title: Conformational dynamics and functional substates during enzyme evolution
authors: Nobuhiko Tokuriki
abstract: Enzymes do not adopt a single rigid structure; instead, they exist as dynamic ensembles of multiple conformational substates. In some cases, distinct conformational substates correspond to different functional states in solution. Understanding how evolution modulates these functional and conformational substates to alter catalytic specificities is key to deciphering the mechanisms of enzyme evolution. In this talk, I will present our studies on enzyme evolution, with a particular focus on the role of functional and conformational substates in enzyme populations. First, I will introduce single-molecule enzyme kinetics using microchambers, which allow us to monitor and characterize metastable functional substates within enzyme populations. I will then discuss how we applied this approach to a series of alkaline phosphatase (AP) and phosphotriesterase (PTE) variants generated through laboratory evolution. Our findings reveal that functional substates are altered by mutations, and large functional shift. For example, PTE evolved toward efficient arylesterase (AE) activity, its functional substates gradually shifted. While PTE exhibited high functional heterogeneity, the evolved AE variant—with reduced PTE activity—displayed a narrower functional distribution. I will show how conformational dynamics are related to the change in functional substate. Finally, I will discuss the broader implications of these findings, highlighting the role of functional substates in shaping enzyme evolution and the potential for leveraging this knowledge in protein engineering.
keywords: functional substates; enzyme evolution; conformational dynamics; conformational substates; enzyme populations

title: A Unified Deep Learning Framework for Predicting DNA Structure
authors: Jinsen Li, Peijun Lin, Tsu-Pei Chiu, Remo Rohs
abstract: High-throughput prediction of three-dimensional DNA structure, represented by DNA shape parameters, has enabled the community to better understand transcription factor binding mechanisms. Protein-DNA recognition can be conceptually divided into base readout and shape readout but ultimately reflects recognition of the overall DNA structure. Each DNA sequence encodes an intrinsically preferred structural conformation. Leveraging either experimentally solved structures or computationally simulated data, it is now possible to construct a general framework for DNA structure prediction, such as Deep DNAshape. However, the current Deep DNAshape framework relies on training separate, independent models for each DNA shape parameter, potentially overlooking informative correlations among them. A unified and cohesive modeling strategy may therefore improve predictive performance by capturing these interdependencies. Here, we present preliminary results from a new version of Deep DNAshape, in which multiple models are integrated into a single framework to predict DNA structure in one pass. This approach incorporates a customized 3D-aware frame loss function that enables the model to learn relationships among different shape parameters. In addition, we outline our ongoing efforts toward modeling protein-induced DNA structural changes within the same unified framework.

title: BiMba: Predicting Protein Binding Sites using Vision Mamba
authors: Azam Shirali, Parshatd Govindasamy, Vitalii Stebliankin, Jimeng Shi, Kalai Mathee, Giri Narasimhan
abstract: Abstract Motivation: Identifying protein binding sites in protein-protein complexes is a central challenge in structural biology. Binding sites, consisting of groups of residues, govern how proteins recognize and interact with protein partners. Thus, identifying them is essential for understanding biological function and guiding the design of effective biomolecules and even drug molecules. Despite major progress in computational approaches, their performance remains limited because most models underrepresent the combined influence of surface properties and residue-level information, leaving room for improvement. Recent advances in state-space models and vision-based deep learning offer an opportunity to address these limitations by efficiently modeling long-range spatial dependencies on protein surfaces. Here, we introduce BiMba (Protein Binding site prediction using Vision Mamba), a state-space–driven deep learning framework that leverages the efficient long-range modeling capability of the Vision Mamba architecture to learn from 3D protein surfaces represented as 2D geometric or physicochemical grids. Results: BiMba integrates complementary sources of information, capturing geometric and physicochemical determinants of molecular recognition as surface patches, encoded as 2D images, along with residue-level descriptors, yielding a unified representation that couples spatial topology with biochemical context. BiMba demonstrates competitive performance across diverse and specialized benchmark datasets, often outperforming existing state-of-the-art methods. In addition, BiMba incorporates perturbation-based and gradient-based interpretability analyses by extracting hidden attentions from Mamba layers, enabling visualization of feature relevance and biologically meaningful residue clusters. Overall, our findings establish state-space models as efficient, interpretable, and scalable architectures for molecular surface learning, advancing the application of deep learning in structural bioinformatics. Availability and Implementation: The BiMba source code, training, test, and benchmark datasets are available at https://github.com/Azam-Shi/BiMba.
keywords: Protein Binding Sites; Vision Mamba; protein surfaces; Binding site prediction; Predicting Protein

title: Investigating the physiological substrates of a putative bacterial serotonin transporter in the gut
authors: Antoniya Aleksandrova, Jonathan Lynch, Lucy Forrest
abstract: Serotonin is critical not only for neuronal signaling, but also for gut functioning. While it has been well-established that gut microbiota regulates serotonin levels in the intestine, recent evidence has suggested that serotonin might also have a functional role in bacteria from the gut. In particular, studies have identified a functional orthologue of the human serotonin transporter (hSERT) that is expressed by a gut bacterium, Turicibacter sanguinis. However, this orthologue, known as TuriSERT, exhibits a few key differences in the serotonin binding site residues identified in hSERT. These differences raise the possibility that its physiological substrates might in fact be amino acids or that serotonin has a distinct interaction mode with TuriSERT compared to hSERT. To investigate these possibilities, we used AlphaFold to construct structural models of TuriSERT in multiple conformations. We then proceeded with docking studies that allow us to refine our model selection and to screen for alternative substrates from a large library of metabolites commonly found in the gut. Our work has implications not only for our understanding of the function of TuriSERT, but also for its ability to interact with commonly used antidepressants.

title: Deciphering Protein Mutation-Phenotype Linkages from CRISPR-based Tiling Mutagenesis Screens
authors: Wei He, Jen-Wei Huang, Yalong Wang, Raphael Guerois, Alberto Ciccia, Han Xu
abstract: CRISPR-based high-throughput mutagenesis screens enables systematic mapping of mutations to phenotypes, yet deciphering mutations-phenotype links remains challenging. Here we present ProTiler-Mut, a versatile computational framework that leveraging tiling mutagenesis screens, which introduce variants across entire protein sequences, to analyze mutation effects at the levels of residues, substructures, and protein-protein interactions (PPIs). Applying ProTiler-Mut to multi-condition base editing (BE) screens targeting DNA damage response proteins and T-cell regulators, we define a separation-of-function (SOF) category beyond the conventional loss-and gain-of-function classes, where SOF mutations show the strongest enrichment for ClinVar-annotated pathogenic variants. ProTiler-Mut also identifies candidate substructures that enable functional inference of unscreened pathogenic mutations and prioritize candidate phenotype-associated PPIs potentially disrupted by functional variants. Using ProTiler-Mut, we identify a substructure harboring pathogenic GOF mutations that disrupt MAPK1-RSK1 interactions, leading to MAPK activation and elevated PD-1 expression. Finally, we show that ProTiler-Mut is applicable across different mutagenesis screening platforms.

title: Multiscale modelling and biophysical validation define a coiled-coil dimeric scaffold in FAZ10 from Trypanosoma brucei
authors: Cleidy Mirela Osorio Mogollon, Gustavo Enrique Olivos Ramírez, Diego Leonardo, Clarice Izumi, Adolfo Poma, Leticia Cioca, Munira Muhammad Abdel Baqui
abstract: Neglected tropical diseases remain a major global health challenge, requiring deeper molecular insight into parasite biology. Trypanosoma brucei, a unicellular flagellated parasite, relies on the flagellum attachment zone (FAZ) to coordinate flagellum positioning, cell morphology, and cytokinesis. The FAZ10 protein (~2 MDa), essential for cleavage-furrow positioning, remains structurally unresolved due to its size and highly repetitive architecture. Here, we characterize the architecture and mechanical properties of the FAZ10 central region by combining structural modelling, multiscale molecular dynamics, and biophysical validation. AlphaFold2 predictions, together with atomistic and coarse-grained simulations (GōMartini 3), support an elongated parallel coiled-coil dimer (~40–50 nm) flanked by symmetric globular domains. The interface is stabilized by canonical knobs-into-holes packing, hydrophobic interactions, salt bridges, and a polar network at e/g positions. In addition, a stammer–stutter pair locally perturbs the heptad repeat, introducing controlled deviations that modulate the superhelical geometry. Simulations indicate that this dimer behaves as a semi-flexible filament, showing axial fluctuations (Ree ≈ 42–48 nm), stable compaction (Rg ≈ 17–18 nm), and localized bending (θ ≈ 160°), consistent with polymer-like behaviour. Biophysical analyses (SEC, SEC–MALS, and circular dichroism) confirm dimerization in solution (~124 kDa) and a predominantly α-helical coiled-coil organization, in agreement with the computational predictions. Together, these results provide the first structural characterization of a FAZ filament component and illustrate how computational and biophysical approaches can be combined to study large, repetitive cytoskeletal proteins and their roles in key cellular processes such as cytokinesis. This integrative strategy not only advances our understanding of parasite biology but also supports the use of in silico methods as reliable tools when complemented by experimental validation, with potential implications for future therapeutic targeting.

title: Protein Language Models Capture Structural and Functional Epistasis
authors: Ananthan Nambiar, Sayantani B. Littlefield, Carlos Cuellar, Rohit Khorana, Sergei Maslov
abstract: Protein language models (PLMs) learn from large collections of natural sequences and achieve striking success across prediction tasks, yet it remains unclear what biological principles underlie their representations. We use epistasis, the dependence of a mutation’s effect on its sequence context, as a lens to probe what PLMs capture about proteins. Comparing PLM-derived scores with deep mutational scanning data, we find that epistasis emerges naturally from pretrained models, without supervision on experimental fitness. Raw model scores align with residue–residue contacts, indicating that PLMs internalize structural proximity. Applying a nonlinear transformation to bring model outputs onto the experimental scale, however, shifts the signal toward functional couplings between distant sites. These findings show that PLMs capture both structural and functional dependencies from sequence data alone, and that epistasis provides a powerful window into the biological principles embedded in their representations.

title: Generalizable and scalable protein stability prediction with SPURS
authors: Ziang Li, Yunan Luo
abstract: Predicting how amino acid substitutions change protein thermostability is essential for understanding disease mech-anisms and engineering robust proteins. Recent protein generative models achieve strong zero-shot performance across mutation-related tasks without task-specific supervision, yet this unsupervised capability remains underused for supervised stability learning. We present SPURS, a deep learning framework that rewires and integrates two complementary protein generative models, a protein language model and an inverse folding model, and reprograms the unified architecture for thermostability prediction using mega-scale ∆∆G data. SPURS injects structure-derived information into sequence-derived representations through lightweight cross-attention adapters and performs parameter-efficient fine-tuning, reducing trainable parameters by 98.5% relative to full language-model tuning. The model is also computationally scalable: it predicts ∆∆G for all single substitutions of a protein in one forward pass, enabling proteome-scale site-saturation analyses. As a concrete example, SPURS can scan the human proteome (19,652 pro-teins, about 109 variants) in about 30 minutes on one GPU. In benchmarking, SPURS improves over baselines on identity-controlled and external datasets, including better recovery of stabilizing mutations and generalization to unseen proteins and mutation contexts. Beyond stability prediction, SPURS supports broad protein-informatics applications, including unsupervised functional-site identification, improved low-N protein fitness prediction, and systematic analysis of stability-pathogenicity relationships in human variants. Together, these results establish SPURS as an accurate, efficient, and generalizable framework for protein stability modeling and as a tool for large-scale protein engineering and disease-variant interpretation.
keywords: SPURS; stability prediction; protein stability; protein generative; low-N protein fitness

title: When Does Protein Structure Help? A Reliability Bottleneck in Mutation-Effect Prediction
authors: Asher Moldwin, Yana Bromberg, Amarda Shehu
abstract: Despite the growing use of 3D structure in variant effect prediction, it remains unclear when and why structure provides information beyond what can be gleaned from sequence-only protein language models (PLMs). We anchor this question on the prediction task of mutation-induced melting temperature shifts Delta Tm. Analysis of multi-modal predictors reveals limited benefit of structure. We show that this does is driven by a reliability bottleneck: mutation-conditioned structural deltas are often unstable, inconsistent across current structure generators, or attenuated by coarse representations, and are therefore difficult for a prediction model to exploit. Our analysis reveals that when strong sequence priors are present, unreliable geometric signal is suppressed; when sequence priors are removed, structural reliability forecasts prediction difficulty. These findings reframe the role of structure in variant effect prediction, changing the question from whether to include structure to how mutation-conditioned structural information can be generated, represented, and integrated so as to reliably complement sequence.
keywords: Protein Structure Help; effect prediction; sequence-only protein language; structural reliability forecasts; forecasts prediction difficulty

title: Func2Seq and Func2Prot: Function-Conditioned Protein Generation for Variant-Effect Prediction and Controllable Design
authors: Shaowen Zhu, Yue Cao, Yihong Yang, Yang Shen
abstract: Protein engineering requires models that can both predict mutational effects and generate new sequences and structures under functional constraints, yet functional intent is difficult to encode and transfer across protein families. We present a function-conditioned generative framework that embeds Gene Ontology (GO) Molecular Function terms using BioBERT text features and a two-stage sequential graph convolutional network over the GO directed acyclic graph, capturing hierarchical relationships among functions. These embeddings condition Func2Seq, an autoregressive decoder modeling P(seq | func) for variant scoring and controllable sampling, and Func2Prot, a joint sequence-structure model for P(seq, str | func) that enables direct backbone generation via a torsion-angle decoder. Meta-pretraining on 8.77M GO-annotated Pfam sequences supports cross-family transfer before family-specific fine-tuning. On a benchmark of 35 DMS datasets across 33 proteins, Func2Seq outperforms an alignment-free baseline in 29/35 tasks (Delta Spearman = +0.041, p = 6.2 x 10^-6) and DeepSequence in 18/35 (Delta Spearman = +0.053, p = 2.9 x 10^-3), with the largest gains in small or low-diversity families, and remains competitive with ESM3 under matched function conditioning on tasks with supported annotations. Func2Prot further improves prediction for compact enzymes such as chorismate mutase, while gains for malate dehydrogenase are endpoint-dependent. For controllable design on the ARID DNA-binding domain, sequences in the 20-30% global-identity twilight zone retain over 40% local identity at DNA-binding regions, and Func2Prot generates representative backbones reaching TM-scores up to 0.867 against natural ARID folds. These results support ontology-guided protein language modeling as a unified framework for variant effect prediction and structure-aware functional design.

title: Simpatico: accurate and ultra-fast virtual drug screening with atomic embeddings
authors: Jeremiah Gaiser, Travis Wheeler
abstract: Virtual screening identifies promising drug compounds from databases containing billions of possible candidates, a true needle-in-a-haystack problem. While computational methods such as docking are often effective in predicting the binding affinity between a given protein and ligand, they are prohibitively slow for primary screening at large scale. Recent developments in deep representation learning have led to a promising new paradigm: retrieval-based virtual screening. In this new approach, deep-learning models convert protein and small-molecule structures into information-rich fixed-dimensional representations. Models are trained such that the output for a given protein identifies the region of molecular-representation space containing good binding candidates. This capability enables direct sampling from arbitrarily large molecular databases. Current state-of-the-art methods represent each protein target with a single embedding, and likewise for each small molecule candidate. Our approach instead produces a unique embedding for each heavy atom in a small molecule or protein pocket. Trained on structural data from resolved protein-ligand complexes, these atom-level embeddings correspond to the expected atomic interaction potentials of each individual atom. As a result, if the embedding of a protein atom and that of a small-molecule atom are observed very near one another in embedding space, then the respective protein-ligand atom pair is expected to produce favorable non-covalent bonding interactions. Therefore, searching for binding candidates for some protein target proceeds as follows: Provided a vector database of pre-computed small molecule atom embeddings, a nearest-neighbor search is performed using the protein pocket atom embeddings as queries. The embeddings returned in this search correspond to small-molecule atoms with high interaction potential with one or more of the protein pocket atoms. Atom embeddings returned by the nearest-neighbor search are aggregated and passed through a scoring function so their parent molecules may be given a final binding score. Our model, Simpatico, achieves state-of-art drug screening enrichment and can scan millions of candidate drugs per minute on a single L40S GPU. Simpatico not only outperforms state-of-the-art, but does so after training in only a few hours on orders of magnitude less data.

title: Learning a PRECISE language for small-molecule binding
authors: Kapil Devkota
abstract: Machine learning now enables screening of billion-scale compound libraries like Enamine and ZINC, shortlisting thousands of candidates for a target protein. Yet without alignment to downstream docking tools, it remains unclear how to prioritize these outputs, creating a bottleneck. Current methods also lack the ability to screen for a specific binding site and do not generalize to important target classes such as metalloproteins and multi-chain complexes. Here, we present PRECISE to address these challenges. PRECISE enables targeted screening by operating directly on the target's 3D structure; to retain billion-compound scalability, it quantizes drug representations. PRECISE's key innovation is reimagining drug-target interaction as compatibility between quantized drug embeddings and the target's surface mesh. Remarkably, these codes, learned from sequence-based binary binding data, transfer to our structure-based setting with a single nonlinear projection. The surface representation is enriched with electrostatic and geometric features and interpreted through a geometric deep learning architecture, enabling PRECISE to identify binding sites more accurately than state-of-the-art methods (DiffDock-L, Chai, and Boltz-2). The codebook formulation ensures billion-scale screening while unlocking zero-shot generalization to complex targets. For downstream alignment, we introduce PRECISE-MCTS, combining PRECISE screening with selective Vina docking via Monte Carlo tree search. By providing both mechanistic understanding and massive scalability, PRECISE delivers capabilities previously mutually exclusive in virtual screening.

title: JointDiff: Simultaneous Generation of Sequence and Structure for Functional Protein Design
authors: Yuxuan Liu, Shaowen Zhu, Siddhant Gulati, Siddhi Kotnis, Qing Sun, Yang Shen
abstract: Protein sequence and structure co-generation can help enable coherent and functionally plausible protein designs. To this end we introduce JointDiff, a unified multimodal diffusion framework that overcomes the limitations of sequential two-stage methods and directly learns the joint distribution of protein sequences and structures, enabling deep cross-modality interactions. JointDiff represents residues through three distinct modalities modeled via specialized diffusion processes: multinomial for amino acid types, Cartesian for positions, and SO(3) for spatial orientations. The diffusion processes are coupled via ReverseNet, including a multimodal graph attention encoder and a modal-specific decoder. We assess JointDiff in both de novo monomer design and motif scaffolding. Operating 1 to 2 orders of magnitude faster than conventional two-stage pipelines, JointDiff efficiently enables accelerated, iterative design-test loops, as demonstrated through classifier-guided sampling. To demonstrate its capability for complex de novo functional design, we applied JointDiff to scaffold the chromophore-forming and structurally critical motifs of green fluorescent proteins (GFPs). By integrating Position-Specific Scoring Matrix (PSSM)-based evolutionary guidance into the rapid sampling process, we generated diverse, stable beta-barrel scaffolds around these fixed functional sites. Experimental validation of these computational designs of GFPs in E. coli yielded high success rates: 11 out of 16 tested variants, filtered and prioritized from 21000 samples, exhibited measurable fluorescence. Remarkably, these functionally active designs included evolutionarily distant variants, demonstrating substantial sequence novelty. For instance, one top-performing variant exhibited fluorescence despite sharing just 39.7% sequence identity with its wild-type avGFP template and the closest known database hits. These laboratory results establish JointDiff as a highly efficient, experimentally validated platform for accelerating complex functional protein design.

title: Thermal Stability- and Binding Affinity-Guided Protein Design with ESM3
authors: Amitash Nanda, Anna Su, Steven Farrell, Nabin Giri, Debashis Sahoo, Mark Gerstein, Jeffrey Brock
abstract: Protein design is crucial for advancing therapeutics and synthetic biology; however, traditional methods are limited by high experimental costs and scale. Recent advances in foundational protein language models and conditional generative models have enabled computational protein design. Guided generation in protein design enables the use of external information to steer a generative model's output towards specific functional goals. However, current state-of-the-art models still face a series of challenges: (1) PLMs often struggle to generate sequences with specific, desired properties that are not strongly represented in the training data; (2) The design candidate sequence space is extremely large; (3) Fine-tuning massive models like ESM-3 is expensive, slow, and requires large datasets; (4) Biological goals (e.g., enhancing solubility, binding, stability) are diverse and context-dependent. In this work, we present a derivative-free optimization framework for computational protein design that leverages ESM3’s guided generation capabilities to refine protein sequences to improve thermal stability and binding affinity. For thermostability, we utilized FoldX, a bio-physics-based external validator to score the stability of each generated sequence. For binding affinity predictions, we used Boltz2, a deep learning model with accuracy comparable to physics-based free-energy perturbation methods. GPU/CPU parallelization are integrated to accelerate candidate scoring by running multiple instances of FoldX and Boltz2 concurrently. To enhance the controllability of the design process, our framework employs an adaptive unmasking schedule that applies large changes initially and fine-tunes the sequence in subsequent optimization steps. This framework has great potential for designing functional protein sequences with thermal stability and binding affinity co-optimization.

title: AlloPep: A Pipeline for De Novo Design of Allosteric Peptides
authors: Dibyajyoti Maity, Baofu Qiao
abstract: Allosteric drugs offer significant advantages over drugs targeting the active site in proteins, such as better selectivity, reduced toxicity, and enhanced tunability of the target protein activity. On the other hand, peptides offer additional advantages compared to small-molecule drugs, including cost-effective synthesis, high bioactivity, absorbability, accessibility, biodegradability, and biocompatibility, as well as low immunogenicity. Allosteric peptides, i.e., peptides that regulate the target proteins allosterically, offer the best of both worlds. Experimentally identifying novel allosteric peptides with the desired properties is a time and resource-intensive process. We present AlloPep, a pipeline for the computational de novo design of novel allosteric peptides. AlloPep seamlessly integrates APOP to identify allosteric binding sites in the target protein, GAPS to obtain the peptide binding hotspots, and PepGLAD, a generative deep learning model for designing peptides based on a binding pocket. After structure validation and quality assessment, the binding potential of the predicted peptides is ranked using an optimized Rosetta Fold Scoring function. Molecular dynamics simulations of the top-ranked peptide-bound and unbound structures are analyzed with MDiGest to estimate the perturbation of the active site from the peptide binding to the allosteric site. We tested the pipeline on the following proteins that have solved PDB structures with bound allosteric peptides from our previously curated AlloBench dataset: human JNK3 (PDB ID: 4H36, 4H39, and 4H3B), human PDK1 protein kinase (PDB ID: 5LVP), and cathepsin D from tick (PDB ID: 5N70). The AlloPep source code is available at https://github.com/djmaity/allopep.

title: Machine Learning-Guided Engineering of Selective Protease Inhibitors by Deep Mutational Scanning
authors: Reut Moshe, Oz Reuveni, Michal Levi, Niv Papo, Yaron Orenstein
abstract: Protein engineering for selective binding remains a major challenge, especially for targets with high structural similarity. Here, we present a machine learning (ML)-guided framework for engineering selective protein-protein interactions using deep mutational scanning (DMS). Using APPI-3M, a variant of the amyloid precursor protein inhibitor, we studied its interactions with two homologous serine proteases: mesotrypsin and KLK6. We trained convolutional neural networks on DMS data to predict the selectivity of APPI variants and used these models to uncover selective epistatic effects and identify key residues driving target specificity. Our models achieved high predictive accuracy and enabled identification of double-mutant variants not observed in the original DMS library. We validated our predictions using yeast surface display and inhibition assays, ultimately discovering novel APPI variants with highly selective binding, including the most selective mesotrypsin inhibitor versus KLK6 reported to date. This approach highlights the value of combining high-throughput mutational data and ML to accelerate selective protein design, with broad implications for therapeutic development.

title: A Hybrid Deep Learning Pipeline for RNA 3D Structure Reconstruction from Cryo-EM Density Maps
authors: Derek Peng, Zhihang Hu
abstract: Determining RNA 3D structures is critical for understanding complex biological functions and developing targeted therapeutics. However, traditional experimental methods are notoriously difficult, leading to data scarcity that severely hinders RNA research. While cryogenic electron microscopy (Cryo-EM) has revolutionized structure determination by improving resolution, converting Cryo-EM maps into accurate RNA all-atom models is still a major computational bottleneck, requiring manual tracing. We present a fully automated hybrid pipeline that reconstructs RNA all-atom coordinates from cryo-EM maps in three stages: (i) voxel-wise segmentation, (ii) backbone construction, and (iii) all-atom completion/refinement. For segmentation, we use a two-step approach that first distinguishes atoms from background and then classifies voxels into phosphate, ribose sugar, and nitrogenous base groups. We design a Swin U-Net Transformer with a multi-resolution (2–7 Å) input pyramid and ensemble learning, achieving a four-class macro-F1 score above 0.85. For backbone construction, we identify a Hamiltonian path through predicted phosphorus atoms while incorporating sequence and secondary structure constraints to enforce plausible chain connectivity. Finally, nucleotide completion and atom refinement produce chemically valid structures consistent with the density, with a mean all-atom RMSD of 4.27 Å, mean phosphorus position RMSD of 1.17 Å, and a mean TM-score of 0.866. This hybrid pipeline enables accurate, fully automated, end-to-end reconstruction of RNA structures, helping accelerate RNA structure determination and structure-based drug discovery.

title: RNAbpFlow: Base pair-augmented SE(3)-flow matching for conditional generation of RNA 3D structures
authors: Sumit Tarafder, Debswapna Bhattacharya
abstract: Despite the groundbreaking advances in deep learning-enabled methods for biomolecular modeling, predicting accurate three-dimensional (3D) structures of RNA remains challenging due to the highly flexible nature of RNA molecules combined with the limited availability of evolutionary sequences or structural homology. Here, we introduce RNAbpFlow, a novel sequence-and base-pair-conditioned SE(3)equivariant flow matching model for generating RNA 3D structural ensemble. Leveraging a nucleobase center representation, RNAbpFlow enables end-to-end generation of all-atom RNA structures without the explicit or implicit use of evolutionary information or homologous structural templates. Experimental results show that base pairing conditioning leads to broadly generalizable performance improvements over current approaches for RNA topology sampling and predictive modeling in large-scale benchmarking. RNAbpFlow is freely available at https://github.com/Bhattacharya-Lab/RNAbpFlow. title: Using MutPred2 Predictions of Molecular Mechanisms to Identify Drug Repurposing Candidates for Genetic Disease
authors: Matthew Neky, Vikas Pejaver
abstract: Missense variants in protein-coding genes are a major driver of rare genetic diseases, yet linking these variants to actionable therapeutic strategies remains challenging. Existing drug repurposing approaches often rely on gene expression, networks, or literature-mining and rarely incorporate mutation-specific molecular mechanisms. This limitation is particularly relevant for gain-of-function variants in enzymatic proteins, where mutations may introduce or alter catalytic or binding sites. We present a computational framework to prioritize variant–drug pairs by integrating variant effect prediction, molecular mechanism inference, structure-based modeling, and molecular simulation. Variants were curated from ClinVar, focusing on pathogenic or likely pathogenic missense variants with sufficient review status. Prioritization leveraged MutPred2 predictions of gain of catalytic or binding sites and curated drug–gene relationships from Pharos. Candidate pairs were restricted to cases where ligands are known to bind the wild-type protein but have not been evaluated for the corresponding variant. Variant-specific protein structures were generated using AlphaFold, followed by docking with AutoDock Vina and molecular dynamics simulations in GROMACS. Binding stability was assessed using two complementary metrics: ligand root mean square deviation (RMSD) and distance to the binding site. Application to 292 variant–ligand systems across 144 proteins and 45 ligands showed that most systems exhibit moderate stability, with a subset demonstrating highly stable binding. Distance analysis indicated that most ligands remain within the binding pocket, although RMSD revealed variability in pose stability. This framework enables systematic evaluation of variant-specific drug interactions and provides a scalable approach for identifying repurposable therapeutics for rare genetic diseases.

title: An Integrative Biophysical Framework for Protein-Nucleic Acid Affinity Prediction from Structure and Sequence
authors: Yafan Zhang, Eduardo Cisneros, Xingcheng Lin
abstract: Accurate prediction of sequence-specific and epigenetic-specific protein–nucleic acid interactions is essential for understanding gene regulation and guiding therapeutic design. High-throughput sequencing (HTS) assays have generated large-scale binding data, yet their utility is often limited by restricted library diversity, batch effects, antibody specificity, and experimental cost. Meanwhile, rapidly growing structural resources—both experimentally determined and AI-predicted—offer complementary mechanistic insights into nucleic acid recognition. Here, we present a family of biophysics-inspired, data-driven frameworks— IDEA, mIDEA, and IRIS—for predicting protein–DNA and protein–RNA binding affinities. Grounded in the principle of minimal frustration, our approach distinguishes native binders from sequence-randomized decoys by maximizing the binding energy gap at the protein–nucleic acid interface, yielding interpretable residue-level interaction matrices. The framework naturally extends to RNA interactions and methylation-aware modeling through the introduction of an additional nucleotide state. Across multiple benchmark datasets, our methods accurately predict binding affinities and discriminate strong binders from weak ones using only sparse structural and sequence information. The framework achieves strong performance on gold-standard protein–DNA and protein–RNA datasets, generalizes across diverse protein families, and remains effective when employing high-confidence AlphaFold3-predicted structures. Furthermore, it captures position-dependent methylation preferences and supports genome-wide identification of transcription factor binding sites. Because the learned energy model can score sequence variants against a target protein structure, the same framework can also guide aptamer design by prioritizing nucleic acid sequences with favorable predicted binding affinities. Collectively, these frameworks provide an interpretable and versatile approach for the mechanistic and quantitative modeling of diverse protein– nucleic acid recognition processes, with potential applications in regulatory genomics and nucleic-acid-based therapeutic design.

title: LocAlign: Local Protein Structural Alignment with Geometric Deep Learning
authors: Jérôme Tubiana, Hagai Ravid, Haim Wolfson
abstract: Identifying common function-determining structural motifs among proteins with different folds is a foundational task in computational biology with no go-to solution. Indeed, standard alignment tools like TM-align are ill-suited for matching small, sequence-order-independent motifs, while specialized tools have limited success. In this talk, we present LocAlign, a local structural alignment algorithm based on geometric deep learning. Given two protein structures, LocAlign iteratively predicts atom-level correspondences and a 3D superimposition. By formulating training as a weakly supervised task on pairs of proteins bound to identical ligands, we bypass the need for ground-truth alignments. LocAlign recovers known functional motifs without explicit supervision, identifying high-quality alignments for 87% and 37% of protein pairs with similar and dissimilar folds, respectively. Equipped with confidence scoring and motif-conditioning capabilities, LocAlign supports diverse applications, including functional annotation of the dark proteome and drug off-target screening. LocAlign is thus a potent, versatile framework for protein functional site comparison.

title: Probabilistic RNA Designability via Interpretable Ensemble Approximation and Dynamic Decomposition
authors: Tianshuo Zhou, David H. Mathews, Liang Huang
abstract: Motivation: RNA design aims to find RNA sequences that fold into a given target secondary structure, a problem also known as RNA inverse folding. However, not all target structures are designable. Recent advances in RNA designability have focused primarily on minimum free energy (MFE)-based criteria, while ensemble-based notions of designability remain largely underexplored. To address this gap, we introduce a theory of ensemble approximation and a probability decomposition framework for bounding the folding probabilities of RNA structures in an explainable way. We further develop a linear-time dynamic programming algorithm that efficiently searches over exponentially many decompositions and identifies the optimal one that yields the tightest probabilistic bound for a given structure. Results: Applying our methods to both native and artificial RNA structures in the ArchiveII and Eterna100 benchmarks, we obtained probability bounds that are much tighter than prior approaches. In addition, our methods further provide anatomical tools for analyzing RNA structures and understanding the sources of design difficulty at the motif level. title: Structural bioinformatics and AlphaFold modeling of the human kinome and its interactions
authors: Roland Dunbrack
abstract: Protein kinases sit at the heart of cellular signaling, and their dysregulation drives many human diseases. The human kinome comprises 480 genes containing one or more “typical” protein kinase domains (similar to PKA or EGFR). These proteins contain 437 catalytically active kinase domains and 56 pseudokinase domains. We describe an integrated framework that combines structural bioinformatics of experimental structures with large-scale AlphaFold modeling to define, model, and interpret the conformational and interaction space of human protein kinases. Leveraging a set of 54 unique substrate-bound kinase complexes, we derived structural criteria that define the active form of a protein kinase. Using these criteria, we modeled all 437 catalytically active human kinase domains in their active, substrate-competent conformations with AlphaFold2. We have used Boltz2 to extend this to ATP/Mg2+ bound and phosphorylated structures. Clustering the conformations of inactive kinase domains enables the identification of likely physiologically relevant inactive forms of kinase domains. We applied AlphaFold2 modeling to all 480 full-length human kinase proteins, identifying and giving consistent names to 1637 folded domains across these multidomain proteins. We find 17 novel, previously unnamed globular domains in 31 kinases, and 8 conserved coiled-coil regions in 25 kinases. Of the assigned domains, ECOD misses 3%, TED misses 7%, and UniProt/InterPro misses 17%. This domain-resolved view enables hypothesis generation for intramolecular autoinhibition, substrate recognition, and scaffolding functions of kinases. Finally, we present a new interaction-scoring approach based on AlphaFold’s predicted aligned error (PAE) matrix (github.com/DunbrackLab/IPSAE) and show how it supports modeling of active and inactive kinase domains, intra-and interprotein domain interactions of kinases spanning activating, inhibiting, and substrate-binding assemblies, and protein design of kinase-inhibiting peptides and mini-proteins. Together, these advances provide a structurally grounded, proteome-scale platform for understanding kinase regulation and for guiding experiments and therapeutic discovery.

title: Predicting the structural impact of human alternative splicing
authors: Yuxuan Song, Chengxin Zhang, Gilbert Omenn, Matthew O'Meara, Joshua Welch
abstract: Protein structure prediction with neural networks is a powerful new method for linking protein sequence, structure, and function, but structures have generally been predicted for only a single isoform of each gene, neglecting splice variants. To investigate the structural implications of alternative splicing, we used AlphaFold2 to predict the structures of more than 11,000 human isoforms. We employed multiple metrics to identify splicing-induced structural alterations, including template matching score, secondary structure composition, surface charge distribution, radius of gyration, accessibility of post-translational modification sites, and structure-based function prediction. We identified examples of how alternative splicing induced clear changes in each of these properties. Structural similarity between isoforms largely correlated with degree of sequence identity, but we identified a subset of isoforms with low structural similarity despite high sequence similarity. Exon skipping (ES) and alternative last exons (ALE) tended to increase the surface charge and radius of gyration. Splicing also buried or exposed numerous post-translational modification sites, most notably among the isoforms of BAX. Functional prediction nominated numerous functional differences among isoforms of the same gene, with loss of function compared to the reference predominating. Finally, we used single-cell RNA-seq data from the Tabula Sapiens to determine the cell types in which each structure is expressed. Our work represents an important resource for studying the structure and function of splice isoforms across the cell types of the human body.

title: DiSPA: Differential Substructure-Pathway Attention for Drug Response Prediction
authors: Yewon Han, Sunghyun Kim, Eunyi Jeong, Sungkyung Lee, Seokwoo Yun, Sangsoo Lim
abstract: Motivation: Accurate prediction of drug response in precision medicine requires models that capture how specific chemical substructures interact with cellular pathway states. However, most existing deep learning approaches treat chemical and transcriptomic modalities independently or combine them only at late stages, limiting their ability to model fine-grained, context-dependent mechanisms of drug action. In addition, standard attention mechanisms are often sensitive to noise and sparsity in high-dimensional biological networks, hindering both generalization and interpretability. Results: We present DiSPA (Differential Substructure–Pathway Attention), a representation learning framework that explicitly disentangles structure-driven and context-driven mechanisms of drug response through bidirectional conditioning between chemical substructures and pathway-level gene expression. DiSPA introduces a differential cross-attention module that suppresses spurious pathway–substructure associations while amplifying contextually relevant interactions. Across multiple evaluation settings on the GDSC benchmark, DiSPA achieves state-of-the-art performance, with particularly strong improvements in the disjoint-set setting (RMSE = 2.453), which assesses generalization to unseen drug–cell combinations. Beyond predictive accuracy, DiSPA yields mechanistically informative representations: learned attention patterns recover known pharmacophores, distinguish structure-driven from context-dependent compounds, and exhibit coherent organization across biological pathways. Furthermore, we demonstrate that DiSPA trained solely on bulk RNA-seq data enables zero-shot transfer to spatial transcriptomics, revealing region-specific drug sensitivity patterns without retraining. Together, these results establish DiSPA as a robust and interpretable framework for integrative pharmacogenomic modeling, enabling principled analysis of drug response mechanisms beyond post hoc interpretation.

title: Cross-attention protein language models infer partner-specific PPI interfaces complementary to AlphaFold3
authors: Alexey Porollo, Jichao Chen
abstract: Accurate identification of protein–protein interaction (PPI) interfaces remains a major challenge in structural bioinformatics, particularly for transient, peptide-mediated, and intrinsically disordered interactions that are often underrepresented in experimentally solved complexes. While recent advances in multimeric structure prediction, especially AlphaFold 3, have substantially improved complex modeling, these methods remain biased toward stable globular assemblies and frequently overpredict interfaces in flexible binding scenarios. Most sequence-based interface predictors likewise analyze proteins in isolation, limiting their ability to capture partner-specific interface selection. We present SPPIDER-seq, a partner-aware residue-level PPI interface predictor that combines pretrained ESM-2 embeddings with a multi-head cross-attention architecture. By explicitly conditioning each residue in a query protein on the sequence context of its interacting partner, the model captures inter-protein dependencies without requiring structural coordinates. Two complementary variants were developed: a receptor-centric model optimized for structured surface patches and a peptide-centric model specialized for motif-driven and disordered peptide interfaces. On non-redundant blind benchmarks derived from BioLiP, SPPIDER-seq achieved AUROC values up to 0.797 and MCC up to 0.269. Direct comparison with AlphaFold 3 revealed strong complementarity: AF3 performed better on well-folded globular complexes, whereas SPPIDER-seq outperformed AF3 on small peptide interfaces and intrinsically disordered peptide-binding regions, improving MCC from 0.239 to 0.314 on disordered peptide benchmarks. These results establish cross-attention over protein language model embeddings as an effective and scalable framework for structure-aware, partner-specific interface inference directly from sequence, particularly for transient, motif-mediated, and disorder-driven PPIs.

title: DEPP: Dynamic Embedding Property-Based Predictor for Protein Conformational Ensembles and Drug-Protein Interactions
authors: Mor Frank, Dana Dayan, Shumeng Ma, Karen S. Anderson, Mark Gerstein
abstract: Understanding protein function requires capturing both structure and dynamics. While modern prediction methods accurately model static conformations, they ignore the conformational ensembles that govern biological activity and bias ligand-binding predictions. Existing methods treat proteins as single static structures, failing to capture the flexibility, critical for accurate affinity prediction. To address this, we introduce DEPP (Dynamic Embedding Property-Based Predictor), a deep learning framework that leverages ESM-2 embeddings, to model protein dynamics as a continuous stochastic process in latent space. DEPP uses a Langevin-type stochastic differential equation (SDE) - combining sequence-based representation with physics-inspired dynamics. By learning trajectory-dependent drift and diffusion terms directly from molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, DEPP captures transitions between conformational states. This probabilistic formulation enables the generation of physically plausible ensembles, prediction of ensemble-specific binding free energies (BFEs), and ranking of candidate drugs according to how each compound reshapes the protein's conformational landscape. The model identifies functionally relevant residues and captures allosteric communication without requiring MD simulation data at inference time. On a diverse held-out test set, DEPP achieves a median BFE MAE of 0.743 kcal/mol and a median Cα RMSD of 2.77Å against MD-simulated conformations, with AUC-ROC of 0.943 and top-k recall of 0.752 for binding site identification, all without MD data at inference time. DEPP delivers a greater than 1,000-fold speedup over MD simulation while outperforming single-structure docking baselines on binding affinity prediction, offering a scalable and mechanistically interpretable framework for virtual screening, polypharmacology, and allosteric regulation.

title: AlphaFold Database expands to proteome-scale quaternary structures
authors: Milot Mirdita, Sreenath Nair, Urmila Paramval, Nilkanth Patel, Risha Patel, Ivanna Pidruchna, Brianda Santini Lopez, Sameer Velankar, Martin Steinegger, Jeniffer Fleming, Maciej Majewski, Christian Dallago, Prashant Sohani, Ahsan Tanweer, Duc Tran, Kyle Tretina, Melanie Vollmar, Quan Vu, Augustin Žídek, Darren Hsu, Maxim Tsenkov, Niccolò Venanzi, Damian Bertoni, Sooyoung Cha, Alejandro Chacón, Nick Dietrich, Boris Fomitchev, Yonathan Goldtzvik, Yewon Han, Jeannie Austin, Joseph Ellaway, Kieran Didi, Oleg Kovalevskiy, Dariusz Lasecki, Agata Laydon, Micha Livne, Paulyna Magaña
abstract: Protein function is governed by molecular interactions, yet structural coverage of these interactions remains sparse. The AlphaFold Protein Structure Database (AFDB) transformed access to accurate monomeric protein structures at scale. Here, we expand AFDB with 1.8M high-confidence protein complexes by conducting a large-scale study of over 31M predicted homo-and heteromeric protein complexes compiled from 4,777 proteomes, including model-and global health organisms, and using STRING physical-interaction annotations. We calibrate confidence metrics to assess the quality of complex predictions, and propose confidence cutoffs. These enabled the discovery of emergent structure and topologies in complex structure prediction that is not present with monomeric predictions. Clustering of high-confidence complexes showed that the largest 1% of non-singleton representatives account for ~25% of all complexes, and that ~9% of clusters are conserved across superkingdoms. In summary, large-scale structural predictions of the interactome serve as a foundational resource to facilitate functional and mechanistic discovery across biology.

title: MDRepo, a community-contributed open molecular dynamics data repository
authors: Ken Youens-Clark, Amitava Roy, Travis Wheeler
abstract: Protein function is governed not by static structure but by conformational dynamics, the fluctuations and transitions that regulate interactions, kinetics, and biological outcomes. Current structure prediction models do not capture this dynamic behavior, and experimental techniques such as NMR and cryo-EM are limited in timescale or resolution. Physics-based molecular dynamics (MD) simulations fill this gap, modeling atomic motion continuously through time and enabling observation of transient states and dynamic properties inaccessible to experiment. MD has consequently become a cornerstone of computational biology, accounting for an estimated 15% of worldwide academic supercomputer usage. Despite this scale of adoption, no dedicated repository has existed for MD simulation data. Petabytes of simulation data are scattered across private servers, general-purpose repositories with no common metadata standards, or lost entirely on decommissioned hardware. This fragmentation stalls reanalysis, prevents revalidation of results, and forecloses the possibility of training the next generation of AI models on dynamic protein behavior, models that could transform drug discovery, enzyme engineering, and protein-protein interaction prediction. To address this gap, we developed MDRepo, a community-contributed open repository for MD simulations released in 2024 and built on NSF-funded CyVerse cyberinfrastructure. MDRepo currently holds more than 21,000 simulations totaling over 150TB, with uniform metadata, automated quality validation, and a fault-tolerant command-line tool supporting petabyte-scale upload and download. All data are released under CC-BY 4.0, ensuring free reuse with attribution. MDRepo is designed to serve as the shared foundation that the MD community has lacked.

title: NoisyFlow: Differentially Private Optimal Transport Using Neural Networks for Secure Biomedical Data Sharing across Multiple Institutions
authors: Yunyang Li, Nikhil Khandekar, Skylar Wang, Varada Khanna, Julian Sanker, Mark Gerstein
abstract: Biomedical models improve when trained on data pooled across institutions, but sensitive patient records (e.g., genomics, clinical data, and medical images) are difficult to share due to privacy constraints. Moreover, data collected at different sites often have shifted distributions because of covariate differences (including batch effects), so privacy-preserving sharing alone cannot simply resolve cross-site mismatch. Methods that protect individuals while explicitly aligning distributions are needed to enable reliable multi-institutional analyses. We present NoisyFlow, a three-stage differentially private framework for cross-institutional harmonization under distribution shift. In stage I, each site learns a differentially private flow-based generator of its local labeled distribution. In stage II, it learns a neural optimal transport map to a shared reference distribution. In stage III, a central server composes the released models to generate reference-aligned pseudo-data for downstream analysis without accessing raw records. Across four biomedical settings spanning single-cell genomics, histopathology, neurogenomics and wearable sensing, NoisyFlow reduces distribution shift while preserving downstream utility under formal differential privacy guarantees.

title: ProMeta: A meta-learning framework for robust disease diagnosis and prediction from plasma proteomics
authors: Han Li, Haoteng Gu, Lei Hu, Zimo Zhang, Yongji Lv, Peng Gao, Johnathan Cooper-Knock, Yaosen Min, Jianyang Zeng, Sai Zhang
abstract: The plasma proteome offers a dynamic window of human health, capturing the real-time intersections between genetics and physiology. However, the application of deep learning to proteomics is currently hindered by a reliance on large-scale labeled datasets, rendering standard models ineffective for rare or novel diseases where patient samples are inherently scarce. Here, we present ProMeta, a meta-learning framework designed to enable robust disease modeling under extreme data restrictions. By integrating knowledge-guided pathway encoding with bi-level meta-optimization, ProMeta projects unstructured proteomic profiles into biologically interpretable functional tokens. This architecture allows the model to learn a global initialization containing transferable biological priors from biobank-scale data, facilitating rapid adaptation to novel tasks. Through comprehensive benchmark experiments, ProMeta consistently outperformed transfer learning and traditional machine learning baselines in both disease diagnosis and prediction tasks. In the most challenging 4-shot scenarios (utilizing only 2 cases and 2 controls), the model achieved robust generalization with an average AUROC of ~0.69, representing a 24.6% relative improvement over the best-performing baseline methods. Mechanistic investigation revealed that ProMeta disentangles cases from controls in the latent space prior to task-specific adaptation, confirming the acquisition of universal biological rules rather than rote memorization. Furthermore, gradient-based interpretation identified disease-specific protein biomarkers and functional pathways consistent with known pathophysiology. Collectively, ProMeta overcomes the data-scarcity bottleneck in precision medicine, providing a scalable, interpretable framework for characterizing the full spectrum of human diseases, particularly for rare conditions lacking extensive clinical cohorts.

title: Towards statistically valid protein structure search: revisiting E-values in Foldseek and Reseek
authors: Lingfeng Shi, Han Zhou, Yang Lu
abstract: Fast protein structure search tools such as Foldseek and Reseek are rapidly becoming indispensable for homology detection, annotation transfer, and structural database mining. Their E-values appear to provide an interpretable statistical assessment of structural similarity, analogous to BLAST in sequence search. Here we show that these E-values can be seriously miscalibrated, with Foldseek tending to be too conservative and Reseek at times too liberal. We instead estimate significance by generating a small query-specific null sample through shuffling the per-residue structural representation used by the search engine and comparing the observed score against the resulting random optimal scores. Across the settings we examined, the resulting p-values were never liberal, substantially improving calibration for Foldseek and correcting anti-conservative behavior for Reseek. Our results suggest that native E-values in modern structure search should be interpreted with caution and that this framework offers a practical route to statistically reliable, error-controlled structure similarity discovery.

title: Unmasking Pathogen-Host Structural Mimicry in the AI era
authors: Tung Nguyen, Elodie Ghedin, Pietro Sormanni
abstract: Molecular mimicry, where pathogen proteins structurally resemble host antigens, is a central hypothesis in autoimmune pathology. However, current detection methods are largely limited to sequence homology or domain-level alignment, failing to identify the subtle, discontinuous structural “patches” that often drive antibody cross-reactivity. To resolve this computational bottleneck, we present JumpMASTER, a high-performance structural motif-search engine written in Rust that extends MASTER-style backbone patch matching. Powered by chemical similarity prefilters and GPU acceleration, JumpMASTER directly queries existing Foldcomp structural databases encompassing the predicted protein universe. Furthermore, it generates an optional, self-sufficient C-alpha acceleration index—further compressing the search space for the entire human proteome to just 60 MB. Motif recovery benchmarks indicate JumpMASTER achieves more than two orders of magnitude acceleration over MASTER C++, enabling the detection of 20-angstrom structural mimics for hundreds of pathogen queries across the entire human proteome in seconds. We integrated this high-speed structural scanning with AlphaFold3 to computationally model antibody cross-reactivity from pathogen epitopes to predicted human mimics. Applying this pipeline to major viral proteomes, including SARS-CoV-2, HIV, RSV, and Epstein-Barr Virus (EBV), we uncovered a broad landscape of both previously characterized and novel host-pathogen structural homologies. As a prominent example, we identified high-confidence mimicry motifs within both surface-exposed and intracellular targets, such as vesicular trafficking proteins. We propose that these intracellular mimics become accessible to circulating antibodies via viral-induced cellular stress or ectopic surface expression, exacerbating inflammatory responses. These findings demonstrate JumpMASTER's utility in unmasking non-obvious, structurally conserved epitopes that evade sequence-based detection. By providing a scalable framework to map the “structural mimicry interactome,” this work generates new hypotheses regarding the etiology of post-infection syndromes and highlights new classes of potential therapeutic targets.

title: The Payoff of FAIR: From Natural Language Queries to GEO Submissions and Nextflow Samplesheets in a Bioinformatics Core
authors: Stuart Levine
abstract: Machine learning across biomedical research datasets is only as good as the metadata underlying it, and most data have not been captured focusing on these applications. Current approaches rely on highly structured relational databases or carefully warehoused data with well-characterized, harmonized data points. These work well for large clinical studies built around consistent data types, but are poorly suited to pre-clinical and multi-omic research where experimental designs vary and upfront harmonization is costly, and they do not take advantage of LLM-based approaches which do not require strict relational structure. NExtSEEK addresses this by pointing to data rather than tagging it directly, tracking samples as nodes in a directed experimental graph with protocols and assays as the connecting edges. Built as an extension of FAIRDOM-SEEK, the structure is defined but not predetermined: the schema is fixed while sample types, attributes, and connections remain fully mutable. This approach has been deployed across seven multi-institutional consortia spanning highly diverse domains including pre-clinical infectious disease, cancer biology, and environmental health, accumulating over 150,000 samples without requiring harmonization upfront. NExtSEEK Assistant was developed to take advantage of the rich metadata available in NExtSEEK. The chat-based multi-agent system responds to natural language requests through specialized agents engineered for the accumulated metadata, protocols, sample types, and assay relationships. Pilot applications directly address common researcher pain points: generating Nextflow samplesheets for nf-core pipelines and preparing submissions to public repositories such as GEO, SRA, and PRIDE. Tasks that previously required hours of manual effort are reduced to a single conversational request.

title: Less Code, More Biology: Carnation for Collaborative Multi-Omics Exploration
authors: Apratim Mitra, Ryan Dale
abstract: Recent reductions in sequencing cost have made complex experimental designs much more accessible, making it routine for transcriptomic or proteomic assays to yield dozens of interesting comparisons. Biological context might further warrant pattern analysis to find co-regulated genes, functional enrichment analysis to detect pathways affected by perturbation or orthogonal assays conducted in parallel, e.g. proteomics or mass spectrometry. In addition, depending on biological or technical factors, tool parameters often need to be fine-tuned over multiple rounds to maximize statistical power and facilitate biological interpretation. In the end, the massive volume of scripts, output files and analysis objects, can be overwhelming to manage not only for biologists but even for computational experts, making the task of extracting biological insight even more challenging. To address this we developed Carnation, an R/Shiny package that integrates various facets of differential expression analysis into a unified, interactive environment designed for both computational and experimental researchers. Carnation offers a clean intuitive graphical interface for exploring differential expression results, clustering patterns, and functional enrichment summaries, supporting multiple modalities and implementing several interactive features, such as highly customizable visualizations, and a global scratchpad for keeping track of genes of interest. Carnation features a modular extensible design allowing easy integration with new tools or visualizations and can be deployed locally or as a sharing platform on public infrastructure. In summary, Carnation democratizes multi-omic genomics analyses, transforming static analysis into a collaborative, interactive experience, enabling research teams to spend less time navigating data and more time generating biological insight.

title: An R Package To Simplify The UK Biobank RStudio Experience
authors: Nathan Kennedy, Christian Anderson, Lea Scheppke, Martin Friedlander, Roberto Bonelli
abstract: The UKB contains one of the largest collections of health data on half a million participants. Access to the data is offered using a bespoke cloud-based computing infrastructure called the UK Biobank Research Analysis Platform (UKB-RAP) via DNAnexus. The UKB-RAP offers a wide array of programming tools for different analyses. While this offers extreme flexibility, learning how to optimally use the platform can take weeks if not months. Several examples of this issue are found in the UKB-RAP and DNAnexus community forums, with multiple users asking for an "easier way to do things". To limit this friction, we are developing an R package for computational researchers who work in UKB RStudio. This package simplifies day-to-day activities while adding functionality to data extraction, backup, and manipulation between the UKB RStudio virtual machines (VMs) and the RAP storage. This is achieved by wrapping many of the established platform-specific command line interface (CLI) client commands provided by DNAnexus into easy-to-use R functions. Rather than manually coordinating DNAnexus commands between the distinct UKB platforms, researchers can interact within a cohesive R-based environment that allows seamless background synchronization. Our package additionally helps create a structured environment for researcher collaboration, including systems to store processed datasets and generalized pipelines for cooperative workflows. Employment of this package simplified daily VM setup, CLI interaction, and collaboration overhead -- demonstrating the potential of a simpler way for research groups to focus on their work rather than platform onboarding and environment configuration.

title: Scaling up support for bioinformatics core facilities training
authors: Patricia Carvajal-López, Kim Tamara Gurwitz, Eva Alloza, Salvador Capella-Gutiérrez
abstract: Bioinformatics core facilities (BCFs) play an essential role in enabling research in life sciences. As AI-based and multi-omics methodologies are increasingly applied to analyse molecular data, the demand continues to grow for highly specialised BCF services and expert personnel. Building on existing initiatives to support BCF scientists, we aim to stimulate discussion on the next steps needed to sustain and scale this support. Several initiatives have emerged to strengthen management-related competencies within BCFs. These include dedicated training initiatives, expanded competency frameworks for BCF scientists (https://doi.org/10.1093/bioadv/vbaf206), and efforts to bridge communities of practice (e.g. ISCB Education, Bioinfo-core). Notably, a number of training events have addressed BCF management, including the 2019 and 2021 EMBO “Research to Service: Planning and running a bioinformatics core facility” practical courses and the annual EMBL-EBI “Managing a Bioinformatics Core Facility” courses (2017– 2025). By December 2025, EMBL-EBI had trained 156 participants (36 countries; ~22% from LMICs), while the EMBO courses hosted 32 participants (https://f1000research.com/slides/11-1569). In addition, despite these efforts, due to the evolving needs of BCF personnel, together with the necessity to reach underrepresented audiences, the need remains to further structure and stratify training provision. Sustained, coordinated e orts are needed to support the BCF community. Many former trainees have become trainers, while others are developing local capacity-building initiatives. Targeted, competency-based training and opportunities to share best practice will be essential to support this growing community and to continue enabling research and innovation in the life sciences.

abstract: Bioinformatics workflows in Roche R&D must balance diverse assay types, scores of users and different compute needs with the utmost operational stability. Introducing our R&D pipeline, which processes data that can reach 30x-900x in coverage and where each sequencing run could be up to 5Tb in FASTQs across germline, somatic, RNAseq or other modalities. While transitioning from legacy DSL1 hybrid architecture to a modular DSL2 aligned towards nf-core principles, we implemented a configuration abstraction layer in the form of an internal CLI tool for flexibility, traceability and a user-friendly interface. This also aids in scalability and optimizes the configurations for performance on one of our many compute environments like AWS or GCP Batch, and a slurm-based HPC using Docker/Singularity images for reproducibility. We have a large supporting suite for this pipeline including operational monitoring by collecting metadata about runs and modules, infrastructure information, etc. and visualising them on multiple dashboards. We further have multiple metrics which look at different aspects of the analytical integrity and output. Which further enhances reliability, along with a suite of nf-tests at module and subworkflow level. This is augmented by integrated GitHub Actions which fire off tests for every pull requests and manually triggerable GitHub Actions for minimal dataset and benchmark testing that can be done with regression testing. This work demonstrates a scalable and modern approach to large scale pipelines designed to handle very high throughput of data and what goes into modernising them and creating a full framework around them.

title: HuBMAP Workspaces: an integrated analysis environment for the Human BioMolecular Atlas Program Data Portal
authors: Thomas C. Smits, John Conroy, Juan Muerto, Tiffany S. Liaw, Austen Money, Nikolay Akhmetov, Mark S. Keller, Morgan L. Turner, Lisa Choy, Philip Blood, Nils Gehlenborg
abstract: The HuBMAP Data Portal (https://portal.hubmapconsortium.org/) is a comprehensive repository for multi-modal spatial and single-cell data from healthy human tissues, with 5032 datasets from 22 different data types spanning 27 organ classes across 310 donors designed with FAIR principles. In addition to the data and metadata search and discovery options and interactive visualizations on dataset and organ pages, the portal supports downstream analysis tasks through an integrated online analysis environment for Python and R, the Workspaces. This project is a collaboration between members of the HuBMAP HIVE teams from Harvard Medical School (HMS) and the Pittsburgh Supercomputing Center (PSC). The Workspaces were designed to bring analysis closer to the data, and support this through offering direct data access, compute resources, analysis templates, and workspace collaborations. Single-cell and spatial biological data are large and analyses are resource intensive, thus direct data access and compute resources from the PSC enable analyses without the need for downloads or local infrastructure. Pre-constructed Jupyter notebook templates help quickly run standard analyses for data exploration, QC, and interactive Vitessce and scellop visualizations. Users can send each other invitations with copies of workspace files for collaboration. The Workspaces feature is deeply integrated into the portal, and can be accessed through different workflows, such as launching analyses directly from selected datasets. It has been used in two hackathons. Together, Workspaces extend the portal from a data repository into a platform for interactive and scalable biological data analysis.

title: Telomere-to-Telomere Genome Assembly of Native Desert-Adapted Sheep Ovis aries Breed “Najdi” From Saudi Arabia
authors: Ibrahim Alhidary, Samer Alharthi, Yara Altuwaijri, Faisal Alsubaie, Maxat Kulmanov, Marwa Abdelhakim, Olga Mashkova, Robert Hoehndorf, Yaqoub Almutairi, Hussain Alawad, Abdulrahman Alharthi, Abdulrahman Alghamdi, Riyadh Aljumaah, Hani Al-Baadani, Abdulkareem Matar, Mohammed Al-Badwi, Esam Fazea, Abdulaziz Algawaan, Marimuthu Swaminathan, Hatim Almutairi, Sulaiman Alajel, Waleed Alsalim, Hend Alotaibi, Aroob Alhumaidy, Othman Aljurayyad, Mohammed Babdullah, Areej Almuhayya, Mashael Alghuraybi, Muhayla Alanazi, Norah Alharbi, Muruj Tukruni, Alanoud Alharthy, Osama Alshehri, Mohammed Alarawi, Nouf F Alharbi, Shahad Alsalman, Saidan Alotaibi, Nuha Bin Tyyash, Afrah Alsulami, Shouq Alqahtani, Jamelah Alabdullatif, Sarah Alsobaie, Ahmad Faraj, Hind Aldakil
abstract: Najdi sheep (Ovis aries), an indigenous Arabian breed uniquely adapted to extreme arid conditions, remain underrepresented in genomic resources despite their high economic and adaptive significance. Existing sheep reference genomes are biased toward cosmopolitan breeds and leave repetitive and pericentromeric regions unresolved. This is exemplified by the widely used Rambouillet reference (ARS-UI_Ramb_v3.0), which remains fragmented across 134 contigs. Addressing this gap is essential to broaden the representation of genetically diverse, climate-adapted breeds in global genomic resources. Here, we present two telomere-to-telomere (T2T) genome assemblies for Najdi sheep, male and female, generated through a robust, scalable, and modular workflow. Assemblies integrate PacBio HiFi, ultra long Oxford Nanopore (ONT), and Hi-C data across four stages: de novo assembly, chromosome-scale scaffolding, chromosomal reconstruction and gap closing, and telomere rescue. The workflow utilizes an in-house developed approach for a gap resolution relies on a sample-specific strategy that draws on internal assembly resources, preserving biological accuracy and avoiding reference bias. Telomere assembly was achieved through a custom rescue workflow. Both assemblies achieved gap-free, chromosome-scale genomes spanning 26 autosomes and sex chromosomes, with genome sizes of 2.69-2.70Gb, N50 of 103.3-104.2Mb, N90 of 53.9-59.0Mb, QV ≥ 41, and completeness of ~97%. These metrics are comparable to the only available T2T sheep assembly (Hu-male) and represent a substantial improvement over the Rambouillet reference. These complete genomes establish a new benchmark for sheep genomics and provide a valuable resource for precision breeding, conservation, and climate resilience in the Arabian Peninsula and beyond.

title: Spatial multi-omics of cancer
authors: Ben Raphael
abstract: Tumors have an intricate spatial organization consisting of cancerous cells growing within the microenvironment of the host tissue. The cell types and cell states within this microenvironment are often related to treatment response and resistance, and thus characterizing the spatial organization of tumors is of great importance. Recent spatial technologies yield high-throughput and high-dimensional measurements of RNA, proteins, metabolites, and other modalities at thousands of locations within tissue sections, revealing spatial patterns of cell types and molecular activity. However, current datasets are often sparse and incomplete due to technological and cost constraints. I will present computational approaches that use machine learning and AI technologies to overcome this sparsity by modeling the latent geometry of individual tissue slices and by integrating measurements across multiple modalities over space and time. We apply the resulting methods to analyze spatial variation in cell types and gene expression across multiple cancer types and to reconstruct three-dimensional multi-modal tumor atlases.

title: Unavailability of experimental 3D structural data on protein folding dynamics and necessity for a new generation of structure prediction methods in this context
authors: Aydin Wells, Khalique Newaz, Jennifer Morones, Jianlin Cheng, Tijana Milenkovic
abstract: Protein folding is a dynamic process during which a protein's amino acid sequence undergoes a series of 3D conformational changes en route to reaching a native 3D structure; these conformations are called folding intermediates. While data on native 3D structures are abundant, data on 3D structures of non-native intermediates remain sparse, due to limitations of current technologies for experimental determination of 3D structures. Yet, analyzing folding intermediates is crucial for understanding folding dynamics and misfolding-related diseases. Hence, we search the literature for available (experimentally and computationally obtained) 3D structural data on folding intermediates, organizing the data in a centralized resource. Also, we assess whether existing methods, designed for predicting native structures, can be utilized to predict structures of non-native intermediates. Our literature search reveals six studies that provide 3D structural data on folding intermediates (two for post-translational and four for co-translational folding), each focused on a single protein, with 2-4 intermediates. Our assessment shows that an established method for predicting native structures, AlphaFold2, does not perform well for non-native intermediates in the context of co-translational folding; a recent study on post-translational folding concluded the same for even more existing methods. Yet, we identify in the literature recent pioneering methods designed explicitly to predict 3D structures of folding intermediates by incorporating intrinsic biophysical characteristics of folding dynamics, which show promise. This work of ours assesses the current landscape and future directions of the field of 3D structural analysis of protein folding dynamics.
