title: F.O.R.E.S.T: Spatially Informed Deconvolution of Cell Type Composition in Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Ranojoy Chatterjee, Prech Uapinyoying, Ali Rahnavard, Jyoti Jaiswal
abstract: Background-Spatial transcriptomics is a widely used approach to understand tissue development and disease. Despite thousands of publicly available 10x Visium datasets, their biological utility is limited by the inability to achieve single cell spatial resolution. Each Visium spot captures the transcriptional signal from a mixture of up to 10 cells, averaging cell-type-specific expression into an unresolved aggregate transcriptome for each 55 µm spot spaced 100 µm apart. Use of single cell transcriptomic data for deconvolution of spot into individual cellular transcriptome can provide spatial atlases resolved at single cell resolution, resulting in high-value spatial data rich in architectural and cellular heterogeneity driving the underlying biology of interest. This is needed to use the existing 10x Visium datasets to answer fundamental questions in tissue biology including cell type composition, proportion, and how those proportions change spatially during development or disease. Methods-To address the above need, we developed Feature-Optimized Robust Ensemble for Spatial Transcriptomics deconvolution (F.O.R.E.S.T), a framework that deconvolutes individual spots in Visium dataset to single-cell proportions. It does so by explicitly integrating spatial context of each spot at every stage of the deconvolution pipeline using large scRNA-seq references through marker-guided stratified subsampling. This approach allowed preserving rare cell populations with substantially reduced computational cost to construct a spatial neighborhood graph using the spot coordinates and per-spot features such as local expression gradients, boundary scores, and heterogeneity entropy to encode tissue architecture directly into a deconvolution model. A weighted ensemble of Random Forest models, trained on Dirichlet-synthesized pseudo-bulk mixtures, generated robust proportion estimates refined by adaptive graph Laplacian smoothing, enforcing spatial coherence across the entire tissue section while preserving true anatomical boundaries. Results-Compared to existing deconvolution algorithms RCTD, CARD, and SPOTlight F.O.R.E.S.T achieved a mean Moran’s index (0.573) substantially higher than RCTD (0.440), SPOTlight (0.437), and CARD (0.381) for Visium data of mouse olfactory bulb-a tissue with well-defined laminar organization. It enabled statistically significant spatial clustering for 100% of cell types compared to 80% for all the other methods. Unlike the spatially incoherent, salt-and-pepper cell type predictions by other tools, F.O.R.E.S.T recovered continuous granule cell, mitral cell, glomerular, and external plexiform layers. In a severe mouse model of muscular dystrophy (D2-mdx) with more heterogeneous cell type mixture, F.O.R.E.S.T ranked first in spatial coherence and delineating discrete zones of fibrosis, regeneration, and immune infiltration. In a milder dystrophic mouse model (BLAJ), at early (7 months) and late (11 months) stage of disease, F.O.R.E.S.T resolved spatial features of disease progression, that were invisible at spot level, identifying progressive expansion of fibroblast (9.5% to 14.8%, p < 0.0001), loss of Type IIB fibers (13.2% to 8.7%, p < 0.01), and tenocyte infiltration into muscle (p < 0.05). These results establish F.O.R.E.S.T as a robust tool to unlock spatial single-cell resolution analysis of existing and rapidly growing corpus of Visium data. Conclusion-F.O.R.E.S.T provides a robust and scalable solution to overcome the inherent resolution limitations of spatial transcriptomics by accurately deconvolving Visium spots into single-cell proportions while preserving spatial architecture. This framework enables researchers to fully exploit the growing repository of Visium datasets, facilitating deeper insights into tissue organization, cellular heterogeneity, and disease progression at near single-cell resolution.

title: scAURA: Alignment- and Uniformity-based Graph Debiased Contrastive Representation Architecture for Self-Supervised Clustering of Single-Cell Transcriptomics.
authors: Jubair Ibn Malik Rifat, Sarthak Engala, Serdar Bozdag
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) allows transcriptomic profiling at single-cell resolution, providing valuable insights into cellular diversity across tissues, developmental stages, and diseases. However, accurately identifying cell types remains challenging due to the high dimensionality, sparsity, and noise inherent in scRNA-seq data. To address these challenges in cell type identification in scRNA-seq data, we introduce scAURA (single cell Alignment-and Uniformity-based Graph Debiased Contrastive Representation Architecture), a unified framework that integrates graph debiased contrastive learning with self-supervised clustering. We evaluated scAURA on 18 real single-cell datasets collected from six sequencing platforms spanning diverse tissue and cell types in human and mouse. scAURA outperformed all state-of-the-art (SOTA) methods in nine and eight datasets in Adjusted Rand Index (ARI) and Normalized Mutual Information (NMI), respectively. On average, scAURA obtained average ranks of 2.28 (ARI) and 2.39 (NMI) across all 13 SOTA methods, demonstrating its consistent superiority across datasets. scAURA also exhibited strong robustness to dropout noise by maintaining stable clustering performance even under increasing sparsity levels. Furthermore, in an external single-cell Alzheimer’s disease dataset, scAURA accurately clustered different cell types, identified novel cell type–specific marker genes, and inferred their potential transcriptional regulators. The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/bozdaglab/scAURA.

title: Differential prevalence study of dust microbiome from rural farming and non-farming homes in Wisconsin
authors: Rene Welch, Heather Floerke, Rose Vrtis, Adan Glawe, Deborah Chasman, Christine Seroogy, Jim Gern, Irene Ong
abstract: Differential prevalence study of dust microbiome from rural farming and non-farming homes in Wisconsin Background The prevalence of asthma has increased with urbanization, but growing up on farms offers protection. We compared 16S rRNA-seq profiles of housedust samples from Wisconsin infants participating in the Wisconsin Infant Study Cohort (WISC), a prospective birth cohort study comparing three levels of exposure to farming environments: traditionally agrarian, dairy farming, and rural, non-farming. Methods We performed 16S rRNA-seq on environmental house dust samples from traditionally agrarian, dairy farming and rural non-farming houses at the age two-month and one-year visits. We analyzed the relationship between the microbial profiles with farm group, pet and farm animal exposure, and respiratory / allergic illness outcomes using statistical tests, classical ecological methods, and machine learning. We developed a data fission motivated differential prevalence model. Our model integrates two of the typical tasks involved in the analysis of microbiome data: estimating bacterial network and differential analysis. Results The differential prevalence analysis identified a core subnetwork of bacteria selected by all models, with some additional bacteria specific to each design variable. The core network included Dolosigranulum, and Moraxella, two healthy airway microbes when comparing against acute respiratory illnesses. Moreover, our differential prevalence method revealed that Aliicoccus, Salinicoccus, and Sinobaca were more prevalent in traditionally agrarian dust communities compared to both farm and non-farm homes. Conclusion Identifying bacteria that are differentially prevalent in house dust may provide clues as to mechanisms for reduced allergic diseases and asthma in farming environments.

title: U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Collaboration: Evaluation of Assays and Control Materials for Characterizing Animal Biotechnology Products Generated by Genome Editing

abstract: Genome editing technology has revolutionized the ability to make targeted changes to an animal’s genome (intentional genomic alterations [IGAs]), offering promise for the development of animal biotechnology products that address animal and public health needs. Characterization of these IGAs is an important part of the regulatory process to ensure that the edit to the animal is as intended and to identify any unintended genomic alterations. However, there are currently no validated measurements and standards for characterizing unintended genomic alterations in animals. In collaboration with FDA-CVM, NIST qualified commercially available porcine and bovine cell lines as potential control materials by characterizing their DNA sequences at on-target and potential off-target loci before and after CRISPR/ Cas9 genome editing with multiple guide RNAs. Eight off-target nomination approaches were compared: five in silico methods (Cas-OFFinder, CCtop, CHOPCHOP, COSMID, CRISPOR), two biochemical assays (CHANGE-seq, SITE-Seq), and one cell-based assay (GUIDE-seq-2), and rhAmpSeq was used for confirming nominated off-target sites. Preliminary outcomes of comparative analyses identified off-target sites that were nominated across multiple nomination methods; however, many off-targets were nominated by a single method. rhAmpSeq analyses identified reproducible off-target editing at predicted loci in edited cells, albeit at low levels. Future work involves expanding off-target analyses to identify reasons that may explain the discordance observed across off-target sites nominated by various methods. Resulting protocols and datasets will be published and made accessible to developers and the general public.

title: Like a Chicken in the Corn: Bioinformatics in the Great Plains
authors: ,, Iddo Friedberg
abstract: The Great Plains are often associated with food crops, livestock, and vast landscapes, yet they also provide fertile soil for bioinformatics research. Here, I will discuss how bioinformatics bridges fundamental biology and agriculture to address some of the region’s most pressing scientific challenges. We examine the promise and limitations of machine-learning approaches for annotating the large fraction of proteins that remain functionally uncharacterized in economically important yet less-studied crop plant genomes. I will also discuss how an abstract model of operon evolution helped us understand what makes a plant symbiont a plant pathogen. Finally, I discuss the importance of community-driven science, open benchmarking, and interdisciplinary training in developing the next generation of bioinformaticians. As biological datasets continue to grow in scale and complexity, progress will depend not only on better algorithms but also on collaborative frameworks that connect computer scientists, biologists, agricultural researchers, and students. Together, these efforts demonstrate how bioinformatics can thrive far from traditional academic hubs while making globally significant contributions.

title: Quantum‑enhanced attention improves expression prediction from cancer histopathology images with limited samples
authors: Kahn Rhrissorrakrai, Aritra Bose, Filippo Utro, Aldo Guzmán-Sáenz, Laxmi Parida
abstract: A major obstacle in cancer genomics is inferring molecular profiles from limited sequencing data, as large-scale sample acquisition remains costly and challenging. Whole slide images (WSIs), in contrast, are more readily available and recent advancements in transformer-based models have shown promise in predicting gene expression profile of a cancer sample from histopathology. However, performance varies widely across cancer types, indicating need for alternative computational approaches. Here, we evaluate the application of quantum-enhanced doubly stochastic attention in hybrid quantum-classical transformers, to the problem of gene expression prediction from WSIs. We integrate a quantum-enhanced doubly stochastic matrix (QDSM) into a state-of-the-art vision transformer, and systematically assess its impact across multiple cancer cohorts.Across all evaluated cancer types, quantum-enhanced attention consistently improves gene expression prediction, both when used throughout training or when applied only during a small number of early epochs as a warm start. Notably, the largest performance gains occur in cancer types with smallest sample sizes, highlighting the potential value of QDSM for rare or data-limited diseases. Experiments on quantum hardware with up to 30 qubits further demonstrate the practical feasibility of constructing quantum-enhanced doubly stochastic attention under realistic quantum hardware constraints. Together, these results establish that quantum-enhanced attention can serve as a data-efficient inductive bias for molecular prediction from histopathology and can be readily integrated into existing vision transformers with fixed attention size.

title: AI Accelerates Biological Discovery. Are We Ready for the Risks?
authors: Michelle Holko,
abstract: Generative agentic models and other applications of AI in molecular biology have the potential to create novel biohazards and increase the capabilities of malevolent actors. While current governance frameworks focus on individual models, technologies, or actors, risks increasingly arise from complex interactions across systems and organizational boundaries. To address these emerging risks, we propose adding an additional layer of relational biosecurity. Developments in generative AI, synthetic biology, cyberbiosecurity, and commercial scientific infrastructure amplify potentially hazardous capabilities while reducing requirements for specialized biological expertise. Agentic approaches increase compositional risks, where individually safe systems produce unexpected outcomes when connected in novel ways. New risks also can arise from inference over apparently mundane biomedical data when it is linked and aggregated at scale. Increasingly distributed and automated workflows present challenges to effective governance. Existing approaches to oversight struggle to manage rapidly evolving capabilities based in complex biomedical data ecosystems and AI-assisted design, as illustrated by recent cyberbiosecurity incidents. Relational biosecurity is a framework that views AI-enabled biology as a connected socio-technical system in which risk arises through relationships among data, models, infrastructure, institutions, and people. The approach emphasizes system-level visibility, uncertainty propagation, feedback, coordination, and alignment with shared values. In practice, this means designing workflows that preserve provenance and uncertainty across system boundaries, monitor interactions between components, and support shared awareness of how decisions, capabilities, and risks propagate through connected biological systems. Envisioned as a complement to existing biosecurity approaches, relational biosecurity offers a framework for understanding and managing risk in an era of increasingly connected AI-enabled biological systems.

title: Integrating genomics and structural biology in one of the earliest computational biology programs in the USA
authors: Remo Rohs, Dylan Kemmerer, Peijun Lin, Alexandra Shewchuk, Wei Yu Tang, Yingfei Wang, Jinsen Li, Tsu-Pei Chiu
abstract: DNA-binding specificity of transcription factors (TFs) can be studied through two complementary approaches: structural biology and genomics. Structural biology provides high-resolution insight by determining the precise spatial positions of atoms and residues in protein–DNA complexes, enabling detailed quantification of chemical and physical interactions. However, such data are typically limited to a small number of complexes, often a single TF bound to one DNA sequence, making it low throughput. In contrast, genomics approaches measure TF binding across thousands to millions of DNA sequences, using in vitro binding assays or in vivo genome-wide experiments. These methods generate high throughput data but represent DNA at low resolution, where each nucleotide (A, C, G, or T) is a coarse representation of the underlying atomic structure (each nucleotide pair comprising about 60 atoms). Historically, these two fields, structural biology and genomics, have operated largely independently. This divide has begun to close with the development of integrative computational methods such as Deep DNAshape (1) and DeepPBS (2). Deep DNAshape (1) takes DNA sequence as input and predicts structural features, effectively bridging low-resolution sequence data and high-resolution structural properties. This enables incorporation of DNA shape information into machine learning models for predicting TF–DNA binding specificity at scale. DeepPBS (2), on the other hand, starts from a protein–DNA complex structure with a single DNA fragment and generalizes binding specificity across sequences using geometric deep learning. It thus expands the utility of structural data into a broader genomic context. This talk will review recent progress in integrating genomics and structural biology and compare how this key principle is implemented in Deep DNAshape and DeepPBS with approaches such as AlphaFold. The talk will conclude with a perspective on how the integration of genomics and structural biology informs educational programs in computational biology, particularly in one of the earliest Ph.D. programs in computational biology and bioinformatics in the United States and worldwide. title: Scalable cell population plots for single-cell data with scellop
authors: Thomas C. Smits, Nikolay Akhmetov, Tiffany S. Liaw, Mark S. Keller, Eric Moerth, Nils Gehlenborg
abstract: Cell population plots are used to visualize cell types, states or clusters, and compare cell types within and between samples across conditions. Cell populations are traditionally shown using a stacked bar chart approach, with samples as bars and cell types as colored segments with lengths corresponding to the number or proportion of cells. These visualizations do not scale well with increasing numbers of samples and cell types, making it hard to identify and compare cell types. This is becoming a larger issue as single-cell atlas studies combine more and larger samples with more and rarer cell types. We conducted a design study to evaluate the user tasks and need for cell population plots, including within-sample and between-sample comparisons and metadata alignment. This highlighted color interpretability limitations and a need for interactive filtering, sorting, and grouping. Here we introduce scellop, a redesigned flexible cell population viewer (https://github.com/hms-dbmi/scellop). scellop combines a heatmap of cell counts with expandable embedded bar charts to support both global pattern detection and detailed investigation of samples. scellop is available as a Python and JavaScript package and integrates in Jupyter environments and web applications. It supports common single-cell data formats and allows flexible configuration and exports. Together, it enables scalable exploration of single-cell datasets and improves comparisons compared to traditional stacked bar chart approaches.

title: Interactive Visualization and Analysis of Genomic Data at NCBI using GDV, CGV, and MCGV
authors: Vamsi Kodali, Andrea Asztalos, Evgeny Borodin, Vadim Lotov, Dong-Ha Oh, Marina Omelchenko, Sanjida Rangwala, Dmitry Rudnev, Francoise Thibaud-Nissen, Joel Virothaisakun
abstract: The National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) provides a suite of interactive, web-based tools to support visualization and analyses of genomic data across a wide range of organisms. Together, the Genome Data Viewer (GDV), Comparative Genome Viewer (CGV), and Multiple Comparative Genome Viewer (MCGV) offer complementary approaches to exploring data at a single genome level to pairwise comparisons to multi-genome comparisons. GDV (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gdv) serves as NCBI's flagship genome browser, displaying gene annotations from multiple sources such as RefSeq, GenBank and Ensembl, variation data from NCBI and EVA, RNA-seq expression, and user-provided custom tracks for over 4500 eukaryotic genome assemblies. GDV integrates with other NCBI resources including BLAST, dbGaP, GEO, and ClinVar, enabling comprehensive genomic analyses within a single platform. For comparative genomics, CGV (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/cgv) visualizes pairwise whole-genome assembly alignments using an interactive ideogram and dotplot views, enabling exploration of structural differences such as inversions and translocations, as well as examining synteny of homologous genes when structural annotations are available. CGV currently supports over 1,600 pairwise alignments across more than 750 species, with new alignments added continuously in response to requests from the scientific community. MCGV (https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/mcgv) extends comparative visualization to multiple genomes simultaneously, displaying synteny blocks and sequence conservation relative to an anchor assembly, with support for pangenome datasets. Developed as part of the NIH Comparative Genomics Resource (CGR) initiative, MCGV—together with GDV and CGV—forms an interconnected ecosystem enabling researchers to navigate genomic data across biological scales without the need for local software installation or data preprocessing.

title: SBGNFlow: An AI-Assisted & Interactive Workflow for Generation, Merging & Layout of Pathway Maps
authors: Hasan Balci, Augustin Luna
abstract: The Systems Biology Graphical Notation (SBGN) provides standardized visual languages for representing complex biological processes, facilitating communication, reproducibility, and model sharing in systems biology. However, generating high-quality SBGN maps from scratch can be challenging, particularly for new users, due to the learning curve associated with SBGN editors and the difficulty of translating informal ideas into structured diagrams. To address this, we present SBGNFlow, an AI-assisted and interactive workflow that streamlines SBGN map generation and refinement through three key steps, supporting both Process Description (PD) and Activity Flow (AF) languages. The first step enables automatic conversion of hand-drawn SBGN sketches into SBGN-ML format using large language models with in-context learning. Quick correction of minor recognition errors and text-based editing are supported through an interactive interface, while biological identifiers are mapped automatically to facilitate annotation. Second, SBGNFlow supports flexible merging and splitting of maps. Digitized maps can be merged with existing ones to create larger networks in incremental steps by identifying shared nodes and edges, or reorganized into smaller components as needed, while preserving the user’s mental map. Finally, we introduce layout refinement methods. A user-guided layout algorithm allows sketch-based hints to influence the arrangement of the entire network or selected subgraphs, while a polishing step improves readability by aligning edges orthogonally or diagonally and organizing nodes by functional role (input, output, modifier). Together, these features provide an end-to-end solution for transforming informal sketches into structured, publication-ready SBGN maps, lowering the entry barrier for new users while offering flexible control for experts.

title: InterSCellar: Surface-Based Cell Neighborhood and Interaction Volume Analysis in 3D Spatial Omics
authors: Eunice Lee, Clarence Yapp, Zoltan Maliga, Luca Marconato, Felix Zhou, Tuulia Vallius, Alex Wong, Peter Sorger, Nils Gehlenborg, Eric Mörth
abstract: InterSCellar (https://pypi.org/project/InterSCellar/) is an open-source Python package for surface-based cell-cell interaction analysis in 3D spatial omics data. Current practices for estimating cell-cell interactions are simply centroid-based and ignore the shape irregularities between different cell types. To address this, InterSCellar implements two core functionalities: (1) construction of cell-neighbor graphs through surface-based detection of adjacent cell pairs; (2) computation of intercellular spaces between neighbors as physical volumes. Therefore, InterSCellar more accurately identifies subcellular interaction contexts grounded in spatial adjacency, redefining how cell-cell interactions are detected, quantified, and interpreted. Applied to highly-multiplexed (>50-channels) 3D CyCIF melanoma datasets of clinical melanoma samples, InterSCellar reveals interaction-specific structural and molecular patterns across different stages of disease progression. We identify distinct shifts in neighborhood organization, with invasive tumors forming more self-associated or immune-enriched clusters, while in situ tumors retain stronger epithelial and stromal architecture. Proteomic expression within interaction volumes uncovers enrichment patterns specific to neighboring cell profiles and differential localization of structural markers across tumor–epithelial interfaces. These results enable downstream analyses such as network-based characterizations of tissue microenvironments and identification of spatial niches associated with disease states. InterSCellar (https://github.com/hms-dbmi/InterSCellar) is interoperable with standard data structures including OME-NGFF and scverse’s SpatialData, and integrates with visualization tools such as Vitessce and Napari. By transforming high-dimensional 3D images into surface-resolved interaction graphs and volumes, InterSCellar bridges the analytical gap between segmentation and biological insight.

title: How Do We Visualize Space in Molecular Biology? A Study of Spatial Transcriptomics Visualization Practices
authors: Denisse Chacon-Ramirez, Mark S. Keller, Eric Mörth, Nils Gehlenborg, Marc Streit, Andreas Hinterreiter
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics enables the study of gene expression while preserving spatial context within tissue, generating datasets that are high-dimensional, multimodal, and spatially structured. These characteristics introduce challenges for visualization, requiring methods that support reasoning across molecular, cellular, and tissue scales during exploration, validation, and communication of biological hypotheses. Despite a growing ecosystem of tools, there remains limited understanding of how visualizations encode data, support biological inquiry, and scale with analytical complexity. To address this gap, we developed a survey of visualization practices in spatial transcriptomics, grounded in the systematic coding of over 3,000 figure panels across 170 published analysis and visualization tools. After excluding benchmarking and schematic ones, over 1,800 were retained for analysis. We systematically coded each figure using a taxonomy inspired by Munzner’s what–why–how framework, capturing three dimensions: data representation (what), analytical tasks (why), and visualization design (how), with interaction characterized as an additional dimension. Through this analysis, we identify recurring design patterns; Visualization is predominantly oriented toward questions of tissue structure, followed by tasks focused on identifying cell types. Comparative analysis is most commonly supported through juxtaposition using small multiples, typically to contrast gene expression patterns within tissue. We also observe that some practices mirror those used in single-cell transcriptomics, discarding spatial context. By linking biological research questions to visualization design, this review establishes a task-oriented perspective on visualization practice in spatial transcriptomics. Our findings highlight design biases and missed opportunities, providing guidance for developing tools that better support spatial reasoning and complex biological inquiry.

title: Interactive Visual Exploration of Antibody Sequence Optimization: Bridging Machine Learning Predictions and Visual Analytics
authors: Khushboo Jain, Yu-Min Chung, Aditeya Pandey
abstract: Modern sequencing technologies generate millions of antibody sequences per experiment, generating complex datasets. Current approaches usually present mutations as static tables or scatter plots, failing to preserve sequence context or integrate predictions from multiple protein language models. Consequently, scientists must manually piece together insights, introducing inefficiency and risking losing critical insights. We present an interactive visualization system addressing fundamental challenges of multi-scale navigation, multi-objective optimization, and exploratory analysis of mutation spaces. Our web-based platform integrates three coordinated views, an interactive sequence navigator with Complementarity Determining Regions (CDR) highlighting, an adaptive multi-position heatmap, and a selection drawer for detailed inspection. This enables intuitive exploration from overview to mutation-level detail. Beyond antibody engineering, this work demonstrates generalizable visualization strategies for biological sequence optimization problems involving multi-model predictions and multi-objective decision-making. The system exemplifies how thoughtful visualization design can transform complex bioinformatics predictions into actionable insights while maintaining critical spatial context throughout exploratory analysis, using simulated antibody sequence data.

title: Cluster stability in spatial transcriptomics: A method agnostic evaluation and visualization framework
authors: Wenshan Wu, Joe Nguyen, Erin Molloy
abstract: Clustering is a fundamental step in many spatial transcriptomics (ST) analysis pipelines, including Space Ranger. Clusters are often used for manual annotations, biological interpretations, and downstream analyses such as differential gene expression analysis (DGEA). However, most clustering methods are stochastic and can yield different partitions even when input and parameter are fixed except for a random seed. The key question is whether clustering are stable or merely artifacts of a particular run? In this talk, we present a model-agnostic framework for quantifying and visualizing clustering instability in ST analyses. We apply this framework to 18 publicly available ST benchmark samples with ground truth labels and 7 clustering methods. Our results revealed that unstable clusters were pervasive across benchmarks, and that cluster stability depended more on the sample itself than the clustering method. Unstable clusters were typically associated with lower purity, lower gene expression coherence, and lower DGEA consistency; while stable clusters showed the reverse. A central contribution of our framework is the visualization of clustering instability in spatial context. We introduce spatial instability maps that allow users to inspect unstable tissue regions, compare instability patterns across methods and samples, and relate instability to biological annotations and downstream analyses. These visualizations help biologists identify regions where cluster-based interpretation should be treated cautiously or where alternative analysis strategies may be needed. Ongoing work extends this framework into an interactive tool for exploring unstable regions, inspecting cluster behavior across repeated runs, and using stability information to guide study conclusions.

title: Evaluating Agentic Schemes for Authoring Interactive Multiview Genomics Visualizations
authors: Astrid van den Brandt, Kiroong Choe, Sehi L'Yi, Devin Lange, Nils Gehlenborg
abstract: Genomics visualizations require the integration of heterogeneous data types, coordinated interactive views, and domain-specific constraints, making authoring more difficult than standard chart generation. Although many visualization tools are available, they are typically either limited in customization or require extensive learning or programming effort, and even when a tool is sufficiently expressive, users may lack the visualization expertise to produce effective designs. Large language models are increasingly used for automatic visualization generation from natural language, but remain limited when applied to complex, domain-specific data such as genomics, where their complexity might also make it more difficult for users to articulate their needs precisely in natural language. We investigate how agent-based LLM schemes can support complex genomics visualization authoring in two steps. We first characterize where vanilla LLM generation succeeds and fails using Gosling, a declarative grammar for genomics visualization, across 159 cases spanning three complexity levels and three query scenarios. We identified eight quality dimensions covering encoding, layout, interaction, and presentation, and found that persistent failure modes emerge as complexity increases, motivating more structured authoring approaches with iteration and correction. We then compare six authoring schemes ranging from direct generation and a fixed pipeline to four agentic configurations, varying in the number of specialist agents and the presence of a reviewer. Our results show that agentic schemes substantially outperform both baselines on perceived quality, while more complex agent architectures did not improve over a single iterative agent, which achieved comparable quality at the lowest cost. Our findings suggest that specialized grammars and flexible agents are complementary: a grammar acts as a guardrail that constrains the solution space, and the agent flexibly searches within those limits. Realizing this potential will require finer-grained tools such as per-track validation and interaction-level debugging, allowing agents to inspect and correct more precisely than static visual and spec-level feedback currently supports.

title: Introducing WWizNet, a fully interactive 3D web-based application for large-scale biomedical network visualization and analysis
authors: Philipp Friedrich, Iker Núñez Carpintero, Celine Sin, Chloé Bucheron, Ines Gerard-Ursin, Jörg Menche
abstract: Network models offer a flexible and effective framework for analyzing large-scale biomedical data. Interactive visualization plays a central role in this process, with tools such as Cytoscape, Gephi, and VRNetzer widely used to explore and interpret network biology models. However, the complexity of large biomedical networks presents a significant challenge for developing intuitive visualizations that enable rapid identification of patterns within intricate topologies. Existing tools, while powerful, do not always fully address the interactivity, scalability, and integrative analysis required for increasingly large and heterogeneous datasets, which often demand customized visual configurations and workflows. Here, we present WWizNet, a fully interactive web-based application that integrates scalable visualization with advanced analytical functionality in a unified environment. The platform supports real-time rendering of large networks alongside rich metadata annotation, including dimensionality reduction approaches such as UMAP applied to functional annotations (e.g., Gene Ontology or Human Phenotype Ontology), enabling discovery of relationships beyond topology. Classical network analysis methods, including community detection and random walk with restart, are implemented to explore structural organization and prioritize relevant nodes. Additionally, we introduce a plugin for visualization of AlphaFold protein structures, with emphasis on amino acid highlighting for phosphoproteomic data and disease-associated variants. The application further incorporates seemingly integrated metadata analysis tools, including interactive heatmaps and UpSet plots that respond dynamically within a unified node selection environment. This unified design enables iterative, exploratory workflows, facilitating efficient hypothesis generation, validation, and knowledge discovery within a single, scalable platform.

title: Interactive Exploration of Cancer Regulatory Landscapes with Reactive Notebooks
authors: Vedat Yilmaz, Conrad Bzura, Nezar Abdennur
abstract: Chromatin accessibility profiling across hundreds of tumor samples[1] and millions of candidate regulatory elements[2] reveals regulatory programs that distinguish cancer subtypes, yet most analyses reduce this complexity to static figures that cannot be interrogated further. Purpose-built data portals support predefined queries but do not empower users to reshape analyses on the fly. We present Epifolio[3,4], a suite of reactive Marimo[5] notebooks that couple curated multi-modal views of the TCGA regulatory landscape with the full analytical flexibility of a computational notebook. Marimo's reactive execution model, combined with custom visualization widgets built on Anywidget[6,7], lets users transition between a purpose-driven "app" interface and an editable notebook interface for bespoke analyses. Since all processed data artifacts are hosted statically, Epifolio runs across a range of environments with zero configuration. Multiple notebooks guide exploration across scales: cohort-level dimensionality reduction (NMF, PCA) linked to clinical metadata, pairwise accessibility comparisons between patients, and side-by-side inspection of healthy and tumor signal tracks at specific loci. The dataflow model propagates selections across linked views, so users can lasso a cluster in a UMAP embedding, immediately see corresponding NMF loadings, clinical annotations, and underlying signal, then modify code to pursue new questions without leaving the notebook. To validate this workflow, we recovered the PAM50 basal versus non-basal breast cancer distinction-traditionally derived from gene expressions-from unsupervised decomposition of chromatin accessibility alone. All notebooks are downloadable, self-contained, and executable. Epifolio's design demonstrates that reactive notebooks can bridge the gap between curated data resources and open-ended multi-omic exploratory analysis. References: 1. M. title: Hierarchical decomposition and visualization of metagenome assembly graphs with MetagenomeScope
authors: Marcus Fedarko, Jay Ghurye, Todd Treangen, Mihai Pop
abstract: Motivation: Metagenome sequence assembly is an increasingly critical step in studying microbial community composition, and the assembly graphs that this process produces provide a unique window into the underlying genomic diversity thereof. Assembly graphs represent this information at both coarse-grained ("which connected components seem like putative plasmid sequences?") and fine-grained ("what caused this bubble?") levels of detail. Visualizing assembly graphs at both scales -- enabling the user to move back and forth between comprehensive high-level overviews of the graph and clear representations of local details of interest -- remains an active area of research. Methods: We present MetagenomeScope, a software tool that facilitates the multilevel exploration of assembly graphs. MetagenomeScope iteratively decomposes the graph into interpretable structural patterns and visualizes them as hierarchical annotations. These patterns are used to inform graph layout, providing a clear view of these small-scale details. MetagenomeScope augments this functionality with a rich set of tools for analyzing higher-level graph structure, including path highlighting and interactive summary plots. Results: MetagenomeScope enables close-up visualizations of densely tangled regions of assembly graphs, such as those caused by rDNA arrays. The tool is able to visualize entire large assembly graphs (up to tens of thousands of nodes) as well as subregions and summaries of even larger graphs. Significance: The ongoing deluge of sequencing data underscores the need for careful validation. The novel algorithms and features supported by MetagenomeScope simplify assembly graph analysis, lowering the barriers to manual inspection of assembly outputs. Code and documentation are available at https://github.com/marbl/ MetagenomeScope.

title: Automating subtype-specific cancer gene prioritization at the OncoTree ontology scale using large language models (LLMs) for exploration in cBioPortal
authors: Suhasini Lulla, Ino de Bruijn, Karl Pichotta, Christopher Fong, Augustin Luna, Sharon Plon
abstract: Disease-specific gene sets are central to genomic data interpretation. However, curation at the cancer subtype resolution remains incomplete and difficult to scale. Therefore, we developed 'OncoTree2Genes-LLM' (https://github.com/SuhasiniLulla/OncoTree2Genes-LLM), a programmatic framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate and evaluate gene-cancer subtype associations across the comprehensive OncoTree ontology of cancer subtypes. Using the December 2025 OncoTree ontology release, we prompted an LLM to generate structured lists of genes classically implicated for each subtype. We then compared these lists with established pan-cancer lists. Novel associations were evaluated through automated PubMed queries. For each gene-disease pair, abstracts were retrieved and assessed using a second LLM acting as an independent evaluator ('LLM-as-a-judge') to determine whether the association is supported by literature evidence. Supported associations were retained. Human review was performed on selected subtypes to assess concordance with LLM-as-a-judge. The pipeline generated gene sets for 896 of 898 cancer subtypes, yielding 11,129 associations (median 12 genes per subtype). Of these, 85.1% were supported by established lists or literature-based evaluation. Manual review demonstrated agreement between LLM-as-a-judge and human judgment (17 of 18 correct classifications). Subtype-specific gene sets showed concordance with curated resources for selected cancers where curations were available. Lists generated by OncoTree2Genes-LLM were integrated into a local deployment of cBioPortal to enable cohort filtering and visualization. This work demonstrates a scalable approach for structured knowledge extraction and evaluation in cancer genomics in combination with pre-existing ontologies, with applications for expert gene curation, focused research, and clinical workflows.

title: Constrained LLM-Assisted Alignment of HPO Terms to Phecodes
authors: Chenjie Zeng, Joshua Denny
abstract: The Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) provides a standardized vocabulary for rare-disease phenotypes. Connecting HPO terms to large-scale electronic health record (EHR) analyses requires alignment to clinical coding systems designed for different purposes. Phecodes, curated groupings of International Classification of Diseases (ICD) codes into clinically meaningful phenotypes, have become standard infrastructure for large-scale EHR-based biobanks. Naive lexical matching between HPO and phecodes, however, is brittle and may force broad developmental phenotypes into semantically incompatible clinical codes. We developed an LLM-assisted curation pipeline that combines OpenAI o1-pro with structured biomedical knowledge resources to align 6,199 HPO terms to phecodes. The pipeline anchors mappings using Callahan et al. OMOP2OBO and OMIM cross-references, then expands unresolved terms with rules prioritizing congenital/genetic interpretations and enforcing organ-level, sex, and congenital-versus-acquired consistency constraints. Rather than serving as an unconstrained generator, the LLM functions as a structured reviewer,proposing candidates, auditing cross-system mismatches, and recording source-tiered provenance, with full decision traces retained for auditability. Of the 6,199 terms, 75 abstract ontological groupings (e.g., "Abnormality of the nervous system") were explicitly excluded and 16 remained unresolved, yielding 6,108 mapped terms with tiered confidence scores. We benchmarked against the Bastarache et al. HPO-to-phecode resource, yielding 1,323 validated terms. On a leakage-free pre-benchmark snapshot, 52.1% exact-code and 81.5% same-category agreement were observed. After iterative harmonization, the final release reached 75.2% exact-code agreement, 91.6% same-category agreement, and 99.9% coverage. These mappings, covering nearly all HPO terms linked to OMIM diseases, now support phenome-wide discovery, genomic screening, and cohort identification across biobank-scale EHR data.

title: BiomarkerKB: A Knowledgebase Supporting a Standardized Biomarker-Centric Knowledge and Data Integration
authors: Raja Mazumder,
abstract: Biomarkers are essential for disease detection, risk assessment, and therapeutic monitoring, but the data describing them are fragmented across diverse resources and inconsistently represented in the literature. This lack of standardization limits data integration and the discovery of novel biomarker-disease relationships. To address this critical gap, we present BiomarkerKB, an integrated knowledgebase designed to harmonize and contextualize biomarker information under a standardized data model. The model follows the FDA-NIH BEST biomarker definition and captures both core elements (biomarker, biomarker entity, condition/exposure agent) and contextual metadata, including specimen, biomarker role, and evidence. This framework provides a structured template for reporting biomarker information, facilitating alignment with and integration into existing knowledge. Biomarker data were curated from publications and aggregated from multiple public resources, including Open Targets, GWAS Catalog, NCI-EDRN, alongside contributions from NIH’s CFDE. Standardization was achieved using ontologies and reference systems, including biomarker-specific controlled vocabulary and ontology, Disease Ontology, UBERON, PubChem, UniProt, and GlyTouCan. This unified representation enables biomarker entities such as genes, proteins, and metabolites to be linked to corresponding entities in different biological databases. As a result, it becomes feasible to link measurements from clinical reports in electronic health records (EHR) to broader knowledge about those molecules, including their function, pathways, and disease relevance, enabling a more comprehensive view of patient data than is currently possible. The current release of BiomarkerKB (https://biomarkerkb.org) contains over 200,000 biomarker-condition associations spanning genes, proteins, metabolites, and glycans.

title: Do Mice Speak Human? Cross-Species Semantic Alignment of Disease Metadata
authors: Yuzhang Fu, Ayesha Saleem Sheikh, Halie Rando
abstract: Mice are widely used to model human diseases due to their genetic similarities, yet few pharmaceutical developments are successfully translated across species. This project develops a cross-species semantic alignment framework to examine how experimental metadata describe disease models and to support systematic comparison between human and mouse studies. Our broader motivation is to understand whether semantic representations can provide a foundation for evaluating the biological similarity. We first introduced MONDO, a unified disease ontology that integrates multiple disease resources into a global hierarchy of disease concepts. Human and mouse GSE (GEO Series) metadata were analyzed separately using txt2onto 2.0, which maps controlled vocabularies onto free text and outputs prior probability scores for disease models. Applying a threshold greater than 1 allowed us to retain predictions with high confidence for cancer-related MONDO terms and assign consistent disease labels to individual studies. To investigate ontology behavior, we examined prediction patterns across six hierarchical levels within the cancer branch of MONDO. Although txt2onto does not encode hierarchical structure explicitly, most studies showed stronger predictions at child nodes and weaker scores at parent terms. This pattern indicates that disease specificity present in experimental metadata aligns with the internal structure of the ontology. We then analyzed human–mouse GSE pairs sharing the same predicted MONDO term. After preprocessing and lemmatization, we applied TF-IDF and generated sentence embeddings to compare studies. Cosine similarity scores were consistently higher for matched human–mouse pairs than for random pairs, suggesting structured alignment at the textual level. To further characterize biomedical entities, we used SciSpaCy (en_ner_bionlp13cg_md) with its AbbreviationDetector and UMLS EntityLinker to normalize differently expressed phrases through shared CUIs, grouping related terms such as gene expression under unified concepts. Ongoing work maps these normalized entities back to the corpus and applies TF-IDF to enable refined cross-species comparison.

title: Signal Over Noise: Semi-Automated Relevancy Scoring for Biomedical Knowledge in Drug Repurposing
authors: Shilpa Sundar, Kathleen Carter, Nicolas Matentzoglu, Melissa Haendel
abstract: Biomedical knowledge graphs integrating heterogeneous biomedical data sources are increasingly central to computational drug repurposing. However, not all sources contribute equally: varying in their scope, content, modeling, provenance, and utility for modeling drug-target-disease relationships. Existing frameworks such as FAIR, Open Targets scoring, and the Venus Score address accessibility/ general data quality, but were not designed for the specific requirements of drug repurposing; namely the need for directed, mechanistic, and clinically-grounded edges connecting drugs to diseases. Moreover, determining each source’s contribution via graph-based filtering is computationally expensive at scale. We present the Relevancy Score Rubric, a framework for prioritizing sources for drug repurposing, combining manual scoring with automated labeling across four criteria: (A) Domain Coverage-entity types and relation families; (B) Source Scope-breadth and scale across diseases, organisms, and modalities; (C) Utility for Drug-Disease Modelling-presence of actionable edges, directionality, evidence, and mapping quality; and (D) Noise Penalty-deduce for text-mined, or low-precision associations. It also includes a boolean indicator from reviewer comments to capture repurposing-relevant edge types (core_edge_family flag). Combined scores yield an auto-label (High, Medium, Low) via deterministic thresholds, validated by expert review. We applied the Rubric to 91 primary knowledge sources in Every Cure's MATRIX, assigning 18 sources as High, 59 as Medium, and 14 as Low. Automated labels agreed with expert manual review across all case studies. By enabling systematic prioritization of high-value sources, the rubric reduces reliance on costly graph experiments and supports more efficient drug repurposing analyses.

title: Constraining Pathogenetic State Hypotheses in Synovial Sarcoma: A Neuro Symbolic Pipeline for SS18::SSX1 Characterization via TTT Linear and Z3 Based SMT Verification
authors: George Anstey, Noel Anstey
abstract: We introduce a neuro-symbolic pipeline for characterizing system level failures driven by the SS18::SSX1 fusion protein in synovial sarcoma. Characterizing this pathogenesis requires bridging molecular level protein disruptions with phenotypic observables a task that challenges standard deep learning models due to the dual requirements of long range sequence dependency and formal causal consistency. The proposed architecture implements an operational interface between test time training (TTT) architectures and satisfiability modulo theories (SMT) based verification using Z3. Within this pipeline a TTT Linear model processes protein sequence data to propose candidate state transition sequences. These sequences are mapped into symbolic predicates and subjected to formal verification against a knowledge base of encoded biological rules. Z3 functions as a constraint-guided pruning layer rejecting candidates that violate consistency constraints involving phenotypic markers such as LDH and CD56. Importantly, Z3 does not merely validate candidate predictions it constrains the admissible hypothesis space generated by TTT Linear outputs. This hierarchical methodology produces reconstructions that are computationally expressive and biologically auditable. Preliminary experiments indicate that this constrained approach reduces the proposal of biologically incoherent states relative to unconstrained sequence modeling baselines.

title: Bridging classical and transcriptomic cell types at scale: agentic AI workflows for the Cell Ontology
authors: David Osumi-Sutherland, Ismail Uğur Bayındır, Hüseyin Kır, Andrea Rivera, Caroline Eastwood
abstract: Cell types have historically been defined by function, morphology, location, and lineage, while single-cell atlases now classify them by transcriptomic profiles. Both perspectives capture essential aspects of cellular identity, but connecting them remains a fundamental knowledge representation challenge. Bridging these definitions relies on multimodal data from techniques including spatial transcriptomics, CITE-seq and Patch-seq. Typically, mapping is done informally during atlas annotation, but the scale of emerging atlases, particularly for the nervous system, means it is often incomplete while supporting evidence, if reported at all, remains buried in the literature. The Cell Ontology (CL) is uniquely placed to bridge these perspectives, already defining classical cell types formally by location, structure, function, lineage, and markers, and increasingly linking to transcriptomic reference data. We have developed agentic AI workflows addressing both scale and evidence challenges. Community-facing workflows on GitHub convert requests into validated draft CL extensions, checking assertions against cited literature and linking terms to atlas data. Evidencell, a deep-search workflow for atlas annotation, combines literature mining, atlas metadata, and bioinformatic analysis to generate structured hypotheses mapping transcriptomic clusters to classical types. Each mapping is backed by typed evidence: literature excerpts with citations, marker gene overlaps, spatial expression data, and electrophysiological or morphological properties. Results are stored in a formal schema ensuring traceability and shared as reports for expert review. Both systems feature anti-hallucination validation and human review gates. As these workflows scale, CL is evolving into an evidence-rich knowledge base bridging classical and transcriptomic cell type definitions.

title: Developing a Semantically Interoperable Knowledge Graph Schema to Support Single Cell Transcriptomics
authors: Matthew Diller, Raymond Leclair, Bingfang Xu, Anne Deslattes Mays, Ajith Viswanathan Asari, Noam Rotenberg, Yun Zhang, Kumar Arvind, Beverly Peng, Richard Scheuermann
abstract: The Cell Knowledge Network (CKN) is a project led by the National Library of Medicine to integrate complex data from high throughput single cell transcriptomics experiments with knowledge about relevant biological systems using a graph-structured knowledgebase. Concurrent with this effort are a multitude of knowledge graph (KG) projects that are actively being developed and maintained that contain rich collections of computable knowledge about various domains of science. To maximize on the potential value of these knowledge graphs—both collectively and individually—it is vital that their development and maintenance place a large emphasis on interoperability with other KGs. With this in mind, CKN version 1 was developed to be a modular KG that is aligned with community adopted data standards. Where possible, we normalize defined node and edge types to terms from biomedical ontologies—such as the Cell Ontology—which are widely used in single cell transcriptomics databases, including CELLxGENE and the Human Biomolecular Atlas Program (HuBMAP). We also map defined nodes, edges, and triple assertions to the Biolink Model, which was designed to be an upper-level data model to facilitate interoperability between biomedical KGs. Additionally, to capture the trustworthiness of the data and knowledge represented in CKN, defined edge properties were developed for various confidence measures and to store the source of an assertion. Ultimately, we believe that efforts such as this to drive integration between KGs will better enable the discovery of new knowledge about cell biology and disease. The schema for CKN is publicly available at https://github.com/NIH-NLM/cell-kn-schema. This research was supported by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institutes of Health (NIH). title: The critical role of human validation in the era of AI-assisted biocuration: Extending competencies and reflecting career progression in current frameworks
authors: Patricia Carvajal-López, Kim Tamara Gurwitz
abstract: Biocuration is fundamental to the integrity and usability of biological references and biological data resources. This critical field requires highly trained specialists with skill sets that are often developed through extensive, non-classical academic pathways.While the ISCB Competency Framework (https:// competency.ebi.ac.uk/framework/iscb/3.0 ), defines a ‘minimum standard’ for a generic, mid-career biocurator (as well as other professional profiles), more detail and nuance is needed to better support career progression in this field. This talk aims to propose a further extension to the ISCB Competency Framework for biocurators. This would include the evolving role of biocurators, particularly in the AI age, and discussion on how best to engage the community to refine and, where necessary, extend the competencies required for this profession. In addition, it seeks to begin formally incorporating a structured career progression pathway for biocurators within the ISCB Competency Framework. This extension could serve as a valuable tool to support recruitment, training, and performance evaluation in a similar way to the extension for bioinformatics core facility scientists, from entry level to a leadership role, which has recently been published (https://doi.org/10.1093/bioadv/vbaf206). Developing a well-defined, competency-based career pathway, alongside appropriate training opportunities, is essential to support the professional development of biocurators. In turn, this will strengthen their contribution to research and innovation in the life sciences and help address emerging challenges in an era increasingly shaped by AI-assisted approaches.

title: SomaModules:A Pathway Enrichment Approach Tailored to SomaScan Data
authors: Julián Candia, Giovanna Fantoni, Francheska Delgado-Peraza, Nader Shehadeh, Toshiko Tanaka, Ruin Moaddel, Keenan Walker, Luigi Ferrucci
abstract: Background: Pathway enrichment analysis, widely regarded as the primary approach for gaining insights into biological processes regulated by differentially expressed genes, relies on gene set repositories derived from gene expression data. For lack of better alternatives, these repositories are also used in pathway analyses of proteomics data. This practice is problematic, because measured protein abundances are affected by a variety of post-translational biological processes and by technical limitations in protein quantification. Results: We developed a greedy, top-down procedure to iteratively identify strongly intra-correlated SOMAmer modules, termed “SomaModules" based, on 11K SomaScan data. We generated two repositories based on the latest MSigDB and MitoCarta releases, containing more than 40,000 SOMAmer-based gene sets combined. We validated our results with two case examples: (i) Alzheimer’s Disease specific pathways in a 7K SomaScan case-control study, and (ii) mitochondrial pathways using 11K SomaScan data linked to physical performance outcomes. Using Gene Set Enrichment Analysis (GSEA), we found that, in both examples, SomaModules had significantly higher enrichment than the original gene set counterparts. These findings were robust and not significantly affected by the choice of enrichment metric or the Kolmogorov enrichment statistic used in the GSEA procedure. Significance: We generated SomaScan-specific public repositories to be utilized by any unstructured pathway enrichment analysis tool. Our framework can be leveraged to analyze SomaModules derived from other sources, including custom, user-generated gene sets, and extended to data from other proteomics platforms, such as Olink and targeted mass spectrometry, and even other omics assays beyond proteomics.

title: Keynote Lecture: AI and ontologies: The beginning of a beautiful friendship
authors: Maryann Martone
abstract: The field of ontology, like almost every other field of human endeavor, is heavily impacted by the AI revolution. Those of us who spend time constructing them are often asked whether they are necessary now that large language models and other tools are able to reason over unstructured text and extract key concepts and their relationships. If an LLM can apparently "understand" that a hippocampal neuron and a CA1 pyramidal cell are related without consulting the Cell Ontology, why are these painstakingly curated knowledge structures necessary? The answer is that ontologies and AI are not substitutes — they are increasingly complementary and mutually reinforcing — but the nature of ontologies' value is shifting. In this presentation, I will argue that human-curated ontologies serve an irreplaceable function as stable anchors in a constantly shifting knowledge landscape. I will illustrate this complementarity and mutual reinforcement through our work over the past few decades to build ontologies and other knowledge structures for biomedicine. I will provide lessons learned in our efforts to construct and maintain effective ontologies for neuroscience, a challenging domain where key entities like brain anatomy and cell types still lack consensus. I will discuss some of our approaches and infrastructure for building multiscale connectivity and cell type knowledge bases to accommodate rapidly advancing knowledge by using a sociology of science framework to propose when and how a concept deserves stable representation. I will also make the case that AI is the “killer technology” that allows us not only to realize our long-standing goal of building comprehensive and complete knowledge artifacts at scale, but to deliver the tools required to exploit them to domain experts.

title: Distributing standardized annotations of public transcriptomics samples and studies with MetaHQ and Meta2Onto
authors: Parker Hicks, Christopher Mancuso, Lydia Valtadoros, Faisal Alquaddoomi, Vincent Rubinetti, Kayla Johnson, Sneha Sundar, Arjun Krishnan, Sean Davis
abstract: Today, there are millions of samples from hundreds of thousands of studies in publicly available repositories like the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) [1] and the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) [2]. These data are an invaluable resource to reuse to investigate novel biomedical questions. However, a key barrier to reusing these data is the poor quality of their metadata. Almost all public metadata are in the form of unstructured plain text using varied terminologies and including extraneous pieces of information. To overcome this barrier, many research groups have independently manually curated annotation sets for public samples and studies, linking them to terms in controlled vocabularies. However, these resources are scattered across online resources in web servers, GitHub repositories, data sharing resources like Zenodo, or supplemental files in publications. Additionally, these resources store annotations in various formats and use a diverse set of controlled vocabularies. To combine annotations across these resources to use at-scale would require an incredible amount of work to harmonize all of the annotation schemas. To that end, we built MetaHQ, a platform to harmonize and distribute standardized tissue, disease, sex, and age annotations for over 188,000 transcriptomics samples and 11,000 studies queryable through a command line interface (CLI) [3] (Figure 1). MetaHQ contains a collection of annotations harmonized across 13 independent sources harmonized into a single database with a standardized annotation schema. Users can use our CLI to seamlessly query the database and retrieve annotations for samples or studies, filter for technology, species, and annotation quality, and select to retrieve either annotations or labels. While ‘annotations’ state what a sample is, ‘labels’ declare what a sample is, what it definitely is not, and what is unknown. These labels explicitly define nuances in MetaHQ annotations in formats ready for machine learning (ML) classification. Lastly, we include references to the original sources of all annotations in all MetaHQ outputs, along with additional documentation and guidance, to enable users to cite the original sources if they use annotations in MetaHQ. Figure 1. (A) The MetaHQ harmonization and standardization process. (B) The number of annotations in MetaHQ across attributes and the number of unique tissue and disease terms represented. (C) The MetaHQ CLI pipeline. MetaHQ is, to our knowledge, the largest collection of standardized tissue, disease, sex, and age annotations. Yet, there are still millions of samples and hundreds of thousands of studies left without standardized annotations. With the exponential growth of public databases like GEO and SRA, manually annotating the remaining samples and studies is, realistically, an impossible feat. Therefore, scalable natural language processing (NLP) methods are essential for inferring standardized annotations of samples and studies directly from their unstructured plain text metadata records. Numerous NLP approaches have been developed to extract contextual information from biomedical texts [4–7]. However, none of these approaches offer all four of the following qualities: interpretability, scalability, predictions to standardized terms, and generalizability. Each method has its strengths with regards to one or two of these qualities, however none possess all. For these reasons, we developed an interpretable, generalizable, and lightweight text-based ML approach, txt2onto [8], to predict standardized tissue, cell type, and disease annotations from biomedical metadata. To maximize the accessibility of our text-based predictions, we developed Meta2Onto, a web server to search for standardized annotations for hundreds of thousands of studies in GEO. Meta2Onto currently stores our predicted tissue and disease annotations for over 270,000 GEO studies (Figure 2). Users can filter results for various study attributes such as technology, platform, study sample size, and annotation confidence. Users can also filter by whether the data from the study is available in large, ready-to-use public expression compendia [9–11]. Transparency and interpretability are at the core of Meta2Onto. Our predictions are highly interpretable where words/phrases that contributed to each prediction are highlighted for each retrieved study. To maximize transparency, we enable users to calibrate their trust based on the performance of our text-based models for the user’s tissue or disease of interest, which we show prominently. Also displayed for each retrieved study is the confidence our model has for that particular annotation. Lastly, we leverage the facts that users can easily read a metadata record and the words/phrases therein that contributed to the prediction to provide prediction-level feedback functionalities. Using these functionalities, researchers can provide high-level and detailed feedback on various attributes of prediction quality for individual studies. Together, MetaHQ and Meta2Onto offer both manually-curated and text-predicted standardized annotations, respectively. Through these resources, we strive to increase the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of public omics data to drive novel biomedical hypothesis generation and discovery at-scale. title: KGXVal: Open-source quality control and curation support for biomedical knowledge graph harmonization.
authors: Daniel Korn, Matthew Brush, Kevin Schaper, Melissa Haendel
abstract: The Knowledge Graph Exchange (KGX) data standard eases harmonization of biomedical data in the creation of knowledge graphs across diverse research domains (e.g. pharmacology, genomics, and proteomics). Existing data sources can be mapped onto the KGX specification and normalized against shared ontologies, supporting interoperable, multi-domain knowledge graphs. However, these conversion and normalization pipelines are imperfect: data sources may carry incorrect annotations, normalization can introduce errors when mapping between ontologies, and the KGX standard itself may lack the flexibility to cleanly represent all biomedical modalities. Manual review of KGX files for such inconsistencies has historically required specialized tooling and considerable expert effort. We present KGXVal, a Python tool that automates this validation step and surfaces errors directly to human curators. KGXVal accepts KGX-formatted files as input and produces three categories of output: (1) summary statistics on the frequency and distribution of unique metalabel combinations, (2) stratified samples across each combination type for targeted review, and (3) a complete enumeration of KGX model violations detected before and after normalization. All outputs are written as XLSX and CSV files, enabling immediate inspection in standard spreadsheet applications without additional tooling. In an initial analysis of 26 data sources harmonized to KGX format, KGXVal identified over 3100 instances of KGX schema errors, demonstrating the scale of quality issues that previously went undetected. KGXVal benefits from an ecosystem of existing open-source tools for working with KGX and biomedical data and is released under the BSD-3-Clause license and is available at https://github.com/monarch-initiative/kgxval.

title: KG-Registry: the open registry of knowledge graphs and their provenance
authors: J. Harry Caufield, Michael Gargano, Justin Reese, Melissa Haendel, Chris Mungall
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) serve a unique and fundamental function in biological and biomedical research: they represent varied types of entities and relationships in flexible but consistent ways. Data stored in KGs supports integration, hypothesis generation, and translational analysis, but realizing the full value of these graphs remains challenging to even the most experienced investigators. The KG-Registry is an open source, openly licensed registry designed to address these difficulties. This resource contains metadata for more than 760 data sources, including 135 knowledge graphs and more than 4,800 of their associated products. Each entry is defined in plain Markdown with human-readable YAML front matter, so the framework easily supports any combination of manual or agentic AI-driven curation. Each entry captures metadata about each data source or product as well as how it is distributed, transformed, accessed, and related to others. Product-level provenance fields, together with metadata on licenses, repositories, activity status, domains, contacts, and standards compatibility, support practical reuse and comparison. The schema is defined using the LinkML modeling language, so it is integrated with tools in the LinkML ecosystem for validation and adaptation to a multitude of use cases. The KG-Registry supports discovery, interoperability analysis, and hybrid human/automated curation of graphs of biological data.

title: Scalable Representation of Categorical Genomic Variation Using Cat-VRS
authors: Daniel Puthawala, Brendan Reardon, James Stevenson, Kori Kuzma
abstract: Accurate representation of genomic variation is essential for integrating knowledge across precision medicine resources. While existing standards effectively describe individual sequence variants, many clinically relevant concepts refer to categories of variants defined by shared functional or structural properties, such as activating mutations or gene fusions. These categorical variants are widely used but remain difficult to represent, compare, and search computationally. The Categorical Variant Representation Specification (Cat-VRS), developed by the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH), addresses this challenge using a constraint-based model in which variant categories are defined by modular, composable properties. This approach enables flexible yet computable representations that support automated matching across genomic knowledge systems. Following the Cat-VRS v1.0 release, early adoption identified the need to represent additional classes of variation commonly encountered in clinical genomics, including functional variants, genomic rearrangements, and gene fusions. We introduce new constraint types and modeling patterns, including Function and Adjacency constraints, that extend the expressive scope of the framework while preserving its formal structure and computational properties. We demonstrate the practical impact of these extensions through implementations in resources including VICC MetaKB and CIViC. These systems integrate Cat-VRS representations across heterogeneous data architectures, including graph, relational, and flat-file databases. These results provide evidence that the Cat-VRS constraint model can be extended to support diverse categories of genomic variation while remaining interoperable with existing systems, supporting scalable and computable genomic knowledge exchange.

title: Curating Gene Symbol Relationships for the Resolution of Gene Symbol Ambiguity
authors: Anastasia Bratulin, James S. Stevenson, Kori Kuzma, Wesley Goar, Matthew Cannon, Alex Wagner
abstract: Although gene symbols are used ubiquitously, community guidelines on their use in the literature and genomic data resources are not commonly followed or enforced. As a result, it is often necessary to disambiguate gene symbols when linking knowledge in genomic research and clinical applications. A common source of ambiguity is when a single gene symbol represents multiple genes, known as a gene alias collision. For example, the symbol “BCR" is, the primary gene symbol for one gene but also the alias symbol of another, RN7SL263P. These are distinct genes with BCR being implicated in two gene fusion events with clinical significance in cancer while RN7SL263P lacks functional characterization in literature. Such ambiguity limits the effectiveness of data aggregation and linking tools. In Ensembl, 3,784 (7.8%) records share an alias with another gene, compared to 2,482 (5.6%) in HGNC and 5,964 (13.4%) in NCBI Gene. Additionally, 767 (1.6%) Ensembl records share a primary gene symbol as an alias with another gene, along with 546 (1.2%) in HGNC and 1,613 (3.6%) in NCBI Gene. To address this, we developed Gene Harmony, a resource for resolving ambiguous gene symbols in biomedical literature and genomic knowledgebases. We curated relationships between gene symbols and gene concepts using manual, programmatic, and automated methods to assign relationship labels. This structured semantic data supports automated symbol disambiguation and lays the foundation for evidence-driven protocols to improve gene harmonization workflows in knowledge aggregation resources such as DGIdb and MetaKB.

title: FAIRSCAPE: Pre-model AI-Readiness and Interpretability for Biomedical Data
authors: Sadnan Al Manir, Maxwell Adam Levinson, Justin Niestroy, Christopher Churas, Nathan Sheffield, Brynne Sullivan, Karen Fairchild, Monica Munoz-Torres, Sarah Ratcliffe, Jilliian Parker, Trey Ideker, Timothy Clark
abstract: Post-model and in-model AI explainability methods have recently received enormous attention. Yet equally important are interpretability methods for complex, and frequently opaque, data preparation tasks in biomedical applications. These may include ethically sensitive decision making and analytic methods such as image segmentation, embedding generation, and multi-stage feature derivation. Pre-model pipelines cannot remain opaque if post-model results are to be trusted and reliable. The FAIRSCAPE AI-readiness framework addresses this problem by operationalizing and scoring 28 AI-readiness criteria developed by the NIH Bridge2AI Standards Working Group across seven categories: FAIRness, Provenance, Characterization, Pre-model Explainability, Ethics, Sustainability, and Computability. FAIRSCAPE packages data and metadata as Research Object Crates (RO-Crates), providing machine-readable metadata in schema.org and PROV/EVI vocabularies; component-resolvable provenance graphs; and an extended Gebru-style human readable datasheet; supplemented by LinkML and Croissant metadata translations. AI-readiness evaluations are provided as multi-factorial scores associated with data packages, enabling targeted identification of quality gaps across each AI-readiness category. The framework is production-deployed and cloud-native, and has been used to packaged multiple Bridge2AI releases. In recent additional work, FAIRSCAPE provenance graphs are resolved, and used for graph-RAG across the data, software, and model provenance components and metadata to produce a layered, audience-targeted interpretation with Likert-scoring of issues such as data leakage, and potential impact on results. Interpretations are stored as annotations in the provenance graph, and provided in severity-coded visualizations to the user. These features help enable the fine-scaled attention to rigor and reliability in pre-model data transformation required for critical decision making in biomedical research.
