title: A FAIR Framework for Structured Biomarker Representation, Discovery, and Hypothesis Generation
authors: Maria Kim, Jeet Vora, Cyrus Chun Hong Au Yeung, Raja Mazumder, Rene Ranzinger
abstract: Biomarker data is dispersed across data sources, impeding discovery and hypothesis generation. Moreover, existing biomedical knowledge graphs record biomarker associations, such as gene X relates to disease Y, but not the measurable change that defines a biomarker according to the NIH-FDA definition. This omission limits both machine reasoning and clinical interpretability. Here we present Biomarker Knowledge Graph, a comprehensive knowledge graph incorporating biomarker information from multiple sources, which represents each biomarker as a structured triple: a change type (e.g., increased), an entity (e.g., IL6), and an assessed aspect (e.g., level). It unifies fragmented biomarker data in a standardized data model and terminology (Biomarker Ontology). Additionally, Biomarker Knowledge Graph enables discovery and design in a complex, interconnected system of biomarkers, entities, diseases, exposure agents, specimens, terminology of health measurements, and publications, by allowing users to identify patterns, and shortest paths between entities. Finally, Biomarker Knowledge Graph allows the user to deduce new facts from existing relationships rather than just recalling stored data. A controlled vocabulary was developed to avoid duplication of biomarker data, and we used our standardized data as nodes and edges to construct the knowledge graph, thus enabling the data to be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). Thanks to Biomarker Knowledge Graph (https://github.com/clinical-biomarkers/ Knowledge-Graph), clinicians and researchers can identify biological patterns of biomarkers (freely available at data.biomarkerkb.org), their interconnections, and use this knowledge in clinical and research practices, and generate new hypotheses. Contributions of the open-source community could include visualization tools, e.g. neo4j implementations, and LLM-based CYPHER query construction.

title: The OBO Foundry in 2026: Building Sustainable Ontology Infrastructure for Interoperable Life Science Data
authors: James Balhoff, Hande McGinty, Sebastian Duesing, Nicolas Matentzoglu, James Stevenson, Christopher Mungall
abstract: The OBO Foundry is a community-driven initiative dedicated to the development, maintenance, and coordination of interoperable ontologies for the life sciences. Its mission is to support semantic consistency, rigorous knowledge representation, and data interoperability across biological and biomedical domains through shared principles, open infrastructure, and collaborative governance. By expanding and clarifying principles and governance procedures, incorporating new member ontologies, operationalizing standards compliance, developing and promoting tools and approaches for an engineering approach to ontology development, and fostering community participation and collaboration, the Foundry plays an outsized role in life sciences knowledge and data interoperability relative to its efficient use of resources. Persistent URLs, shared repository structures, lightweight web infrastructure, and community-maintained practices together provide the technical backbone that makes OBO ontologies discoverable, resolvable, and reusable. Widely adopted tools such as ROBOT and the Ontology Development Kit support release workflows, ontology quality control, automated checks, mapping workflows, and repository maintenance. In addition to these established tools, the OBO community is beginning to incorporate AI-assisted approaches into ontology curation and development workflows. As the number of ontologies and ontology-enabled applications continues to grow, the challenge is no longer simply to create ontologies, but to ensure that they are interoperable, well-maintained, technically sound, and sustainable over time. The Foundry addresses this challenge by combining clear principles, practical development technologies, community review, transparent validation, and shared infrastructure. These efforts position OBO as both a mature semantic resource and an evolving sociotechnical framework for life science knowledge representation.

title: In a genAI world, does structured knowledge still have a role in science?
authors: Karin Verspoor
abstract: The paradigm of generative AI, based on foundation models that have absorbed vast volumes of scientific knowledge captured in digital artefacts including publications, ontologies, and databases, threatens to disrupt disciplines such as bioinformatics which have traditionally relied on curated, structured knowledge. Models which rely on implicit knowledge representation through complex, data-driven mathematical models, and which reproduce knowledge through language, stand in stark contrast to carefully constructed, curated information captured through relational structures and formal semantics. This talk will explore the tensions this creates, and consider connections between these apparently opposing paradigms. I may raise more questions than I can answer, but isn’t that the point of science?

title: STAR-GO: Improving Protein Function Prediction by Learning to Hierarchically Integrate Ontology-Informed Semantic Embeddings
authors: Mehmet Efe Akça, Gökçe Uludoğan, Arzucan Ozgur, Inci Baytaş
abstract: Accurate prediction of protein function is essential for elucidating molecular mechanisms and advancing biological and therapeutic discovery. Yet experimental annotation lags far behind the rapid growth of protein sequence data. Computational approaches address this gap by associating proteins with Gene Ontology (GO) terms, which encode functional knowledge through hierarchical relations and textual definitions. However, existing models often emphasize one modality over the other, limiting their ability to generalize, particularly to unseen or newly introduced GO terms that frequently arise as the ontology evolves, and making the previously trained models outdated. We present STAR-GO, a Transformer-based framework that jointly models the semantic and structural characteristics of GO terms to enhance zero-shot protein function prediction. STAR-GO integrates textual definitions with ontology graph structure to learn unified GO representations, which are processed in hierarchical order to propagate information from general to specific terms. These representations are then aligned with protein sequence embeddings to capture sequence–function relationships. STAR-GO achieves state-of-the-art performance and superior zero-shot generalization, demonstrating the utility of integrating semantics and structure for robust and adaptable protein function prediction.

title: GIMME: Graph Inference for Microbial Metabolism Exploration using Knowledge Graphs
authors: Winston Anthony, Sam Donald, Sumit Purohit, Adam Deutschbauer, Kaizad Patel, Rob Egbert
abstract: Predicting gene fitness across environmental conditions remains a central challenge in predictive phenomics. High-throughput fitness assays generate large volumes of genotype–phenotype measurements that are difficult to integrate with experimental metadata and biological function in a form that supports mechanistic reasoning. A key obstacle is that the predictive signal is distributed across heterogeneous modalities, including free-text experiment descriptions, media composition, and structured biological annotations. We present GIMME (Graph Inference for Microbial Metabolism Exploration), a knowledge-graph-augmented framework for microbial gene fitness prediction that combines pretrained language representations of experimental metadata with relational message passing over a semantically grounded biological graph. In addition to model development, we implement GIMME as an interactive platform for natural-language querying, evidence retrieval, and graph-based exploration of microbial metabolism and gene fitness.

title: DGLink: automated knowledge graph construction from biomedical data repositories
authors: Woodward Galbraith, Benjamin Gyori
abstract: Numerous biomedical data repositories host vast collections of multi-modal experimental and clinical datasets. However, non-standardized formats and challenges in comprehensively traversing such repositories severely limit their utility at scale. We present DGLink, an automated system for constructing semantically grounded knowledge graphs (KGs) from biomedical data portals, enabling data discovery, reusability and knowledge-driven hypothesis generation. DGLink traverses a portal's studies and experimental files, extracting semantic annotations through named entity recognition and normalization against key biomedical ontologies (including HGNC, UniProt, ChEBI, MeSH, DOID, HP and EFO) using Gilda. Unlike existing approaches such as DUG, which annotate only study-level metadata, DGLink performs schema-free ingestion of both tabular and modality-specific experimental files (e.g. VCF, DICOM), substantially increasing annotation depth. To reduce false positives during tabular file annotation, DGLink implements three column selection strategies: rule-based filtering, LLM-based schema matching inspired by Magneto, and a hierarchical combination of both. The resulting KG conforms to the Biolink data model, ensuring semantic interoperability and reusability. The KG is further queryable via a Neo4j graph database, a structured semantic-search web interface or an LLM-based chat interface through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, enabling natural language data discovery and hypothesis generation. We demonstrate DGLink across three portals: the NF Data Portal, NCI General Commons, and NCI Genomic Data Commons, showing generalizability across portals with heterogeneous modalities, study scales and APIs. Across all three portals, DGLink achieves 96-100% tabular coverage. Per-column LLM schema matching achieves an F1 of 0.819, while Gilda achieves 96% grounding accuracy on manually evaluated annotations.

title: Transforming PubChem BioAssay Data into Linked Open Data through the Resource Description Framework (RDF) and Standard Ontologies
authors: Sunghwan Kim, Tiejun Cheng, Qingliang Li, Evan Bolton
abstract: The PubChem BioAssay collection is a critical resource for biological activity data in the public domain. However, its full potential is hindered by challenges in large-scale data integration and analysis. To address this, we have semantically annotated the bioactivity data in PubChem BioAssay using the Resource Description Framework (RDF) and a suite of standard ontologies, including the Basic Formal Ontology (BFO), Ontology for Biomedical Investigations (OBI), Information Artifact Ontology (IAO), BioAssay Ontology (BAO), Citation Typing Ontology (CiTO), Protein Ontology (PRO), and Gene Ontology (GO). By encoding bioactivity data in this machine-readable format, we have made it available as Linked Open Data. This enables researchers to perform sophisticated queries, grouping, and reasoning across chemical and biological domains that are not possible with traditional relational databases. The resulting RDF data set facilitates the discovery of previously hidden relationships between chemical structures and their biological activities, thereby enhancing data sharing, reuse, and interoperability across the life sciences.

title: ImmPort: A Foundational Data Repository Facilitating AI-Enabled Immunology Research
authors: Sanchita Bhattacharya, Catherine Hypes, Sammi Smith, Jayalakshmi Kannan, Matthew Strub, Parisa Pirani, Ruth Monteiro, Srinivas Chepuri, Emma Kendris, Steven H. Kleinstein
abstract: Introduction: Immunology research generates diverse molecular and clinical datasets spanning autoimmunity, infectious diseases, allergy, transplantation, vaccine response and beyond. Decades of accumulated data in generalist and domain-specific repositories present an unprecedented opportunity for machine learning and artificial intelligence (AI)-powered analyses of large-scale, multi-modal datasets, accelerating scientific discovery. Methods: ImmPort, the NIH-NIAID sponsored open-access immunology data portal, houses over 1,300 studies, 5,000 experiments, and over 7.5 million data points, supporting conventional and emerging technologies for capturing molecular and clinical datasets at subject level. To fully unlock this potential, ImmPort is advancing towards semi-automate repository data management, reformatting data for AI-readiness, and establishing integrated AI ecosystems that maximize the value of existing immunology data for reproducible research and discoveries. Results: AI-driven automation streamlines data curation and enhances metadata quality through intelligent extraction and validation. Standardized provenance frameworks, ontologies, machine-readable metadata, and Application Programming Interface (APIs) transform data into computationally accessible resources. ImmPort has developed methods for integrating Common Data Elements (CDEs) and piloted automated pipelines to facilitate systematic mapping for promoting Findability, Accessibility, Interoperability, and Reuse (FAIR) principles. ImmPort disseminates Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) formatted data and is piloting Data Mesh architecture using ImmPort as a domain-oriented, interoperable data node to enable AI-assisted biomedical discovery. Conclusion: The ImmPort AI ecosystem enables immunology-specific foundation models trained on multimodal data to capture immune system dynamics, transforming repositories into AI-enabled platforms that accelerate biomarker discovery and advance personalized, translational research.

title: Sage Brain: An AI-Powered Cross-Disease Knowledge Graph Connecting Neurodegenerative Research Communities
authors: Susheel Varma, Milan Vu, Jessica Malenfant, Thomas Yu, Orion Banks
abstract: Neurodegenerative disease research remains fragmented across disease-specific data portals. Despite significant overlap in molecular pathways between Alzheimer's Disease (AD), Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS), Frontotemporal Dementia (FTD), and Parkinson's Disease (PD), researchers lack computational tools to query across disease boundaries. Cross-disease investigations, such as identifying shared neuroinflammatory mechanisms across AD and ALS cohorts, currently require months of manual data harmonisation. We present Sage Brain, an open knowledge graph platform that aims to connect 16 biomedical research portals encompassing over 3.9 petabytes of genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, and clinical data. The platform employs a five-stage fan-in/fan-out architecture: heterogeneous data sources are harmonised through a common data model with ontology alignment, ingested into a graph database, and exposed through an AI layer supporting natural language queries, cross-disease pattern detection, and automated hypothesis generation. A structured ""Hypothesis Games"" framework guides researchers through iterative cross-disease mechanism discovery grounded in existing cohort data. Initial subgraphs targeting shared AD-ALS biology are under construction, with ontology harmonisation leveraging SysBio FAIRplex mappings across Accelerating Medicines Partnership programmes. The platform will support SPARQL, Gremlin, and natural language query interfaces accommodating diverse researcher expertise. Sage Brain represents the first community-governed knowledge graph infrastructure designed for cross-disease neurodegenerative research. By bridging siloed communities through standardised ontologies and AI-assisted querying, the platform will enable a new class of investigations, accelerating identification of shared therapeutic targets, biomarkers, and drug repurposing candidates across disease boundaries.

title: Distributing standardized annotations of public transcriptomics samples and studies with MetaHQ and Meta2Onto
authors: Parker Hicks, Christopher Mancuso, Lydia Valtadoros, Faisal Alquaddoomi, Vincent Rubinetti, Kayla Johnson, Sneha Sundar, Arjun Krishnan, Sean Davis
abstract: Today, there are millions of samples from hundreds of thousands of studies in publicly available repositories like the Gene Expression Omnibus (GEO) [1] and the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) [2]. These data are an invaluable resource to reuse to investigate novel biomedical questions. However, a key barrier to reusing these data is the poor quality of their metadata. Almost all public metadata are in the form of unstructured plain text using varied terminologies and including extraneous pieces of information. To overcome this barrier, many research groups have independently manually curated annotation sets for public samples and studies, linking them to terms in controlled vocabularies. However, these resources are scattered across online resources in web servers, GitHub repositories, data sharing resources like Zenodo, or supplemental files in publications. Additionally, these resources store annotations in various formats and use a diverse set of controlled vocabularies. To combine annotations across these resources to use at-scale would require an incredible amount of work to harmonize all of the annotation schemas. To that end, we built MetaHQ, a platform to harmonize and distribute standardized tissue, disease, sex, and age annotations for over 188,000 transcriptomics samples and 11,000 studies queryable through a command line interface (CLI) [3] (Figure 1). MetaHQ contains a collection of annotations harmonized across 13 independent sources harmonized into a single database with a standardized annotation schema. Users can use our CLI to seamlessly query the database and retrieve annotations for samples or studies, filter for technology, species, and annotation quality, and select to retrieve either annotations or labels. While ‘annotations’ state what a sample is, ‘labels’ declare what a sample is, what it definitely is not, and what is unknown. These labels explicitly define nuances in MetaHQ annotations in formats ready for machine learning (ML) classification. Lastly, we include references to the original sources of all annotations in all MetaHQ outputs, along with additional documentation and guidance, to enable users to cite the original sources if they use annotations in MetaHQ. Figure 1. (A) The MetaHQ harmonization and standardization process. (B) The number of annotations in MetaHQ across attributes and the number of unique tissue and disease terms represented. (C) The MetaHQ CLI pipeline. MetaHQ is, to our knowledge, the largest collection of standardized tissue, disease, sex, and age annotations. Yet, there are still millions of samples and hundreds of thousands of studies left without standardized annotations. With the exponential growth of public databases like GEO and SRA, manually annotating the remaining samples and studies is, realistically, an impossible feat. Therefore, scalable natural language processing (NLP) methods are essential for inferring standardized annotations of samples and studies directly from their unstructured plain text metadata records. Numerous NLP approaches have been developed to extract contextual information from biomedical texts [4–7]. However, none of these approaches offer all four of the following qualities: interpretability, scalability, predictions to standardized terms, and generalizability. Each method has its strengths with regards to one or two of these qualities, however none possess all. For these reasons, we developed an interpretable, generalizable, and lightweight text-based ML approach, txt2onto [8], to predict standardized tissue, cell type, and disease annotations from biomedical metadata. To maximize the accessibility of our text-based predictions, we developed Meta2Onto, a web server to search for standardized annotations for hundreds of thousands of studies in GEO. Meta2Onto currently stores our predicted tissue and disease annotations for over 270,000 GEO studies (Figure 2). Users can filter results for various study attributes such as technology, platform, study sample size, and annotation confidence. Users can also filter by whether the data from the study is available in large, ready-to-use public expression compendia [9–11]. Transparency and interpretability are at the core of Meta2Onto. Our predictions are highly interpretable where words/phrases that contributed to each prediction are highlighted for each retrieved study. To maximize transparency, we enable users to calibrate their trust based on the performance of our text-based models for the user’s tissue or disease of interest, which we show prominently. Also displayed for each retrieved study is the confidence our model has for that particular annotation. Lastly, we leverage the facts that users can easily read a metadata record and the words/phrases therein that contributed to the prediction to provide prediction-level feedback functionalities. Using these functionalities, researchers can provide high-level and detailed feedback on various attributes of prediction quality for individual studies. Together, MetaHQ and Meta2Onto offer both manually-curated and text-predicted standardized annotations, respectively. Through these resources, we strive to increase the findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability of public omics data to drive novel biomedical hypothesis generation and discovery at-scale. title: KGXVal: Open-source quality control and curation support for biomedical knowledge graph harmonization.
authors: Daniel Korn, Matthew Brush, Kevin Schaper, Melissa Haendel
abstract: The Knowledge Graph Exchange (KGX) data standard eases harmonization of biomedical data in the creation of knowledge graphs across diverse research domains (e.g. pharmacology, genomics, and proteomics). Existing data sources can be mapped onto the KGX specification and normalized against shared ontologies, supporting interoperable, multi-domain knowledge graphs. However, these conversion and normalization pipelines are imperfect: data sources may carry incorrect annotations, normalization can introduce errors when mapping between ontologies, and the KGX standard itself may lack the flexibility to cleanly represent all biomedical modalities. Manual review of KGX files for such inconsistencies has historically required specialized tooling and considerable expert effort. We present KGXVal, a Python tool that automates this validation step and surfaces errors directly to human curators. KGXVal accepts KGX-formatted files as input and produces three categories of output: (1) summary statistics on the frequency and distribution of unique metalabel combinations, (2) stratified samples across each combination type for targeted review, and (3) a complete enumeration of KGX model violations detected before and after normalization. All outputs are written as XLSX and CSV files, enabling immediate inspection in standard spreadsheet applications without additional tooling. In an initial analysis of 26 data sources harmonized to KGX format, KGXVal identified over 3100 instances of KGX schema errors, demonstrating the scale of quality issues that previously went undetected. KGXVal benefits from an ecosystem of existing open-source tools for working with KGX and biomedical data and is released under the BSD-3-Clause license and is available at https://github.com/monarch-initiative/kgxval.

title: KG-Registry: the open registry of knowledge graphs and their provenance
authors: J. Harry Caufield, Michael Gargano, Justin Reese, Melissa Haendel, Chris Mungall
abstract: Knowledge graphs (KGs) serve a unique and fundamental function in biological and biomedical research: they represent varied types of entities and relationships in flexible but consistent ways. Data stored in KGs supports integration, hypothesis generation, and translational analysis, but realizing the full value of these graphs remains challenging to even the most experienced investigators. The KG-Registry is an open source, openly licensed registry designed to address these difficulties. This resource contains metadata for more than 760 data sources, including 135 knowledge graphs and more than 4,800 of their associated products. Each entry is defined in plain Markdown with human-readable YAML front matter, so the framework easily supports any combination of manual or agentic AI-driven curation. Each entry captures metadata about each data source or product as well as how it is distributed, transformed, accessed, and related to others. Product-level provenance fields, together with metadata on licenses, repositories, activity status, domains, contacts, and standards compatibility, support practical reuse and comparison. The schema is defined using the LinkML modeling language, so it is integrated with tools in the LinkML ecosystem for validation and adaptation to a multitude of use cases. The KG-Registry supports discovery, interoperability analysis, and hybrid human/automated curation of graphs of biological data.

title: Scalable Representation of Categorical Genomic Variation Using Cat-VRS
authors: Daniel Puthawala, Brendan Reardon, James Stevenson, Kori Kuzma
abstract: Accurate representation of genomic variation is essential for integrating knowledge across precision medicine resources. While existing standards effectively describe individual sequence variants, many clinically relevant concepts refer to categories of variants defined by shared functional or structural properties, such as activating mutations or gene fusions. These categorical variants are widely used but remain difficult to represent, compare, and search computationally. The Categorical Variant Representation Specification (Cat-VRS), developed by the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH), addresses this challenge using a constraint-based model in which variant categories are defined by modular, composable properties. This approach enables flexible yet computable representations that support automated matching across genomic knowledge systems. Following the Cat-VRS v1.0 release, early adoption identified the need to represent additional classes of variation commonly encountered in clinical genomics, including functional variants, genomic rearrangements, and gene fusions. We introduce new constraint types and modeling patterns, including Function and Adjacency constraints, that extend the expressive scope of the framework while preserving its formal structure and computational properties. We demonstrate the practical impact of these extensions through implementations in resources including VICC MetaKB and CIViC. These systems integrate Cat-VRS representations across heterogeneous data architectures, including graph, relational, and flat-file databases. These results provide evidence that the Cat-VRS constraint model can be extended to support diverse categories of genomic variation while remaining interoperable with existing systems, supporting scalable and computable genomic knowledge exchange.

title: A FAIR Framework for Structured Biomarker Representation, Discovery, and Hypothesis Generation
authors: Maria Kim, Jeet Vora, Cyrus Chun Hong Au Yeung, Raja Mazumder, Rene Ranzinger
abstract: Biomarker data is dispersed across data sources, impeding discovery and hypothesis generation. Moreover, existing biomedical knowledge graphs record biomarker associations, such as gene X relates to disease Y, but not the measurable change that defines a biomarker according to the NIH-FDA definition. This omission limits both machine reasoning and clinical interpretability. Here we present Biomarker Knowledge Graph, a comprehensive knowledge graph incorporating biomarker information from multiple sources, which represents each biomarker as a structured triple: a change type (e.g., increased), an entity (e.g., IL6), and an assessed aspect (e.g., level). It unifies fragmented biomarker data in a standardized data model and terminology (Biomarker Ontology). Additionally, Biomarker Knowledge Graph enables discovery and design in a complex, interconnected system of biomarkers, entities, diseases, exposure agents, specimens, terminology of health measurements, and publications, by allowing users to identify patterns, and shortest paths between entities. Finally, Biomarker Knowledge Graph allows the user to deduce new facts from existing relationships rather than just recalling stored data. A controlled vocabulary was developed to avoid duplication of biomarker data, and we used our standardized data as nodes and edges to construct the knowledge graph, thus enabling the data to be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). Thanks to Biomarker Knowledge Graph (https://github.com/clinical-biomarkers/ Knowledge-Graph), clinicians and researchers can identify biological patterns of biomarkers (freely available at data.biomarkerkb.org), their interconnections, and use this knowledge in clinical and research practices, and generate new hypotheses. Contributions of the open-source community could include visualization tools, e.g. neo4j implementations, and LLM-based CYPHER query construction.

title: Curating Gene Symbol Relationships for the Resolution of Gene Symbol Ambiguity
authors: Anastasia Bratulin, James S. Stevenson, Kori Kuzma, Wesley Goar, Matthew Cannon, Alex Wagner
abstract: Although gene symbols are used ubiquitously, community guidelines on their use in the literature and genomic data resources are not commonly followed or enforced. As a result, it is often necessary to disambiguate gene symbols when linking knowledge in genomic research and clinical applications. A common source of ambiguity is when a single gene symbol represents multiple genes, known as a gene alias collision. For example, the symbol “BCR" is, the primary gene symbol for one gene but also the alias symbol of another, RN7SL263P. These are distinct genes with BCR being implicated in two gene fusion events with clinical significance in cancer while RN7SL263P lacks functional characterization in literature. Such ambiguity limits the effectiveness of data aggregation and linking tools. In Ensembl, 3,784 (7.8%) records share an alias with another gene, compared to 2,482 (5.6%) in HGNC and 5,964 (13.4%) in NCBI Gene. Additionally, 767 (1.6%) Ensembl records share a primary gene symbol as an alias with another gene, along with 546 (1.2%) in HGNC and 1,613 (3.6%) in NCBI Gene. To address this, we developed Gene Harmony, a resource for resolving ambiguous gene symbols in biomedical literature and genomic knowledgebases. We curated relationships between gene symbols and gene concepts using manual, programmatic, and automated methods to assign relationship labels. This structured semantic data supports automated symbol disambiguation and lays the foundation for evidence-driven protocols to improve gene harmonization workflows in knowledge aggregation resources such as DGIdb and MetaKB.

title: FAIRSCAPE: Pre-model AI-Readiness and Interpretability for Biomedical Data
authors: Sadnan Al Manir, Maxwell Adam Levinson, Justin Niestroy, Christopher Churas, Nathan Sheffield, Brynne Sullivan, Karen Fairchild, Monica Munoz-Torres, Sarah Ratcliffe, Jilliian Parker, Trey Ideker, Timothy Clark
abstract: Post-model and in-model AI explainability methods have recently received enormous attention. Yet equally important are interpretability methods for complex, and frequently opaque, data preparation tasks in biomedical applications. These may include ethically sensitive decision making and analytic methods such as image segmentation, embedding generation, and multi-stage feature derivation. Pre-model pipelines cannot remain opaque if post-model results are to be trusted and reliable. The FAIRSCAPE AI-readiness framework addresses this problem by operationalizing and scoring 28 AI-readiness criteria developed by the NIH Bridge2AI Standards Working Group across seven categories: FAIRness, Provenance, Characterization, Pre-model Explainability, Ethics, Sustainability, and Computability. FAIRSCAPE packages data and metadata as Research Object Crates (RO-Crates), providing machine-readable metadata in schema.org and PROV/EVI vocabularies; component-resolvable provenance graphs; and an extended Gebru-style human readable datasheet; supplemented by LinkML and Croissant metadata translations. AI-readiness evaluations are provided as multi-factorial scores associated with data packages, enabling targeted identification of quality gaps across each AI-readiness category. The framework is production-deployed and cloud-native, and has been used to packaged multiple Bridge2AI releases. In recent additional work, FAIRSCAPE provenance graphs are resolved, and used for graph-RAG across the data, software, and model provenance components and metadata to produce a layered, audience-targeted interpretation with Likert-scoring of issues such as data leakage, and potential impact on results. Interpretations are stored as annotations in the provenance graph, and provided in severity-coded visualizations to the user. These features help enable the fine-scaled attention to rigor and reliability in pre-model data transformation required for critical decision making in biomedical research.

title: The OBO Foundry in 2026: Building Sustainable Ontology Infrastructure for Interoperable Life Science Data
authors: James Balhoff, Hande McGinty, Sebastian Duesing, Nicolas Matentzoglu, James Stevenson, Christopher Mungall
abstract: The OBO Foundry is a community-driven initiative dedicated to the development, maintenance, and coordination of interoperable ontologies for the life sciences. Its mission is to support semantic consistency, rigorous knowledge representation, and data interoperability across biological and biomedical domains through shared principles, open infrastructure, and collaborative governance. By expanding and clarifying principles and governance procedures, incorporating new member ontologies, operationalizing standards compliance, developing and promoting tools and approaches for an engineering approach to ontology development, and fostering community participation and collaboration, the Foundry plays an outsized role in life sciences knowledge and data interoperability relative to its efficient use of resources. Persistent URLs, shared repository structures, lightweight web infrastructure, and community-maintained practices together provide the technical backbone that makes OBO ontologies discoverable, resolvable, and reusable. Widely adopted tools such as ROBOT and the Ontology Development Kit support release workflows, ontology quality control, automated checks, mapping workflows, and repository maintenance. In addition to these established tools, the OBO community is beginning to incorporate AI-assisted approaches into ontology curation and development workflows. As the number of ontologies and ontology-enabled applications continues to grow, the challenge is no longer simply to create ontologies, but to ensure that they are interoperable, well-maintained, technically sound, and sustainable over time. The Foundry addresses this challenge by combining clear principles, practical development technologies, community review, transparent validation, and shared infrastructure. These efforts position OBO as both a mature semantic resource and an evolving sociotechnical framework for life science knowledge representation.

title: Science for the People: Open science to engage and build trust with communities
authors: Maryam Zaringhalam
abstract: The open science movement positions scientific knowledge as a global public good — yet in practice, open science is often not designed with public participation in mind. Policy efforts, including landmark federal public access policies to expand access to research, have largely focused on lowering barriers to accessing scholarly literature, datasets, and code. But access alone does not guarantee that research can meet communities where they are and address their most pressing needs. This gap has real consequences. The research community is increasingly discussing the erosion of public trust in science without fully reckoning with the gap between the research we produce and whether it actually reaches or serves the broader public. Simply put, we can do more to include and engage the communities with whom we seek to build trust. Open science, intentionally practiced, is a way to do that. Drawing on her experience spanning federal open science policy, biomedical research, and science communication, Dr. Zaringhalam will argue that open science represents an underutilized opportunity to rebuild that trust. By layering science communication and community engagement onto open research outputs, researchers, institutions, and practitioners can create genuine on-ramps for diverse publics — connecting the products and process of science to the communities who stand to benefit from them. This talk will explore practical approaches to bridging open science and community engagement, centering the needs of communities as a starting point for more meaningful and trustworthy science. Biography Maryam Zaringhalam, Ph.D., is the Senior Director of Policy at the Center for Open Science (COS). In that position, she leads COS’s policy efforts to increase openness, integrity, and trustworthiness of research. Prior to joining COS, Maryam served as the Data Science and Open Science Officer at the National Library of Medicine (NLM) at the National Institutes of Health (NIH), working to enhance capacity in the biomedical research community for data science and open science. From 2022 to 2024, she also served as the Assistant Director for Public Access and Research Policy at the White House Office of Science and Technology Policy (OSTP) where she oversaw federal policy development around public access, open science, and scientific integrity. Maryam is also a Senior Producer for the Story Collider, where she co-hosts the science policy podcast Science Soapbox, bringing true, personal stories of science to live audiences in Washington, DC. She received her PhD in Molecular Biology from the Rockefeller University.

title: Designing CWL‑Based Medallion Pipelines: A Spatial Aggregation Case Study for Climate and Air‑Pollution Exposures
authors: Michael Bouzinier, Dmitry Etin
abstract: Population health research frequently requires integrating tabular data keyed by administrative units with gridded environmental variables defined on regular rasters. The geospatial steps involved, such as overlay, aggregation, and missing-data handling, are typically implemented with bespoke GIS scripts that are difficult to reproduce, audit, or incorporate into automated pipelines. We present a design approach in which Common Workflow Language (CWL) is augmented with a declarative YAML data model and a small set of helper utilities to support medallion-style data pipelines that are reproducible, portable across CWL runners, and accessible to data engineering teams without GIS expertise. Our design follows five principles: characterize source formats; define consumer-facing outputs organized as Bronze/Silver/Gold medallion layers; express transformation logic declaratively, independently of CWL; use CWL strictly for DAG topology; and auto-generate provenance documentation and lineage diagrams from the same sources used to execute the pipeline. We illustrate this approach with a spatial aggregation pipeline that maps daily climate variables on a ~4 km grid and monthly PM2.5 estimates on a ~1 km grid to U.S. counties and ZCTAs. We evaluate three rasterization strategies (center-point, all-touched, and downscaled) and show that the default center-point strategy leaves 12.5% of ZCTAs without climate data, while alternative strategies eliminate this extrinsic missingness with negligible accuracy loss (Pearson r ≥ 0.998). Built-in monitoring utilities help users calibrate coverage-accuracy-cost trade-offs for their infrastructure. All utilities, the pipeline and pre-computed datasets are part of the open"‘source Dorieh Data Platform and are available under the Apache 2.0 license.

title: WILDS WDL Library: Modular Bioinformatics Workflow Components for Researchers and Developers
authors: Taylor Firman, Emma Bishop
abstract: Reproducibility and scalability are challenges for many bioinformatics analyses. Workflow languages, such as Nextflow and Workflow Description Language (WDL), address this by defining analyses as portable, version-controlled scripts paired with containerized environments. Our team at Fred Hutch Cancer Center has adopted WDL for its readability and approachable learning curve. However, the upfront investment of writing workflows from scratch remains a significant barrier for many bench researchers. To lower this barrier, we developed the WILDS WDL Library, a rigorously tested, well-documented collection of modular WDL scripts. The scripts are organized into two tiers: modules, that wrap popular commands for over 50 bioinformatics tools into reusable tasks, and pipelines, which use the tasks in end-to-end workflows. Modules can be imported via their GitHub URLs and combined in numerous ways. With developmental guardrails in place, we have begun exploring the use of large language models to assist with prototyping new modules, with all generated code undergoing thorough review and validation by human researchers. At Fred Hutch, this library has encouraged workflow adoption by researchers and in some cases reduced computational wait times from weeks to hours. Since releasing the library in January, we have had contributions from fourteen researchers across nine labs and been cited in a manuscript. We have built this community through an introductory workshop and a workflow development program. The WILDS WDL Library serves as a resource for the distributed development of WDL workflows and as an example of how to build an open source community among biologists from scratch.

title: Raw Counts to Trusted References: A Reproducible QC Workflow Supporting the NLM Cell Knowledge Bases
authors: Anne Deslattes Mays, Richard Scheuermann, Yun Zhang, Bingfang Xu, Matthew Diller, Ajith Viswanathan Asari, Raymond Leclair, William Spear, Arvind Kumar, Latoya McDonald, Beverly Peng, Daniel Pintard
abstract: Downstream analyses of single-cell RNA sequencing studies benefit from rigorous quality assessment, yet standardized, reproducible workflows for this purpose remain underutilized. We present best practices for assembling bioinformatics packages into production-grade Nextflow workflows, demonstrated through the sc-nsforest-qc-nf pipeline. This workflow integrates a newly developed scsilhouette Python package with the containerized NSForest marker discovery machine learning package, combining them for systematic single-cell dataset quality assessment. The workflow produces 50 artifacts including an interactive HTML visualization combining per-cluster silhouette scores, displayed as box-and-whisker plots, with NSForest F-scores for the same clusters used for dataset quality assessment. Median-of-medians statistics for both metrics guide assessment, with high-quality datasets expected to show the majority of clusters above zero for both measures. Environment control is managed via Conda; packages are containerized with Docker, with Apptainer images readily generated for HPC environments. Continuous integration via GitHub Actions automates Docker image publication and keeps documentation synchronized with the codebase. Sphinx-based documentation, integrated with HTML and SVG outputs from both packages, is deployed on GitHub Pages, enabling researcher review and feedback. The pipeline was validated on 84 published single-cell datasets across 10 tissues from CellxGene, and forked for application to a non-CellxGene endometriosis dataset from the Jackson Laboratory, supporting a Springer-Verlag volume forthcoming in 2026. Agentic AI (Claude Code) was employed as a collaborative tool during software development. These datasets inform reference dataset selection for the NLM Cell Knowledge Base. This work illustrates best practices in reproducibility, provenance, containerization, and reusability for single-cell bioinformatics. All software is open source and publicly available.

title: Where did the algorithms go?
authors: Zebulun Arendsee
abstract: Bioinformatics has a software engineering problem. The current paradigm for writing pipelines is based on monolithic applications communicating through files. This forces every tool to handle parsing, validation, iteration, parallelization, and formatting. File formats constrain data and obscure the elegant data structures that are the true inputs to algorithms. The core algorithm, the thing we really care about, is buried in boring code that we must reimplement in every tool. Workflow managers further bury the algorithm under more layers of wrappers. We present Morloc as a foundation for an alternative paradigm where functions and data structures replace applications and files. Morloc allows researchers to write algorithms in their preferred language and compose them across language boundaries. The Morloc compiler generates interprocess communication code and CLI/API interfaces. Source functions are idiomatic with no Morloc dependencies or special syntax. With Morloc, a short read trimmer is a single function whose input is one sequence and its quality scores (not a FASTQ file) that is passed as an argument to a generic mapping function. Our benchmarks show that cross-language communication is near the UNIX domain socket floor and within-language calls run at native speeds. We present three Morloc case studies: a polyglot influenza strain classification algorithm, a hybrid system where Morloc-generated CLI tools are orchestrated by a conventional workflow manager, and the translation of a conventional workflow to Morloc. By replacing the application/file paradigm, Morloc provides a foundation for high-performance, modular, polyglot scientific libraries. We can scrap the frameworks and get back to writing algorithms.

title: From the Human Genome Project to the Realization of Genomic Medicine: A Scientific, Medical, and Societal Journey
authors: Eric Green
abstract: The coming decade offers great promise for human genomics and genomic medicine. Since the completion of the Human Genome Project over two decades ago, genomics has become progressively entrenched within the bedrock of the biomedical research enterprise. Capitalizing on the momentum of the project’s successful completion, the field of genomics has increasingly expanded and matured, such that genomics is now central and catalytic in basic and translational research, and studies now regularly demonstrate the vital role that genomic information can play in clinical care. Looking ahead, the anticipated advances in technologies, biological insights, and clinical applications (among others) will lead to more widespread dissemination of genomics throughout biomedical research, a growing adoption of genomics into medical and public health practices, and an increasing relevance of genomics in everyday life. At the same time, many challenges remain and require ongoing attention, such as understanding the biological complexities of the human genome, untangling the complex roles that genomic variants play in health and disease, and ensuring that genomics gets broadly and equitably integrated in medicine around the world. title: MuSAlS: Fast Multiple Sequence Alignment Using Hierarchical Clustering
authors: Emily Light, Noah Daniels, Najib Ishaq
abstract: Motivation: The multiple sequence alignment (MSA) problem has been extensively studied, with numerous approaches developed over recent years. With the rapid growth of sequence data, there is an increasing need for fast and accurate MSA tools that scale effectively to large datasets. Building on our previous work on CLAM, we are able to use exact dynamic programming (Needleman-Wunsch) while scaling to large datasets. We introduce MuSAlS (Multiple Sequence Alignment at Scale), a fast and scalable de novo MSA aligner. MuSAlS uses hierarchical clustering to construct a guide tree based on the Levenshtein distance metric, enabling efficient and accurate alignment through a bottom-up approach. Results: MuSAlS achieves competitive accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods while significantly improving runtime performance. This makes it a valuable tool for researchers analyzing large-scale genomic and metagenomic datasets, addressing the growing demand for scalable bioinformatics solutions. Availability and Implementation: MuSAlS is implemented in the Rust programming language, and available at https:// github.com/URI-ABD/clam.

title: Combining RNA-seq and MS proteomics boosts sensitivity to detect differentially expressed genes by rpMeta
authors: Xijun Zhang, Clifton Dalgard, Craig Shriver, Matthew Wilkerson
abstract: Differential gene expression (DGE) is a powerful analytical technique to characterize biology. DGE analysis is most often applied to RNA sequencing revealing transcripts overexpressed and underexpressed among experimental groups. DGE analysis is also applied to global MS-based proteomics datasets revealing proteins overexpressed and underexpressed. A growing number of multi-omic studies combine RNA sequencing and proteomics from matched specimens. A common multi-omic DGE practice involves separate DGE analysis by RNA, DGE analysis by proteins and comparison of results by log ratios or Venn Diagrams. This disjoint approach may not utilize all of the available signal from both platforms as RNA transcripts and proteomics are known to have correlated expression levels. To integrate DGE analysis between RNA and proteomics, we developed a new method, RNA protein meta-analysis called rpMeta. rpMeta takes RNA and protein expression matrices as input. rpMeta then calculates DEGs by RNA, by protein, and by meta-analysis, according to user-provided options. To evaluate rpMeta’s performance, we used two published lung cancer datasets for benchmarking to detect DEGs between known lung cancer subtypes, Terminal Respiratory Unit and Proximal-Proliferative. The benchmarks included a spike-in analysis, a down-sampling analysis, and a cross-cohort validation. Among genes co-measured by RNA and protein, the meta-analysis model displayed greater performance than the RNA and protein models (AUCs of 0.912,0.862 and 0.828). rpMeta includes utilities to produce publication-ready data visualizations of the integrated DGE. rpMeta is an open-source R package under the MIT license, available at https:// github.com/zhangx8/rpMeta and therefore enabling data analysis and workflow integration for the community.

title: Generalized linear models for clustering of RNA-seq time series experiments
authors: Jherson Medina Correa, Juan Diego Enriquez-Ramos, Jorge Duitama
abstract: RNA-seq in time series experiments is a fundamental experimental design model for identification of important changes in gene expression along a biological process. Gene clustering allows to identify groups of genes with similar expression patterns throughout the process. Clusters can be interpreted as shared regulation mechanisms, which can be related to biological functions. Most current methods for gene clustering in time series implement classical unsupervised learning techniques which do not take into account the structure of the experiment, including management of replicate samples. We present a generalized linear model (GLM) implemented in a new open source software for gene clustering in time series RNA-seq experiments. Given an input matrix of raw counts and metadata file, the model calculates log fold changes (LFC) across the time points relative to the basal expression level at time zero, according to a GLM similar to that implemented in DeSeq2 for differential expression. The LFC values can be interpreted as normalized expression values, considering the variance across replicates. Three different alternatives (K-means, Neighbor joining and DBScan) with two different distance functions (euclidean and correlation) were implemented to perform gene clustering over the LFC values. The software was implemented in Java with minimal dependencies, following an interface driven design with object oriented best practices. Benchmark experiments against Clust and WGCNA using real time series datasets shows that the new model has improved computational efficiency and provides clusters with better internal consistency than previous solutions.

title: The AOP-Wiki EMOD Tool Suite: An Open Source Foundation for Enhanced Integration Between Adverse Outcome Pathways (AOPs), New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), AOP-Supporting Evidence, and Agentic Support for AOPs
authors: Virginia Hench, Harry Caufiled, Rebecca Boyles, James Balhoff, Sierra Moxon, Matthew Watson, Gaurav Vaidya, Nyssa Tucker, Alex Tropsha, Chris Mungall, Jason O'Brien, Kristie Sullivan, Stephen Edwards
abstract: Adverse outcome pathways (AOPs) are logic models used to organize heterogeneous evidence for causal relationships between biomechanisms and phenotypes, characterized by upstream molecular initiating events leading to downstream adverse outcomes through intermediate key events (KEs). AOPs help contextualize New Approach Methodologies (NAMs), in vitro and in silico methods, that offer alternatives to animal testing. The AOP-Wiki Knowledge Base is the central AOP repository that serves a global community of NAMs developers, linked data system architects, toxicologists, and regulatory decision-makers. As the sole AOP authoring tool, the AOP-Wiki plays a pivotal role in defining AOP standards. Yet, further growth and evolution is limited by the AOP-Wiki’s outdated infrastructure and data model. To address these limitations, we introduce three open source tools to facilitate a much needed AOP-Wiki data modernization overhaul. A CLI tool offers functions to filter and extract AOP entities from the AOP-Wiki XML into multiple formats for further analysis and curation. As the most recent AOP-Wiki evidence model (EMOD) prototype, the AOP-Wiki EMOD 3.0 web app features a seizure use case that demonstrates how new data model classes enable semantic mapping between AOPs, NAMs and biological targets, harmonization to reduce redundancies and enhance utility, and provenance tracking to source citations and contributors. We introduce an integration score for classifying KEs, which is needed for AOP-Wiki content quality improvement and agentic curation priorities. Lastly, our AOP EMOD LinkML schema defines a standard to support computational and agentic approaches to AOP development.

title: Bridging the Metadata Gap: A Two-Stage Federated Learning Architecture and Visual Audit Tool (FedViz) for Global Biobank Consortia
authors: Aditya Karna, Hieu Ngo, Yuan-Ting Hsieh
abstract: The harmonization of heterogeneous biomedical data remains a critical bottleneck for global collaborative research. During the 2026 CMU-NVIDIA Hackathon, a global consortium collaborated to build prototype software for federated learning (FL) across biobanks using NVIDIA FLARE. Across various prototype tracks—including federated GWAS meta-analysis—a universal challenge emerged: deploying FL at scale requires strict feature alignment across institutional nodes before training can safely execute. To operationalize this alignment, we developed FedViz, an open-source visual architecture designed to audit federated readiness prior to model execution. Built with a React/TypeScript frontend and an Elasticsearch backend, FedViz executes a two-stage approach: Consortium-Wide Discovery and Targeted Model Execution. As a demonstration, we used FedViz to audit metadata across 14 simulated international biobank cohorts (e.g., CANPATH, CHoP). Out of 11,511 unique clinical variables detected, the visual dashboard revealed a baseline Readiness Index of just 1.04%, mapping the severe fragmentation of genomic and imaging metadata. We then filtered for this high-quality harmonized subset (120 variables), so targeted federated models could be safely executed. After users conduct auditing and associated filtering, the FedViz Evaluation Layer integrates post-training metrics from NVIDIA FLARE, utilizing site-specific ROC curves and confusion matrix distributions to enable researchers to visually detect local domain drift. This prototype demonstrates that combining robust FL infrastructure with rigorous, visual data-readiness auditing (FedViz) provides a scalable blueprint for leveraging open biomedical data across global biobanks.

title: Large-scale Reference-Guided Cell Type Re-annotation of Single-Cell Brain Data
authors: Rachel Schwartz, Paul Pavlidis
abstract: Cell type annotation is a critical but poorly standardized step in single-cell transcriptomics. Across publicly available human and mouse brain datasets, cell-type specific meta-analysis is impeded by diverse annotation strategies, inconsistent cell type nomenclature, and varied granularity of annotation. To address these inconsistencies in a reproducibile manner and enable large-scale re-analysis of single-cell brain datasets, we developed a reference-guided Nextflow pipeline for hierarchical cell type annotation, now deployed in the Gemma gene expression database. In developing the pipeline, we benchmarked deep learning (scVI) and PCA-based (Seurat) label transfer across 9 human cortex and 7 mouse brain single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq cohorts, varying reference atlas, confidence threshold, and other parameters. A Random Forest classifier trained on scVI embeddings typically achieves higher macro-F1 scores than Seurat and is more computationally efficient, though Random Forest confidence scores are poorly calibrated for filtering. Study of origin accounts for more variance in annotation accuracy than method, reference, disease or experimental perturbation status. Some cell types fail systematically across all configurations; we mitigate this by grouping poorly discriminated cell types into higher-level categories for re-analysis. The recommended pipeline configuration achieves macro-F1 = 0.940 for human and 0.770 for mouse. In a reanalysis of PsychENCODE, differential expression (DE) concordance with author labels was high overall, but as expected, cell types with annotation failures and/or label harmonization issues showed poorer reproducibility. The framework presented here, deployed in Gemma for over 200 brain experiments, provides a reusable alternative to per-study annotation with documented caveats tied to annotation quality.

title: The MoTrPAC Data Hub: An AI-Enabled, Open-Science Ecosystem for the Molecular Map of Exercise
authors: Eric Leslie, Matthew Wheeler, Euan Ashley, Malene Lindholm, David Amar, Motrpac Study Group, Mihir Samdarshi, Crystal Han, Shruti Marwaha, Daniel H. Katz, Mia Levanto, Nik Vetr, Jeren Olsen, Samuel Montalvo, Pauline Brochet, Jay Yu, David Jimenez-Morales, Jimmy Zhen
abstract: The diverse benefits of exercise are mediated by a system-wide, multi-tissue, multi-omic response. However, the molecular mediators of these benefits remain incompletely understood. The Molecular Transducers of Physical Activity Consortium (MoTrPAC) aims to build a multi-omic molecular map of exercise. To disseminate this map as widely as possible, we present the MoTrPAC Data Hub (https:// motrpac-data.org/), an open source for all MoTrPAC data with multiple tools to support the bioinformatics community and meet FAIR principles. After data are processed through standard pipelines, the Data Hub provides multiple approaches for utilization. Currently, two datasets comprising data from 2 species, 19 tissues, and >60,000 exercise-responsive molecules are available. We highlight four elements of the ecosystem: 1) Data search and visualization uses Elasticsearch for low-latency retrieval over thousands of features, with interactive visualizations of MoTrPAC data in real time. 2) GitHub repositories and R packages (https://motrpac-data.org/code-repositories) provide both programmatic data access and functional code to reproduce and extend results. 3) The ExerWise Chatbot is embedded in the Hub to answer questions across the consortium knowledge base; and 4) the Model Context Protocol Server provides AI-mediated interactivity with MoTrPAC data and integrates with any agent for custom analysis using vetted MoTrPAC tools. All data and code are offered under the CC-BY-4.0 license and are provided with reference materials to support users. Together, the MoTrPAC Data Hub maximizes the impact of this science and serves as a blueprint for multi-omic data integration in the era of generative AI.

title: An Open-Source Platform for Quantitative Interactomics

abstract: The project Life123.science, about Dynamical Modeling for Systems Biology, takes an extremely integrative approach, with long-range goals towards filling what may be a gap in Computational Biology that the current focus on Big Data and AI doesn't address. title: Canopy: An Open-Source Platform for FAIR Research Data Hubs
authors: Marcos Martínez-Romero, Yan Cao, Attila L. Egyedi, Matthew Horridge, Mete Akdogan, Martin O'Connor, Mark Musen
abstract: Scientific research relies on data hubs that coordinate dataset submission, search, access, and reuse across distributed programs and institutions. Despite this shared need, such hubs are frequently built as one-off systems, forcing teams to independently solve difficult, recurring challenges, including access control, data harmonization, and secure authorization. The result is duplicated engineering effort and fragmented infrastructure. There is a clear need for reusable, open-source platforms that encode proven data hub practices in a form other communities can adopt and adapt. In response, we developed Canopy, an open-source research data hub platform targeting data coordinating centers, institutional hubs, and multi-site biomedical consortia, designed to be deployed and customized for different scientific communities. Canopy supports end-to-end data management, from submission through validation and expert curation, to controlled discovery and reuse. Canopy is derived from the NIH RADx Data Hub, a production system hosting nearly 200 studies from more than 100 US organizations. This real-world foundation distinguishes Canopy from purely conceptual frameworks or prototypes: its architecture, data pipeline, and metadata framework have been stress-tested at NIH scale across four research programs spanning diagnostic technologies, health disparities, digital health, and experimental approaches. Canopy supports FAIR data practices by enforcing structured metadata capture through CEDAR templates, using standardized terminology from BioPortal-linked controlled vocabularies, and providing a common data element framework to support variable harmonization across studies. Canopy is released under a BSD 2-Clause license (https://github.com/canopy-datahub). We invite the BOSC community to explore, use, and contribute to Canopy.

title: Templated Collaborative Science Resources for Fostering and Sustainably Cataloging FAIR and Reproducible Digital AI Research Products
authors: Elizabeth G. Campolongo, Matthew J. Thompson, Net Zhang, Yuehua Duan, John Bradley, Iuliia Zarubiieva, Graham Taylor, Hilmar Lapp
abstract: The frontier of AI innovation for biological discovery is often highly collaborative, distributed, and multidisciplinary. Across such teams, the understanding and application of FAIR and Reproducible Research concepts and practices can be very uneven, which can lead to training and know-how gaps for nextgen researchers, those most directly involved with creating AI research products. As a downstream effect, it can also make it challenging to comprehensively catalog a team’s output in terms of code, datasets, and ML models. To this end, we developed two templated resources that can be adapted and deployed with little effort. One is the Collaborative Distributed Science Guide. Inspired by challenges encountered in two large-scale research collaboratives aiming to develop new AI capabilities for ecology, evolutionary, and biodiversity science, the Guide adapts and distills established best practices to create a common lexicon and practical workflows for incrementally developing FAIR and reproducible AI research products. It promulgates the consistent application of established best practices across a team, including version control, FAIR repositories on GitHub and Hugging Face, and templates for READMEs, model cards, and dataset cards. The other resource is a dynamic yet serverless product catalog. As a single-page web application, the Catalog pulls content client-side directly from GitHub and Hugging Face using their respective APIs. It presents products as searchable cards that can be flexibly filtered and ordered. In this way, the Catalog not only promotes product findability and reuse, but also incentivizes team members to adhere to the FAIR product pathways promulgated in the Guide.

title: Posters.science: Building Open Infrastructure for FAIR and AI-ready Scientific Posters
authors: Bhavesh Patel, Jamey O'Neill, Dorian Portillo, Sanjay Soundarajan
abstract: Every year, millions of scientific posters are presented at conferences. They are particularly relevant to biomedical research, where conference posters often represent the earliest public glimpse of ideas and findings that will eventually shape clinical guidelines and drug targets. Yet, most posters disappear by the end of conferences, rolled up under chairs or stuffed into recycling bins. Through our investigation of poster-sharing practices, we found only ~150,000 posters online across 86 platforms, and even those lacked basic metadata, like author identifiers, funding sources, and conference information, making them hard to find and reuse. To address this, we are developing Posters.science, a free and open-source platform that simplifies poster sharing. User only need to upload a PDF of their poster, review auto-extracted metadata, and publish to a repository of their choice, like Zenodo. We developed a custom LLM pipeline that handles the metadata extraction and generates a poster.json file, which is a structured, machine-readable version of the poster that makes it interoperable and AI-ready. The platform also works as a registry, currently indexing over 1,500 posters from Zenodo and Figshare, with more on the way. For the biomedical community specifically, this could open new possibilities for systematically mining early-stage findings on a disease or gene across thousands of posters. In this talk, we will present our analysis of current poster-sharing practices, introduce the poster.json schema design, and give a live demonstration of Posters.science.

title: As Open as Possible; As Closed as Necessary: Enabling Openness for Sensitive Human Data
authors: Mallory Freeberg
abstract: As the volume and complexity of human genomic and health data continue to grow, the need to balance openness with responsible data management is becoming increasingly important. While individual-level human data usually require tight access controls for analysis and sharing, these restrictions do not preclude the application of open principles. Rather, the definition of "openness" highlights specific challenges for sensitive data. Here we describe a framework for responsible openness for sensitive human data, enabled by FAIR principles and community-driven standards. We highlight how controlled-access resources such as DECIPHER and the European Genome-phenome Archive (EGA) demonstrate the approach of "as open as possible; as closed as necessary". DECIPHER enhances clinical diagnosis by enabling upload of patient variants and their interpretation by integrating bioinformatics resources and biomedical knowledge. The EGA supports sharing of personally identifiable genetic, phenotypic, and clinical data generated for biomedical research or research-focused healthcare. The recent expansion of EGA to a Federated EGA Network was a direct response to tighter controls of genomic and health data in Europe. Enabling interoperability between these and similar resources is the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health, a standards-setting and policy-framing initiative aiming to expand the use of genomic data to benefit human health. These examples illustrate how openness can be achieved at data, standards, software, and governance levels even when data access is restricted. Embracing open principles is key to building scalable and flexible resources which both promote responsible data sharing and adhere to evolving data protection regulations locally and globally.

title: CTRL: A Dynamic open source e-Consent Platform
authors: Maxime Hebrard, Ignatius Menzies, Tim Kallady, Peter Louk, Rishi Israni, Katherine Champ, Filippo Ammazzalorso, Leonard Goldstein, Sarah Kummerfeld
abstract: Dynamic consent represents a transformative approach to the traditional informed consent model, fostering continuous engagement between researchers and participants. Unlike static methods, this framework facilitates ongoing communication, allowing researchers to provide study updates and solicit renewed consent for amended protocols. Simultaneously, it empowers participants to proactively manage their involvement. Transitioning from paper-based systems to electronic platforms enhances research efficiency through robust audit trails, stringent access controls, and adherence to the principle of least privilege, thereby streamlining data management and institutional accountability. Initiated by Australian Genomics and developed by Garvan Institute, the open source CTRL platform (pronounced ""control"") is a component of the Australian BioCommons’ GUARDIANS program. CTRL serves as a critical module in national infrastructure for human genomic research. The platform comprises two specialized web interfaces: Researcher Portal: This administrative hub allows clinicians to manage multiple studies within a secure environment. Researchers can design bespoke consent forms featuring modular sections, embedded educational media, and ontology-integrated terms to ensure machine-readability. The portal further enables participant invitation and real-time oversight of consent statuses. Participant Portal: This interface provides a secure environment for individuals to register personal data, review consent statements, and provide authorizations. A dedicated news feed ensures participants remain informed of research milestones, while integrated communication tools facilitate direct contact with study teams. In summary, CTRL is an open source, electronic dynamic consent solution that delivers an intuitive, secure, and engaging interface for both the scientific community and the public.

title: Legal interoperability as infrastructure: Enabling computable licensing in biomedical knowledge graphs
authors: Shilpa Sundar, Daniel Korn, Seth Carbon, Andrew Su, Matthew Brush, Melissa Haendel
abstract: Biomedical knowledge graphs have become central components of computational biology, supporting data integration, machine reasoning, and AI. While the FAIR principles emphasize reusability and interoperability, these aspirations are largely implemented in the form of identifiers, schemas, and APIs. In practice, legal constraints function as hidden system dependencies that determine what data can be programmatically combined, redistributed, or used in downstream applications (no matter whether they are academic, commercial, or clinical). Building on prior work from our (Re)usable Data Project, we consider licensing as a computable dimension of data integration. We conducted a systematic licensing audit of 39 biomedical data sources integrated into the NCATS Biomedical Data Translator, a federated knowledge graph collection used for biomedical reasoning. For each source, we extracted license type, terms of use, commercial and redistribution permissions, attribution requirements, and component-level licensing heterogeneity. Sources were classified into five operational categories reflecting what Translator can and cannot do with the data. Less than half of the sources assessed (19/39) carry permissive licenses (CC0 or CC BY), 6 require ShareAlike (CC BY-SA), 12 restrict non-commercial use or require proprietary agreements, and 2 lack an explicit data license. We identified recurring governance challenges including mixed licensing within single resources, portal-level terms diverging from dataset-level terms, ShareAlike propagation across merged graphs, and access models that conflate availability with reuse rights. This work treats legal interoperability as a first-class dimension of FAIR and contributes a reusable audit framework, machine-actionable classification, and implementation guidance for computably encoding licensing constraints in reproducible computational workflows.

title: Evaluating the Performance of LLMs in Drafting Data Management Plans
authors: Nahid Zeinali, Xuebin Dong, Rebecca Hofstein Grady, Maria Praetzellis, Brian Riley, Bhavesh Patel
abstract: Data Management Plans (DMPs) are now required by most funders for grant proposals to ensure researchers plan in advance for effective data management and sharing. Preparing a DMP is usually difficult for researchers because they often lack training and knowledge in data management practices. Moreover, funding organizations have different policies that require adherence to specific data management strategies and DMP formats. In this work, we evaluated the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs) in drafting DMPs compliant with the National Institutes of Health (NIH)™s 2023 guidelines. The goal was to investigate whether LLMs were ready, off-the-shelf, to assist biomedical researchers in preparing their DMPs. We evaluated the performance of an open-source LLM, Llama 3.3, and a commercial LLM, GPT 4, in drafting NIH-compliant DMPs. We used comparisons to NIH-provided human-written DMP samples to quantify the performance of Llama and GPT models. We also asked domain experts to evaluate LLM-generated DMPs. Overall, we found that LLMs can accelerate initial draft creation, but would still require expert review before submission to ensure full correctness and compliance. Moreover, open-source LLMs may not be as ready off-the-shelf as commercial ones for drafting funding-compliant DMPs.

title: Toward domain-specific genomic AI agents: benchmarking sequencing library structure extraction
authors: Michael Goneos, Chi-Lam Poon
abstract: Novel single-cell sequencing technologies require fast and accurate quality control (QC) to evaluate data quality and identify protocol-level issues that limit throughput and sensitivity. AI agents powered by frontier large language models (LLMs) have the potential to automate tasks in this workflow and accelerate protocol iteration. While downstream computational QC is highly standardized, the first step, deriving the oligonucleotide library structure from heterogeneous experimental protocols, remains a manual bottleneck that requires deep domain expertise. We benchmarked nine frontier LLMs across the Gemini, Claude, GPT, Grok, and Kimi families on their ability to extract library structure from sequencing protocols, using 13 ground-truth library structures manually curated from the scg_lib_structs community resource, explicitly testing whether models understand the underlying biochemistry rather than pattern-matching variable regions. We tested three input modes: (i) raw PDF upload, (ii) text extracted from PDFs, and (iii) assay-name-only prompting with web-search tools enabled. LLM outputs were scored against ground truth using normalized Levenshtein similarity, and mean similarities are 0.801, 0.805, 0.836, respectively. All models scored substantially worse on academic protocols than on commercial 10x kits. This gap suggests that current LLM performance is mostly driven by memorized chemistry rather than document comprehension, and indicates that such domain-specific tasks requiring perfect accuracy will need dedicated agent fine-tuning and specialized training data despite the rapid progress in general-purpose LLMs.

title: PosterSentry: a light-weight multimodal classification system for scientific poster quality assurance in open repositories
authors: James ONeill, Parth Sarin, Adam Buttrick, Bhavesh Patel
abstract: The Posters.science project aims to build an index of findability, accessibility, interoperability, and reusability (FAIR) of posters by extracting machine-actionable metadata from PDFs stored in open access repositories. During harvesting of poster records from Zenodo and Figshare, we found that many were mislabeled, containing multi-page papers, proceedings, abstract books, or presentations. Label noise at this scale severely limits the viability of automated FAIR pipelines. To mitigate this, we developed PosterSentry, a lightweight, open-source multimodal classifier that identifies whether a PDF is a true scientific poster. We fused three complementary feature streams in PosterSentry: 1) text embeddings via model2vec (512 dimensions), 2) visual features including color statistics, edge density, and spatial complexity (15 dimensions), and 3) structural PDF layout features such as page geometry, font diversity, and text density (15 dimensions). We concatenated these streams into a 542-dimensional vector and used logistic regression to classify them. PosterSentry was trained on 3,606 heuristically selected real-world examples with no synthetic augmentation. It achieved 87.3% accuracy, runs on CPU in under one second per file, and requires only a 10kb model head, which is orders of magnitude smaller than other LLM-based alternatives. PosterSentry is publicly available under an MIT license on Hugging Face alongside its training data, and is currently deployed in the Posters.science quality control pipeline. In this presentation, we will present the development of PosterSentry, results across 30,205 poster PDFs from open repositories, and discuss future work planned in collaboration with the Collaborative Metadata (COMET) initiative.
