title: Using AI to develop, maintain, and translate bioinformatics training materials
authors: Geraldine Van der Auwera, Jonathan Manning, Phil Ewels
abstract: Keeping training materials accurate and up-to-date for a rapidly evolving software ecosystem is a major challenge, particularly when learners must interact directly with code. As the team responsible for the nextflow-io/training repository, we have experimented with AI tools to address three key bottlenecks: (1) maintenance and version updates, (2) new content development, and (3) multilingual translation. For maintenance and content development, we developed custom Claude skills: structured, reusable prompt templates that guide Claude (Anthropic) through consulting reference documentation, identifying affected materials, implementing changes, and executing hands-on exercises in a containerised environment to validate results. This has accelerated update cycles by orders of magnitude: days to hours, hours to minutes. For new content development, results have been more mixed. Claude can produce technically accurate exercises, but lacks the pedagogical insight needed to structure learning progressions or anticipate learner confusion. Curriculum design still requires human expertise in both subject matter and instructional design. For translation, we implemented an AI-assisted system based on the FastAPI project's approach, using language-specific LLM prompts integrated into GitHub Actions. Human review focuses on improving prompts rather than edited translated files directly, ensuring that fixes propagate to all future translations. As a result, our materials are now available in ten languages besides English, and the translations are always up-to-date. All Claude skills and LLM prompts are published in the nextflow-io/ training repository for the community to reuse and adapt. We hope that our experience will prove useful for others in the bioinformatics community.

title: Learning in public, losing in private? How AI chatbots and LLMs are reshaping bioinformatics culture
authors: Van Quynh Truong, Sebastian Lobentanzer, Nomi Harris, Marylyn Ritchie
abstract: Decades of free and open-source software movements helped nurture a culture of openness in bioinformatics through code-sharing, public troubleshooting, and examples of learning in public. Chat forums like Biostars, Stack Overflow, and GitHub Issues act as Q&A sites, but they also serve as digital “third spaces" to solve problems aloud. As large language models (LLMs) become everyday research assistants, a subtle shift is taking place. Instead of debugging and learning in public, scientific problem-solving has become fractured between public forums to private one-on-one chats with generative artificial intelligence (AI). This perspective piece explores what is at stake in that shift. Using bioinformatics as a case study, we argue that LLMs are quietly transforming how scientific knowledge is created and shared. While conversational AI assistants help with debugging and maybe even accelerate discovery, they risk eroding five cornerstones of open science: 1) ambient mentorship, 2) peer validation, and 3) collective memory, compounded by the loss of 4) granular resource authority and 5) decentralized tool control. Furthermore, this transition creates a practical problem of liability without ownership for tool builders whose resources are misrepresented by LLM-generated instructions. Rather than resisting the technology, we propose five mutually reinforcing strategies to counteract the “AI chatbot silo effect" and preserve the digital commons: 1) Make the invisible visible with “AI protocols" 2); Reinvest in our digital and physical third places; 3) Build openly where possible with community tools; 4) Demand attribution and tool authority from commercial LLMs; and 5) Champion institutionally-owned, open infrastructure.

title: Differential Connectivity Analysis of Integrated Gut Microbiome Networks for Disease Prediction
authors: Yulin Li, Somnath Datta
abstract: Gut microbiome studies often focus on which bacteria are more or less abundant in disease. However, disease may also change how microbes are connected with each other. In this study, we analyzed the CAMDA 2026 Gut Microbiome Interaction Network Challenge data to compare microbial association networks in healthy and non-healthy samples, and to test whether network-based taxa could help predict disease status. After data filtering, our analysis included 3,314 samples from 15 studies and 206 taxa. We first built study-specific microbial association networks using SparCC. We then combined these networks separately for healthy and disease samples using inverse-variance weighting. To find taxa with the largest network changes, we calculated a differential connectivity score for each taxon. This score measures how much a taxon’s connections changed between the healthy and disease networks. We used 1,000 study-stratified permutations to assess statistical evidence. Finally, we tested whether the top 50 taxa from this network analysis improved disease prediction beyond metadata alone, using elastic-net logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. The healthy and disease networks showed different strongest microbial associations. Several taxa showed relatively large changes in connectivity, including Hungatella hathewayi, Flavonifractor plautii, Bacteroides galacturonicus, and Eubacterium sp. CAG 38. track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Metabolic Pathways as Ecological Niches: Topological Reorganization of Gut Microbiome Functional Networks Across Health and Disease
authors: Nelly Selem, Shaday Guerrero Flores, Lilia Leticia Ramírez Ramírez, Victor Muñiz Sánchez, Jose Abel Lovaco-Flores, Rafael Pérez-Estrada, Pedro Rojas Salas, Hassim Olvera Castillo, Javier Roberto Ruvalcaba Cortés, Gerardo Escamilla, Diego Benjamín Tafolla Herrera, Erika Correa Hernández, Mario Jardon, Roberto Álvarez Martínez
abstract: Gut microbiome dysbiosis has been associated with multiple diseases, yet traditional microbiome analyses based on taxonomic composition or diversity metrics are often insufficient to explain ecosystem-level changes. Here, we propose a pathway-centered ecological framework in which metabolic pathways are treated as ecological niches (“submicrobiomes" ) composed of interacting taxa contributing to shared functions. Using metagenomic datasets from the CAMDA microbiome challenge, we combined ecological diversity analyses and functional network reconstruction to characterize pathway-level organization across healthy and disease-associated microbiomes. We first analyzed the taxonomic α-diversity (Shannon index) of taxa contributing to individual metabolic pathways. Pathways were grouped according to whether their mean diversity was significantly higher in healthy or unhealthy samples using Welch two-sample t-tests in R. Pathways enriched in healthy microbiomes generally displayed high α-diversity, suggesting functions supported by broad and redundant microbial communities, whereas pathways enriched in unhealthy microbiomes showed lower diversity, indicating functions dominated by fewer taxa. To investigate higher-order organization, we reconstructed function-function interaction networks in which nodes represent metabolic pathways and edges represent pathway associations. Comparative analyses revealed extensive rewiring between healthy and disease-associated microbiomes. Although many pathways remained present across conditions, the structure of their interactions changed substantially. Healthy versus Crohn’s disease networks showed a Jaccard similarity of 37.62%, while healthy versus infection-associated networks showed only 21.27% similarity, indicating major reorganization of functional interactions during dysbiosis. Disease-associated networks also exhibited increased connectivity and density, with one disease network containing 1,215 interactions compared with 876 in healthy samples. Functional gains were concentrated in carbohydrate metabolism pathways, whereas central metabolism and energy pathways showed connectivity loss. Together, these results suggest that disease-associated microbiomes are characterized not only by taxonomic shifts, but by ecological and topological reorganization of metabolic interactions. Our framework provides a new perspective for studying microbiome stability, redundancy, and dysbiosis through pathway-level ecological organization.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: A Dual-Layer Network Framework Reveals Hidden Functional Drivers of Gut Microbiome Dysbiosis
authors: Safa Bushnaq, Irina Chelysheva
abstract: Gut microbiome dysbiosis contributes to chronic diseases, yet standard taxonomic profiling poorly predicts functional consequences. One taxon can perform multiple functions, and one function can be executed by multiple taxa, necessitating integrated taxon-function analysis. We developed a two-layer framework combining bias-corrected differential abundance (ANCOM-BC2) with confounder-adjusted association networks. Across 3,727 metagenomic samples spanning 18 diseases, Layer 1 identified disease-associated taxa and pathways while controlling for compositional bias, study heterogeneity, age, BMI, and gender. Layer 2 used correlations between residualised taxon and pathway abundances to infer disease-specific taxon–function networks while reducing host and technical confounding. Streptococcus parasanguinis emerged as a universal oral-gut translocation marker, enriched across IBD, ACVD, and liver disease (LFC +0.99 to +1.99, q<0.05), consistently negatively correlated with essential biosynthetic pathways (queuosine, adenosine ribonucleotides; |Ï |>0.2, q<0.05). Strikingly, we discovered a previously unannotated association in liver disease: Veillonella parvula linked to adenine/adenosine salvage III downregulation— not represented in current BioCyc annotations, and visible only after residualisation. End-stage liver disease exhibited extensive functional disruption with 41 taxa and 10 pathways altered compared with 6 taxa and 2 pathways in early cirrhosis, reflecting progressive microbiome disruption across disease severity. Additionally, BMI confounding masked peptidoglycan maturation pathway upregulation in T2D, highlighting BMI-sensitive inflammatory axes. Across multiple cohorts and sequencing platforms, our framework provides a robust and translatable strategy for resolving microbiome functional activity and identifying candidate disease-associated taxon–function interactions. Experimental validation will be required to establish causality.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Knowledge Graph-Guided Interpretation of Disease-Specific Taxon--Taxon Interaction Networks in the Gut Microbiome
authors: Shiyue Hu, He Cheng, Lucas Gillenwater, Yanjun Gao
abstract: Gut microbiome dysbiosis is associated with several diseases, including obesity, type 2 diabetes, and inflammatory bowel disease. Analyses that only focus on individual taxon abundance miss changes in how microbial communities organize. In this work, we propose a knowledge graph (KG)-guided framework for analyzing disease-specific taxon--taxon interaction networks in the gut microbiome. We constructed microbial interaction networks separately for healthy and disease samples using FastSpar on species-level taxonomic profiles. We compared these networks to identify healthy-specific, disease-specific, and preserved edges. To support biological interpretation, we used LogosKG to retrieve multi-hop neighborhoods from a microbial KG produced by the KG-Microbe construction framework. The retrieved nodes were grouped into disease, resource, function, phenotype, and environment categories, and typed Jaccard scores were computed to quantify shared biological context. In a preliminary colorectal cancer analysis, disease-specific and preserved edges had higher typed Jaccard scores in their KG neighborhood overlap than healthy-specific edges. This finding suggests that interactions retained or gained in disease are linked through shared prior biological knowledge. Overall, this framework prioritizes data-driven taxon-- taxon interaction hypotheses using external microbial knowledge.

title: Network-based optimal transport analysis of gut microbiome data in colorectal cancer
authors: Wei Wei, Rena Elkin, Joseph Deasy, Jung Hun Oh
abstract: Background: Metagenomic studies of the gut microbiome face challenges from high cross-study variability and conventional abundance-based methods often overlook microbial interaction structure. We developed an unsupervised network-based clustering method coupled with optimal transport to stratify colorectal cancer (CRC) and healthy cases using large-scale metagenomic data. Materials and Methods: Metagenomic gut microbiome data from 3,752 participants, including the relative abundance of 1,135 bacterial species and 603 biological pathways, were obtained from the Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis (CAMDA) challenge. After filtering low-prevalence species, a co-occurrence network was constructed using Spearman correlation coefficients. A Wasserstein distance-based K-means clustering algorithm that we developed was applied to the largest connected component of the network, enabling geometry-aware, structure-informed stratification of CRC and healthy cases. Results: Two clusters were identified; Cluster A was enriched with healthy samples (n = 991/1,630) whereas Cluster B was enriched with CRC samples (n = 291/468; chi-squared p = 1.8 Ã— 10â »¹â ¸). Cluster B also showed significantly older age and higher body mass index (BMI) compared to Cluster A (p = 2.8 Ã— 10â »²² and p = 9.2 Ã— 10â »â respectively). ¹, The proposed method outperformed traditional K-means and consensus K-means clustering in stratifying CRC from healthy samples. Pathway analysis revealed 28 pathways that differed significantly between the two clusters. Conclusion: The network-based K-means clustering method applied to gut microbiome profiles effectively distinguishes CRC from healthy samples while accounting for microbial interaction structure, demonstrating potential as a robust tool for large-scale microbiome analysis.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Metabolite-centric functional annotation with context-specific starting points
authors: Ivory Blakley
abstract: (Not yet implemented-in progress) Although this approach was born out of the Gut Microbiome Interaction Network Challenge, it requires starting from sequences, and the approach is therefore not suitable for the challenge data. A poster could facilitate discussion of the merits and challenges of the approach. Abstract: Human fecal WGS captures information from gut microbes, the human host, dietary organisms, and foodborne microbes. Misidentifying non-microbial reads as gut community members introduces error; correctly separating them offers multiple insights from one data source. Removing human reads is already standard. FooDB and MEDI extend this by identifying food-derived reads — enabling their removal from community tabulations while informing which metabolites are available as gut inputs. Host-derived enzymes (e.g., released into the lumen) should similarly be treated as present reactions, even when not microbiome-derived. Functional assessment should shift from pathway abundance tables to per-metabolite probability estimates. For each metabolite, we model both sides: production (relevant genes present and required inputs available; chained in series until reaching either an available input or an impasse) and consumption (consuming reactions and any required co-reactants present). This frames function around a specific metabolite endpoint with context-defined starting points — e.g., ""a host who recently ate a banana"" — rather than universally defined pathways that lack environmental grounding. Datasets with joint metabolomics and WGS provide an avenue to refine and validate the model, identifying metabolites that fit the model well and those that do not. Diet-and microbiome-associated plasma metabolites should be the highest priority for model validation and refinement. Direct taxa-to-outcome relationships remain important. But the complex interplay of host, diet, and microbiome — and its effect on health — is most powerfully modeled through the metabolite environment the host actually experiences.

abstract: We present BIOTIA-DX Resistance, our submission to the CAMDA 2026 AMR Challenge. We achieved a mean accuracy of 86.1% across the six species-drug pairs on the CAMDA test set, ranking first on four pairs, tied for first on Streptococcus pneumoniae (penicillin), and second on Campylobacter jejuni (nalidixic acid). track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Quantifying uncertainty in protein representations across models and tasks
authors: R. Prabakaran, Yana Bromberg
abstract: Embeddings, derived by language models, are widely used as efficient sequence and structure representations of biomolecules, enabling similarity search, structure and function prediction, and estimation of biophysical properties. However, employing these embeddings without assessing representational fidelity may compromise inferences and downstream reliability. Here, we propose a framework to evaluate language model-derived protein embeddings. For each protein, representation uncertainty is quantified as the fraction of non-biological “synthetic" sequences among its nearest neighbors in latent space. Our analysis reveals that underperforming embeddings often fail to capture meaningful biology, displaying vector properties indistinguishable from those of randomly generated sequences. Our model-and task-agnostic scoring framework enables embedding screening prior to downstream applications. We argue that incorporating such screening strategies will enhance the reliability and interpretability of deep learning models in science.

title: Towards Privacy-Preserving Genomics: Understanding and Mitigating Risks
authors: Hoon Cho
abstract: As genomic datasets continue to expand in scale, diversity, and modality, the privacy implications of sharing massive amounts of human data are becoming increasingly urgent. I will discuss how principled mathematical frameworks for quantifying privacy risk can deepen our understanding of genomic privacy while guiding the development of practical methods for privacy-preserving data sharing and analysis. I will highlight recent work on vulnerabilities in genome imputation services, linkage risks in transcriptomic data, and formal approaches for genetic association studies with privacy guarantees. I will conclude with an outlook on how community-driven efforts can accelerate progress in this area, enabling the scientific community to maximize the value of data sharing while safeguarding the individuals who make such research possible.

title: A rigorous benchmarking of alignment-based HLA typing algorithms for RNA-seq data
authors: Serghei Mangul, Ram Ayyala, Dottie Yu, Nicolae Drabcinski, Viorel Munteanu, Walter Wolfsberger, Taras K. Oleksyk
abstract: Accurate identification of human leukocyte antigen (HLA) alleles is essential for various clinical and research applications, such as transplant matching and drug sensitivities. Recent advances in RNA-seq technology have made it possible to impute HLA types from sequencing data, spurring the development of a large number of computational HLA typing tools. However, the relative performance of these tools is unknown, limiting the ability for clinical and biomedical research to make informed choices regarding which tools to use. Here we report the study design of a comprehensive benchmarking of the performance of 12 HLA callers across 682 RNA-seq samples from 8 datasets with molecularly defined gold standard at 5 loci, HLA-A, -B, -C, -DRB1, and-DQB1. For each HLA typing tool, we comprehensively assess their accuracy, compare default with optimized parameters, and examine for discrepancies in accuracy at the allele and loci levels. We also evaluate the computational expense of each caller in terms of CPU runtime and RAM usage, the influence of read length on accuracy for each tool, and the performance of HLA callers across European and African groups to determine any discrepancies in accuracy that is associated with ancestry. Our results demonstrate that while most RNA-Seq HLA callers are capable of returning accurate results, particularly for Class I loci, there is still some variation in prediction performance across different alleles. Additionally, we find that all tools are more accurate for individuals of European ancestry compared to those of African ancestry, highlighting systemic disparities in accuracy across different ancestry groups. However, tools that offer a good balance between accuracy and computational efficiency for all ancestry groups have yet to be developed. Our study provides clinicians and researchers with up-to-date guidance to inform their selection of an appropriate HLA caller.

title: A Unified Weighted-Distance Framework for No-Box Membership Inference Attacks on Synthetic Gene Expression Data
authors: Owen Tucker, Lily Wang, Harutoshi Okumura, Ruixuan Liu, Li Xiong
abstract: Membership Inference Attacks (MIA) assess whether individual records were used to train a generative model, and are a key tool for privacy auditing of synthetic data. We present our red-team submission to the ELSA Health 2026 Challenge, which tasks participants with inferring training membership from synthetic bulk RNA-seq gene expression data (TCGA) produced by four blue-team generators (MVN, CVAE, Noisy Diffusion, DP-PGM); we focus on CVAE and will include results of other target models in the full version. Building on prior works, we unify a family of no-box MIAs under a single weighted-distance framework: each variant is a LOGAN-style cosine score that differs only in its choice of feature weights: uniform (baseline), per-gene variance, KL divergence between synthetic and reference distributions, top-k PCA residualization (zero weight on dominant components), and biologically-informed pathway selection. We further compose this framework with two orthogonal augmentations: subtype-stratified candidate pools and a MinK-style surrogate signal. Our best variant on TCGA-COMBINED, PCA residualization, reaches AUC=0.8951, TPR@1=0.5970 (LOGAN baseline 0.8251 / 0.3842); on TCGA-BRCA, KL-weighted distance reaches AUC=0.7231 (baseline 0.7166), with {TPR@1%}=0.1853 comparable to baseline.

authors: Steven Golob, Patrick McKeever, Sikha Pentyala, Martine De Cock, Jonathan Peck
abstract: Team PPML-Huskies — CAMDA 2026 Track II We present a dual red-team and blue-team submission to CAMDA 2026 Track II. On the blue team, we submit Noisy-scDesign2, a differentially private adaptation of last year's top-performing generator, scDesign2. Noisy-scDesign2 injects calibrated Gaussian noise into scDesign2's per-cell-type copula covariance matrices, offering a partial privacy defense while preserving much of the generator's fidelity at small cohort sizes. On the red team, we present scMAMA-MIA, the first membership inference attack effective against synthetic scRNA-seq data. By fitting a shadow copula on the released synthetic data, scMAMA-MIA computes a Mahalanobis distance in the copula's latent space for each target cell, exploiting the fact that training cells lie anomalously close to the learned gene-covariance structure. Cell-level scores are aggregated per donor to produce donor-level membership predictions. Together, these submissions provide both a practical privacy defense and a rigorous auditing tool for synthetic scRNA-seq data.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Does Synthetic Bulk RNA-seq Data Protect Donors? Privacy Auditing through Membership Inference Attacks
authors: Charlene Jarrell, Daniil Filienko, Jonathan Kim, Emma Szebenyi, Sikha Pentyala, Steven Golob, Martine De Cock
abstract: Synthetic bulk RNA-seq data generation promises privacy-preserving genomic data sharing, but whether released synthetic datasets adequately protect individual donors from membership inference attacks (MIAs) remains underexplored. Through the red team track of the Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis (CAMDA) 2026 Health Privacy Challenge, we develop three generator-tailored MIAs targeting four generators spanning deep learning and statistical paradigms: MeLoMIA for diffusion-and VAE-based generators, MahalaMIA for the multivariate generator, and MAMA-MIA for the differentially private PGM. Our attacks operate under a black-box threat model in which the adversary has access to released synthetic datasets and public generator implementations, but not the trained model parameters or original training data. Evaluated on the TCGA-BRCA and TCGA-COMBINED cohorts, our tailored attacks substantially outperform baseline challenge attacks, achieving AUC values up to 0.922 and demonstrating that model-specific knowledge is critical for effective privacy auditing. High-fidelity non-DP generators are consistently vulnerable, whereas DP-PGM (epsilon = 10) provides meaningful resistance to membership inference. These results highlight the importance of formal privacy protections alongside fidelity and utility in synthetic transcriptomic data release.

title: Privacy-Preserving Synthetic Single-Cell RNA-seq via NMF-Compressed Truncated Vine Copulas
authors: Andrew Wicks
abstract: Sharing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data from human cohorts raises real privacy risks: gene expression profiles are highly individual and can be used to re-identify donors even in anonymized datasets. Synthetic data generation (producing artificial cells that statistically resemble a real cohort without containing any actual individual’s records) is a principled approach to this problem. However, existing copula-based generators either cannot scale to the tens of thousands of genes in a typical scRNA-seq experiment, or provide no mechanistic account of where privacy comes from. We introduce a three-stage generator called Vine-NMF. First, Non-negative Matrix Factorisation (NMF) compresses 25,834 genes into k = 75 biologically interpretable factors, reducing the problem to a tractable size. Second, a truncated vine copula captures how those factors co-vary within each of 14 annotated cell types. Third, Negative Binomial count sampling converts continuous factor values back to integer gene counts. Trained on 490 donors and 634k cells from the OneK1K cohort, the model produces synthetic data with strong cell-type and covariance fidelity (LISI = 0.686, SCC = 0.924) and passes all privacy attacks tested: membership inference and singling-out success rates are statistically indistinguishable from random guessing. A rank sweep (k âˆˆ {20, 30, 50, 75, 100}) reveals why: at k = 75, NMF compression is sufficient to erase individual donor distinctiveness. This suggests a general rank selection principle for privacy-sensitive single-cell synthesis: choose the smallest latent dimension at which donor uniqueness in synthetic pseudo-donors no longer correlates with donor uniqueness in real data. Code Availability: https://github.com/ AndrewJWicks/Vine-NMF-Single-Cell-Generator

abstract: Genomic data remains heavily siloed due to privacy regulations, limiting reproducibility and collaboration in biomedical research. Synthetic Data Generation (SDG) offers a promising alternative, yet new tabular SDG methods remain largely unevaluated on high-dimensional biological data. We assess two recent state of the art SDG methods, namely MIAV, a deep learning approach extending TabPFN via in-context learning, and TabSDS, a lightweight non-parametric shuffle-based alternative. We evaluate them on bulk RNA-seq datasets from the CAMDA'26 Health Privacy Challenge, with differentially private Private-PGM as a baseline. We measure the performance of the methods across utility, fidelity, and empirical privacy metrics on two TCGA datasets. We find that both MIAV-TabPFN and TabSDS achieve significantly higher fidelity compared to the baseline.

title: Benchmarking Recent Single-Cell Synthetic Data Generation Methods on the OneK1K Dataset
authors: Buse Giledereli, Başar Temiz, Amirreza Sattarzadeh Khanehbargh
abstract: Synthetic single-cell RNA-seq data generation offers a promising route for privacy-aware biomedical data sharing, but donor-linked datasets require careful balancing of biological utility and privacy risk. In this work, we benchmark synthetic generation methods for the CAMDA 2026 ELSA Health Privacy Challenge using the donor-split OneK1K dataset, comparing scGFT, scLDM, and Cell2Sentence across statistical fidelity, downstream biological preservation, and membership inference vulnerability. Because full-transcriptome generation is computationally demanding, we focus generative modeling on highly variable genes and evaluate alternative strategies for reconstructing non-HVG expression. Our results show that invariant gene handling is a central determinant of privacy severe leakage, where a Poisson-based reconstruction substantially reduces membership inference risk. We further find that scGFT and scLDM better preserve biological structure than an independent Poisson baseline, while maintaining near-random privacy profiles under appropriate configurations. These findings highlight the importance of evaluating synthetic single-cell data beyond marginal similarity alone, emphasizing privacy-conscious design choices throughout data generation.

title: Harmonization and Integration of Pharmacogenomics Screens
authors: Aleysha Chen, Marcus Kelly, Trey Ideker, Nicole Mattson
abstract: Large pharmacogenomics screens have generated a wealth of information cataloguing the responses of more than a thousand tumor cell-line models to FDA-approved and exploratory drugs. Although centralized repositories have consolidated data access, the diversity of experimental platforms and response metrics used in these screens have made it challenging to integrate and compare their measured drug responses. Towards better pharmacogenomic data harmonization, we surveyed a range of data analysis protocols based on different curve-fitting functions (sigmoid, piecewise linear), different response metrics (IC50, EC50, integrated AUC), and different drug concentration windows (full range or truncated). We found that an AUC derived from a sigmoidal curve fitted to a truncated dose range yields the strongest agreement between screening platforms, significantly bettering other protocols surveyed. This harmonization procedure also best aligns drug responses across successive iterations of the same platform. These findings broadly inform efforts to integrate drug response data in large-scale analyses.

track: CAMDA: Critical Assessment of Massive Data Analysis
title: Adapting Mamba 2 For EHR Data Using Continual Learning
authors: Conrad Testagrose, Simone Rancati, Micheal Sy, Riccardo Bellazzi, Ziyi Chen, Cheng Peng, Simone Marini, Marco Salemi, Christina Boucher, Mattia Prosperi
abstract: Clinical language models have demonstrated the value of pretraining on electronic health records (EHRs), but most prior clinical transformers are limited to context windows of 512 to 8,192 tokens. Full hospital admissions linearized with laboratory events, medications, transfers, and clinical notes frequently exceed these limits. State space models (SSMs) such as Mamba 2 offer a promising alternative due to their linear scaling with sequence length, but whether their recurrent state dynamics can maintain coherent representations across very long clinical sequences has not been established. We present a continually pretrained Mamba 2 2.7B model trained at 131,072 token context on structured linearizations of 383,222 MIMIC-IV hospital admissions, using a blend of medical text and EHR data. Through a sequence length ablation spanning 1,024 to 131,072 tokens, we characterize how base and continually pretrained SSMs respond to increasing context length. The base model performs reasonably at short context (NLL) of 1.58 at 1,024 tokens) but degrades beyond its training range, reaching NLL 12.14 and perplexity 187,543 at 131,072 tokens. The continually pretrained model exhibits the opposite trend, with NLL decreasing from 0.62 to 0.48 across the same range. Linear probing for discharge disposition prediction confirms that these gains translate to downstream clinical utility, the pretrained model improves monotonically from AUROC 0.803 at 25% of admission to 0.844 at full admission, while the base model declines from 0.776 to 0.751. Results demonstrate that domain-specific training at the target context length is critical for SSMs to maintain clinically meaningful representations across full hospital admissions.

title: Insights from a Large Community Challenge Benchmark Applicable to AI/ML-based Complex Biomarkers
authors: Wendell Jones
abstract: Machine learning (ML) methods are widely applied to develop diagnostic, prognostic, and predictive biomarkers in clinical and biomedical research, yet robust clinical success remains limited. To better understand potential determinants of performance, we conducted a large-scale, multi-team empirical study (community challenge) examining how sample size, feature representation, model complexity, validation behavior and other factors jointly influence the performance, stability, and reproducibility of ML-based biomarkers derived from tabular but high-dimensional clinical data. Using real-world oncology datasets comprising 14,882 breast cancer and 7,718 lung cancer patients, 22 independent analysis teams developed and evaluated hundreds of distinct ML models across five training-set sizes ranging from 2% to 80% of available subjects. Models were assessed on blinded held-out test sets using multiple performance measures appropriate for imbalanced outcomes. Several factors were found to be strongly associated with performance beyond the often-cited selection of ML framework. The results suggest best practices for complex biomarker development related to model performance.

title: Data-Driven Modeling of TLR4 Signaling Identifies Missing Negative Feedback Underlying Prolonged Inflammatory Outcomes
authors: TBD, Aleksandra Nita-Lazar
abstract: The Toll-like receptor (TLR) signaling pathway has a vital role during activation of the innate immune response. Tight regulation is essential to mount an effective defense against infection by pathogens while preventing runaway inflammation, and dysregulation can cause life-threatening acute and chronic pathologies. In this project, experimental and computational techniques were integrated to generate a model of the mouse macrophage TLR4 signaling pathway at the molecular interaction level. The model was parameterized using protein concentration values measured using mass spectrometry or estimated using RNA-seq, and reaction rate constants retrieved from published studies or predicted using molecular simulations. Model training used Simmune software and a dataset of experimentally measured (phospho)protein abundance ratios. The model successfully reproduced most of the experimentally measured data, however, it failed to reproduce some of the negative regulation, identifying feedback nodes warranting further experimental input. One of these potential regulatory nodes involved the non-canonical IκB kinase IKKε, whose role downstream of MyD88 is not well understood and could explain the inconsistency between the model and experimental data. We found that IKKε and TANK act downstream of the myddosome to restrain excessive ubiquitylation and activation of TRAF6 and IRAK, acting as cooperative negative regulators of the MyD88 branch of TLR signaling. To our knowledge, this is the first TLR pathway model developed using rule-based modeling at the molecular interaction level with quantitatively measured parameters, and thus it is the most strongly data-driven TLR signaling pathway model yet developed. This work highlights the critical need to elucidate pathway deactivation mechanisms to achieve predictive fidelity and identifies one of the missing mechanisms. This research was supported by the Intramural Research Program of the National Institutes of Health (NIH).

title: mzPeak - A new cloud-native community format for mass spectrometry data
authors: Oliver Kohlbacher
abstract: The growth in size of mass spectrometry (MS) data and is increasingly creating challenges for the management and analysis of MS data. Vendor formats tend to be compact, but are difficult to process and archive. Open formats such as mzML are open, but were designed with much smaller data sets in mind and do not scale well on today's data. We present mzPeak (mzpeak.org), a community format under development as a HUPO-PSI Recommendation, built on Apache Parquet. Parquet's columnar layout enables selective array loading, random access to spectra, and direct integration with cloud object-storage systems — capabilities absent from XML-based formats. The format is more typically more space-efficient than vendor formats (20-80%). We describe the current format specification, reference implementations in seven languages, available tooling, and invite community participation.

title: Detecting brain cancer-specific proteoforms from peptide-level proteomics using the ProteoPy framework
authors: Ian Dirk Fichtner, Levente Temesvari-Nagy, Fuat Kaan Aras, Gianluca Sigismondo, Christel Herold-Mende, Sandro Krieg, Wolfgang Wick, Andreas von Deimling, Felix Sahm, Moritz Gerstung, Isabell Bludau
abstract: Background: Proteoform inference-the detection of distinct molecular species arising from a single gene through alternative splicing, proteolytic cleavage, or post-translational modifications-is typically ignored in standard mass spectrometry-based proteomics workflows, despite their clinical potential as biomarkers and therapeutic targets. Here, we present ProteoPy, a lightweight Python library for protein-and peptide-level proteomics analysis built on the established AnnData class, offering an accessible proteoform inference implementation, native extensibility toward single-cell and multi-omics modalities, and a familiar entry point for researchers with a transcriptomics background through the scanpy and muon ecosystem. ProteoPy is open-source and freely available on GitHub (https://github.com/UKHD-NP/proteopy). Materials and Methods: ProteoPy provides modular functions for data import, quality control, preprocessing, statistical testing, and visualization, and is natively compatible with established packages such as scanpy and muon. A reimplementation of the COPF algorithm (Bludau et al., 2021) enables proteoform group inference from peptide-level covariation patterns. We used ProteoPy to detect and characterize proteoforms in a clinical brain cancer proteomics dataset comprising 30 samples across four subtypes: astrocytoma, meningioma, glioblastoma, and oligodendroglioma. Results: Proteoform inference revealed meningioma-specific differential regulation of RTN4 and LIMA1 proteoform groups. The inferred groups were consistent with known RNA splice isoforms and would have been missed by conventional protein-level analysis. Conclusions: ProteoPy unifies proteomics data analysis into a single, flexible framework based on the AnnData format, promoting reproducibility and cross-ecosystem interoperability. Its proteoform inference functionality extends standard proteomics workflows, enabling the identification of biologically meaningful proteoform-level regulation.

title: MiRROR: fast and accurate de novo peptide sequencing by aligning mirror symmetries in spectrum subgraphs.
authors: George Glidden-Handgis, Travis Wheeler
abstract: The de novo sequencing of peptides from tandem mass spectrometry data is challenging due to the massive volume of spectra generated by even a single experiment and the high levels of noise afflicting these data, comprising both insertion and occlusion of peaks. To address this challenge, we developed MiRROR, an explainable, deterministic algorithm for highly sensitive de novo peptide sequencing that is fast, robust to peak noise, and tolerant of charge state, post-translational modifications, and neutral losses. The MiRROR algorithm consists of three phases. Each can be accelerated using a transcriptome to restrict the space of explored peptide candidates. The first phase enumerates target masses from a library of possible amino acids, losses, modifications, and ion types. Using these target masses, initial and terminal fragments and fragment pairs are annotated. M/z values that serve as axes of mirror symmetry in the spectrum are identified as pivots. Each pivot splits the spectrum into lower and upper portions, and a corresponding spectrum graph pair is constructed. The second phase aligns these graph pairs to reveal approximately equivalent fragment paths through both lower and upper peaks. Alignments correspond to affixes of peptide sequences. The third phase composes affixes into full sequences and fills occlusion-induced breaks using branch and bound search. On preliminary benchmarks of synthetic spectra with simulated losses, random insertion and occlusion of peaks, and truncated boundaries, using a ten-core commodity laptop, MiRROR sequenced tens of spectra per second and achieved near-perfect recall and approximately zero FDR.

title: Benchmarking Fine-Tuned Large Language Models for Tandem Mass Spectrum Prediction: Competitive In-Distribution but Limited Cross-Dataset Generalization
authors: Dongyeop Jang, Youngchan Kim
abstract: Predicting tandem mass spectra (MS/MS) from chemical structure aids compound identification, and fine-tuned large language models (LLMs) have been proposed as a general-purpose alternative to mechanistic and graph-based predictors. Their accuracy has not been systematically benchmarked, however, and their transfer across reference collections is uncharacterized. We benchmark fine-tuned LLMs against established chemistry-informed predictors (CFM-ID, ICEBERG, 3DMolMS, MassFormer), comparing spectral similarity on a held-out MassBank test set (institutes absent from training) and on an independent external collection (MassSpecGym) with overlapping molecules removed. Within the training collection, the best LLMs are comparable to the chemistry-informed predictors and improve with model size, though their advantage is partial and complementary, covering only a subset of spectra. This performance is not explained by memorization: a same-molecule retrieval baseline surpasses the LLM for seen but not novel molecules. On the external collection, all LLMs perform markedly worse than the chemistry-informed predictors. This decline tracks the change of collection rather than of laboratory or molecule: accuracy is largely retained across laboratories within a collection and after accounting for molecular and instrumental factors, and mirrors the limited agreement between spectra of the same compound from different collections; under matched conditions, LLMs appear more sensitive to this change than a mechanistic predictor. These findings suggest that fine-tuned LLMs are reliable mainly on data resembling their training collection, with cross-collection generalization constrained by acquisition style rather than chemical coverage. We recommend evaluating spectral predictors on an independent, differently sourced collection, with overlapping molecules removed, before broad generalization is claimed.
keywords: Limited Cross-Dataset Generalization; tandem mass; Mass Spectrum Prediction; chemistry-informed predictors; fine-tuned LLMs

title: A threshold-free replacement for prevalence filtering in untargeted LC-MS metabolomics
authors: Chiraag Gohel, Ali Rahnavard
abstract: Untargeted LC-MS metabolomics workflows commonly apply hard prevalence filters before differential testing, forcing analysts to choose cutoffs such as 50% pooled detection or 80% per-group detection. These rules are convenient but arbitrary and unstable across datasets and sample sizes, and they exclude low-observation features before inference. We present a threshold-free alternative that keeps the full analyzable feature universe and moves feature observability into the multiple-testing step. Using observed-value moderated two-group tests, we assign each feature a positive weight based on effective sample size, a continuous proxy for pooled observed information. We also show that standard prevalence filtering is a special case of full-universe weighted BH, corresponding to a binary step-function weight on the detection axis. We benchmarked the method on two public untargeted LC-MS studies: a large inflammatory bowel disease comparison and a second family spanning four pulmonary hypertension-related contrasts across two ion modes with balanced and unbalanced resampling. Across both benchmarks, observation-based weighting was competitive with or better than ordinary BH and common hard filters regarding true positive rate, while maintaining FDR control, without dataset-specific threshold tuning. Threshold sweeps showed that no single hard cutoff remained optimal across sample sizes, while weighted BH stayed near the top of the performance range. In sparse untargeted LC-MS feature tables, prevalence may be better handled as a continuous inferential weight than as a manually chosen exclusion threshold.

title: SHINE: Decoding transcriptional-metabolic microenvironments through higher-order spatial integration
authors: Bingxue Du, Jason Wing Hon Wong, Yuanhua Huang
abstract: Spatial omics technologies are expanding to co-profile transcriptomics and metabolomics on the same tissue slide, providing complementary views of gene expression and biochemical activity to reveal molecular programs within native tissue microenvironments. However, integrating the transcriptome and metabolome remains technically challenging due to spatial misalignment, resolution disparity, and higher-order cross-modality interactions. Here, we present SHINE, a hypergraph-based computational framework for the joint analysis of spatial gene expression and metabolic networks derived from the co-profiling slide, focusing on representation learning and cross-modality interaction. Across multiple datasets, SHINE consistently outperformed existing methods for domain segmentation and biomarker co-localization, and provided interpretable insights into metabolic-transcriptional microenvironments. Specifically, on Parkinson’s disease mouse models, SHINE accurately delineates dopaminergic neuron-depleted regions and reconstructs coherent dopamine-associated axes. In human lung and breast cancers, SHINE resolves tumor-associated spatial regions and identifies spatially organized gene–metabolite programs associated with the tumor microenvironment. SHINE enables scalable spatial multi-omics integration across diverse biological systems.

title: Foundation Model Enables Interpretable Open and Error-Tolerant Searching for Mass Spectrometry-Based Proteomics
authors: Tom Altenburg, Thilo Muth, Patrick van Zalm, Hanno Steen, Bernhard Renard
abstract: Mass spectrometry-based proteomics allows to study all proteins of a sample on a molecular level. However, mass spectra are noisy and contain complex patterns, making them inherently challenging to analyze with purely algorithmic approaches. In terms of the protein sequence landscape, most recent bottom-up MS-based proteomics studies consider either a diverse pool of post-translational modifications, employ large databases – as in metaproteomics or proteogenomics, study multiple isoforms of proteins, include unspecific cleavage sites or even combinations thereof. All this makes peptide and protein identifications challenging due to sheer size of the search space. To cope with this two-sided challenge, i.e. the complexity of real spectra and the search space size, we present a foundation model, called yHydra, that jointly embeds spectra and peptides. This allows us to implement various downstream tasks and search modes in Euclidean space. In particular, we implement an open search which allows to query multiple ten-thousands of spectra against millions of peptides. Furthermore, we implement an error-tolerant search for identifying additional proteoforms that are not included in off-the-shelf reference proteomes. Our foundation model provides meaningful embeddings, as we interpret learned peptide embeddings in comparison to the peptide’s physico-chemical properties. yHydra’s open search, assigns delta masses to each identification which allows to unrestrictedly characterize post-translational modifications. The error-tolerant mode of yHydra can be used as post-processing to existing search engines or as a standalone. yHydra is evaluated on several real life data sets for the identification of modified protein sequences and shows up to 25% increase in protein identification at constant false discovery rate compared to the current state-of-the-art. Code available: https://gitlab.com/dacs-hpi/yHydra

title: Using Proteome Priors to improve De Novo Peptide Sequencing performance without constraining the search space
authors: Samuel Khan, Daniela Klaproth-Andrade, Yanik Bruns, Mathias Wilhelm, Julien Gagneur
abstract: De novo peptide sequencing (DNPS) can identify any peptide directly from mass spectrometry data, but lacks the accuracy benefits that database search methods gain from leveraging reference proteome information. Recent hybrid approaches have begun bridging this gap by incorporating peptide language models or retrieval steps, but these target broad generalization rather than supplying information about a specific reference proteome. The one prior method that incorporated target proteome information (SMSNet) applied it as a post-processing correction, meaning these corrections could not influence subsequent autoregressive token predictions. We present Proteome Priors (PP), a method that integrates target-proteome-specific information directly into the DNPS inference loop. We trained a GPT-based peptide language model on reference proteome peptides using a triplet training scheme designed to reproduce reference sequences, tolerate single-amino-acid mutations, and suppress confident predictions on out-of-distribution inputs. During inference, the language model's prefix outputs are combined with those of the base DNPS model through a single-hidden-layer fusion network with batch normalization. On the nine-species benchmark, guiding Casanovo with a same-species PP yielded a 6.0 percentage point median improvement in final precision, while a mismatched prior caused only a 1.1 percentage point drop, confirming that open search capability is preserved. When integrated with Modanovo for phosphopeptide identification in monkeypox virus-infected human cells, the PP improved the area under the precision-coverage curve from 0.747 to 0.838. These results establish late fusion of autoregressive DNPS with mutation-tolerant peptide language models as an effective architecture for hybrid peptide identification that enhances accuracy without constraining the search space.

title: Advancing Proteomic Discovery through Optimized Multi-stage Scoring and Deep Learning-Enhanced Open Search
authors: Chen Qian, Kaifei Wang, Pengzhi Mao, Ranfei Chen, Hao Chi
abstract: Protein search engines are essential for interpreting mass spectrometry data into biological insight. Current tools often face limitations in sensitivity when analyzing complex modern datasets, and lack a unified framework that effectively integrates deep learning features for both restricted and open searches, especially for scenarios aimed at discovering unknown modifications. Here, we present pFind+, a high-performance search engine extending pFind. It introduces a high-precision raw scoring module that delivers substantially improved pre-filtering ability, while recovering most of the associated computational overhead through a tailored acceleration strategy. Coupled with an enhanced rescoring framework that effectively integrates deep learning features, pFind+ uniquely supports high-sensitivity, DL-enhanced open search, enabling comprehensive PTM discovery while incorporating hardware-aware inference optimizations for practical deployment. Evaluations across diverse datasets demonstrate its superior sensitivity, with gains of 12.7–32.9% in restricted search and 8.0–38.4% in open search over the best existing tools.

title: JMod: Enabling increased multiplexing and throughput for sensitive proteomics
authors: Kevin McDonnell, Daniel Geiszler, Nathan Wamsley, Jason Derks, Zachary Cohen, Sarah Sipe, Maddy Yeh, Lina Warinner, Andrew Leduc, Harrison Specht, Nikolai Slavov
abstract: The throughput of mass spectrometry (MS) proteomics can be increased substantially by multiplexing that enables parallelization of data acquisition. Such parallelization in the mass domain (plexDIA) and the time domain (timePlex) increases the density of mass spectra and the overlap between ions originating from different precursors, potentially complicating their analysis. To enhance sequence identification and quantification from such spectra, we developed an open source software for Joint Modeling of mass spectra: JMod. It uses the intrinsic structure in the spectra and explicitly models overlapping peaks as linear superpositions of their components. This modeling enabled performing 9-plexDIA using 2 Da offset PSMtags by deconvolving the resulting overlapping isotopic envelopes in both MS1 and MS2 space. The results demonstrate 9-fold higher throughput with mostly preserved quantitative accuracy and coverage depth. This support for smaller mass offsets increases multiplexing capacity and thus proteomic throughput for a given plexDIA tag. We demonstrate JMod’s generalizability with the analysis of protein abundance and half-lives with >500 in vivo hepatocytes labelled with mTRAQ and acquired at 150% increased throughput. We identified established hepatocyte zonation markers that may be regulated by protein degradation. Single cell proteomics in particular can benefit from the accuracy and increased throughput provided by this software. By supporting enhanced decoding of DIA spectra multiplexed in the mass and time domains, JMod provides an open and flexible software that enables increasing the throughput of sensitive proteomics.

title: SPRINT-MS: A high-throughput platform for identifying protein-protein interactions using pooled IP-MS and sparse signal recovery
authors: Lena Street, Moitrish Majumdar, Katherine Rothamel, Esin Gogus, Gloria Brar, Gene Yeo, Tomas Rube, Marko Jovanovic
abstract: Protein-protein-interactions (PPIs), which govern critical cellular and physiological processes such as development and disease, form extensive networks that vary across time, conditions, and cell types, creating a complex and high-dimensional problem. There is thus a pressing need for universally applicable tools capable of mapping and quantifying PPI networks and their context-dependent dynamics with high efficiency. This talk will present SPRINT-MS (SParse Reconstruction of INTeractions by Mass Spectrometry), an integrated computational-experimental platform that leverages the signal-processing technique compressed sensing to accelerate PPI discovery. The central observation underlying the SPRINT-MS is that most protein pairs do not interact, meaning the matrix of PPIs is sparse. SPRINT-MS leverages this sparsity and implements a compressed measurement by using an algorithmically optimized antibody (or lysate) pooling scheme to transforms the PPI signal into a low-dimensional measurement vector, measuring this vector using immunopurification-mass spectrometry (IP-MS), and finally using a novel sparse signal reconstruction algorithm to recover the PPIs. This approach significantly increases throughput while reducing sample input requirements. This talk will both discuss the computational methods underlying the platform and demonstrate that SPRINT-MS, applied to 30 bait proteins of interest via either antibody or lysate pooling, is comparable to standard individual IP-MS experiments in the identification of PPIs and recapitulation of known interactions. The talk will conclude by discussing how the principles underlying SPRINT-MS can be applied to other problems in proteomics and genomics.

title: Defining context-specific molecular mechanisms from human autoimmune disease loci: Application to the CD40 locus
authors: Soumya Raychaudhuri
abstract: It is important to define causal mechanisms driving autoimmune disease. While thousands of autoimmune risk loci have been identified, it is unclear how these loci alter gene function, cell states, and the immunological dysfunction that leads to disease. If these mechanisms could be defined, then it may be possible to use this information to define curative therapies. We discuss how we use statistical genetics methods to define the causal variant. We demonstrate how many of these alleles have context-specific cis-regulatory effects. That is, they influence local gene regulation in specific immune cell contexts. To do this, we develop Dynema (Dynamic eQTL mapping in single cells), a fast and accurate single-cell model that maps context-dependent expression quantitative trait loci. Unlike existing single-cell methods. Dynema is fast enough to scale to genome-wide analyses in large-scale genotyped cohorts of single-cell data. We then demonstrate how our CRAFT-seq platform can be combined with single-base resolution editing to molecularly confirm context-dependent effects of individual SNP alleles. CRAFTseq is a quad-modal single-cell sequencing assay that links specific CRISPR edits in a cell directly to its functional and transcriptional behavior. It overcomes traditional limitations by simultaneously reading genomic DNA, full-length RNA transcripts, and cell-surface proteins in the same individual cell. We use this approach to functionally fine-map the CD40 autoimmune locus, implicated in rheumatoid arthritis, multiple sclerosis and other autoimmune conditons. Our data reveal that the causal SNP is a protective SNP that disrupts a Kozak sequence, selectively reducing CD40 protein levels without altering mRNA expression in B cells. This reduction raises the threshold for B cell activation and triggers significant trans-regulatory effects. These trans regulatory effects cannot be detected in population data, and is most prominent in activated naive B cells. In this specific context, the SNP suppresses gene modules essential for downstream signaling. These results not only point to the causal gene in that locus and the mechanistic impact of the causal SNP, but also points to a key cellular context that drives autoimmunity. These results are particularly notable given recent clinical results that non-specific B cell ablation can lead to immune reset and cure for autoimmunity. These findings demonstrate how subtle non-coding variation scales into systemic disease. They provide a blueprint for how non-coding variants can be used to define disease mechanisms.

title: Using Interpretable Latent Representations of Spatial Transcriptomic Datasets to Identify Molecular Mechanisms of Immunomodulation
authors: Hanxi Xiao, Niranjana Natarajan, Javad Rahimikollu, Partha Dutta, Jishnu Das
abstract: Modern spatial transcriptomic technologies enable the study of cellular organization and interaction in complex tissues, but the resulting data are high dimensional, sparse, and strongly multicollinear. These properties make inference difficult: the goal is not to recover large sets of correlated markers, but to identify a small, mechanistically meaningful set of causal targets that can be experimentally perturbed. Here, we present an end-to-end, interpretable machine learning framework designed for this task. The framework integrates Significant Latent Factor Interaction Discovery (SLIDE), an interpretable inference method with statistical guarantees, with regulatory network inference and in silico perturbation. Rather than introducing new architectures, we constrain latent representations to be sparse, identifiable, and biologically actionable. Latent factors capture coordinated gene programs rather than individual markers, while regulatory network integration provides mechanistic structure that constrains interpretation and filters correlations that are not experimentally actionable. Together, these components prioritize a minimal set of context-specific therapeutic targets from tens of thousands of measured features. Applied to spatial transcriptomic profiles of human heart tissue after myocardial infarction (MI), the framework disentangles macrophage transcriptional programs defined by proximity to activated fibroblasts and reveals microniche-specific regulatory drivers. Guided by latent-factor prioritization, we identify candidate genes and transcription factors whose perturbation in human and mouse macrophages alters fibroblast activation in vitro and ex vivo. We show that in vivo silencing of Tvp23b, Tdrd6, and B3galnt1, as well as the transcription factors Mafk and Maz in microniche-specific macrophages, improves cardiac function longitudinally and suppresses fibrosis in a murine model of MI.

title: Segmentation-free discovery of spatial niches in image-based spatial transcriptomics
authors: Tamjeed Azad, Yuri Pritykin
abstract: Image-based spatial transcriptomics technologies such as Xenium, MERFISH, and CosMx now generate millions of precisely localized transcript coordinates per tissue section, enabling analyses at subcellular to multicellular resolution. Many organs and complex tissues are organized into spatial niches, which could be defined as recurrent microenvironments composed of one or several cell types that share signaling cues, metabolic states, and functional interactions. However, current analyses often depend on imperfect cell segmentation, limiting the accuracy of downstream spatial clustering and niche discovery. To overcome these limitations, we developed Ecoton (Expression colocalization of transcripts for niche discovery), a new segmentation-free framework that identifies spatial niches directly from transcript coordinates. Ecoton first aggregates nearby transcripts into metatranscripts using density-based clustering, learns a gene-gene spatial colocalization graph, and identifies archetypal modules of colocalized genes. The spatial data is then scanned for dense regions of transcripts encoded by genes from these modules, defining transcript-level niches. Optionally, these transcript niches are then mapped back to segmented cells. In simulations and applied to datasets from various technologies, including Xenium, MERFISH, CosMx, and across biological systems, including brain, lymph nodes, intestine, melanoma, lung and colorectal cancer, Ecoton outperforms existing niche detection methods and identifies previously described and new niches. By operating directly at the transcript level, Ecoton enables robust multi-scale characterization of tissue architecture, even when cell segmentation is noisy or incomplete. Ecoton provides an efficient and flexible framework for spatial niche detection broadly applicable across complex biological systems.

title: Hist2Pheno enables nuclei-resolved phenotypic prediction from histological images in esophageal squamous cell carcinoma
authors: Lingyu Li, Lu Yu, Yuanhua Huang
abstract: Cellular phenotypes within the tumor immune microenvironment are critical for understanding tumor progression and response to immune checkpoint inhibitors, yet are largely shaped by spatial tumor-immune colocalization[1]. Spatial profiling technologies such as CODEX[2] or PhenoCycler Fusion (PCF) enable high-dimensional, spatially resolved characterization of cell states, but are limited by cost, throughput and scalability. In contrast, haematoxylin and eosin (HE) histopathology is widely available yet lacks direct phenotypic resolution, as highlighted in our recent FineST work[3], motivating computational approaches to infer spatial phenotypes from histological images. In this study, we propose Hist2Pheno (Fig. 1B), a computational framework that enables transforming histological images to nuclei-resolved phenotype predictions by leveraging histological foundation models. Hist2Pheno first performs cross-modality preprocessing, including image registration between HE and PCF imaging data, then expert-guided cell-type annotation to construct hierarchical phenotype labels y_level1, y_level2âˆˆRnÃ—1, and finally segments nuclei and extracts tile-level embeddings to represent single-cell morphological features XâˆˆRnÃ—p (Fig. 1B, Step 1). Based on these features, Hist2Pheno employs an MLP backbone with a dual-head design to jointly predict fine-and coarse-grained phenotypes, with hierarchical constraints to ensure consistency across levels (Fig. 1B, Step 2). Finally, the trained model generalizes to in-sample and out-of-sample HE images to predict nuclei-resolved phenotype maps at whole-slide scale without requiring additional molecular profiling (Fig. 1B, Step 3). To evaluate the performance of Hist2Pheno in cell-type prediction, we assembled a large-scale dataset of human esophageal squamous cell carcinoma (ESCC; Fig. 1A), comprising paired HE and PCF images across multiple clinical conditions, including untreated (SA) and treated cohorts (NCRT, NICT and NCT), totaling over 8 million annotated cells with hierarchical cell-type compositions. Taking the SA and NCRT datasets as a case study (Fig. 1D), we first assessed nuclei segmentation quality and observed strong concordance with CODEX across 28 tumor ROIs (Pearson r = 0.887 for SA and r = 0.898 for NCRT), with mean cell areas (56.94 Î¼m2) consistent with the predefined patch size (8Ã—8 Î¼m2). We then evaluated prediction accuracy by comparing inferred cell types with CODEX annotations from clinical experts on NCRT tumor1 ROI, where Hist2Pheno achieved high accuracy across ROIs (e.g., Acc = 0.832 for Tumors, 0.787 for Epithelial). Visually, from local to global, predicted phenotype maps closely matched the ground truth across all 28 tumor regions under NCRT treatment. Furthermore, we assessed generalization on external datasets and found that Hist2Pheno accurately predicts nuclei-resolved cell types from HE images in a VisiumHD lung dataset, consistent with its adjacent Xenium ground truth. As a computational toolbox, Hist2Pheno enables refined cell-type annotation to provide insights into context-specific cellular interactions and signaling (Fig. 1C), including accurate single-cell mapping, spatial cell-state transitions, and intercellular communication networks. The results on the ESCC dataset are illustrated in Fig. 1D, where we show that the predicted phenotypes achieve strong performance in annotating fine-grained cell types and reveal spatial cell-cell interaction patterns across tumor regions. In particular, Hist2Pheno captures heterogeneous cellular compositions and delineates spatial niches that are consistent with CODEX measurements. Moreover, it extends phenotypic prediction to regions where only histological images are available, enabling whole-slide, nuclei-resolved mapping without additional molecular profiling. This computational framework significantly reduces experimental cost and complexity, offering strong potential for scalable analysis of histopathology images in both research and clinical settings. title: Single-cell spatial transcriptomics of archived colitis biopsies uncovers cellular neighborhoods defining two distinct archetypes of vedolizumab resistance
authors: Alexis Combes
abstract: Imaging-based single-cell spatial transcriptomics (iSCST) on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded (FFPE) tissue enables comprehensive analysis of archived specimens while preserving spatial context, critical to understanding ulcerative colitis (UC) pathology. Here, we deployed a robust framework for applying iSCST to clinical FFPE mucosal biopsies from patients with UC, immune checkpoint inhibitor-induced colitis, and healthy controls. iSCST using custom Xenium gene panels enabled precise detection of diverse cell subsets and disease-specific genes. By resolving cells within their native tissue context, we mapped transcriptionally distinct fibroblast subsets within mucosal niches, including inflammation-associated fibroblasts (IAFs), and identified colitis-specific cellular neighborhoods formed by IAFs, monocytes, and neutrophils. Critically, transcriptional signatures and spatial cellular neighborhoods stratified vedolizumab (VDZ) response and revealed two mechanistically distinct patient archetypes of treatment resistance: an innate archetype defined by an IAF–monocyte–neutrophil cellular neighborhood, and an adaptive archetype characterized by a gut-associated lymphoid tissue cellular neighborhood. In contrast, VDZ responders were defined by enrichment of an epithelial cellular neighborhood, underscoring that response and resistance to VDZ are encoded not by individual cell types alone but by the spatial organization of cells into discrete tissue niches. These cellular neighborhood signatures were validated in internal and external datasets, supporting two reproducible archetypes of VDZ resistance in UC. Together, these findings establish a novel framework for understanding patient-specific resistance mechanisms directly from archived clinical tissue, while offering a powerful iSCST approach for analyzing FFPE specimens and identifying spatially-defined biomarkers to enhance risk stratification in routine clinical workflows

title: A multimodal foundation model for single-cell immune profiling
authors: Xu Liao, Wenpin Hou, Zhicheng Ji
abstract: Single-cell immune-profiling technologies that jointly measure gene expression and T cell receptor (TCR) sequences have transformed our ability to dissect the functional states and antigen specificities of T cells in health and disease. While existing computational methods enable integration of these modalities, most are limited to narrow tasks such as clonotype annotation or TCR-based clustering and lack the generalizability required for broad biological inference. Here, we present a multimodal foundation model that integrates gene expression and immune receptor data for comprehensive single-cell immune profiling. Unlike previous models that rely solely on numerical features, our model incorporates the structured nature of TCR sequences to enable joint representation learning across modalities. It supports a wide range of inference tasks, including prediction of tissue origin, disease state, antigen specificity, and gene expression profiles from receptor sequences. It generalizes across diverse datasets and consistently outperforms existing methods, offering a scalable and versatile framework for advancing computational immunology and understanding T cell biology.

title: Keynote - Golnaz Vahedi
authors: Golnaz Vahedi
abstract: Adaptive immunity depends on naïve CD4 T cells accurately interpreting cytokine cues and committing to specialized T helper lineages. Cytokine-activated signaling cascades relay extracellular signals to the nucleus, reprogramming transcription through coordinated remodeling of the chromatin landscape. Cytokines and their downstream transcription factors have been reported to shape chromatin accessibility and histone modifications. Yet, their influence on three-dimensional (3D) genome architecture in CD4 T helper cells remains inadequately defined. Although population-based sequencing approaches relying on chromatin fragmentation have been used, they obscure intact chromatin fiber organization and prevent single-allele resolution. Here, we directly visualize the 3D configuration of a locus containing the ETS family paralogs Ets1 and Fli1 in thymocytes and CD4 Th1 cells using a sub-diffraction, sequential imaging strategy that preserves native chromatin architecture at single-allele resolution. We demonstrate that Th1-polarizing cytokines actively reposition a T cell–specific super-enhancer toward the geometric center of the locus. This radial reorganization is accompanied by increased multi-way enhancer-promoter contacts linking Ets1 and Fli1 to the super-enhancer, resulting in coordinated activation of both paralogs. Strikingly, deletion of the super-enhancer eliminates these architectural features, rendering thymocytes and Th1 cells structurally comparable at this locus. Together, cytokine signaling can drive lineage-specific gene activation by spatially repositioning a super-enhancer within local chromatin architecture. These findings provide a structural framework for understanding how disease-associated genetic variants at the Ets1– Fli1 locus may perturb super-enhancer positioning and multi-way promoter interactions in cis, thereby predisposing to CD4+ T cell–mediated immune disorders.

title: Comprehensive Mapping of Immune Nanobody Repertoires with NanoMAP
authors: William White, Edward Moseley, Jacqueline M. Tremblay, Jackson Reilly, Akram A. Da'Dara, Patrick J. Skelly, Lenore J. Cowen, Charles B. Shoemaker
abstract: Nanobodies have recently emerged as alternatives to classical antibodies in therapeutic and diagnostic contexts from parasites to bacteria to viruses, promising improved stability and simpler manufacturing. To improve nanobody discovery efficiency, we developed an integrated experimental and computational pipeline for detailed characterization of the target binding properties of complete alpaca immune repertoires using our custom Nanobody Meta-clustering Analysis Platform (NanoMAP). We tested our pipeline on three distinct pools of targets, immunizing two alpacas with each pool and generating cDNA and phage display libraries from their immune repertoires. We then panned the phage libraries on each target. To produce more detailed binding information, we performed panning variations using subunits, natural variants, intact pathogens, and binding site competitors. Deep sequencing reads from nanobody libraries before and after each panning were pooled and analyzed with NanoMAP to identify nanobody clonal families and assess their levels of enrichment from the library in each panning, reflecting their affinities. NanoMAP outperformed standard clustering methods, producing clonal families that are coherent in sequence and function and detecting rare but high affinity families. By aggregating sequencing data within clonal families, NanoMAP produced reliable and rich data on nanobody repertoire binding phenotypes for each antigen, enhancing nanobody discovery capabilities.

title: Deep learning TCR-pMHC structure prediction differentiates epitope specific interactions
authors: Michael Robben
abstract: T-cell receptor (TCR) targeting is a computationally complex problem that, if solved, could accelerate CAR-T cell therapy development, Vaccine testing, and high-throughput research of infectious disease, autoimmune disease and cancer. Current solutions rely solely on sequence identity but fail to generalize to unseen epitopes, because epitope specificity is dependent on biophysical interactions between the protein molecules. In this study, we determined that deep-learning generated TCR-pMHC structures contain features that predict epitope specificity. Machine learning models trained on these features and generated structures show higher accuracy and AUC than sequence based models. We determined that non-interacting structures lacked the physics interactions that are observed in interacting structures. This was confirmed in molecular dynamic simulations through an increase in time to stabilize binding energy and reduced hydrogen bond lifetimes. Steered molecular dynamics simulation revealed alternative conformations predicted by deep learning inference may be key to understanding why epitope specific interactions lead to an intracellular immune response. The models developed in this study were compiled into a notebook-based webserver environment to empower immunology researchers to predict TCR-epitope specificity. This study reinforces the potential for deep learning structure prediction algorithms to make important discoveries related to immune and non-immune protein-protein interactions.

title: Scalable Unmutated Common Ancestor Inference of Paired B Cell Receptor Ancestors Across Immune Repertoires
authors: Cole Jensen, Steven H. Kleinstein, Kenneth Hoehn
abstract: B cells play a central role in adaptive immunity by producing antibodies that recognize and neutralize pathogens. Each B cell expresses a unique B cell receptor (BCR) composed of paired heavy and light chains generated through V(D)J recombination, creating a diverse repertoire of antigen-inexperienced (naive) B cells capable of recognizing a wide range of antigens. During immune responses, naive B cells become activated, proliferate, and diversify through somatic hypermutation and selection, generating related descendants whose evolutionary relationships can be reconstructed using phylogenetic methods. These lineage trees illuminate affinity maturation trajectories, key mutations, and antibody evolution. A key goal is inferring unobserved ancestors, including the naive unmutated common ancestor (UCA). However, accurate UCA inference is challenging because phylogenetic methods alone do not fully account for diversification processes shaping BCR sequences, specifically those imposed by V(D)J recombination. Integrating recombination-based generation probabilities with phylogenetic likelihoods enables accurate, scalable UCA inference. We can analyze entire repertoires (hundreds to thousands of clones) with comparable or improved accuracy and faster runtimes than existing methods. It uniquely infers paired heavy-light chain UCAs from single-cell data. We present two complementary analyses: paired reconstruction of UCAs and intermediates for a broadly neutralizing antibodies HIV lineage, and identification of shared mutations across entire BCR sequences in convergent clones. Scalable reconstruction of lineage origins allows repertoire-wide study of mutations in critical antibody regions. This capability will strengthen the interpretation of immune repertoire data and accelerate progress in vaccine design, antibody engineering, and immunotherapy. Our method is implemented in the R package Dowser.
