title: A signaling-informed sequence-to-function model identifies mechanisms of cytokine-specific gene regulation
authors: Anamarie Martinez, Yaxuan Yang, Ali Tugrul Balci, Laura F. Strube, Caroline I. Larkin, Neha Cheemalavagu, Karsen E. Shoger, James R. Faeder, Maria Chikina, Rachel A. Gottschalk
abstract: Signal transducer and activator of transcription (STAT) transcription factors are activated by diverse cytokines to regulate distinct gene programs and cellular outcomes. How STAT activation patterns are decoded at the gene level to produce context-specific transcriptional responses remains poorly understood. Building on our published computational workflow that combines mechanistic modeling of STAT dynamics with machine learning to predict gene expression (Cheemalavagu et al. 2024), we now use a sequence-to-function (S2F) framework to predict gene expression based on STAT phosphorylation dynamics and promoter sequences. The model inputs DNA sequence (16,384 base pairs centered on the transcription start site) and simulated STAT1/STAT3 phosphorylation trajectories to predict cytokine-induced gene expression across 6 cytokine stimulation conditions. Adding signaling features improves per-gene correlation predictions for 70% of unseen genes in unseen conditions compared to a model trained on sequence alone. FIMO-based motif scanning shows that sequence regions with high model attribution are enriched for STAT motifs across all conditions, and STAT motif enrichment scales with response magnitude. Leveraging novel STAT1 and STAT3 CUT&RUN data, our S2F model supported identification of sequence features associated with STAT1-and STAT3-specific binding sites. Finally, the model identifies motifs associated with non-STAT transcription factors that we are relating to STAT1 and STAT3 binding to identify cooperating pathways supporting gene-level decoding of cytokine context.

title: TyCHE enables time-resolved lineage tracing of B cells, tumors, and other heterogeneously evolving cell populations
authors: Kenneth Hoehn, Jessie Fielding, Sherry Wu, Hunter Melton, Nic Fisk, Louis du Plessis
abstract: Phylogenetic methods for cellular lineage tracing have driven significant insights into cell development, immune responses, and tumor evolution. While most methods estimate mutation trees, in which branches represent mutation, time-resolved lineage trees have branches that represent calendar time, meaning they could relate events like cellular migration and differentiation to perturbations like vaccines and drug treatments. However, somatic mutation rates can vary dramatically by cell type, biasing existing methods. For example, B cells undergo rapid somatic hypermutation during immune responses before becoming quiescent memory cells, while tumors, bacteria, and viruses can develop rapidly evolving “hypermutator" variants. To build accurate cellular time trees, we introduce TyCHE (Type-linked Clocks for Heterogenous Evolution), a Bayesian phylogenetics package that infers time-resolved lineage trees even if sub-populations evolve at dramatically different rates. We show through simulations of B cell germinal center reactions that TyCHE estimates more accurate trees, dates, and ancestral cell types than existing methods. We applied TyCHE to single cell and bulk B cell receptor sequences to reconstruct memory cell differentiation during chronic HIV infection, as well as the timing of recall germinal center reactions following repeated influenza vaccination. We further use TyCHE to infer clinically useful lineage trees of a hypermutating glioma tumor lineage and progression of an acute bacterial lung infection, applications where existing methods fail. TyCHE opens new avenues for testing how cell proliferation, differentiation, and migration shape responses to vaccines, drug treatments, and other stimuli. TyCHE and SimBLE are available as open-source software compatible with the BEAST2 and Immcantation ecosystems.

title: Agentic AI for screening ligand– target binding affinity
authors: Simona Rabinovici-Cohen, Jeff Weber, Alex Golts, Yoel Shoshan, Efrat Hexter, Bum Chul Kwon, Joao Bettencourt-Silva, Wendy Cornell, Ella Barkan, Michal Ozery-Flato
abstract: Advances in high-throughput discovery technologies, computational design, and sequencing methods are generating unprecedented numbers of candidate ligands—including small molecules, antibodies, and other molecules—binding to disease-relevant targets. However, validating binding activity through wet-lab experiments remains costly and time-consuming. To address this bottleneck, we investigate the application of fine-tuned foundation models and agentic AI to computationally prioritize ligand candidates based on their predicted binding affinity to target molecules. Our system leverages MAMMAL, an open-source biomedical foundation model trained on billions of biological samples spanning multiple modalities, including proteins, small molecules, and single-cell gene expression data. To evaluate its ability to prioritize ligand–target interactions across diverse modalities, we fine-tuned MAMMAL on multiple binding prediction tasks. For antibody binding prediction, we fine-tuned the model on the SAbDab dataset, achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.90 on the test set and outperforming baseline approaches based on ESM-2 embeddings coupled with classifiers. For small-molecule binding prediction, we fine-tuned MAMMAL on the SGC DEL dataset, achieving an AUC-ROC of 0.95 on the test set. These results demonstrate the ability of foundation models to learn binding-relevant representations across diverse ligand classes. To make these models accessible to researchers without machine-learning expertise, we integrated them into an agentic AI system. The fine-tuned models were exposed as tools within agentic workflows, enabling interactive research dialogues in which AI agents select tools, perform inference, and interpret results. For selected models, we additionally provide optimized inference through vLLM plugins to support efficient, scalable deployment. This framework lowers technical barriers while enabling efficient triage of ligand– target pairs and reducing experimental workload. The architecture is designed to accommodate additional ligand modalities and binding prediction tasks, supporting scalable virtual screening and therapeutic discovery. This work was conducted in part within the scope of the LIGAND-AI EU project.

title: Systems Vaccinology Reveals Shared and Distinct Early Transcriptional Predictors of High Antibody Responses Across Vaccines
authors: Stephanie Hao, Ivan Tomic, Pawel Przytycki, Adriana Tomic
abstract: Vaccination against infectious diseases is an effective public health intervention. However, vaccine efficacy varies widely among individuals, as immunity arises from complex interplay between genetic, environmental, and immunological factors. To date, immunogenicity analyses are largely pathogen-specific, limiting discovery of shared immune architecture governing durable immunity. To this end, we leveraged three vaccine cohorts, yellow fever (YF), influenza (Flu), and hepatitis B (HB; n=1,121), across 25 studies. Within each pathogen, machine learning predicted high antibody response from early post-vaccination transcriptomic features summarized as blood transcriptional modules (BTMs) quantified using GSVA scores (AUC = 0.82, 0.75, and 0.69 for YF, HB, and Flu, respectively). Predictive BTMs were identified using bootstrapped permutation feature importance and interpreted with surrogate decision trees. This systems vaccinology approach revealed both shared and pathogen-specific immunological programs differentiating responses. Durable responses to yellow fever were associated with lymphocyte activation programs including B-cell receptor signaling and MAIT-related signatures. Hepatitis B responses were enriched for Th2-associated pathways and innate immune programs including plasmacytoid dendritic cell and M1 macrophage modules. Influenza responses were characterized by cellular proliferation and metabolic activation signatures, including c-Myc–regulated transcription, mitotic replication pathways, and enrichment of CD4+ T cells and M2 macrophages, including higher expression of POLA1 (FDR < 0.001). 50% of shared BTMs exhibited concordant directional regulation across cohorts, threefold greater than expected by chance (permutation p = 0.009), indicating partially conserved immune architecture across pathogens. Taken together, these findings suggest that durable vaccine responses emerge from partially conserved immunological processes that manifest through pathogen-specific transcriptional programs.

title: Ever more applications of the Burrows-Wheeler transform in computational genomics
authors: Richard Durbin
abstract: I will discuss a series of applications of the Burrows-Wheeler transform, based on suffix sorting, for sequence matching and compression in computational genomics. Initial applications, as in bwa with Heng Li, were for finding maximal exact matches as an alternative to fixed length seeds based on hashing for sequence read mapping. Next the Positional Burrows-Wheeler Transform (PBWT) incorporating run-length encoding gave both excellent compression and very fast maximal matching of haplotype sequences; this underlies most modern genotype imputation tools. More recently, the Graph Burrows-Wheeler Transform (GBWT) was introduced to provide path indices over pangenome graphs, again providing both compression and efficient search. Finally, I will describe a new dynamic GBWT framework based on doubly-linked skip lists that when implemented over a sparse de-Bruijn graph enables rapid O(log_N) time insertion and matching, supporting single-threaded pangenome graph construction and indexing at ~15 seconds per gigabase.

title: Toward Predictive Models of Human Biology and Disease
authors: Olga Troyanskaya
abstract: A central goal of precision medicine is to develop predictive, mechanistic models of human health and disease that connect molecular processes to organismal physiology and clinical outcomes. Achieving this requires integrating information across scales—from genomic sequence and regulatory programs to cellular systems, organs, and longitudinal phenotypes—within models that are both mechanistically grounded and predictive. In this talk, I will describe AI frameworks that connect sequence, regulation, multi-omic networks, and biological context into unified representations of dynamic biological systems. These include models that interpret genomic variation through its biochemical and regulatory effects, network-aware approaches that perform in silico genetics by modeling how perturbations propagate through cellular circuits and pathways, and genetics-informed models of phenotype that link molecular programs to disease heterogeneity and trajectories. These purpose-built, multimodal, and multi-scale approaches integrate genomic, molecular, and clinical data to uncover drivers of disease, define biologically grounded subtypes, and predict outcomes across diverse contexts, including cancer, autism, and chronic kidney disease. The next frontier lies in combining these multi-scale models with verifiable, agentic AI systems that can reason over biological evidence, support hypothesis generation and testing, and enable transparent, reproducible scientific discovery.

title: Uncovering the Palimpsest of India's Population History Using Genome-Scale Analysis: Implications for Disease Epidemiology
authors: Partha P Majumder
abstract: Robust reconstruction of human population history has been possible because of major advances in molecular, computational and statistical genetics. The ability to determine DNA sequences of a large number of humans and to study the sequence variation by calibrating the rate of accumulation of changes with evolutionary time has enabled robust inferences about our population history. These data indicate that (a) ancestors of all present-day people, i.e., modern humans and other humans, evolved in Africa about 600,000 years ago; (b) a large group of humans came out of Africa and evolved as Nearderthals, Denisovans and other archaic humans; (c) modern humans evolved in Africa and spread out within Africa, and (d) modern humans started to come out of Africa about 100,000 years ago, and admixed with both Neanderthals and Denisovans. After modern humans emerged out of Africa, one of the first waves of migration entered India. Contemporary India has a rich tapestry of cultures and ecologies. There are about 400 tribal and more than 4000 groups of castes and subcastes, all largely endogamous, speaking languages that belong to four major linguistic families. We shall provide genomic evidence of how India may have been peopled, the nature and extent of its genomic diversity, and genomic structure among the extant populations of India. We shall then provide a narrative, with evidence, of how the genomic diversity may have impacted on disease epidemiology – susceptibility to disease and response to treatment.

title: Foundations of Human-AI Co-Science
authors: Marinka Zitnik
abstract: AI scientists are AI systems that reason, hypothesize, and experiment alongside human researchers. In this talk, I will show how human-AI co-science is emerging through three capabilities: understanding disease, discovering interventions, and reasoning about treatments. Across these settings, we evaluate AI through discovery loops that pair AI with experiments in biological and clinical labs. I will begin with disease understanding. Foundation models trained on multimodal relational data predict disease mechanisms that are difficult to identify from any single dataset. Drawing on studies of Parkinson disease, bipolar disorder, and Alzheimer disease, I will show how these models generate hypotheses about disease mechanisms and therapeutic opportunities that are evaluated in vitro, in vivo, and through longitudinal health trajectories of five million patients. I will then turn to intervention discovery. AI scientists search large experimental spaces to identify therapeutic targets, predict synthetic lethal interactions in cancer, and model personalized responses to immunotherapy. Finally, I will discuss treatment reasoning. Therapeutic decisions require integrating disease context, comorbidities, medications, and biomedical evidence. I will present AI scientists that combine language models with biomedical tools to reason about treatments developed over the past century. We evaluate these systems through blinded expert assessments in rare diseases, real-world treatment decisions, and population-scale analyses of longitudinal health records. These systems define a foundation for human-AI co-science. They are powered by scientific environments that connect language models to an open universe of scientific tools, democratizing AI scientists.

title: SEA-Alzheimer Disease Challenge
authors: Marina Sirota
abstract: Alzheimer’s disease (AD) is the most common neurodegenerative disorder, affecting approximately 1 in 9 individuals (10.9%) aged 65 and older. title: Olfactory Mixtures Prediction Challenge
authors: Pablo Meyer
abstract: A central goal of sensory sciences is to establish systematic rules linking shifts in physical stimuli to corresponding shifts in perception. While these rules are well defined in vision and audition, they remain elusive in olfaction, which hinders digitization of this sensory domain. Prediction of pairwise olfactory perceptual similarity is widely seen as a promising framework for establishing such rules. The DREAM Olfactory Mixtures Prediction Challenge aimed to advance such framework by inviting participants to develop predictive models of perceptual similarity of molecular mixture pairs from a curated cross study dataset. Throughout this DREAM community challenge, international teams competed for three months to develop machine-learning models predicting how close two molecular mixtures are in odor perceptual space. We demonstrate that an ensemble of diverse models yields a quantitative and generalizable metric for odor mixture similarity that reliably surpasses existing state-of-the-art methods. Our model provides a machine-readable and common framework for neuroscientist, chemists, and engineers to tackle the remaining challenges toward achieving full-fidelity digital olfaction.

title: Target2035-DREAMQ Challenges
authors: Gustavo Stolovitzky
abstract: Rapid progress in artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) is expected to dramatically accelerate the way therapeutic strategies and drugs are discovered. One of the first steps in a drug discovery campaign is to identify bioactive “hit” molecules that can be optimized into drugs. DNA-encoded libraries coupled with ML (DEL-ML) is a novel hit-finding technique where ML models are trained on ultra-large DEL screening data and used to predict hits from catalogs of readily available molecules. However, best strategies for data representation, model architecture, or hit selection are not yet clearly established. In this first open DEL-ML Target 2035 drug discovery challenge, AI experts combined their ML models with computational chemistry approaches to discover hits for the target protein WDR91, both retrospectively and prospectively. A great variety of computational strategies and tools were deployed, and novel WDR91 ligands were discovered. While a clear differentiating factor was the choice in data to train ML models, variations in fingerprint representation or model architecture had comparatively little impact on the outcome, emphasizing the need for impactful AI-driven technological improvement. A second similar challenge is being organized using PGK as a target and a version of this challenge using Quantum Computing will also be organized.

title: Digital Pen Feature Extraction Challenge
authors: Solveig Sieberts,
abstract: Cognitive assessments using digital pen capture offer significant advantages over traditional pen-and-paper tests by capturing both final answers and real-time data on how those answers are produced. This includes timing, pressure, stroke patterns, and pauses—providing a richer, more granular view of cognitive processes. These fine-grained metrics can help detect subtle cognitive changes earlier than standard scoring alone, improving sensitivity and diagnostic accuracy. However, open source packages to extract relevant features are limited. The Digital Pen Feature Extraction Challenge aims to develop open-source feature extraction methods which can be used to better contextualize traditional pen-and-paper cognitive assessments and provide the research community with open-source alternatives to proprietary software, which is prohibitively expensive for academic researchers. Planned to launch in Fall 2026, this challenge will focus on Digital Clock Drawing Assessments (dCDT), a popular digital pen cognitive assessment, and will assess algorithms on their ability to predict various cognitive domains and risk factors.

title: BioAgentBench: Reliable LLM Agents for End-to-End Omics Workflow Orchestration
authors: Sajib Acharjee Dip, Adrika Zafor, Liqing Zhang
abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents offer a promising interface for automating bioinformatics analyses, yet their reliability in executing real-world omics workflows remains largely uncharacterized. We present BioAgentBench, a unified framework for developing, integrating, and rigorously evaluating agentic systems that orchestrate end-to-end bioinformatics pipelines. Our approach introduces domain-specific Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers that wrap standard command-line omics tools—covering RNA-seq preprocessing, differential expression, and pathway enrichment—into structured, machine-interpretable interfaces. These components are seamlessly integrated with existing workflow systems, enabling reproducible and production-ready execution. We define a suite of reliability-focused metrics, including execution success rate, tool-call correctness, recovery from runtime errors, and biological validity of outputs. Across diverse transcriptomic and multi-omics tasks, our system achieves over 85% end-to-end pipeline completion, with a 30–45% improvement in error recovery compared to unconstrained agent baselines. Downstream analyses demonstrate that agent-generated outputs preserve biological signal, yielding consistent differential expression profiles and significantly enriched pathways aligned with known disease mechanisms. Our results reveal that structured tool interfaces and constrained reasoning substantially improve agent robustness, highlighting the importance of standardized protocols for scientific AI systems. BioAgentBench establishes a foundation for scalable, trustworthy, and accessible AI-driven bioinformatics, enabling domain scientists to interact with complex analytical pipelines through natural language while maintaining rigorous computational guarantees.

title: Evidence Agents: evaluating a multi-agent framework for evidence-based scientific discovery
authors: Joao Bettencourt-Silva, Natasha Mulligan, Scott Espenschied, Mallory Zammataro, Laura Gardiner, Jennifer Kelly, Ashley Evans, Ritesh Krishna, Simona Rabinovici-Cohen, Timothy Rumbell, Vibha Anand, Ryan Musich, James Kozloski, Jianying Hu, Thaddeus Stappenbeck
abstract: Recent advances in single-cell technologies and biomedical foundation models are generating new insights and high-volume, data-intensive challenges that require careful examination and benchmarking. Novel scientific discoveries arising from these data need to be supported by knowledge gathered through multiple rigorous experiments as well as a foundation of prior knowledge. Here, we introduce a multi-agent AI framework designed to automate the search, extraction, and reasoning of biomedical information to accelerate single-cell scientific discovery. The primary objective is to provide accurate, evidence-based responses to complex research questions regarding human cells in the context of single-cell RNA-seq analyses. The agentic framework’s modular architecture includes a planner agent responsible for orchestrating workflows as well as specialist tools and agents to mine scientific literature (e.g.,PubMed Central), biological and omics experiment databases (e.g.,CellXGene), knowledge bases or graphs (e.g.,OpenTargets), and biomedical foundation model results (e.g.,BMFM-RNA). Specialized tools and agents were evaluated individually (e.g., relation extraction from scientific literature, algorithms for querying and ranking experiment databases) and the overall system performance was evaluated through a structured, non blinded survey in which four human domain-expert were asked to answer three specific questions about cells and genes. The reviewers then compared the agentic framework outputs with the responses obtained through their own bioinformatic workflows and methods when answering the same research questions. Finally, the overall framework outputs were compared against a state-of-the-art general-purpose biomedical AI agent (Biomni). The challenges and bottlenecks of benchmarking individual tools and agents within the framework as well as the overall multi-agent system output are discussed.

title: A Framework for Benchmarking Artificial Intelligence Agents on Crowdsourced Computational Biology Competitions
authors: Nikolaos Kalavros, Lun Ai, Orion Banks, Joseph Yu, Elias Chaibub Neto, Gaia Andreoletti, Solveig Sieberts, Jineta Banerjee, Adi Tarca, Tomiko Oskotsky, Marina Sirota, Luca Foschini, Julio Saez-Rodriguez, Gustavo Stolovitzky
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM) agents have emerged as a paradigm shift in software development, with rapidly rising use, as shown by Github commit statistics. Initial benchmarks have showcased their abilities in completing computational biology tasks where the answers are either multiple choice or a specific value in a well researched task that occurs often.While many sophisticated solutions exist to enhance these agents’ performance, such as multiple agents with different personalities or equipping agents with skills, their performance on more open-ended tasks remains poorly characterized. We present here a framework that performs automated execution of multiple commercial and open source coding agents. We include general coding agents and specialized bioinformatics agents. These agents are run on DREAM challenge gated data, benchmarked against real human crowdsourced solutions. We showcase that agents can rank within the top few teams but not yet outperform the top humans in performance. Furthermore, we zoom in and address how we can optimize these agents by leveraging evolutionary solutions that iterate on the input prompt, swarms of agents and the effect of increasing the agents’ test time compute. We highlight promising results from AutoResearch, an agent swarm method, which measurably improves performance, albeit at the cost of potential overfitting. We present a leaderboard of agents, and a set of carefully stewarded challenges to evaluate new solutions, as well as an initial comparison of optimization methods that work on these agents. We hope that our work contributes to the responsible adoption of AI agents in the life sciences.

title: Prospective Benchmarking of Generalist AI Agents Across Biological Prediction Challenges
authors: Gaia Andreoletti, Elias Chaibub Neto, Orion Banks, Jineta Banerjee, Luca Foschini, Solveig K Sieberts
abstract: Open prediction challenges provide rigorous blind benchmarks for evaluating computational methods in biomedicine. As AI agents from general-purpose coding assistants to domain-specific co-scientist systems become increasingly prevalent in computational biology, these frameworks offer a valuable lens for assessing agent performance relative to human expertise. We report AI agent performance across seven biological prediction tasks spanning two major challenge series: variant effect prediction (CAGI7) and Alzheimer's disease neuropathology staging from single-nucleus RNA-seq data (SEA-AD DREAM Challenge). In CAGI7, a co-scientist agent participated across five challenges including TSC2 stability prediction, LPL abundance prediction, ARSA missense stability, ATP7B functional scoring, BARD1 variant effect prediction, and FGFR kinase drug resistance prediction. Performance was markedly task-dependent. On the FGFR drug resistance challenge, the agent's mechanistic reasoning about the molecular brake mechanism was recognized by assessors as well-suited for predicting Pemigatinib resistance. Performance was more modest on high-dimensional continuous regression tasks where deep learning methods trained on saturation mutagenesis data hold advantage. In the SEA-AD DREAM Agentic Track, a multi-agent AutoML framework autonomously orchestrated single-cell preprocessing, model selection, and pipeline execution across 1.2 million cells. For categorical neuropathological staging, the framework achieved an ADNC quadratic weighted kappa of 0.525, ranking 6th overall. Continuous regression tasks remained more challenging. These results reveal that current AI agents perform competitively on tasks requiring categorical reasoning and mechanistic knowledge synthesis, while continuous molecular phenotype regression remains a persistent challenge. Crowdsourced benchmarks are well-positioned to track and guide the development of autonomous AI systems in biomedical research.

title: The MecCog open science challenge: Discovering mechanism in preclinical biology
authors: John Moult, Lindley Darden, Gustavo Stolovitzky, Jan Pedersen, Goergia Channing, Jeff Lam, Krzysztof Fidelis, Andriy Kryshtafovych, Nikolas Kalavros, Oishi Deb, Ankitha Shenoy
abstract: It is widely acknowledged that there is a replication crisis in preclinical biology, and that this crisis impedes the development of new therapeutics. This project addresses the problem using principles of critical assessment and benchmarking developed in other domains (e.g., CASP, DREAM, and others), combined with the current generation of foundation AI models. The goal is to use a community science critical assessment framework to create a trustworthy disease-mechanism knowledge resource. The project is conducted in collaboration with Hugging Face, leveraging its open science culture and large community of machine learning experts. The first phase focuses on critically assessing the ~40 mechanisms proposed to explain the large effect of a single genetic variant on the risk of late-onset Alzheimer’s disease (the E4 variant of APOE). The tools developed in this phase are intended to be generalizable and the second phase of the challenge will address mechanisms for many diseases. Challenge participants will develop AI tools to address a sequence of tasks, from identifying relevant papers to assigning confidence to proposed mechanisms and suggesting informative experiments. A pilot group is currently exploring how best to structure the challenge. Initial results indicate that even the most advanced current paper-retrieval tools are inadequate for the task, and that extracting and comparing experimental findings remains an unsolved problem. Criteria for evaluating evidence and extrapolation are based on guidelines compiled through detailed human analysis of many APOE4 studies.

title: DREAMx: Deploying Federated DREAM Challenges Behind Institutional Firewalls to Evaluate Cross-Institution Generalizability of Computational Models
authors: Arushi Shrivastava, Kristin Ayers, Jonathan Mccafferty, Aravinda Chakravarti, Gustavo Stolovitzky
abstract: We introduce DREAMx, a distributed benchmarking framework that deploys synchronized DREAM Challenges across multiple institutions while keeping sensitive data securely behind local firewalls. Under this framework, identical challenge protocols are executed in parallel across sites A, B, etc. (e.g. DREAMx@A, DREAMx@B), enabling each institution to internally crowdsource the development of models using its own data but with shared task definition and standardized evaluation scheme across institutions. Rather than sharing data, DREAMx enables the systematic exchange of models across sites. These models trained at one institution can be evaluated at others, creating a fully cross-institutional validation performance matrix (Models x Organizations) without exposing private data. This design provides direct, scalable, and realistic assessment of model transportability, potentially capturing performance degradation, calibration shifts, and failure modes that may arise in cross-institutional deployment. By harmonizing tasks, metrics, and evaluation timelines, DREAMx establishes reproducible framework for comparing generalization across heterogeneous clinical environments. Beyond benchmarking, it supports structured interrogation of dataset shift (e.g. covariate, prior, and concept shift)—allowing investigators to identify the drivers of performance gaps and evaluate mitigation strategies such as reweighting, local adaptation, and model updating. Our initial deployment consisted of running the “deciphEHR Polygenic Risk Score DREAMx Challenge @ NYU Langone," a challenge focused on developing and benchmarking disease risk prediction models using the NYU Langone Health deciphEHR dataset. This dataset comprises genomic, demographic, and outcome data from approximately 12,000 individuals, generated by the NYU Center for Human Genetics and Genomics. The phenotypes evaluated include breast cancer, type 2 diabetes, and coronary artery disease.

title: Benchmarking large language models for predictive modeling in biomedical research with a focus on reproductive health
authors: Reuben Sarwal, Victor Tarca, Claire Dubin, Gaurav Bhatti, Nikolas Kalavros, Gustavo Stolovitzky, Sanchita Bhattacharya, Tomiko Oskotsky, Adi Tarca, Marina Sirota
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for code generation and data analysis. This study assessed LLM performance across four predictive tasks from three DREAM challenges: gestational age regression from transcriptomics and DNA methylation data, and classification of preterm birth and early preterm birth from microbiome data. We prompted LLMs with task descriptions, data locations, and target outcomes and then ran LLM-generated code to fit prediction models and determined accuracy on test sets. Among the eight LLMs tested, o3-mini-high, 4o, DeepseekR1, and Gemini 2.0 completed at least one task. R code generation was more successful (14/16) than Python (7/16). OpenAI's o3-mini-high outperformed others, completing 7/8 tasks. Test set performance of the top LLM-generated models matched or exceeded the median-participating team for all four tasks and surpassed the top-performing team for one task (p = 0.02). These findings underscore the potential of LLMs to democratize predictive modeling in omics and accelerate research output.

title: OpenChallenges: A FAIR-Aligned, Centralized Platform for Crowdsourcing in Biological Research
authors: Gaia Andreoletti, Hallie Swan, Rongrong Chai, Jake Albrecht, Jay Hodgson, Solveig K Sieberts, Thomas Schaffter, Luca Foschini, Susheel Varma, Verena Chung
abstract: Rigorous benchmarking is a critical bottleneck in the responsible development of AI agents for biomedical applications. Community challenges, where teams evaluate models on held-out data, provide the gold standard for objective, scalable AI assessment. Yet over 2,000 such challenges are scattered across hosting platforms without a centralized registry, fragmenting the landscape and preventing it from meeting FAIR data principles at the metadata level. We developed OpenChallenges (OC), a centralized, FAIR-aligned repository that aggregates and standardizes challenge metadata from 26 hosting platforms into a unified, searchable registry. OC is built on the Minimal Information About a Challenge (MIAC) schema, derived from an analysis of 47 DREAM challenges and enriched with ontologies for semantic search. The platform currently indexes 836 biomedical challenges spanning oncology, genomics, imaging, and drug discovery, with challenge creation accelerating markedly: 80 launched in 2025, 68 in 2024. Critically, 38.5% of indexed challenges originate from long-tail and independent platforms which are competitions lacking the inherent visibility of major hubs like Synapse or Kaggle, for which OC provides the greatest discoverability benefit. A metadata completeness scoring framework assigns each challenge one of four tiers (Baseline, Standard, Comprehensive, Gold Standard), revealing mean FAIR dimension scores of Findable 80.0%, Accessible 50.2%, Interoperable 45.7%, and Reusable 11.0% with the latter driven by sparse coverage of evaluationMetric (6.5%), submissionLicense (14.6%), and dataLicense (11.8%), the primary targets of ongoing curation. By consolidating a fragmented ecosystem into a FAIR-aligned knowledge base, OC provides essential infrastructure for transparent, reproducible benchmarking of AI agents across the biomedical sciences.

title: Empowering African Life Scientists Through R: Outcomes of a Community-Led Bioinformatics Training Initiative
authors: Seun Olufemi
abstract: Computational skills remain a major barrier for life scientists in sub-Saharan Africa, limiting equitable participation in open and data-driven research. Community-led initiatives offer a scalable pathway to address this gap. We report outcomes from a 3-day intensive R training organized by Bioinformatics Outreach Nigeria (BON), designed to build foundational data science skills using domain-relevant biological datasets. The curriculum covered base R, data structures, data cleaning, and reproducible data analysis workflows using the tidyverse, alongside data visualization with ggplot2. Training materials emphasized real-world applications, including gene expression analysis, ecological datasets, and clinical data interpretation. Pre-training survey responses (n ≈ 200) indicated that 65–70% of participants had no prior experience with R, with self-reported confidence levels in core competencies (base R, tidyverse, ggplot2) clustering at 1–2 on a 5-point scale. Despite this, participants expressed strong motivation, with the majority rating R proficiency as critical to their academic and professional development. Post-training evaluation showed substantial gains in both confidence and applied knowledge. Participants demonstrated improved understanding of key concepts, including data structures and common tidyverse operations (e.g., filtering, transformation, grouping), as well as data visualization principles. Satisfaction levels were high, with most participants rating the training as “Excellent" or “Good" and highlighting the relevance of life sciences-focused examples. Feedback underscored demand for deeper engagement: most participants recommended extending the training duration and increasing hands-on components. Requests for improved access to learning resources, including recorded sessions, were also prominent. Our findings demonstrate that short, context-aware, and community-driven training can significantly enhance computational literacy in underrepresented regions. This work contributes practical insights into designing inclusive, reproducible, and scalable R training models that support broader participation in open bioinformatics and open science ecosystems.

title: Hackathons as a Scalable Model for Training and Community Engagement
authors: Allissa Dillman, Lafrancis Gibson, Padmashri Saravanan, Kelli Bursey
abstract: The Common Fund Data Ecosystem (CFDE) integrates diverse programs, multi-omics datasets, tools, and user communities to enable biomedical discovery. However, this complexity presents challenges for new users seeking to engage with its resources. Traditional training formats such as lectures, and short-format skills building workshops, are valuable but often insufficient on their own. They tend to lack the practical application needed to translate knowledge into sustained engagement. Within the CFDE Training Center (TC), hackathons have been used as an effective mechanism for onboarding users through hands-on, collaborative exploration of data, tools, and workflows. These events foster peer-to-peer learning, mentorship, and community building, enabling participants to develop foundational skills in an applied context. A separate FAIR Forward initiative built on the hackathon model, combining structured workshops with a culminating hackathon. During the workshops, participants iteratively develop core competencies in open-source tools including R programming, and FAIR data principles. Students then apply these skills in a team-based, problem-solving environment during the hackathon. This progression aligns with Bloom’s taxonomy: moving learners from remembering and understanding concepts in workshops to applying, analyzing, and creating during hackathons. These components demonstrate that structured, sequenced training can transform hackathons from informal entry points into rigorous capstone experiences, advancing individual competency and long-term community engagement with CFDE resources. The TC is now implementing this model to a CFDE summer institute, where a hackathon will serve as a capstone experience that reinforces learning through real-world application, accelerating skill acquisition, building user confidence, and strengthening professional networks.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Teaching biological data science with generative and agentic artificial intelligence
authors: Steven Brenner
abstract: Artificial intelligence is transforming how biologists interact with data, through code generation and agentic systems that perform entire analyses. This poses a fundamental challenge for educators: how do we prepare students for a future where AI mediates most computational work? In Spring 2026 I heavily revised my biological data science course at the University of California, Berkeley to have students extensively use AI. The course is organized around active learning, with students helping each other as instructors circulate. Ethics pervades the course and has become even more central with AI. This model has proven surprisingly accommodating of widespread AI use. Several findings have emerged. AI provides substantial educational benefit: students receive customized assistance, and vibe coding lets them focus on concepts rather than syntax. Allowing AI also resolves an increasingly intractable academic integrity problem. However, the course revealed how AI can function as a false-conclusion generator. When students transcribed and translated a DNA strand step by step manually, each produced correct results. When teams instead had AI generate code, nearly half made substantial undetected errors—they did not recognize that certain steps required decisions and did not notice when AI chose incorrectly. Red-teaming proved engaging and effective. We also had students deploy agentic tools: from short prompts, every student had an AI agent locate, download, and analyze genomic data, producing a chromosome gene-count plot. These findings illuminate skills essential as AI becomes the primary interface for biological data analysis: framing the right questions, understanding analytical logic, and detecting errors AI introduces silently.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: From Survey to Syllabus: Evidence‑Informed Integration of Bioinformatics into Required Undergraduate Biology Courses
authors: Adena Collens, Charles Delwiche
abstract: Contemporary biology is increasingly data driven, but many undergraduate biology programs still offer limited, fragmented exposure to bioinformatics and coding. This project developed, implemented, and evaluated modular bioinformatics curricula for a large R1’s undergraduate Biological Sciences program that combines authentic, RNA-seq–based gene expression analysis into required junior-and senior-level courses. These modules combine pre-class conceptual preparation, low-stakes assessment, and a guided 3-hour data analysis lab built on real, publicly available transcriptomic data, enabling students to practice core skills in R and RStudio, data visualization, and interpret differential gene expression data in biologically meaningful ways. These activities explicitly align with the national bioinformatics and biology education competency frameworks (e.g. NIBLSE, ISCB), emphasizing tool use, data management, reproducibility, and communication of computational results to biologist audiences. These design choices were driven by a year-long mixed-methods needs assessment of the existing bioinformatics curriculum. In Spring 2024, 40 biology faculty and 166 undergraduate majors completed surveys that cataloged where and how students encountered bioinformatics concepts, which tools and coding practices were taught, how much time was spent on computational work, and what kinds of support (e.g. TA help, office hours, online resources) were available. Faculty were asked to identify courses containing any computational biology components, estimate the proportion of course time devoted to bioinformatics, list specific tools and teaching methods (live coding, lecture, worksheets), and indicate their interest in collaborating on new modules. In parallel, students reported which required biology courses included coding or bioinformatics assignments, how many hours they spent on these tasks in-and outside of class, which topics they found most frustrating and why, and how well-supported they felt on a 1-5 scale. Graduating seniors completed further questions on how bioinformatics training influenced their job applications and perceived career opportunities. Comparing faculty reports with student experiences revealed curricular gaps that guided module design. Faculty frequently reported including bioinformatics content broadly defined, yet students often did not recognize these activities as computational biology, especially when instruction used small, highly curated datasets or point-and-click interfaces. Students described limited exposure to coding applied to molecular and genetic questions, inconsistent opportunities to work with larger, more realistically complex datasets, and uncertainty about the relevance of bioinformatics skills beyond individual assignments. Both faculty and students, however, endorsed the importance of integrating bioinformatics throughout the curriculum and identified specific needs for: 1) direct instruction in fundamental coding syntax and workflows, 2) clear connections between existing lecture content and computational analyses, and 3) explicit illustration of real-world research applications. To meet these demonstrated needs, this work adapted Carpentries materials and other open-source resources into course-embedded curriculum modules tailored to two key courses: Cell Biology, a required 300-level laboratory, and Molecular Genetics, a 400-level lecture course. The Cell Biology module consists of a pre-lab assignment introducing RNA sequencing concepts and the experimental context, an associated pre-lab quiz to ensure conceptual readiness, and a three-hour lab where students use R to import, explore, visualize, and interpret RNA-seq count data in small groups. The Molecular Genetics module builds on the same publicly available dataset, but it extends the analysis to more complex gene enrichment analysis questions and interpretations appropriate for their coursework. This creates a linked integration of bioinformatic skills across the curriculum. Both modules are designed for implementation by instructors and teaching assistants who may be novice programmers, using widely used R environments and packages, step-by-step code templates, and detailed TA guides to reduce technical barriers. The study protocol, including all faculty and student surveys and the use of de-identified performance data, was reviewed by the university Institutional Review Board and classified as exempt from full IRB review according to federal regulations. Participants completed online consent procedures, and student responses were collected without names or university identifiers, with classroom-level linkage only used when necessary to interpret aggregate patterns. Surveys, curriculum materials, and analysis code are being made publicly available via GitHub to enable reuse and adaptation by instructors at other institutions. By building on widely used, open-source educational materials while providing course-tested implementation sin large-enrollment required classes, this work offers a portable model for integrating bioinformatics coursework into undergraduate biology programs that may lack the capacity for stand-alone bioinformatics majors or extensive faculty training. Overall, this project answers recent national calls for local curricular assessment by 1) empirically characterizing mismatches between faculty and student perceptions of bioinformatics instruction, 2) translating those findings into modular, competency-aligned, open-source curricula that can be integrated into existing coursework, and 3) demonstrating the feasibility of scaling these interventions to hundreds of students with realistic implementation constraints. By doing so, we demonstrate how biology departments can move beyond treating bioinformatics as an isolating elective and highlight how computational analysis of real biological datasets can be an expected, supported component of undergraduate biology training.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Enhancing Computational Biology Education in Pharmacy Students through a Structured Training Program in Drug Discovery
authors: Sara Munir
abstract: Background: Developments in Computational Biology, Bioinformatics, and Artificial Intelligence are reshaping drug discovery, which has led to a need of pharmacy graduates who have computational skills. Conventional courses generally do not provide systematic opportunities to familiarize themselves with such practices restricting the ability of students to be prepared to work in contemporary research and industries. This research determined the effect of a short-term educational intervention incorporating computational biology into pharmacy education. Method: The study involved 60 undergraduate pharmacy students, which was a three-month quasi-experimental study. A standardized pre-test was used to measure the baseline knowledge. Students were then subjected to a structured training program that included Python programming, bioinformatics tools, molecular docking, and network-based analysis, through interactive lectures, practical sessions, and project based learning. To measure outcomes, a student feedback and a post-intervention assessment were gathered. Results: Baseline testing revealed a low level of previous exposure: 76% of students scored below 50 and only 18% showed the basic level of competence in computations. Post-training, the mean score increased from 42% to 78% (p < 0.001). The level of competency in computational tools increased to 72 and 68% completed molecular docking and data analysis activities. Moreover, 81% said that they felt more confident using computational methods to discover drugs, even in complex disease settings such as cancer. Student comments emphasized the importance of practical learning and the interdisciplinary approach. Conclusion: Training Pharmacy students with a focused short training program can significantly improve their computational skills to provide a transition between traditional training and the current drug discovery. These efforts create industry-prepared workforce and innovation in pharmaceutical research.

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Navigating Career Pathways with the EMBL-EBI Competency Hub
authors: Daria Sokolova, Kim Gurwitz, Catherine Brooksbank, Vera Matser, Denise Bianco, Giulia Tomba, Emma Karoune
abstract: In today’s skills-based economy, professional success depends on demonstrating measurable competencies rather than relying on static job titles. A competency-based approach provides a structured ""common language"" that clarifies career paths and helps organisations build resilient teams through better role definition and targeted development. The Competency Hub from EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) is a specialised web infrastructure designed to operationalise these frameworks. As a centralised, open-access repository, it empowers users to assess their attributes (KSAs/ KSBs) against recognised frameworks, explore professional personas, and identify training resources mapped to specific skills gaps. Access to such a repository is critical in biomedical data science, where the convergence of biology, medicine, and computation requires a highly adaptable workforce. The Hub’s utility is demonstrated by the Advancing Biomedical Data Science Careers (ABDC) project led by The Alan Turing Institute and EMBL-EBI. We’re utilising the Hub to host a comprehensive competency mapping that synthesises existing frameworks to identify 12 Minimum Standard Requirements and specific personas. Following this mapping, a gap analysis will identify training needs to be reflected in the Hub. Furthermore, the Hub supports granular professional extensions, such as the recently published career pathway for bioinformatics core facility scientists, serving as a blueprint for other specialists, such as biocurators. By hosting these outputs, the Competency Hub translates complex ecosystem analyses into practical, live templates for organisations to standardise roles and support inclusive workforces. Additionally, we developed the ""10 Simple Rules for producing FAIR competency frameworks"" to foster a connected global training ecosystem.

title: Quantifying domain-specific relevance of computational biology Wikipedia articles using TF-IDF and cosine similarity
authors: Arya Menon, Trenton Davis, Megha Hegde, Nicolas C Näpflin, Audra Anjum, Sarah Barman, Dan DeBlasio, Pradeep Eranti, Jean-Christophe Nebel, Nelly Sélem-Mojica, Sayane Shome, Lonnie Welch, Alastair Kilpatrick, Farzana Rahman
abstract: Wikipedia is one of the world's most visited websites and serves as the principal open educational resource for computational biology. However, identifying which articles are most relevant to distinct sub-disciplines of computational biology remains largely subjective. This study collected short descriptions for 22 Communities of Special Interest (COSI) groups maintained by the International Society for Computational Biology and downloaded 1,536 computational biology articles from English Wikipedia. Following standard text preprocessing, COSI descriptions and Wikipedia articles were embedded in a common TF-IDF vector space. Semantic relatedness was quantified using cosine similarity, yielding a real-valued relevance matrix that maps each COSI to the most pertinent computational biology articles. The resulting scores, typically low in absolute value, captured nuanced differences: general-interest pages such as "Computational biology" and "Bioinformatics" ranked highest, whereas niche pages showed high relevance only for specific COSIs. Unsupervised analysis using principal component analysis, k-nearest neighbours, and Leiden community detection revealed clusters of articles corresponding to the particular COSIs and highlighted inter-COSI relationships. This automated pipeline reduces bias compared with manual tagging and enables more precise curation of domain-specific educational resources. The relevance matrix developed in this study is available in the Zenodo repository (doi: 10.5281/ zenodo.18311878).

track: Education: Computational Biology and Bioinformatics Education and Training
title: Leveraging a hybrid cross-disciplinary training model to accelerate global bioinformatics capacity
authors: Serghei Mangul, Daryna Yakymenko, Taras K. Oleksyk, Viorel Munteanu, Sylwia Bożek, Paweł Łabaj
abstract: Disparities in formal bioinformatics training exacerbate the global skills gap, impeding the democratized application of advanced genomic technologies. To bridge this divide, we introduce a scalable, hybrid training framework designed to rapidly accelerate regional bioinformatics capacity. We exemplify this approach through the Eastern European Bioinformatics and Genomics (EEBG) workshop series — a cross-disciplinary initiative that pairs international faculty with local institutions to deliver modular, hands-on curricula. Functioning as a structured knowledge-transfer pipeline, the series has catalyzed a sustainable educational ecosystem, evidenced by the establishment of multiple independent summer schools across the region. The assessment of the 2025 EEBG workshop in Kraków, Poland, validates the model's viability; participant metrics confirm high efficacy in skill acquisition (mean satisfaction: 4.4/5.0) and community building. Crucially, the hybrid delivery mode dismantled geographic barriers, serving as a vital mechanism for maintaining scientific continuity for researchers facing displacement and crisis. Synthesizing these outcomes, we define the core features of a replicable blueprint for scientific readiness in resource-constrained environments. We conclude by presenting a strategic roadmap — organized around infrastructure standardization, governance sustainability, and geographical expansion — for adapting this regional proof-of-concept into a global export-ready model, offering a critical path toward ensuring universal access to genomic innovation. The full version is available as a preprint under the link: https://doi.org/10.64898/2026.01.21.700760 The manuscript was in principle accepted to Nature Biotechnology.

authors: Rebeca Campos-Sánchez, Jose Arturo Molina-Mora, Juanita Riveros, Cindy Aguilar-Bartels, Kim Gurtwitz, Lizzie Divala, Cath Brooksbank
abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is transforming biosciences by enabling the analysis of complex, large-scale biological and medical data. In Latin America, however, the integration of AI into research and healthcare faces several structural challenges, including limited infrastructure, lack of specialized training, fragmented research systems, and scarce funding. These obstacles contribute to a regional gap in AI readiness compared to high-income countries. To reduce this gap, we created the BiotrAIn program in 2024. A partnership involving EMBL-EBI, the University of Costa Rica, and CABANAnet, with support from the Chan Zuckerberg Initiative. The project is structured around three pillars: knowledge exchange, curriculum development, and regional training. Every part of the program was developed by Latin American faculty and early-career scientists using regional datasets as examples. Over the years, the program has generated open training resources and has strengthened the collaborations among scientists in Latin America. In particular, the one-week training program has been delivered eight times across seven Latin American institutions, with 189 students. The evaluations demonstrate the impact of this program on the region. BiotrAIn exemplifies how targeted, regionally adapted programs can build AI capacity and promote equitable scientific development.

title: Keynote: Growing bioinformatics capacity through mentorship and community in Peru and Latin America
authors: David Requena,, David Requena
abstract: Bioinformatics is essential for modern biomedical research, yet access to computational infrastructure, advanced training, expert mentorship, and international scientific networks remains limited and uneven across Peru and Latin America. In this talk, I will discuss how community-building, knowledge-sharing events, and pro-bono mentorship can expand regional bioinformatics capacity while promoting scientific excellence, equity, and long-term sustainability. I will share my experience bringing together professionals across bioinformatics and data science to create and support the growth of the Peruvian Society for Bioinformatics and Computational Biology and the Regional Student Group Peru. I will also describe the creation of the Bioinformatics Group for Multiomics and Immunology, a voluntary mentorship and research initiative for students and early-career researchers that provides technical training, scientific guidance, exposure to rigorous research practices, and personalized support for trainees pursuing opportunities in highly competitive international institutions. Together, these initiatives have helped identify national gaps, decentralize training, support underrepresented groups, build regional and international collaborations, and expand access to Spanish-language educational activities. They are examples of how mentorship and community networks can transform individual opportunities into collective capacity, strengthening Latin America’s global participation in bioinformatics through inclusive ecosystems where young scientists can grow, collaborate, lead, and contribute to world-class science.

track: Equity and Diversity in CompBio Research
title: A Systematic Fairness Evaluation of Racial/Ethnic Bias in Alzheimer’s Disease Diagnosis Using Machine Learning Models
authors: Neha Goud Baddam, Bizhan Alipour Pijani, Serdar Bozdag, Melissa Petersen
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD) is a global health concern, expected to affect 12.7 million Americans by 2050. Machine learning (ML) algorithms developed for AD diagnosis and progression prediction raise concerns about generalizability across demographic groups due to lack of racial/ethnic diversity in datasets. Studies show that ML algorithms inherit biases from data, leading to biased AD predictions. We hypothesized that models trained on one racial/ethnic group perform best for that group but may not generalize to others. We utilized the Health & Aging Brain Study-Health Disparities (HABS-HD) dataset, comprising 2,060 individuals and 1,017 features across Non-Hispanic White, Mexican American, and African American participants, with three diagnostic classes: Cognitively Normal, Mild Cognitive Impairment, and AD. To select informative predictors, we applied filter-based (Mutual Information), wrapper-based (Recursive Feature Elimination, SelectFromModel, SelectBySingleFeaturePerformance, SHAP), and embedded (LASSO) feature-selection methods. Random Forest models were trained under four scenarios: (1) train on one racial/ethnic group and test across all groups, (2) train on combined multi-racial/ethnic data, (3) a pre-processing approach merging results from multiple feature selection methods, selecting consistent features, and (4) re-weighting training samples to increase underrepresented group influence. Performance (macro F1, balanced accuracy) and fairness (Demographic Parity, Equal Opportunity, Equalized Odds Difference) were evaluated for our three-class, multi-group setting. Our results show that models achieved significantly better performance within their training group, supporting our hypothesis. Fairness-aware pre-processing and in-processing methods reduced disparities while preserving performance. This study highlights the need for diverse datasets and fairness constraints to ensure equitable AD predictions.

track: Equity and Diversity in CompBio Research
title: Large-scale automated detection reveals pervasive sex bias in biomedical research
authors: Lydia Valtadoros, Parker Hicks, Hao Yuan, Mansooreh Ahmadian, Kayla Johnson, Arjun Krishnan
abstract: Female study subjects have historically been excluded from human, animal, and cell culture research, resulting in considerable sex bias in biomedical studies. Quantifying this bias is critical for identifying areas for future balanced investigations. Sex bias has been documented in limited research areas through manual review of publications. However, assessing sex bias across a wide range of research areas at-scale remains a major challenge. Here, we present a multimodal computational approach to address this challenge by inferring the sex of publicly available human samples, and identifying diseases enriched in the associated metadata of the samples. Applying this approach to ~230,000 public human transcriptomics samples and their associated ~5,000 publications revealed hundreds of diseases associated with sex-biased studies but are not biologically sex-specific. Even after adjusting for the prevalence of diseases in males and females, up to 56% of all disease terms demonstrated a male study bias without biological justification. These diseases, including cirrhosis, glioblastoma, and idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, are critical areas for both new studies focused on females to correct our sex-biased knowledge and others with a balanced representation of sex to understand sex differences in disease pathogenesis and treatment.

track: Equity and Diversity in CompBio Research
title: Keyboard accessibility of biomedical data portals and visualization tools
authors: Thomas C. Smits, George Bandek, Lawrence Weru, Nils Gehlenborg, Sehi L'Yi
abstract: Biomedical research relies heavily on data resources, such as visualization tools and data portals, to discover and explore datasets and advance our understanding of health and disease. We previously showed that many resources are inaccessible to users with visual impairments. However, insight into how accessible these resources are for keyboard users remains limited. People use keyboard navigation predominantly for various reasons, ranging from permanent and temporary motor disabilities to personal preference (e.g., quicker navigation). Furthermore, many assistive technologies, such as screen readers and switch access devices, rely on keyboard bindings. Therefore, it’s important to understand the state of keyboard accessibility in these resources. Here, we examine the accessibility of biomedical data resources through (1) automated analysis of visualization tools and (2) a user study of biomedical portals and embedded visualization tools with actual keyboard users. In our automated analysis, we found that almost all 141 surveyed web-based visualization tools (97.2%) have keyboard accessibility issue violations. In our user study, we further evaluated keyboard accessibility of three biomedical data portals with seven study participants and explored the potential effect of using a shortcut-based accessibility tool. In total, participants completed only 66.4% of study tasks. Although participants did not have significantly better task success rates using the shortcut-based tool, it significantly improved the experience of navigation. Tasks were perceived as less challenging and frustrating, and participants felt substantially greater levels of confidence and satisfaction. Still, our user study showed fundamental interaction barriers for biomedical data resources in real-life experiences.

track: Equity and Diversity in CompBio Research
title: Exploring the Human Gut Microbiome Diversity in Latin America: Focus on Populations at Nutritional Risk
authors: Rebeca Campos, Maria Alejandra Soto, Lilliam Marín Arias, Trevor D. Lawley, Adrián Turjanski, Karina Salvatierra, Mariana Rosales, Maria Adelaida Gomez, Alejandro Reyes
abstract: The gut microbiome plays a central role in human health, yet Latin American populations remain underrepresented in microbiome research. Because diet, lifestyle, and socioeconomic factors strongly shape microbial communities, studying populations with non-Western dietary patterns is essential for expanding our understanding of microbiome diversity and disease. This study aimed to generate a comprehensive catalog of metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) from adults in three Latin American countries. We analyzed variation in gut microbiota composition by country of origin, diet, lifestyle, and body mass index (BMI), and assessed the prevalence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes and potential pathogens. Stool samples were collected from 250 adults in Colombia (n = 50), Argentina (n = 50), and Costa Rica (n = 150), of whom 188 were classified as overweight or obese (BMI ≥ 25). Standardized protocols for sample collection, metadata recording, and DNA extraction were used across all countries. Shotgun metagenomic sequencing was performed on the Illumina NovaSeq 6000 platform (150 bp paired-end), followed by a standardized assembly-based pipeline for MAG reconstruction. We reconstructed 13,532 MAGs, including 260 species not previously reported in public databases. Microbiome diversity was significantly influenced by country, lifestyle, and BMI, with reduced diversity observed in urban and obese individuals. Prevotella was enriched in rural populations, whereas Bacteroides, Parabacteroides, Alistipes, and Phocaeicola predominated in urban settings. AMR genes were widespread, particularly those conferring resistance to tetracyclines, aminoglycosides, and MLSb antibiotics, mainly associated with Klebsiella, Enterobacter, Enterocloster, Sellimonas, and Bacteroides. These findings demonstrate the importance of underrepresented populations for understanding microbiome diversity, antimicrobial resistance, and nutrition-related disease.

abstract: The Open-Source Enablers project addresses inequalities in bioinformatics education and practice. In Mexico, opportunities, infrastructure, and training are concentrated in a few institutions, which limits the participation of underrepresented communities. In this context, the Regional Student Group Mexico (RSG-Mexico) received funding from the International Society for Computational Biology (ISCB) to strengthen the project. The project's initial phase proposed an integrated model based on three pillars: access to computational infrastructure, open science training, and developing reproducible and repeatable skills. The initiative was firmly established through collaboration with student communities, including RSG-Mexico and R-Ladies. Intensive workshops based on inclusive methodologies, such as those offered by The Carpentries, were implemented. These workshops covered version control, multi-omics analysis, reproducibility and repeatability. For the first pillar, computing infrastructure was upgraded to support 50 users working simultaneously, up from 20. For the second and third pillars, three main workshops were held: (1) an introduction to bioinformatics practices with a focus on Linux and Git, with 49 participants (Guerrero); (2) bacterial genomic mining with a focus on microbial diversity and antibiotic resistance in R, with 42 participants (Queretaro); and (3) metagenomics with a focus on data analysis and management in computational environments, with 37 participants (Chiapas). Overall, these free workshops achieved high levels of satisfaction and adoption of open, reproducible, and repeatable tools. The project culminated in a hackathon (Michoacan) aligned with the CAMDA 2025 challenge. This event promoted interdisciplinary collaboration, which ultimately led the team to win the CAMDA 2025 trophy. This initiative also contributed to closing equity and diversity gaps, strengthening a more inclusive, decentralized community committed to reproducible practices in computational biology.

track: Equity and Diversity in CompBio Research
title: Generalization Performance of RNA-Based Predictors of Homologous Recombination Deficiency in Diverse Populations
authors: Samantha Lopez Alvarez, Katherine A Lawson-Michod, Courtney E Johnson, Lindsay J Collin, Xintian Song, David A Nix, Chad D Huff, Andrew Berchuck, Lucas A Salas, Casey S Greene, Jeffrey R Marks, Lauren C Peres, Joellen M Schildkraut, Jennifer A Doherty, Natalie R Davidson
abstract: Homologous recombination deficiency (HRD) influences tumor behavior and treatment response in high-grade serous ovarian carcinoma (HGSC). Clinical HRD tests guide therapy but are often unavailable in public datasets, limiting population-scale research. Transcriptome-based predictors provide a functional readout of HR activity, but performance remains underexplored. Because these models are developed in European ancestry cohorts, they may not generalize across populations due to potential differences in tumor biology and variant interpretation, including higher rates of variants of uncertain significance (VUS) in non-European populations. We benchmarked transcriptome-based IdentifiHR, expHRD, and MultiscaleHRD in HGSC tumors from self-identified Black (n=272) and White (n=316) participants. Mutation-based HRD status was defined using pathogenic/likely pathogenic variants in ASCO-prioritized HR genes (BRCA1/2, RAD51C/D, BRIP1, PALB2) and SBS3 mutational signature. Performance was evaluated using concordance, error rates, and precision-recall AUC. The top-performing method was assessed across groups. IdentifiHR showed strongest overall performance (ROC-AUC 0.781 [95% CI: 0.727-0.834]; PR-AUC 0.783) compared to expHRD (0.685 [0.623, 0.746], 0.648) and MultiscaleHRD (0.68 [0.619, 0.742], 0.634), with the lowest misclassification rate (34.8%). Error analysis revealed discordance between transcriptome-based predictions and mutation-based HRD definitions, with high false negative rates across groups (~60-64%), indicating many transcriptome-defined HRD cases were not captured. False positive rates were higher in self-identified White patients compared with Black patients (12.3% vs 4.9%), suggesting classification differences despite similar overall accuracy. IdentifiHR most reliably captured HRD status, but performance varied by groups. Highlighting the potential and limitation of transcriptome-based HRD prediction and the need for improved generalizability and more equitable HRD classification.

title: Comparative Genomics in the Open Ocean

abstract: Genomic approaches are rapidly transforming our understanding of some of the least known organisms on Earth: the animals of the open ocean. title: Topology-Based Analysis of Gene Tree Heterogeneity with Applications to Incomplete lineage Sorting and Introgression
authors: Tanjeem Zaman, Yuting Xiao, Maureen Stolzer, Dannie Durand
abstract: Incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) and introgression drive gene tree heterogeneity, leaving characteristic signatures in gene tree topology distributions. These patterns make gene tree sampling a compelling approach for inferring ancestral population processes among species. For species trees with k=3 leaves, gene tree heterogeneity can be assessed simply by counting tree topologies. Comparing the empirical distribution with theoretical models allows for hypothesis testing and parameter estimation. For larger gene trees, current approaches subsample rooted triplets targeting species tree branches of interest, because the number of unique gene tree topologies scales super-exponentially with k. However, accurate assessment requires sampling several rooted triplets for each species tree branch. Counting and combining results from multiple triplets is computationally expensive and becomes intractable when extended to whole-clade analyses. Here, we present a scalable, topology-based algorithm that characterizes gene tree heterogeneity at each species tree internode without triplet subsampling. Given a species tree and a set of gene trees, the method maps gene tree internodes to species tree internodes and tabulates the gene tree heterogeneity statistics for each species tree branch in a single, unified calculation. The algorithm automatically excludes uninformative cases arising from paralogy, gene loss, or reconstruction error. It runs in time linear in the total number of gene tree internodes. Applied to simulated and genuine datasets, the algorithm recovers topology frequency distributions consistent with theoretical predictions under ILS, even in the presence of paralogy and missing data.

title: Leveraging horizontal gene transfer networks to predict the host of Staphylococcus aureus isolates
authors: Katerina Terwelp, Evan Brenner, Janani Ravi
abstract: Spillover events, when pathogenic bacteria switch hosts, can have catastrophic consequences (e.g. black death, Yersinia pestis). To anticipate the next infectious disease outbreak, we need to investigate mechanisms of bacterial host adaptability. One essential mechanism of bacterial host adaptation is the horizontal transfer of genetic material outside of inheritance (HGT). For example, HGT-acquired genetic elements enable Staphylococcus aureus strains to jump from humans to poultry. Previously, our lab used k-sized genome snippets, k-mers, and genes to predict the host of S. aureus isolates. However, these machine learning (ML) models can struggle to generalize across phylogenetically diverse clades because top genomic features may be clade-specific. In contrast, HGT occurs across species, producing naturally cross-species features. Therefore, I hypothesize that leveraging HGT networks to predict S. aureus hosts will improve generalizability compared to previous approaches. To test this hypothesis, I constructed an HGT network linking S. aureus genomes with their inferred gene transfers. Then, I trained ML models using HGT-derived features (ex: transfer events per genome pair by host), k-mers, and genes. To evaluate model robustness and generalizability, I generated phylogenetic data splits by training on closely related genomes and testing on distant genomes. Gene and k-mer models performed significantly worse on phylogenetic compared to random splits, suggesting difficulty generalizing across divergent clades. The best-performing model combined HGT and gene-based features, indicating complementary predictive value. Because HGT is a key driver of bacterial niche adaptation, incorporating gene flow into host tropism predictions will improve surveillance of zoonotic pathogens.

title: Machine learning identifies the fingerprints of host adaptation in bacterial genomes
authors: Evan Brenner, Landon Buskirk, Katerina Terwelp, Clay Griffin-Derr, Sarah Mentzer, Janani Ravi
abstract: Emerging and expanding infectious diseases threaten human and animal health worldwide, but different bacterial species and strains pose different risks. As exposures to novel microbes continue to rise at the wildland-urban interface and animal agriculture increases cross-species exposures and spillover risks, how can we classify whether a bacterial isolate is likely to affect different hosts? Benchside microbiology cannot alone keep pace with the expanding scale of the challenge. We apply comparative genomics and machine learning approaches to identify predictors of host specificity. Using publicly available microbial genomics data and metadata, we extract features across molecular scales (genes, k-mers, virulence factors), train machine learning models that classify the host of origin, and extract the features driving model performance. At the whole genome sequence level, we find strong predictive performance (F1 scores > 0.9) in multiple bacterial species (e.g., Staphylococci, Streptococci), and that these models are underpinned by biological features with known involvement in host adaptation and host cell tropism. We also find predictive power in individual proteins using basic amino acid composition properties or ESM-2-based protein language model embeddings, supporting the use of multiple approaches for bacterial host specificity. Finally, errors and inconsistency in available metadata for hosts and isolation sources, and potentially confounding bacterial population structures motivate our additional work to harmonize and normalize metadata values, and test how phylogenetic relatedness affects ML model robustness. Collectively, I find that bacterial host specificity can be predicted across molecular feature scales, and that the driving motifs shed biological insights into pathogenesis.

title: AmpliPhy improves gene trees by adding homologous sequences without affecting alignments
authors: Dongwook Kim, Manuel Gil, Kazutaka Katoh, Christophe Dessimoz
abstract: In phylogenomics, gene tree reconstruction depends on multiple sequence alignment (MSA) and tree inference, and ongoing work continues to improve inference quality. Denser taxon sampling has been associated with improved gene tree inference, suggesting that adding homologs could be a practical route to higher accuracy as sequence databases continue to expand. However, adding sequences can influence multiple steps of typical inference pipelines, and little is known on its specific effect on the multiple sequence alignment, tree reconstruction, and rooting steps. We performed a large-scale empirical and simulated benchmarks to quantify how homolog enrichment affects alignment and phylogenetic inference. Using an enrichment-impoverishment design and a measure of tree accuracy based on taxonomic congruence, we found that enrichment consistently improves tree inference quality, while effects on alignment quality are marginal. We show that this improvement is associated with, but not restricted to accurate root placement on enriched trees when sensitive homolog search is accompanied. Notably, much of the benefit can be retained with relatively compact alignments produced by sequence addition. Building on these observations, we provide a tool, AmpliPhy, which efficiently improves phylogenetic reconstruction of protein families through homolog enrichment. The AmpliPhy open-source pipeline software is available at https://github.com/DessimozLab/ampliphy.
