title: Phlag: Scalable detection of genomics regions with unexplained phylogenetic heterogeneity
authors: Ali Osman Berk Şapcı, Shayesteh Arasti, Edward L. Braun, Siavash Mirarab
abstract: Motivation: Phylogenetic analyses of entire genomes (phylogenomics) have revealed abundant heterogeneity of evolutionary histories. While much has been done to model this heterogeneity and to infer species trees despite it, the current toolkit has a limitation. Existing methods assume that gene trees across the genome differ but are all sampled from the same distribution, defined by models such as the multi-species coalescent (MSC), and parametrized consistently across the genome. Empirical data strongly suggest this assumption is often violated because the species tree, its parameters, or the process generating the gene trees can all change across the genome. Errors in the data can further compound this heterogeneity. Results: To address this challenge, we define the problem of detecting what segments of the genome are inconsistent with a putative species tree, even after allowing discordance according to MSC. We model gene trees not as a set, but rather as a series (a realization of a stochastic process) along genomic positions. We propose a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) approach applied to quartet statistics measured from gene trees and tie the model to MSC using simulations. The combined use of these three ideas leads to a scalable method called Phlag. On simulated and real data, we show that Phlag can detect many cases of change in underlying evolutionary processes, including reduced recombination rates, population size changes, and admixture, all using the same algorithm. Availability and Implementation: Phlag is available at github.com/bo1929/phlag. All results and scripts can be found at github.com/ bo1929/shared.phlag.

title: To peel the pangenome
authors: David Sankoff
abstract: A pangenome can be represented by a multigraph on a set of genes as vertices with non-negative edge weights. It may be constructed and displayed in many ways, but it is basically formed by amalgamating a number of "constituent" genomes, each a forest path graph where the vertices of each component (chromosome) has at most 2 adjacencies. The genes (or homology set of genes) in all constituents is called the core, the remaining are called the shell.The data giving rise to a pangenome are experimentally determined constituent genomes, from a single species or closely related species. There has been no previous call to solve the "inverse" problem: given a pangenome, deduce the set of genomes that generated it, since thes latter are already known. In one context, however, the reconstruction of an ancestral pangenome from a set of of extant pangenomes, not closely related, we start with the pangenome and try to infer the constituent genome. We assume the set of edge-weights are determined by the given extant pangenomes and the reconstruction procedure (which we do not discuss, there being many possibilities). We "peel" off the the constituent genomes, one at a time, or in a simultaneous decomposition, trading off the number of constituent genomes thus created against the weight discordance between the values associated with the given pangenome and the set of adjacencies in all the constructed constituent genomes.

title: PINNOU: Physics-Informed Neural Networks for Ornstein–Uhlenbeck Inference in Phylogenetics
authors: Ojas Chaudhary, Anand Swaroop, Soumitra Pal
abstract: Evolution of gene expression patterns underlies phenotypic diversity and cellular heterogeneity across species, yet modeling global expression dynamics remains a major challenge. The Ornstein–Uhlenbeck (OU) process provides a principled framework for capturing stabilizing selection on continuous traits. However, existing likelihood-based implementations rely on covariance matrix operations that scale cubically with the number of taxa, limiting their applicability to large comparative and single-cell datasets. Here we introduce PINNOU, a physics-informed neural network framework for scalable inference of phylogenetic OU processes. By embedding the governing differential equations of OU dynamics directly into a neural network, PINNOU avoids explicit covariance matrix construction while concurrently enabling parameter inference from sparsely observed data. We evaluate PINNOU on simulated datasets spanning a range of evolutionary regimes and tree sizes. We demonstrate that it achieves accuracy comparable to state-of-the-art likelihood-based methods with improved scaling behavior. In particular, PINNOU reliably distinguishes among neutral, constrained, and adaptive regimes and maintains performance as the number of taxa increases. We apply PINNOU to retinal transcriptomic datasets across multiple species, where it recovers expression patterns consistent with known adaptations of rod and cone photoreceptor systems. Our results establish physics-informed neural networks as a flexible and scalable alternative for modeling trait evolution. More broadly, our approach provides a bridge between comparative phylogenetics and modern machine learning, enabling the study of evolutionary dynamics in high-dimensional and single-cell data.

title: What is the best strategy for building gene trees and species trees?
authors: Erik Wright
abstract: Many methods have been proposed for phylogenetic reconstruction, yet it remains unclear which approach is most appropriate for empirical data. Recent studies quantified gene tree accuracy using gene-to-species tree discordance and have unexpectedly shown that computationally intensive approaches, such as maximum likelihood and Bayesian inference, are less accurate than faster distance-based methods. Here, we introduce Treeline, a unified optimization framework for phylogenetic inference that facilitates comparison of trees optimized under alternative criteria. Treeline employs a novel strategy for exploring tree space based on structured perturbation of patristic distances, allowing optimization of balanced minimum evolution, maximum likelihood, and maximum parsimony objectives within a single framework. Benchmarking on large empirical datasets shows that Treeline often achieves accuracy, runtime, or memory efficiency comparable to programs designed for individual optimization objectives. Using Treeline, we confirm that the balanced minimum evolution criterion produces gene trees with greater concordance to species trees than maximum likelihood. Moreover, we show that maximum parsimony is competitive with maximum likelihood when biologically realistic, non-uniform cost matrices are applied. These advantages extend to species tree inference, where minimum evolution gene trees yield increased species tree consistency across diverse empirical datasets. Together, our results support the growing evidence that distance-based methods offer superior performance for gene and species tree inference and challenge the prevailing assumption that greater computational complexity necessarily leads to more accurate phylogenetic trees.

title: The Impact of Species Tree Shape on Method Performance
authors: Yunzhuo Liu, Wesley Demontigny, Seyed Mohammad Saleh Ghaemi, Stratis Aloimonos, Jenan El-Hifnawi, Erin Molloy
abstract: Gene tree discordance caused by incomplete lineage sorting (ILS) is a hallmark of rapid radiations and has motivated the development of many methods for species tree inference. Simulation studies are the gold standard for evaluating these methods, yet most prior work has relied on relatively balanced species trees generated under the Yule model. By comparing published phylogenies with Yule-generated trees, we found that simulations under the Yule model failed to capture much of the imbalance observed in real datasets, motivating a systematic evaluation of whether species tree shape affects method performance. We generated species tree topologies spanning a broad spectrum of imbalance using Ford's alpha model. Because tree-shape simulators generate topologies but not branch lengths, we developed a pipeline that fits branch lengths by sampling node ages under a Yule prior in RevBayes, allowing balanced and imbalanced trees to be compared under a common branch length model. We then simulated gene trees under the multispecies coalescent, generated sequence data, estimated gene trees with IQ-TREE, and benchmarked concatenation, summary, and site-based coalescent methods. In baseline simulations, greater species tree imbalance led to shorter internal branches, increasing ILS and gene tree estimation error; species tree estimation error also increased across all methods. Surprisingly, concatenation with IQ-TREE was often among the most accurate methods, even under high ILS. Weighted ASTRAL-IV and weighted TREE-QMC were also consistently accurate, whereas the site-based methods CASTER-site and CASTER-pair were generally the least accurate. Overall, our study highlights species tree shape as an important dimension of realistic phylogenomic benchmarking.

title: ADAMIXTURE: Adaptive First-Order Optimization for Biobank-Scale Genetic Clustering
authors: Joan Saurina-i-Ricos, Daniel Mas Montserrat, Alexander Ioannidis
abstract: Motivation: Estimating genetic clusters from sequencing data is a fundamental task in population and medical genetics, enabling demographic inference and adjustment for population structure in association studies. ADMIXTURE, a widely used model-based clustering method, employs an accelerated Expectation–Maximization (EM) algorithm to infer population parameters; however, its computational demands scale poorly, limiting its usefulness for modern biobank-sized datasets. While recent EM acceleration strategies employing second-order quasi-Newton schemes preserve accuracy, they remain computationally intensive. Conversely, EM-free approaches that prioritize speed often compromise solution quality. Results: We introduce ADAMIXTURE, a novel optimization framework that integrates the EM algorithm with Adaptive Moment Estimation (Adam). Unlike traditional acceleration methods, ADAMIXTURE utilizes first-order gradients with adaptive learning rates derived from raw and squared moments to approximate curvature information, bypassing the computational overhead of Hessian approximations. This approach surpasses the convergence efficiency of second-order methods while maintaining the low computational complexity of first-order updates. Across simulated and large-scale empirical datasets, ADAMIXTURE demonstrates substantial reductions in wall-clock runtime and enhanced scalability compared to state-of-the-art methods, while maintaining comparable or improved inference accuracy. Its GPU implementation runs in under 2 hours on half a million samples and variants, a two order of magnitude speedup over current state-of-the-art.

title: Phylogenetic Placement Achieves Near-Haplotype Resolution in Wastewater-Based Epidemiology using WEPP
authors: Pranav Gangwar, Pratik Katte, Manu Bhat, Yatish Turakhia
abstract: Wastewater-based epidemiology (WBE) is a cost-effective, unbiased, and time-efficient tool for public health surveillance. Although widely adopted since the COVID-19 pandemic, WBE remains underutilized in genomic epidemiology, as most tools are limited to lineage-level resolution and focus only on estimating lineage abundances from wastewater sequencing reads. In this talk, we present WEPP, a pathogen-agnostic pipeline that improves both the resolution and capabilities of WBE analysis. WEPP uses phylogenetic placement of sequencing reads onto mutation-annotated trees (MATs) - daily updated phylogenies of all globally available clinical sequences and their inferred ancestors-to sensitively and precisely identify a subset of haplotypes likely present in a sample. It also reports the abundance of each haplotype and lineage, and flags "unaccounted alleles" - those found in the sample but not explained by selected haplotypes-that may indicate novel variants. WEPP includes a powerful interactive dashboard for high-resolution visual analysis, allowing users to explore haplotype and lineage abundances, read-to-haplotype mappings, and unaccounted alleles within a global phylogenetic context. Applied to wastewater samples from multiple cities and pathogens, WEPP uncovered biological insights sometimes missed by other tools and enabled new WBE applications previously confined to clinical sequencing, such as identifying (i) intra-lineage haplotype clusters, (ii) multiple cluster introductions in a city, (iii) early haplotype detection up to five weeks before clinical confirmation, (iv) mutations from novel variants, and (v) circulating lineages missed by clinical surveillance. With these capabilities, WEPP can transform wastewater-based epidemiology into a more powerful tool for monitoring and managing infectious disease outbreaks.

title: Ok-k-mer: Integrating multiple k-mers for calculating genomic distance
authors: Stephen Hwang, Ben Langmead
abstract: Advances in sequencing and assembly have led to an exponential increase in available genomes, necessitating higher resolution and precision in calculating genomic similarity, such as average nucleotide identity (ANI). While k-mer-based approaches offer increased computational efficiency, fixed-length k-mer-based taxonomic read classification loses specificity as databases grow. Using the EvANI benchmarking framework, we previously showed that no single k-mer length is universally optimal across taxonomies. We found evidence that combining two k-mer lengths can improve concordance, but didn’t provide a principled way to select these k-mers and apply these k-mer recommendations to datasets. Here, we introduce Ok-k-mer, a tool to systematically select and integrate multiple k-mers for pairwise genomic distance estimation. Given a phylogenetic tree, Ok-k-mer ranks genome pairs by Jaccard distance across a range of k and uses a progressive search to maximize the Spearman correlation between weighted-average k-mer ranks and true branch distances. Across six GTDB datasets, Ok-k-mer identified ensembles that outperform single k-mers. For example, in a Chlamydiales dataset (n=288), a k-mer ensemble of 22, 18, and 8 achieved a correlation of rho = 0.5253, substantially surpassing the best single k-mer (k=20, rho = 0.4240) and the standard 31-mer (rho = 0.3843). We demonstrate that our recommendations are robust to missing data and vary across subtrees, reflecting diverse evolutionary complexities. Ok-k-mer provides a formal framework for moving beyond a "one-k-fits-all" k-mer analysis, improving genomic distance estimation and informing tree placement in the era of massive-scale genomics.

title: Recombination on genotype representation graphs: toward fast forward-time genetic simulation with arbitrary complexity
authors: Sahana Senthilkumar, Akshay Anand, Wilson Pan, Drew DeHaas, Xinzhu Wei, Richard Border
abstract: Forward-time and coalescent simulators such as SLiM and msprime can record ancestry and mutations in succinct tree sequences over long evolutionary horizons. However, many analyses require explicit access to genotypes at each generation, for example, to implement assortative mating or indirect genetic effects. Such operations effectively require the genotype matrix implied by the tree sequence, but the representation stops being succinct when performing per-generation genotype-level computations. By contrast, frameworks that operate on dense genotype matrices support arbitrary operatios at every generation but incur O(nm) storage (given n samples and m variants) and corresponding costs for repeated recombination at whole-genome scale. All together, existing tools tend to optimize either long-horizon compression or flexible per-generation linear algebra, but not both. Genotype representation graphs (GRGs) compress shared haplotype structure while still supporting matrix-vector products with subquadratic complexity, but prior work employs a static representation and does not incorporate meiotic recombination. Here we extend GRGs with interval-annotated edges specifying the genomic region covered, enabling recombination directly on the graph without matrix conversion. Given two parent haplotypes and a crossover breakpoint, our algorithm creates an offspring node by recursively traversing each parent's ancestry within the appropriate genomic interval. Our work thus successfully narrows the gap between succinct long-horizon simulations and matrix-based trait models. Future directions include parallelizing recursive graph traversal and benchmarking against matrix-based recombination.

title: LAML-Pro: Joint Maximum Likelihood Inference of Cell Genotypes and Cell Lineage Trees
authors: Gillian Chu, Henri Schmidt, Ben Raphael
abstract: Motivation. Recent dynamic lineage tracing technologies use genome editing to induce heritable mutations, or edits, that accumulate across successive cell divisions. These edits are measured using single-cell sequencing or imaging, providing data to reconstruct cell lineages at single-cell resolution. Current computational approaches to infer cell lineage trees, or phylogenies, from these data perform two separate steps: (1) Identify each cell’s edits (genotype) from the raw sequencing or imaging data; (2) Infer a cell lineage tree from the cell genotypes. However, genotyping cells is an inexact process and genotype errors can yield an inaccurate lineage tree. For example, using fluorescence based-imaging to measure edits results in a high fraction (≈25-50%) of uncertain or erroneous genotypes. Results. We introduce Lineage Analysis via Maximum Likelihood with PRobabilistic Observations (LAML-Pro), an algorithm that jointly infers cell genotypes and a cell lineage tree. LAML-Pro is based on the Probabilistic Mixed-type Missing Observation (PMMO) model, which we derive to describe both the genome editing and genotype observation processes. LAML-Pro constructs lineage trees from thousands of cells in under an hour by leveraging the sparsity of transitions under the PMMO model. On simulated data, we demonstrate that LAML-Pro corrects genotype errors and infers substantially more accurate trees than existing methods which are vulnerable to genotype errors. Applied to data from two recent imaging-based lineage tracing systems, LAML-Pro reduces genotype errors by 5-fold and produces more spatially coherent lineage trees compared to existing methods. Availability and Implementation. LAML-Pro is freely available at: github.com/raphael-group/LAML-Pro. Supplementary information. Supplementary Methods includes additional derivations and Supplementary Results includes additional descriptions of evaluation metrics, reproducibility details, and additional experiments.

title: Bounding mutations for a subsampling-placement strategy to reconstruct clonal lineage trees for somatic evolution
authors: Nishat Anjum Bristy, Russell Schwartz
abstract: Phylogenetics, like many areas of data-intensive discovery in biology, faces challenges from the ever-growing scale and complexity of modern sequencing data sets. This challenge is particularly acute in studies of somatic evolution, such as in cancers, where single-cell technologies now make it possible to sequence hundreds of thousands of genetically distinct cells and mutations on genome-wide scales. At the same time, the biological complexity of somatic evolution has led to the development of phylogenetic methods that can capture more complex evolutionary models than classic phylogenetics but often do not scale well even to moderately sized data sets. In this work, we investigate the theoretical and empirical foundations for addressing this problem through a strategy of subsampling mutations for phylogeny reconstruction followed by efficient placement of additional mutations onto an inferred guide tree. Our primary goal is to set lower bounds on the number mutations needed to recover a correct phylogeny at a desired level of resolution with high probability. We provide theoretical bounds for variants of several standard models that form the basis of several widely used clonal tree reconstruction methods. We further test the robustness of the resulting bounds using simulations and real biological datasets. The results suggest that, for typical numbers of clones, only modest numbers of mutations are needed to recover clonal trees accurately, providing support for mutation subsampling as a general approach for scaling phylogenetic inference to rapidly growing data.

title: New evolutionary dynamics emerge from phenotypic uncertainty
authors: Anna Sappington, Vaibhav Mohanty, Eugene Shakhnovich, Bonnie Berger
abstract: Classical population genetics has largely relied on the same stochastic differential equations (SDEs) for over 60 years to describe evolutionary dynamics. However, these SDEs ignore the fact that phenotype heterogeneity and noise are ubiquitous in biological systems from bacteria to cancers. Here, we develop Probabilistic Phenotype Genetics (ProP Gen) theory as a mathematical framework for evolutionary dynamics under phenotypic uncertainty. Our newly introduced class of SDEs show that, remarkably, phenotypic uncertainty causes many central tenets of classical population genetics to break down, such as invariance of evolutionary dynamics to global shifts in absolute fitness at fixed population size. We discover that lower-probability, high-fitness “phenotypic bridges" can substantially accelerate fitness valley crossing even at low mutation rates. We show our theory explains a paradoxical concept we call “phenotypic buoying" whereby low-fitness phenotypes can exist at surprisingly high frequencies when carried by a high-fitness phenotype. ProP Gen theory uncovers complex phase diagrams of simultaneous coexistence between genotype-phenotype pairs due to phenotypic buoying, which we derive analytically exactly and verify numerically. Notably, the standard Wright-Fisher branching process is unsuitable for probabilistic phenotype numerics. Thus, we develop a more general discrete-time simulation algorithm, Probabilistic Serial Dilution (ProSeD), which allows for overlapping generations and phenotypic uncertainty. Finally, we show the new diffusion limit of population genetics recapitulates the experimentally observed resuscitation and partitioning dynamics of bacterial “persister" strains. ProP Gen theory offers promise for describing and predicting the evolutionary dynamics of cancers, which have been empirically observed to exploit phenotypic uncertainty to evade treatment.

title: CAMUS: Scalable Phylogenetic Network Estimation
authors: James Willson, Tandy Warnow
abstract: Motivation. Phylogenetic networks are models of evolution that go beyond trees, and so represent reticulate events such as horizontal gene transfer or hybridization, which are frequently found in many taxa. Yet, the estimation of phylogenetic networks is extremely computationally challenging, and nearly all methods are limited to very small datasets with perhaps 10 to 15 species (some limited to even smaller numbers). Results. We introduce CAMUS (Constrained Algorithm Maximizing qUartetS), a scalable method for phylogenetic network estimation. CAMUS takes an input constraint tree T as well as a set Q of unrooted quartet trees that it derives from input, and returns a level-1 phylogenetic network N that is built upon T through the addition of edges, in order to maximize the number of quartet trees in Q that are induced in N. We perform a simulation study under the Network Multi-Species Coalescent and show that a simple pipeline using CAMUS provides high accuracy and outstanding speed and scalability, in comparison to two leading methods, PhyloNet-MPL used with a fixed tree and SNaQ. CAMUS is slightly less accurate than PhyloNet-MPL used without a fixed tree, but is much faster (minutes instead of hours) and can complete on inputs with 201 species while PhyloNet-MPL fails to complete on the inputs with more than 51 species. Availability and Implementation. The source code is available at https:// github.com/jsdoublel/camus.

title: DO-tanglegrams for phylogenetic trees and networks
authors: Daniel Huson
abstract: Phylogenetic trees and networks play a central role in biology, bioinformatics, and mathematical biology, and producing clear, informative visualizations of them is an important task. Tanglegrams, which display two phylogenies side by side with lines connecting shared taxa, are widely used for comparing evolutionary histories, host-parasite associations, and horizontal gene transfer. Existing layout algorithms have largely focused on trees and on minimizing the number of inter-taxon edge crossings. We introduce displacement-optimized tanglegrams (DO-tanglegrams), a new approach that applies equally to trees and rooted phylogenetic networks. Our method explicitly minimizes taxon displacement-the vertical misalignment of corresponding taxa across the two sides-and reticulate displacement-the vertical distance spanned by reticulation edges within a network. We formalize one-sided and two-sided optimization problems, show that exact minimization is computationally intractable, and propose a heuristic that combines exhaustive local search with simulated annealing. The algorithm naturally accommodates unresolved nodes (multifurcations or multicombinations) and missing taxa. To evaluate performance on trees, we compared our DO-tanglegram implementation in SplitsTree with a recently updated and widely-used method for trees, the cophylo function in the R package phytools. To evaluate perform on networks, we compared against the NN-tanglegram algorithm implemented in Dendroscope on a collection of synthetic networks. The results indicate that DO-tanglegram performs significantly better than cophylo on trees and than NN-tanglegram on networks.

title: Tracing Input Trees Inside PhyloFusion Network
authors: Banu Cetinkaya, Daniel Huson
abstract: Reticulate evolutionary processes such as hybridization, recombination, and horizontal gene transfer are commonly represented using rooted phylogenetic networks. PhyloFusion constructs such networks by combining multiple rooted phylogenetic trees into a single tree-child network that displays all input trees. Although this provides a compact representation of incongruent evolutionary histories, it is often difficult to determine how each individual input tree is embedded in the resulting network. We extend PhyloFusion by making tree membership explicit throughout the construction process. Each lineage taxon hypersequence entry is annotated with the identifier of the input tree from which it originates. During shortest common supersequence alignment, matching labels are merged and their associated tree sets are combined, so that every resulting network node retains information about the subset of input trees that support it. In addition, reticulate edges are explicitly annotated with tree-trace information, which is essential for resolving ambiguity at reticulation vertices. Since different incoming edges correspond to different input trees, these annotations are required to correctly propagate and reconstruct tree-specific paths through the network. Starting from annotations, we propagate tree-trace information through the network by postorder traversal, thereby obtaining a complete tree-specific annotation of nodes and edges. This makes it possible to trace, extract, and visualize each input tree directly within the PhyloFusion network. The result is a network construction framework that not only displays all input trees but also reveals their individual embeddings in an explicit and interpretable way.

title: Structure-Aware Reinforcement Learning for Reconstructing Duplication Event Histories in Gene Families
authors: Jeonghoon Choi, Sanghun Sel, Giltae Song
abstract: Segmental duplications account for ~5% of the human genome and are key drivers of gene family evolution and disease-associated copy number variation. Reconstructing duplication histories in gene family loci is critical for understanding the emergence of novel functions and inferring the roles of poorly characterized genes. However, this remains challenging because present-day genome assemblies provide only a static snapshot of these regions, obscuring the sequence of historical duplication and insertion events. To study such events, gene family loci are analyzed via self-alignment, where duplications followed by insertions can split a single event into multiple disjoint alignment blocks, making it difficult to recover event grouping and ordering. In this work, we propose a structure-aware reinforcement learning framework for reconstructing duplication event histories. Our approach uses noise filtering and one-step chain simulation as structural features to distinguish true alignments from spurious ones and identify locally chainable fragments. We then learn event ordering using reinforcement learning under partial dependency constraints and incorporate geometry-aware heuristics to capture long-range interactions beyond local decisions. We train and evaluate our model on synthetic gene family sequences generated from empirical alignment statistics. On scenarios with known ground truth, our method achieves 91–94% recall of true duplication events under medium complexity (30–70 events), compared to 81–88% for size-based greedy and 68–73% for random ordering. The learned policy generalizes to unseen tandem duplication patterns without retraining and demonstrates applicability to real gene families such as KIR and IFN.

title: In Pursuit of Forbidden Protein Domain Architectures
authors: Yu-Hsiang Chen, Xiaoyue Cui, Maureen Stolzer, Dannie Durand
abstract: The domain architecture of a protein is defined as the sequence of domains it encodes in N to C terminal order. Human domain architectures exhibit strong deviation from random expectations, suggesting that some domain combinations are "forbidden" by intrinsic constraints. Examining the properties of forbidden architectures has the potential to reveal these constraints. However, this requires distinguishing unseen architectures that are truly forbidden from those that are absent due to incomplete sampling and evolutionary contingency. To identify candidate forbidden architectures, we embedded genuine architectures and artificial architectures generated using a variety of randomization models in a high dimensional space. This revealed a cluster of artificial architectures that are distant from almost all genuine architectures. We hypothesize that this well-separated cluster represents a forbidden zone containing domain combinations that violate intrinsic constraints. To further investigate this hypothesis, we set out to compare properties of genuine architectures and architectures in the well-separated cluster. As a pilot study, we asked how often extracellular (EC) and DNA-binding (DB) domains co-occur in the same architecture; EC and DB domains represent functions associated with distinct, non-adjacent cellular compartments. We found that EC and DB domains co-occur in 48% of architectures in the well-separated cluster versus 1% of genuine architectures, suggesting that incompatible localization is likely a constraint on domain composition. Overall, our analysis suggests a quantitative framework for probing constraints shaping multidomain protein evolution.

title: BATH2: splice-aware translated search of protein sequences or profile HMMs against genomic DNA
authors: Genevieve Krause, Travis Wheeler
abstract: Annotation of protein-coding DNA in sequenced genomes is a foundational task in computational biology. A common workflow is to first identify and translate the open reading frames, then to annotate the resulting peptides by comparison to a database of protein sequences or profile hidden Markov models (pHMMs), and finally to map those annotations back to the genome. BATH is a tool that directly compares protein queries against genomic DNA, simplifying annotation by eliminating the translate-align-map paradigm. BATH's frameshift-aware pHMM alignment algorithm also provides sensitivity gains when annotating sequences containing frameshift-inducing indels. However, frameshift detection carried a runtime cost prohibitive for larger datasets, and like BLAST, MMSeqs2, and HMMER, BATH could not join genes split across multiple exons, yielding fragmented alignments for eukaryotic genomes. Here we present BATH2, which addresses both limitations. BATH2 uses a new spliced alignment pipeline that stitches hit fragments across exon boundaries, employing a graph algorithm to identify optimal join paths and a spliced Viterbi algorithm to recover missed exons and precisely detect splice sites. In benchmarks across animal, plant, and fungal species, BATH2 correctly annotates more than twice as many spliced genes as Miniprot and Spaln3. Splice-aware annotation runs at 1.3-2x the runtime cost of splice-oblivious search. BATH2 also improves frameshift alignment through updated parameterization and new SIMD implementations, yielding up to 20x runtime improvements and large gains in sensitivity and specificity.

title: Systematic inference of mutation rates and spectra across the tree of life via a scalable read-based framework
authors: Asaf Pinhasi, Keren Yizahak, Yosef Efraim Maruvka
abstract: The rapid expansion of available genomes across the tree of life promises to transform comparative genomics, opening the door to systematic, genome-wide analyses of evolutionary processes. Mutation rates and spectra have attracted growing interest as quantitative descriptors of molecular evolution. However, genome-genome alignment remains a major computational bottleneck, limiting large-scale, cross-phyla examination of mutational processes. To address this, we developed CORAL-Comparative Orthologous Read-based Analysis of Lineage Mutations. CORAL infers branch-specific mutations by fragmenting each sister genome into synthetic short pseudo-reads, aligning them to an outgroup reference with the fast and efficient BWA-MEM aligner, and then reconstructing changes by simple parsimony. When benchmarked on well-studied clades, mutation rates inferred by CORAL accurately aligned with UCSC Multiz-based whole-genome alignments (Pearson r>0.95). For each species branch, we extracted 96-category mutation spectra defined by substitution type and trinucleotide sequence context. We applied CORAL to 5,090 species with known divergence times, generating the largest comparative dataset of per-branch mutation rates and spectra assembled to date across animals, plants, fungi, and protists. This analysis revealed that mutation rates vary by orders of magnitude and exhibit a clear, strong negative correlation with life-history traits such as lifespan and body weight. Normalized spectra accurately recapitulate each clade’s genomic trinucleotide composition, indicating that mutational processes shape species genomic triplet content. At the same time, normalized spectra exhibit strong phylogenetic structure across eukaryotes, revealing mutation spectra as evolvable molecular traits that encode evolutionary relationships across the tree of life. Ultimately, we characterized seven distinct mutational signatures active across species. Of these, two are novel, three were previously observed only in somatic cancer contexts rather than in germline evolution, and two were previously reported in evolutionary contexts. The activity of these signatures varied considerably: while some appeared ubiquitous (e.g., an SBS5-like signature), others were lineage-specific, such as the SBS12-like signature in fungi and the newly identified SBSB, which was abundant only in a subset of fish lineages. Notably, the activity of some signatures correlated with life-history traits, suggesting distinct etiologies for established mutational processes. CORAL thus provides a flexible, high-throughput framework for comparative genomics, enabling systematic, large-scale inference of mutation rates and signatures across the tree of life.

title: Identifying Coevolution in Multiple Sequence Alignments with Machine Learning Anomaly Detection Methods
authors: Matthieu Vilain, Stéphane Aris-Brosou
abstract: Identifying pairs of sites that evolve in a correlated manner is central to predicting amino acid contacts within proteins, inter-molecular interfaces, viral immune escape, and drug resistance. A number of methods have been developed to detect coevolution in multiple sequence alignments (MSAs), including mutual information (MI), direct coupling analysis, or phylogeny-based models. Yet, despite their natural fit for the problem, anomaly detection approaches in machine learning (ML) have never been systematically applied to coevolution detection. Our key framing insight is that while the number of possible site pairs grows quadratically with sequence length, truly coevolving pairs scale linearly, making this a natural anomaly detection task. We propose to combine MI measurements and phylogenetic structure to construct an evolutionary matrix for each pair of sites in an MSA, and then evaluate three ML models: an Isolation Forest, an autoencoder, and a convolutional autoencoder, for identifying anomalous (coevolving) matrices. We performed parameter tuning on a held-out set of simulated MSAs and benchmarked the models on a separate dataset where coevolution strength, tree length, sequence number, and length, as well as the number of coevolving sites, were systematically varied. Our results indicate that the Isolation Forest outperformed both MI and other ML methods under most conditions. Future work includes validation on experimentally confirmed coevolving sites in viral datasets and expanding the framework towards epistasis detection, that is, predicting the phenotypic effect of paired mutations, to move beyond detection of correlated evolution to identifying genuine coevolution.

title: A Unified Substitution– Mutation Rate Ratio (c/µ) Framework and Near-Neutral Selectionist Theory for Molecular Evolution: Insights from SARS-CoV-2
authors: Chun Wu, Nicholas Paradis, Khushi Jain
abstract: Understanding how mutations shape genome evolution remains a central challenge, particularly in resolving the neutralist–selectionist debate. Traditional frameworks such as Ka/Ks and mutation–selection (MutSel) models provide important insights but have key limitations. Ka/Ks assumes synonymous mutations are neutral and is restricted to coding regions, while MutSel requires equilibrium assumptions and significant computational complexity, limiting genome-wide applicability, especially in untranslated regions (UTRs). To overcome these limitations, we introduce a unified framework based on the substitution–mutation rate ratio (c/µ), which quantifies selection at the nucleotide level across entire genomes. Here, c represents the substitution rate and µ the mutation rate. The ratio c/µ directly measures fitness effects, classifying mutations as beneficial (c/µ > 1), neutral (c/µ = 1), or deleterious (c/µ < 1), without assuming synonymous neutrality and with applicability to both translated and untranslated regions. We further derive the relationship c/µ = Ps(Ks/µ) + Pa(Ka/µ), showing that Ka/ Ks is equivalent to c/µ only when synonymous mutations are neutral. Empirical SARS-CoV-2 analysis demonstrates frequent violations of this assumption, leading to misclassification by Ka/Ks. Building on this, we develop the Near-Neutral Selectionist Theory (NNST), supported by L-shaped distributions of fitness effects dominated by deleterious mutations with smaller fractions of neutral and beneficial mutations. Two regimes emerge: Near-Neutral Balanced Selectionist Theory (NNBST), explaining strict molecular clocks through balanced near-neutral effects, and Near-Neutral Unbalanced Selectionist Theory (NNUST), explaining deviations from clock behavior. Analysis of 49 genomic segments shows both regimes coexist, indicating evolution is governed by a spectrum of near-neutral dynamics. Together, c/µ and NNST provide a unified, data-driven framework that reconciles neutral and selectionist perspectives, offering a more complete model of genome evolution.

title: AI-Driven Protein Functional Annotation and Biomedical Discovery
authors: Cathy Wu
abstract: We have witnessed the transformative impact of artificial intelligence and accelerated biomedical knowledge discovery with advancements in large language models (LLMs), retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), knowledge graphs (KGs), and agentic AI. In this talk, I will highlight several areas of AI development in the UniProt Consortium for protein functional annotation and biomedical discovery. These include: (1) using protein language models (pLMs) as a scalable approach for protein name and function prediction, (2) combining text mining with LLMs as a generalizable framework for both relation extraction and summarization from scientific literature, and (3) developing a protein knowledge network (ProKN) in partnership with the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem as an interoperable and sustainable means for data integration and knowledge discovery. All functional annotations generated by the pLMs, text mining tools, and LLMs are clearly labelled as AI annotations with evidence tagging and literature reference. The ProKN knowledge graph integration expands the utility of interconnected biomedical data for drug repurposing, understanding disease mechanisms and functional genomics. Collectively, the AI-driven approach allows the UniProt Consortium to improve the functioning of the UniProt knowledgebase while making UniProt data AI-ready to democratize access by the broad user community.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: AMR-Fold: Structure-Aware Deep Learning for Antibiotic Resistance Gene Discovery and Classification
authors: Sergio Sánchez Carrillo, Dearbháile Morris
abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is a major global health threat, yet most current tools for antibiotic resistance gene (ARG) detection rely on sequence similarity to known databases and may fail to identify divergent or novel ARGs. To address this limitation, we developed AMR-Fold, a structure-aware deep learning model for simultaneous ARG detection and ARG-class prediction from protein sequences. AMR-Fold integrates complementary representations from a protein language model and predicted structural features, combining residue-level embeddings, 3Di structural tokens, and confidence scores within a dual-input transformer architecture. The model was trained and evaluated on a curated dataset of 54,044 proteins, including 27,022 ARGs spanning 15 resistance classes and 27,022 non-ARG proteins. To minimise homology-driven information leakage, sequences were clustered and split at the cluster level into training, validation, and test sets using an 80:10:10 partition. Hyperparameters were optimised with Optuna in a multi-task framework combining binary ARG detection and ARG-class classification. Across five independent retraining seeds, AMR-Fold achieved highly stable performance. Mean validation and test macro-F1 for ARG-class prediction on ARG-positive sequences were 0.9542 and 0.9449, respectively, while binary ARG/non-ARG discrimination reached test F1 values up to 0.9882 in the final ensemble. These results indicate strong generalisation beyond near-identical homologues. AMR-Fold provides a promising framework for improved ARG discovery, benchmarking against current state-of-the-art methods, and future validation in coastal metagenomic datasets generated within the BlueAdapt project.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Leveraging phenomic variation and knowledge graphs to elucidate molecular functionality
authors: Yannick Mahlich, Dylan Ross, Lummy Monteiro, Sutanay Chowdhury, Jasmin Alvarez, Heather Olson, Tong Zhang, Sneha Couvillion, Jeffrey Czajka, Jason McDermott
abstract: Linking different biological data modalities from multi-omics experiments to elucidate functional relationships remains challenging largely due to limitations in feature annotation. For mass spectrometry-based multi-omics measurements, these issues stem from reliance on incomplete reference databases for the annotation of detected features. This issue is especially pronounced in poorly characterized biological systems. Failing to resolve functional descriptions for proteins and chemical compounds leads to dead-ends for interpreting biology from these experiments, and approaches that can improve annotation rates independent from necessary improvements to reference database coverage are desperately needed. We present a novel knowledge graph-based integration approach using on our Variation-Leveraged Phenomic Association Study (VaLPAS) framework, that is suited to the task of functional interpretation from partially annotated multi-omics data. In this approach, edges are associations calculated from mass-spectrometry data between proteins and metabolites and nodes are augmented with prior biological knowledge from sources like KEGG and Gene Ontology. Our knowledge graph can then be used to infer functional annotations for otherwise unannotated metabolites and proteins by strongly associating them with other known molecular features. We demonstrate that this knowledge graph approach is successful at predicting both chemical annotations for unknown metabolites as well as offering insight into the potential functionality of unannotated proteins using an experimental dataset investigating lipid yields of Lipomyces starkeyi under a range of growth and stress conditions. Our approach presents a promising avenue to elucidate previously unexplored molecular dark matter in a way that is not possible using existing tools.

title: Enhancing Protein Function Annotation through Explainable Reasoning with LLM
authors: Huiying Yan, Hancheng Liu, Shanfeng Zhu
abstract: Automated protein function prediction/annotation (AFP) is essential for bridging the gap between the exponential growth of protein sequences and very limited experimental knowledge. Recent text-based methods, such as GORetriever and GOAnnotator, have demonstrated that scientific literature provides rich and effective signals for protein function annotation. However, they function as "black boxes" that lack interpretability, which prevents them from effectively assisting human experts in manual curation. We present GOReasoner, a framework built on the "Initiate-Reason-Propagate" paradigm that employs a fine-tuned LLM, GOExplainer, to enhance in-depth functional reasoning for existing AFP methods. It integrates weighted direct preference optimization(W-DPO) for precise judgment scoring and a Dynamic Propagation (DPP) mechanism to ensure hierarchical consistency. This enables GOReasoner to effectively refine functional candidates derived from different AFP methods. Experiments across multiple benchmarks confirm GOReasoner’s versatility and strong performance across diverse literature sources, from expert annotated to automatically retrieved. By offering verifiable biological explanations and reducing hallucinations, GOReasoner turns automated predictions into interpretable insights, aiming to narrow the gap between large-scale prediction and expert validation. The code and data are available at https:// github.com/ZhuLab-Fudan/GOReasoner.

title: Protein embeddings to address functional specificity in protein families
authors: Ana Rojas, Ildefonso Cases
abstract: Nuclear receptors (NRs) and small GTPases are major protein superfamilies with distinct classification principles-ligand-binding properties in NRs and sequence features in GTPases. Both exhibit multidomain architectures, often requiring analyses to focus on conserved regions. Here, we assess whether protein sequence embeddings can capture functional relationships within these families. Using an alignment-free framework, we generated embeddings from full-length sequences and specific domains, and analyzed them through clustering and classification with multiple protein language models. Embeddings effectively recapitulate GTPase classifications, particularly when using full-length sequences, but perform less well for NRs, where function depends on binding modes not directly encoded in sequence. Overall, whole-protein embeddings outperform domain-based ones, and model choice significantly impacts performance. These results highlight the strengths and limitations of embeddings for protein sub-family classification.

title: Knowledge-guided Contextual Gene Set Analysis with Large Language Models

abstract: Motivation: Gene set analysis (GSA) is a foundational approach for interpreting genomic data of diseases by linking genes to biological processes. However, conventional GSA methods overlook clinical context of the analyses, often generating long lists of enriched pathways with redundant, nonspecific, or irrelevant results. Interpreting these requires extensive, ad-hoc manual effort, reducing both reliability and reproducibility. Results: We introduce cGSA, a novel AI-driven framework that enhances GSA by incorporating context-aware pathway prioritization. cGSA integrates gene cluster detection, enrichment analysis, and large language models to identify pathways that are not only statistically significant but also biologically meaningful. Benchmarking on 102 curated gene sets across 19 diseases and ten disease-related biological mechanisms shows that cGSA outperforms baseline methods by over 30\%, with expert validation confirming its increased precision and interpretability. Two independent case studies in melanoma and breast cancer further demonstrate its potential to uncover context-specific insights and support targeted hypothesis. title: Alpha&ESMhFolds: An updated database for the comparison and functional annotation of predicted structural models for the human proteome

abstract: The adoption of predicted models of protein structures generated by methods such as AlphaFold and ESMFold is ever-increasing. We release an updated version of a public database available at https://alpha-esmhfolds.biocomp.unibo.it/, storing pairs of models for 48,815 human proteins enriched with functional characterization. This release, synchronized with the latest updates of resources like UniProt, PDB, AlphaFold DB, and Pfam, introduces new functionalities. We extract for each protein Pfam annotations and known pathogenic variants. Both are mapped on the predicted structures and can be visualized from the web server. Moreover, we complement the structural superimposition of AlphaFold2 and ESMFold models with an external validation performed by three state-of-the-art Quality Assessment tools, providing a consensus to suggest the best model for each protein. Exploiting those functionalities, we perform large-scale analysis to identify two interesting trends. First, both AlphaFold2 and ESMFold are consistently better at predicting regions of the proteins covered by Pfam entries. Not only do both methods exhibit higher average pLDDT scores in those regions when compared to the average of the full models, but their agreement, measured by the TM-score upon structural superimposition, also increases from 0.58 to 0.88. Second, focusing on the subset of proteins for which the two methods produce diverging models, we observe that the consensus of external QA tools assigns better scores to AlphaFold for only 51% of the cases, supporting the usefulness of having different models available to exploit the strengths of each method, particularly when the models differ.

title: A Deep Positive-Unlabeled Learning Approach to Cell-Penetrating Peptide Discovery
authors: Jérôme Tubiana, Omri Yakir, Chieh Chang, Maayan Gal
abstract: Cell-penetrating peptides (CPPs) are a promising approach for the intracellular delivery of diverse molecular cargos. However, although hundreds of CPPs have been characterized, most are cationic peptides with poor pharmacoproperties or limited uptake efficiency; new high-throughput discovery approaches are thus imperative. Here, we introduce BaggingCPP, a machine learning-based CPP virtual screening framework that integrates inductive Positive-Unlabeled (PU) learning, protein language models, and parameter-efficient fine-tuning algorithms. Unlike prior works, we do not use an artificial negative set to train the model. Instead, we use PU learning to simultaneously train on, and screen a library of candidate peptides-a large corpus of naturally expressed peptides such as hormones, neuropeptides, and small proteins. We show that BaggingCPP is competitive with the state-of-the-art model GraphCPP when training and evaluating on the standard public CPP1708 benchmark. More importantly, we demonstrate that the PU learning formulation effectively addresses the distribution shift problem commonly encountered in the standard train-then-screen protocol, thereby significantly reducing the false positive rate. Using BaggingCPP, we identified several candidate CPPs with low similarity to any known CPP, and experimentally tested them with cellular permeability assays. We notably found two cyclic peptides with favorable pharmacoproperties and comparable uptake efficiency to the gold-standard Tat peptide. Bagging CPP thus represents a data-driven, biologically grounded route to expand the chemical diversity of known CPPs.

title: PUFFIN: Protein Unit Discovery with Functional Supervision
authors: Gökçe Uludoğan, Elif Ozkirimli, Arzucan Ozgur, Buse Giledereli
abstract: Motivation: Proteins carry out biological functions through the coordinated action of groups of residues organized into structural arrangements. These arrangements, which we refer to as protein units, exist at an intermediate scale, being larger than individual residues yet smaller than entire proteins. A deeper understanding of protein function can be achieved by identifying these units and their associations with function. However, existing approaches either focus on residue-level signals, rely on curated annotations, or segment protein structures without incorporating functional information, thereby limiting interpretable analysis of structure-function relationships. Results: We introduce PUFFIN, a data-driven framework for discovering protein units by jointly learning structural partitioning and functional supervision. PUFFIN represents proteins as residue-level structure graphs and applies a graph neural network with a structure-aware pooling mechanism that partitions each protein into contiguous, multi-residue units, with functional supervision that shapes the partition. We show that the learned units are structurally coherent, exhibit organized associations with molecular function, and show meaningful correspondence with curated InterPro annotations. Together, these results demonstrate that PUFFIN provides an interpretable framework for analyzing structure–function relationships using learned protein units and their statistical function associations. title: How Not to be Seen: Predicting Unseen Enzyme Functions using Contrastive Learning

While it is not possible to assign a not-yet-existent label to such a sequence, there is high value in placing it as accurately as possible in known function space. Our method, EnzPlacer, predicts the third, second and first EC numbers when given a protein whose 4th EC number was not in the training corpus. track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Improving protein function annotation with balanced representations and evolutionary profiles
authors: Jiaqi Luo, Shitong Dai, Yunan Luo
abstract: Accurate protein function prediction is essential for interpreting the rapidly growing sequence databases, yet current computational methods remain unreliable for proteins associated with rare functions or lacking close annotated homologs. This challenge is driven by the imbalanced annotation distributions and by the limited ability of existing methods to exploit evolutionary context for remote homologs. To address these issues, we developed two complementary sequence-based representation learning frameworks, MSRep and EPERep, for robust protein function annotation. MSRep improves prediction for underrepresented functions by refining pretrained protein language model embeddings with a neural collapse-inspired objective that promotes a more evenly distributed representation space across function classes. EPERep further enhances prediction by retrieving homologous sequences from a large unlabeled database and integrating them with the query to construct a contextualized evolutionary profile. Across four major annotation benchmarks — Enzyme Commission numbers, Gene3D domains, Pfam families, and Gene Ontology terms — both methods consistently outperform strong machine-learning and alignment-based baselines. MSRep shows the largest gains for underrepresented function classes and maintains strong performance across functions with different frequencies in the training set. EPERep is especially effective for proteins with low sequence identity to the training set and improves remote homology detection by leveraging unlabeled evolutionary neighborhoods. Together, these results show that balanced representation learning and retrieval-based evolutionary profiling are complementary strategies for improving protein function prediction in the most challenging real-world regimes. Our work provides scalable approaches for annotating understudied proteins and narrowing the gap between sequence availability and functional characterization.

title: Learning Protein Post-Translational Modification Sites Prediction via Spatially-Aware Local Conditioning of Embeddings on Proximal Evidences
authors: Pawel Pratyush, Bhawana Prasain, Meenal Chaudhari, Stefan Schulze, Dukka B Kc
abstract: Existing Post-Translational Modification (PTM) predictors often treat site predictions as independent, overlooking the rich biochemical context provided by neighboring modifications. In this work, we introduce Evidence Maps, a novel representation that encodes the annotated PTM sites within the local sequential neighborhood of a target site. We propose a multi-task framework that utilizes these maps as the primary conditioning signal for PTM site prediction. By incorporating Evidence Maps with latent protein embeddings through Feature-wise Linear Modulation (FiLM), the model performs evidence-aware feature transformations. To ensure these interactions are physically grounded, we augment the conditioning with geometric descriptors derived from residue-centered local 3D coordinate frames. To capture the interdependence among distinct PTM tasks, we further introduce a Neighborhood Attention mechanism featuring cross-talk gates. These gates allow task-specific heads to interact with both peer predictions and evidence maps simultaneously, iteratively updating their own output. The framework is designed for residue-specific learning, jointly predicting multiple PTM types for a shared amino acid type, enabling shared representation learning and modeling inter-modification dependencies. Our proposed approach substantially outperforms existing predictors across multiple PTM prediction tasks, demonstrating the benefits of integrating intra-protein relational evidence with spatial geometry.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: nail: high-speed sequence annotation with profile hidden Markov models
authors: Jack Roddy, Travis Wheeler
abstract: The dominant method for accurate annotation of a protein is sequence database search, in which an unlabeled sequence is classified by aligning it to an established database of sequences or profile hidden Markov models (pHMMs). Alignment with HMMER has long been the gold standard for sensitive alignment-based annotation, but is often not used due to runtime limitations; meanwhile recent algorithmic advances (as in MMseqs2 and DIAMOND2) have resulted in hyper-fast annotation tools with reported sensitivity close to that of the venerable BLAST. Here, we introduce a new tool, called nail, that addresses the tension between competing needs for sensitivity and speed in sequence annotation. On a protein benchmark, nail recovers almost all of the recall difference between MMseqs2 and HMMER, with run time only ~2x slower than MMseqs2 with sensitive settings. The core computation of pHMM alignment is performed in the Forward/Backward (FB) algorithm, which fills in a dynamic programming (DP) matrix with size that is the product of the lengths of the pHMM and sequence. The nail software implements a heuristic approximation of the FB algorithm by computing a sparse subset of the cells in the DP matrix that contains nearly all of the probability mass. The method produces an accurate approximation of HMMER-based pHMM scores and E-values with high speed and small memory requirements. As a proof of concept, nail aligns a 5GB dataset of viral proteins with the entire geNomad database of ~228K viral protein family pHMMs in under 4 hours on a 48 core machine.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Critical Assessment of Protein Function Annotation algorithms: CAFA6 preliminary results and CAFA Forever
authors: An Phan, Iddo Friedberg, Predrag Radivojac, M. Clara De Paolis Kaluza, Paul D. Thomas, Damiano Piovesan, Walter Reade, Parnal Joshi, Maria Martin, Sandra Orchard, Martyna Plomecka, María Cruz, Chris Mungall
abstract: The Critical Assessment of protein Function Annotation (CAFA) is an ongoing community effort to independently assess computational methods for protein function prediction, to highlight well-performing methodologies and provide a forum for the dissemination of results and exchange of ideas. In its fifth and sixth rounds (CAFA5 and CAFA6), CAFA has expanded its scope and community reach by partnering with Kaggle to engage a broader community of machine learning practitioners and data scientists. Participants are provided with protein targets and are free to apply diverse data sources and computational strategies to generate functional annotations, which are centrally collected and subsequently evaluated after a waiting period during which new experimental annotations accumulate. In this talk, we present a preliminary analysis of the prediction models in CAFA6. We now include the partial-knowledge assessment of proteins, that is, proteins that accumulated deeper GO annotations beyond what has already been known, on the largest test set so far in CAFA, with more than 224,000 proteins. Finally, we turn our attention to the future and discuss the plan and implementation of CAFA Forever, a continuous assessment framework designed to complement and extend the existing CAFA beyond the punctuated competition paradigm. CAFA Forever enables ongoing evaluation of containerized prediction methods on regularly updated annotation data, thereby transforming CAFA from a periodic challenge into a persistent benchmarking ecosystem. This transition aims to accelerate methodological iteration, support reproducibility, and provide a more dynamic and fine-grained view of progress in protein function prediction.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Extending CAFA to Natural Language: Towards Evaluating Free-Text Protein Function Descriptions
authors: M. Clara De Paolis Kaluza, An Phan, Iddo Friedberg, Predrag Radivojac
abstract: Computational methods for protein function prediction have advanced considerably, yet evaluation paradigms remain largely confined to structured ontology terms. With the advancement of generative natural language models and specifically the emergence of models that generate free-text functional descriptions, there is a growing need for rigorous evaluation frameworks that assess the factual correctness, completeness, and utility of natural language predictions. Here, we present an ongoing effort to extend the CAFA evaluation paradigm to free-text protein function descriptions. We propose a two-level evaluation framework. First, we assess high-level semantic similarity between generated descriptions and reference UniProt text summaries using biomedical language model embeddings (PubMedBERT), providing a coarse measure of alignment with curated knowledge. Second, we decompose generated into individual factual assertions and map each claim to structured Gene Ontology terms, and verify them against GO annotations, yielding fine-grained measures of factual precision and completeness. Following the CAFA temporal holdout design, we evaluate predictions only against information accrued after each model's training cutoff, enabling assessment of genuinely novel predictive content. We apply this framework to outputs from 18 models collected as an optional challenge in the CAFA 6 competition. Automated scores from both evaluation levels are used to rank predictions and select subsets for expert bio-curator review, supplemented by random sampling to calibrate the relationship between automated metrics and human judgment. We discuss preliminary findings on the reliability of claim decomposition and structured term mapping, and outline challenges including reference coverage gaps and the granularity of atomic claims in biological text.
keywords: Free-Text Protein Function; Function Descriptions; natural language; CAFA; Evaluating Free-Text

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: The Variation-leveraged phenomic Foundation Model (VFM): A novel multi-omic AI model for understanding biological systems context
authors: Jason McDermott, Yannick Mahlich, Ben Drucker, Kate Schultz, Sayan Ghosh, Nathan Tallent, Christopher Oehmen
abstract: Despite continuing advances in sequencing and computational function determination, large fractions of a biological systems gene and protein function potential remain unresolved. The advent of AI approaches applied to biological data has resulted in transformational advances in structure prediction from sequence, and in gene-and protein-language models trained on millions of sequences, that can reveal hidden evolutionary patterns and rules driving functional classes. However, these approaches are fail to incorporate system and environmental context, which is an important – yet underappreciated – component of gene and protein function. The availability of large quantities of high-throughput molecular functional data from transcriptomics, proteomics, and high-throughput phenotypic screens for genetic fitness provide an opportunity for new models to understand patterns of functional activation and regulation across many conditions and organisms. Under the Department of Energy (DOE)’s new Genesis Mission we have developed a multi-modal transformer-based foundation model called the Variation-leveraged Phenomic Foundation Model (VFM) that is trained on bacterial multi-omics data and represents molecular components (genes, proteins, and pathways) in a high-dimensional functional systems embedding space. The unsupervised model has been trained on thousands of bacterial genomes, and phenotypic fitness profiling datasets, transcriptomics and proteomics datasets with different environmental conditions. Embeddings from the model represent individual features (ortholog groups) and their relationships as they function in the bacterial system, interact in different complexes and pathways, and respond to environmental signals. We have benchmarked VFM using KEGG metabolic pathways, STRING database, and experimentally-determined regulons. Our results show that VFM can predict interactions, module and pathway membership, and regulatory relationships across many organisms with high confidence, and that novel interactions show strong phenotype associations. To demonstrate the utility of VFM and the model’s standout feature of incorporating system and environmental context into the predictions, we analyzed a dataset of Variovorax transcriptomes from an experimental study investigating microbe interaction with a plant host and the resulting effect on the host’s thermoprotection phenotype. To this end we use VFM feature embeddings to cluster genes, then identify subnetworks that are associated with conferring plant thermoprotection phenotype. The demonstration shows how VFM can be used to rapidly analyze functional activity for useful phenotypes and predict underlying biological mechanisms.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: Agentic evaluation of AI function prediction pipelines
authors: Harry Caufield, Marcin Joachimiak, Chris Mungall
abstract: Assigning functions to gene products is a foundational task of molecular biology, accomplished through literature-based expert curation and computational prediction. Most annotation databases deploy HMM-and family-based pipelines. Recently, protein language models and other AI methods have triggered an explosion of new prediction tools. Reviewing these presents challenges. The Critical Assessment of Functional Annotation (CAFA) series tracks aggregate progress against Gene Ontology database snapshots, but its scores often reward annotations curators later reject. A second, acute problem is that modern agentic and foundation-model predictors no longer emit only GO terms: BioReason-Pro, for example, outputs a free-text functional summary and a chain-of-thought reasoning trace alongside its term list, which CAFA cannot grade. de Crécy-Lagard et al. manually reviewed 453 predictions from a top deep learning method on uncharacterised *E. coli* proteins: only 3/453 were genuinely novel and correct, the remainder falling into systematic error classes. But performing this level of extensive manual review of a broad range of annotations is challenging. Here we demonstrate an agentic review system (AIGR) that synthesizes multiple lines of evidence and performs biological reasoning to evaluate sequence-based predictions. AIGR complements CAFA-style benchmarks by grading narrative and reasoning content in qualitative terms, providing human-readable explanations, and assigning failed predictions to a failure mode taxonomy. Applied to a large-scale evaluation of BioReason-Pro and a replication of the de Crécy-Lagard taxonomy, we find that recent reasoning and embedding-based predictors either make systematic errors or, when correct, recapitulate baseline HMM-based approaches.
keywords: AI function prediction; de Cr cy-Lagard; Agentic evaluation; providing human-readable explanations; manually reviewed 453

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: PU-GRAIL: residue-level graph learning for identifying protective bacterial antigens under positive–unlabeled supervision
authors: Jaemin Jeon, Sangwook Jung, Inuk Jung, Kwangsoo Kim, Jinki Yeom
abstract: Motivation: The identification of protective antigens is fundamentally constrained by sparse annotations and pervasive label uncertainty in reverse vaccinology. Protective antigen–antibody interactions are mediated by a limited subset of surface-accessible residues that form spatially coherent epitopes. This motivates modeling antigenicity at the residue level, where three-dimensional structure provides critical context for functional immune recognition. Moreover, antigen datasets are inherently positive unlabeled: unannotated proteins may contain hidden positives, making reliable negatives difficult to obtain. Results: We present PU-GRAIL, a graph neural network framework that integrates protein language model embeddings with predicted 3D structures under positive–unlabeled learning. Trained and evaluated on three benchmark datasets, PU-GRAIL achieves competitive performance compared with existing methods. Importantly, the model’s attention mechanism enables residue-level interpretation, identifying putative epitope regions that correspond to experimentally validated antibody-binding sites. Beyond standard benchmarks, we demonstrate practical utility through (i) severity-associated antigenicity patterns in SARS-CoV-2 patient cohorts, and (ii) proteome-wide vaccine candidate prioritization across 11 bacterial species

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: In a genAI world, does structured knowledge still have a role in science?
authors: Karin Verspoor
abstract: The paradigm of generative AI, based on foundation models that have absorbed vast volumes of scientific knowledge captured in digital artefacts including publications, ontologies, and databases, threatens to disrupt disciplines such as bioinformatics which have traditionally relied on curated, structured knowledge. Models which rely on implicit knowledge representation through complex, data-driven mathematical models, and which reproduce knowledge through language, stand in stark contrast to carefully constructed, curated information captured through relational structures and formal semantics. This talk will explore the tensions this creates, and consider connections between these apparently opposing paradigms. I may raise more questions than I can answer, but isn’t that the point of science?

title: GO-CAM: thousands of curated pathways using GO, and new tools for using them
authors: Paul Thomas, Chris Mungall
abstract: The Gene Ontology Causal Activity Modeling (GO-CAM) framework was introduced to extend GO annotations to represent gene functions in the context of larger systems such as metabolic and signaling pathways (Thomas et al., Nat Genet 51:1429-1433, 2019). In a recent publication (GO Consortium, Nucleic Acids Res 54:D1779-D1792, 2026), we described how the GO Consortium has rapidly increased coverage of expert-curated GO-CAM models for human genes, as well as for a few other well studied organisms. Here, we provide the latest updates on GO-CAM curation progress and plans, and describe new software tools for accessing and using GO-CAM models, such as the gocam-py package.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: STAR-GO: Improving Protein Function Prediction by Learning to Hierarchically Integrate Ontology-Informed Semantic Embeddings
authors: Mehmet Efe Akça, Gökçe Uludoğan, Arzucan Ozgur, Inci Baytaş
abstract: Accurate prediction of protein function is essential for elucidating molecular mechanisms and advancing biological and therapeutic discovery. Yet experimental annotation lags far behind the rapid growth of protein sequence data. Computational approaches address this gap by associating proteins with Gene Ontology (GO) terms, which encode functional knowledge through hierarchical relations and textual definitions. However, existing models often emphasize one modality over the other, limiting their ability to generalize, particularly to unseen or newly introduced GO terms that frequently arise as the ontology evolves, and making the previously trained models outdated. We present STAR-GO, a Transformer-based framework that jointly models the semantic and structural characteristics of GO terms to enhance zero-shot protein function prediction. STAR-GO integrates textual definitions with ontology graph structure to learn unified GO representations, which are processed in hierarchical order to propagate information from general to specific terms. These representations are then aligned with protein sequence embeddings to capture sequence–function relationships. STAR-GO achieves state-of-the-art performance and superior zero-shot generalization, demonstrating the utility of integrating semantics and structure for robust and adaptable protein function prediction.

track: Function: Gene and Protein Function Annotation
title: GIMME: Graph Inference for Microbial Metabolism Exploration using Knowledge Graphs
authors: Winston Anthony, Sam Donald, Sumit Purohit, Adam Deutschbauer, Kaizad Patel, Rob Egbert
abstract: Predicting gene fitness across environmental conditions remains a central challenge in predictive phenomics. High-throughput fitness assays generate large volumes of genotype–phenotype measurements that are difficult to integrate with experimental metadata and biological function in a form that supports mechanistic reasoning. A key obstacle is that the predictive signal is distributed across heterogeneous modalities, including free-text experiment descriptions, media composition, and structured biological annotations. We present GIMME (Graph Inference for Microbial Metabolism Exploration), a knowledge-graph-augmented framework for microbial gene fitness prediction that combines pretrained language representations of experimental metadata with relational message passing over a semantically grounded biological graph. In addition to model development, we implement GIMME as an interactive platform for natural-language querying, evidence retrieval, and graph-based exploration of microbial metabolism and gene fitness.

title: Long-read sequencing of single cell-derived melanoma sublines reveals divergent and parallel genomic and epigenomic evolutionary trajectories
authors: Anton Goretsky, Yuelin Liu, Salem Malikic, Chi-Ping Day, Ayse G. Keskus, Tanveer Ahmad, S. Cenk Sahinalp, Mikhail Kolmogorov
abstract: Tumor evolution is driven by various mutational processes, ranging from single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) to large structural variants (SVs) to dynamic shifts in DNA methylation. Current short-read sequencing methods struggle to accurately capture the full spectrum of these genomic and epigenomic alterations due to inherent technical limitations. To overcome that, here we introduce an approach to identify and analyze the genomic and epigenetic events in different stages of tumoral evolution from long-read sequencing of single-cell derived sublines. We then use it to profile 23 sublines of a mouse cutaneous melanoma cell line, characterized with distinct growth phenotypes and treatment responses. We develop a computational framework for harmonization and joint analysis of different variant types in the evolutionary context. Uniquely, our framework enables detection of recurrent amplifications of putative driver genes, generated by independent SVs across different lineages, suggesting parallel evolution. In addition, our approach revealed gradual and lineage-specific methylation changes associated with aggressive clonal phenotypes. We also show our set of phylogeny-constrained variant calls along with openly released sequencing data can be a valuable resource for the development of new computational methods.
keywords: single cell-derived melanoma; sublines reveals divergent; epigenomic evolutionary trajectories; long-read sequencing; single-cell derived sublines
