title: CN-SigBench: A benchmarking pipeline for pan-cancer copy-number signature analysis
authors: Keshav Gandhi, Chenxi Nie, Katyayni Ganesan, Alexander Nicolay, Adam Streck, Tom L. Kaufmann, Roland F. Schwarz
abstract: Background: Chromosomal instability (CIN) causes chromosome-level gains, losses, and rearrangements and occurs in ~90% of tumors. Copy-number (CN) alteration patterns can be summarized into quantitative profiles that reflect mixtures of underlying CIN processes. CN signature detection depends on how CN events are encoded and binned into distinct features. However, existing CN feature representations have not been systematically benchmarked. Methods: Using simulated CN profiles with known mixtures of predefined CIN mechanisms, we benchmarked three representations (named after their bin counts): two established approaches (CN-43 and CN-48) alongside our novel CN-14. With signature inference approaches to generate signatures (e.g., variants of non-negative matrix factorization), we evaluated (1) reconstruction errors, (2) solution stabilities, (3) multi-label classification metrics against ground-truth CN signature memberships, and (4) soft clustering sample assignment errors relative to ground truth. Results: Across matched conditions, reconstruction errors (1) were lower in CN-43 than in CN-14 or CN-48 (Wilcoxon test, p < 0.0001). Reproducibility (cosine similarity) (2) was highest in CN-48, though uniformly high across all representations (> 0.99 across replicates). Multi-label classification (3) yielded a higher mean micro-F1 score for CN-14 (0.919) than CN-48 (0.794) or CN-43 (0.778). Soft clustering (4) produced a similar trend, with a lower mean absolute error for CN-14 (0.160) than CN-43 (0.365) or CN-48 (0.469). Conclusion: This simulation-based benchmarking framework reveals potential task-dependent trade-offs: CN-43 minimizes reconstruction error, CN-48 yields the most reproducible signatures, and CN-14 achieves the best classification and clustering performance, motivating further evaluation across additional simulated datasets and annotated tumor cohorts.

title: Benchmarking sample mispairing detection tools in complex cancer datasets
authors: Emma Lathouwers, Casey Greene
abstract: Transcriptomics datasets containing different modalities (e.g. single-cell (sc), single-nucleus (sn), and bulk RNA-seq) from the same donors are very valuable since they can reduce bias from technical artifacts introduced by any one method, and they bring together different pieces of information. A crucial aspect of quality control is to check that the samples are paired correctly (i.e. samples from the same donor are labelled as such). We benchmarked the available bioinformatic tools for assessing sample mispairing in multimodal transcriptomic cancer datasets. The benchmarking consists of three parts: (1) pseudobulk experiments to assess the accuracy, (2) experiments comparing different RNA-seq modalities with the expected sample matches to assess the performance in real data, and (3) experiments comparing demultiplexed sc/snRNA-seq and bulk RNA-seq with the expected samples per pool. We found that some older tools are no longer maintained and not performing well, and some require a large read depth, which prevents them from making accurate calls when comparing bulk and sc/snRNA-seq data. We concluded that Vireo had the best performance across pseudobulk experiments. The robustness of the tools was tested by searching for potential sample mispairs in several multimodal RNA-seq cancer datasets. We were able to identify samples originating from the same donors in a multimodal RNA-seq high-grade serous ovarian cancer dataset, including the identification of misannotated samples.

title: Super-silencers safeguard cell identity and are repurposed as super-enhancers in cancer metastasis.
authors: Di Huang, Ivan Ovcharenko
abstract: Super-silencers (SSs) – genomic regions marked by exceptionally strong repressive chromatin signatures – remain poorly characterized across health and disease contexts, despite emerging evidence of their importance in establishing and stabilizing cellular identity. To address this gap, we designed a sequence-based deep learning model to profile silencers, including SSs and typical silencers, and investigated distinct biological roles of SSs in physiology and disease. As a pilot, we applied our framework to the B-cell line GM12878, identifying 879 SS regions comprising more than 4,600 predicted silencers (Huang, Petrykowska et al. 2025). Genes associated with these SSs exhibit the lowest expression levels in GM12878 but are highly expressed in stem cells and are frequently located near key regulators of B-cell development, including BCL6, BACH2, and CXCR4. These observations suggest that SSs help maintain cell identity by repressing developmental programs in differentiated B cells. Notably, GM12878 SSs frequently convert into super-enhancers (SEs) during B-cell lymphoma development. Approximately 13% of normal B-cell SS components become SEs in diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (DLBCL), with many of these conversions recurring across patients. The converted regions harbor the highest density of B-cell lymphoma mutations and chromatin translocation breakpoints. For example, four B-cell SSs located within the locus of BCL6 – a hallmark gene in B-cell lymphoma – convert into SEs in 70% of DLBCL patients and display approximately twofold higher bromodomain-containing protein 4 (BRD4) occupancy than other DLBCL SEs. Inhibiting BRD4 binding deactivates these converted elements and rapidly downregulates BCL6. Together, these findings highlight the pivotal role of these converted elements in establishing lymphoma transcriptional programs. Next, we extended this framework to eight normal tissues – including breast epithelium, pancreas, osteoblast, etc. – and their histotype-matched cancer cell lines (such as MCF7, PANC1, SJSA1, etc.), systematically profiling SSs across these contexts (Fig. a). Across nearly all normal and tumor contexts examined, SSs are consistently associated with genes exhibiting the lowest expression, reflecting their strong repressive potency. In normal cell types, SSs preferentially repress genes that are highly expressed in both developmental and cancer states (Fig. b), suggesting that these elements are important for stabilizing differentiated cell states by constraining developmental transcriptional programs. Consistent with this role, normal-cell SSs also show a 4.61-fold enrichment for genetic variants linked to both development and cancer traits, positioning these elements as a pivotal safeguard against aberrant gene activation. Importantly, normal-cell SSs are frequently reprogrammed into SEs in matched cancer cells (nSSï‚®cSE), occurring ~2.7-fold more often than genome-wide expectations, consistent with the findings in the study of B cells and DLBCL. nSSï‚®cSE elements harbor the highest density of metastasis-associated GWAS variants (16.9-fold enrichment versus the genome-wide expectation, Fig. c) and are most enriched in the loci of literature-curated EMT genes (5.1-fold versus the genome-wide expectation and 1.5-fold versus cancer SEs). Moreover, these elements preferentially control genes that are upregulated in metastatic cells (as reported in TCGA) and/or essential for metastatic survival (as measured in DepMap), highlighting nSSï‚®cSE conversions as a crucial yet largely underappreciated regulatory axis that facilitate EMT activation and metastatic progression. Mechanistic analyses further reveal that nSSï‚®cSE conversions often establish self-reinforcing regulatory circuits. Examples include the auto-regulation of FOXA1 in ER+ breast cancer MCF7 cells, HOXB8 in pancreatic cancer PANC1 cells, and PAX9 in small-cell lung cancer cells. In normal breast epithelium, FOXA1, flanked by intronic and intergenic nSSs, is expressed at moderate levels. In MCF7, conversion of nSSs into cSEs coincides with FOXA1 occupancy, enabling the overexpression of FOXA1. In parallel, the emergence of FOXA1-bound cSEs in the ESR1 locus contributes to the overexpression of ESR1, which in turn upregulates FOXA1, forming an additional positive feedback regulatory loop. Together, nSSâ†’cSEs proximal to FOXA1 initiate the coordinated overactivation of FOXA1 and ESR1, a hallmark of endocrine-drug-resistance ER+ breast cancer and its metastatic progression. Oncogenic self-reinforcing circuits are well-recognized as stabilizing malignant, stem-like cellular states and as contributing to therapeutic resistance. Our findings pinpoint nSSâ†’cSE conversions as the backbone of some of these oncogenic regulatory networks. Collectively, our analyses establish that SSs are critical for maintaining cellular integrity and suppressing stem-like transcriptional programs in normal cells. Most notably, our work advances the prevailing enhancer-centric model of tumorigenesis, by highlighting regulatory state conversion – from strong repression to substantial activation as a pivotal but largely underexplored driver for EMT activation and metastatic propagation across cancer types. These discoveries provide gene-regulatory mechanistic insight into metastatic progression and offer potential avenues for cancer therapeutic interventions. Huang, D., H. M. Petrykowska, D. Kumar, L. title: Phasing Tumor Clones By Timing Somatic Mutations In Bulk Long-Read Sequencing
authors: Ataberk Donmez, Ayse Keskus, Anton Goretsky, Cenk Sahinalp, Mikhail Kolmogorov
abstract: Cancer cells genetically differ from healthy cells due to somatic aberrations (e.g., somatic mutations and structural variations). Studying these mutations in cancerous cells enhances our understanding of tumor evolution by identifying driver mutations, which, in turn, aids clinicians in improving diagnostics and selecting optimal treatment strategies. Reconstruction of tumor clones is a multi-allelic phasing problem. Obtaining a relative ordering of detected somatic single nucleotide variants (SNVs) is a key step toward phasing these mutations into different clones. We propose a tool to infer the relative ordering of pairs of SNVs in bulk long-read sequencing, based on their co-occurrence patterns. We then extend this pairwise information into larger regions by exploiting the transitivity of these relationships and represent this as a mutation graph. We apply our tool to two datasets: one consisting of two human cell lines and the other comprising a mouse model with 8 sublines. We show that our tool can provide evolutionary information for regions that span up to 10 Mbs and the relationships we detect between SNV pairs are 90% consistent with an independently constructed phylogeny. Our tool is freely available at https://github.com/atabeerk/ cancer_phasing.

title: Bridging Ancestry Gaps in Genomic Risk Prediction with Tabular Foundation Models
authors: Anirban Das, Yan Cui
abstract: Motivation: Models deployed for genomic prediction of diseases perform unevenly across populations, limiting clinical utility. Two factors drive this limitation: large imbalances in sample availability across ancestry groups and non-stationarity of genotype–phenotype effect sizes across the ancestry continuum. While tabular foundation models with in-context learning (ICL) have shown strong sample efficiency in other domains, their effectiveness for genotype-to-phenotype prediction and their robustness to ancestry-driven effect heterogeneity remain unclear. Results: Using large, ancestrally diverse biobank data, we show that ICL-capable tabular foundation models reduce performance degradation in under-sampled ancestry groups compared to conventional supervised approaches. However, we find that prevailing models trained on existing synthetic tabular tasks fail when allele effect sizes vary across ancestry space. Treating genetic ancestry as a continuous variable, we introduce an instruction-tuning framework that exposes models to synthetic tasks with ancestry-dependent non-stationary effects. Instruction-tuned models achieve improved and more stable predictive performance across the genetic ancestry continuum, including for individuals distant from in-context exemplars in ancestry space. Availability and Implementation: All code for instruction-tuning models, synthetic task generation, data wrangling, and model evaluation, is publicly available at https://github.com/ai4pm/Bridging-Ancestry-Gaps-in-Genomic-Risk-Prediction-with-Tabular-Foundation-Models. The final instruction-tuned model (ICL-NS-G2P-proto) is also released in this repository. Detailed documentation is provided, including environment setup instructions and guidelines for running various parts. The instruction-tuning task datasets are available at https://zenodo.org/records/18309187. Contact: adas23@uthsc.edu, ycui2@uthsc.edu. Supplementary Information: Supplementary data are available online.

title: A disentangled transformer-based transfer learning framework to predict patient drug response from tumor single-cell transcriptomics
authors: Xinliang Sun, Li Shen, Linconghua Wang, Xinyi Zhang, Zhangli Lu, Jing Tang, Min Li
abstract: Motivation: Intratumoral cellular heterogeneity limits therapeutic efficacy in cancer patients. Although single-cell transcriptomics offers highresolution profiling, translating these insights into clinical drug response prediction remains challenging. Recently, transfer learning approaches have attempted to predict patient drug response by leveraging pre-clinical data. However, these approaches operate at the bulk level, often masking the cellular heterogeneity essential for prediction. Results: In this study, we propose scTAPE, a disentangled transfer learning framework to predict patient drug response using tumor single-cell transcriptomics. scTAPE follows a pre-training and fine-tuning paradigm. During the pre-training stage, scTAPE employs a disentangled learning strategy to extract intrinsic pharmacological signals masked by confounding factors from the matched bulk and single-cell expression profiles. Subsequently, a supervised drug response model is trained on labeled cell-line data to fine-tune the aligned common embedding, thereby achieving cross-domain generalization to patient single-cell data. Experimental results demonstrate that scTAPE successfully predicts drug response in cell-line data and two independent clinical cohorts, outperforming state-of-the-art single-cell-based predictors. Furthermore, by analyzing tumor cell subpopulations, scTAPE not only predicts patient drug response to both single and combination treatments but also identifies potential therapeutic agents targeting drug-resistant subpopulations.

title: SAD-DRP: A Subspace-Aware Domain Adaptation Model with Explicit Prototype-Based Local Alignment for Cancer Drug Response Prediction
authors: Ruisheng Wang, Xianchuan Chen, Ying Li, Xiaofeng Liu, Zehua Zhang, Bin Wang
abstract: Motivation: Drug Response Prediction (DRP) is one of the key technologies enabling precision oncology. In real-world clinical settings, ground-truth drug response labels for patients are often difficult to obtain. Therefore, practical deployments commonly transfer knowledge learned from cell lines (source domain) to unlabeled patient cohorts (target domain), where distribution shift becomes a major challenge. Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA), as an effective transfer learning paradigm, has been increasingly adopted. However, most existing UDA methods mainly pursue domain-invariant representations, without explicitly strengthening task-relevant shared signals. Meanwhile, contrastive-learning-based domain adaptation methods usually induce cross-domain alignment indirectly via discriminative prototype learning, without directly modeling the alignment of target samples to same-class prototypes across the source and target domains. Results: We propose SAD-DRP, a novel UDA model. During pretraining, we introduce a subspace-aware encoder to extract a cross-domain shared representation subspace that is central to DRP discrimination. In the domain adaptation stage, we adopt an explicit prototype-based local distribution alignment objective that pulls target samples toward the corresponding source domain prototype while reducing their dependence on the distribution represented by the same-class target domain prototype. In addition, at the inference stage, we incorporate a lightweight post-processing module —drug-specific decision operating point transfer—to improve the rationality of binary response decisions. Extensive experiments demonstrate that SAD-DRP outperforms mainstream existing methods in unsupervised domain adaptation for cancer drug response prediction. title: Sex-dependent and cell-type specific transcriptional responses to sleep deprivation caused by mutations in the autism gene Shank3 in early development
authors: Caitlin Ottaway, Elizabeth Medina, Kaitlyn Ford, Abrar Al Maghribi, Kristan Singletary, Lucia Peixoto
abstract: Sleep problems are prevalent in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) as early as the first year of life and negatively impact quality of life. Mice with a mutation in the high confidence ASD gene Shank3 recapitulate the clinical ASD sleep phenotype and show an inability to properly respond to sleepiness (acute sleep deprivation, SD) as early as postnatal 24 (P24, ~1 year old). However, the molecular basis of sleepiness and how ASD associated mutations may impact this early in life is poorly understood. We have previously shown that SD in the brain of adult mice leads predominantly to an excitatory-neuron heavy transcriptional response. We hypothesize that the Shank3 mutation impairs the transcriptional response to sleepiness starting at young ages in neurons. To test this, we measured the cell-type specific transcriptional response to SD in Wild-Type and Shank3 (male and female) mice at P24 using single nuclear RNA-sequencing. Our results show that, like in adults, SD predominantly impacts excitatory neuronal transcription but does so differently in males than females. The Shank3 mutation seems to impair transcriptional responses in excitatory neurons in males but not in females. However, the transcriptional response in inhibitory neurons is enhanced by the mutation regardless of sex. Overall, the molecular basis of sleepiness is altered by the Shank3 mutation in early life, but the effect of sex on cell-type specific gene expression is more complex than previously anticipated. Current work focuses on identifying cell-type specific pathways underlying mutation and sex-dependent effects and independent validation using spatial transcriptomics.

title: Accurate detection of mosaic mutations at short tandem repeats from bulk sequencing data
authors: Weixiang Wang, Wenlong Li, Chunyi Wang, Wenxuan Fan, Yonghe Xia, Xiaoxu Yang, Chong Chu, Yanmei Dou
abstract: Short tandem repeats (STRs) are among the most mutable regions of the human genome, yet their somatic mosaicism remains poorly characterized due to the technical challenges of distinguishing genuine mutations from high intrinsic polymorphism and sequencing noise. Here, we introduce BulkMonSTR, a computational framework that combines STR-specific error modelling with machine-learning classification to enable accurate detection of mosaic STR mutations from bulk next-generation sequencing data. BulkMonSTR identifies nucleotide-resolution mutations—including insertions, deletions, and single-nucleotide variants (SNVs)—and supports both control-independent and case-control study designs. Leveraging a comprehensive training dataset derived from pedigree-based validation and in silico spike-in simulations, our random forest classifier effectively discriminates true mosaic events from germline variants and technical artifacts. Benchmarking on simulated and real datasets demonstrates that BulkMonSTR achieves substantially improved precision and F1 scores across diverse coverages and variant allele frequencies. In normal samples, cancer samples and controlled in silico mixing experiments, BulkMonSTR consistently outperforms existing methods, capturing a broader spectrum of STR mutations—including those arising on non-reference alleles—while achieving high validation rates. By enabling systematic, genome-wide interrogation of STR mosaicism, BulkMonSTR provides a scalable foundation for investigating the contributions of somatic STR mutations to aging and disease.

title: inSTRbility: a computational framework for quantifying somatic mosaicism at tandem repeat loci
authors: Akshay Kumar Avvaru, Harriet Dashnow, Caroline Dias, Anna Dischler
abstract: Tandem repeats (TRs) are highly polymorphic genomic elements exhibiting variation in both germline and somatic contexts and are implicated in >60 Mendelian disorders. TR disorders display marked repeat instability: the accumulation of length polymorphisms in somatic cells over time, leading to a distribution of allele lengths within a tissue. This instability is directly implicated in disease pathogenesis and often predicts age of onset. Somatic TR instability remains poorly characterized due to difficulty in distinguishing somatic variation from sequencing errors. Advances in long-read sequencing technologies enable direct observation of native DNA molecules, capturing true somatic alleles along with methylation. We present inSTRbility, a computational framework for quantifying somatic TR instability from long-read sequencing data. The method extracts locus-specific reads, phases alleles, and models somatic allele-length distributions using principled statistical approaches to derive biologically interpretable instability metrics. We demonstrate the utility of inSTRbility by characterizing regional somatic instability at the FMR1 CGG repeat locus in the brains of FXTAS carriers, revealing expansions >6000bp far beyond the full mutation range and unexpected patterns of methylation mosaicism on pre and full mutations. At the genome-wide level, our analysis of population genomes from the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium reveals that instability increases with length in simple TRs and is greater in compound TR loci of comparable length. inSTRbility includes visualization for locus-specific inspection of repeat length and methylation variation. Overall, inSTRbility provides a scalable, comprehensive approach for studying somatic instability, enabling deeper insights into the role of TR variation in human disease.
keywords: Somatic TR instability; quantifying somatic; inSTRbility; tandem repeat loci; Tandem repeats TRs

title: SIVA: Diagonal Integration of Spatial Multi-omics Data via Spatially-Informed Variational Autoencoders and Anchor Guidance
authors: Peng Jiang, Sishuo Chen, Xingye Wu, Juan Liu, Tian Tian
abstract: Motivation: Understanding cellular states and regulatory programs requires integrative analysis of multiple omics layers. Although recent spatial sequencing technologies allow molecular profiling of cells within their tissue context, paired spatial multi-omics assays are still limited by technical complexity and cost. This creates a pressing need for diagonal integration methods that enable joint analysis of unpaired spatial omics datasets. Results: We propose SIVA, a deep generative framework based on Spatially-Informed Variational Autoencoders with Anchor Guidance, for diagonal integration of spatial multi-modal data. SIVA employs modality-specific variational autoencoders with a hybrid latent embedding that integrates Gaussian process and standard Gaussian priors, enabling joint modeling of spatially structured variation and dominant underlying data distributions across modalities. To facilitate cross-modal alignment in the absence of one-to-one cell correspondence, SIVA adopts a dual integration strategy combining global distribution alignment via Maximum Mean Discrepancy and local correspondence guidance using mutual nearest neighbor anchors. Extensive experiments across multiple cross-slice integration scenarios demonstrate that SIVA achieves robust and accurate integration of unpaired spatial omics datasets, consistently outperforming existing methods. title: Meta-CCC: Deciphering Cell–Cell Communication through Integrative Single-Cell
authors: Jia-Jun Liu, Mengying Xia, Michael Bambha, Qingqi Lin, Silvia Liu
abstract: Modern single-cell technologies enable detailed exploration of cell-cell communication (CCC) across diverse cell types, which is critical for understanding how cells coordinate functions within complex tissues, maintain homeostasis, and drive disease processes. Numerous computational tools, such as CellChat and CellPhoneDB, have been developed to infer ligand-receptor (LR) interactions. However, over 100 CCC-related methods show substantial variability due to differences in databases, algorithms, and dataset biases. Spatial transcriptomics offers complementary insights but suffers from low sensitivity, limited gene coverage, and challenges in integration with single-cell transcriptomics. Moreover, challenges such as poor reproducibility, limited generalizability, and low comparability across datasets, further limit cross study consistency. To address these issues, we present Meta-CCC, a meta-analysis-based framework that integrates CCC results across multiple studies and datasets. Meta-CCC employs machine learning to prioritize biologically meaningful interactions and reduce inflated significance in large-scale single-cell data. This approach enhances statistical power and estimation precision, enabling identification of both conserved and context-specific LR interactions. Beyond pairwise comparisons, Meta-CCC captures dynamic changes across conditions and time series to refine predictions. Our framework can be broadly applicable across various experimental settings. In this study, we demonstrated its uses on mouse kidney AKI single-cell datasets and performed cross-species integration with human data, showing improved robustness and biological interpretability of inferred CCC networks. These results highlight Meta-CCC as a reliable and biologically informative tool for studying intercellular communication, providing a framework that can improve insights into intercellular communication and support downstream biological and translational research.

title: CLEAR-ST: Physics-informed probabilistic decontamination of spatial transcriptomics by modeling mRNA lateral diffusion
authors: Kun Ma, Joshua Wing Kei Ho
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics data are frequently distorted by lateral transcript diffusion, a structured contamination process that redistributes signal across neighboring capture locations and obscures the underlying biological pattern. This problem is challenging because the contamination is spatially organized, heterogeneous across samples, and often directionally biased, making simple denoising or post hoc normalization insufficient. We present CLEAR-ST, a physics-informed probabilistic framework for recovering latent clean expression from spatially contaminated count data. CLEAR-ST combines a denoising autoencoder with a graph-Laplacian-based forward diffusion model, enabling latent expression to be reconstructed jointly with the spatial contamination process. The framework integrates count data, spatial neighborhood structure, tissue masks, and histology-derived image context; image-derived niche labels capture local tissue architecture, while expression-derived diffusion-rate labels provide data-driven initialization of spot-specific diffusion propensity. Model parameters are learned jointly using stochastic variational inference under an explicit count-based observation model. Across public and custom spatial transcriptomics datasets, we found that contamination exhibits diverse regimes of spatial extent and directional coherence, motivating a shared but spatially adaptive diffusion formulation. CLEAR-ST reduced contamination-associated signal mixing, improved recovery of spatial structure, and enhanced downstream analyses including domain identification, differential expression, and cell type deconvolution. These results highlight CLEAR-ST as a general computational strategy for structured spatial decontamination and latent signal recovery in spatial omics data.
keywords: Physics-informed probabilistic; CLEAR-ST; mRNA lateral diffusion; spatial transcriptomics; spot-specific diffusion propensity

title: SpaReg: Sparsity-based scalable reconstruction of three-dimensional microenvironments at subcellular resolution
authors: Rajdeep Pawar, Thomas Jacob, Rebecca Raphael, Elaine Byrnes, Simon Watkins, T. Rinda Soong, Aatur Singhi, Shikhar Uttam
abstract: A comprehensive understanding of healthy and diseased tissue biology requires accurate characterization of the tissue microenvironment in three dimensions (3D). Recent studies have shown that spatial gradients in cellular composition and gene expression, in 3D, govern critical processes such as immune surveillance, tumor development, and therapeutic resistance. Yet, extending currently available methods to study large-scale tissues in 3D remains challenging due to limitations in resolution and scalability. Specifically, high-resolution WSIs are exceptionally information-rich, capturing cellular and subcellular detail across entire tissue sections, but this richness comes at the cost of gigapixel-scale image sizes, making volumetric 3D reconstruction at sub-cellular resolution prohibitively difficult. We present SpaReg, a sparsity-based, multi-scale framework for 3D reconstruction of tissue microenvironments from serial sections of high-resolution WSIs. The sparsity-based formulation enables reconstruction of large-scale tissues while remaining robust to common tissue artifacts and partially damaged sections, achieving this with just 0.002% of the most informative pixels. The multi-scale approach then leverages this sparse representation to reconstruct entire environment at subcellular resolution while preserving native tissue integrity. This uniquely enables training a model to identify and localize major cellular populations, including T cells, B cells, and Epithelial, along with larger tissue structures, directly in stain space (H&E and IHC). Together,SpaReg enables high-resolution, large-scale 3D reconstruction without compromising on tissue integrity, laying down the foundation for quantitative, spatially resolved characterization of tissue microenvironments at scale.

title: Is a Win-Win Possible? Achieving Pareto-Optimal Privacy-Utility Balance in Fine-Tuned Genome Language Model Embeddings Against Embedding Reconstruction Attacks
authors: Reem Al-Saidi, Erman Ayday, Ziad Kobti, Rola Alseidi
abstract: Motivation: Genomic data is among the most sensitive categories of personal information, and the growing adoption of language models for sequence analysis raises significant privacy concerns. Prior work demonstrated that embeddings from general-purpose language models adapted for genomic sequences leak substantial single-nucleotide information under reconstruction attacks and that fine-tuning embeddings can reduce this vulnerability at certain positions. However, three critical questions remain unaddressed: (1) whether privacy-utility tradeoffs are inherent constraints or configuration-dependent phenomena; (2) whether genomic-specialized models such as DNABERT and Nucleotide Transformer exhibit different vulnerabilities than adapted general-purpose models; and (3) how to statistically validate whether observed privacy improvements represent meaningful gains. Addressing these gaps is essential for guiding model selection in privacy-sensitive genomic applications. Results: We systematically evaluated 13 transformer architectures, 9 general-purpose and 4 genomic-specialized, under embedding reconstruction attacks for splice-site prediction. We assessed the vulnerabilities of both pre-trained and fine-tuned models to the single-nucleotide inference-reconstruction attack using our new metrics, such as error-based privacy gain and Pareto dominance scores. With statistical validation, we identified models that improved both privacy and utility. On the HS3D benchmark, XLNet-Large provided the strongest privacy protection (+19.5% privacy gain) while maintaining competitive prediction performance. General-purpose models outperformed genomic-specialized models in 56% of pairwise comparisons. Tokenization strategy, rather than domain specialization, determined the balance between privacy and utility. These findings give evidence-based guidance for selecting models in privacy-sensitive genomic applications.

title: Deciphering Key Factors of Active Learning Performance in Biomolecular Design
authors: Yixuan Zhi, Qixiu Du, Han Yu, Lei Wei, Xiaowo Wang
abstract: Motivation: Employing machine learning (ML) to efficiently design biomolecules has become an emerging trend in genetic engineering. Active learning (AL) algorithms, as scalable approaches for ML-guided discovery, can automatically identify promising samples for function (i.e., fitness) optimization, and have therefore attracted growing interest across scientific domains. However, applying AL in genetic engineering presents several challenges. The regulatory patterns between sequence and fitness are highly complex, noisy, and sparse, making the existing evaluation of AL algorithm efficiency unreliable. Therefore, a comprehensive benchmark and thorough investigation into the key determinants of AL performance are urgently required to resolve these challenges. Results: We created a benchmark across multiple large-scale libraries of proteins and DNA regulatory sequences, evaluating uncertainty quantification (UQ) algorithms on metrics including calibration and accuracy, demonstrating the robustness and generality of ensemble-based algorithms. Moreover, we systematically assessed the efficiency of existing sampling strategies for fitness optimization. Our results show that no single sampling strategy is universally optimal across datasets, although greedy iterative strategies perform well in many practical scenarios. Finally, we evaluated the factors influencing optimization efficiency, and found that optimization efficiency is mainly determined by the choice of initial settings, distribution sparsity, and sequence similarity in high-fitness regions, rather than by the specific AL algorithm. Meanwhile, we proposed two quantifiable metrics to measure the factors. These findings provide practical guidance for more effective application of AL algorithms in practical genetic engineering scenarios. title: Optimizing Protein Tokenization: Reduced Amino Acid Alphabets for Efficient and Accurate Protein Language Models
authors: Ella Rannon, David Burstein
abstract: Motivation: Protein language models (pLMs) typically tokenize sequences at the single-amino-acid level using a 20-residue alphabet, resulting in long input sequences and high computational cost. Sub-word tokenization methods such as Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) can reduce sequence length but are limited by the sparsity of long patterns in proteins encoded by the standard amino acid alphabet. Reduced amino acid alphabets, which group residues by physicochemical properties, offer a potential solution but their performances with sub-word tokenization have not been systematically studied. Results: We investigate the combined use of reduced amino acid alphabets and BPE tokenization in protein language models. We pre-train RoBERTa-based pLMs de novo using multiple reduced alphabets and evaluate them across diverse downstream tasks. Our results show that reduced alphabets enable substantially shorter input sequences and faster training and inference. These findings suggest that alphabet reduction may facilitate more effective sub-word tokenization, enabling increased efficiency with marginal impact on predictive performance, and for specific tasks even improving accuracy. title: Fairness-aware Supervised Hierarchical Contrastive Semantic Learning for Sexual Dimorphism Analysis
authors: Euiseong Ko, Sai Phani Parsa, Sai Kosaraju, Tesfaye B. Mersha, Mingon Kang
abstract: Motivation: Sexual dimorphism is a fundamental biological determinant driving systematic differences in disease susceptibility, progression, and clinical outcomes. However, current AI-based genomic models often exhibit algorithmic bias and fail to capture these sex-specific mechanisms, creating a critical barrier to unbiased precision medicine. Ensuring fairness in the context of sexual dimorphism requires understanding and addressing the distinct biological mechanisms functioning in each sex, rather than focusing solely on equalizing predictive performance. Results: We propose a fairness-aware supervised hierarchical contrastive learning approach, called FairHICON, to discover unbiased sex-common and sex-specific genomic drivers. Evaluations on cancer and asthma transcriptomic datasets demonstrate that FairHICON significantly outperforms state-of-the-art benchmarks, improving predictive performance by up to 9% while effectively reducing the performance gap between male and female cohorts. Furthermore, prognostic validation confirms that the identified sex-specific pathways stratify patient survival significantly better within their corresponding sex groups. This validates FairHICON to elucidate the molecular heterogeneity of sexual dimorphism, advancing inclusive precision medicine. title: ATTNSOM: Learning Cross-Isoform Attention for Cytochrome P450 Site-of-Metabolism Prediction
authors: Hajung Kim, Eunha Lee, Sohyun Chung, Jueon Park, Seungheun Baek, Jaewoo Kang
abstract: Motivation: Identifying metabolic sites where cytochrome P450 enzymes metabolize small-molecule drugs is essential for drug discovery. Although existing computational approaches have been proposed for site-of-metabolism prediction, they typically ignore cytochrome P450 isoform identity or model isoforms independently, thereby failing to fully capture inherent cross-isoform metabolic patterns. In addition, prior evaluations often rely on top-k metrics, where false positive atoms may be included among the top predictions, underscoring the need for complementary metrics that more directly assess binary atom-level discrimination under severe class imbalance. Results: We propose ATTNSOM, an atom-level site-of-metabolism prediction framework that integrates intrinsic molecular reactivity with cross-isoform relationships. The model combines a shared graph encoder, molecule-conditioned atom representations, and a cross-attention mechanism to capture correlated metabolic patterns across cytochrome P450 isoforms. The model is evaluated on two benchmark datasets annotated with site-of-metabolism labels at atom resolution. Across these benchmarks, the model achieves consistently strong top-k performance across multiple cytochrome P450 isoforms. Relative to ablated variants, the model yields higher Matthews correlation coefficient, indicating improved discrimination of true metabolic sites. These results support the importance of explicitly modeling cross-isoform relationships for site-of-metabolism prediction. title: Improving Hit Discovery by Integrating Activity Cliff Sensitivity into Active Learning
authors: Junha Kim, Youngkuk Kim, Bonil Koo, Dongmin Bang, Sun Kim
abstract: Motivation: Active learning has emerged as an effective strategy for accelerating molecular discovery under limited labeling budgets. However, existing method primarily focus on global information, often overlooking activity cliff—sharp changes in bioactivity caused by small structural perturbations—leading to suboptimal sample selection. In this work, we propose a model-agnostic, activity cliff–aware active learning framework designed to improve hit discovery efficiency without imposing constraints on the underlying molecular representation. Our framework introduces an auxiliary activity cliff scoring module trained on pairwise molecular relationships to explicitly capture local structure–activity sensitivity. The outputs of this module are integrated into a cliff-aware acquisition function that prioritizes structurally informative molecules whose labels are expected to be most beneficial for model improvement. Notably, the proposed strategy is agnostic to backbone architectures and molecular feature, enabling seamless integration with a wide range of existing active learning pipelines. Result: We evaluate our approach on benchmarks under a fixed labeling budget. Across all targets, the proposed method consistently identifies more active compounds than baseline acquisition strategies, demonstrating improved robustness in early, data-scarce learning stages. Ablation studies further confirm the contribution of activity cliff awareness to the observed performance gains. Overall, our results underscore the importance of explicitly modeling activity cliffs within active learning frameworks and highlight the effectiveness of a model-agnostic design for accelerating hit discovery in data-limited drug discovery settings. Availability and implementation: The source code is accessible online at https://github.com/wnsgk/AC-Active.

PIMO provides biologically interpretable analyses that identify important pathways, genes, and inter-omics interactions with DNA methylation and copy number alterations. title: Attention-driven accurate deconvolution of bulk transcriptomes using population-scale single-cell references
authors: Xing Zheng, Sicheng Luo, Lina Ma, Zhang Zhang
abstract: Deconvolution of bulk transcriptomes using single-cell references enables cost-effective profiling of tissue heterogeneity. However, leveraging population-scale single-cell atlases to jointly and accurately infer cell-type abundances and cell-type-specific gene expression profiles (GEPs) remains computationally prohibitive and methodologically challenging. Here, we present DCAT (Deconvolution of Cell-type Abundance Toolkit), a scalable deep-learning framework employing an attention-based encoder-decoder architecture to jointly decode cell-type abundances and specific GEPs from bulk data. To alleviate computational bottlenecks and enhance signal resolution, DCAT integrates cell-type-aware feature selection with a vectorized, batched pseudo-bulk simulation strategy. This substantially reduces the memory footprint and processing time, seamlessly accommodating million-cell reference cohorts. Across diverse simulated and gold-standard real bulk datasets, DCAT consistently delivers superior predictive accuracy and lower absolute error over current state-of-the-art (SOTA) approaches in both abundance estimation and the recovery of cell-type-specific transcriptomic landscapes. Furthermore, application to a clinical pancreatic islet cohort demonstrates that DCAT robustly recovers underlying biological dynamics. It accurately links reduced beta-cell abundance to elevated HbA1c levels and reconstructs the precise expression trajectories of identity markers and stress-response genes, successfully capturing the beta-cell dedifferentiation process across type 2 diabetes progression. Together, DCAT provides an efficient, biologically interpretable, and broadly applicable framework for high-precision transcriptome deconvolution at the population scale.

title: Qombucha identifies distinct developmental methylation programs and cell type compositions in Glioblastoma
authors: Xuan Li, Ananth Hari, Yuelin Liu, Omkar Singh, Zhichao Wu, Zied Abdullaev, Stephen Mount, Kenneth Aldape, Eytan Ruppin, Alejandro Schäffer, S. Cenk Sahinalp, H Lalchungnunga
abstract: Motivation: Glioblastoma (GBM) is an aggressive brain cancer characterized by high intratumoral heterogeneity and treatment resistance. Prior research has shown that GBM tumors may comprise one or more developed brain cell types. The interplay between the developmental program of the brain cells and GBM progression remains unclear. DNA methylation provides a reliable signal for brain cancer subtyping and for understanding tumor evolution and brain development. However, no existing methods leverage methylation to decode the developmental signals in GBM. Results: We present Qombucha (Quadratic prOgraMming Based tUmor deConvolution with cell HierArchy), a novel computational framework that uniquely integrates a tree-structured brain cell hierarchy into deconvolution of bulk tumor methylation data. We applied Qombucha to a large GBM cohort from TCGA, representing the three most common methylation-defined subtypes: receptor tyrosine kinase (RTK) I, RTK II, and mesenchymal typical (MES TYP). Qombucha reveals subtype-specific developmental programs and shows that higher abundance of certain progenitor cells is associated with shorter overall survival. Qombucha-imputed mature and progenitor cell fractions can be used to obtain clustering that is more concordant with the three subtypes by the McClain-Rao or silhouette scores than alternative clustering methods. Inferred cell fractions improved subtype-concordant clustering and enabled accurate subtype classification in an independent NCI dataset using only 11 inferred cell-type features, achieving performance comparable to models based on 10,000 methylation sites. Qombucha is a method to aid in understanding the crosstalk between brain development and tumor progression. title: STEP2h: Detecting transposable element exonization with multi-task deep learning
authors: Zitong He, Liliana Florea
abstract: Transposable element (TE)-derived exons have contributed to species diversity and polymorphic variation, including disease-causing variants, yet they are poorly represented in gene annotation databases. Machine learning-based annotation methods are poorly equipped to detect them, and many TE-exons are condition-specific or expressed at low levels and therefore missed by sequencing-based methods. We developed a two-tier multitask convolutional segmentation method, STEP2h, to predict hard-to-annotate transposable elements (TE)-derived exons, generalizable across TE families and species. We tested STEP2h alongside the foundation model SegmentNT for the ability to detect TE-derived exons in human (Alu, LINE1) and mouse (B1, LINE1). STEP2h shows significantly higher accuracy as measured by the F1-value, by 2.6-fold in human and 2.0-and 7.6-fold in mouse. Altogether, STEP2h identified 24,610 Alu and 8,328 LINE1 exonizable elements in human, and 3,974 B1 and 3,506 LINE1 elements in mouse, including thousands of novel exon candidates with protein coding potential, and therefore is a promising tool for TE-exon annotation.

title: absuite: A Package in R for Antibody Repertoire Profiling and Clonotype Analysis
authors: Favour Igwezeke, Olaitan I. Awe
abstract: B-cell receptor (BCR) repertoire sequencing enables detailed characterization of antibody responses in infection, vaccination, and autoimmunity. However, comprehensive repertoire analysis typically requires integrating multiple specialized tools, limiting accessibility for experimental immunologists. We present absuite, an R/Bioconductor package providing an integrated workflow for BCR repertoire analysis. The package implements ten core analytical functions: V-gene usage profiling, convergent clonotype identification across samples, clonality quantification via Shannon entropy and normalized entropy metrics, isotype class-switching analysis, diversity calculations (richness, evenness), clonotype similarity networks with community detection, and repertoire comparison with statistical testing. absuite accepts data from major repositories (OAS, IMGT) and standard formats (AIRR, CSV), handling preprocessing automatically to allow researchers to focus on biological interpretation. We validated absuite using 187,342 antibody sequences from three published COVID-19 cohorts. V-gene analysis correctly identified established COVID-19 signatures (IGHV3-30, IGHV4-34 enrichment). Convergent analysis detected 57 public clonotypes shared across multiple patients, consistent with published findings. Network analysis using Louvain clustering revealed 447 communities with high modularity (0.86), exposing clonotype relationships and somatic variant lineages. Clonality metrics distinguished expanded clonal responses from diverse repertoires, with values ranging from 0.001 to 0.11 across samples. absuite consolidates BCR repertoire analysis into a single R package, eliminating the need for multiple tools and custom scripting. By providing an accessible, well-documented workflow, absuite enables experimental immunologists to perform sophisticated repertoire analyses independently. The absuite package is currently under development and will soon be submitted to Bioconductor.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Scalable computation of ultrabubbles in pangenomes by orienting bidirected graphs
authors: Juha Harviainen, Francisco Sena, Corentin Moumard, Aleksandr Politov, Sebastian Schmidt, Alexandru I. Tomescu
abstract: Motivation: Pangenome graphs are increasingly used in bioinformatics, ranging from environmental surveillance and crop improvement to the construction of population-scale human pangenomes. As these graphs grow in size, methods that scale efficiently become essential. A central task in pangenome analysis is the discovery of variation structures. In directed graphs, the most widely studied such structures, superbubbles, can be identified in linear time. Their canonical generalization to bidirected graphs, ultrabubbles, more accurately models DNA reverse complementarity. However, existing ultrabubble algorithms are quadratic in the worst case (and thus do not scale to large graphs) or compute only partial solutions. Results: We show that all ultrabubbles in a bidirected graph containing at least one tip, a common property of pangenome graphs, can be computed in linear time. Our key contribution is a new linear-time orientation algorithm that transforms a bidirected graph with a tip into a directed graph of linear size. Orientation conflicts are resolved by introducing auxiliary source or sink vertices. We prove that ultrabubbles in the original bidirected graph correspond exactly to superbubbles in the resulting directed graph, enabling the use of existing linear-time superbubble algorithms. Our approach achieves speedups of up to 30x over the ultrabubble implementation in vg, enabling scalable pangenome analyses. For example, on the v1.1 pangenome graph constructed by the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium from 47 individuals, our method completes in 12 minutes, compared to 2 hours for vg. On the v2.0 graph built from 232 individuals and containing more than 200 million edges, our method finishes in 18 minutes, while vg requires 9 hours and four times more RAM. Availability and implementation: Our method is implemented in the BubbleFinder tool, available at www.github.com/algbio/BubbleFinder, via the new ultrabubbles command.
keywords: bidirected graph; population-scale human pangenomes; pangenome graphs; orienting bidirected; directed graphs

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: RLBWT-Based LCP Computation in Compressed Space for Terabase-Scale Pangenome Analysis
authors: Ahsan Sanaullah, Nathaniel Brown, Pramesh Shakya, Arun Deegutla, Ardalan Naseri, Benjamin Langmead, Degui Zhi, Shaojie Zhang
abstract: Motivation: Lossless full text indexes are utilized in a myriad of applications in bioinformatics. The continuously decreasing cost of generating biological data has resulted in the need to build full text indexes on biological datasets of increasing size. Many compressed full text indexes have been developed to address this problem. In particular, run-length Burrows-Wheeler transform (RLBWT) based compressed full text indexes have seen wide development and adoption. However, the construction of these RLBWT-based compressed full text indexes is still computationally expensive, sometimes prohibitively so, even for current dataset sizes. Results: Therefore, we present algorithms for the construction of RLBWT-based compressed full text indexes and their supporting data structures in compressed space. The algorithms have a space complexity of $O(r)$ words and run in $O(n)$ time for repetitive datasets, where $r$ is the number of runs in the BWT, $n$ is the length of the text, and repetitive data sets implies $\frac{n}{r}\in \Omega(\log n)$. We provide the first algorithm to compute LCP-related information for repetitive datasets in optimal time and $O(r)$ space, greatly reducing memory requirements. The key idea behind this algorithm is the utilization of $r$ samples of the inverse suffix array at regular intervals. For example, on the Human Pangenome Reference Consortium Release 2 dataset, this reduces peak memory from 2,135 GiB to 170 GiB (12.6x reduction) compared to the previous best method (pfp-thresholds). Availability: The implementation is available at https://github.com/ucfcbb/TeraTools.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: ImpuT2T: Pangenome-Based Patching for Human Genome Assemblies
authors: Mao-Jan Lin, Vikram Shivakumar, Ben Langmead
abstract: With improvements in long-read sequencing and assembly methods, many high-quality telomere-to-telomere (T2T) assemblies have become available. These assemblies now serve as important reference collections for sequencing data analyses. However, the long-read sequencing required to generate such a high-quality assembly remains expensive, and is often out of reach for many research groups and applications. Here, we propose ImpuT2T, a tool to scaffold and patch de novo assemblies with a panel of high-quality assemblies. ImpuT2T takes a fragmented assembly as input and uses the pangenome panel to scaffold and fill inter-contig gaps. Unlike single-reference patching methods, ImpuT2T leverages haplotype diversity in a pangenome panel to infer gap sequences consistent with the underlying haplotype structure. Specifically, ImpuT2T uses flanking region homology to infer the most probable gap sequence between two neighboring contigs, producing more contiguous and user-friendly personalized assemblies at lower cost with minimum error. Benchmark comparison demonstrates that ImpuT2T is highly effective at patching human HiFi assemblies and outperforms existing gap-filling approaches, highlighting the advantages of pangenome-based patching over single-reference methods.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Optimizing sparse and skew hashing: faster k-mer dictionaries
authors: Giulio Ermanno Pibiri, Rob Patro
abstract: Motivation: Representing a set of k-mers — strings of length k — in small space under fast lookup queries is a fundamental requirement for several applications in Bioinformatics. A data structure based on sparse and skew hashing (SSHash) was recently proposed for this purpose [Pibiri, 2022]: it combines good space effectiveness with fast lookup and streaming queries. It is also order-preserving, i.e., consecutive k-mers (sharing a prefix-suffix overlap of length kâˆ’ 1) are assigned consecutive hash codes which helps compressing satellite data typically associated with k-mers, like abundances and color sets in colored De Bruijn graphs. Results: We study the problem of accelerating queries under the sparse and skew hashing indexing paradigm, without compromising its space effectiveness. We propose a refined data structure with less complex lookups and fewer cache misses. We give a simpler and faster algorithm for streaming lookup queries. Compared to indexes with similar capabilities and based on the Burrows-Wheeler transform, like SBWT and FMSI, SSHash is significantly faster to build and query. SSHash is competitive in space with the fast (and default) modality of SBWT when both k-mer strands are indexed. While larger than FMSI, it is also more than one order of magnitude faster to query. Availability and Implementation: The SSHash software is available at https://github.com/jermp/sshash, and also distributed via Bioconda. A benchmark of data structures for k-mer sets is available at https://github.com/jermp/kmer_ sets_benchmark. The datasets used in this article are described and available at https://zenodo.org/ records/17582116.
keywords: skew hashing; faster k-mer dictionaries; Optimizing sparse; hashing indexing paradigm; space effectiveness

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: 10-minimizers: a promising class of constant-space minimizers
authors: Arseny Shur, Ido Tziony, Yaron Orenstein
abstract: Minimizers are sampling schemes which are ubiquitous in almost any high-throughput sequencing analysis. Assuming a fixed alphabet of size Ïƒ, a minimizer is defined by two positive integers k, w and a linear order Ï on k-mers. A sequence is processed by a sliding window algorithm that chooses in each window of length w + k âˆ’ 1 its minimal k-mer with respect to Ï. A key characteristic of a minimizer is its density, which is the expected frequency of chosen k-mers among all k-mers in a random infinite Ïƒ-ary sequence. Minimizers of smaller density are preferred as they produce smaller samples, which lead to reduced runtime and memory usage in downstream applications. Recent studies developed methods to generate minimizers with optimal and near-optimal densities, but they require to explicitly store k-mer ranks in Î©(2^k) space. While constant-space minimizers exist, and some of them are proven to be asymptotically optimal, no constant-space minimizers was proven to guarantee lower density compared to a random minimizer in the non-asymptotic regime, and many minimizer schemes suffer from long k-mer key-retrieval times due to complex computation. In this paper, we introduce 10-minimizers, which constitute a class of minimizers with promising properties. First, we prove that for every k > 1 and every w ≥ k âˆ’ 2, a random 10-minimizer has, on expectation, lower density than a random minimizer. This is the first provable guarantee for a class of minimizers in the non-asymptotic regime. Second, we present spacers, which are particular 10-minimizers combining three desirable properties: they are constant-space, low-density, and have small k-mer key-retrieval time. In terms of density, spacers are competitive to the best known constant-space minimizers; in certain (k, w) regimes they achieve the lowest density among all known (not necessarily constant-space) minimizers. Notably, we are the first to benchmark constant-space minimizers in the time spent for k-mer key retrieval, which is the most fundamental operation in many minimizers-based methods. Our empirical results show that spacers can retrieve k-mer keys in competitive time (a few seconds per genome-size sequence, which is less than required by random minimizers), for all practical values of k and w. We expect 10-minimizers to improve minimizers-based methods, especially those using large window sizes. We also propose the k-mer key-retrieval benchmark as a standard objective for any new minimizer scheme.
keywords: constant-space minimizers; 10-minimizers; k-mer key-retrieval; non-asymptotic regime; promising class

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: The gift of novelty: repeat-robust k-mer-based estimators of mutation rates
authors: Haonan Wu, Paul Medvedev
abstract: Estimating mutation rates between evolutionarily related sequences is a central problem in molecular evolution. Due to the rapid expansion of datasets, modern methods avoid costly alignment and instead focus on comparing sketches of sets of constituent $k$-mers. While these methods perform well on many sequences, they are not robust to highly repetitive sequences such as centromeres. In this paper, we present three new estimators that are robust to the presence of repeats. The estimators are applicable in different settings, based on whether they need count information from zero, one, or both of the sequences. We evaluate our estimators empirically using highly repetitive alpha satellite sequences. Our estimators each perform best in their class and our strongest estimator outperforms all other tested estimators. Our software is open-source and freely available on https://github.com/medvedevgroup/Accurate_repeat-aware_kmer_based_estimator.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Incorporating indel channels into average-case analysis of seed-chain-extend
authors: Spencer Gibson, Yun William Yu
abstract: Motivation: Given a sequence $s_1$ of $n$ letters drawn i.i.d. from an alphabet of size $\sigma$ and a mutated substring $s_2$ of length $m < n$, we want to recover the mutation history that generated $s_2$ from $s_1$. Many modern sequence aligners for this task employ seed-chain-extend with $k$-mer seeds. Previously, Shaw and Yu showed linear-gap cost chaining can produce a chain with $1-O\left(\frac{1} {\sqrt{m}}\right)$ recoverability, the proportion of the mutation history that is recovered, in $O\left(mn^{2.43\theta} \log n\right)$ expected time for seed-chain-extend (assuming pre-seeded reference), where $\theta < 0.206$ is the mutation rate under a substitution-only channel and $s_1$ is uniformly random. A gap remains between theory and practice, as real genomes include insertions and deletions (indels). Results: We introduce mathematical machinery to deal with the two new obstacles introduced by indel channels: the dependence of neighboring anchors and the presence of anchors that are only partially correct. We prove that expected recoverability of an optimal chain is $\ge 1-O\Bigl(\frac{1}{\sqrt{m}}\Bigr)$ and expected runtime is $O(mn^{3.15 \cdot \theta_T}\log n)$, given the total mutation rate $\theta_T = \theta_i + \theta_d + \theta_s$ (sum of substitution, insertion, and deletion rates) is $\theta_T\le 0.159$. We thus narrow (but not close) the gap between theory and practice. Availability and implementation: https://github.com/Lazarus42/seed_chainer_indels Supplementary Information: extended and auxiliary proofs in external appendices.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: ORION: A High-Performance Barcode and UMI Correction Tool for Oxford Nanopore Single-Cell Sequencing
authors: Dohun Yi, Jin-Wu Nam
abstract: Oxford Nanopore long-read single-cell RNA sequencing captures full-length transcripts, enabling isoform-level and variant-level analyses within individual cells. However, Nanopore INDEL errors corrupt cell barcodes and UMIs at multiple stages of preprocessing, and existing tools do not fully account for these stage-specific error structures, often discarding reads that could be rescued with more targeted correction. We present ORION, a barcode and UMI correction tool implemented in C that employs stage-specific error modeling across a five-stage disk-based pipeline, integrating statistical frameshift diagnosis, progressive barcode merging, and transcript-aware UMI deduplication. ORION accepts raw FASTQ and produces corrected, tagged FASTQ compatible with existing workflows, supporting multiple 10x Chromium chemistries. We benchmarked ORION against 7 tools across 3 datasets spanning simulated, CRISPR-edited, and primary cell data on both R9.4.1 and R10.4.1 chemistries. ORION achieved the highest read retention at 91.7% compared to 52-86% for other tools, the highest BC F1 of 0.954 and UMI F1 of 0.625, and the fastest throughput, completing 41 million reads in under 10 minutes with roughly 10 GB memory. Downstream gene expression quantification across 31 pipeline configurations showed that ORION's correction quality translated to expression-level improvements, with ORION-based chains achieving the highest correlations to short-read reference.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: SpatiaXen: An Open-Source Interactive Platform for Cell-Type-Resolved Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis
authors: Anirban Chakraborty, Cort Thompson, Lauren Wade-Kleyn, Mark Reimers, Erin Purcell
abstract: Background: In-situ spatial transcriptomics technologies, such as the 10x Genomics Xenium platform, enable single-cell-resolution analysis of gene expression while also preserving the spatial organization of tissue. These platforms can provide new insights into cellular responses to diseases and injuries, as well as therapeutic interventions. They generate tens of millions of spatially resolved transcript coordinates per tissue section. This enables new opportunities to investigate spatially organized biological phenomena, such as neurodegenerative processes and tissue responses around implanted biological devices. However, fully leveraging this potential requires complex computational methods that can handle all the unique features of the in situ spatial transcriptomics data, as they are very large and complex datasets. There are also imaging-related spatial artifacts that need to be addressed before downstream analysis. Also, in most cases, we need to relate gene expression patterns to the locations of known tissue structures or regions rather than only assigning them to individual cells. The current analysis pipelines assign transcripts to individual cells using the cell segmentation technique. But in tissues such as the brain, where cellular processes are intertwined and most reads come from the dense neuropil rather than cell bodies, similar segmentation approaches may introduce errors and obscure spatial information. When studying the brain tissue response to implanted microelectrode arrays, devices that interface with the central nervous system to treat various neurological disorders, these issues can come to the fore. It is important to understand how the individual cell types, including neurons, astrocytes, microglia, etc., respond to the implanted devices at the single-cell resolution to improve the design and biocompatibility of the electrodes. However, the existing computational tools are not well-suited to the spatial complexity of brain tissue. To address this challenge, we developed SpatiaXen, an open-source interactive computation platform that provides a complementary analytical framework alongside conventional segmentation-based algorithms. SpatiaXen works with the raw transcript coordinates treated as spatial point data. It generates a spatial map of gene expression using kernel density estimation and classifies cell types using a marker gene-based scoring framework based on the spatial clustering of cell type-specific transcripts around nuclei. This density-based approach captures expression from both the bodies of the cells and the processes as a function of distance from the locations selected by the users. In the future, a cell segmentation pipeline will be incorporated as an option, which will allow users to try both the density-based and segmentation-based approaches within a single software package. Although we developed and tested this software for brain tissues, this approach can be used for spatial transcriptomics analysis of any Xenium data. We implemented SpatiaXen in Python, and it is structured as an interactive desktop application. SpatiaXen processes standard Xenium output files, including parquet or CSV transcript tables, nucleus boundary files and user-defined region coordinates within a modular analysis pipeline. Transcript coordinate data are loaded and can be visualized as a spatial map of downsampled transcripts. Then the users can interactively define the region coordinates, which are used as the region of interest for our analysis. We have also included an option to store the data for reproducibility. This software estimates the gene expression at each spatial location by computing the weighted averages of nearby transcript counts. Total transcript density is estimated on a coarse grid (40 µm spacing, 80 µm bandwidth) to capture spatial variations. Gene-specific densities are calculated on a finer grid (5 µm spacing and 7 µm bandwidth). To reduce the spatial artifacts in the data, the gene-specific densities are normalized by the local total transcript density relative to the average total read density. This approach corrects the systematic differences in the read density, including periodic 30-40% variations caused by the field-of-view stitching, without altering the true biological variation. Cell type inference is done using user-defined marker gene sets for each cell type of interest. High-resolution density maps (2.5 µm grid, 3.5 µm bandwidth) were constructed for each marker gene and converted the bounded scores between 0 and 1 using a rank-based exponential scaling because of the right-skewed distribution of the sparse markers. Principal component analysis is applied to per-pixel marker scores, and normalized PC1 loadings of marker genes are used as weights to compute the composite cell type scores. Each nucleus is assigned to the cell type with the highest total score, with confidence defined by the difference between the top scores, allowing ambiguous assignments to be excluded. For studies related to spatial perturbations, including devices, lesions, or tumors, our software measures the distance of each transcript from a user-defined reference surface. The expression values for each cell type are grouped by distance. It enables the analysis of spatial expression patterns and comparison between tissue close to and far from the perturbation. We used ANOVA to evaluate statistical significance with Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate corrections at the biological replicate level. Results: We applied SpatiaXen to Xenium in situ spatial transcriptomics data from rat motor cortex implanted with silicon and polyimide electrodes of 10 and 100 µm cross-sectional sizes at 1 and 6 weeks post-implantation [1]. The software's cell-type inference identified excitatory neurons, interneurons, astrocytes, oligodendrocytes, and microglia. Our analysis indicates that implants are associated with increased inflammatory gene expression in glial cells, accompanied by damage-related reductions in synaptic transmission and activation of protective responses, including remyelination and antioxidant production to preserve the nearby neurons. While our bulk tissue analysis confirmed previously reported glial scar consolidation over time, SpatiaXen's per-cell analysis discovered a progressive increase in inflammatory gene expression (GFAP, Serping1, Gpnmb) within individual reactive astrocytes between 1 and 6 weeks. Using the software’s distance analysis, we identified spatial gradients of gene expression extending from the implant location, specifically in microglia (C3, Dock8, and Itgam), astrocytes (Gpnmb and Serping1), oligodendrocytes (Hcn2), and neurons (Kif5a). SpatiaXen revealed that smaller implants were associated with fewer reactive cells, rather than decreased per-cell reactivity, an effect revealed by separate tissue-level and per-cell analysis. Conclusion: While developed for neural device-tissue interfaces, SpatiaXen applies to any in situ spatial transcriptomics study involving complex tissues or spatially structured perturbations, including tumor microenvironments, neurodegeneration, TBI, and tissue-biomaterial interfaces. The interactive modular design of the software allows researchers to adapt marker-gene panels and analysis parameters to their tissue type without requiring programming expertise. [1] A systematic analysis of brain tissue response to microelectrode material and size with single-cell spatial transcriptomics. track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Detecting and reconstructing breakage-fusion-bridge cycles from long-read sequencing using BFBArchitect
authors: Chaohui Li, Siavash Raeisi Dehkordi, Daniel Muliaditan, Ramanuj Dasgupta, Jens Luebeck, Kaiyuan Zhu, Vineet Bafna
abstract: Motivation: Focal oncogene amplification is a key driver of tumor progression. Remarkably, the increased pathology depends on the context-whether the amplification is extrachromosomal (ecDNA) or intrachromosomal. EcDNA amplifications promote heterogeneity, therapy resistance, and poor prognosis. Focal intrachromosomal amplifications often arise through breakage-fusion-bridge (BFB) cycles, which produce highly rearranged but stable chromosomes. Distinguishing BFB from ecDNA remains challenging due to overlapping genomic signatures. To address this, we present BFBArchitect, a computational method leveraging long-read Oxford Nanopore data to identify BFB sequences consistent with both copy number and foldback structural variation. Results: We provide a novel combinatorial characterization of BFB, which naturally leads to an integer linear programming (ILP) optimization. The ILP optimization generates a BFB sequence that best explains experimentally observed copy numbers and structural variants. We implement this idea in a tool called BFBArchitect. BFBArchitect achieves near-perfect accuracy in distinguishing BFB from non-BFB structures in extensive simulations as well as on 18 validated examples. Moreover, it generates sequence-level BFB reconstructions that provide mechanistic insights into BFB formation, including repair mechanisms with template switching and other foldback variants, and recapture of telomere for stabilization. Availability and Implementation: BFBArchitect is available at https://github.com/AmpliconSuite/BFBArchitect. Contact: vbafna@ucsd.edu

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: scVarSim: A Unified Simulator for Benchmarking Genetic Variant Calling and RNA Editing Detection in Single-Cell RNA-seq Data
authors: Weijian Wang, Jingyi Jessica Li
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing enables the capture of genetic variants (SNPs and indels) and post-transcriptional RNA editing events without paired whole-genome sequencing data. However, accurate detection of these genetic and RNA variants from scRNA-seq data alone remains technically challenging. Existing benchmarks for genetic variant calling and RNA editing detection lack realistic simulations with explicit single-cell-level ground truth for variant locations, types, allelic ratios, and editing levels. This limits rigorous assessment of detection accuracy and error source across methods. To fill this gap, we present scVarSim, a simulation framework trained on real scRNA-seq data that generates realistic synthetic reads with ground truth for genetic and RNA variants. scVarSim models DNA-level features, including SNP and indel locations, types, and allelic ratios, and RNA-level features, including gene expression distributions, transcript splicing structures, and RNA editing locations, types, and levels. Using scVarSim, we systematically benchmarked four genetic variant callers and four RNA editing detection tools across three aligners, identifying DeepVariant and JACUSA2 as the most reliable methods for genetic variant calling and RNA editing detection, respectively. We further show that inference at single-cell resolution is primarily limited by sensitivity rather than quantification accuracy. Together, these results establish practical guidelines for genetic variant calling and RNA editing detection from scRNA-seq data and provide a testbed for method development.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Spatiotemporal cell type deconvolution leveraging tissue structure
authors: Macrina Lobo, Ziqi Zhang, Xiuwei Zhang
abstract: Spot-based spatial transcriptomics (ST) captures aggregated transcriptomic profiles at spatial locations (spots) in tissues. Deconvolution methods are needed to estimate the proportion of each cell type in every spot and usually leverage a single cell transcriptomic reference (scRNA-seq). Though there are an increasing number of experiments that profile multiple adjacent tissue slices, no deconvolution method leverages 3D tissue structure. Some methods utilize the 2D spatial organization assuming neighboring spots are similar, which is not true in heterogeneous environments. Moreover, most methods aggregate reference scRNA-seq profiles of the same cell type, missing subtle cell state variations. We present SpaDecoder, a parallelized per-spot deconvolution method for multiple neighboring spatial or temporal ST slices that predicts cell type proportions with a matrix factorization-based objective. SpaDecoder uses slice alignment and intermediate slice imputation, per-spot spatio-transcriptomic neighborhood inference, and 3D Gaussian kernel weights to effectively leverage 3D structure and adapt to homogeneous and heterogeneous tissue environments. We model individual scRNA-seq profiles, instead of cell type aggregated, with a learned scRNA-seq cell to cell type association matrix to capture cell state variability. The mathematical framework of SpaDecoder supports several downstream analyses. It uncovers key cell type regions and changing composition across slices, identifies colocalized cell types, imputes spatial gene expression, and predicts 3D spatio-temporal scRNA-seq cell locations. SpaDecoder outperforms baseline methods on various metrics, datasets, scenarios, and ablations, and yields interpretable biology, showing it effectively harnesses 3D structure and single cell reference profiles to improve deconvolution. SpaDecoder is available at https://github.com/ZhangLabGT/spadecoder}{https://github.com/ ZhangLabGT/spadecoder with the preprint at https://www.biorxiv.org/ content/10.64898/2026.02.10.705204v1.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: MethylSeg: Context-Aware Methylome Segmentation Enables Robust PMD Detection in Array and WGBS Data
authors: Jacob Tye, Kendell Clement
abstract: DNA methylation is a repressive epigenetic mark that regulates gene expression. Partially methylated domains (PMDs) are extended regions that capture large-scale methylation dysregulation and are a hallmark of cancers. Many segmentation algorithms have been developed to identify these domains, but they are limited to whole-genome bisulfite sequencing data, excluding more cost-effective and widely available array-based datasets. Furthermore, current methods lack a consistent definition of features that characterize PMDs. To address these limitations, we present MethylSeg, a context-aware methylome segmentation framework that enables PMD detection across assay types. MethylSeg refines the definition of PMDs by incorporating additional methylation features, including intermediate methylation percentages. It also improves cross-assay compatibility by employing a three-step approach: emission generation, state assignment, and region construction. To generate biologically meaningful emissions, MethylSeg summarizes CpG methylation across genomic windows, allowing each CpG to be interpreted locally and within its broader genomic context. These context-aware emissions are used to assign CpGs to biologically meaningful states using k-means clustering. Finally, contiguous regions are defined by applying a Hidden Markov Model to smooth CpG state transitions and group adjacent same-state CpGs. To assess the biological relevance of our methodology, we evaluated PMDs identified by MethylSeg and other established methods using chromatin enrichment and functional annotations analyses. MethylSeg-derived PMDs captured expected epigenetic patterns, including depletion of H3K36me2 within PMDs. Overall, MethylSeg provides a flexible and interpretable framework for PMD identification, with improved cross-assay compatibility and improved biological interpretability compared to existing methods.
