track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Amaranth: Enhanced Single-Cell Transcript Assembly via Discriminative Modeling of UMI Reads and Internal Reads
authors: Xiaofei Carl Zang, Tasfia Zahin, Irtesam Mahmud Khan, Qian Shi, Yi Xing, Mingfu Shao
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing has transformed transcriptome profiling at cellular resolution. A central yet unsolved challenge is the accurate reconstruction of full-length transcripts for individual cells. Emerging scRNA-seq protocols can produce reads that span entire transcripts, enabling the isoform-level expression analysis. For example, Smart-seq protocols combine UMI-linked reads that index and stitch together multiple reads from the same molecule, with internal reads filling coverage gaps. Here, we report a previously unrecognized phenomenon that, UMI reads and internal reads exhibit markedly different biological and statistical properties in strandness, 5'/3' coverage bias, and locality distribution. Existing assemblers fail to leverage these distinctions and consequently yielding suboptimal assembly. We show that discriminative modeling of UMI reads and internal reads can drastically increase the assembly accuracy. Based on these insights, we developed Amaranth, a new single-cell assembler that implements a set of new heuristics specifically designed to address the distinct biases of UMI-linked and internal reads. These heuristics enable accurate assignment of strandness for internal reads, reliable refinement of the splicing graph, and precise determination of transcript start and end sites, collectively resulting in substantial improvements. We also developed Amaranth-meta, that integrates all cells to produce improved assembly for individual cells. Benchmarked on Smart-seq3 datasets from human and mouse, Amaranth outperformed other state-of-the-art assemblers in assembling individual cells and in meta-assembly. Amaranth advances isoform-level analysis in single-cell transcriptomics, facilitating detailed studies at cellular resolution.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Minerva: Breakpoint-Guided Allele-Specific Copy Number Inference in Long-Read Cancer Genomes
authors: Ayse Keskus, Tanveer Ahmad, Isabel Rodriguez, Anton Goretsky, Ataberk Donmez, Sonam Tulsyan, Nicholas Syracuse, Michael Dean, Mikhail Kolmogorov
abstract: Copy-number alterations (CNAs) and structural rearrangements play a key role in cancer evolution, but resolving allele-specific copy-number structure remains difficult in highly rearranged genomes. Existing methods often rely on segmentation and phasing strategies that do not account for structural variant (SV) breakpoints, leading to smoothing across rearrangements and limited resolution, especially for small or focal events. While long-read sequencing provides accurate breakpoint detection and long-range haplotype information, these signals are typically not used together. We present Minerva, a method for inferring total and allele-specific copy number by directly incorporating SV information. Minerva uses breakpoint-guided segmentation, defining genomic segments based on SV breakpoints so that copy-number states follow the underlying genome structure. Total copy number is estimated using a mixed integer linear program that combines segment-level coverage with constraints from SV junctions, producing consistent integer copy-number states across the genome. For allele-specific inference, Minerva integrates haplotype-tagged read coverage with B-allele frequency (BAF), weighting each based on how informative it is locally, and uses SV junctions to extend haplotype phase across distant regions. We evaluated Minerva on the CASTLE long-read cancer cell-line panel using a truth set derived from diploid assemblies of matched normal samples. Across nearly all cell lines, Minerva improves chromosome-scale accuracy, yields more stable purity and ploidy estimates, and increases sensitivity and precision in detecting copy-number events. By incorporating SV breakpoints, Minerva resolves segments smaller than 100 bp and avoids smoothing across rearrangements, enabling more accurate reconstruction of complex genomic structures.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Unravelling genome-wide mosaic microsatellite mutations at single-cell resolution
authors: Yanmei Dou
abstract: Short tandem repeats (STRs), or microsatellites, are highly mutable genomic elements that modulate gene regulations and are implicated in a range of human diseases. However, detecting mosaic STR mutations at single-cell resolution remains challenging due to both technical and biological complexities. To address this, we developed BayesMonSTR, a robust algorithm that enables accurate detection of mosaic STR mutations. Using this tool in single-cell analysis of human tissues, we reveal an accumulation of longer mosaic STR insertions and deletions (indels) in aging mitotic and post-mitotic cells. Strikingly, prefrontal cortex (PFC) neurons accumulate a higher burden of STR mutations than B cells or lung epithelium, with aged neurons exhibiting a particularly pronounced increase in longer STR deletions. These mutations are enriched at transcription start sites (TSSs) and active enhancers of highly expressed genes. Our work establishes a foundation for genome-wide, hypothesis-free discovery of disease-associated mosaic STR mutations and reveals a previously unexplored landscape of mosaic STR variation in development and aging.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: SQANTI-epi: Functional and Quality Annotation of Single-Molecule Epigenomic Data
authors: Tianyuan Liu, Ana Conesa
abstract: A rapidly expanding family of single-molecule chromatin-profiling assays now reads per-molecule epigenomic state directly from long reads: m6A-methyltransferase methods (Fiber-seq, SAMOSA, SAM-seq), GpC-methylation approaches (nanoNOMe, MeSMLR-seq), multi-mark protocols (SMAC-seq), deaminase footprinting (DAF-seq, FOODIE), and protein-targeted strategies (DiMeLo-seq). Each rests on distinct enzymatic chemistry, yet no framework exists to assess data quality or to compare protocols against common reference epigenomes. Without QC, treatment artifacts propagate silently, and there is no principled way to test whether different technologies recover concordant regulatory-element maps. SQANTI-epi is, to our knowledge, the first QC framework for single-molecule epigenomics. It implements a three-level architecture. Library-level metrics — a Chromatin Signal-to-Noise score from base-modification autocorrelation, methylation rate, and nucleosome framing — flag improperly treated libraries. A region-level 53-element feature vector, including a 9-bin spatial profile analogous to positional k-mer representations, serves as a quality descriptor for every inter-nucleosome region. Cross-annotation against user-supplied reference tracks (ENCODE cCREs, DNase-/ATAC-seq, histone ChIP-seq) both measures concordance between single-molecule and bulk data and supplies weak labels — regulatory-element positives and heterochromatin/no-overlap negatives — that train FLARE, a gradient-boosted per-molecule accessibility classifier. The protocol-agnostic feature model enables direct cross-protocol comparison against identical references. Implemented in Rust with a streaming parallel architecture, SQANTI-epi extracts the 53-element descriptor for all 1.68 billion inter-nucleosome regions of a genome-wide GM12878 Fiber-seq dataset. On 128.7 million held-out chr1 regions, FLARE raises precision-recall AUC over the established FIRE caller by 4.4–5.8× across three orthogonal bulk references (DNase rep1/rep2, scATAC; mean ∆ +0.19). As a complementary diagnostic, TSS-proximal regions show 4.3× higher concordance with reference peaks than intergenic regions (59.9% vs 14.0%) — a ratio whose collapse would reveal over-treatment or systematic false-positive calls.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Likelihood-based optimization enables accurate copy number estimation for paralogous genes using exome data
authors: Sang Yoon Byun, Vikas Bansal
abstract: Motivation: Exome sequencing is widely used for genetic studies; however, accurate detection of copy number variants (CNV) in paralogous genes is challenging due to short-read mapping ambiguity and extensive copy-number variation. The human genome contains several hundred paralogous genes, many of which are known to harbor disease-associated CNVs. Existing exome CNV callers are primarily designed for rare CNV detection in uniquely mappable regions and are not well-suited for paralogous genes. Methods: We describe a computational method (EdgeCopy) for copy number profiling of paralogous genes using whole-exome sequence data. EdgeCopy aggregates reads mapped to all copies of paralogous genes and relates observed read depth to copy number for multiple exome samples using an approximate composite likelihood function. The likelihood function is optimized using numerical optimization to obtain gene-level fractional copy number estimates which are discretized and refined using a Hidden Markov Model to obtain exon-level copy number estimates. Results: Benchmarking of Edgecopy using experimental copy number data showed high concordance (mean = 0.975) for six disease-associated paralogous genes. We evaluated performance using whole-exome data from approximately 2,400 samples across five continental populations from the 1000 Genomes Project. EdgeCopy shows robust concordance with whole-genome sequencing based estimates (0.974-0.982) across populations and 130 paralogous genes spanning a wide range of copy-number variation. In comparison, copy number analysis using a state-of-the-art exome CNV caller failed to estimate copy number for paralogous genes with very high mapping ambiguity and showed much lower concordance (0.565) for CNV events compared to EdgeCopy (0.908). Availability: EdgeCopy is freely available at https://github.com/byunsy/edgecopy.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Seqwin: Ultrafast identification of signature sequences in microbial genomes
authors: Michael X. Wang, Bryce Kille, Michael G. Nute, Siyi Zhou, Lauren B. Stadler, Todd J. Treangen
abstract: Motivation: Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) enables rapid, cost-effective diagnostics but requires prior identification of genomic regions that allow sensitive and specific detection of target microbial groups, herein referred to as microbial signature sequences. We introduce Seqwin, an open-source framework designed to automate microbial genome signature discovery. Tens of thousands of microbial genomes are now available for a single species, limiting the application of existing manual and automated approaches for identifying signatures. Modern approaches that are capable of leveraging all available microbial genomes will ensure sensitive and accurate DNA signature identification and enable robust pathogen detection for clinical, environmental, and public health applications. Results: Seqwin builds weighted pan-genome minimizer graphs and uses a traversal algorithm to identify signature sequences that occur frequently in target genomes but remain rare in non-targets. Unlike earlier tools that depend on strict presence or absence of sequences, Seqwin accommodates natural sequence variation and scales to very large genome collections. When applied to genomes from C. difficile, M. tuberculosis, and S. enterica, Seqwin recovered more high-quality signatures than alternative methods with lower computational burden. Seqwin’s analysis of nearly 15 000 S. enterica genomes yielded over 200 candidate signatures in three minutes. Seqwin provides an open-source solution for the long-standing need for scalable microbial signature discovery and diagnostic assay design. Availability and Implementation: Seqwin is available on GitHub (https://github.com/treangenlab/Seqwin) and can be installed via Bioconda (https:// bioconda.github.io/recipes/seqwin/README.html). Benchmarking datasets, outputs, and scripts are available on Zenodo (https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.19874011). track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: pHapCompass: Probabilistic Assembly and Uncertainty Quantification of Polyploid Haplotype Phase
authors: Marjan Hosseini, Ella Veiner, Thomas Bergendahl, Tala Yasenpoor, Zane Smith, Margaret Staton, Derek Aguiar
abstract: Motivation: Computing haplotypes from sequencing data, i.e. haplotype assembly, is an important component of molecular and population genetics problems, including interpreting the effects of genetic variation on complex traits and reconstructing genealogical relationships. Assembling the haplotypes of polyploid genomes remains a significant challenge due to the exponential search space of haplotype phasings and read assignment ambiguity; the latter challenge is particularly difficult for haplotype assemblers since the information contained within the observed sequence reads is often insufficient for unambiguous haplotype assignment in polyploid genomes. Results: We present pHapCompass, probabilistic haplotype assembly algorithms for diploid and polyploid genomes that explicitly model and propagate read assignment ambiguity to compute a distribution over polyploid haplotype phasings. We develop graph theoretic algorithms to enable statistical inference and uncertainty quantification despite an exponential space of possible phasings. Since prior work evaluates polyploid haplotype assembly on synthetic genomes that do not reflect the realistic genomic complexity of polyploidy organisms, we develop a computational workflow for simulating genomes and DNA-seq for auto-and allopolyploids. Additionally, we generalize the vector error rate and minimum error correction evaluation criteria for partially phased haplotypes. Benchmarking of pHapCompass and several existing polyploid haplotype assemblers shows that pHapCompass yields competitive performance across varying genomic complexities and polyploid structures while retaining an accurate quantification of phase uncertainty. Availability and implementation: The source code for pHapCompass, simulation scripts, and datasets are freely available at https://github.com/bayesomicslab/pHapCompass.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: Pilot discovery of allele-specific modification QTLs from long-read RNA sequencing
authors: Michael Goneos, Theodore Nelson, Christopher Mason
abstract: RNA modifications are a major regulatory layer of gene expression, but the field still lacks a robust way to ask a mechanistic question: does genetic variation change RNA modification stoichiometry on one allele but not the other? Short read approaches break the link between haplotype, transcript structure, and modification state, and thus are restricted from allele-specific modification detection. Oxford Nanopore direct RNA sequencing changes that by reading all three features on the same molecule. Here, we present PLASMA (Phased Long-Read Analysis of Splicing and Modification with Alleles), a framework for transcript aware, allele specific modification quantification trait locus (modQTL) discovery that integrates transcript structure, per read modification quantification, and within sample haplotype resolved association testing. Across 18 samples, PLASMA tested 10,696 transcript site comparisons and identified 94 FDR significant modQTLs. This represents a discovery rate of roughly 0.8% of tested comparisons in a modestly sized cohort. m6A sites dominated the discovery set, accounting for 90 of 94 significant events. Critically, some of the strongest effects were linked to variants outside the canonical DRACH motif window rather than to direct motif rewriting. These results suggest that genetic control of RNA modification extends beyond canonical sequence motifs, even in this limited scale dataset. PLASMA thus provides a proof of concept path toward studying the genetic architecture of the modified transcriptome at the level where regulation occurs, that is, phased, transcript resolved, and molecule specific.

track: HiTSeq: High Throughput Sequencing Algorithms & Applications
title: CRANE: Correcting Errors in Raw Nanopore Signals Using Hidden Markov Models
authors: Simon Ambrozak, Ulysse McConnell, Bhargav Srinivasan, Burak Ozkan, Ernest Zhang, Can Firtina
abstract: Nanopore sequencing can read substantially longer sequences of nucleic acid molecules, called reads, than other sequencing methods, which has led to advances in genomic analysis such as the gapless human genome assembly. By analyzing the raw electrical signal reads that nanopore sequencing generates from molecules, existing works can map these reads without translating them into DNA characters (i.e., basecalling), allowing for quick and efficient analysis of sequencing data. However, raw signals often contain errors due to noise and processing errors, which limits the overall accuracy of raw signal analysis. Our goal in this work is to detect and correct errors in raw signals to improve the accuracy of raw signal analyses. To this end, we propose CRANE, a mechanism that trains and utilizes a Hidden Markov Model (HMM) to accurately correct signal errors. Our extensive evaluation on various datasets shows that CRANE 1) consistently improves the overall accuracy of the underlying raw signal analysis tools, 2) minimizes the burden of optimizing analysis pipelines for newer nanopore technologies, and 3) does not introduce substantial computational overhead. We conclude that CRANE provides an effective mechanism to systematically identify and correct the errors in raw nanopore signals before further analysis, which can enable the development of a new class of error correction mechanisms purely designed for raw nanopore signals. Source Code: CRANE is available at https://github.com/STORMgroup/ CRANE. We also provide the scripts to fully reproduce our results on our GitHub page.

title: Rules for 3' splice site choice inferred from high-throughput in silico mutagenesis
authors: Steve Mount, Wanru Lin
abstract: The selection of the 3' splice site in human introns is complex. Recognition of the 3' splice site sometimes depends on a branchpoint motif. However, in some introns, a branchpoint with little similarity to the consensus is used. Here, we have used splicesai-10k for high-throughput in silico mutagenesis. Thousands of sequence variants were systematically generated and evaluated on three exons selected because of branchpoint-dependent 3' splice sites and flanking exons within the 10,000 bp analysis window. When all possible pentamers were compared for their ability to function as a branchpoint, the three exons showed a very high degree of correlation. Perhaps surprisingly, significant differences were observed between poor matches to the branchpoint motif, suggesting that sequences with very little match to the consensus differ meaningfully in their ability to function at a branchpoint-dependent intron. To see how branchpoint-dependent introns differ from others, the effect of every possible single-nucleotide substitution was compared between the wild-type intron and the branchpoint mutation. We found that branchpoint-dependence often requires an AG dinucleotide upstream of the branch, or a complete absence of A residues well upstream, but some contribution of nucleotides in the exon or even in the adjacent intron was observed. Because spliceai recognizes compatibility between splice sites on either end of a long intron, we hypothesize that branchpoint-dependence may depend on the partner 5' splice site, but we have yet to explore the role of remote upstream 5' splice site sequences in branchpoint-dependence.

title: Expanding RNA Biology with XNAs: In Vitro Evolution of Non-natural Nucleic Acids for Recognition and Catalysis
authors: Lijun Zhou
abstract: In vitro evolution has greatly expanded the functional repertoire of RNA and highlights opportunities to explore beyond natural nucleic acid chemistry. Here, I will present our efforts to extend RNA biology using non-natural nucleic acids (XNAs). We focused on an XNA-SELEX platform that enables in vitro evolution of XNAs with programmable binding and catalytic activities. This approach has yielded XNA molecules capable of precise RNA targeting and protein modulation in complex biological contexts. Our work further demonstrates how alternative backbone chemistries can access functional properties not readily available to canonical RNA. Together, these results establish XNAs as a versatile molecular toolkit for probing and modulating RNA and protein function, and provide a general framework for extending nucleic acid structures and functions beyond natural systems.

title: Deep Learning to Accelerate Discovery of Functional Synthetic Nucleic Acids
authors: Jiatao Liang, Hong Kang, Lijun Zhou, Yoseph Barash
abstract: Nucleolytic xeno nucleic acid enzymes (XNAzymes) offer a promising new modality to directly and selectively cleave oncogenic mRNA sequences for the treatment of cancer. Because of their non-canonical backbones, XNAzymes have higher cellular stability compared to canonical RNAs, translating to longer persistence in a potential new therapy. Functional XNAzymes can be discovered via directed evolution procedures such as Systematic Evolution of Ligands by Exponential Enrichment (SELEX). However, amplification-driven biases often confound the results of selection experiments, which can be especially acute for XNAs, where enzymatic fidelity is limited and no nucleic-acid language models exist to alleviate these issues. To address this gap, we developed a backbone-agnostic machine learning framework that extracts sequence fitness directly from the generational sequencing data produced by SELEX, without requiring additional activity measurements. This attention-based framework accounts for long-range interactions within sequences and jointly models a linear term to capture amplification bias and a non-linear term to capture the true fitness underlying the desired activity or characteristics. When applied to an XNAzyme evolution dataset, the model successfully distinguished a highly enriched but bias-driven false-positive sequence from lower-enriched yet genuinely functional candidates. It also identified additional sequences with strong predicted fitness that were not highly enriched. These results demonstrate that transformer-based modeling of generational abundance can overcome PCR-associated biases in directed evolution. This framework provides a generalizable strategy for interpreting selection dynamics across diverse nucleic-acid chemistries and potentially reducing the number of costly and labor-intensive SELEX generations required in future campaigns, ultimately accelerating the development of XNA-based treatments.

title: RNA Language Model learns structure prediction of Internal Ribosome Entry Sites despite sequence only training
authors: Adam Sychla, Pierre Bongrand, Grant Yang, Jacob Rulison, Silvi Rouskin, R. Alexander Wesselhoeft, Namita Bisaria
abstract: RNA is a dynamic, yet structured molecule bridging high information density with complex higher-order assemblies and interactions. Far from being an inert translator, RNA uses both sequence and structure to enable function. Despite its importance, computational and experimental evaluation of RNA structure remains a core challenge. RNA's dynamic nature means that there are limited ""ground truth"" structures available by traditional methods. Given the lack of high-quality training data, machine learning models have been relatively ineffective when evaluating RNAs outside a subset of well-resolved structures. For this work, we were interested in Internal Ribosome Entry Sites (IRESes), large and complex structures used by viruses to recruit the ribosome. Although IRESes are well studied, they typically fall far outside the predictive capabilities of other computational methods. In trying to find a method to study IRESes as a broad class, we found that, paradoxically, our best structure predictions were derived without any a priori data on structure. We achieved this by fine-tuning an RNA Language Model on 50,000 IRES sequences on the task of masked-token prediction. Although this model was provided no external knowledge of secondary structure or base pairing rules, an encoding of structure nonetheless emerges. Evaluating structure with this model, we outperformed covariance in F1 and precision. This pipeline enabled us to seek new family-wide patterns of IRES structures and provides a path towards more accurate functional prediction. Together, we demonstrate that emergent properties of RNA can be derived from their sequence alone by carefully probing RNA Language Models.

title: RNA Design with Language Models
authors: Milan Gautam, Ning Dai, Tianshuo Zhou, Bowen Xie, David Mathews, Liang Huang
abstract: RNA design, the task of finding a sequence that folds into a target secondary structure, has broad biological and biomedical impact but remains computationally challenging due to the exponentially large sequence space and exponentially many competing folds. Traditional approaches treat it as an optimization problem, relying on per-instance heuristics or constraint-based search. We instead reframe RNA design as conditional sequence generation and introduce a reusable neural approximator, instantiated as an autoregressive language model (LM), that maps target structures directly to sequences. We first train our model in a supervised setting on random-induced structure-sequence pairs, and then use reinforcement learning (RL) to optimize end-to-end metrics. We also propose methods to select a small subset for RL that greatly improves RL efficiency and quality. Across four datasets, our approach outperforms state-of-the-art systems on key metrics such as Boltzmann probability while being 1.7Ã— faster, establishing conditional LM generation as a scalable, task-agnostic alternative to per-instance optimization for RNA design.

title: Sampling-based Continuous Optimization for Messenger RNA Design
authors: Feipeng Yue, Ning Dai, Wei Yu Tang, Tianshuo Zhou, David Mathews, Liang Huang
abstract: Designing messenger RNA (mRNA) sequences for a target protein requires searching an exponentially large design space while optimizing properties that affect stability and downstream performance. This is challenging because practical mRNA design involves multiple objectives beyond the classical minimum free energy, and different applications prefer different trade-offs. We cast this discrete optimization problem as continuous optimization, where we define a distribution over valid mRNA sequences, compute the expectation of the objective function over this distribution, and use gradient descent to update the distribution towards better sequences. To make it universally applicable to any objective function, we use sampling to approximate the objective function and gradients. Across a set of UniProt proteins and the SARS-CoV-2 spike protein, our method consistently improves the chosen objective, with particularly strong gains on average unpaired probability and accessible uridines compared to LinearDesign and EnsembleDesign. title: Nuclear speckles enable processing of RNA from GC-rich isochores
authors: Ferhat Ay, Tugce Aktas, Michał Małszycki, Lisa Martina, Ibrahim Avsar Ilik, Daniela Salgado Figueroa, Nirmalya Dasgupta, Menşura Feray Çoşar, Keun-Tae Kim, Gil Carraco, Beatrix Fauler, David Meierhofer, Thorsten Mielke, Hiroo Imai, Cantaş Alev
abstract: Nuclear speckles are conserved, membrane-less organelles linked to various post-transcriptional processes. Here, we examined their roles in human cells by engineered, acute removal of SON and SRRM2, two conserved speckle core components characterized by intrinsically disordered regions (IDRs). Their removal results in a significant downregulation of GC-rich genes with short introns clustered within GC-rich isochores, caused by inefficient and chaotic splicing; in contrast, the expression or splicing of genes outside these isochores remains unaffected. Comparative analysis across eukaryotes, from fungi to mammals, reveals that both GC-rich isochores and speckles are found exclusively in amniotes; moreover, the IDRs of SON have undergone notable expansion in the latter. title: ERV-Seq: Revealing The Hidden Transcriptome of Human Endogenous Retroviruses
authors: Isabelle Heifetz Ament, Zelin Liu, Lan Lin
abstract: Human endogenous retroviruses (HERVs), remnants of ancient retroviral integrations, comprise a substantial yet largely uncharacterized fraction of the human genome. To systematically resolve the complexity of the HERV transcriptome, we developed ERV-seq, a targeted long-read RNA sequencing approach that combines probe-based enrichment with full-length sequencing to robustly capture HERV-derived transcripts from both intragenic and intergenic loci. Leveraging ultra-deep, full-length reads, ERV-seq achieves locus-specific resolution not attainable with short-read methods. Using this approach, we identified over 2,000 expressed proviral HERV loci and more than 27,000 transcript isoforms, the vast majority of which are novel and previously unannotated, substantially expanding the known HERV transcriptome. This comprehensive atlas enabled reanalysis of GTEx short-read RNA-seq datasets, revealing over 700 HERV loci with strong genotype-expression associations and more than 40 loci showing eQTL-GWAS colocalization, implicating previously unrecognized HERV loci in human trait and disease associations. By generating the most comprehensive and precise catalogue of expressed human HERV loci and transcript isoforms to date, ERV-seq provides a powerful platform to investigate the functional contributions of HERVs to human development, disease, and genome evolution.

title: Statistical guarantees for identifying RNA-binding protein interaction sites
authors: Young-suk Lee
abstract: Technological advancement in mapping protein-RNA interaction networks is key to decoding post-transcriptional regulation. However, existing computational tools often fail to account for the technical noise inherent in data generation, leading to a lack of statistical guarantees for downstream analysis. We present a full nonparametric approach for identifying RNA-binding protein (RBP) interaction sites that directly controls the False Discovery Rate (FDR) using size-matched input data. By accounting for sequence depth and zero-inflation, our method demonstrates superior statistical robustness and reproducibility in genome-wide site identification. Reanalyzing ENCODE CLIP-seq data (120 RBPs in K562; 103 RBPs in HepG2), our framework provides unique insights into mitochondrial RNA, noncoding RNA, and splicing regulation. Finally, by integrating variant databases such as ClinVar, COSMIC, and GTEx, we link RBP interaction sites to pathogenic and regulatory variants, thereby providing mechanistic insights for functional genomics in RNA biology.

title: Nearest Neighbor Parameters for Estimating the Folding Stability of RNA Sequences Including Pseudouridine
authors: Thandolwethu Shabangu, Elzbieta Kierzek, Sebastian Arteaga, Gregory Orf, Julia Stone, Olivia Hiltke, Megan Miaro, Elizabeth Jolley, Marta Soszyńska-Jóźwiak, Philip Bevilacqua, Brent M Znosko, Ryszard Kierzek, David Mathews
abstract: Nearest neighbor parameters are widely used in software for estimating the conformational stability of a given RNA sequence folding into a specific structure. Folding stability for RNA folding with canonical nucleotides A, C, G, and U has been widely studied, but the same is not true for most modified nucleotides. In this work, we present a comprehensive set of nearest neighbor parameters for estimating the folding stability of RNA sequences including pseudouridine in helical or loop contexts. These parameters are derived from 199 optical melting experiments involving helices with pseudouridine-A and pseudouridine-G pairs and with pseudouridine in loop motifs. The experiments include sequences with pseudouridine and U in the same strand, including U-A and U-G pairs, allowing us to consider the folding stability of sequences with both U and pseudouridine. On average, pseudouridine stabilizes the folding compared to U in an analogous motif, although this effect is sequence-context dependent. These parameters improve the modeling of folding stability for RNA secondary structures containing pseudouridine. We demonstrate that these parameters successfully model, for S. cerevisae U2 snRNA, the secondary structure change when two additional inducible pseudouridines are present. These parameters are freely available and incorporated into the RNAstructure software package.

title: Deciphering Fusion Transcript Complexity Using Targeted RNA Sequencing
authors: Bohu Pan, Paweł P. Łabaj, David P. Kreil, Joshua Xu, Donald J. Johann Jr
abstract: Fusion transcripts arising from chromosomal rearrangements are critical diagnostic and therapeutic biomarkers in oncology. Accurate detection and quantification of fusion transcripts in the cancer transcriptome is key for research and clinical application. We performed a comprehensive assessment of fusions detected in a standardized reference RNA sample by eight targeted panels and two whole transcriptome sequencing protocols followed by both short-read and long-read sequencing and seven fusion calling tools. Our study establishes a benchmark fusion dataset derived from the commonly used Universal Human Reference RNA (UHRR) sample by orthogonal RT-qPCR based validation and provides a publicly accessible multi-platform resource to rigorously evaluate existing and emerging fusion detection algorithms. Furthermore, we systematically evaluate performance metrics for both short-read and long-read targeted panels, offering actionable insights for optimizing experimental design and bioinformatic pipelines. This comprehensive compendium of fusion transcripts in the reference sample serves as a valuable resource for improving the accuracy and reproducibility of clinical fusion detection, ultimately supporting precision oncology initiatives.

title: Systematic identification and multi-omic characterization of human chromatin-associated long non-coding RNAs
authors: Zhao Li, Yue Qi, Shaosen Zhang, Zhang Zhang, Lina Ma
abstract: Chromatin-associated long non-coding RNAs (ca-lncRNAs) play crucial roles in genome organization and gene regulation, yet systematic identification and comprehensive characterization of human ca-lncRNAs remain inadequate. Here, we identified human ca-lncRNAs genome-wide using high-throughput sequencing datasets that assess RNA-chromatin association, and comprehensively characterized their multi-dimensional molecular features via integrative multi-omics analysis. Across six cell lines, we identified 17,875 high-confidence ca-lncRNAs among 323,950 lncRNAs from LncBook. These constitute nearly 80% of all detected chromatin-associated RNAs and display significantly higher cell-type specificity. Multi-omics analysis across more than 1,000 samples indicates that, compared with chromatin-disassociated lncRNAs, ca-lncRNAs exhibit significantly higher expression levels, lower protein-coding potential, and more frequent interactions with RNA-binding proteins such as hnRNPs and transcription factors. Notably, ca-lncRNA genes are generally young and predominantly originate in the Eutheria and Homo sapiens-specific lineages. To investigate the sequence basis for chromatin binding, we applied an interpretable machine learning framework and revealed that Alu repeats are the key drivers of chromatin binding. Mechanistically, integrative interactome analysis combined with computational prediction suggested that Alu repeats facilitate RNA-chromatin interactions through Alu-DNA triplex formation. Collectively, our study provides a comprehensive resource of human ca-lncRNAs, delineates their multi-omics characteristics, and highlights Alu repeats as key sequence elements of chromatin binding.

title: modulator: Fragment-Specific Modification Calling for Nanopore Direct-RNA Sequencing Data
authors: Theodore Nelson, Michael Goneos, Caroline Aufgebauer, Paul Collier, Jacqueline Proszynski, Krista Ryon, Evan Violette, Nadia Houerbi, Stacy Horner, Christopher Mason
abstract: Nanopore direct RNA sequencing (DRS) enables simultaneous measurement of RNA sequence and chemical modifications at single-molecule resolution. However, existing epitranscriptomic analysis workflows typically operate at the gene level or rely on predefined reference transcriptomes, limiting resolution of isoform-specific RNA modification patterns. Here, we introduce modulator, a unified pipeline for transcript-aware epitranscriptomic analysis that operates on fragmentforms: read-supported, 3prime-anchored RNA structures defined by shared splice junctions and transcript end sites (TES). Unlike canonical transcripts, which represent full-length isoforms often derived from reference annotations, fragmentforms are data-driven partial isoform representations that prioritize reliable features of Nanopore DRS reads, namely splice structure and poly(A)-anchored ends, while accommodating incomplete or variable coverage. This distinction enables robust modeling of RNA populations in contexts where full-length transcript reconstruction is ambiguous or unsupported. modulator reconstructs fragmentforms directly from aligned reads using TES clustering and splice-chain collapsing, and assigns reads to these structures using a 3prime-anchored suffix-based strategy. Transcript identity is encoded in BAM tags and used to partition modification calls generated by ONT modkit, yielding fragmentform-specific modification profiles across multiple RNA modification types. Downstream modules aggregate genotype and modification signals across samples, apply site-level quality filtering, and perform differential analysis. Across experimental datasets, modulator reveals widespread fragmentform-specific differences in RNA modification stoichiometry, including substantial heterogeneity among structures derived from the same gene and condition-specific modulation of these patterns. These results demonstrate that fragmentform-level resolution is critical for disentangling RNA processing from epitranscriptomic regulation. modulator provides a reproducible framework for integrative RNA biology, enabling sample-specific transcript-resolved modification analysis without reliance on incomplete reference annotations. title: Beyond the known genome: expanding the vertebrate lncRNA universe through targeted full-length RNA sequencing
authors: Barbara Uszczynska-Ratajczak, Roderic Guigo, Tomasz Madry, Monika Kwiatkowska, Silvia Carbonell
abstract: Long non-coding RNAs (lncRNAs) are among the largest yet least characterized gene classes in vertebrate genomes. Fragmented catalogs, limited cross-species conservation data, and poor transcript-level resolution have collectively hindered their systematic functional analysis. Here we present complementary efforts that substantially expand lncRNA annotations across human, mouse, and zebrafish using targeted long-read RNA sequencing, revealing previously unrecognized transcriptomic complexity. Through manually supervised computational annotation of full-length long-read sequencing data across matched embryonic and adult tissues, GENCODE added 17,931 human genes (140,268 transcripts) and 22,784 mouse genes (136,169 transcripts) to its reference catalog, representing the largest increase in annotated human genes since the initial sequencing of the human genome. New human-mouse ortholog assignments tripled the number of disease-associated lncRNAs with murine counterparts, directly enabling functional and translational studies. Although many novel lncRNAs are lowly abundant in bulk RNA-seq, they display high cell-type-specific expression, suggesting roles in cell identity and genome regulation. Extending this framework to zebrafish (Danio rerio), we applied CapTrap-seq to capture 5"²-capped full-length transcripts across developmental stages and adult tissues. Analysis of polyadenylation dynamics and isoform-specific expression revealed regulatory complexity absent from current annotations. Locus-level studies of carmn and dancr identified novel full-length isoforms with distinct domain structures. These results establish a reproducible, genome-agnostic framework for high-confidence lncRNA discovery across vertebrates, with direct implications for comparative genomics, disease gene characterization, and the functional interpretation of non-coding regions of the genome.

title: Decoding the temporal landscape of mRNA modifications at single-molecule resolution
authors: Eduardo Eyras
abstract: Despite their pivotal roles in gene regulation, the precise timing of mRNA modifications during biogenesis has remained elusive due to the lack of methods that can simultaneously resolve modification status and RNA processing states at the single-molecule level. Here we describe two complementary nanopore-based approaches to establish a temporal framework for mRNA modification. First, we developed SWARM (Single-molecule Workflow for Analysing RNA Modifications) (Prodic et al. 2026), an AI-based tool that overcomes the high false-positive rates plaguing modification detection. By employing a training strategy that accounts for signal crosstalk from non-target modifications and incorporates orthogonally validated cellular signals, SWARM enables high-precision detection of m6A and pseudouridine (Ψ) at single-nucleotide and single-molecule resolution and outperforms existing tools on rigorous cellular benchmarks. Second, to place these modifications in time, we created dFORCE (direct Fractionated Observation of RNA Coupled to Elongation) (Sethi et al. 2025), a technique that separates transcriptionally engaged pre-mRNA from mature, polyadenylated transcripts, allowing us to pinpoint the order of processing events on a transcriptome-wide scale. Applying these technologies across cell lines, mammalian tissues, and targeted perturbation experiments with splicing and modification enzyme inhibitors reveals two key temporal principles of RNA modification. First, we find that m6A deposition substantially precedes splicing catalysis, with m6A accumulating near-cytoplasmic levels on unspliced pre-mRNA. Crucially, the canonical suppression of m6A near exon boundaries is already in place before splicing and the deposition of the exon junction complex, challenging prevailing models of how m6A topology is established. Second, we discover a splicing-shaped mode of Ψ deposition in which TRUB1-mediated pseudouridylation near exon boundaries preferentially occurs after exon-exon ligation, driven by local RNA structure stabilisation in spliced transcripts. We validate this mechanism using both nascent RNA sequencing and in vitro biochemical assays. Together, these findings suggest that m6A and Ψ modifications follow distinct temporal trajectories during mRNA maturation, arguing against a globally coordinated epitranscriptomic code and instead pointing to a more intricate, stepwise regulatory logic. and challenge models of widespread coordination between these marks. By integrating high-precision detection with temporal resolution, our integrated approach provides a robust framework for decoding the dynamic life of RNA.

title: Decoding the Cancer Splicing Landscape: From Aging Associated Isoforms to Regulatory Networks and Therapeutic Targets
authors: Olga Anczuków
abstract: Alternative RNA splicing exponentially expands the functional proteome, yet its systematic dysregulation across cancer and aging remains incompletely understood. Our work integrates multi-modal genomic approaches to decode how splicing programs are remodeled during aging, malignant transformation, and tumor immune evasion. Using long-read RNA-sequencing of human breast and lung tumors, we have mapped the landscape of full-length cancer isoforms, uncovering thousands of novel transcripts that are often missed by short-read approaches. Building on this isoform atlas, we reveal that aging drives broad splicing remodeling in mammary epithelial cells, and that select tumor-associated isoform signatures are in fact age-driven, positioning splicing alterations as early preneoplastic events. We further define the regulatory architecture controlling these splicing programs, demonstrating that post-transcriptional autoregulatory mechanisms within splicing factors are selectively disrupted in tumors, representing novel intervention points. Finally, we show that specific splicing events have direct clinical relevance: intron retention in immune-regulatory genes predicts patient response to checkpoint inhibitor immunotherapy, and splice-switching oligonucleotides that correct tumor-associated isoforms exert selective anti-proliferative effects across cancer models. Together, this work defines splicing dysregulation as a molecular hallmark of aging and cancer, and identifies novel isoforms and splicing regulators as actionable biomarkers and therapeutic targets.

title: ASPECT: Alternative Splicing Event Classification with Transformers for Cancer Transcriptomics
authors: Sahil Thapa, Miguelangel Tamargo, Oluwatosin Oluwadare
abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) is a fundamental regulatory mechanism that expands transcriptomic and proteomic diversity by generating multiple mRNA isoforms from a single gene and plays a key role in numerous diseases, such as cancer. However, most existing studies focus predominantly on exon skipping and constitutive splicing, with limited attention to other biologically relevant AS event types. In addition, many computational approaches rely on short genomic sequence windows and conventional deep learning architectures, limiting their ability to capture long-range regulatory dependencies underlying complex splicing decisions. Here, we present ASPECT, a transformer-based framework for alternative splicing event classification built on DNABERT-2 with Byte Pair Encoding (BPE) tokenization. Using fixed-length sequence inputs of 1,024 nucleotides, ASPECT captures extended regulatory context and demonstrates strong performance across multiple splicing event classification tasks. Comparative evaluation shows that ASPECT consistently outperforms the state-of-the-art model across all evaluated tasks, while maintaining robust performance across alternative 3"² (acceptor) and alternative 5"² (donor) splice-site prediction. To address the complexity of splicing patterns, we further introduce a hierarchical transformer cascade for multi-class splicing event identification, incorporating additional event types such as mutually exclusive exons (ME) and retained introns (RI). Extensive evaluation on cancer-associated splicing events derived from TCGA SpliceSeq datasets and independent cohorts demonstrates the robustness and generalizability of ASPECT across diverse datasets. These results establish ASPECT as a scalable framework for sequence-based analysis of alternative splicing in disease contexts.

title: An integrative framework links cryptic splicing to neoantigen generation and candidate splicing factor regulation in lupus neutrophils
authors: Rayan Najjar, Xiaoxing Wang, Ning Wang, Farheen Shaikh, Ethan Le, Jie An, Cecilia Mustelin, Fatemeh Moadab, Vincent Gurghian, Sadie Van den Bogaerde, Stephen Schoenberger, Tomas Mustelin
abstract: Aberrant RNA splicing can generate non-reference protein sequences, yet its contribution to autoimmune antigen landscapes and its upstream regulatory basis remain incompletely understood. Here, we developed an integrative computational framework to identify cryptic splicing events in neutrophils from patients with systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE), infer their coding consequences, and assess their potential to generate neoantigens. Compared with neutrophils from healthy donors and patients with rheumatoid arthritis, SLE neutrophils exhibited widespread aberrant splicing, including intron retention, exon skipping, and noncanonical splice junction usage. Many of these events were predicted to disrupt canonical reading frames and generate novel peptide sequences absent from annotated isoforms and the reference proteome, defining a disease-associated landscape of candidate cryptic neoantigens. Using this framework, we systematically prioritized cryptic splice-derived peptides with predicted antigenic potential and disease specificity in SLE. A subset of these candidates was supported by experimental evidence, including immunopeptidomic detection on class I MHC molecules, antigen-specific T cell reactivity, and serum class-switched antibody recognition in patient-derived samples. To investigate potential upstream mechanisms, we integrated event-level splicing results with external RNA-binding protein perturbation and binding datasets, identifying candidate splicing factor regulatory programs associated with the SLE cryptic splicing landscape. Together, these findings establish a computational framework linking aberrant splicing, candidate upstream regulation, and neoantigen potential in lupus neutrophils, while providing a foundation for broader studies of immune-relevant splicing dysregulation across autoimmune disease.

title: Alternative RNA processing-informed deep learning models boost gene expression-based patient outcome prediction and reveal novel prognostic indicators
authors: Zachary Wakefield, Ana Fiszbein
abstract: Alternative splicing (AS) is a fundamental mechanism of gene expression (GEX) regulation that allows a single gene to produce multiple protein isoforms, contributing to the proteomic complexity essential for cellular functions. This process is intricately regulated and crucial for the normal development and maintenance of tissues. Deviations in AS are increasingly implicated in cancer progression, generating oncogenic protein variants that drive tumorigenesis. However, the molecular mechanisms underlying AS's role in cancer prognosis remain unclear. Recently, several prognostic deep-learning methods have been developed using GEX and other omics data. However, these all ignore the vital mechanism of alternative RNA processing (aRNAp). We developed a deep-learning framework based on a Cox proportional hazards neural network to evaluate the prognostic utility of GEX, AS, alternative transcript termination and start, and exon-type usage. Across 26 TCGA cancer types and ~9000 samples, aRNAp features showed predictive performance comparable to GEX for patient outcome. Remarkably, aRNAp-derived features frequently outperformed GEX. Using SHAP-based interpretation, we identified prognostic features from nonlinear models, including candidates not detected by standard survival analyses. Thus, highlighting the added value of deep learning for capturing complex survival-associated signals. We then built a multimodal survival model that fused modality-specific encoders with MLP-Cox architecture. This approach further improved prognostic performance over single-data-type models and shows that aRNAp events often ranked among the most influential predictors of patient outcome. Together, these results demonstrate that aRNAp provides substantial prognostic information beyond traditional expression-based analyses and offers a framework for discovering novel biomarkers and therapeutic targets in cancer.

title: predNMD: prediction of nonsense-mediated mRNA decay for enhanced clinical variant pathogenicity classification
authors: Yaqi Su, Steven Brenner
abstract: We developed predNMD, which predicts whether human transcripts harboring nonsense variants undergo nonsense-mediated mRNA decay (NMD). For nonsense variants predicted not to trigger NMD, predNMD additionally predicts whether the resulting transcript will produce a C-terminal or N-terminal truncated protein through SHAP-based feature analysis. NMD is a conserved RNA surveillance pathway that degrades transcripts with premature termination codons (PTCs), critically modifying genotype-phenotype relationships in human disease. Accurate NMD prediction is essential for applying PVS1, the strongest pathogenic evidence criterion in the ACMG/AMP variant classification framework, yet current guidelines rely on the 50-nucleotide (50nt) rule, which incompletely captures NMD biology. predNMD is a random forest classifier trained on 5,304 nonsense variants curated from four independent allele-specific expression datasets (GREGoR, GEUVADIS, GTEx, and TCGA). From 166 candidate features spanning transcript structure, sequence context, evolutionary conservation, translational signals, RNA modifications, and population genetics, Boruta feature selection identified 20 informative predictors, including novel features such as TranslationAI-derived translation initiation and termination scores and m6A modification density. On an independent MMRF-TARGET validation set, predNMD achieved an AUC of 0.78, outperforming NMDetective-A, NMDetective-B, Ensembl VEP NMD prediction, and the 50nt rule. Validation against BRCA1 saturation genome editing data yielded a Spearman correlation of âˆ’0.64 between predNMD scores and experimentally measured transcript abundance, compared to âˆ’0.43 for NMDetective-A. predNMD's mechanism predictions also showed stronger concordance with ClinGen expert panel decisions than the 50nt rule. predNMD is available as a Python package, Docker container, and web interface at prednmd.org.

title: Charting the Axes of Isoform Variation using Long Read Single-cell Transcriptomics with Allos
authors: Eamon Mcandrew, Pascal Barbry, Kevin Lebrigand, Laure-Emmanuelle Zaragosi, Sylvie Leroy
abstract: While single-cell atlases chart the cellular landscape shaped by complex human diseases, they remain limited to gene-level expression, leaving an entire regulatory dimension unmapped. Around 90% of human multi-exon genes undergo alternative splicing, generating distinct mRNA isoforms that independently shape cell identity, function, and disease susceptibility. To address this question in the airway, we documented the isoform landscape across cell types, anatomical compartments at the level of the human airway during early stages of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease. We first developed Allos, an open-source Python framework for isoform-level single-cell and spatial transcriptomics, built on AnnData and integrated with the scverse ecosystem. Allos screens for differential isoform usage across all pairwise cell-type contrasts transcriptome-wide in seconds, with pseudobulk-aware testing available for multi-donor designs, and provides structure-aware visualisation linking transcript architecture to PSI values across cell types with protein-level domain interpretation. Applying this platform to human airway biopsies, we generated over 1.1 billion long reads across 14 samples from 10 donors, capturing single-cell long-read transcriptomes from 60,037 cells across 49 distinct cell types, spanning four nasal and ten tracheobronchial biopsies, including healthy controls and COPD patients. Across these cells, we quantify 228,258 isoforms, with over 60% of expressed genes producing two or more distinct isoforms, a layer of transcript diversity inaccessible to standard gene-level atlases. We identify differential isoform usage across all major compartments and splicing programmes that shift continuously along epithelial differentiation trajectories, generating the first isoform-resolution single-cell atlas of the human airway.

authors: Lieke Michielsen, Andrey Prjibelski, Careen Foord, Yelizaveta Spiegelman, Taewoo Kim, Wen Hu, Julien Jarroux, Justine Hsu, Rebecca Pfeill, Xinyi Zhang, Li Gan, Alexandru Tomescu, Iman Hajirasouliha, Hagen Tilgner
abstract: Spatial long-read technologies are becoming increasingly common but lack nanometer and therefore often single-cell resolution. This leaves the question unanswered of whether spatially variable isoforms represent spatial variability within one cell type or differences in cell-type composition between different regions. Here, we developed Spl-ISO-Seq2 (220nm spot size and 500nm resolution), and the accompanying software packages Spl-IsoQuant-2 and Spl-IsoFind, enabling long-read sequencing using up to 500 million barcodes compared to 80,000 previously. Applying this to the adult mouse brain, we compared spatial variability by examining (a) differential isoform abundance between known brain regions and (b) spatial isoform patterns that do not align with predefined regions. While the former revealed more spatial isoform differences, both approaches identified overlapping hits, e.g., Rps24 in oligodendrocytes. For Snap25, previously known to exhibit spatial isoform variation, we now show that this variability occurs in excitatory neurons. The second approach also uncovered patterns not captured by predefined-region comparisons, e.g., Tnnc1 in excitatory neurons. Furthermore, we show that a surprising number of spatial isoform signals is not driven by cell-type composition alone. Finally, we applied our software to newly generated Visium HD 3' long-read data to demonstrate its applicability and strong reproducibility across protocols and biological replicates. Taken together, our experimental and analytical methods enrich spatial transcriptomics with a so-far elusive isoform view of spatial variation for individual cell types.

title: BenchDrop-seq: a microfluidics-free platform for benchtop single-cell long-read RNA sequencing
authors: Avi Srivastava
abstract: Single-cell long-read RNA sequencing enables direct measurement of full-length transcripts but has remained difficult to deploy at scale due to reliance on microfluidic barcoding, specialized instrumentation, and high per-cell cost. Here we present BenchDrop-seq, a benchtop platform for single-cell long-read transcriptomics that leverages particle-templated partitioning for single-cell molecular barcoding and couples this workflow to Oxford Nanopore sequencing for full-length transcript capture. By integrating established bead-based partitioning chemistry with long-read sequencing and a dedicated open-source analysis pipeline for barcode recovery, alignment, and transcript quantification, BenchDrop-seq enables isoform-resolved measurements from thousands of individual cells using standard laboratory equipment. We validate the platform in both a homogeneous cell line and a heterogeneous primary tissue, demonstrating high barcode recovery, accurate gene-level quantification, and reproducible detection of cell-type-specific transcript usage that is not readily accessible to short-read assays. Together, BenchDrop-seq establishes a practical and accessible framework for single-cell long-read RNA sequencing, lowering experimental barriers while enabling transcript-level analyses in routine single-cell experiments.

title: Three-Dimensional RNA Spatial Mapping Reveals Microcircuit Organization of the Nucleus Accumbens
authors: Lauren Wills, Sarah Claypool, Adam Catto, Paul Kenny
abstract: The nucleus accumbens (NAc) is a central hub in the brains reward circuitry and plays a critical role in addiction-related behaviors, including reinforcement, motivation, and relapse. Despite its importance, the cellular architecture of the NAc has largely been studied using dissociative approaches or two-dimensional (2D) RNA spatial assessment methods, which do not fully capture tissue organization in intact brain circuits. While single-nucleus RNA sequencing (snRNA-seq) identifies expected NAc cell populations, it does not resolve RNA spatial positioning or cellular relationships within native microenvironments. Here, we perform three-dimensional (3D) RNA spatial assessment of the mouse NAc using the Pyxa platform (Stellaromics), based on STARmap-like technology. Control C57BL/6J male mice were used for spatial RNA profiling (N=2, preliminary sample run). Brains were removed, dissected into a 250µm slab containing the NAc, preserved in OCT, and sectioned to capture a 50µm spanning region. Samples then underwent hydrogel embedding, clearing, and in situ RNA spatial mapping. Data were analyzed using a customized Python pipeline and visualized using early access Pyxa Studio. This volumetric RNA spatial profiling enables mapping of cell types and their relative positioning in three-dimensional space, allowing interrogation of local cellular neighborhoods. Using this approach, we identify distinct patterns of medium spiny neuron (MSN) organization, including densely packed MSN aggregates versus more isolated MSNs. These spatial RNA analyses reveal non-random cellular relationships, with both aggregated and isolated MSNs showing preferences for specific neighboring cell types within their microenvironment. These findings are displayed briefly in figures 1 and 2. Together, these findings demonstrate that 3D RNA spatial positioning uncovers previously unappreciated features of NAc architecture that are not accessible with snRNA-seq or conventional 2D spatial RNA approaches alone, providing new insight into the microcircuit organization of an addiction-relevant brain region.

title: Single-cell RNA editing identifies aggressive and favorable cellular states in chronic myelomonocytic leukemia
authors: , Nisansala Wickramasinghe, Doan Bui, Surendra Neupane, Meghan Ferrall-Fairbanks, Michael Deininger, Eric Padron, Tongjun Gu
abstract: Chronic myelomonocytic leukemia (CMML) is a clinically heterogeneous myeloid malignancy with limited therapeutic options and inadequate risk stratification. Although single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) has improved CMML classification through gene expression profiling, post-transcriptional regulatory layers remain poorly understood. Adenosine-to-inosine (A-to-I) RNA editing, catalyzed primarily by ADAR1 and ADAR2, is a pervasive RNA modification, but its role in CMML at single-cell resolution has remained unclear because accurate detection from scRNA-seq is technically challenging. We developed a single-cell–aware computational framework for high-confidence discovery of RNA editing events at pseudo-bulk depth followed by sensitive quantification at single-cell resolution. Applying this approach to discovery and independent validation CMML cohorts, we identified 3,326 single-cell–resolved A-to-I editing sites and defined reproducible RNA editing–based cellular states with distinct biological and clinical associations. A granulocyte-monocyte progenitor–like editing state, edClu1_sub0, aligned with a previously described inflammatory, monocytic-biased transcriptional program associated with adverse outcomes. In contrast, other editing-defined states, including edClu3 and edClu6, mark more favorable states associated with earlier-stage disease, TET2 wild-type status, and improved survival. Editing states also changed systematically following hypomethylating agent treatment and showed locus-and cluster-specific regulation by ADAR1 and ADAR2, with edClu1_sub0 characterized by high ADAR1 and low ADAR2 expression. Integrative analyses further nominated immune-related genes, including LAPTM5, CTSS, and CD83, as candidate targets of CMML-associated oncogenic RNA editing programs. These results identify RNA editing as a previously underappreciated source of cellular heterogeneity and a distinct regulatory layer in CMML, extending disease characterization beyond gene expression alone.

title: Leveraging Long-Read Transcriptomics and Ribo-seq to Expand the Noncanonical Proteome
authors: Nuo Xu, Bharti Kukreja, Brian Kalish, Shreejoy Tripathy
abstract: Long-read RNA sequencing has revealed that the transcript landscape is far more complex than captured by standard genome annotations, uncovering thousands of novel isoforms with potentially distinct coding potential. A major challenge, however, is determining which of these novel transcripts are actually translated. Computational tools can predict open reading frames (ORFs) from long-read assemblies, but prediction alone cannot confirm active translation. Experimental approaches are needed to bridge the gap between isoform discovery and functional protein output. Here, we present a framework combining long-read RNA sequencing with ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq) to provide direct evidence of translation for ORFs in novel isoforms. Using a custom long-read-derived transcriptome as the reference, we benchmarked two complementary ORF-calling approaches: RiboTIE, a supervised deep learning method, and Ribo-TISH, an unsupervised translation initiation site detector. RiboTIE showed superior recovery of GENCODE-annotated ORFs, while Ribo-TISH recovered a larger but noisier candidate set. A high-confidence consensus set yielded 188 noncanonical ORFs mapping to transcript sequences labeled as intergenic in GENCODE, demonstrating that long-read transcriptomes substantially expand the discoverable ORF space beyond what short-read data or canonical annotations provide. Ongoing bottom-up mass spectrometry using the long-read-derived ORF catalog as a search database will provide an additional layer of proteomic confirmation. We apply our framework to study human iPSC-derived astrocytes, comparing resting and reactive states to characterize astrogliosis at the isoform and translational level. Our analyses reveal differential isoform usage between conditions, which we connect to the noncanonical ORF landscape identified above. We are further intersecting splicing quantitative trait loci from differentially translated isoforms with disease-associated SNPs to link isoform-level translational regulation to genetic risk for neurological disease. This work demonstrates that anchoring Ribo-seq ORF calling to full-length long-read isoform assemblies markedly improves sensitivity for noncanonical ORF detection. The framework is generalizable beyond astrocytes and opens new avenues for understanding how isoform diversity shapes the proteome in disease-relevant contexts.

title: seq2ribo: Structure-aware integration of machine learning and simulation to predict ribosome location profiles from RNA sequences
authors: Gün Kaynar, Carl Kingsford
abstract: Motivation: Ribosome dynamics are vital in the process of protein expression. Current methods rely on ribosome profiling (Ribo-seq), RNA-seq profiles, and full genomic context. This restricts their use in de novo sequence design, like messenger RNA (mRNA) vaccines. Simulation-only approaches like the Totally Asymmetric Simple Exclusion Process (TASEP) oversimplify translation by focusing solely on codon elongation times. Results: We present seq2ribo, a hybrid simulation and machine learning framework that predicts ribosome A-site locations using only an mRNA sequence as input. Our method first employs a novel structure-aware TASEP (sTASEP), which models translation using a comprehensive set of fitted parameters that include codon wait times and structural features, such as local angles, base-pairing, and discrete positional buckets. The ribosome locations generated by sTASEP are then processed by a polisher model, which learns to refine the simulated ribosome distributions. seq2ribo provides high-fidelity predictions of ribosome locations across diverse cell types (iPSC, HEK293, LCL, and RPE-1), significantly outperforming baselines. When benchmarked against Translatomer, seq2ribo achieves reductions in transcript-level error up to 36.4%, while simultaneously reducing codon-level mean absolute error (MAE) by up to 78.7% and bucket-level MAE by up to 72.6%. By adding a task-specific head, seq2ribo achieves Spearman correlations up to 0.795 with experimental translation efficiency (TE) across several cell lines, and 0.689 with measured protein expression. By operating from sequence alone, seq2ribo provides a new tool for synthetic biology, enabling the rational design and optimization of mRNA sequences without the need for expression-level data or genomic context. Availability: seq2ribo is available at https://github.com/ Kingsford-Group/seq2ribo. Contact: gkaynar@cs.cmu.edu, carlk@cs.cmu.edu.

title: An Integrative Approach to Predictive Modeling of Translation
authors: Can Cenik
abstract: The overarching vision of our research program is to construct predictive models that explain how cells determine their protein abundance. Achieving this goal involves two major components: (1) higher-resolution and higher-precision measurements of gene expression modalities, and (2) computational and theoretical advancements capable of integrating these quantitative measurements into cohesive, predictive frameworks. Towards these goals, we have compiled measurements of translation from more than 3,500 experiments and introduced the concept of translation efficiency covariation(TEC), revealing that transcripts associated with shared biological functions and those that are members of the same protein complexes exhibit TEC. We then leveraged our expansive compendium of translation efficiency measurements to develop a deep neural network model, called RiboNN, capable of predicting mRNA translation rates across numerous cell types based solely on the full-length mRNA sequence. R RiboNN can evaluate the impact of genetic variants in the human population, providing insight into diseases driven by abnormal mRNA translation. This approach has implications for bioengineering applications, genetic diagnostics as well as the design and optimization of mRNA therapies.

title: The Genome Taxonomy Database and identification of new stop codon reassignments
authors: Donovan Parks
abstract: The Genome Taxonomy Database (GTDB) provides a complete, phylogenetically consistent, and rank-normalized taxonomy for prokaryotic genomes. In this presentation, I will discuss the principles underlying this framework, provide an update on the current state of this resource (now in its 11th release), and highlight future developments, including initial work to incorporate Fungi. I will conclude the talk with findings from gTranslate, a tool for predicting prokaryotic genetic codes. Specifically, we identified two Actinomycetota genera within the family Eggerthellaceae with a UGA stop-to-tryptophan reassignment. We also report the first instances of UGA-to-tryptophan reassignment in the Patescibacteriota, establishing it as the first bacterial phylum with members capable of using translation tables 4, 11, and 25. This stop reassignment was previously known in only three other bacterial phyla: Bacillota, Pseudomonadota, and Verrucomicrobiota.

title: PhageMind: Generalized Strain-level Phage Host Range Prediction via Meta-learning
authors: Yang Shen, Chen Yu, Keming Shi, Rui Zhang, Yanni Sun, Jiayu Shang
abstract: Motivation: Bacteriophages (phages) are key regulators of bacterial populations and hold great promise for applications such as phage therapy, biocontrol, and industrial fermentation. The success of these applications depends on accurately determining phage host range, which is often specific at the strain level rather than the species level. However, existing computational approaches face major limitations: many rely on genus-specific features that do not generalize across taxa, while others require large amounts of training data that are unavailable for most bacterial lineages. These challenges create a critical need for methods that can accurately predict strain-level phage–host interactions across diverse bacterial genera, particularly under data-limited conditions. Results: We present PhageMind, a learning framework designed to address this challenge by enabling efficient transfer of knowledge across bacterial genera. PhageMind is trained to identify shared principles of phage–bacterium interactions from well-studied systems and to rapidly adapt these principles to new genera using only a small number of known interactions. To reflect the biological basis of infection, we represent phage–host relationships using a knowledge graph that explicitly incorporates phage tail fiber proteins and bacterial O-antigen biosynthesis gene clusters, and we use this representation to guide interaction prediction. Across four bacterial genera (Escherichia, Klebsiella, Vibrio, and Alteromonas), PhageMind achieves high prediction accuracy and shows strong adaptability to new lineages. In particular, in leave-one-genus-out evaluations, the model maintains robust performance when only limited reference data are available, demonstrating its potential as a scalable and practical tool for studying phage–host interactions across the global phageome.

title: Metagenomic Strain-Resolved DNA Modification Patterns Link Extrachromosomal Elements to Host Strains
authors: Daniel Portik, Rohan Sachdeva, Jillian Banfield, Spencer Diamond, Matthias Hess, Michael Morowitz, Susan Lynch, Jeremy Wilkinson, Siyuan Zhang, Shuai Wang, Holly Steininger, Marie Schoelmerich, Ling-Dong Shi, Ming Yan, Pengfan Zhang, Rebecca Garner, Luis Valentin-Alvarado, Allison Guitor
abstract: DNA modification is central to microbial defense against extrachromosomal elements (ECEs), consequently ECEs tend to adopt their host’s modification patterns. Shared ECE–host modification patterns enable linking ECEs to their hosts, but modification detection tools are designed for single genomes and are ineffective at metagenome scale. Here, we present MODIFI, software for detecting DNA modifications in metagenomes. MODIFI assumes that each k-mer in a metagenome is mostly unmodified and calculates background signal levels for that k-mer from PacBio HiFi reads, eliminating the need for matched control experiments. MODIFI ECE–host linkages were validated using >1,000 isolate and mock microbiome datasets. Illustrating the approach, we identified 315 strain-resolved, non-redundant ECE–host linkages in environmental and human metagenomes. In infant gut microbiomes, a chromosomal inversion in Enterococcus faecalis alters host and associated plasmid methylation motifs simultaneously. Overall, MODIFI solves a major bottleneck in DNA modification analysis and provides a foundational tool for understanding microbial epigenomics.

title: UniqSketch: sensitive and resource-efficient strain-level detection in metagenomes
authors: Bonnie Hurwitz, Hamid Mohamadi, Keith Turner, Rob Schmieder
abstract: Microbial communities contain diverse organisms, including multiple strains of the same species that coexist and display phenotypic differences influencing pathogenicity and host interactions. Detecting strains is challenging due to computational demands and low-abundance in metagenomes. We present UniqSketch, an open-source toolkit for identifying target strains across species within a single metagenome. It tracks specific microbial signatures or contaminants even in complex, multi-species samples. UniqSketch uses unique genomic fingerprints and a compact Bloom filter for efficient computation and accurate abundance estimation. Results demonstrate improved precision and accuracy over existing tools, performing reliably even at low coverage levels of 0.1x sequencing depth.

title: ICICLE: Transformer-Based Detection of Integrative and Conjugative Elements from Genomic and Metagenomic Sequences
authors: Sakshi Pandey, Noelle Noyes, Yun William Yu, Christina Boucher
abstract: Integrative and Conjugative elements(ICEs) are potent agents of bacterial evolution, combining stable chromosomal maintenance with autonomous conjugative transfer to disseminate antimicrobial resistance, virulence, and symbiosis genes across species. For instance, the SXT system in the bacteria Vibrio cholerae can transform susceptible strains into multi-drug resistant pathogens in a single transfer event. However, despite being one of the most abundant mobile genetic elements(MGEs) in nearly all prokaryotic clades, ICEs remain difficult to detect. Their modular, mosaic architecture lacks any single conserved backbone, and current tools relying on rigid heuristics often truncate large elements and miss divergent families. To address this we present ICICLE, a ~126M-parameter transformer-based classifier that learns compositional signatures of ICE directly from nucleotide sequences as short as 2000bp. Unlike existing methods, ICICLE does not require annotation, or a curated database, enabling ICE detection in metagenomic reads, draft genomes, and fragmented assemblies where current tools falter. Benchmarked against five state-of-the-art methods across 131 genomes (191 ICEs), ICICLE outperformed all competitors with 99% detection and 95% mean sequence coverage. This coverage marks an 8% improvement over the next-best tool, scaling to a 22% advantage for elements exceeding 100 kbp, highlighting ICICLE's superiority for large ICEs. Beyond standard benchmarks, ICICLE detected a novel, experimentally validated 61.6 kbp composite ICE unseen in its training data with 92% coverage. Leveraging its short sequence context, ICICLE also enables extraction of a dynamic "ICE burden" metric from metagenomic datasets, offering a proof of concept for real-time, culture-free surveillance of ICE prevalence across microbial communities.

title: Phylogenetic Placement Enables Near-Haplotype Resolution of Metagenomic Samples using metaWEPP
authors: Pranav Gangwar, Qiwen Xu, Jaden Seangmany, Pratik Katte, Yatish Turakhia
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing is transforming diverse areas of health and biological sciences, including pathogen surveillance, clinical diagnostics, and microbiome research. However, the inherent complexity of metagenomic data limits most existing computational tools to species-level classification and abundance estimation, overlooking within-species genetic diversity that drives key phenotypes. In this talk, we present metaWEPP, a novel computational pipeline that overcomes this limitation by achieving near-haplotype resolution in metagenomic analysis. Specifically, metaWEPP first assigns sequencing reads to species using standard taxonomic classifiers, and then leverages WEPP to phylogenetically place them onto species-specific mutation-annotated trees of publicly available sequences and select the subset of haplotypes that best explain the sample. It also reports unaccounted alleles indicative of novel variants and provides an interactive dashboard for detailed, read-level visualization. Applied to diverse metagenomic and mixed-genome samples from prior studies, metaWEPP produced concordant species-level results, while also revealing finer lineage-and haplotype-level insights beyond the capabilities of existing tools. For instance, across various clinical samples, in addition to identifying the pathogens infecting patients, metaWEPP provided credible lineage-and haplotype-level information that can support clinical decision-making by identifying mutations in haplotypes associated with key phenotypes. In wastewater samples, metaWEPP uncovered previously undetected, epidemiologically relevant haplotype clusters of human-infecting pathogens, as well as clusters associated with plant-infecting pathogens. These findings demonstrate metaWEPP's ability to advance various clinical, epidemiological, and research applications by providing deeper, actionable insights.
