title: Quantifying classification stability under reference database perturbation
authors: Elizabeth Hunter, Rob Patro
abstract: Metagenomic classification of mixed biological samples is commonly performed using marker-gene surveys, contig assembly and binning, or direct classification of individual reads against reference databases. The latter approach has become popular because it is rapid, scalable, and well suited to large shotgun sequencing datasets. However, its accuracy depends strongly on the composition of the reference database, raising concerns about the quality and stability of the resulting taxonomic assignments. In many cases, a label may reflect not only the biological signal in the read, but also the presence or absence of related genomes in the database. As databases expand, some assignments become more robust, whereas others become more ambiguous. To investigate this, we applied a bootstrap framework to three reference sets representing distinct biological contexts: Viridiplantae, the Kraken2 Standard database, and Enterobacteriaceae. For each set, we generated ten Kraken2 databases by sampling genomes with replacement and used kraken-inspect summaries to calculate the coefficient of variation for each taxon across the replicates. Taxa with high and low variability were selected for downstream analysis, and simulated Illumina reads were classified across the bootstrapped databases. Classification changes were quantified using a basic edge-walking metric and a custom ontology aware weighted entropy score that penalizes taxon changes according to phylogenetic distance and rank. Across all datasets, high variability taxa showed significantly greater classification instability than low variability taxa. These findings were used to inform confidence scores that account for database composition, and develop more robust, database aware methods for sequence classification.

title: Medival Can Detect Mobile Genetic Elements Without a Reference Database
authors: Grace Oualline, Sakshi Pandey, Christina Boucher, Yun William Yu
abstract: Motivation: Mobile genetic elements (MGEs) are DNA sequences that move within or between genomes, driving horizontal gene transfer and accelerating bacterial evolution. Detecting MGEs is crucial for understanding their evolution and managing antibiotic resistance. Existing tools rely on reference databases or trained models, imposing a fundamental ceiling on what they can find, as they are structurally unable to detect MGEs absent from their reference data. Results: We present Medival (https:// github.com/graceoualline/Medival), a method that identifies MGEs by comparing against databases of unannotated bacterial genomes. Our previous work, skandiver, identified large intercellular MGEs by detecting genomic regions with high sequence similarity to phylogenetically distant species. Medival extends this divergence-based approach to small and fragmented MGEs. Medival uses BLAT against the Genome Taxonomy Database to get short alignments, filtered by divergence or average nucleotide identity, providing strong statistical evidence for horizontal transfer. On a synthetic benchmark of 100 plasmid insertions, Medival detected 66 MGEs, recovering an average of 7.7% of each element while reporting 1.1% of the host genome as signal. By comparison, geNomad detected 10 MGEs with higher per-element recovery (84.1%) but flagged 5.02% of the host genome, and MobileElementFinder detected 24 MGEs with 20.5% average recovery and no host-genome signal. Reference-based tools thus achieve higher coverage of recognized elements, but miss the majority of MGEs entirely. Medival also recovered 55% of a plasmid from newly discovered species Photobacterium toruni, a species absent from existing reference databases and undetected by the existing tools.

title: VirBinn improves viral genome binning from metagenomic Hi-C through graph diffusion
authors: Shiyuan Wang, Yuxuan Du
abstract: Motivation: Metagenomic Hi-C provides in situ proximity signals that can improve genome binning and enable virus-host association analysis. However, viral genome recovery remains difficult because virus-virus Hi-C contact matrices are extremely sparse. Viral genomes are small, often low-abundance, and frequently assemble into short contigs, leaving many true within-genome links unobserved and causing viral bins to fragment. Results: We present VirBinn, a graph-diffusion framework for viral binning from metagenomic Hi-C. VirBinn enhances virus-virus connectivity through two complementary mechanisms: random-walk-with-restart enhancement on the sparse virus-virus contact graph and host-guided diffusion that propagates viral seeds through the host network to infer indirect virus-virus associations. The enhanced views are integrated and clustered using Leiden community detection to produce viral metagenome-assembled genomes (vMAGs). On dataset-specific simulation benchmarks with ground truth, VirBinn consistently recovers more high-quality vMAGs than Hi-C-based and shotgun-based baselines and substantially increases the number of near-complete genomes. On four real metagenomic Hi-C datasets spanning human gut, pig gut, sheep gut (long-read assembly), and wastewater, VirBinn yields more high-completeness vMAGs under CheckV and produces bins with strong within-cluster contact support. Finally, host linkage analysis using reconstructed host MAGs reveals habitat-specific host-association patterns and plausible host taxonomic profiles. Availability and Implementation: VirBinn is available at https://github.com/dyxstat/VirBinn. The scripts to reproduce the results and figures in this manuscript are available at https://github.com/dyxstat/Reproduce_VirBinn. Contact: yuxuan.du@utsa.edu

title: Comparative metagenomics using pan-metagenomic graphs
authors: Lily He, Tal Korem, Anne-Catrin Uhlemann, Itsik Pe'er, Aya Brown Kav, Yael R. Nobel, Heekuk Park, Dwayne Seeram, Amanda Simkhovich, Izaak Coleman, Ayushi Sharma, Aviya Litman, Yoli Meydan, Lisa Yu, Peiwen Cai, Andrey Zaznaev, Natalya Mametyarova
abstract: Identifying microbial genomic factors underlying human phenotypes is a key goal of microbiome research. Sequence graphs are a highly effective tool for genome comparisons because they enable high-resolution de novo analyses that capture and contextualize complex genomic variation. However, applying sequence graphs to complex microbial communities remains challenging due to the scale and complexity of metagenomic data. Existing multi-sample sequence graphs used in these settings are highly complex, computationally expensive, less accurate than single-sample alternatives, and often involve arbitrary coarse-graining. Here, we present copangraph, a multi-sample sequence-graph-based analysis framework designed for comprehensive comparisons of genomic variation across metagenomes. Copangraph uses a novel homology-based graph, which provides both non-arbitrary, evolutionary-motivated grouping of sequences into the same node and flexibility in the scale of variation represented by the graph. Its construction relies on hybrid coassembly, a new coassembly approach in which single-sample graphs are first constructed separately and are then merged to create a multi-sample graph, and an algorithm that uses paired-end reads to improve detection of contiguous genomic regions, increasing accuracy. Our results demonstrate that copangraph captures sequence and variant information more accurately than traditional graphs, provides graphs that are more suitable for comparative analysis than de Bruijn graphs, and is computationally tractable. We show that copangraph reflects meaningful metagenomic variation across diverse scenarios. Importantly, it enables significantly better performance than other metagenomic representations when predicting the gut colonization trajectories of Vancomycin-resistant Enterococcus. Our results underscore the value of our multi-sample, graph-based framework for comparative metagenomic analyses.

title: Modeling Scale Uncertainty Improves Microbiome Analysis
authors: Maxwell Konnaris, Manan Saxena, Gregory Gloor, Nicole Lazar, Justin Silverman
abstract: Microbiome sequencing measures relative abundances, leaving total microbial load (scale) un-observed and confounding inference about absolute abundances. Existing approaches either fix scale through normalization (e.g. TSS, DESeq2, and ANCOM-BC2) or predict it from taxonomic profiles using machine learning (ML), thereby treating scale as identifiable and risk distorting effect sizes, false discovery rates, and predictive performance. To benchmark these strategies, we assembled mutt, a curated database of 35 studies comprising more than 15,000 samples with paired sequencing data and direct microbial load measurements across diverse study settings. Using mutt, we compared normalization-based methods, ML-based load prediction, and Bayesian Partially Identified Models (PIMs) using a Scale-Reliant Inference perspective under realistic cross-study heterogeneity conditions. ML predictors failed to generalize: sample correlations were near zero and R2 was frequently negative. Normalization-based methods yielded median FDR above 75% and PPV below 25%. By contrast, Bayesian PIMs achieved near-zero median FDR, PPV ≈99%, and NPV ≈97%. Re-analysis of 19 autism case–control cohorts showed that previously reported autism microbiome associations are study-specific and more consistent with scale misspecification than reproducible biology. Microbial load is not recoverable from sequencing data alone, and strategies that assume otherwise systematically inflate false discoveries. Bayesian PIMs, which model scale uncertainty rather than imputing a point estimate, substantially improve false-discovery control without loss of power and materially alter biological conclusions in a prominent multi-cohort application. These results argue that microbiome studies should treat scale as a source of uncertainty to be modeled explicitly, not a nuisance to be normalized or imputed away.

title: Inferring gut butyrate resilience from sparse longitudinal metabolomics via effective landscapes
authors: Javad Aminian Dehkordi, Mohammad Mofrad
abstract: Human stool metabolomics is typically sparse and noisy. This limits what dynamical structure can be reliably inferred about gut metabolic regulation. We use a metabolite-only approach to quantify butyrate resilience from longitudinal measurements using an effective landscape view of stochastic dynamics. Using toy stochastic systems, we show that true multistability can appear monostable under sampling densities comparable to human studies. The outcome motivates a shift away from discrete state classification toward statistically identifiable continuous stability metrics. We apply the approach to longitudinal stool metabolomics and find no robust evidence for alternative stable states at the observational timescale. Instead, butyrate dynamics are consistent with smooth return toward subject-specific equilibria, with inter-individual heterogeneity in recovery strength. We further screen auxiliary metabolites as modulators of butyrate return dynamics and identify bile acids and fermentation intermediates with strong associations. Together, these results provide a practical route to quantify metabolic resilience under realistic sampling constraints.

title: LaBay: Scalable Bayesian Modeling of Longitudinal Microbiome Dynamics After Sleeve Gastrectomy
authors: Ali Reza Taheriyoun, Ali Rahnavard
abstract: Longitudinal microbiome studies generate sparse, compositional, and zero-inflated relative abundance measurements that challenge conventional generalized linear mixed models (GLMMs) based on negative binomial or Gaussian assumptions. These limitations reduce power for detecting treatment-associated microbial dynamics in high-dimensional settings. We introduce LaBay, a Bayesian regularization framework for Tweedie GLMMs that enables scalable inference for longitudinal omics data by combining compound-Poisson modeling with Laplace priors for coefficient shrinkage and efficient MCMC posterior sampling. We applied LaBay to a longitudinal 16S microbiome cohort of adolescents with severe obesity followed for 24 months after sleeve gastrectomy (SG) alongside non-surgical controls. Samples collected at baseline and multiple post-surgical visits were profiled as amplicon sequence variant relative abundances and analyzed jointly with clinical and metabolomic metadata. Compared with standard mixed-effects approaches, LaBay improved sparsity recovery and stability of feature selection while accommodating zero inflation and heterogeneous sequencing depth. The model identified time-dependent shifts in several genera, including Streptococcus, Haemophilus, and Lachnospiraceae groups, and detected surgery-associated trajectories consistent with metabolic remodeling after SG. Associations between microbial features and bile acid exposure and glucose-related markers further highlighted links between microbiome dynamics and host metabolic adaptation. These results demonstrate that Bayesian regularized Tweedie GLMMs provide a principled framework for modeling longitudinal compositional microbiome data and enable interpretable discovery of treatment-associated microbial signatures. LaBay extends existing differential-abundance strategies by integrating mixed-effects structure with high-dimensional shrinkage, supporting robust biomarker discovery in complex multi-timepoint microbiome studies.

title: Creation and validation of LIMON -Longitudinal Individual Microbial Omics Networks
authors: Suzanne Alvernaz, Niket Pathak, Beatriz Penalver Bernabe
abstract: Microbial communities are dynamic structures that continually adapt to their surroundings and play pivotal roles in countless ecosystems, from environmental to human health. Multiple diseases dynamically perturb crosstalk among microorganisms in the community; thus, it is essential to build robust methods for detecting longitudinal changes in microbial interactions. Existing methods have mostly focused on changes in individual taxa rather than on relationships between taxa. Identifying these interactions over time provides a deeper understanding of how the microbial ecosystem changes as a whole. To fill this gap, we have developed a pipeline that addresses the complex nature of repeated compositional count data: LIMON – Longitudinal Individual Microbial Omics Networks. This novel computational approach addresses key challenges in modeling temporal and microbial data, including overdispersion, zero-inflated count data, compositional data, repeated-measures designs, time-varying sample covariates, and the identification of individualized or sample-specific networks. LIMON allows users to denoise covariate effects from their data, identify changes in interactions across time points, and return individual networks and network characteristics per sample and time point. In doing so, LIMON provides a platform for identifying the relationship between microbial community interactions and the sample features of interest over time (e.g., disease severity). In simulated datasets, we showed that LIMON could accurately remove covariate effects, reconstruct sample-specific networks, and recover underlying network edges from covariate-confounded data. Analysis of the effect of diet type on infant microbiome evolution illustrates LIMON’s novel utility for identifying key microbial interactions associated with diet type.

title: Semi-supervised Genome Annotation Using a Mixture-of-Experts Genome Foundation Model
authors: Junho Hong, Rob Egan, Fengchen Liu, Lizhen Shi, Zhong Wang
abstract: Functional annotation of microbial genomes relies on homology to reference databases and generalizes poorly to non-cultured clades that dominate environmental communities. Genomic foundation models could recover this structure directly from sequence, but dense transformers expose no per-token handle on what they encode. We drop-upcycle GenomeOcean-100M into an 8-expert, top-2 Mixtral MoE (714M total, 205M active parameters) and continue training on 52B additional metagenomic tokens. We then analyze per-token expert routing on five reference bacterial genomes with various GC percentages. Without any annotation supervision, individual experts emerge as sharp functional class detectors. Compared to per-bp GFF labels from known annotations, one layer-7 expert is over-selected on tRNA by 13-fold, and a separate layer-6 expert is simultaneously over-selected on rRNA, tRNA, ncRNA, and intergenic tokens — a coherent non-CDS detector. These preliminary results suggest that MoE routing is a potential candidate for semi-supervised functional annotation of novel genomes, independent of BLAST/ Rfam/tRNAscan, and applicable to any contig without reference-database biases. We are currently investigating potential applications of MoE to classify protein families and other types of functional elements.

title: Limousia bacteria encode mucinolysome for mucin utilization in animal gut microbiomes
authors: Jerry Akresi, Siva Shanmugam Nallattinputhur Radhakrishnan, Yanbin Yin, Thi Van Thanh Do, Jennifer M Auchtung
abstract: Mucins create a physical barrier that protects human and animal tissues from microbial pathogens. Here, we provide evidence that mucin degradation can be mediated by unique mucinolysomes, defined as extracellular cellulosome-like multi-enzyme complexes specializing in mucin degradation. We predicted the presence of mucinolysomes across 63 metagenome-assembled genomes (MAGs) and two isolated genomes of three anaerobic species of Limousia, including seven MAGs from human gut microbiome samples from six countries. We validated that mucins can support the growth of the Limousia strain ET540 as its sole carbon source, triggering the upregulation of most mucinolysome-related genes in ET540. We modeled the mucinolysome assembly by predicting cohesin"’dockerin interactions among most of the mucinolysome proteins using AlphaFold3. We performed metagenomic read mapping of 2897 fecal samples from various human cohorts and wild/domesticated animals against Limousia MAGs. We found that Limousia has a greater abundance and prevalence in farm animals than in humans. This study characterizes and adds the Limousia bacteria as unique member to the list of human and animal gut mucin glycan-degrading bacteria. Overall, we discovered that this novel gut bacteria genus (Limousia) uses a previously unrecognized molecular mechanism for highly organized mucin glycan degradation, shedding new light on microbe"’host interactions in the gastrointestinal tracts of diverse animal hosts, including humans. This work was recently published in the journal Gut Microbes: https:// pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12997984/

title: dbcan-nf: a scalable Nextflow pipeline for CAZyme annotation in metagenomes
authors: Xinpeng Zhang, Haidong Yi, Jinfang Zheng, Yanbin Yin
abstract: Metagenomic sequencing has greatly expanded our understanding of complex microbiomes, particularly in the human gut, where carbohydrate-active enzymes (CAZymes) drive carbohydrate metabolism and host-microbe interactions. However, accurate and reproducible profiling of CAZyme abundance from whole-genome shotgun (WGS) data remains challenging due to fragmented analytical workflows and inconsistent tool configurations. Here we present dbcan-nf, a scalable and reproducible Nextflow pipeline built within the nf-core framework for automated CAZyme annotation from metagenomes. The pipeline integrates commonly used metagenomic processing steps, including read quality control, assembly (MEGAHIT/Flye), gene prediction (pyrodigal), CAZyme annotation (run_dbcan), and read mapping-based CAZyme abundance quantification. dbcan-nf supports multiple analytical modes, including individual sample assembly, co-assembly, and assembly-free analysis, and processes both short reads and long reads. We evaluated dbcan-nf using simulated reads of synthetic mock community as well as reads from an ultra-deep sequencing dataset from Hadza hunter-gatherer microbiome samples. Benchmark analyses revealed that assembly-based modes provided higher CAZyme annotation accuracy, while the assembly-free mode significantly overestimated CAZyme abundance despite lower computational cost. dbcan-nf produces interpretable and publication-ready outputs, including CAZyme abundance table/plot, substrate-level summary table/plot, and read mapping plots for CAZyme gene clusters (CGCs). dbcan-nf provides a standardized and scalable solution for functional characterization of microbiome carbohydrate metabolism and facilitates reproducible analysis of CAZyme repertoires across large metagenomic cohorts. The source code is freely available at: https://github.com/bcb-unl/dbcan-nf.

title: RAmpSim: A Thermodynamic Simulator for Hybridization Capture in Metagenomic Sequencing
authors: Aidan Zhang, Christina Boucher, Noelle Noyes, Yun William Yu
abstract: Motivation: Simulators that generate synthetic datasets help address the lack of ground truth for developing and benchmarking computational tools. Many read simulators assume uniform sampling across reference genomes; however, for newer capture-based sequencing technologies (e.g. TELSeq), this assumption is intentionally broken to oversample regions of interest. Along with systematic biases arising from probe multiplicity, sequence composition, and species abundances inherent to capture-based sequencing, this mismatch between modeling assumptions and the characteristics of real data necessitates the design of a new capture-based sequencing-specific simulator. Results: We present RAmpSim, a fast simulator that models bait–target hybridization and fragment capture using a thermodynamic nearest-neighbor energy model and Boltzmann-weighted sampling of binding sites. Fragments are generated through multinomial sampling parameterized by bait concentration, binding energy, and genomic abundance before being passed to existing models of platform-specific errors. Implemented in Rust, RAmpSim reproduces empirical within-genome coverage and cross-species enrichment patterns observed in capture-based metagenomic datasets. Compared to uniform-coverage baselines, RAmpSim’s simulated coverage distributions are up to an order of magnitude closer to real data with respect to earth mover’s distance. Classification analysis reveals high recall in classifying high coverage regions between simulated and experimental distributions while outperforming a uniform baseline. Availability: Code and example scripts are available at https://github.com/az002/RAmpSim.git. Contact: ywyu@cmu.edu Supplementary information: Supplementary appendices include additional figures.

title: The Kenyan Human Gut Virus Catalogue Reveals Extensive Virome Diversity
authors: Simeon Nthuku, James Mordecai, Abiola Babajide, David Makoko, Yacouba Sawadogo, Olaitan Awe
abstract: The human gut virome is a critical yet poorly characterized component of the microbiome that shapes microbial community structure and host–microbe interactions. To date, most virome studies have focused on high-income populations, leaving African low-and middle-income regions markedly understudied despite their distinct diets, lifestyles, and environmental exposures. To address this gap, we present the Kenyan Human Gut Virome Catalogue (KHGVC), the first comprehensive catalogue of the human gut virome from Kenya using metagenomic data from diverse populations. Metagenomic sequencing data were retrieved from four publicly available Kenyan microbiome studies and analyzed using a standardized viromics pipeline. From these datasets, we identified 116,968 viral clusters, of which 92% could not be classified at the viral family level, underscoring the vast uncharacterized viral diversity in this population. Among annotated viral operational taxonomic units (vOTUs), members of the families Anelloviridae, Microviridae, and Peduoviridae were most abundant. Temperate bacteriophages dominated the virome, accounting for approximately 70% of vOTUs. Functional annotation revealed that only ~27% of predicted viral proteins could be assigned known functions, highlighting extensive viral genetic “dark matter." Overall, this study reveals substantial previously undescribed viral diversity within the Kenyan gut virome and establishes the KHGVC as a foundational resource. These findings advance our understanding of African human gut viral ecology and provide a critical framework for future microbiome research and virome-based therapeutic strategies relevant to populations of African descent. The Kenyan Human Gut Virus Catalogue is freely and publicly available as a user-friendly graphical user interface (https://igmr.org/software/kenyavirocat).

title: WWBio: Control-Calibrated Multi-Evidence Inference for Robust Marker Detection in Long-Read Wastewater Metagenomics
authors: Ayesha Wasim, Susana Ladra, Margarita Poza, Todd Treangen
abstract: Wastewater metagenomics enables population-level monitoring of disease-associated microbial signatures, but detecting predefined markers in long-read sequencing data remains challenging under low-depth and heterogeneous conditions. Sparse and fragmented signals cause nucleotide-only approaches to miss true markers or produce spurious alignments. We present WWBio, a control-calibrated multi-evidence inference framework that integrates nucleotide and protein signals while explicitly modeling background noise using matched shuffled controls. WWBio combines read support, coverage breadth, and translated protein homology into a unified confidence score, enabling robust and interpretable marker detection under realistic sequencing constraints. We evaluated WWBio on Oxford Nanopore wastewater metagenomic datasets at two sequencing depths (2 Gb and 5 Gb) against a nucleotide-only baseline (â‰ ¥2 reads and ≥10% coverage thresholds). At higher depth, both approaches detected established markers (bft, clbB, clbN), while WWBio additionally identified radD supported by protein evidence. At reduced depth, the baseline detected only bft, whereas WWBio recovered multiple markers (clbB, clbN, fap2, radD) by integrating complementary evidence sources. Shuffled-marker controls yielded no detections for either method, confirming that improved sensitivity does not arise from spurious alignments. These results demonstrate that explicit background calibration combined with multi-evidence integration substantially improves sensitivity and reduces false positives of marker detection in low-depth long-read metagenomic data, providing a scalable and interpretable framework for biomarker detection in complex environmental sequencing settings.

title: The gut microbiome and mycobiome landscape of treatment-naïve lymphoma
authors: Andrey Zaznaev, Ruben Mars, Purna Kashyap, Tal Korem, Tom Witzig
abstract: Lymphomas are a group of immune cancers accounting for 88,000 new cases in the United States in 2026. Since the gut microbiome is tightly connected with the host immune system, its composition may play a role in the efficacy of chemoimmunotherapy, a common lymphoma treatment strategy, and modulate patient prognosis. In addition, intestinal microbiota experiences compositional shifts in lymphoma patients due to treatment effects, dietary changes, gastrointestinal involvement, and antimicrobial exposure. Therefore, characterizing gut microbiome in treatment-naÃ¯ve lymphoma patients could assist in evaluating clinical outcomes and informing therapeutic strategies. To investigate the connection between gut microbiome and patient outcomes in lymphoma patients, stool samples from 462 treatment-naÃ¯ve lymphoma patients and 278 healthy controls were collected to perform shotgun metagenomics, quantitative metabolomics, and amplicon fungal sequencing. Gut microbial, fungal, and metabolite profiles were compared between lymphoma patients and healthy controls and survival models were used to characterize the association between microbiome features and overall and event-free survival across lymphoma subtypes. It was found that lymphoma patients had a distinct microbiome composition and decreased prevalence of purine-and pyrimidine-derived metabolites compared to healthy controls. Certain microbial and fungal taxa were associated with lymphoma prognosis. Anaerobutyricum hallii had the strongest positive association with overall and event-free survival, while fungal species Malassezia restricta correlated with poorer clinical outcomes. This study comprises the largest cohort of pretreatment lymphoma where gut microbiome, mycobiome, and metabolome were characterized. The results of this study lay the groundwork for future microbiome-targeted interventions for improving clinical outcomes in lymphoma patients.

title: End-to-end evaluation of pipelines for metagenome-assembled genomes reveals hidden performance gaps
authors: Izaak Coleman, Jiong Ma, Gordon Qian, Yusheng Jiang, Aya Brown-Kav, Tal Korem
abstract: The generation of Metagenome-assembled Genomes (MAGs) has become a staple of metagenomic data analysis. This multi-step process, which includes assembly, binning, refinement, and quality control, has many alternative algorithms and parameters. Determining the ideal approach for a given ecosystem and study, or highlighting algorithmic gaps in need of additional development, requires rigorous benchmarking. We present MAG-E (MAG pipeline Evaluator), a generalizable and expandable framework for end-to-end evaluation of MAG pipelines, which relies on simulations that are built to match an ecosystem of interest and provide a ground truth for accurate evaluation. To demonstrate its capabilities, we benchmark two assemblers, six binning algorithms, three binning modes, and three quality control and refinement methods in the context of the human gut microbiome. Our findings offer multiple insights into optimal MAG generation: We find that metaSPAdes consistently outperforms MEGAHIT in terms of recall (completeness), and that COMEBin overall outperforms alternative binning algorithms, but has lower precision than SemiBin2. While multi-sample binning results in higher precision, as previously shown, single-sample binning has higher recall and leads to better overall performance with modern binners. Binning refinement, which combines bins from multiple different algorithms, leads to reduced performance. We further show that CheckM2 systematically overestimates completeness and underestimates contamination, and that this is partially ameliorated when using GUNC. Finally, we demonstrate that binning algorithms systematically underperform for prophages and fail to bin contigs that are shared between genomes. Overall, MAG-E (https://github.com/korem-lab/MAG-E) offers deep insights into successes and gaps in this important analytic process.

title: RECAST: A Reproducible Workflow for Updating Taxonomic and Functional Classifications for Metagenome Analysis
authors: Julia U. B. Fischer, Anupam Gautam, Daniel H. Huson
abstract: Accurate taxonomic and functional interpretation of metagenomic sequencing data requires current and well-maintained reference classifications such as NCBI or GTDB for taxonomic binning and SEED, eggNOG or gene ontology (GO) for functional annotation. The widely used metagenomic tool MEGAN performs both tasks using integrated hierarchical representations of these classifications and mappings from protein accessions to classification-specific identifiers. However, maintaining these resources is challenging: the underlying databases evolve rapidly, and updating MEGAN’s internal representations requires substantial manual effort, often leading to outdated annotations. This highlights the need for reproducible workflows that enable regular updates while producing outputs reusable beyond a single software environment. Here, we present RECAST (REproducible Classification Assembly and Standardisation Toolkit), an automated Nextflow pipeline combined with standard operating procedures (SOPs) for updating and integrating multiple classifications used in MEGAN. The workflow includes the NCBI and GTDB taxonomies and the functional classification systems SEED, eggNOG and GO. For each resource, source data are retrieved from their respective reference database and processed to generate standardised outputs, including hierarchical trees in Newick format, corresponding mappings between node names and internal identifiers, and protein accession mappings to internal classification identifiers. RECAST improves the maintainability of the reference classifications provided in MEGAN, supports more accurate binning and enables reproducible metagenome analyses, while also delivering a reusable, standardised classification resource that can be integrated into other tools and pipelines to promote consistent and sustainable reference data management.

title: Multi-sample binning increases MAG recovery from Empty Quarter desert soils with minimal benefit from geographic sample grouping
authors: Alejandra Lopez-Velazquez, Robert Hoehndorf
abstract: Multi-sample metagenomic binning exploits co-abundance patterns to improve genome recovery, but two practical questions remain: the optimal configuration for low-biomass environments with fragmented assemblies, and whether geographically informed sample partitioning improves recovery when scaling to large cohorts. We benchmarked five SemiBin2 configurations on 20 hyperarid desert metagenomes (median N50: 1,796 bp) from Saudi Arabia's Empty Quarter, selected from an ongoing collection of over 500 metagenomes, then compared geographic versus random grouping across 130 metagenomes. Multi-sample binning yielded 31% more high-quality bins than the best single-sample mode (465 vs 355 HQ), but was not strictly dominant: cross-mode dereplication at 95% ANI revealed that multi-sample uniquely recovered 293 MAGs (22.9%) while single-sample uniquely recovered 120 MAGs (9.4%), suggesting a union strategy may maximize recovery. A union of both methods yielded 1,280 dereplicated MAGs, of which 96.6% lacked GTDB species assignments. Geographic grouping showed no advantage over random assignment (TOST equivalence p < 0.05; 80% of MAGs shared), indicating that the assumption of stronger co-abundance signal among geographically similar samples is not supported. Researchers can therefore partition samples arbitrarily, by sequencing batch or submission date, simplifying pipeline design without sacrificing recovery.

title: A Novel Transformer Model of Protein Domains for Viral Taxonomy Classification
authors: Jihye Shin, Qingyang Xiao, Yuzhen Ye
abstract: Motivation: Viruses with carefully curated taxonomic assignments (such as those in the ICTV taxonomy) still represent only a small fraction of viruses identified through sequencing data from virome or microbiome projects. It is therefore critical to develop methods that can assign viruses at multiple taxonomic ranks, so that a virus deemed novel at a given rank may still be placed into a higher-level taxon. Sequence-similarity–based approaches can classify viruses that share substantial genomic similarity with known viruses (e.g., those belonging to the same species or genus); however, their performance drops significantly when applied to more divergent viruses. Recent deep learning models, such as ViTax, which utilize DNA language models, aim to address these limitations, but their performance also degrades when applied to novel viruses lacking genus-level similarity to known references. Proteins are more conserved than genomic sequences, and the multiple proteins encoded by a virus can be leveraged to reveal evolutionary relationships among viruses. Results: We propose a new tool, D2T (Domain-to-Taxonomy), that leverages recent advances in protein language models to improve viral taxonomic assignment. D2T represents a virus as a sequence of protein domain tokens and learns a transformer-based model for taxonomic classification. Experiments on multiple closed-set and open-set datasets show that D2T excels at assigning higher-level taxonomic labels (family and above). Furthermore, by combining D2T with Kraken2, which performs well at the genus level, the hybrid method (K+D2T) achieves accurate viral taxonomic classification across multiple taxonomic ranks. title: MetaKSSD: boosting the scalability of the reference taxonomic marker database and the performance of metagenomic profiling using sketch operations
authors: Huiguang Yi
abstract: The performance of metagenomic profiling is constrained by the diversity of taxa present in the reference taxonomic marker database (MarkerDB) used. However, continually updating MarkerDB to include newly determined taxa using existing approaches faces increasing difficulties and will soon become impractical. Here we introduce MetaKSSD, which redefines MarkerDB construction and metagenomic profiling using sketch operations, enhancing MarkerDB scalability and profiling performance. MetaKSSD encompasses 85,202 species in its MarkerDB using just 0.17 GB of storage and profiles 10 GB of data within seconds. Leveraging its comprehensive MarkerDB, MetaKSSD substantially improves profiling results. In a microbiome-phenotype association study, MetaKSSD identified more effective associations than MetaPhlAn4. We profiled 382,016 metagenomic runs using MetaKSSD, conducted extensive sample clustering analyses and suggested potential yet-to-be-discovered niches. MetaKSSD offers functionality for instantaneous searching of similar profiles. It enables the swift transmission of metagenome sketches over the network and real-time online metagenomic analysis, facilitating use by non-expert users.

title: Perseus: Lineage-Aware Refinement of Kraken2 Taxonomic Classification for Long Read Metagenomes
authors: Matthew Nguyen, Michael Schatz
abstract: Motivation: Long-read sequencing has enabled more contiguous assemblies and improved resolution of complex microbial communities. Despite these benefits, assigning accurate taxonomic labels to long reads and contigs remains a persistent challenge. Widely used k-mer-based methods such as Kraken2 offer exceptional speed and scalability, but often produce overly specific classifications on long-read data. In particular, small regions of ambiguous or shared sequences can disproportionately affect assignments, leading to elevated false positive rates. This issue is particularly worsened in environments with substantial taxonomic novelty. Results: We present Perseus, a lineage-aware confidence estimation framework for taxonomic classification that models the spatial distribution and hierarchical consistency of k-mer evidence along sequences. Instead of treating classification as a single-label prediction problem, Perseus formulates it as hierarchical confidence estimation across taxonomic ranks. The method refines k-mer-level taxonomic signals from Kraken2 using a multi-headed convolutional neural network that estimates calibrated confidence scores for taxonomic correctness at each canonical rank. Using these estimates, Perseus retains reliable assignments, backs off to higher taxonomic ranks, or abstains when evidence is insufficient, prioritizing correctness and lineage consistency over overly specific assignments. Across taxonomic novelty simulations and real-world metagenomic datasets, Perseus consistently and substantially reduces the false assignment rate while improving precision and lineage-consistent accuracy. These improvements are most pronounced for long reads and assembled contigs, where spatial context enables reliable discrimination between consistent taxonomic signal and spurious matches. Availability and implementation: Perseus is designed to integrate seamlessly with existing Kraken2 workflows and is available at https://github.com/matnguyen/perseus.

title: Improving Metagenomics Classification with Kmask: Entropy-Based Masking of Low-Complexity Regions
authors: Peter Ge, Edward Li, Harun Mustafa, Ales Varabyou, Steven Salzberg
abstract: Accurate taxonomic classification in metagenomics is often compromised by low-complexity sequences, which lead to chance k-mer matches that in turn cause read misclassifications. We present Kmask, an entropy-based masking tool implemented for use as part of Kraken (1,2) database construction, which selectively replaces low-entropy regions with Ns. Using a sliding window size aligned with Kraken’s default k-mer length, an entropy unit size, and a threshold optimized across 12 control bacterial genomes spanning a broad range of GC content, Kmask efficiently removes low-complexity sequences while retaining high-complexity regions. To benchmark performance, we applied Kmask to Microbial2025, a database that contains over 71,000 RefSeq bacterial, archaeal, viral, and fungal genomes, and we then classified CHM13 human reads against it using KrakenUniq (2). Compared to the unmasked database, Kmask substantially reduced misclassifications without sacrificing sensitivity, driving down the false positive rate from 6.31% to 4.37%. Notably, Kmask outperformed the DUST-masked (3) database by achieving a near identical false positive rate (4.29% vs. 4.37%) while masking out fewer bases (1.56% vs. 2.07%), thereby preserving nearly 33% more discriminative sequences for classification. These results demonstrate that Kmask is a simple yet effective method for masking low-complexity sequences in large microbial databases, thus improving the accuracy of metagenomic classification. title: Integrating cross-platform metagenomics studies - high taxonomic concordance and functional analysis challenges
authors: Kinga Zielińska, Kateryna Pantiukh, Paweł P. Łabaj, Tomasz Kościółek, Elin Org
abstract: As microbiome research shifts from taxonomic descriptions toward a metabolism-centric understanding of dysbiosis, the integration of diverse, large-scale datasets becomes essential. Recent developments, such as our function-based index q2-predict-dysbiosis (Q2PD), have demonstrated that analyzing the microbiome’s functional potential offers superior disease prediction and robustness to sequencing depth compared to traditional taxonomy-reliant methods [1]. However, the effective integration of multi-cohort data is often hindered by variations in sequencing technologies and experimental protocols. To evaluate the impact of sequencing platforms on data comparability, we conducted a comprehensive large-scale analysis of 1,351 matched human gut microbiome sample pairs [2]. Each sample was sequenced using both the MGISEQ-2000 (MGI) and NovaSeq 6000 (Illumina) platforms. We performed a comparative assessment of taxonomic and functional profiles to identify platform-specific biases and determine the feasibility of cross-platform data integration for functional studies. Taxonomic profiles exhibited high concordance between the two platforms, with over 97% of species shared between MGI and Illumina pairs. The proportion of platform-specific species was remarkably low (< 6%), and no significant differences were observed in alpha-diversity metrics. In contrast, functional profiles revealed significant discrepancies and appeared to be severely impacted by differences in sequencing protocols. Our analysis indicates that these functional shifts are not inherent to the sequencing chemistry but are primarily driven by pre-sequencing protocols and the degree of sample multiplexing. Our results demonstrate that while MGI and Illumina platforms are highly comparable for taxonomic profiling, functional potential is more sensitive to technical variation. These findings are crucial for the field; they suggest that while a shift toward functional indices like Q2PD is necessary for clinical accuracy, these methods require stringent standardization of experimental design. We recommend prioritizing sequencing depth and limiting multiplexing to ensure the breadth of coverage necessary for reliable functional annotations. Such considerations are vital for the successful integration of diverse datasets in the context of large-scale functional microbiome analyses. title: A modular framework to evaluate statistical methods for microbiome differential analysis
authors: Shri Vishalini Rajaram, Priyanka Singh, Erliang Zeng
abstract: Selecting appropriate normalization and differential abundance (DA) methods has a substantial impact on microbiome analysis outcomes. However, many studies still rely on fixed, convenience-driven method combinations without accounting for differences in study design or fundamental data characteristics such as sparsity, compositionality, and overdispersion. The lack of systematic, data-driven guidance has contributed to inconsistent biological interpretations and limited reproducibility across microbiome research. To address this gap, we developed an R package, Microbiome Normalization and Differential Analysis – Statistical Evaluation and Testing (MiNDSET). MiNDSET implements a registry-based architecture that integrates 20 normalization approaches and 35 DA methods, including those with implicit built-in normalization assumptions, and supports binary, multiclass, longitudinal, and zero-inflated study designs. The framework introduces a multi-criteria scoring system, paired with visualizations, to benchmark method combinations based on statistical performance, reproducibility under bootstrap resampling, biological consistency, and computational efficiency. MiNDSET further quantifies feature-level stability across resampled datasets and ranks normalization-DA pairs by agreement in detected features. We applied MiNDSET to publicly available microbiome datasets and simulated data to assess the consistency of detected features across methods and resampling schemes. Performance is strongly data-dependent, and no single method is optimal across all settings. Score-based benchmarking demonstrated pronounced variability across methodological choices, often surpassing variation attributable to biological condition alone. Overall, MiNDSET-selected strategies yield more stable effect estimates, improved reproducibility, and more biologically interpretable results, whereas non-adaptive approaches showed inflated false discoveries or unstable feature rankings. By enabling transparent, scalable benchmarking, MiNDSET provides a reproducible, data-driven framework for selecting normalization-DA methods for microbiome studies.

authors: Ilana Brito, Ian Lee, Daniel Lamm

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Benchmarking AI scientists for omics data-driven biological discovery
authors: Erpai Luo, Jinmeng Jia, Yifan Xiong, Xiangyu Li, Xiaobo Guo, Baoqi Yu, Minsheng Hao, Lei Wei, Xuegong Zhang
abstract: Motivation: Recent advances in large language models have enabled the emergence of AI scientists that aim to autonomously analyze biological data and assist scientific discovery. Despite rapid progress, it remains unclear to what extent these systems can extract meaningful biological insights from real experimental data. Existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning in the absence of data or focus on predefined analytical outputs, failing to reflect realistic, data-driven biological research. Results: Here, we introduce BAISBench (Biological AI Scientist Benchmark), a benchmark for evaluating AI scientists on real single-cell transcriptomic datasets. BAISBench comprises two tasks: cell type annotation across 15 expert-labeled datasets, and scientific discovery through 193 multiple-choice questions derived from biological conclusions reported in 41 published single-cell studies. We evaluated several representative AI scientists using BAISBench and, to provide a human performance baseline, invited six graduate-level bioinformaticians to collectively complete the same tasks. The results show that while current AI scientists fall short of fully autonomous biological discovery, they already demonstrate substantial potential in supporting data-driven biological research. These results position BAISBench as a practical benchmark for characterizing the current capabilities and limitations of AI scientists in biological research. We expect BAISBench to serve as a practical evaluation framework for guiding the development of more capable AI scientists and for helping biologists identify AI systems that can effectively support real-world research workflows. track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Agentomics: An Agentic System that Autonomously Develops Novel State-of-the-art Solutions for Biomedical Machine Learning Tasks
authors: Vlastimil Martinek, Andrea Gariboldi, Dimosthenis Tzimotoudis, Mark Galea, Elissavet Zacharopoulou, Aitor Alberdi Escudero, Edward Blake, David Čechák, Luke Cassar, Alessandro Balestrucci, Panagiotis Alexiou
abstract: Motivation: Extracting knowledge from biomedical data is crucial for advancing our understanding of biological systems and developing novel therapeutics. The quantity, quality, and resolution of biomedical data constantly evolves, requiring the automation of biomedical machine learning (ML). Existing Automated ML tools lack flexibility, while Large Language Models (LLMs) struggle to consistently deliver reproducible machine learning codebases, and existing LLM Agent-powered solutions lag behind human-engineered ML models. Results: Here, we introduce Agentomics, an autonomous LLM-powered agentic system for end-to-end ML experimentation. Given a biomedical dataset, Agentomics implements various ML modeling strategies, and produces a ready-to-use ML model. Agentomics introduces strict validation checkpoints for standard ML development steps, allowing gradual development on top of working code with defined interfaces and validated artifacts. Further, it offers native support for biomedical foundation models that can be leveraged during experimentation. The generic nature of Agentomics allows the user to create ML solutions for a large variety of datasets and use various LLMs. We evaluate Agentomics across 20 datasets from the domains of Protein Engineering, Drug Discovery, and Regulatory Genomics. When benchmarked against other agentic systems, Agentomics outperformed them in all tested domains. When benchmarked against human expert solutions, Agentomics generated novel state-of-the-art models for 11/20 established benchmark datasets. track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Data-driven AI system for learning how to run transcript assemblers
authors: Yihang Shen, Zhiwen Yan, Carl Kingsford
abstract: Biological research increasingly depends on complex software tools, many of which include tunable parameters that can strongly influence performance. The optimal parameter settings often vary across input datasets, yet systems that can automatically select input-specific parameters are still lacking. We introduce AutoTuneX, the first data-driven AI system designed to automatically predict optimal parameters for transcript assemblers, which reconstruct transcripts from RNA-seq reads in a given sample. By combining Bayesian optimization with contrastive learning, AutoTuneX learns a latent representation of RNA-seq samples in which samples with similar optimal parameter settings are placed close together. Once trained, AutoTuneX predicts parameters for a new RNA-seq sample by identifying representative nearby samples in the latent space and transferring their best-performing parameter settings. Across 1,588 human RNA-seq samples evaluated with two transcript assemblers, Scallop and StringTie, AutoTuneX predicted parameters that led to more accurate transcript assembly than default settings for 98% of samples, with some samples showing up to a 600% improvement in AUC. AutoTuneX offers a new strategy for improving the performance of sequence analysis tools, particularly transcript assemblers, by optimizing the use of existing methods rather than developing entirely new ones. More broadly, the framework underlying AutoTuneX can be naturally extended to parameter optimization for other bioinformatics tools. This work has received in-principle acceptance at Genome Biology.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: The Virtual Biotech: A Multi-Agent AI Framework for Therapeutic Discovery and Development
authors: Harrison Zhang, Peter Eckmann, Jiacheng Miao, Andrew Mahon, James Zou
abstract: Drug discovery and development requires integrating diverse evidence across biological scales and data modalities. However, relevant data, tools, and expertise remain fragmented across teams and organizations, making integration difficult. To address these challenges, we introduce the Virtual Biotech, a coordinated team of AI agents that mirrors the structure of human therapeutic research organizations to support end-to-end computational discovery. The Virtual Biotech is led by a Chief Scientific Officer agent that receives scientific queries, delegates them to domain-specialized scientist agents, and integrates their outputs through data-driven reasoning. Scientist agents leverage complementary tools and knowledge sources spanning statistical genetics, functional genomics, pathways and interactions, chemoinformatics, disease biology, and clinical data. We showcase the Virtual Biotech across three translational applications. First, the agents autonomously annotated and analyzed outcomes from 55,984 clinical trials to identify genomic features of drug targets associated with trial success. More than 37,000 clinical-trialist agents curated structured trial outcomes and linked targets to multi-omic annotations, including cell-type-specific features derived by the agents from single-cell RNA-sequencing atlases. The agents discovered that drugs targeting cell-type-specific genes were 40\% more likely to progress from Phase I to Phase II and 48\% more likely to reach market (Phase IV), while exhibiting 32\% lower adverse event rates. Second, the Virtual Biotech evaluated B7-H3 as a lung cancer target, integrating statistical genetics, single-cell, spatial, and clinicogenomic evidence to propose an antibody–drug conjugate strategy while identifying key liabilities and differentiation opportunities. Third, the platform analyzed a terminated ulcerative colitis trial targeting OSMR$\beta$ to infer potential failure mechanisms and proposed biomarker-guided enrollment strategies to address precision-medicine gaps. Together, these results illustrate how the Virtual Biotech can enable more transparent, efficient, and comprehensive multi-scale therapeutic analyses, helping to accelerate early-stage drug discovery workflows while keeping human scientists in the loop.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A Conversational Multi-Agent AI Framework for Integrated Multi-Omics Analysis and Biomedical Discovery
authors: Pankaj Rajdeo, Shunya Asanuma, Michal Kouril, Peixin Lu, Jichao Chen, Aman Chadha, V. B. Surya Prasath, Bruce J. Aronow, Nathan Salomonis
abstract: Single-cell and spatial transcriptomics have transformed our ability to resolve cellular heterogeneity across development and disease, yet extracting reproducible, integrative insight from these datasets demands multi-modal expertise, iterative analytical workflows, and access to validated tools that remain beyond the reach of most researchers. LungChat addresses this gap through a hierarchical multi-agent AI framework in which a Supervisor Agent decomposes natural-language queries into parallel sub-tasks delegated to four specialized agents (Single-Cell, Spatial Omics, Research, and Atlas) each grounded in a curated library of 51 bioinformatics tools selected via hybrid semantic and lexical matching. Complementing this architecture, DART (Direction-Aware Repurposing and Targeting) provides cell-type-resolved drug prioritization by classifying perturbation-induced gene signatures as reversing or reinforcing disease transcriptional programs to enable safety-aware compound ranking across heterogeneous cell populations. Across 1,080 ablation evaluations, the hierarchical design reduced token consumption approximately 2Ã— and improved refusal of out-of-scope queries by 35 percentage points over a flat single-agent baseline. Applied to idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis via a single natural-language query, LungChat recovered canonical fibrosis markers, ECM organization and TGF-β/VEGFA pathways, and spatially resolved fibroblast–basaloid ligand–receptor interactions. DART ranked Saracatinib, an SRC/ ABL inhibitor as the top repurposing candidate, demonstrating 90.9% reversal of pathogenic myofibroblast programs (Pearson r = âˆ’0.82), a prediction independently supported by the STOP-IPF trial (NCT04598919). LungChat is deployed within the NHLBI-funded LungMAP ecosystem (chat.lungmap.net) to provide community access to harmonized lung multi-omics analysis. These results establish that conversational multi-agent systems can enable rigorous, reproducible multi-omics discovery at scale without supplanting expert judgment.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Transfer learning from datasets with unshared features for detecting Autism Spectrum Disorder using AutDB
authors: Ruslan Kurmashev, Adina Yessimova, Denis Traore, Olaitan I. Awe
abstract: Machine learning models for autism spectrum disorder (ASD) screening based on video analysis often achieve high accuracy when evaluated on the same dataset used for training, but their performance deteriorates sharply when transferred to external datasets. This leads to a limitation of their practical application and reduces the credibility of the results obtained. To address this challenge, we present a simple and reproducible benchmark on two open, privacy-preserving datasets: Multi-Modal ASD dataset (MMASD) and Engagnition. Both datasets were harmonized in a unified metadata table, with the introduction of a common proxy activity label, derived from 2D skeleton dynamics and accelerometry. We compared two simple tabular models, Logistic Regression and XGBoost, under within-dataset independent and identically distributed (IID) and cross-dataset leave-one-dataset-out (LODO) scenarios. We then explicitly quantified the cross-dataset domain shift between MMASD and Engagnition using summary movement features and Wasserstein distances, and visualised the joint feature space with UMAP. Building on this, we evaluated standard domain adaptation baselines (CORrelation ALignment (CORAL) and importance weighting) and a simple PCA-based representation of movement intensity. These analyses show that movement statistics and task structure differ substantially between datasets, basic covariance alignment can partially recover cross-dataset performance for a low-level intensity proxy, whereas naive importance weighting is unstable and collapsing movement descriptors onto a single principal component degrades transfer performance. In addition, minimal TRIPOD-AI reporting elements and PROBAST-AI risk assessment were applied to increase transparency and reproducibility.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Enabling direct nanopore sequencing of non-canonical bases using bootstrapped learning and signal splicing
authors: Mauricio Lisboa Perez, Niranjan Nagarajan
abstract: Non-canonical bases (NCBs) that expand the nucleic acid alphabet beyond canonical A, T, C, G, and U have sparked interest in applications across synthetic biology, DNA storage and viral genomics. However, the inability to directly and efficiently sequence NCBs remains a major barrier to their development and practical use. We address this challenge with an AI framework for training a de novo basecaller capable of decoding NCBs at high throughput. For model training, we leverage nanopore sequencing technology to extract raw signals from a complex pool of synthetic xeno-nucleic acids (XNAs) comprising 1,024 oligonucleotides with NCBs in diverse 6-mer contexts and high purity. We devise a bootstrapped learning approach for data preparation, where we construct training data from initially imperfect labels and iteratively refine basecalling models. To enable training of generalizable models, we introduce a signal-splicing data-augmentation strategy that generates artificial reads using real nanopore signals across diverse contexts. Our approach enables us to obtain a basecaller model capable of directly decoding NCB-containing sequences with high accuracy (>80%) and specificity (99%). These results highlight the versatility of nanopore sequencing and AI for interrogating unusual nucleic acids, and the potential to transform the study of genetic material beyond those that use canonical bases. Besides enabling practical sequencing of expanded genetic alphabets, this work demonstrates a general strategy for decoding novel nanopore signals from noisy and limited training data, laying the foundation for obtaining generalizable basecallers for identifying diverse molecular classes, including novel nucleotides, modified bases and proteins.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Linear-time prediction of proteome-scale microbial protein interactions
authors: Andre Cornman, Yunha Hwang, Matt Tranzillo, Nicolo Zulaybar, Imane Bouzit
abstract: Protein-protein interactions (PPIs) underpin biological function, yet proteome-scale interaction prediction remains bottlenecked by the quadratic computational complexity of all-vs-all pairwise comparisons. Here, we present FlashPPI, a contrastive learning framework, grounded in residue-level interactions, that enables linear-time prediction of physical protein interfaces across a microbial proteome. By leveraging a genomic language model that captures cross-protein co-evolutionary signals from metagenomic sequences, FlashPPI aligns interacting partners in a shared latent space. We demonstrate a four-fold performance increase over existing sequence-based methods, while reducing proteome-wide screening time from days to minutes. Crucially, FlashPPI achieves comparable screening performance to state-of-the-art structure-folding models at a fraction of the computational cost. Finally, we integrate FlashPPI into seqhub.org, an interactive web platform that combines predicted networks with functional annotations and genomic context, making proteome-wide network analysis rapid and accessible for microbial discovery.

title: Learning from evolutionary trajectories
authors: Yun Song
abstract: Accurately predicting the functional effects of genetic variants is a central challenge in modern biology, with applications ranging from disease diagnosis to understanding complex trait architectures and engineering novel biomolecules. In this talk, I will present my lab’s recent work on developing evolution-informed language models for biological sequences that learn the constraints shaping natural variation. I will highlight two frameworks: one that leverages evolutionary and contextual information to predict the effects of coding and non-coding variants, and another that explicitly models evolutionary trajectories to enable realistic sequence generation. Through applications in human genetics and biomolecular engineering, I will demonstrate how grounding AI models in evolutionary principles can improve predictive accuracy while producing biologically plausible sequences, providing powerful new tools for variant interpretation and biomolecular design.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: BRIDGE-SP: Bridging Single-Cell Foundation Models for Spatial Transcriptomics-to-Proteomics Prediction via Spatially Aware Adaptation
authors: Zijie Fang, Yimeng Qiao, Ran Liu, Zhidong Yang, Yuyan Ruan, Jihong Tang, Jiguang Wang
abstract: Spatial proteomics (SP) provides spatially resolved protein measurements and captures cellular states that cannot be fully inferred from RNA alone. However, SP assays remain costly and difficult to scale, whereas spatial transcriptomics (ST) is more accessible across platforms and tissues. This motivates computational translation from ST to SP as a scalable alternative to direct SP measurement. To this end, we present BRIDGE-SP, a multimodal framework for SP prediction from ST. Considering foundation models (FMs) pretrained on large-scale single-cell (SC) RNA-seq data encode rich and transferable transcriptomic priors, we first develop a morphology-driven SC-ST calibration strategy to adapt SC FMs trained under an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) assumption and lacking spatial awareness to non-i.i.d. ST data. To address the limitation that rank-based encoding in widely used SC FMs underuses quantitative RNA abundance relevant to protein expression, we further introduce a multi-scale adaptive RNA quantification modeling module to recover absolute RNA signals across neighborhoods of varying radii. Finally, BRIDGE-SP is trained with a multimodal contrastive objective aligning rank-based transcriptomic, quantitative transcriptomic, and histologic-related transcriptomic representations. In the STP Open Challenge, BRIDGE-SP ranked first among 100 teams. Besides, it achieved the best Top-10 Mean SCC (78.19%), PCC (75.41%), and Moran’s BV (66.50%) across four in-sample evaluation datasets from two SP technologies. In cross-sample evaluation, it also achieved the best performance in 6 transfer settings. Together, these results show that spatially aware adaptation of SC FMs is an effective strategy for robust ST-to-SP translation, which promotes future study of spatially resolved mRNA-protein correlation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: SpatioVelo: Spatial RNA velocity inference by integrating scRNA-seq and spatial transcriptomics
authors: Guan-Ting Chen, Yeuh-Hua Tu, Hsueh-Fen Juan, Hsuan-Cheng Huang
abstract: Advances in single-cell sequencing have established RNA velocity as a key tool for inferring cell trajectories. However, applying it to spatial transcriptomics (ST) remains challenging. Unspliced mRNA counts in ST often suffer from low capture efficiency and high sparsity, leading to unreliable estimates. Furthermore, existing methods typically assume constant kinetic dynamics across all cells and ignore spatial context. Models lacking spatial context and cell-specific kinetics fail to capture these environmental constraints, resulting in velocity vectors inconsistent with known tissue biology. To overcome these limitations, we present SpatioVelo, a framework that integrates high-quality splicing dynamics from scRNA-seq with spatial transcriptomics. SpatioVelo introduces a spatial constraint mechanism that downweighs associations between transcriptionally similar but spatially distant cells, ensuring that velocity vectors align with the tissue's physical architecture. Additionally, SpatioVelo estimates cell-specific kinetic parameters, capturing variations in transcription, splicing, and degradation rates driven by local microenvironments. By combining spatial proximity with cell-specific gene kinetic parameters, SpatioVelo produces RNA velocity projections that are more biologically interpretable within the tissue space. Benchmarking across diverse ST datasets, we show that SpatioVelo more accurately reconstructs known differentiation trajectories compared to existing models. By yielding inferences consistent with the biological logic of complex tissues, SpatioVelo provides a powerful tool for uncovering how spatial positioning governs cell fate, offering broad potential for studies in tissue development and disease progression.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Characterizing Functional Microniches with SpaceTravLR
authors: Alyson Wang, Koushul Ramjattun, Amanda Poholek, Youjin Lee, Jishnu Das
abstract: Motivation Cellular microniches influence cell fate and function through spatially restricted cytokine and cellular interactions. Existing approaches define microniches based on spatially resolved gene expression, which often lack functional interpretability. Here, we introduce SpaceTravLR (Spatially Perturbing Transcription Factors Ligands and Receptors), a first-in-class machine learning approach for in-silico perturbations with spatial resolution to uncover functional microniches. Results SpaceTravLR discovered a novel mechanism for CCR4 that could not be captured by existing approaches that drives the compartmentalization and spatial location of a pathogenic population of Th2 cells in allergic asthma, which was validated in a murine model. Availability https://github.com/jishnu-lab/SpaceTravLR https:// spacetravlr.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html Implementation SpaceTravLR infers how single or combinatorial genetic perturbations rewire signals across the tissue neighborhood by propagating effects through underlying spatially resolved molecular networks. We first construct a gene-modulatory network linking target genes to upstream transcription factors, ligands, and receptors. Based on this regulatory network, the expression of a target gene at every location is modeled as a linear combination of its intrinsic transcription factors, and extrinsic ligand-receptor and ligand-TF signaling activities. SpaceTravLR then estimates the coefficients for each modulator by first estimating global cell-type level baselines, and then utilizes a vision model to generate location-specific spatial multipliers. This factorization isolates spatial signals from fundamental cell-type biology, improving model interpretability. Further, with these coefficients, we can compute derivatives to propagate perturbations spatially, thereby modeling how perturbations can reshape both the targeted cell and its surrounding neighborhood. track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Correcting cell count bias improves perturbation effect estimates and virtual cell models
authors: Gerold Csendes, Bence Czakó, Gema Sanz, Zsolt Gyüre, Milán Sztilkovics, László Mérő, Gábor Kovács, Kristóf Szalay, Bence Szalai
abstract: Artificial intelligence-based virtual cell (AIVC) models aim to predict post-perturbation cellular states, such as gene expression changes following genetic or chemical perturbations. A key challenge for these models is generalization to new biological contexts, including unseen cell types and perturbations. Since generalization critically depends on the consistency of perturbation effect estimates across datasets, we analyzed seven recent Perturb-seq datasets, commonly used benchmark datasets in the AIVC field. While the direction of pseudo-bulk differential expression (PB-DE) profiles showed moderate agreement across studies (median Pearson correlation > 0.4 for strong perturbations), the magnitude of perturbation effects (L1 norm of PB-DE vectors, effect size) varied substantially. We observed a strong inverse relationship between the number of cells per perturbation (n_cell) and effect size, indicating systematic inflation of effect sizes at low cell counts. Importantly, PB-DE magnitude and n_cell did not correlate with independent biological measures such as gene essentiality from DepMap, and the same relationship was recapitulated by downsampling control cells, supporting a technical rather than biological origin. We therefore introduce a simple scaling approach based on the empirical relationship between n_cell and PB-DE magnitude. This correction substantially improves cross-study agreement of perturbation effects and their association with biological readouts. track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Topographical Archetypes of Somatic Mutagenesis in Cancer
authors: Allen W. Lynch, Sangmi Sandra Lee, Jan P. Hummel, Benedikt Geiger, Hu Jin, Doga C. Gulhan, Peter J. Park
abstract: The genome of every cancer cell carries a record of the mutational processes that have acted throughout its history. Mutational signature analysis, which infers the activity of mutagenic processes from their characteristic base-change patterns, has become an indispensable tool for interpreting somatic mutations. However, this framework captures only which types of mutations a process generates and not where in the genome they occur -- a distribution influenced by replication timing, chromatin organization, transcription, DNA secondary structure, and other genomic features. Here, we present a generative probabilistic framework (MuTopia) that jointly infers mutational spectra and their genome-wide topography as nonlinear functions of genomic and epigenomic state. Applied to whole-genome sequencing data from 15 tumor types, MuTopia reveals that mutational processes fall into eight conserved topographical archetypes, or topotypes, structured primarily by replication timing and chromatin state. Diverse mutational processes converge upon this limited repertoire, indicating that the genomic distribution of mutagenesis is constrained less by the source of damage than by how that damage is processed. Individual mutational processes exhibit state-dependent variation in their genomic distributions: the same signature can adopt distinct topotypes depending on repair proficiency and replication stress. For instance, SBS8 shifts from a canonical late-replicating profile in homologous recombination (HR)-proficient tumors to an early-replicating, stress-associated topotype in HR-deficient tumors, and replication stress similarly reshapes the genomic distribution of APOBEC editing. Topotypes, therefore, provide a classification of mutagenesis distinct from spectral signatures, capturing aspects of tumor biology that spectra alone cannot resolve. The resulting pan-cancer topographical catalog provides a resource for investigating the genomic patterns of mutagenesis across human cancers.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Toward an In Silico Tissue Laboratory: From Virtual Staining to Executable Tissue Modeling
authors: Young Hwan Chang
abstract: This presentation introduces the concept of an in silico tissue laboratory: a new computational paradigm for studying tumor microenvironments by integrating molecularly anchored virtual staining with executable tissue modeling. The goal is to move beyond static tissue characterization toward scalable, interpretable, and mechanistic interrogation of tissue states, transitions, and therapeutic response. I will first present miniMTI, a virtual staining framework that combines routine H&E with a minimal set of experimentally measured molecular markers to reconstruct high-dimensional multiplex tissue imaging (MTI) panels. This approach enables molecularly rich tissue profiling across large cohorts while preserving cellular phenotypes, spatial architecture, and clinically relevant programs. I will then introduce an executable tissue modeling framework based on agent-based modeling and trajectory-centric analysis. Here, simulated tumor–microenvironment dynamics are used to define a reference landscape of tissue states and transitions. Patient MTI data can then be mapped onto this landscape to interpret observed tissue states, infer likely trajectories and transition regimes, and contextualize samples within different phases of treatment response. Together, these approaches establish an interpretable in silico tissue laboratory for scalable molecular inference, mechanistic hypothesis testing, and trajectory-informed therapeutic discovery.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Spatial-ZEDNet: A Unified Spatial Transcriptomics Framework for Detecting Differential Gene Activation and Expression
authors: Osafu Egbon, Benedict Anchang
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) has enabled the study of spatial biological variations across conditions. However, identifying spatially variable genes (SVGs) and differentially expressed genes (DEGs) across multiple conditions is often hindered by spatially misaligned tissues, limiting cross-condition spatial inferences. Moreover, the presence of zero-inflated expressions in ST complicates the analysis further. Most existing methods are designed to identify SVGs and DEGs among cellular neighborhoods per tissue, limiting their applicability to cross-condition inferences. To address these challenges, we propose Spatial-ZEDNet, a computational framework that jointly learns differentially expressed genes (DEGs) and differentially activated (on/off) genes (DAGs) using a spatially informed two-part model that explicitly accounts for zero inflation. The method also simultaneously detects SVGs by aligning biological signals across misaligned tissue sections and conditions using network-regularized Bayesian learning, overcoming a key limitation in comparative spatial transcriptomics without requiring coordinate matching. Through extensive simulations in an ablation study and analyses of real datasets, Spatial-ZEDNet demonstrates improved power and specificity relative to existing DEG and SVG methods, particularly in the presence of strong spatial structure and identification of DAGs, while maintaining competitive performance in non-spatial settings. Importantly, the framework effectively disentangles perturbation-induced differential expression from intrinsic spatial variability, making it a competitive analysis tool for ST across conditions. Applied to ulcerative colitis and Plasmodium infection ST datasets, the method identified spatially localized differential expression and activation of immune genes missed by conventional methods, including Mmp7, Olr1, Ifitm3, and Gbp3, several of which correspond to validated inflammatory disease loci. Spatial-ZEDNet offers an interpretable Bayesian learning framework for cross-condition inference in spatial transcriptomics, enabling mechanistic insights into biological systems without explicit tissue coordinate matching.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Spatiotemporal Modeling with ATLIS: Anchored Tissue Landscapes in an Interpretable Space
authors: Wenjun Zhao, Ying Ma
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics data are increasingly collected across developmental time points, yet most existing methods analyze slices independently or rely on pairwise alignment, without explicitly modeling how cellular composition and spatial structure evolve over time. This limits interpretability, temporal coherence, and the ability to reconstruct unobserved intermediate tissue states. We develop ATLIS, an interpretable spatial-temporal modeling that represents tissue organization in a low-dimensional latent space anchored to cell type compositions. By modeling gene expression as a noisy linear projection of latent tissue states, ATLIS enables spatial and temporal regularization to be imposed directly on biologically interpretable quantities. Spatial smoothness is enforced within slices, and temporal continuity is encoded through optimal transport–based coupling across time points, yielding a unified framework for alignment, clustering, and whole-slice imputation. Benchmarks on both simulations and real data applications demonstrate consistent improvements in accuracy, interpretability, and biological coherence over existing approaches.
