track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Interaction-aware multitask deep learning reveals cross-species receptor compatibility landscapes across sarbecoviruses
authors: Kritika Prasai, Jeffrey C. Chandler, Constanza Espada, Riley Wiese, Yingyi Long, Sean P. Streich, Jonathon Heale, Nathan Roberts, Yizhi Jane Tao, Thomas J. DeLiberto, Xiu-Feng Wan
abstract: Predicting compatibility between interacting proteins across diverse hosts and rapidly evolving viral variants remains a fundamental challenge in computational biology, particularly when binding function diverges a lot from sequence similarity. In the context of SARS-CoV-2 and related sarbecoviruses, the receptor binding domain (RBD)–ACE2 interaction exemplifies this challenge, even the closely related sequences exhibit divergent binding affinities, making classical homology-based approaches unreliable. Here, we present CompatNet, a multitask deep learning framework that jointly predicts categorical binding strength and quantitative dissociation constant (KD) from paired ACE2–RBD. CompatNet encodes paired RBD and ACE2 sequences using LoRA-adapted ESM-2 embeddings, refines them through a dual-branch local–global encoder (CNN + self-attention), and learns residue-level interaction patterns via gated multi-head cross-attention. The multi-task objective jointly optimizes regression (pKD) and classification (four binding strength categories) over a shared representation, enabling both continuous affinity prediction and interpretable risk classification. We train and evaluate on a curated experimental dataset using 17 wildlife ACE2 orthologs, 16 sarbecovirus RBDs, and additional public dataset of 414(ACE-RBD paired data) and 20,000 deep mutational scanning variants. CompatNet outperforms classical and deep learning baselines and identifies key interface determinants and generalizes well to held-out Omicron sub lineages (Pearson correlation R = 0.95). This framework maps receptor compatibility landscapes across peri-domestic U.S. wildlife and provides a scalable platform for prioritizing receptor-compatible host–virus pairs for surveillance and experimental evaluation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Multimodal spatial alignment and morphology mapping with MOSAICField
authors: Hongyu Zheng, Xinhao Liu, Peter Halmos, Julian Gold, Erik Storrs, Li Ding, Ben Raphael
abstract: Recent efforts to build comprehensive tissue and tumor atlases leverage diverse spatial technologies to measure transcriptomic, proteomic, epigenetic, and other modalities with hundreds to thousands of features at thousands to millions of spatially resolved locations in a tissue slice. Integrating such data across spatial technologies that differ in molecular features, spatial resolution, and tissue morphology remains a major challenge. We introduce MultimOdal Spatial Alignment and Integration with Coordinate neural Field (MOSAICField), a unified framework for aligning spatial slices across arbitrary combinations of experimental modalities. MOSAICField computes two types of spatial alignments across multiple slices from the same tissue: physical alignment, which reconstructs a contiguous 3D model of the original tissue, and morphological alignment, which maps distinct morphological or anatomical structures, such as ducts, veins, or neurons, that may traverse the tissue at different angles relative to the direction of slicing. MOSAICField computes both alignments using a deep neural network that estimates a nonlinear deformation field with a multimodal feature loss. We evaluate MOSAICField on simulated data and a prostate cancer sample from the Human Tumor Atlas Network (HTAN), containing more than a dozen spatial slices with multimodal profiling data. MOSAICField constructs an accurate 3D tumor model, tracks the architecture of the prostatic ductal system, and improves analysis of features within and across modalities, outperforming existing methods.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Domain-Aware Enzyme Classification via Multiple Instance Learning
authors: Qingyang Xiao, Yuzhen Ye, Haixu Tang
abstract: Accurate Enzyme Commission (EC) number prediction is fundamental to protein function annotation and metabolic pathway reconstruction. Recent methods based on protein language model embeddings or 3D structure have improved EC prediction, but important limitations remain. Whole-sequence embeddings can dilute local functional signals, such as catalytic residues and functional domains, whereas structure-based methods depend on accurate protein structures and are therefore difficult to apply broadly. We present MIL-BC, a multiple instance learning framework for EC prediction that models each protein as a bag of domains rather than a single sequence-level object. This design is motivated by the observation that enzymatic function is often determined by constituent functional domains instead of the full-length sequence alone. Domain instances are generated automatically using our DCTdomain algorithm, avoiding dependence on curated domain annotations. MIL-BC aggregates domain-level evidence into protein-level EC predictions and assigns interpretable weights to domains that contribute most strongly to each prediction. We further combine domain embedding with global embedding as MIL-BC+. MIL-BC+ achieved F1 improvements of 0.03, 0.04, 0.06, and 0.17 over the sequence-based baseline on New-392, Price-149, uniprot2025-all, and uniprot2025-multi, respectively. The largest gains were observed for proteins with multiple enzymatic functions, where domain-level modeling better separates mixed functional signals. These results show that domain-centric multiple instance learning is an accurate and interpretable strategy for enzyme classification. By improving EC prediction without requiring structural data or curated domain labels, MIL-BC provides a scalable framework for large-scale protein function annotation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: CROP: A feature-independent context-aware method for CRISPR-Cas9 frameshift prediction
authors: Ido Tziony, Yaron Orenstein
abstract: Motivation: The CRISPR-Cas9 complex has revolutionized genome-editing technologies. By designing a 20 nt-long guide RNA, a Cas9 nuclease can be guided to cleave almost any genomic target site (followed by NGG). The cleavage induces double-stranded DNA breaks, which are then repaired by cellular pathways. Accurate CRISPR-Cas9 repair-outcome prediction is essential for designing guide RNAs with desired genomic effects, such as gene knockout. A central challenge is quantifying the rate of frameshifts, i.e. repair-outcomes that lead to a change in the local length that is not a multiplicity of 3. Previous methods for frameshift-rate prediction were trained on only few experimental or cellular contexts, mostly rely on manually defined microhomology features, and are limited by sparse features and class labels. Results: We developed CROP, the first feature-independent context-aware repair-outcome prediction method. By aggregating specific repair outcomes as Δlength classes, CROP overcomes class sparsity. We designed CROP to work with variable input sequence lengths and output classes in order to utilize multiple datasets simultaneously. We benchmarked CROP against state-of-the-art repair-outcome prediction methods over 18 datasets, which we curated and standardized from various studies. Across all datasets, CROP outperformed all competing methods in frameshift-rate prediction. We performed cross-experiment and cross-cellular frameshift predictions to investigate the generalizability of repair mechanisms. Finally, we show that CROP learned microhomology principles from raw sequences without explicit feature engineering, establishing the first end-to-end architecture for CRISPR-Cas9 repair-outcome prediction which learns from multiple datasets. Availability and implementation: CROP is available at https:// github.com/OrensteinLab/CROP.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: PertAdapt: Unlocking Single-Cell Foundation Models for Genetic Perturbation Prediction via Condition-Sensitive Adaptation
authors: Ding Bai, Le Song, Eric Xing
abstract: Motivation: Single-cell foundation models (FMs) pretrained on massive unlabeled scRNA-seq data show strong potential in predicting transcriptional responses to unseen genetic perturbations (e.g. knockouts, variants). However, existing approaches do not effectively transfer pretrained knowledge and overlook the imbalance between perturbation-sensitive and insensitive genes, yielding only marginal improvements over non-pretrained baselines. Results: To address these limitations, we introduce PertAdapt, a framework that unlocks FMs to accurately predict genetic perturbation effects by integrating a plug-in perturbation adapter and an adaptive loss. The adapter employs a gene-similarity-masked attention mechanism to jointly encode perturbation conditions and contextualized representations of unperturbed cells, enabling more effective knowledge transfer. To better capture differential expression patterns, the adaptive loss dynamically reweights perturbation-sensitive genes relative to global transcriptomic signals. Extensive experiments across seven perturbation datasets, including both single-and double-gene settings, demonstrate that PertAdapt consistently outperforms non-pretrained and FM baselines. Moreover, PertAdapt demonstrates strong capacity to model multiplexed gene interactions, to generalize in limited-data regimes, and to maintain robustness across backbone sizes.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: A Palma Ratio–Driven Graph-Fusion Approach for Detecting Ultra-Rare Cell Types in scRNA-seq Data
authors: Xingzhi Niu, Jieqiong Wang, Shibiao Wan
abstract: Single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) is routinely used to build atlases of tissues, resolve developmental trajectories, and characterize disease microenvironments. Yet many biologically and clinically meaningful populations such as transient progenitors, therapy-resistant tumor subclones, and antigen-specific lymphocytes, occur at very low frequencies (<1%) and are easily missed by standard clustering pipelines. Existing approaches often require extensive manual curation, rely on known marker genes, or trade sensitivity for unacceptable false positive rates due to the insensitivity of metrics like the Gini index to heavy-tailed distributions. A scalable, statistically grounded method is needed to sensitively detect rare populations while providing calibrated confidence and interpretable molecular signatures. To address these concerns, we present PalmaClust, a graph-fusion clustering framework that repurposes Palma ratio, a tail-sensitive inequality metric in sociology, to identify marker genes driven by extreme sparsity. PalmaClust constructs and fuses multiple K-Nearest Neighbor (KNN) graphs derived from complementary gene-selection statistics including the Palma ratio, Gini index, and Fano factor. It employs a local refinement strategy that re-prioritizes Palma-ranked genes within parent clusters. Benchmarking across diverse public scRNA-seq datasets confirms that PalmaClust consistently outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, improving rare-class F1 scores by at least 20% (absolute) while maintaining high global clustering stability. Further studies demonstrate that the Palma ratio-derived graph layer is essential for capturing ultra-rare signatures that other views miss.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Bridging the negative data gap in bioactivity prediction using InertDB
authors: Seungchan An, Minsoo Noh
abstract: Small molecule bioactivity prediction is frequently limited by "publication bias," where the scarcity of negative data hinders model reliability. To address this gap, we present InertDB, a comprehensive database of 3,205 Curated Inactive Compounds (CICs) and 64,368 Generated Inactive Compounds (GICs). CICs were identified from 4.6 million PubChem records using a natural language processing (NLP)-based bioassay diversity metric to ensure consistent inactivity across diverse biological contexts. Remarkably, 97.2% of CICs adhere to the Rule of Five, with a minimal pan-assay interference compounds (PAINS) rate of 1.2%, offering superior drug-like properties compared to general chemical sets. To further navigate sparsely populated chemical space, we employed a recurrent neural network-based generative AI to produce GICs, providing unique scaffolds (e.g., dioxaspiroundecane) absent from existing datasets like Dark Chemical Matter. Validation on LIT-PCBA and MUV benchmarks shows that models trained with InertDB significantly outperform those using random sampling or property-matched decoys. By integrating extensive curation with generative AI, InertDB serves as a pivotal resource for robust virtual screening and bioactivity prediction.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: ChromCodes: interpretable discrete representations enable controllable design of cell-type-specific regulatory DNA sequences
authors: Luca Pinello
abstract: Deep learning models for regulatory DNA either achieve interpretability or enable sequence generation, but rarely both. Discriminative models like ChromBPNet and Enformer predict chromatin accessibility from sequence but cannot generate sequences with specified properties. Generative methods like DNA-Diffusion enable cell-type-conditional design but operate as black boxes whose outputs cannot be decomposed into interpretable features. We present ChromCodes, an architecture unifying these capabilities through three components: motif-detecting convolutional filters, vector quantization into a discrete codebook, and a cross-attention decoder. ChromCodes encodes 200 bp DNA using 512 reverse-complement-equivariant filters, quantizes embeddings through a 512-entry codebook, and reconstructs via cross-attention with no skip connections—forcing all information through an interpretable bottleneck. Trained on 48,000 chromatin accessible peaks across four human cell types (GM12878, hESCT0, K562, HepG2), the model recovers known TF motifs in 48% of filters (GATA1, HNF4A, NANOG, SPI1) and predicts accessibility from a bag-of-codes representation (Pearson r=0.780). This creates a traceable chain from nucleotides through motifs and discrete codes to cell-type identity. We introduce CodeProp, a gradient-based method that designs DNA sequences with target activity by optimizing the input sequence directly through the frozen ChromCodes pipeline. CodeProp achieves high tunability while generating genuinely novel sequences. Cell-type transformations recover expected master regulators: stem cell to erythroid transformations gain GATA1/GATA2/TAL1 while losing SOX2/FOXH1. External validation with ChromBPNet, an independent accessibility model, confirms generated sequences match endogenous profiles. ChromCodes unifies interpretation, representation, regression, and generation of regulatory DNA in a single differentiable framework, enabling controllable design without sacrificing transparency.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: CPS: Mapping Physical Coordinates to High-Fidelity Spatial Transcriptomics via Privileged Multi-Scale Context Distillation
authors: Lei Zhang, Kai Cao, Shuqiao Zheng, Shu Liang, Lin Wan
abstract: Motivation: Spatial transcriptomics enables the dissection of tissue heterogeneity within native contexts, yet current platforms are inherently constrained by high sparsity and low signal-to-noise ratios that obscure fine-grained biological signals. Current efforts to recover these signals are limited by image registration dependencies or the inherent context-blindness of implicit neural representations. Method: We introduce the Cell Positioning System (CPS), a context-aware implicit neural representation framework designed to map physical coordinates to high-fidelity spatial transcriptomics via a privileged multi-scale context distillation strategy. CPS treats multi-scale tissue niches as privileged information, employing a teacher network equipped with a multi-scale niche attention mechanism to capture adaptive biological interactions during training. This structural knowledge is explicitly distilled into a student coordinate network, enabling the generation of context-aware expression landscapes solely from spatial coordinates during inference. Results: Benchmarking on the DLPFC dataset demonstrates that CPS achieves state-of-the-art performance in spatial imputation and denoising. Furthermore, CPS enables super-resolution to recover subcellular mouse brain anatomical details and offers interpretability by identifying the scale effective size of biological interactions on human breast cancer. Finally, the framework exhibits superior scalability for large-scale datasets with linear computational complexity. Availability: Software is available online at https://github.com/tju-zl/CPS.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Riemannian Metric Learning for Alignment of Spatial Multiomics
authors: Peter Halmos, Yufan Xia, Benjamin Raphael
abstract: Recent spatial technologies measure the transcriptome, epigenome, proteome, metabolome, and other modalities from thousands of cells across a tissue. Most assays typically profile only one modality from a tissue slice, raising the question of how to align spatial data from heterogeneous feature spaces. While multiple approaches have been developed for multi-modal integration of single-cell datasets, few existing techniques perform spatial alignment across arbitrary modalities incorporating both spatial and feature information. We introduce Manifold Gromov-Wasserstein (MGW), a metric-learning framework that exploits the product structure of spatial multiomics to infer modality-specific Riemannian pull-back metrics with neural fields. MGW aligns Riemannian distances induced by these metrics via Gromov-Wasserstein optimal transport, yielding a hyperparameter-free cost across arbitrary modalities sharing a spatial base. The formulation enjoys theoretical invariances -- including orthogonal transformations of the spatial and feature domains as well as global feature scalings. We demonstrate the advantages of MGW on multiple alignment tasks, including Stereo-Seq spatiotemporal transcriptomics of mouse embryo, Xenium and Visium spatial transcriptomics of colorectal cancer, and spatial metabolomics-transcriptomics from human striatum and kidney cancer. MGW recovers biologically meaningful correspondences and spatially coherent tissue structures, outperforming existing OT and non-OT based multi-modal baselines.

title: Opportunities and challenges in sequence-based deep learning

abstract: Deep neural networks that take DNA sequence as input have immense potential to decode the cis-regulatory code, reveal sequence determinants of chromatin organization, and predict the effects of genetic variation on cell state and health. This means that effects of sequence differences on important motifs can be upweighted, and rare or de novo variants never used in model training can be analyzed. To date, however, sequence-based deep learning models tend to under-perform and have not fully capitalized on these advantages. This talk will use simulations, explainable AI techniques, and data analysis to reveal the main roadblocks and shed light on a path forward towards deep-learning enabled personal genome interpretation.

track: MLCSB: Machine Learning in Computational and Systems Biology
title: Diffusion-based Representation Integration for Foundation Models Improves Spatial Transcriptomics Analysis
authors: Atishay Jain, Tuan M. Pham, David H. Laidlaw, Ying Ma, Ritambhara Singh
abstract: Motivation: We propose DRIFT, a framework that integrates spatial context into the input representations for foundation models by leveraging diffusion on spatial graphs derived from spatial transcriptomics (ST) data. ST captures gene expression profiles while preserving spatial context, enabling downstream analysis tasks such as cell-type annotation, clustering, and cross-sample alignment. However, due to its emerging nature, there are very few foundation models that can utilize ST data to generate embeddings generalizable across multiple tasks. Meanwhile, well-documented foundational models trained on large-scale single-cell gene expression (scRNA-seq) data have demonstrated generalizable performance across scRNA-seq assays, tissues, and tasks; however, they do not leverage the spatial information in ST data. We use heat kernel diffusion to propagate embeddings across spatial neighborhoods, incorporating the local neighborhood context of the ST data while preserving the transcriptomic representations learned by state-of-the-art single-cell foundation models. Results: We systematically benchmark five foundational models (both scRNA-seq and ST-based) across key ST tasks such as annotation, alignment, and clustering, ensuring a comprehensive evaluation of our proposed framework. Our results show that DRIFT significantly improves the performance of existing foundational models on ST data over specialized state-of-the-art methods. Overall, DRIFT is an effective, accessible, and generalizable framework that bridges the gap toward universal models for modeling spatial transcriptomics. title: Striping artifact removal in VisiumHD data through nuclear counts modeling] {Striping artifact removal in VisiumHD data through nuclear counts modeling

abstract: Motivation: 10x Genomics VisiumHD enables spatial transcriptomics at 2 µm2 resolution but exhibits slide-specific, non-periodic striping artifacts due to lane-width variability. These multiplicative row/column e!ects distort bin total counts and can bias downstream analyses. The state-of-the-art destriping approach is the normalization procedure used as a preprocessing step in bin2cell; it applies sequential high-quantile row-then column-wise normalization, which is asymmetric and can introduce edge e!ects/macro-stripes and distortions of large-scale total-count structure. Results: We propose a statistical destriping approach that leverages nuclei segmentation from the co-registered H&E image. Assuming transcript abundance is constant within each nucleus, we model bin counts with a negative binomial distribution whose mean is a product of a nucleus-specific concentration and row-and column-specific stripe-factors reflecting lane-width variation. We fit all parameters in a generalized linear modeling framework with cross-validated regularization on stripe-factors and iterative dispersion estimation, and use the fitted parameters to correct the observed counts into a destriped image. On synthetic data with known ground truth, our method improves stripe-factor estimation accuracy and reduces error in corrected counts relative to bin2cell and bin2cell-derived baselines. Across four public VisiumHD slides, it consistently lowers striping intensity while substantially better preserving biological signal present in the large-scale global count structure and avoiding the artifacts introduced by other methods. title: Taming the complexity of large-scale metabolic networks
authors: Zoran Nikoloski
abstract: Metabolism provides the energy and building blocks to sustain diverse functions in every living cell. This is achieved via a network of biochemical reactions that transform input nutrients into a plethora of metabolites. Given the diverse functions supported by metabolism, it is not surprising that the underlying metabolic networks have been deemed complex. These results have been obtained by relying on transformation of the hypergraph structure of metabolic networks into uni-or bipartite graph representations. These transformations, however, do not allow establishing a connection between the structure of metabolic networks and metabolic phenotypes—given by reaction rates and metabolite concentrations. In the first part of the talk, I will first advocate the use of a hypergraph as a metabolic network representation and will show how its underlying algebraic structure allows us to glean surprising simplicity in the seemingly complex metabolic networks from species across all domains of life. To this end, I will introduce the concept of multi-reaction dependencies and will show how such dependencies can be efficiently determined from the algebraic structure and operational constraints of metabolic networks. I will then demonstrate how the multi-reaction dependencies can be used to partition a metabolic network into so-called concordance modules that allow substantial reduction of metabolic models. In the second part of the talk, I will introduce the concept of a kinetic module in metabolic network endowed with mass action kinetics, enabling us to study the relation between network structure and metabolic phenotypes. I will then show how kinetic modules can be identified in large-scale networks in absence of parameter values using the concordance modules determined solely based on the network structure. Finally, I will link the kinetic modules of metabolic networks with robustness of metabolite concentrations to perturbations. By analyzing 34 metabolic network models of 26 organisms from all domains of life, I will show that the introduced concepts are pervasive in metabolic networks allowing us to tame their complexity.

title: A Novel Network Approach to Identify Sample-Specific Context-Informed Metabolic Signatures During Developmental Processes
authors: Emma Lee, Ashwin Koppayi, Almudena Veiga-Lopez, Beatriz Peñalver Bernabé
abstract: Metabolism is fundamental during cellular development and understanding how metabolic processes change over time and between cell types is essential. Genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) are network-based tools that allow the mathematical representation of metabolism within a system. By integrating cell-, tissue-, or organ-specific omics data (e.g., transcriptomics), GEMs can be tailored to specific biological contexts by constraining the model to the predicted metabolic processes. Flux balance analysis (FBA), estimates metabolic flux distributions but requires significant amounts of prior knowledge, making the results less insightful in complex and understudied biological contexts. To address these challenges, we developed a pipeline to study dynamic differences in individual, context-specific GEMs of complex multicellular developmental processes. To demonstrate the capabilities of our novel framework, we utilized transcriptomic data from two major cell types that comprise the ovarian follicle, the oocyte (female germ-cell) and granulosa cells (somatic cells), at multiple stages during their development (primordial, primary, secondary, and antral stages) and the human GEM, Recon3D to develop the first human ovarian follicle GEMs for each cell type and at each developmental stage. Our framework identified 99 metabolic subsystems, 2,618 genes, and 4,799 metabolites with dynamic, cell-specific activity during human ovarian follicle development, revealing coordinated metabolic programs that reflect distinct functional demands of oocytes and granulosa cells. These results highlight underexplored processes that can serve as testable hypotheses to guide future experimental studies involving biomarkers for ovarian follicle quality and can be expanded to other understudied biological contexts utilizing our pipeline.

title: Bayesian Likelihood-based Inference of Metabolic Modules for Prokaryotes (BLIMMP)
authors: Neha Sontakke, Amy E Zimmerman, William C Nelson, Jason McDermott, Travis J Wheeler
abstract: A major challenge in metagenomic analysis of microbial communities is that most assembled genomes are incomplete. Sequencing depth and abundance biases produce fragmented assemblies with missing or incomplete contigs and only a small fraction of metagenome-assembled genomes meet near-complete quality thresholds. This incompleteness makes it difficult to distinguish genes that were not recovered from genes that are truly absent, undercutting any downstream inference on the metabolic functions an organism can perform. We present BLIMMP a probabilistic, graph-based framework for inferring metabolic pathway presence in bacterial genomes and metagenomes, even when incomplete. BLIMMP fills a unique gap in metabolic reconstruction with a completeness-aware, probabilistic, and interpretable model for metabolic annotation. We evaluated BLIMMP on the complete Pseudomonas fluorescens SBW25 genome and found that BLIMMP predicts the presence of several modules missed by other tools. We also synthetically degraded the SBW25 genome to simulate a fragmented metagenome-assembled genome; at 70% protein completeness, BLIMMP recovers nearly all modules identified in the full genome, while other approaches miss a large fraction. BLIMMP also provides an interactive web-based visualization tool that renders each module's directed graph as an interactive diagram. Users can inspect individual enzyme nodes, along with the evidence behind each probability estimate, and can trace the best path through the module. This supports inquiry into reasons for calling a module present or absent, which enzymes contributed the most uncertainty, and where co-occurring influencers impacted the outcome. This exploratory approach bridges the gap between statistical outputs and biological interpretation.

title: Rawk: Metabolic pathway local enrichment analysis via random walks on metabolic reaction network
authors: Yuanchao Zhang, Benjamin J. Stear, Kelsey Keith, Dana Mitchell, Aditya Lahiri, Taha Mohseni Ahooyi, Deanne Taylor
abstract: Background: In metabolic reaction networks, the local enrichment of a biologically regulated property, such as gene transcriptions level, within a metabolic pathway indicates that the pathway is preferentially regulated over its neighboring pathways. However, present pathway enrichment analysis methods generally compare a pathway of genes to a background distribution constructed by resampling all genes and therefore lack the sensitivity and specificity to locally enriched pathways. To improve the performance for analyzing local enrichment, we present Rawk, a metabolic pathway local enrichment analysis method. Methods: Rawk compares a pathway to a background that represents the local neighborhood of the pathway, via biased random walks on a metabolic reaction network, to test whether the pathway is locally enriched. We applied Rawk to two simulated gene transcription datasets and three previously published datasets of mouse and human gene transcription levels profiled using bulk RNA-seq, single-cell RNA-seq, or L1000 assay. Rawk is implemented in Python. Results: We show that Rawk has higher sensitivity and specificity to identify locally enriched metabolic pathways on the simulated datasets than commonly used methods. From the previously published transcriptional datasets, Rawk identified locally enriched metabolic pathways with both biologically validated and relatively less well-characterized links to the studied perturbations. The local enrichments of gene transcription levels could be interpreted as metabolic capacities, considering that actual metabolic activities are regulated by various other factors, such as metabolite concentrations. Conclusion: Rawk is a new method for analyzing metabolic pathway local enrichment, which can facilitate the functional characterizations of metabolic variations from genomics data.

title: DyGraphTrans: A temporal graph representation learning framework for modeling disease progression from Electronic Health Records.
authors: Most Tahmina Rahman, Mohammad Al Olaimat, Serdar Bozdag, Alzheimer'S Disease Neuroimaging Initiative
abstract: Motivation: Electronic Health Records (EHRs) contain vast amounts of longitudinal patient medical history data, making them highly informative for early disease prediction. Numerous computational methods have been developed to leverage EHR data; however, many process multiple patient records simultaneously, resulting in high memory consumption and computational cost. Moreover, these models also often lack interpretability, limiting insight into the factors driving their predictions. Efficiently handling large-scale EHR data while maintaining predictive accuracy and interpretability therefore remains a critical challenge. Methods: To address this gap, we propose DyGraphTrans, a dynamic graph representation learning framework that represents patient EHR data as a sequence of temporal graphs. In this representation, nodes correspond to patients, node features encode temporal clinical attributes, and edges capture patient similarity. DyGraphTrans models both local temporal dependencies and long-range global trends, while a sliding-window mechanism reduces memory consumption without sacrificing essential temporal context. Unlike existing dynamic graph models, DyGraphTrans jointly captures patient similarity and temporal evolution in a memory-efficient and interpretable manner. Results: We evaluated DyGraphTrans on Alzheimer’s Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) and National Alzheimer’s Coordinating Center (NACC) for disease progression prediction, as well as on the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care (MIMIC-IV) dataset for early mortality prediction. DyGraphTrans achieved state-of-art performance across all three datasets. We also demonstrated the interpretability of DyGraphTrans aligned with known clinical risk factors. Conclusion: DyGraphTrans is an efficient and interpretable dynamic graph framework that effectively models temporal EHR data to achieve accurate disease progression prediction.
keywords: graph representation learning; electronic health records; disease progression; dynamic graph; progression prediction

title: Genetic Interaction-based Machine Learning Models for Disease Risk Prediction
authors: Mathew Fischbach, Wen Wang, Chad Myers
abstract: Genome-wide association studies (GWAS) aim to find associations between genotypes and phenotypes to identify specific genetic loci that affect disease risk. GWAS has been successful in discovering new risk loci for diseases, yet it is still difficult to clinically predict complex polygenic diseases. We have previously shown that genetic interactions underlying human diseases form structured networks connecting within and between biological pathways and have developed a method called BridGE for the systematic discovery of genetic interactions. BridGE has discovered many complex genetic interactions from human genotype cohort data for multiple diseases; however, these genetic interactions have not yet been used as features to predict disease risk. In this work, we created a machine-learning (ML) pipeline for predicting Parkinson's disease case-control phenotypes that leverages combinatorial (pairwise) genotype information and curated gene sets (e.g., pathways). We evaluated our pipeline with two types of genetic interaction data models: pairwise SNPs and pathway-based aggregated SNP pairs. These are compared against a data model of single SNPs with no knowledge of pathways or genetic interactions. Aggregating SNP pairs into biological pathways on average outperformed SNP-pair only data models in all but one ML model. We also found that even though the aggregated SNP-pairs are derived from the single SNPs, the two data models fundamentally predict the same individuals differently. These results demonstrate that pathway-based genetic interactions are complementary to single SNPs when predicting Parkinson's disease and these genetic interactions could be used for other genomic-based predictive tasks.

title: PICDGI: Dynamic Gene Interaction Network Modeling Reveals Cancer Driver Genes from Single-Cell Data
authors: Komlan Atitey, Benedict Anchang
abstract: Understanding how gene-gene interactions shape tumor progression is essential for identifying cancer driver genes (CDGs), yet most existing approaches overlook dynamic regulatory dependencies and focus on mutation frequency alone. We introduce PICDGI, a network-based computational framework that reconstructs time-evolving gene interaction structures from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data to identify regulatory drivers of cancer progression. PICDGI models gene expression dynamics through a time-varying interaction network, where latent gene-gene dependencies are inferred using a probabilistic state-space formulation. By combining variational Bayesian inference with MCMC sampling, the framework estimates posterior distributions over interaction strengths, enabling robust quantification of both regulatory influence and uncertainty. These inferred networks are used to derive a driver coefficient, which prioritizes genes based on their dynamic impact on system-wide expression changes. In lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) scRNA-seq data, PICDGI reconstructs biologically meaningful interaction patterns and recovers established oncogenes and tumor suppressors. It further identifies novel candidate drivers, including JPH1 and CHEK1, which occupy central positions in inferred interaction networks and are linked to calcium signaling, mitochondrial function, and DNA repair. These genes exhibit trajectory-aligned regulatory influence consistent with tumor evolution and immune modulation. Compared to spatial autocorrelation-based methods implemented in Monocle 3, PICDGI identifies genes with stronger network-driven and progression-consistent activity patterns. Validation on an independent pediatric AML cohort demonstrates that PICDGI generalizes across cancer types, consistently recovering known drivers and relapse-associated regulatory modules. By integrating dynamic network inference with single-cell resolution data, PICDGI provides a systems-level framework for uncovering rare and context-specific drivers of cancer progression.

title: Sample-Specific Differential miRNA Network Rewiring Associated with Asthma Exacerbation Using LIONESS
authors: Parham Hadikhani, Shraddha Piparia, Alvin T Kho, Michael McGeachie, Rinku Sharma, Scott T. Weiss, Kimberly Glass, Kelan Tantisira
abstract: Background: Asthma exacerbations confer considerable clinical and economic burden, and the molecular regulatory mechanisms are not well understood. MicroRNAs (miRNAs) are post-transcriptional modulators of immune and inflammatory pathways that may regulate exacerbations. Differential expression analysis cannot account for changes in miRNA regulatory interactions. Sample-specific network analysis may be useful for understanding the co-regulatory architecture and network rewiring within individual omics samples. Methods: We analyzed serum miRNA sequencing data from two CAMP cohorts of children with asthma (n = 491 discovery cohort and n = 485 replication cohort). Sample-specific miRNA co-expression networks were constructed using both standard LIONESS and a sparsity-aware LIONESS approach. Using both methods, differential edges were identified by comparing exacerbators (>1 exacerbation events during Year 1) and non-exacerbators (≤1 event) using ordinary least squares regression with FDR correction. Results were replicated in the second cohort and compared to standard LIONESS. Results: Analysis of networks derived using sparsity-aware LIONESS identified 18 differential edges, whereas the standard LIONESS identified 46 differential edges; one edge was identified using both approaches miR-483-5p–miR-92a-3p. Although standard LIONESS identified a larger number of differential edges, it did not replicate in the second cohort (p = 0.15). In contrast, the sparsity-aware approach identified a more constrained network topology with stronger replication (p = 0.0042). Conclusions: Sample-specific miRNA rewiring differentially identifies exacerbators and non-exacerbators and is reproducible across cohorts and can be used to understand changes in miRNA regulation with asthma exacerbation. Our comparison of standard versus sparsity-aware LIONESS demonstrated a trade-off between sensitivity and reproducibility.
keywords: LIONESS; Network Rewiring; Asthma Exacerbation; Sample-Specific Differential miRNA; differential edges

title: BIRDccNEST: Interpretable single cell characterization with inferred cell networks
authors: Gizem Cicekli, Adrita Samanta, Hao Zhu, Donna Slonim
abstract: Motivation: Trajectory inference for single cell RNA sequencing data aims to elucidate continuous biological processes like differentiation by ordering cells along a pseudo-temporal trajectory. While there are nominally-unsupervised trajectory inference algorithms, many still require designating a root node to create the directed trajectory relationship ordering amongst cell clusters. Here, we introduce BIRDccNEST (pronounced “bird’s nest”), an efficient unsupervised framework for characterizing cells and defining trajectories in scRNA-seq data by inferring directed cell-cell relationship networks. Methods: The BIRDccNEST framework infers directed cell networks by applying our RegDiffusion network inference algorithm to the transposed scRNA-seq expression matrix, learning a weighted directed adjacency matrix whose edge weights capture the similarity of expression distributions between individual cells. These networks are then transformed into cell flow networks, where the directed relationships between cell-cell communities are found with oriented maximum spanning trees, yielding interpretable trajectories and characterizing subgroups of cells. Results: We demonstrate on BEELINE datasets that BIRDccNEST finds new cell subtypes more coherent than the cell states identified in their original publications, while automatically capturing the known underlying temporal or developmental trajectories. For all datasets, we show that the BIRDccNEST cell clusters are significantly more coherent, as measured by the Davies-Bouldin Index and Silhouette Score. Availability: The full manuscript appeared in Proceedings of the 20th annual Machine Learning in Computational Biology meeting, PMLR 311:270-279, September, 2025. Code is available at: https://bcb.cs.tufts.edu/BIRDccNEST.html

title: From Spatial Transcriptomics to Network Biology in Health and Disease
authors: Helder Nakaya
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics is opening new ways to study how tissue architecture shapes disease. In this seminar, I will present our work integrating spatial transcriptomics and network biology to investigate infection and cancer. I will highlight computational tools developed in our group, especially CellReach, which measures spatial distances and neighborhood relationships between cell types across tissue regions. I will also discuss how we analyze gene networks within cells as a function of their spatial location, connecting local tissue context to transcriptional states and cellular interactions. This framework helps move from descriptive tissue maps to a network view of health and disease.

title: Spatially Varying Gene Regulatory Network Inference from Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Yurui Li, Jin Chen, Ting Lu, Nien-Pei Tsai, Haohan Wang
abstract: Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) govern cellular functions and are shaped by heterogeneous local microenvironments, leading to spatially varying regulatory patterns across tissues. Thus, high-resolution GRN inference with spatial context is essential. However, most existing approaches either operate at the cell-type level or infer cell-specific GRNs without modeling spatial organization and neighborhood effects, limiting their ability to capture microenvironment-driven regulatory variation. To address this, we propose SVGRN, a deep learning framework that infers spatially resolved, cell-or spot-specific GRNs by conditioning regulatory inference on spatial context and local neighborhood information. SVGRN integrates gene expression, regulatory interactions, and spatial coordinates within a structural equation modeling framework implemented using a conditional variational autoencoder, enabling nonlinear modeling of spatially varying regulatory programs in an unsupervised manner. By conditioning on target locations and incorporating neighborhood information, SVGRN refines tissue-level regulation into cell-or spot-specific GRNs. Across simulated datasets, SVGRN consistently outperforms state-of-the-art methods under diverse and challenging conditions, demonstrating robust recovery of regulatory interactions. Applications to seqFISH mouse embryo and Visium human cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma (cSCC) and fallopian tube datasets show that SVGRN captures spatially varying regulatory programs across distinct microenvironments, providing insights into development, tumor progression, and tissue organization. Notably, SVGRN reveals microenvironment-dependent, cell-or spot-specific regulatory interactions missed by non-spatial or cell-type level methods, highlighting its ability to resolve fine-grained regulatory heterogeneity. Together, these results position SVGRN as a robust and broadly applicable framework for uncovering spatially resolved regulatory mechanisms in complex tissues.

title: Inferring and Evaluating Network Medicine-Based Disease Modules with Nextflow
authors: Johannes Kersting, Chloé Bucheron, Lisa M. Spindler, Joaquim Aguirre-Plans, Quirin Manz, Tanja Pock, Mo Tan, Fernando M. Delgado-Chaves, Cristian Nogales, Harald H. H. W. Schmidt, Jörg Menche, Andreas Maier, Jan Baumbach, Emre Guney, Markus List
abstract: Motivation: Most diseases result from complex molecular interactions of genes and proteins. Various network-based methods characterize these mechanisms by expanding seed genes into disease modules. Their underlying algorithmic strategies differ, making it difficult to determine which of the created modules are most useful or biologically plausible. Results: To address this challenge, we developed an all-in-one pipeline that handles installation, input preparation, execution, and systematic evaluation of six widely used module detection tools, considering module topology, functional coherence, robustness, and the capacity to recover seeds. To showcase the value of our pipeline and provide guidance to potential users, we conducted a comprehensive evaluation across 50 different disease-network combinations, revealing substantial variability among the derived disease modules, driven by both network and algorithm choices. We show that methods are robust to minor perturbations but struggle to recover omitted seeds. None consistently outperforms all others, underscoring the need for careful method selection. Our work enables the systematic comparison of disease module discovery approaches and promotes reproducible network medicine research. Integrated into the nf-core project, it is intended as an extendable, long-term resource for tracking progress in the field. Availability and Implementation: The pipeline is implemented in Nextflow. Code and documentation are available through GitHub (https://github.com/nf-core/ diseasemodulediscovery) and the nf-core website (https://nf-co.re/diseasemodulediscovery). title: EPIC: Event Prototyping via Information Constrained graph learning for personalized cancer driver gene prediction
authors: Sang-Pil Cho, Young-Rae Cho
abstract: Motivation: Precision oncology relies on accurately distinguishing patient-specific driver mutations from the vast background of passenger alterations. While graph-based computational methods have emerged as powerful tools for this task, they often struggle to preserve the distinct genomic context of individual mutations within complex biological networks. Consequently, subtle patient-specific driver signals are frequently obscured by dominant topological patterns, critically impeding the identification of individualized oncogenic events essential for personalized cancer therapy. Results: To address this, we propose EPIC, a novel framework for Event Prototyping via Information Constrained Graph Learning. Unlike traditional node-centric approaches, EPIC redefines driver prediction as a metric learning task in an event embedding space. We introduce an information constrained learning strategy that imposes explicit geometric constraints on feature variance, effectively preventing feature collapse and ensuring that low-frequency driver signals are distinctively preserved. Experiments on large-scale cancer cohorts demonstrate that EPIC significantly outperforms established baselines. Notably, the model prioritizes low-frequency driver variants typically overlooked by population-based methods, mapping them to critical oncogenic mechanisms associated with drug resistance and metastasis. Furthermore, clinical actionability analysis confirms that EPIC substantially expands the patient population eligible for targeted therapies. EPIC provides a robust and context-aware solution for personalized cancer driver discovery, bridging the gap between genomic data and actionable therapeutic insights. Availability: The source code and datasets are available at https://github.com/spcho-dev/EPIC

title: Single-Cell Multiome Analysis Links Genetic Risk to a Cell-Type–Specific Regulatory Program in L6 IT Car3 Neurons Following Opioid Exposure
authors: Fengge Chang, Alexey Kozlenkov, Jinyoung Jung, Gregory Rompala, Yasmin Hurd, Zhana Duren, Stella Dracheva
abstract: Opioid use disorder (OUD) is a major public health crisis, however the mechanisms underlying its molecular pathology remain unclear. Here, we performed single-nucleus multiome profiling (snRNA-seq + snATAC-seq) of 331,015 nuclei from postmortem human orbitofrontal cortex across 14 heroin users and 12 controls. Differential expression analysis revealed most of the differentially expressed genes (DEGs) are observed in intratelencephalic (IT) neuron populations. Especially L6 IT Car3 and L6b neurons showed significant enriched in KEGG morphine addiction pathway (hsa05032). Co-expression analysis identified a gene program (Module 5) that is highly enriched for differentially expressed genes and morphine addiction pathways in L6 IT Car3 neurons. Notably, this module exhibits markedly stronger enrichment compared to all other detected modules in L6 IT Car3. Integration with previous GWAS study revealed significant enrichment of OUD heritability within regulatory elements linked to this module. Multiple genome-wide significant and sub-threshold risk loci overlap these regions, indicating that genetic risk preference maps to this transcriptional program. We next integrated transcription factors with Module 5 to reconstruct a hierarchical regulatory architecture underlying this gene program. This analysis defined three functional classes of regulators: (i) candidate upstream regulators, (ii) core regulators, and (iii) downstream effectors. Together, these regulators form a coordinated network that drives this gene program. Representative factors include HIF1A and ARNT (upstream), EGR family members (core), and CREB1 and NPAS2 (downstream). Together, our results identify a cell-type-specific regulatory network in L6 IT Car3 neurons that links genetic susceptibility to a cell-type-specific transcriptional program in OUD.

title: Deep integrative multiplex network-based analysis of rare neuromuscular disorders reveals overlapping multiscale endotypes involved in cardiac and skeletal muscle myopathies
authors: Iker Núñez Carpintero, Philipp Friedrich, Davide Cirillo, Alfonso Valencia, Jörg Menche, Julia Guthrie
abstract: Applying these integrative methods to analyze large-scale biomedical data to rare diseases remains challenging due to limited data availability. A central difficulty is interpreting molecular relationships linking clinically overlapping conditions, knowledge that could uncover opportunities for drug repositioning. Addressing such scenarios requires strategies that combine scarce disease-specific data with biomedical knowledge databases. Here we showcase how multiplex networks can address this challenge: we introduce multiCore, a network diffusion–based approach to perform endotype definition using multiplex networks. Focusing on 13 monogenic neuromuscular disease (NMD) categories, we build a biomedical multiplex network comprising 71 layers spanning phenome, tissue-specific interactome and co-expression, pathways, and drug–target relationship knowledge. Disease-specific layer relevance is then used to compute NMD modules, from which molecularly and functionally coherent endotypes are derived. Overlap analysis among the resulting endotypes reveals a densely connected landscape: 97.2% share genes with endotypes from other NMD categories, with a major cluster of 11 highly overlapping endotypes being enriched for processes underlying skeletal and cardiac muscle development, providing mechanistic insight into the co-occurrence of skeletal and cadiomyopathic myopathies and highlighting therapeutically actionable bridging genetic interactors currently under study with clinical partners. We further study how multiplex-based disease module identification remains robust under systematic layer-removal perturbations, and we introduce netviz-interactive, a 3D visualization framework that enables intuitive analysis of multiplex networks, revealing strong contributions from heart and skeletal muscle protein–protein interaction and coexpression layers. Our results establish multiplex networks as a robust framework for integrating large-scale knowledge for uncovering shared rare disease pathomechanisms.

title: GATSBI: Improving context-aware protein embeddings through biologically motivated data splits
authors: Gowri Nayar, Russ B. Altman
abstract: Motivation-Understanding protein function requires integrating diverse biological evidence while accounting for strong contextual dependence. Recent protein embedding methods increasingly leverage heterogeneous biological networks, yet their evaluation protocols often fail to reflect the specific biological tasks for which the embeddings are intended. Prediction of missing interactions, annotation of new proteins, and discovery of functional modules require fundamentally different data partitions, such as edge-masked versus node-held-out splits. Moreover, most approaches report performance primarily on well-studied proteins, where computational predictions are least needed, risking substantial overestimation of real-world utility. Results-We introduce a graph attention–based framework (GATSBI) to construct context-aware protein embeddings from integrated protein–protein interactions, co-expression, sequence representations, and tissue-specific associations. Using task-aligned evaluation protocols, we show that models trained with biologically appropriate partitions achieve markedly better generalization. Across interaction, function, and functional set prediction, GATSBI consistently outperforms existing pretrained embeddings for both well-studied and understudied proteins, with the largest gains observed for the understudied regime and under inductive node-held-out evaluation. To enable broad reuse, we provide the learned embeddings for download for application to other protein prediction tasks. Availability and Implementation-Code and models for our experiments are available at https://github.com/Helix-Research-Lab/GATSBI-embedding

title: The NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem Data Distillery Knowledge Graph: A Scalable Framework for Multimodal Integration and Network-Based Biomedical Discovery
authors: Shankar Subramaniam, Dubravka Jevtic, Jyl Boline, Jeet Vora, Jared Nedzel, Clara Bakker, Julia Markowski, Michael Tiemeyer, Rene Ranzinger, Andrew Schroeder, Aleks Mihajlovic, Jeffrey Grethe, Bernard de Bono, Matthew Roth, Robert Fullem, Kristin Ardlie, Peter Park, Raja Mazumder, Christophe Lambert, Kristina Cole, Sarah Tasian, Adam Resnick, Aleksandar Milosavljevic, Elizabeth Goldmuntz, Avi Ma'Ayan, Sharon Diskin, Jonathan C. Hill, Shiping Zhang, Tiffany Callahan, Patricia J. Sullivan, Aditya Lahiri, Varduhi Petrosyan, Benjamin J. Stear, Daniel Clarke, Jeremy Yang, Heesu Kim, Sherry Jenkins, Zhourui Xie, James Terry, Vincent T. Metzger, Praveen Kumar, Srinivasan Ramachandran, Eoin Fahy, Thomas H. Gillepsie, Fahim Imam, Natalia Kokash
abstract: Integrating heterogeneous biomedical data in basic, translational and clinical research domains remains a central challenge in network biology. We present the NIH Common Fund Data Ecosystem Data Distillery Knowledge Graph (CFDE DDKG), a large-scale, ontology-aligned property graph designed to enable graph-native integration and analysis of multimodal biomedical data including genomics data. Built on the Unified Biomedical Knowledge Graph (UBKG) framework, the DDKG harmonizes over 180 ontologies and data sources and millions of data points into a unified UMLS-like concept-code–term graph schema, supporting semantically consistent, multi-hop querying across heterogeneous data domains. The DDKG integrates data from large-scale NIH Common Fund resources, including GTEx, HuBMAP, Kids First, LINCS, and Metabolomics Workbench, alongside additional curated resources such as ClinVar, STRING, and MSigDB. This architecture enables direct traversal across genomic variation, gene expression, regulatory features, pathways, and phenotypes without requiring manual data harmonization or intermediate pipelines. To demonstrate its analytical capabilities, we applied the DDKG to several use cases, including the investigation of the causal genetics behind the observed co-occurrence between certain pairs of childhood cancers and structural birth defects. We integrated variants from whole-genome sequencing data from four pediatric cohorts hosted in the Kids First Data Resource Center. We also integrated developmental single-cell RNA-seq data from embryonic and fetal heart tissue into the DDKG. The DDKG provides a scalable, extensible framework for multimodal integration and supports reproducible network-based inference across heterogeneous biomedical data.

title: Predicting Phosphatase-Substrate Association using a Heterogeneous Knowledge Graph
authors: Jannatul Fardaus, Mahmudul Hasan Robin, Mehmet Koyuturk, Marzieh Ayati
abstract: Protein phosphorylation is a central regulatory mechanism in cellular signaling, controlled by the opposing actions of kinases and phosphatases. While kinase-substrate interactions have been extensively characterized both experimentally and computationally, phosphatase-substrate associations remain poorly understood. Existing computational methods are either limited to a small subset of phosphatases or rely primarily on sequence-based features, which often capture shared motif patterns and lack the resolution to distinguish specific phosphatase-substrate interactions. In this talk, we present PSNet, a heterogeneous knowledge graph-based computational framework for predicting phosphatase-substrate associations. PSNet integrates diverse biological data sources, including phosphatase-substrate interactions, kinase-substrate associations, protein-protein interactions, pathways, disease annotations, and drug-target relationships. These heterogeneous data are unified into a multi-relational knowledge graph that captures both direct enzymatic regulation and broader biological context. Network embedding methods are then applied to learn low-dimensional molecular representations, which are then used in supervised machine learning models to predict phosphatase-substrate associations. The framework is evaluated using experimentally validated data from the Human Dephosphorylation Database under both link prediction and phosphatase prioritization settings. Results demonstrate that PSNet achieves strong predictive performance (AUC of 0.97) across multiple embedding methods and classifiers. Furthermore, systematic analysis reveals that diverse relationship types contribute complementary predictive signals, highlighting the value of integrative graph modeling. Overall, this work presents a scalable and integrative computational approach for large-scale phosphatase-substrate discovery. This approach addresses the current knowledge gap in phosphatase biology and facilitates the discovery of novel regulatory mechanisms and therapeutic targets

title: From General-Purpose to Disease-Specific Features: Aligning LLM Embeddings on a Disease-Specific Biomedical Knowledge Graph for Drug Repurposing
authors: Suman Pandey, Muhammed Talo, David Siderovski, Nathalie Sumien, Serdar Bozdag
abstract: General-purpose Large-Language Model (LLM) embeddings encode rich semantics but often lack the task-specific context needed for biomedical inference tasks such as computational drug repurposing. We introduce a novel framework called Contextualizing LLM Embeddings via Attention-based gRaph learning (CLEAR). CLEAR is a multimodal representation-fusion framework that aligns LLM embeddings using the topological information of a context-specific Knowledge Graph (KG). CLEAR achieved state-of-the-art results on five benchmark datasets, improving predictive performance (i.e., F1 score) by up to 30% over prior methods. Furthermore, we applied CLEAR to identify FDA-approved drugs for potential repurposing / re-labeling to treat Alzheimer disease (AD) and related dementias such as Parkinson disease-related dementia and Lewy Body dementia (collectively referred to as ADRD by the U.S. National Institute on Aging). CLEAR learned a biologically coherent embedding space, prioritized top ADRD candidate drugs, and correctly summarized known therapeutic relationships for FDA-approved AD drugs. Overall, CLEAR grounds biomedical LLM embeddings with context-specific KG signals to advance drug repurposing in data-sparse, real-world settings.

title: drGT: Attention-Guided Gene Assessment of Drug Response Utilizing a Drug-Cell-Gene Heterogeneous Network
authors: Yoshitaka Inoue, Hunmin Lee, Tianfan Fu, Rui Kuang, Augustin Luna
abstract: Background: For translational impact, accurate drug response prediction and biological plausibility of predictive features are needed. We present drGT, a heterogeneous graph deep learning model over drugs, genes, and cell lines that couples prediction with mechanism-oriented interpretability via attention coefficients (ACs). Results: We assess predictive generalization (random, unseen-drug, unseen-cell, and zero-shot splits) and biological plausibility (text-mined PubMed co-mentions and comparison to a structure-based DTI predictor) on GDSC, NCI60, and CTRP datasets. Across benchmarks, drGT delivers top regression performance while maintaining competitive classification accuracy for drug sensitivity. Under random 5-fold cross-validation, drGT attains an AUROC of up to 0.945 (3rd overall) and an R2 of up to 0.690, outperforming baselines on regression. In leave-one-out tests for unseen cell lines and drugs, drGT achieves AUROCs of 0.706 and 0.844, and R2 values of 0.692 and 0.022, the only model yielding positive R2 for unseen drugs. In zero-shot prediction, drGT achieves an AUROC of 0.786 and a regression R2 of 0.334, representing the highest scores among models. For interpretability, AC-derived drug-gene links recover known biology: among 976 drugs with known DTIs, 36.9% of predicted links match established DTIs, and 63.7% are supported by either PubMed abstracts or a structure-based predictive model. Enrichment analyses of AC-prioritized genes reveal drug-perturbed biological processes, providing pathway-level explanations. Conclusions: drGT advances predictive generalization and mechanism-centered interpretability, offering state-of-the-art regression accuracy and literature-supported hypotheses, leveraging graph learning from heterogeneous data for biological discovery. title: Challenges and Opportunities in Single-Sample Network Modeling
authors: Marieke Lydia Kuijjer, Margherita De Marzio, Kimberly Glass
abstract: Analysis of biological networks can provide critical insights into disease. Many methods have been developed to estimate biological networks using multiple experimental samples, an approach that may not capture population-level heterogeneity. Other methods have been developed to infer networks for individual samples, i.e. single-sample networks. However, single-sample network methods have been formulated differently, making it challenging to compare them. To address this issue, we re-cast the mathematics of several single-sample network methods using common variables. We then systematically explore the parameters, caveats, and underlying assumptions of these methods. We find that the mathematics of two methods, SWEET and BONOBO, includes a scale factor that drives the predicted single-sample networks toward a background network. The impact is that the networks predicted by these methods tend to have high accuracy but low specificity. In contrast, SSN estimates the most specific but least accurate networks, while LIONESS straddles these domains, with an accuracy almost as high as SWEET and BONOBO and a specificity almost as high as SSN. Our results highlight the challenges encountered when modeling single-sample networks. However, they also point to important methodological synergies, providing an opportunity to create a common framework that can be used to improve single-sample network inference.

title: VDJ-REMIX: Repertoire Module Identification and eXploration
authors: Sakina Amin, Lauren Overend, Felicia Tucci, Bo Sun, Justin Whalley, Michael Dustin, Julian Knight, Rachael Bashford-Rogers
abstract: Motivation: High-throughput sequencing of B and T cell repertoires provides unprecedented insights into adaptive immunity but generates high-dimensional feature sets that are challenging to interpret. Standard dimensionality reduction techniques are often suboptimal for adaptive immune receptor repertoire (AIRR) data, which exhibits multi-collinearity, heterogeneous data types, and missingness. Results: Here, we present VDJ-REMIX, an R package implementing a robust, network-based framework to deconstruct complex repertoire feature matrices into biologically interpretable modules. By refactoring weighted correlation network analysis (WGCNA), VDJ-REMIX provides a tailored workflow for preprocessing, imputation, and modularization of immune repertoire data. We demonstrate its utility across diverse contexts, including autoimmunity, inflammation, and acute infection. In autoimmune patients, VDJ-REMIX identified distinct B cell signatures that stratified diseases and revealed opposing dynamic responses to B cell-depleting versus anti-proliferative therapies. In COVID-19 and non-COVID-19 sepsis patients, it distinguished disease-specific signatures from shared severe infection responses and identified modules correlated with severity. Analysis of flow-sorted B cell populations stratified by FCGR2B genotype recapitulated known tolerance defects and uncovered population-specific repertoire signatures linked to inhibitory receptor dysfunction, providing orthogonal validation of module biological coherence. Finally, applied to a single-cell multi-omics dataset of immune cells in pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) combining gene expression with AIRR-seq, VDJ-REMIX recovered modules linking BCR isotype usage and clonality to cytotoxic, interferon-responsive, and regulatory immune programmes. VDJ-REMIX is a versatile tool enabling systematic exploration of immunological variation and biomarker discovery from complex immune repertoire data. Availability and Implementation: VDJ-REMIX is freely available at https:// github.com/Bashford-Rogers-lab/vdjremix.

title: Traditional machine learning vs. deep learning from dynamic graph representations of proteins’ 3D folds in the task of protein structure classification
authors: Aydin Wells, Francis Gatsi, Aaron Striegel, Tijana Milenkovic
abstract: Determining protein function experimentally is resource-consuming. This has motivated computational prediction of protein function. A protein’s amino acid sequence determines its 3D structure/fold, which in turn determines its function. Consequently, computational methods extract features from sequences or 3D structures to predict functions. Before such features are used for function prediction, it is desirable to first validate that they actually meaningfully reflect the proteins' folds. Protein structure classification (PSC) serves exactly this purpose. PSC is a supervised task of linking proteins' features to their CATH/ SCOP/SCOPe structural classes. Historically, features for PSC have been extracted from sequences or 3D structures. More recently, features extracted from protein structure network (PSN) representations of 3D structures have emerged, which have often outperformed sequence or direct (non-network) 3D structural approaches. The earlier successes were based on static PSNs. More recently, we introduced a dynamic PSN to mimic a protein's folding dynamics. In our PSC evaluation on ~44,000 CATH/SCOPe domains, dynamic PSNs were significantly superior to static PSNs, and thus by transitivity to sequence and direct (non-network) 3D structural approaches. This existing dynamic PSN approach is a "traditional ML" approach: it uses manual, pre-engineered features with an off-the-shelf classifier. Hence, we examine whether deep learning (DL) can automatically extract additional signal from dynamic PSNs; we examine multiple DL architectures/variants. In our PSC evaluation, traditional ML holds value even in presence of the methodologically more advanced DL, i.e., traditional ML is comparable to the best of the DL variants in terms of accuracy, while also being much faster.

title: stem.MAP: A mouse embryonic stem cell specific protein complex map
authors: Akshaya Rajaraman, Samantha N. Fischer, Ron Sistrunk, Ryan S. Gray, Kevin Drew
abstract: Proteins assemble into protein complexes to coordinate all cellular processes, with each complex shaped by cell-type, diseases, and environmental conditions. Identifying context-specific protein complexes is necessary to build insight into development and diseases. Most systemic studies overlook this, instead offering a static, one-size-fits-all atlas of complexes. Current methods to identify context-specific complexes require thousands of mass spectrometry experiments, are costly and laborious. To address this, we present stem.MAP, a mouse Embryonic Stem Cell (mESC)-specific protein complex map generated using Co-Fractionation Mass Spectrometry (CF-MS) experiments and machine learning(ML). CF-MS measures protein co-elution in orthogonal separations to predict their interactions in a label-free manner. We apply three ML strategies to improve the predictive power while minimizing reliance on large orthogonal datasets. We integrate (1) prior knowledge from a cell-type agnostic map, hu.MAP 3.0, (2) refine benchmarks to be cell-type specific, and (3) introduce randomness in priors to recognize true interactions not supported by priors. We evaluated our stem-cell specific protein complex map and observed that the prior-weighted model markedly outperforms an unweighted model. stem.MAP ultimately predicts >375,000 interactions and ~4,000 complexes. We identify stem-cell specific variants of major chromatin remodeling assemblies including the BAF-pBAF and the NuRD complex. stem.MAP also predicts ~1,400 high confidence novel interactions, which we validated using AlphaFold3. Further, we used stem.MAP to prioritize candidate genes for congenital heart defects in early zebrafish development, where 66% candidate gene knockouts produced heart-related phenotypes like edema and hemorrhage. Together, our results establish stem.MAP as a validated and scalable approach for identifying context-specific interactions and prioritizing disease-relevant complexes in early development.

title: The AI Revolution in Protein Science: From Prediction to Discovery and Cure
authors: Qian Cong
abstract: Protein–protein interactions (PPIs) are central to biological function, yet mapping the complex human interactome and translating these insights into therapeutics has long remained a formidable challenge. By integrating advanced deep learning with large-scale genomic data, our work establishes a comprehensive framework for interpreting protein sequences, structures, interactions, and function. To address the limitations of traditional in silico screening, we enhanced coevolutionary signals using 30 petabytes of unassembled genomic data and developed a novel deep-learning model trained on millions of predicted protein structures. This approach enabled a systematic survey of the human proteome, leading to the high-precision prediction of thousands of previously uncharacterized PPIs. Beyond uncovering new mechanisms of human disease and identifying cancer vulnerabilities, these high-confidence 3D interaction models provide a direct structural foundation for therapeutic development. Building on this expanded interactome, we are leveraging generative AI for precise protein design and deploying highly accurate computational methods to identify ligandable cysteines. Together, this integrated pipeline accelerates the progression from fundamental interaction discovery to the rational design of targeted therapeutics and novel covalent drugs.

title: ADAPTS -Autoimmune Disease Analysis Platform Testing Space using a Trusted Federated Platform for Research Data Interoperability
authors: Richard Scheuermann, John Greene, Davide Aloi, Jeffrey Brabec, Sangram Sahu, Anne Deslattes-Mays, Victoria Shanmugam
abstract: Autoimmune diseases represent the most common group of chronic conditions affecting Americans. More than 140 known autoimmune diseases have been identified. Importantly, people with one autoimmune disease have a higher probability of developing another. Advances in molecular and clinical profiling are helping define disease subgroups (endotypes) more precisely through cross disease immuno-clinical phenotyping. The Autoimmune Disease Analysis Platform Testing Space (ADAPTS) is supported by the NIH Office of Autoimmune Disease Research in the Office of Research on Women’s Health (OADR-ORWH) and the National Library of Medicine (NLM). This federated digital ecosystem supports research across multiple autoimmune diseases being studied in the NIH Intramural Research Program (IRP). ADAPTS aims to enable scaled cross-cohort analysis of shared and disease-specific biological mechanisms. Objectives include enabling federated data analysis at scale, multi-omics data integration, identification of new disease endotypes, and development of Common Data Elements (CDEs) for autoimmune disease research. ADAPTS’s instance of the Lifebit Trusted Research Environment data platform, a Platform-as-a-Service, enables cross-cohort analysis of autoimmune disease datasets through federated approaches that allow analysis of in situ data without centralizing or replicating sensitive data, which remains Federal Information Security Modernization Act (FISMA) Moderate protected with a complete audit trail. The autoimmune disease-specific data sets are maintained across multiple IC-specific secure environments, preserving governance, and data access control. Data are mapped to the OMOP Common Data Model with AI assistance to standardize clinical and research variables, enabling consistent cross study analysis. This methodology enhances reproducibility and standardization across cohorts through harmonized data and shared analytical approaches, supporting the identification of shared and disease-specific biological mechanisms and the development of precision medicine strategies and improved patient outcomes for autoimmune diseases. Initial analysis results will be presented.

title: The NIAID Discovery Portal: A federated ecosystem for finding infectious and immune-mediated disease resources
authors: Chunlei Wu
abstract: Enabling meaningful reuse of infectious and immune-mediated disease (IID) data requires researchers to efficiently discover and evaluate relevant data across distributed, heterogeneous resources. Inconsistent metadata standards and fragmented repository landscapes create persistent barriers to data reuse and cross-study integration. The NIAID Data Ecosystem (NDE) Discovery Portal addresses this challenge by providing a unique, centralized interface that aggregates datasets, samples, computational tools, and other resources from diverse biomedical repositories. Currently indexing over 4.3 million resources at the data level and 43 at the resource level, the NDE Discovery Portal standardizes and augments key IID metadata fields to enable intuitive filtering, semantic search, and programmatic access via API. AI-assisted search interprets user intent and surfaces semantically-related results, while dynamic filtering and visual metadata summaries allow users to quickly assess data relevance. Program Collections highlight data from NIH-funded initiatives, supporting structured discovery workflows across subdomains. The NDE can be accessed at https://data.niaid.nih.gov. In this session, we demonstrate how the NDE supports discovery strategies ranging from exploratory browsing to targeted data search. This approach enhances researchers’ ability to integrate data across the IID landscape. We also discuss future applications of NDE metadata infrastructure to support knowledge generation, data citation, and FAIR data practices across biomedical research.
