title: AnVIL: A Federated Cloud Ecosystem for Scalable, Secure, and Reproducible Genomic Data Science and Clinical-Genomic Harmonization
authors: Jonathan Lawson
abstract: Recent years have seen explosive growth in human genomics, single‑cell, functional, and clinical datasets that promise transformative insights for human health. These opportunities come with substantial challenges as moving protected datasets to local institutional compute is costly, complex, difficult to secure and govern. NHGRI's Genomic Data Science Analysis, Visualization, and Informatics Lab‑space (AnVIL) addresses these challenges by inverting the data‑sharing model, bringing researchers to secure data and compute. AnVIL is federally approved infrastructure for NHGRI and beyond, hosting 5 PB of open and controlled-access datasets from flagship programs such as GREGoR, PRIMED, eMERGE, HPRC, T2T, CCDG, and CMG. Quarterly releases and integration with DUOS and dbGaP streamline discovery while meeting NIH's latest requirements for secure, identity-verified access to controlled data. AnVIL provides integrated ecosystems for reproducible, scalable analysis. Terra delivers secure compute for collaborative projects. Dockstore shares reusable, containerized workflows. Galaxy offers a zero‑code, end‑to‑end analysis environment, while Bioconductor supports interactive, programmatic exploration and advanced statistical workflows and seqr enables Mendelian variant interpretation. The AnVIL Data Explorer lets users build metadata‑driven cohorts across studies. New services include an All of Us + AnVIL Imputation Service powered by 500,000+ genomes and the AnVIL Clinical Resource, which supports clinical‑genomic harmonization through REDCap ingestion, MapDragon vocabulary management, and OMOP transformations to accelerate discovery. AnVIL has matured into a secure platform used across hundreds of institutions, supporting thousands of users, with hundreds active monthly. The platform offers an expanding workflow catalog and continued scale‑ups in Galaxy and Bioconductor. These capabilities have produced measurable scientific impact through consortium analyses and method development. Community activities such as annual AnVIL Community Conferences, the AnVIL Champions Program foster broader adoption and training. By reducing redundant data movement, providing secure and auditable access, and offering shareable, reusable workflows together with harmonized clinical‑genomic infrastructure, AnVIL enables reproducible cross‑study analyses at consortium scale and accelerates translation of genomic data into discovery and clinical benefit.

title: Seven Bridges Core Infrastructure (SB-CI): A public–private model for secure, interoperable, and reusable data science with NIH stewardship
authors: Surya Saha, Garrett Rupp, Cera Fisher, Raegan O’Lone, Pavel Gongora, Johanna Samuelsson, Pavan Kalantri, Indhu Subramanian, Danilo Jovanovic, Selena Vukadinovic, Gaurav Mehta, Jitendra Deshmukh, Mike Kling, Jack Digiovanna
abstract: Motivation. Scalable analyses of genomic, multi-omic, clinical and imaging datasets for advanced biomedical research requires tiered and flexible security controls in a performant cloud infrastructure. Recent updates to the NIH Genomic Data Sharing Policy underscore the importance of trusted, and policy aligned environments that reduce barriers to collaboration and adoption without compromising security. Approach. We describe the Seven Bridges Core Infrastructure (SB CI), a proprietary, cloud based core developed through more than a decade of sustained NIH co design and shared governance. SB CI serves as the common technical foundation for three NIH funded, open science platforms, the NCI Cancer Genomics Cloud (CGC), CAVATICA, and NHLBI BioData Catalyst (BDC). Each platform serves a distinct user community. Integration between communities is enabled through SB CI’s implementation of the Global Alliance for Genomics and Health (GA4GH) standards for data access, portable workflow execution, and NIH governed authentication and authorization. SB CI operates within a FedRAMP Moderate environment aligned with NIST SP 800 53 controls, exceeding NIST SP 800 171 requirements for controlled access data. Results. Adoption of a shared, standards based core has enabled the three platforms to offer interoperable, secure cloud workspaces that support multi-cloud (AWS, GCP and Azure) native analysis. Platform features such as file management, API access, cloud cost billing, Jupyter and RStudio notebooks, imaging viewers, workflow management tools with rich provenance incentivize reuse of data, tools, and promote best practices across research programs. Impact. SB CI will be presented as a mature public–private partnership model in which NIH stewardship, open standards, and a secure proprietary core align technical implementation with policy objectives. This provides a foundation for AI enabled capabilities to support scalable analysis across large and heterogeneous datasets. The experience of CGC, CAVATICA, and BDC demonstrates how long term governance and standards based design can enable compliant access to controlled data, interoperability, and durable incentives for sharing and reuse in NIH funded health research.

title: FAIR Knowledge Graphs On-Demand
authors: Chris Bizon, Evan Morris, Kathleen Carter, Hina Shah, Alex Tropsha
abstract: Biomedical knowledge graphs draw from resources that are Findable, Accessible, Interoperable, and Reusable (FAIR) in principle but do not interoperate in practice. Differences in identifier systems, semantic models, provenance conventions, and deployment patterns make it difficult for researchers to reproducibly integrate the precise graph needed for a specific health research question. ROBOKOP addresses this gap through ORION, a graph-building framework that transforms independently maintained biomedical resources into modular, Biolink-compatible knowledge graphs (KG). ORION ingests source data, normalizes identifiers, harmonizes semantic types and predicates, preserves provenance, and emits reusable graph artifacts that can be combined into larger application-specific graphs. Building on this infrastructure, we have introduced the ROBOKOP Graph Repository: a distribution mechanism for installable knowledge graphs. Rather than requiring each user to rebuild or manually integrate source resources, the Graph Repository allows users to discover, retrieve, and compose prepared graph modules using package-manager-like mechanics; creating a customized knowledge graph is as simple as installing python packages. This tooling shifts biomedical KG construction from a centralized, one-size-fits-all release model toward an on-demand model in which researchers can create the dataset they need when they need it. The same infrastructure supports ROBOKOP’s production graph while also enabling smaller, targeted graphs for method development, reproducible analysis, and reuse by other software systems. By pairing ORION’s semantic harmonization with a practical graph distribution layer, ROBOKOP converts interoperable-but-not-interoperating resources into a reusable ecosystem of fully interoperating knowledge graphs. Furthermore, these consistent interoperable KGs can become the platform for creating an ecosystem of KG tools. This work advances social and technical infrastructure for health research by making biomedical data integration more modular, reproducible, and accessible to software communities beyond the original ROBOKOP deployment.

title: Clinical Dataset Structure: A Universal Framework for Structuring Clinical Research Datasets
authors: Bhavesh Patel, Aydan Gasimova, Sanjay Soundarajan, Nayoon Gim, Jamie Shaffer, Julia Owen, Aaron Lee
abstract: Motivation Clinical studies collect rich multimodal data, such as surveys, wearables, and eye images. There is currently no consensus on how to structure that data into a consistently organized dataset in line with the FAIR principles. As a result, clinical datasets are hard to reuse, and datasets from different studies are not interoperable, which limits the ability to pool data across studies and particularly undermines the development of AI models. Methodology To address this challenge in the NIH Bridge2AI-supported AI Ready and Exploratory Atlas for Diabetes Insights (AI-READI) project, we developed the Clinical Dataset Structure (CDS). The CDS is a standardized framework for organizing clinical research data and metadata, developed by unifying and extending existing domain-specific standard structures (e.g., Brain Imaging Data Structure), metadata schemas (DataCite, ClinicalTrials.gov), and AI/ML-focused standards (Datasheet, Healthsheet). Key results The CDS recommends organizing multimodal clinical research datasets into one folder per data type, named according to a set convention, where applicable standard structure must then be followed within each folder. It also recommends including multiple metadata files at the root level in human-friendly (e.g., README, Healthsheet) and machine-friendly (e.g., dataset_description.json, study_description.json) formats that collectively capture over 80 metadata elements. The CDS specification is documented openly at cds-specification.readthedocs.io. The AI-READI dataset, which is structured following the CDS, has already been downloaded over 950 times and contributed to multiple publications, demonstrating real-world impact. Impact The impact of the CDS is already evident through the AI-READI dataset. We expect greater impact as adoption scales, a goal we are pursuing through community outreach and tooling development to lower implementation barriers. In this presentation, we will introduce the CDS, present its implementation in the AI-READI dataset, and explain how the community can adopt and build on it.

title: CEDAR: A platform to drive standardization of metadata for FAIR data sharing and reuse
authors: Mark Musen
abstract: Scientists strive to make their datasets available in open repositories, with the goal that they might be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). Although it is hard for most investigators to remember all the “guiding principles” associated with FAIR data, there is one overarching requirement: The data need to be annotated with “rich,” discipline-specific, standardized metadata that can enable third parties to understand who performed the experiment, who or what the subjects were, what the experimental conditions were, and what the results appear to show. The CEDAR Workbench provides a library of templates that encode community standards for metadata in machine-actionable form, allowing investigators to annotate their data in a manner to promote FAIRness. CEDAR has been used to standardize metadata for a variety of large scientific consortia, including HuBMAP, SenNet, and HEAL. The system uses its metadata templates to acquire standardized metadata through Web forms or through spreadsheets, and it can help correct metadata to ensure adherence to standards. CEDAR templates thus provide a mechanism for scientific communities both to create shared metadata standards and to deploy those standards in a range of intelligent systems to promote open science.

title: Enabling Recognition and Reward of Artificial Intelligence Research Objects
authors: Kristi Holmes, Faraz Ahmad, Matt Carson, Mohammad Hosseini, Luke Rasmussen, Yuan Luo, John Chodacki, Arjun Krishnan
abstract: Researchers’ use of Artificial intelligence (AI) in biomedical research has generated a new class of research outputs for recognition. Since incentives, metrics, and impact stories remain largely human-centric, AI outputs can lack proper governance and context, potentially impacting reuse and reproducibility. This gap can be addressed through technical and social infrastructures to incentivize and reward AI research products. Make Data Count (MDC) advances data as a first-class research object, promoting responsible metrics for evaluating data use and impact. MDC supports repositories like Zenodo in producing compliant, high-quality data outputs by providing guidance and infrastructure for data metrics, metadata, and citation practices. Last year, MDC and partners produced a public Toolkit which includes: (1) a maturity model for evaluating institutional readiness; (2) a practical guide with implementation-ready resources; and (3) a set of real-world case studies. These efforts can help inform recognition and reward of AI generated outputs. Here, we extend MDC principles and the Toolkit to consider AI-enabled research outputs. We have developed a comprehensive structured taxonomy of AI research outputs to inform efforts. Other updates include an enhanced maturity model, guidance for communicating AI contributions on researcher CVs and to reviewers; and an initial set of use cases in Zenodo from NIH AI projects, including HF-ETIOLOGY and NUCATS, among others. This presentation will also address ethical considerations, provide context for other NIH sharing and reuse initiatives, and recommend additional activities to further support and advance recognition and reward of AI research outputs. By advancing infrastructure that captures the full spectrum of scholarly products, this work helps accelerate data-driven discovery, enables more meaningful evaluation and impact, and supports an open and trustworthy ecosystem for AI-driven biomedical research.

title: A Blueprint for FAIR Data Sharing Across a Distributed Biomedical Data Ecosystem
authors: Nancy Hoebelheinrich, Reed Shabman, Christine Kirkpatrick, Willem Van Panhuis, Rachel Waymack, Matthew Mayernik, Keith Maull, Bert Meerman, Barbara Magagna, Lisa Mayer, Meghan Hartwick, John Graybeal, Ismael Kherroubi Garcia, Sydney Foote, Doug Fils, Chris Erdmann, Julianne Christopher-Ohlin, Darya Pokutnaya
abstract: The National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID) has a long history of data sharing. However, the absence of requirements for data standards or repositories has led to a fragmented data landscape, preventing discovery, reuse, and interoperability of the millions of publicly available NIAID-funded datasets. To reduce these barriers, NIAID’s Office of Data Science and Emerging Technologies (ODSET) is developing a strategic framework across 11 NIAID-funded repositories with support from GO FAIR US (GFU). GFU data experts completed an initial evaluation, developing key findings and opportunities for future work, that ODSET developed into the first unified approach to NIAID research data, called A Blueprint for Including Digital Objects in the NIAID Data Ecosystem (the NIAID Blueprint). This flexible, minimal specification spans five focus areas: Minimal Metadata Schema, Persistent Identifiers, Minimal API Specifications for Metadata, Minimal Citation Requirements, and Point of Contact for Outreach and Training. These guidelines represent ways to make data easier to find and reuse, such as supporting integration with the NIAID Data Ecosystem Discovery Portal, a metadata catalog indexing over 4 million data records as of this date. Since the NIAID Blueprint’s launch in March 2025, ODSET and GFU have fostered a community of practice to implement and iteratively improve the recommendations. Initial repository adoption typically aligns with either: 1) using the NIAID Blueprint specification to develop new tools or methodologies, or 2) mapping existing practices to NIAID Blueprint recommendations. This framework demonstrates the impact of continuous learning through collaboration with interdisciplinary stakeholders, fostering critical conversation, and seeding new projects to connect NIAID data. This project provides a model for enhancing FAIRness and interoperability for complex biomedical research data that could apply to other complex data management ecosystems.

title: Accelerating Research Across the Biosciences Using Experimentally-Determined 3D Biostructures and Computed Structure Models of Proteins Generated using Artificial Intelligence/ Machine Learning
authors: Stephen K. Burley
abstract: RCSB Protein Data Bank (RCSB PDB; RCSB.org) is the United States data center for the global Protein Data Bank (PDB) archive of 3D structure data for large biological molecules (proteins, DNA, and RNA) essential for research and training in fundamental biology, health, bioenergy, and biotechnology. RCSB PDB, in collaboration with its Worldwide Protein Data Bank (wwPDB) partners, hosts structure deposition, data processing, and distribution centers for PDB data. The wwPDB rigorously validates and expertly curates 3D biostructure information essential for understanding human health and disease. The enormous wealth of 3D biostructure data stored in the PDB has underpinned significant advances in our understanding of protein architecture, culminating in recent breakthroughs in de novo protein structure prediction driven by artificial intelligence approaches and machine learning methodology. RCSB.org is the research-focused web portal of the RCSB PDB that provides open access to >250,000 PDB structures alongside >1 million predicted Computed Structure Models (CSMs) generated using AlphaFold (from AlphaFold DB v6) and RoseTTAFold or AlphaFold2 (from the ModelArchive). Both AlphaFold DB and the ModelArchive utilize the ModelCIF data standard, which interoperates with the PDBx/mmCIF data dictionary and is jointly managed by RCSB PDB, our wwPDB partners, and the wwPDB ModelCIF Working Group. RCSB.org is a “living data resource.” PDB structures and CSMs are integrated weekly with related functional annotations from ~50 trusted external resources, providing up-to-date information for each 3D biostructure. For the avoidance of doubt, experimentally-determined PDB structures and CSMs delivered on RCSB.org by the RCSB PDB are clearly identified as to their respective provenance and reliability. Both PDB structures and CSMs can be searched, analyzed, and visualized using powerful online resources and tools freely available at RCSB.org. RCSB PDB is funded by the National Institutes of Health (R01GM157729), the United States National Science Foundation, and the United States Department of Energy.

title: EMAI: A Universal Computational Framework to Develop Ethics-Aware Multimodal Disease Foundation Models
authors: Farnoush Banaei-Kashani, MohammadJavad Zohrabi, Sundous Hussein, Shreyas Patel, Iain Konigsberg, Claire Guo, Spencer Mahaffey, David Baraghoshi, Andrew Hill, Katerina Kechris, David DeCamp, Russell Bowler
abstract: Multimodal disease foundation models can serve as general-purpose systems adaptable to diverse research and clinical tasks, including prevention, detection, diagnosis, treatment, and disease management. We present EMAI (Ethics-aware Multimodal AI), a universal framework for developing such models from heterogeneous biomedical data, including omics (genomics, proteomics, metabolomics), medical imaging (CT, X-ray), audio (e.g., cough sounds), electronic health records, and wearable data. EMAI comprises two integrated components: (1) a tiered multimodal model development and evaluation pipeline, and (2) an ethics module that measures and enforces key ethical properties. Together, these components provide a systematic blueprint for building disease-specific multimodal foundation models that balance predictive performance with fairness, interpretability, and privacy. The development pipeline includes modality-specific data preprocessing and a three-tier modeling strategy. Tier 1 establishes unimodal baselines using both classical and state-of-the-art methods to assess data quality and learn reusable representations. Tier 2 introduces bimodal modeling through fusion, coordination, fission, and transfer techniques, alongside metrics to characterize cross-modal heterogeneity and interaction dynamics, guiding architectural choices. Tier 3 supports full multimodal modeling via tensor fusion, mixture-of-experts, universal tokenization, and bottlenecked architectures for modality-dominant settings. The ethics module targets fairness, interpretability, and privacy, providing quantitative metrics and mitigation strategies for each. EMAI is implemented as a system with automated versioning and both web-based and conversational interfaces, enabling use by researchers, clinicians, patients, and policymakers. We demonstrate EMAI by presenting EMAI-COPD, a multimodal foundation model for chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

title: Governing Controlled-Access Data Reuse in the LLM Era: Policy-Aligned Frameworks and Technologies for Secure Model Sharing
authors: Jonathan Lawson
abstract: Motivation: The rapid adoption of Large Language Models (LLMs) in biomedical research introduces significant governance challenges for the stewardship of controlled-access genomic and clinical data. While LLMs promise to accelerate discovery, using controlled-access data in these models risks inadvertent redistribution and secondary use violations. Recent NIH policy notices highlight a strengthened federal posture on data security and consent governance, a broader definition of controlled access data, and further policy guardrails on use of AI in NIH research, elevating the urgency for technical infrastructure that supports AI innovation while maintaining compliance. Methodology: We propose a governance framework asserting that core principles of controlled data access: consented data use limitations, non-redistribution, and Data Access Committee (DAC) oversight, are adaptable guardrails for AI-based research. We address two primary reuse use cases: (1) analyzing controlled-access data with existing LLMs, and (2) training or fine-tuning models on controlled-access datasets. In the latter case, the resulting models are treated as derivative datasets. We developed a preliminary cloud-based software platform that enables DAC-governed secondary access workflows, allowing approved users to execute controlled-access trained models "in place". Key Results: Our framework successfully operationalizes DAC oversight for AI-derived research products. By enabling "in place" execution, the system reduces the need for model downloads, thereby strengthening compliance with non-redistribution policies. This approach ensures that the "memory" of a model trained on sensitive data is managed with the same rigor as the raw data itself. Impact: This work provides a policy-aligned prototype for the secure reuse of NIH-funded data in AI development. By establishing clear pathways for the stewardship of derivative AI products, we preserve participant protections and institutional accountability without stifling technological innovation. This infrastructure is essential for the responsible scaling of AI-driven health research in a complex regulatory landscape.

title: spatiAlytica: A Viewer-Coupled Multi-Sub-Agent System with Agentic Memory for Conversational Spatial-Biology Analysis by Non-Coding Biomedical Researchers
authors: Arun Das, Shou-Jiang Gao, Lei Li, Yufei Huang
abstract: Motivation. Spatial transcriptomic and proteomic technologies (Xenium, MERFISH, CODEX, Visium) now resolve cellular neighborhoods linked to immune evasion, therapy response, and clinical outcome. Translating these data into biological insight requires coding fluency and computational-methods expertise (spatial statistics, niche analysis, differential expression) that most biologists, including domain experts in pathology and tumor immunology, lack. Graphical viewers ease browsing but not analysis, and recent LLM agents (BioMANIA, CellAgent, BioMedAgent) remain text-only, decoupled from the viewer, rely on flat conversation histories, and emit code whose biological validity non-experts cannot judge. Methodology. We developed spatiAlytica, a viewer-coupled multimodal agentic system for non-coding biologists. Embedded in the Napari spatial viewer, it treats plots, layers, and selected regions as queryable objects, so users can ask questions about the current view. A central orchestrator sub-agent coordinates specialized sub-agents for data resolution, code generation, error correction, image-grounded visual question answering, and natural-language reporting. A hybrid tool repository combines curated reusable functions with on-demand code synthesis, and an agentic memory subsystem persists intermediate results across turns to support a unified exploratory-analysis and interpretation-reporting workflow. Key Results. We released spatiAlyticaBench, an open benchmark of 222 single-turn analytical questions, 178 sequential multi-turn workflows, and 7,350 image-grounded question-answer pairs. spatiAlytica outperformed baseline LLM agents in analysis accuracy, multi-turn reasoning, and viewer-grounded interpretation. Ablations showed agentic memory is essential for multi-turn robustness and the code-debugger sub-agent recovers first-pass failures. Case studies on Xenium Kaposi sarcoma, CODEX colorectal cancer, and Visium ovarian cancer reproduced published findings and surfaced a progressive CD8 T-cell dysfunction trajectory during Kaposi-sarcoma progression not reported in the original analysis. Impact. spatiAlytica lowers the analytic barrier for non-coding biomedical researchers, demonstrates a reusable viewer-coupled multi-sub-agent pattern for the NIH data-science ecosystem, and openly releases its code, benchmark, and case-study transcripts for community reuse and integration with NIH-funded data infrastructure.

title: Data to Discovery: AI-Powered Analysis in BRC Analytics
authors: Michael Schatz
abstract: BRC Analytics (brc-analytics.org) is a free, cloud-based platform for pathogen, host, and vector genomics that enables researchers to transform public genomic data into reproducible scientific analyses. Developed as part of the NIAID-funded Bioinformatics Resource Centers, BRC Analytics integrates thousands of curated reference genomes, biological metadata, community-developed workflows, and national-scale computational infrastructure within a single browser-based environment. By combining data resources from NCBI Datasets and the UCSC Genome Browser with scalable analysis capabilities provided through Galaxy and high-performance computing resources from the Texas Advanced Computing Center (TACC), BRC Analytics enables researchers to move from raw sequencing data to publication-ready results without specialized local infrastructure. This presentation will describe how BRC Analytics supports infectious disease research through integrated data resources, reproducible workflows, scalable computing, and emerging artificial intelligence technologies. I will highlight recent advances that leverage AI throughout the analytical lifecycle, from natural-language interfaces for workflow planning and execution to machine learning models for taxonomic classification, variant interpretation, and biological discovery. This will include Orbit, an AI-powered research assistant that translates scientific questions into executable analysis plans; Galaxy-ML, a framework for training, validating, and deploying machine learning models within reproducible workflows; and Perseus, a deep learning framework for improving taxonomic classification of long-read metagenomic sequences. I will also discuss emerging applications of foundation models, including AlphaGenome, for predicting regulatory effects and prioritizing candidate functional variants across host-pathogen systems. Together, these capabilities illustrate a broader vision in which AI serves not only as a predictive technology, but also as an interface between biological questions and computational methods. By combining curated biological data, reproducible workflows, scalable computing, and AI-assisted analysis, BRC Analytics helps democratize access to advanced computational biology and accelerate the translation of genomic data into biological insight.

title: AI in scientific publishing and peer review

abstract: Biomedical publishers have long used AI and machine learning to support image and integrity screening in peer review, but the development of LLMs and release of frontier models has driven a greater adoption of AI in academic publishing. Though publishers have been slower to adopt LLM-driven tools, some are partnering with third-party providers to develop and implement GenAI tools in editorial and peer review workflows. While some publishers are piloting agentic solutions, most lack the in-house technical expertise and partnerships with technology partners needed for such resource-intensive initiatives. Other barriers to the use of GenAI in peer review include integration with legacy technology systems, cultural resistance to AI, and concern around the limitations AI technologies. title: Rigorous Benchmarking for Bioinformatics Methods: From Universal Rankings to Context-Specific Evaluation
authors: Jingyi Jessica Li
abstract: The bioinformatics community has long relied on universal rankings to benchmark competing methods, yet no single method performs best across all data types, experimental designs, or biological contexts. We advocate for a paradigm shift: from aggregate leaderboards to context-specific evaluation that accounts for the conditions under which a method is applied. Achieving this rigorously requires three pillars: synthetic data with known ground truth to enable controlled comparisons, negative controls derived from real data (via permutation or model-based null generation) to calibrate false positive rates, and real-data-based positive controls to quantify power across varying signal-to-noise ratios. Beyond benchmark data design, since the optimal method is context-specific, method selection for a given dataset is crucial and should be made transparent in analysis papers. We illustrate these principles through differential expression analysis as a case study, where we developed DE-Rigor-Agent: an AI-driven framework that enforces pre-specified, expert-defined statistical assessment, executes appropriate methods in parallel, and produces fully auditable reports that eliminate subjective cherry-picking. We close by proposing concrete community reporting standards: stratified performance evaluation across data scenarios, pre-registered benchmarking protocols, and transparent documentation of methodological assumptions and decision criteria.

title: Quantum Hamiltonian-Based Generative Modeling of Gene Regulatory Networks: Inference algorithms and sample complexity analysis.
authors: Arvind Rao, Sandeep Pradhan, Mohammed Aamir Sohail, Raghunath Ranga Sudharshan
abstract: We introduce a novel quantum Hamiltonian-based gene expression model (QHGM), a generative framework for modeling pseudotime-ordered single-cell gene expression (scRNA-seq) data. In QHGM, gene interactions are encoded through a parameterized Hamiltonian that governs the evolution of discretized gene-expression states along pseudotime trajectories. The resulting pseudotime-ordered single-cell gene expression profiles are represented as measurements from a fixed, local, informationally complete POVM. Unlike classical generative modeling approaches, which often struggle to capture nonlinear, context-dependent, beyond-pairwise, and order-dependent dependencies in gene interactions, QHGM provides a unified framework for modeling directional regulatory dynamics by explicitly encoding network topology within a parameterized Hamiltonian. This framework naturally captures context-dependent and non-commutative interaction effects underlying cellular state evolution, while providing a flexible foundation for modeling higher-order regulatory interactions and integrating multimodal and multi-omics cellular data. To learn the regulatory interactions encoded within the Hamiltonian and infer gene regulatory networks, we develop a scalable variational quantum network inference algorithm (VQ-NET) based on maximum-likelihood estimation from pseudotime-ordered scRNA-seq data. We further derive finite-sample recovery guarantees and establish upper bounds on the number of pseudotime samples and single-cell observations required for accurate parameter estimation with high probability, demonstrating polynomial scaling with the number of genes

title: Quantum Computing Approaches for Biological Network Inference and Analysis
authors: Mhaned Oubounyt, Jan Baumbach
abstract: Biological networks, including gene regulatory networks (GRNs) and protein–protein interaction (PPI) networks, provide a powerful framework for understanding cellular processes, disease mechanisms, and complex traits. However, their inference and analysis remain challenging due to the high dimensionality, sparsity, and combinatorial complexity of multi-omics and clinical data. In this talk, we present a set of emerging quantum computing approaches for biological network inference and analysis. We explore the use of QUBO-based formulations for enhancing topological GRN inference, and apply the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm (QAOA) to graph mapping problems in PPI networks. In addition, we investigate quantum reservoir computing for classification tasks in electronic health record data, as well as quantum-inspired strategies for detecting network-wide epistatic interactions. Across these approaches, preliminary results indicate improved sensitivity to complex structures and higher-order dependencies compared to classical methods. While current hardware imposes limitations, our findings highlight the strong potential of hybrid quantum–classical frameworks to advance systems biology and network medicine.

title: RotorMap and Quantum Fingerprints of DNA Sequences via Rotary Position Embeddings
authors: Sergii Strelchuk, Danylo Yakymenko, Maksym Chernyshev, Illia Savchenko
abstract: For strings of letters from a small alphabet, such as DNA sequences, we present a quantum encoding that empirically provides a strong correlation between the Levenshtein edit distance and the fidelity between quantum states defined by the encodings. It is based on the principles of Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE), employed in modern large language models. Classically, this encoding yields RotorMap: a GPU-accelerated DNA mapping algorithm that achieves speedups of 50–700× over single-thread Minimap2 in proof-of-concept tests on human and maize genomes. For use on quantum devices, we introduce the Angular encoding, which is built from RoPE and directly outputs state preparation circuits. To verify its properties and utility on NISQ devices, we report results of experiments conducted on real quantum hardware. As a potential application, we consider a quantum DNA authentication problem and conjecture that a quantum advantage in one-way communication complexity could be achieved over any comparable classical solution.

title: When Regulators Become Mutagens: Transcription Factor-Induced Mutagenesis
authors: Raluca Gordan
abstract: Transcription factors (TFs) are critical regulators of gene expression that bind to specific DNA sites throughout the genome. But this regulatory activity comes with an unexpected mutagenic cost: TFs can inadvertently bind to DNA replication errors and act as roadblocks for the repair of these errors by the mismatch repair machinery, leading to localized hypermutation at TF binding sites. In recent work, we provided the first direct evidence for this TF-dependent mutagenesis paradigm (Zhu et al., Cell 2025), building on our previous results showing unexpectedly strong binding of TFs to DNA mismatch lesions (Afek et al., Nature 2020). In addition to competing with the mismatch repair machinery, we have shown that TFs contribute substantially to UV-induced mutagenesis through two distinct mechanisms (Wasserman et al., in review). First, TF-induced distortions in DNA structure can enhance the formation of UV lesions—we found evidence of this mechanism for more than two hundred human TFs. Second, by binding strongly to damaged DNA in a subset of their binding sites, TFs can act as physical barriers to nucleotide excision repair. We assessed the extent to which TFs influence UV damage formation and repair, and linked these molecular mechanisms to patterns of somatic mutations observed in human cells. Our findings establish a new paradigm in which transcription factors function not only as regulators of gene expression but also as determinants of genome stability. In this talk, I will discuss mechanisms of TF-induced mutagenesis and their implications for understanding mutation landscapes, DNA evolution, and the origins of disease-associated mutations in regulatory DNA.

title: REGA: an interpretable hierarchical network representation learning framework for reference regulatory element– guided gene expression analysis
authors: Lixin Ren, Ishita Debnath, Zhana Duren
abstract: Gene regulatory network (GRN) inference is essential for deciphering cellular identity and disease mechanisms. While advanced foundation models utilizing single-cell multiome data have significantly improved inference accuracy, their broad application is hindered by steep financial costs and technical barriers. The vast majority of transcriptomic studies lack paired epigenomic profiles, locking high-accuracy GRN inference behind a restrictive data wall. To resolve this trade-off between data accessibility and performance, we propose REGA, an interpretable hierarchical network representation learning framework for Reference regulatory Element–Guided gene expression Analysis. REGA utilizes ubiquitous gene expression data alongside non-sample-specific reference regulatory element (RE) lists. By relying on robust, cell-type-level static chromatin accessibility blueprints and dynamic gene expression fluctuations, REGA bypasses the noise of single-cell ATAC-seq and eliminates the need for expensive paired multi-omics data. REGA effectively maps the complete transcription factor (TF)–RE–target gene regulatory axis. It captures a substantial portion of multi-omics accuracy (average improvement of 68% over random) while maintaining the low data burden of expression-only methods. Furthermore, REGA demonstrates broad versatility across bulk, single-cell, spatial transcriptomics, and perturb-seq datasets. Beyond fundamental inference, REGA successfully connects individual-level regulatory activities with clinical phenotypes and identifies cross-cell-type regulatory programs, revealing how cell-specific impacts are communicated across tissues to drive systemic disease phenotypes. REGA drastically lowers the data barrier for high-accuracy GRN analysis, enabling mechanistic insights into complex diseases.

title: STORMI: Inference of mechanistic gene regulation dynamics from multimodal and interventional data
authors: Alexander Aivazidis, Stefan Schrod, Paul Kaegy, Cameron Smith, Tara Chari, German Passarello, Mikdad Talpur, Fatih Erkan, Jonathan Kunz, Vitalii Kleshchevnikov, Luca Pinello, Oliver Stegle, Smaran Nair
abstract: A long-standing goal in biology is to understand the causes behind cell state changes. This requires inference of interpretable dynamical equations for both intrinsic DNA-dependent regulation, extrinsic environment dependencies and biochemical stochasticity. Yet, scalability and parameter identifiability limits for such ambitious dynamical models have prevented their realization. With STORMI we introduce a foundational framework to close this gap. We introduce analytical and numerical advances to scale the inference of mechanistic stochastic differential equations to the entire regulatory hierarchy from DNA accessibility, over transcription, splicing to TF protein translation. We advance parameter identifiability with inference on an unprecedented breadth of data modalities, including flexible, joint inference on RNA, ATAC and CRISPR perturbation data from different experiments. Furthermore, we use STORMI's posterior uncertainty metric to highlight non-identifiable parameters for follow up experiments. We apply STORMI to three single cell datasets that capture differentiation into multiple cell states across multiple time points with joint or disjoint RNA and ATAC readouts and TF CRISPR perturbations, anchored by an internal, unpublished cardiac organoid atlas with 400 perturbations. STORMI strongly outperforms alternative GRN methods in predicting cell fates or differentially expressed genes and improves with additional data modalities (e.g. perturbations), mechanistic fidelity (e.g. bifurcations) and a lower uncertainty metric. Moreover, our mechanistic model structure allows interpreting cell fate decisions by causal chains of environment to TF to regulatory region cascades. Overall, STORMI provides a mechanistic foundation to leverage the next generation of complex genomic experiments and continuously refine the governing equations underlying biological systems.

title: MiRformer: a dual-transformer-encoder framework for predicting microRNA-mRNA interactions from paired sequences
authors: Jiayao Gu, Can Chen, Yue Li
abstract: Motivation: MicroRNAs (miRNAs) regulate gene expression by binding to target messenger RNAs (mRNAs), inducing translational repression or mRNA degradation. Accurate prediction of miRNA–mRNA interactions and precise localization of binding and cleavage sites are critical for understanding post-transcriptional regulation and for enabling RNA therapeutics. Existing computational methods often rely on handcrafted or indirect features, scale poorly to kilobase-long mRNA sequences, or provide limited interpretability. Results: We present MiRformer, a transformer-based framework that jointly predicts miRNA–mRNA interactions and localizes miRNA binding and cleavage sites directly from raw sequence pairs. MiRformer employs a dual-transformer encoder architecture for miRNA and mRNA sequences and incorporates a sliding-window attention mechanism to efficiently model kilobase-length mRNA contexts while preserving nucleotide-level resolution. Across multiple benchmarks, MiRformer achieves state-of-the-art performance on interaction prediction, binding-site localization, and cleavage-site identification from Degradome-seq data. Beyond accuracy, MiRformer provides strong interpretability: attention patterns consistently highlight miRNA seed regions within 500-nt mRNA windows, revealing clear and biologically meaningful interaction signals. When applied to jointly infer binding and cleavage sites across 13k miRNA-mRNA pairs, predicted sites frequently co-localize, supporting a miRNA-mediated degradation mechanism.

title: NEXIS: Disentangling Cell-Autonomous and Intercellular Gene Regulation from Spatial Transcriptomics
authors: Wenjun Zhao, Geoffrey Schiebinger
abstract: Gene expression in tissue reflects both cell-autonomous regulation and intercellular signals, yet existing methods for spatial transcriptomics conflate these effects. We present NEXIS, a spatiotemporal framework that decomposes gene expression dynamics into cell-autonomous and neighbor-mediated regulatory components using a structured dynamical model. Applied to zebrafish embryogenesis and aging mouse brain spatial transcriptomics data, NEXIS recovers functionally distinct regulatory programs: autocrine programs capture intracellular processes while paracrine programs recover tissue-level signaling and coordinated cell behavior.

title: SpiderNet reveals a meta-interaction basis for cell-cell communication in tissues
authors: Junjie Tang, Shaoheng Liang, Shahul Alam, Jian Ma
abstract: Cell-cell communication in tissues emerges from spatially organized, directional signaling programs that couple sender state, intercellular ligand--receptor interactions, and receiver transcriptional responses, yet these programs remain difficult to resolve in situ. Here we present SpiderNet, an interpretable framework for learning cell-cell meta-interactions (MIs) from spatial transcriptomics. Each MI represents a directional communication module linking sender-side regulators, ligand--receptor bridges, and receiver-side target genes, thereby connecting intercellular coupling to intracellular regulatory consequences. SpiderNet models ordered neighboring cell pairs and is trained end-to-end to jointly reconstruct ligand--receptor co-expression and gene expression, yielding a compact and mechanistically interpretable representation of multicellular regulation. Across simulations and diverse spatial transcriptomic datasets, SpiderNet robustly recovers biologically coherent meta-interactions, more faithfully links intercellular signaling to curated regulatory activity than existing approaches, and supports downstream analyses including cell-subtype discovery, in silico spatial perturbation, phenotype prediction, and multi-hop communication cascade detection. In ovarian cancer, SpiderNet identifies a thrombospondin (THBS)-associated fibroblast--tumor program coupled to an upstream osteopontin (SPP1) monocyte--fibroblast relay marking aggressive tumor states. In aging brain, it resolves a T cell-associated pro-aging communication module linked to local transcriptional remodeling and transferable age prediction across regions and platforms. In perturbation-resolved melanoma, it uncovers coordinated remodeling of melanoma--T cell communication following NF-KB perturbation. By organizing tissue communication into a small set of reusable meta-interactions, SpiderNet provides a general framework for resolving, comparing, and perturbing multicellular regulatory programs across tissues and experimental settings.

title: Chromatin-informed inference of cell-type-specific regulatory programs in Alzheimer’s disease using single-cell multi-omics
authors: Jiahui Hou, Hatice Osmanbeyoglu
abstract: Computational inference of transcription factor (TF) regulatory programs from single-cell data remains challenging due to sparsity and the weak coupling between chromatin accessibility and gene expression. To address this, we develop a chromatin-informed multitask framework that integrates single-cell RNA-seq and single-cell ATAC-seq data for cell-type-resolved TF activity inference. Our approach extends PSIONIC by combining pseudobulk aggregation with multitask learning across cell type–sample pairs, enabling robust estimation of TF activity while sharing information across contexts. We further improve regulatory specificity by incorporating ChIP-seq–derived priors, replacing motif-based features with empirically informed TF–gene regulatory potentials. Applied to Alzheimer’s disease (AD) data, our framework recovers biologically coherent regulatory programs that distinguish neuronal and glial identities and identifies cell-type-specific TF activity changes across disease stages. These include known AD-associated regulators as well as novel candidate TFs, highlighting disease-specific regulatory rewiring. Overall, our method improves TF–target inference through chromatin-informed priors and multitask learning, providing a scalable and generalizable framework for dissecting regulatory mechanisms in complex diseases.

title: TFScope: Learning the DNA-binding specificity of transcription factors from protein sequence
authors: Lei Huang, Zain Patal, Luca Pinello
abstract: Decoding the DNA-binding specificity of transcription factors (TFs) from protein sequence remains a fundamental challenge in gene regulation, and synthetic biology. Current methods are often limited by sequence homology or TF family specific codes and struggle to generalize across different TF families. Here, we present a structure-guided framework (TFScope) for de novo inference of TF–DNA binding specificity from protein sequence. Our approach first uses a family-aware seed model to predict candidate motif lengths and coarse DNA-binding preferences directly from the TF sequence, generating a small library of candidate DNA targets. We first construct in silico structural models of candidate TF–DNA complexes using AlphaFold 3. We then apply Rosetta-based single-nucleotide mutational scanning across DNA positions to estimate base-resolved interaction energetics, enabling the derivation of a calibrated position weight matrix (PWM). By combining learned priors with structure prediction and physics-based refinement, our framework transforms TF sequence into a DNA specificity landscape. We envision this hybrid strategy as a general route toward motif prediction, TF specificity profiling, and programmable TF design, particularly for engineered DNA-binding proteins and transcription factor families lacking rich experimental characterization.

title: NPBIP: Predicting binding preferences of uncharacterized nucleic-acid-binding proteins
authors: Noam Shimshoviz, Safwan Butto, Yaron Orenstein
abstract: Motivation Nucleic-acid-binding proteins (NBPs) are crucial regulators of gene expression, recognizing specific RNA or DNA binding sites. While high-throughput experiments have generated vast amounts of binding data, a significant challenge remains in predicting binding affinities of a novel query NBP to any nucleic-acid sequence. Current computational methods often require prior experimental data for the query NBP or are limited to predictions over predefined short RNA or DNA sequences. Results Here, we present NPBIP (New Protein Binding Intensity Predictor), a new method to predict the binding of a query NBP to any DNA or RNA sequence by integrating two complementary components: (i) a similarity-based method that computes a weighted average of binding predictions over the training NBPs; and (ii) a deep-learning model that combines a large protein language model with a hybrid convolutional-transformer network to predict binding directly. We trained and evaluated NPBIP on 420 and 464 RNA-and DNA-binding protein experiments, respectively. NPBIP significantly outperformed each of its components and all competing baselines, achieving an average Pearson correlation of 0.414 ± 0.20 and 0.581 ± 0.22 over the RNA-and DNA-binding experiments, respectively. This prediction performance was statistically comparable to an experimental k-mer upper bound over RBPs and statistically superior to an upper bound over DBPs. Furthermore, interpretability analysis demonstrates that NPBIP recovers canonical binding motifs for both RBPs and DBPs, providing biological validation for the model’s predictions.

title: Multi-modal functional mapping of non-coding sequences regulating fetal hemoglobin
authors: Lucas DaSilva, Daniel Bauer, Luca Pinello, Davide Seruggia, Hyejung Won, Michael Love, Justin Delano, Sean Jones, A. Trent Ledford, Jessica Bell, Jonathan Rosen, Basheer Becerra, Jing Zeng, Steve Coyne, Sabine Studer, Sébastien Levesque, Gue-Ho Hwang, Marlena Starrs, Eric Che, Zain Patel, Ting Wu
abstract: Transcriptional regulation by non-coding elements and their associated DNA-binding transcription factors governs the developmental transition from fetal to adult hemoglobin ("hemoglobin switching"). Reactivation of fetal hemoglobin (HbF) is a major therapeutic strategy for beta-hemoglobinopathies such as sickle cell disease. Defining the cis-regulatory logic of HBG1 and HBG2, which encode the gamma-globin chains of HbF, is therefore essential for understanding hemoglobin switching and enabling improved therapeutic design. Although population genetics studies have identified single-nucleotide variants associated with HbF induction, they are limited to naturally occurring variation and do not provide a comprehensive view of regulatory function. To address this gap, we systematically compared multiple mutagenesis approaches across HbF regulatory sequences in immortalized erythroid progenitors (HUDEP-2). We integrated four complementary modalities: in-situ dense adenine base-editing (ABE8e-SpRY) and dual base-editing (TadDE-SpRY) mutagenesis, in-situ prime-editing saturation mutagenesis, ex-situ massively parallel reporter assay (MPRA) saturation mutagenesis, and in-silico ChromBPNet saturation mutagenesis. These assays targeted the HBG1/2 promoters and the BCL11A +55 kb and +58 kb enhancers. This multi-modal strategy uncovered new regulatory features of hemoglobin switching, including a BCL11A autoregulatory binding site within the BCL11A +55 kb enhancer. We also identified novel therapeutic editing strategies including TadDE-SpRY base editing and prime editing of the BCL11A distal motif in the HBG1/2 promoter, which may enable stronger HbF induction than editing strategies currently being pursued clinically. Together, this functional map highlights how in-situ, ex-situ, and in-silico approaches can be combined to resolve regulatory element function and guide therapeutic genome-editing design.

title: ExoShorkie: Predicting RNA-seq coverage of exogenous genomes in yeast by transfer learning
authors: Jonathan Mandl, Yaron Orenstein
abstract: Predicting the RNA-seq coverage of native and exogenous sequences is central to many endogenous and synthetic-biology applications. Substantial progress has been made in developing methods to predict the RNA-seq coverage of native genomic sequences, with the recently developed Shorkie achieving state-of-the-art performance in yeast. However, prediction performance of these methods over the challenging out-of-distribution exogenous DNA is still unknown. Recent studies measured RNA-seq coverage of large exogenous genomes in yeast, providing a unique opportunity to train machine-learning models on a large exogenous sequence space and to improve both prediction performance and our understanding of regulatory mechanisms. Here, we introduce ExoShorkie, a method we developed by extending Shorkie through transfer learning across multiple exogenous RNA-seq datasets. We demonstrate that ExoShorkie significantly improves prediction performance on held-out exogenous genomes and outperforms both a native-genome-trained Shorkie baseline and Yorzoi, the only competing method in predicting exogenous RNA-seq coverage in yeast, in cross-validation and in leave-one-genome-out evaluations. Furthermore, through interpretability analyses we reveal biologically meaningful regulatory motifs and distinct regulatory rules in exogenous genomes in yeast, providing new insights into transcriptional regulation beyond native genomic contexts.

title: Developing a methylation and SNP-aware DNA large language model
authors: Dante Bolzan, Ferhat Ay
abstract: The development of foundation models that learn a general grammar of DNA (DNA language models) has accelerated in recent years. The vast majority of DNA language models, such as DNABERT-2 and Nucleotide Transformer, are pretrained on reference genomes, thereby omitting sequence variation and epigenetic base modifications. Single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and methylated cytosine (5mC) are associated with gene expression and genome function. We hypothesize that a single model that incorporates both SNPs and 5mC during pretraining would learn representations that better capture functional genomic contexts. To test this hypothesis, we developed ModBERT, a DNA language model that was pretrained on the human reference genome with the addition of SNP and CpG methylation information from the 1000 Genomes Long Read Sequencing Consortium. ModBERT takes as input a probabilistic representation of the genome where each locus is a probability distribution over A, C, G, T, M (5mC). The probabilities reflect the frequency of alleles for each SNP and the percent methylation of each CpG site. We show that ModBERT effectively utilizes methylation information to classify peaks from functional genomic assays, outperforming ab initio models and models pretrained on sequences without methylation. Furthermore, ModBERT demonstrated predictive power on prediction tasks in heldout donors, suggesting that ModBERT has learned associations of SNPs and 5mC with gene regulation. We also show that ModBERT may be extended to include additional base modifications. This work paves the way for in silico assessment of genetic variants and their epigenetic status in their prioritization for experimental validation.

title: Chorus: An Agentic Framework for Comparative Regulatory Genomics with Sequence-to-Function Oracles
authors: Dmitry Penzar, Lorenzo Ruggeri, Rosalba Giugno, Luca Pinello
abstract: Sequence-to-function deep learning models —Enformer, Borzoi, AlphaGenome, ChromBPNet, Sei, LegNet— predict chromatin accessibility, transcription factor binding, histone modifications, gene expression, and splicing from DNA sequence across hundreds of human cell types. Yet each model inhabits its own ecosystem with unique dependencies, input requirements (2 kb to 1 Mb), output resolutions, and prediction formats. Cross-model comparison requires heroic engineering effort, leaving these tools underutilized. We present Chorus, a unified framework addressing these barriers through three innovations: a standardized oracle abstraction, a multi-layer analysis framework, and an agentic AI interface. Chorus treats each model as an ""oracle"" returning predictions for genomic coordinates or sequences. Each oracle runs in an isolated environment with automatic dependency management, yet all are accessed through a single Python API. Predictions across thousands of tracks are organized into regulatory layers with modality-specific scoring and quantile-based contextualization against empirical backgrounds. Integrated modules support causal variant prioritization from GWAS loci, cell-type discovery, saturation mutagenesis, and sequence engineering. Most transformatively, Chorus exposes its capabilities as a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, letting AI agents orchestrate regulatory genomics from natural-language requests such as ""score rs12740374 across AlphaGenome, Borzoi, and Enformer in liver cell types and report convergent evidence."" The agent autonomously selects oracles, picks cell-type-matched tracks, runs reference and alternate predictions, and synthesizes multi-oracle evidence into an interactive report. This turns cross-oracle variant interpretation from a specialist engineering task into a conversational one, letting clinicians, biologists, and synthetic biologists use state-of-the-art models without code. Chorus is freely available at https://github.com/pinellolab/chorus.

title: FIREFate: Functional and Interpretable Regulatory Encoding of Fate determination
authors: Swapnil Keshari, Jishnu Das
abstract: Cell fate determination integrates gene regulatory programs with epigenetic signals to coordinate differentiation and functional specialization across tissues. Yet how fate decisions are encoded in regulatory programs, how these programs dynamically rewire during transitions, and whether fate bias can be detected prior to phenotypic divergence remain unresolved. Existing approaches are insufficient: GRN methods miss transition-driving dynamics, differential expression is univariate, ML models sacrifice interpretability, and co-expression frameworks cannot resolve causal regulation. We introduce FIREFate (Functional and Interpretable Regulatory Encoding of Fate determination), which integrates interpretable ML with mechanistic regulatory modeling through high-resolution static and dynamic GRNs to identify regulatory programs that define and drive cell states. Applied to primary human B cells, FIREFate resolves the bifurcation between plasmablast (PB) and germinal center (GC) fates, recovering canonical regulators—PAX5, PRDM1, and IRF4—without prior knowledge, and identifying CREB3L2 as a central hub linking ER stress to PB commitment. Benchmarking against SCENIC+ confirms more compact, higher-specificity regulatory modules with improved mechanistic interpretability. To resolve dynamic regulation, FIREFate reconstructs time-resolved TF activity integrating expression, regulatory edge strength, and downstream regulatory force, uncovering sequential regulatory waves: a CREB3L2–RUNX2–PRDM1 activation cascade for PB commitment and a repression-dominated IRF4/NFKB1–PAX5 program locking in GC identity. Finally, perturbation-guided transfer learning predicts fate bias prior to phenotypic commitment, revealing GC-primed subsets within early activated B cells and identifying IKZF2 and RBPJ as episodically active regulators invisible to conventional analyses. FIREFate shifts cell fate inference from descriptive characterization to predictive, mechanistic resolution across biological systems.

title: Sequence basis of heterogenous and dynamic single-molecule chromatin states
authors: Jian Zhou,,,,
abstract: Much of our understanding of the regulatory code has been built upon the view of chromatin as a single, sequence-determined, state, typically measured through population average across cells. Single-molecule techniques provide the opportunity to push measurement and modeling closer to the molecular mechanisms, by capturing the distribution of heterogeneous chromatin states at near basepair resolution. Here we present a sequence-based generative modeling approach that faithfully captures the distribution of single-molecule chromatin states, including co-accessibility patterns not visible from bulk data. This sequence-to-distribution framework allows us to uncover distinct modes of transcription factor effects on nucleosomes, including roles of motifs in positioning the +1 nucleosome in transcription start sites, the dependencies between accessibility and methylation across transcription factor motifs, and identifying factors that mediate long-range regulatory coupling. Extending beyond static snapshots, we generated single-molecule simulations of pseudo-dynamic chromatin trajectories as a step toward a true dynamic model of chromatin. Furthermore, our models enable interpretation of the genetic variant effects at single-molecule resolution. Together, this work establishes a sequence-to-distribution framework that effectively transforms single-molecule regulatory measurements into a virtual chromatin model, providing a foundation for decoding how genomic sequence encodes heterogeneous and dynamic chromatin behavior and how genetic variation perturbs it, one molecule at a time.

title: An Expanded Registry of cis-Regulatory Elements Enables Systematic Analysis of Transcriptional Regulation
authors: Jill Moore, Nishigandha Phalke, Jonathan Fisher, Matthew Lacadie, Jair Meza, Mansi Khandpekar, Zhiping Weng
abstract: Understanding how cis-regulatory elements (CREs) encode cell type-specific gene expression remains a central challenge in genomics. Here, we present an expanded and computationally unified Registry of candidate cis-Regulatory Elements (cCREs) that provides a scalable framework for systematic analysis of regulatory activity across biological contexts. Building on our previous work, we expanded the Registry to 2.37 million human and 0.97 million mouse cCREs across 1,679 biosamples, representing a threefold increase over previous versions and substantially improving coverage of low-accessibility and repetitive genomic regions. Using an updated framework integrating chromatin accessibility, histone modification, and transcription factor binding data, we systematically classify cCREs into eight biochemical classes and enable both cell type-specific and aggregate regulatory annotations. To functionally characterize cCREs, we integrated STARR-seq, MPRA, CRISPR perturbation, and transgenic assays, collectively profiling over 97% of human cCREs. We also developed CAPRA, a CRE-centric method for resolving element-level reporter activity, enabling systematic identification of enhancers, silencers, and combinatorial regulatory interactions. Leveraging this unified framework, we identified nearly 10,000 silencer cCREs, including REST-bound elements with context-dependent enhancer/silencer activity, and uncovered MAFF/MAFK-associated latent enhancers poised for stimulus-responsive activation. Finally, we demonstrate the utility of the Registry for interpreting noncoding variation and nominating likely causal genes, including KLF1 for red blood cell traits. Together, this work establishes a scalable framework for regulatory annotation, predictive modeling, and interpretation of genome function.

title: Unlocking the Microglial Storm: The Genetic “Off-Switch” Failure in Alzheimer’s Disease.
authors: Di Huang, Ivan Ovcharenko
abstract: The genetic mechanisms of ~90% of Alzheimer's disease (AD)-associated variants residing in noncoding DNA remain poorly understood. To address this, we developed a deep learning framework that integrates bulk histone modification data with single-cell open chromatin profiles to evaluate the regulatory potential of noncoding variants. This model identified 1457 silencer and 3084 enhancer AD-associated variants in dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, classifying gene loci as silencer-only (SL), enhancer-only (EN), or dual-function (ENSL). EN loci predominantly regulate housekeeping metabolic processes, SL loci (including MS4A6A and HLA-D) are linked to immune responses (with ~70% substantially up-regulated in AD microglia), while ENSL loci are implicated in neurofibrillary tangle assembly. Our model achieves robust power in assessing the impact of regulatory variants, with ~70% directional concordance with experimental results. It identified rs636317 as a putative causal silencer variant, distinguishing it from a neutral variant located 11 base pairs away. This study advances understanding of the AD-associated regulatory landscape and provides a framework for ascertaining noncoding variants in AD pathogenesis. D. Huang and I. title: Interpreting deep learning models via concept attribution
authors: , Shaun Mahony, Shaun Mahony,, Shaun Mahony
abstract: Interpreting genomics deep learning models remains challenging. Existing feature attribution methods are largely restricted to one-hot DNA inputs and therefore cannot assess the influence of more general genomic features such as chromatin states or genomic repeats. Concept attribution methods offer an input-agnostic global interpretation framework, yet they have not been systematically applied to interpret neural network applications in genomics. I will present the first application of concept attribution to interpret genomics deep learning models by adapting the Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV) method. I will show that incorporating a PCA-based decorrelation transformation to address correlated and redundant embedding features improves over the original TCAV, resulting in the Testing with PCA-projected Concept Activation Vectors (TPCAV) approach. I will show that TPCAV provides comparable motif interpretation to TF-MoDISco on one-hot encoded DNA-based transcription factor binding prediction models. TPCAV also enables robust interpretive analysis of more general biological concepts such as repetitive elements, genome annotations, and chromatin states. It also generalizes to interpreting important features in tokenized foundation models as well as models incorporating chromatin signals as inputs. I will further show that TPCAV can identify representative regions associated with specific concepts, motivating downstream investigation of distinct regulatory mechanisms. TPCAV can be applied to a wide range of model architectures and genomics applications, and provides a flexible and robust complement to existing model interpretation techniques.

title: Cherimoya: Lightweight Sequence-to-Function Models For Large-Scale Regulatory Element Design
authors: Jacob Schreiber, Christian Ramirez, Achsah Marlene Aruva
abstract: Genomic sequence-to-function (S2F) models have become essential tools for understanding regulatory genomics, enabling motif discovery, the prediction of non-coding variant effects, and increasingly, the design of synthetic regulatory elements. However, current state-of-the-art models are large, with AlphaGenome exceeding 400M parameters and aggregating information across expansive receptive fields. Although a single ChromBPNet model has far fewer parameters, because each model only makes predictions for a single cell type, pursuing tasks in important cellular systems with dozens or hundreds of cell types remains computationally prohibitive. This parameter burden limits the use of these models for downstream interpretation and design tasks that may require thousands or millions of evaluations. We introduce Cherimoya, a compact neural network architecture that outperforms ChromBPNet at predictive performance with a fraction of the parameter count. The core building block, the Cheri Block, adapts the ConvNeXt block for noisy genomic signals and introduces a custom fused GPU kernel combining the depthwise convolution and layer normalization operations. With fewer than 5% of ChromBPNet's parameters, Cherimoya surpasses it on chromatin accessibility benchmarks and achieves comparable performance on non-coding variant effect prediction, running ~10x faster at inference. We anticipate that such compact architectures will be invaluable not only for those seeking to apply existing interpretation methods more broadly across compendia of data but also for those who are trying to pursue large-scale DNA design tasks that require the simultaneous usage of many models.

title: When Less Is Enough: Low-rank Structure in DNA Sequence-to-Function Models
authors: Elizabeth Gilfeather, Maria Chikina, Dennis Kostka
abstract: Motivation: Sequence-to-function models have been developed to predict assays that measure chromatin state, transcription factor binding, and gene expression of DNA sequences with high accuracy, allowing for in silico prediction of variant effects. These models are useful for investigating the role of sequence variability on the regulation of gene expression and complex diseases. However, these models typically have many parameters, resulting in slow CPU inference times and large GPU memory requirements, making prediction at scale or in resource-limited research environments impractical. Results: Here we create low-rank approximations of linear layers within four sequence-to-function models, Sei, Enformer, Borzoi, and AlphaGenome to significantly reduce their number of parameters, while maintaining predictive accuracy. We create quantized versions of these low-rank models, finding significantly reduced CPU inference time for the Sei models. The quantized low-rank Sei models maintain predictive accuracy across cell-type specific variant prediction tasks and perform comparably to state-or-the-art models, while reducing model size by up to 90.6% and reducing inference time on CPUs to approximately 0.34 seconds per sequence. We demonstrate that this model can be quickly finetuned on a CPU for increased performance on downstream prediction tasks. We present a python package, seilora, to easily download a suite of small, fast, low-rank Sei models, for use on a laptop, that predict cell-type specific chromatin tracks from DNA sequences. Availability: Reduced-rank Sei models are available as a Python package at https://github.com/kostkalab/seillra.

title: Sequence-to-function modeling uncovers the context-specific grammar of Drosophila chromatin insulation
authors: Brendan Wang, Gabriel Dolsten, Wenfan Ke, Yuri Pritykin
abstract: Chromatin is organized into self-interacting topologically associating domains, yet the regulatory principles governing their boundaries (insulators) are incompletely understood. It is unclear whether the known architectural factors are sufficient to explain the global diversity of chromatin insulation, or how specific combinations of factors dictate boundary strength and type. Nonetheless, studying how cells decode instructions for chromatin organization encoded in sequence remains crucial for understanding gene regulation. Leveraging the nucleosome-resolution of Drosophila melanogaster Micro-C, we developed Domino, a sequence-to-function deep learning framework that quantitatively models insulation across tissues. Unlike traditional transcription factor motif scanning, which merely identifies motif presence, Domino is a predictive model leveraging local sequence context to accurately score the functional contribution of motif instances to insulation. We validated the model performance experimentally through perturbations of insulator sequences. Domino uncovers a comprehensive motif grammar, revealing that nearly all sequence-dependent chromatin insulation in the embryo (4,195 boundaries) is driven by a compact set of just 20 primary motifs, with an average of only two active motifs per boundary. Using Domino, we identified and experimentally validated previously unreported insulation factors, including the homologous zinc-finger proteins CG4854 and Trem, uncovered distance-and orientation-dependent synergy between insulation motifs, and traced tissue-specific shifts of active insulator landscape in the larval and adult brain. This framework provides a generalizable approach for decoding the complex regulatory logic of 3D genome architecture in any high-resolution system.

title: DNA-aware evaluation and debiasing of sequence-to-function models
authors: Doruk Cakmakci, Yue Li
abstract: Genome sequence-to-function (S2F) models are widely used to interpret base-resolution functional genomics assays. Most S2F models are trained and evaluated against observed counts and profile-shapes using statistical objectives and fidelity metrics. These choices are well motivated, but they are DNA-independent. At the same time, experimental measurements arise from DNA-dependent assays with distinct characteristics. This mismatch motivates a complementary DNA-aware evaluation of S2F-predicted and experimental functional genomic tracks. We study DNA-dependency of experimental and S2F-predicted tracks using track-conditional genome language models (cgLMs). cgLMs predict masked nucleotides from a conditioning track under controlled DNA visibility. Across ATAC-seq and TF ChIP-seq peaks from GM12878 and K562, cgLM probing reveals a consistent \emph{masked DNA-decodability gap} between many experimental and S2F-predicted tracks. In particular, single-task (e.g., BPNet) and multi-task (e.g., AlphaGenome) S2F-predicted tracks enabled cgLMs to recover masked nucleotides with significantly higher accuracy and confidence than matched experimental tracks. Analyses of nonpeak and dinucleotide-shuffled sequences show that this gap is not confined to peaks and is not captured by standard DNA-agnostic profile-shape fidelity metrics alone. ChromBPNet Tn5-denoised predictions were an exception and behaved closer to the experimental regime, suggesting that staged training may reduce the gap. We then convert this diagnostic into a critic-derived objective, \emph{DNA-dependency matching} (DDM), using a frozen multi-headed cgLM critic. We introduce Critic-Guided Profile-Shape Editing (CGPSE), a preliminary post hoc debiasing framework for frozen S2F models. In GM12878 ATAC-seq, CGPSE partially reduces the masked DNA-decodability gap for AlphaGenome and BPNet predictions, while exposing a tradeoff with profile-shape fidelity.

title: stORCA: Correspondence-aware differential spatial expression analysis across biological conditions
authors: Yeojin Kim, Saurabh Sinha
abstract: Spatial transcriptomics (ST) enables gene expression profiling in tissue context, yet identifying genes whose spatial expression patterns change across biological conditions, termed differential spatial expression (DSE), remains an open challenge. Existing approaches are confounded by within-sample spatial autocorrelation, which inflates scores for spatially smooth genes regardless of cross-condition differences, and rely on implicit alignment choices not designed for cross-condition composition shifts. We introduce stORCA, a modular framework that explicitly decouples cross-condition alignment (stORCA-A) from DSE scoring (stORCA-D). stORCA-A learns a joint cell-state and niche representation across conditions, then computes cell-to-cell correspondence via high-entropy unbalanced optimal transport, accommodating cell-type composition imbalance without requiring strict one-to-one matching. The transport plan is independently replaceable with alternative aligners (PASTE2, SLAT). stORCA-D maps one condition's expression into the other's coordinate frame and computes per-gene residuals. A novel statistic, the Normalized Residual Moran's I (NRMI), scores the spatially coherent component of the residual while normalizing by each condition's intrinsic autocorrelation, directly addressing the autocorrelation confound. Significance is assessed by label permutation. An interpretation module then localizes changes via local Moran's I and attributes them to specific cell types or spatial domains. We benchmark stORCA on a synthetic tissue with controlled categories of genes whose spatial expression patterns change in a given domain or in a given cell type within a domain, and on two real datasets: a MERFISH mouse hypothalamus dataset spanning distinct behavioral states, and a Visium mouse brain APOE4 dataset. stORCA is positioned as a general framework for cross-condition spatial comparative genomics.

title: Integrative Inference of Spatially Resolved Cell Lineage Trees using LineageMap
authors: Xinhai Pan, Yiru Chen, Xiuwei Zhang
abstract: Understanding the spatio-temporal processes of tissue growth, including how new cell types emerge and how cells form the tissue architecture, is a fundamental problem in biology. The emerging spatially resolved lineage tracing data, where three modalities, lineage barcodes, gene expression profiles, and spatial locations, are measured for each single cell, provides an unprecedented opportunity to understand these processes. Computational methods that take advantage of all three modalities to reconstruct cell lineage tree and ancestral cell states and locations are needed. We introduce LineageMap, a hybrid lineage inference algorithm that integrates the scalability of distance-based tree reconstruction methods with the flexibility of likelihood-based methods under a unified probabilistic framework. The input to LineageMap is spatially resolved lineage tracing data, where for each single cell, the gene expression, lineage barcode and spatial locations are available. LineageMap enables accurate, interpretable, and scalable inference of high-resolution lineage trees as well as locations of ancestral cells from the tri-modality single-cell data. Across simulated and experimental datasets, LineageMap consistently outperforms existing methods in the accuracy of reconstructed cell lineage trees, while revealing biologically coherent spatiotemporal trajectories. Our framework bridges molecular lineage tracing with spatial and transcriptomic information, advancing computational reconstruction of dynamic cellular ancestries in both time and space. LineageMap is available at: https://github.com/ZhangLabGT/LineageMap
