title: CellPace: a generative framework for modeling continuous single-cell dynamics
authors: Chen Su, Amin Emad
abstract: Single-cell transcriptomic assays provide detailed but static snapshots of developmental processes, making it difficult to reconstruct the continuous dynamics that connect observed cell states. Existing generative models typically treat time as a categorical label, limiting their ability to recover coherent dynamics or to interpolate and extrapolate across sparsely sampled stages. To address this gap, we introduce CellPace, a generative framework for learning continuous developmental dynamics from sparse single-cell snapshots. CellPace uses a Temporal Diffusion Forcing (TDiF) module to model gap-aware temporal structure and enables iterative generation from pure Gaussian noise. Across four mouse developmental datasets, CellPace achieved the strongest overall performance among evaluated methods in simulation, interpolation, and extrapolation. Generated cells showed strong manifold alignment and preserved continuous temporal dynamics, with pseudotime trajectories closely tracking real developmental progression. Beyond distributional fidelity, CellPace preserved biologically meaningful structure: it captured fine-grained lineage organization in the posterior embryo, retained sufficient positional identity to map concordantly to the MOSTA spatial atlas, and extended naturally to joint RNA–chromatin accessibility modeling in a mouse secondary palate dataset. Even when temporal ordering was inferred from pseudotime, CellPace preserved coherent temporal manifold structure across both modalities. Together, these results establish CellPace as a generative framework for modeling continuous developmental dynamics from sparse developmental snapshots.

title: An interpretable model of the cell-type-specific Protein-RNA regulatory relationship
authors: Donglu Bai, Mark Gerstein, Prashant Emani
abstract: The well-documented discordance between mRNA and protein abundance (ρ ~ 0.4–0.6) means transcriptomic measurements are poor proxies for protein levels. Yet cell-type-resolved protein measurements remain limited: single-cell proteomics has low throughput, CITE-seq covers only ~200 surface targets, and bulk proteomics averages across cell types. Existing computational methods— supervised CITE-seq models, zero-shot surface protein predictors, generative transcriptome-to-proteome translators, and bulk deconvolution—each address part of this gap, but none separate transcriptional from post-transcriptional regulation at cell-type resolution. We present the first mechanistic framework integrating scRNA-seq, bulk RNA-seq, and bulk proteomics through steady-state constraints from the joint master equation for mRNA and protein. For each gene and cell type, we fit transcriptional bursting parameters via a scalable Beta-Poisson model, obtain cell-type fractions from bulk RNA-seq, and recover cell-type-specific translational efficiencies by positivity-constrained regression against bulk proteomics. Every protein estimate decomposes into a transcriptional and a translational component. On CITE-seq PBMC data, our framework matches state-of-the-art accuracy (Spearman ρ = 0.64), comparable to DESP and outperforming pretrained scTranslator, with the inferred translational component further improving protein-level accuracy over transcription alone. On heart intracellular proteomics—where deep-learning baselines fail—our framework remains competitive. Inferred burst kinetics are orthogonally validated against promoter accessibility, revealing neuron-specific transcriptional strategies. Applied to the ROSMAP Alzheimer's cohort, the framework decomposes bulk mRNA-protein discordance into cell-type-specific transcriptional and translational programs, providing complementary disease signatures for AD staging.

title: R4ST: A Reference-guided Graph-generative Model for Robust Reconstruction of Spatial Transcriptomic Profiles
authors: Mingyue Wei, Wenrui Li, Wei Zhang, Zhi-Ping Liu
abstract: The trade-off between spatial granularity and transcriptome coverage in current spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies results in sparse and incomplete expression profiles. Meanwhile, the rich local and global spatial topology inherent in spatial data are crucial for accurate biological interpretation but remain underutilized by existing methods. Here, we propose R4ST, an end-to-end framework designed to complete ST data. R4ST leverages scRNA-seq data as a reference and employs dual learning channels based on graph inductive and transductive modeling to capture complementary spatial topology information in ST data, enabling accurate reconstruction of missing gene expression. Extensive evaluations across multiple datasets from different platforms demonstrate that R4ST enables accurate recovery of large-scale gene expression profiles from a small subset of measured genes, uncovers novel spatial patterns associated with rare cell types, and substantially enhances the biological interpretability of ST data.

title: MARCA: Detecting Micro-compartment Anchors in 3D Genome utilizing Spatial Relationships
authors: Boshuai Zhang, Ferhat Ay
abstract: Background/Motivation: Recent advances in chromosome conformation capture methods reveal complex 3D architectures of chromatin such as compartments, topological domains and loops, which are fundamental to genome function. More recently, micro-compartments (via Region Capture Micro-C at 500-1kb resolution) and micro-compartment domains (MCDs, via Hi-C at 5-10kb resolution) have been identified as unique chromatin interaction patterns that occur during cell cycle and are amplified through certain perturbations. Current computational approaches for detection of these micro-compartment/MCD patterns suffer from low sensitivity and detection specificity. Method: We developed MARCA (Micro-compartment-AnchoR CAtcher), an automated tool utilizing image-processing techniques and scale-space analysis. MARCA applies a multi-scale Hessian-based filter and a specialized response function to detect candidate rectangle/ellipse-like interactions. After extracting local maxima, an anchor summarizer projects interactions to the diagonal, iteratively consolidates anchors while filtering out low-confidence candidates. Results: MARCA detects nearly twice as many anchors as previous methods on early G1 Hi-C data with depletion of nuclear transport and captures significantly higher number of MCD anchors on other cell-cycle phases where MCDs are expected. Results show strong coherence across cell-cycle and align with previously reported anchors features. On two high-resolution Region Capture Micro-C (RCMC) datasets, MARCA outperforms existing loop caller-based approach. Conclusion: MARCA provides a robust, highly sensitive framework detecting micro-compartment/MCD patterns across different resolutions and scales as well as their temporal dynamics during cell cycle. By improving MCD detection, MARCA enables studying the dynamic regulation of MCDs alongside other 3D genome organization features. Our code can be found at: https://github.com/alovesupr3me/MARCA

title: HiC-LEGO: A Modular Graph-Based Architecture for High-Resolution 3D Genome Reconstruction from Hi-C Data
authors: Abhishek Pandeya, Oluwatosin Oluwadare
abstract: Chromosome conformation capture techniques, such as Hi-C, provide insights into the three-dimensional (3D) organization of chromosomes by measuring interaction frequencies between genomic loci. Reconstructing 3D chromosome structures from TADs and Hi-C data remains a challenging task due to variability in domain detection methods. In this paper, we propose a novel framework for 3D chromosome reconstruction that leverages ensemble domains and a hierarchical model for enhanced structural prediction. As a key advancement, we incorporate a graph attention network (GAT)-based modeling approach to capture complex interaction patterns more effectively. This GAT-based technique serves as an initial backbone for improving structural embeddings and is further integrated into our TAD-based high-resolution reconstruction pipeline. Our method first identifies optimal topologically associating domains (TADs) by integrating domain lists from multiple TAD detection tools and computing pairwise domain similarity using a modified Measure of Concordance (MoC) metric. Using this refined domain set, we then construct individual 3D structures by leveraging pre-trained models and domain-specific structural embeddings. These domain structures are assembled into megabase (MB)-region structures, referred to as LEGOs. Finally, these LEGO structures are assembled into a complete chromosome structure while preserving consistency across different scales. Our method enhances domain accuracy through TAD refinement and produces structurally consistent chromosome models. We demonstrate that our approach achieves superior reconstruction accuracy compared to state-of-the-art methods and preserves TAD boundary consistency. Additionally, the reconstructed structures show improved alignment with known biological features, including chromatin loops and regulatory domain organization, providing an interpretable framework for 3D genome modeling.

title: Similarity-based counts weighting improves differential T cell clonotype abundance analysis
authors: Thomas C. Smits, Franka Buytenhuijs, Ankur Ankan, Radu-Florian Diaconescu, Johannes Textor
abstract: Differential T cell clonotype abundance analysis can give insight into clonal expansion following vaccination, infection, and other immune responses. However, because the majority of T cell receptor (TCR) sequences are private, data is highly sparse and overdispersed, causing both the sensitivity and specificity of differential abundance analysis to be limited. It has been shown that TCRs that bind the same antigen are highly similar in sequence and structure. Based on this, we propose a similarity-based weighting strategy to increase true positive detection in differential abundance analysis, by first finding TCR neighbourhoods and subsequently weighting the read counts of sequences. This preprocessing step can be combined with any downstream differential analysis. Using both simulated and real datasets, we show that similarity-based weighting can improve the true positive rate (TPR) while controlling the false positive rate (FPR). We simulated datasets using immuneSIM and incorporated sequences from the VDJ database in the treatment group, enabling assessment of the TPR and FPR. We observe increases in TPR from under 20% without weighting to over 90% with similarity-based weighted counts, while the FPR remains under 5%, using the Wilcoxon signed-rank test and DESeq2. We also show the power of similarity-based weighting in TCR data from SRBC-infected mice, using permutation testing to assess false positive control. This simple preprocessing step can be integrated in existing pipelines through our accompanying R package (https://github.com/thomcsmits/simweightR). We examined local neighbourhoods with the Hamming distance and BLOSUM62 alignment, although this can easily be extended towards other similarity metrics.

title: 3R-Fold: Enhancing RNA Secondary Structure Prediction via Retrieval-Augmented Self-Representation
authors: Chaimae Toubali, Kunpeng Xu, Shengrui Wang, Aida Ouangraoua
abstract: RNA secondary structure is a key determinant of RNA function, governing processes such as gene regulation, catalysis, and RNA–protein interactions. Despite decades of research, accurate computational prediction of RNA secondary structure remains challenging. Classical thermodynamic methods such as ViennaRNA rely on minimum free-energy optimization and often struggle to capture complex structural motifs and long-range interactions. Recently, pretrained RNA foundation models have demonstrated a remarkable ability to encode structural information directly from sequence data. However, how to effectively leverage these representations for retrieval-guided RNA folding remains largely unexplored. We introduce 3R-Fold, a retrieval-augmented framework for RNA secondary structure prediction that integrates RNA foundation model embeddings with representation learning and structural similarity search. In the first stage, RNA sequences are encoded using RNA-FM together with a Deep Self-Representation (DSR) model to learn structure-aware embeddings capturing global relationships between RNA sequences. In the second stage, FAISS similarity search retrieves structurally related RNAs from a knowledge base, and their secondary structures are aggregated to produce a consensus structural signal that guides folding prediction. Experiments across multiple RNA families and sequence lengths show that retrieval-based guidance substantially improves prediction accuracy compared with classical thermodynamic folding. The proposed 3R-Fold framework achieves the strongest overall performance among evaluated approaches and does not require prior knowledge of RNA family annotations. More broadly, 3R-Fold can be viewed as a modular retrieval layer that augments existing RNA folding algorithms and provides a promising direction toward scalable, data-driven RNA structure prediction.
keywords: RNA secondary structure; structure prediction; 3R-Fold; RNA foundation; RNA folding

title: Benchmarking LLMs on SMILES-Based Metabolite Property Prediction and Identifying Structural Determinants of Prediction Success
authors: Youngchan Kim, Dongyeop Jang
abstract: Background. Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to predict molecular properties from SMILES, but whether their accuracy depends on token patterns or chemical structure remains unclear. Methods. We benchmarked six LLMs (Claude Sonnet 4.0, GPT-4.1 Mini, Gemini 2.0 Flash, Gemma 12B, LLaMA 8B, NatureLM) on two databases (HMDB, TMMC) and three properties (molecular weight, LogP, carbon count). Per combination, we tested 0/1/3-shot baseline prompts and three 0-shot auxiliary strategies (SMILES decoding, IUPAC name, property hint). Random forest meta-models predicted correctness from 43 chemical descriptors and 440–525 SMILES n-grams, and chemical-feature enrichment among top SHAP predictors was assessed by permutation (100,000 permutations; Benjamini– Hochberg correction). Results. Claude Sonnet 4.0 was most accurate, but accuracy varied across properties (69% molecular weight, 9% LogP). Spearman correlations exceeded accuracy in all 18 pairs (HMDB), surpassing 0.99 (molecular weight, carbon count) and 0.89 (LogP). Prompt-strategy effects depended on model and property, with no single optimal strategy. Chemical features contributed half of SHAP importance, comparable to token features, but were enriched among top predictors in most pairs (P < 0.05). This enrichment was inversely correlated with molecular-weight accuracy (Spearman ρ = -0.81; P = 0.003; n = 11). Conclusions. LLMs ranked molecules more reliably than predicting absolute values, supporting rank-based screening. Prompts should be tailored to each model and task. Although all models used chemical information, greater reliance on chemical features was associated with lower accuracy, suggesting performance depends on how chemical and textual signals combine rather than on chemical sensitivity alone, requiring direct investigation.

title: EMBL-EBI Competency Hub as a Tool to Navigate Career Pathways
authors: Daria Sokolova, Kim Gurwitz, Catherine Brooksbank, Vera Matser, Denise Bianco, Giulia Tomba, Emma Karoune
abstract: In today’s skills-based economy, professional success depends on demonstrating measurable competencies rather than relying on static job titles. A competency-based approach provides a structured ""common language"" that clarifies career paths and helps organisations build resilient teams through better role definition and targeted development. The Competency Hub from EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) is a specialised web infrastructure designed to operationalise these frameworks. As a centralised, open-access repository, it empowers users to assess their attributes (KSAs/ KSBs) against recognised frameworks, explore professional personas, and identify training resources mapped to specific skills gaps. Access to such a repository is critical in biomedical data science, where the convergence of biology, medicine, and computation requires a highly adaptable workforce. The Hub’s utility is demonstrated by the Advancing Biomedical Data Science Careers (ABDC) project led by The Alan Turing Institute and EMBL-EBI. We’re utilising the Hub to host a comprehensive competency mapping that synthesises existing frameworks to identify 12 Minimum Standard Requirements and specific personas. Following this mapping, a gap analysis will identify training needs to be reflected in the Hub. Furthermore, the Hub supports granular professional extensions, such as the recently published career pathway for bioinformatics core facility scientists, serving as a blueprint for other specialists, such as biocurators. By hosting these outputs, the Competency Hub translates complex ecosystem analyses into practical, live templates for organisations to standardise roles and support inclusive workforces. Additionally, we developed the ""10 Simple Rules for producing FAIR competency frameworks"" to foster a connected global training ecosystem.

title: Sex-dependent cell-type specific transcriptional responses to sleep deprivation caused by mutations in the autism gene Shank3 in early development
authors: Caitlin Ottaway, Elizabeth Medina, Kaitlyn Ford, Abrar Al Maghribi, Kristan Singletary, Lucia Peixoto
abstract: Sleep problems are prevalent in autism spectrum disorder (ASD) as early as the first year of life and negatively impact quality of life. Mice with a mutation in the high confidence ASD gene Shank3 recapitulate the clinical ASD sleep phenotype and show an inability to properly respond to sleepiness (acute sleep deprivation, SD) as early as postnatal 24 (P24, ~1 year old). However, the molecular basis of sleepiness and how ASD associated mutations may impact this early in life is poorly understood. We have previously shown that SD in the brain of adult mice leads predominantly to an excitatory-neuron heavy transcriptional response. We hypothesize that the Shank3 mutation impairs the transcriptional response to sleepiness starting at young ages in neurons. To test this, we measured the cell-type specific transcriptional response to SD in Wild-Type and Shank3 (male and female) mice at P24 using single nuclear RNA-sequencing. Our results show that, like in adults, SD predominantly impacts excitatory neuronal transcription but does so differently in males than females. The Shank3 mutation seems to impair transcriptional responses in excitatory neurons in males but not in females. However, the transcriptional response in inhibitory neurons is enhanced by the mutation regardless of sex. Overall, the molecular basis of sleepiness is altered by the Shank3 mutation in early life, but the effect of sex on cell-type specific gene expression is more complex than previously anticipated. Current work focuses on identifying cell-type specific pathways underlying mutation and sex-dependent effects and independent validation using spatial transcriptomics.

title: The Shank3∆C mutation differentially impacts the molecular response to sleep deprivation across development
authors: Elliot Wald, Elizabeth Medina, Caitlin Ottaway, Christine Muheim, Kaitlyn Ford, Kristan Singletary, Hannah Schoch, Taylor Wintler, Ashely Ingiosi, Lucia Peixoto
abstract: Insomnia is prevalent in autism spectrum disorder (ASD), worsening core symptoms and negatively impacting quality of life. We previously showed that mice with a mutation in the high-confidence ASD gene Shank3 (Shank3∆C) recapitulate the clinical insomnia phenotype. Specifically, Shank3∆C mice do not respond properly to sleepiness after acute sleep deprivation (SD) starting as early as postnatal day 24 (P24, ~1 year old infant). However, the molecular basis of sleepiness and how ASD-associated mutations impact it remains unclear. In this study, we used RNA-sequencing to define the effect of Shank3∆C on the molecular basis of sleepiness by comparing cortical gene expression following SD in Wild-Type (WT) and mutant mice between P24 and P90 (adults). We found that at P90, the typical WT response involves upregulating DNA damage repair systems and neuronal activity-dependent transcription. At P24, WT animals upregulate neuronal growth and development pathways. The Shank3∆C mice do not show these changes, with the mutation largely repressing the transcriptional response to SD. However, mutants do consistently upregulate oxidative stress/neurodegeneration after SD regardless of age. We conclude that mutant mice are unable to accumulate sleepiness at the molecular level, instead showing an aberrant oxidative stress response. Enhancing the recruitment of neuronal growth and DNA repair pathways while diminishing the impact of oxidative stress following SD may therefore be actionable strategies to improve sleep in ASD. Future studies will focus on validating top candidates using low-throughput spatial transcriptomics to identify key targets and cell-types for further investigation.

title: Therapeutic Target Discovery for Rare Diseases via Machine Learning Integrating GWAS and TWAS
authors: Satoko Namba, Michio Iwata, Shin-Ichi Nureki, Noriko Otani, Yoshihiro Yamanishi
abstract: Identifying therapeutic targets for diseases is important in drug discovery. However, the depletion of viable therapeutic targets has a major bottleneck, contributing to the recent stagnation in drug development, especially for rare and orphan diseases. Here, we propose a disease signature, TRESOR, which characterizes the functional mechanisms of each disease through genome-wide association study (GWAS) and transcriptome-wide association study (TWAS) data. Based on TRESOR and target perturbation signatures (TGPs)—i.e., gene knockdown and overexpression profiles of target-coding genes —we develop machine learning methods for predicting inhibitory and activatory therapeutic targets for various diseases. TRESOR enables highly accurate identification of target candidate proteins based on inverse correlations between TRESOR and TGPs. Furthermore, Bayesian integrative method combines TRESOR-based inverse correlations and omics-based disease similarities, providing more reliable predictions for rare and orphan diseases with few or no known targets. We make comprehensive predictions for 284 diseases with 4,345 inhibitory target candidates and 151 diseases with 4,040 activatory target candidates. These predictions were validated through literature-based cross-referencing and independently assessed using human cohort data, supporting their therapeutic potential. For instance, multiple endocrine neoplasia, a rare disease with only one known inhibitory target, was predicted to have new candidate targets such as FHL2, whose downregulation correlated with improved survival in independent cohorts. The proposed method was also applied to orphan diseases lacking any known targets, such as tauopathies, identifying promising candidates including RAB1B. Proposed methods are expected to be useful for understanding disease–disease relationships and identifying therapeutic targets for rare and orphan diseases.

title: Bioinformatics Analysis of Circulating Tumour DNA Sequencing Data: A Promising Approach to Monitor Prostate Cancer Progression
authors: Samira Rahimirad, Eleonora Scarlata, Lucie Hamel, Seta Derderian, Ginette McKercher, Fadi Brimo, Fred Saad, Armen Aprikian, Simone Chevalier
abstract: Background: Although prostate cancer (PCa) has a high survival rate, several patients progress to late stages. Indeed, current blood PSA and imaging modalities cannot accurately predict therapy response/ resistance and progression. We sought to identify new indicators by tracking changes in genomic alterations emerging during progression in the serial liquid biopsies of patients with lethal PCa. Methods: Banked fresh frozen prostate tissues from ten radical prostatectomy cases with lethal PCa were processed to identify tumour foci and macro-dissect cores of high cellularity (>75%) for DNA extraction. Their serial plasma collections (<4mL) were used to isolate cell-free DNA (cfDNA), next sequenced along with matched primary tumour and germline (blood) DNA. Results: Already established and novel copy number variations (CNVs), mostly deletions, were found in patients' primary tumours. Longitudinal cfDNA sequencing and bioinformatics analysis unveiled rising circulating tumour DNA (ctDNA) fractions when patients reached the metastatic and later stages. Although genomic amplifications were rare in primary tumours, they were common in ctDNAs. Tumour-shared alterations were found in ctDNA during progression, along with newly discovered ctDNA-exclusive modifications. Furthermore, the clonality of ctDNA alterations was related to treatment resistance over time and revealed PCa cellular heterogeneity in the advanced stage. Conclusion: The identification of novel genomic changes in tumour DNA and emerging ctDNAs during progression is enhancing our knowledge of PCa severity. Findings on ctDNA underscore the significance of longitudinal liquid biopsy for monitoring recurrent disease less invasively and could contribute to the development of novel diagnostic tests and more effective treatments impacting PCa lethality.

title: DrugAgent: Explainable Multi-Agent Large Language Model-based Reasoning for Aggregating Heterogeneous Biomedical Evidence
authors: Yoshitaka Inoue, Tianci Song, Xinling Wang, Augustin Luna, Tianfan Fu
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems can integrate heterogeneous biomedical evidence but often produce unfaithful reasoning due to hallucinations of source material, leading to unsupported mechanistic claims. We introduce a triangulation framework using multiple LLM-based agents for drug-target interaction (DTI) reasoning, enforcing agreement across three complementary sources: ML-based affinity prediction, multi-hop knowledge graph (KG) reasoning, and PubMed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A reasoning module aggregates these signals under an explicit cross-source consistency constraint, thereby restricting inference by preventing the composition of unsupported cross-source evidence. We evaluate DrugAgent on 900 kinase drug-target pairs using an LLM-as-a-judge protocol for biological plausibility by citing multiple evidence sources. Without this multi-source triangulation, two-source combinations (ML+KG, ML+RAG, KG+RAG) produce 15-20% unfaithful explanations due to unsupported evidence bridging and speculative reasoning. Enforcing agreement across all three sources reduces unfaithful outputs to ≤0.2%, reaching near-zero failure rates while maintaining competitive predictive performance. The framework shows high stability (98.3% label agreement) and strong semantic consistency (>0.7 cosine similarity). It also improves biological plausibility, producing more calibrated predictions citing various evidence sources. Evidence combination analysis shows that triangulation resolves conflicts and prevents dominance of noisy sources, while stabilizing prediction trajectories and preserving consensus signals. These failures arise from under-constrained reasoning, where evidence is combined without sufficient cross-validation. Cross-source agreement acts as a regularizer for scientific reasoning, preventing hallucinated mechanisms and constraining inference to evidence-grounded pathways. This highlights triangulation as a general design principle for reliable multi-source reasoning in biomedical AI and other knowledge-intensive domains.

title: drGT: Interpretable Drug Response Prediction with Attention-Guided Gene Attribution on a Drug-Cell-Gene Heterogeneous Graph
authors: Yoshitaka Inoue, Tianfan Fu, Rui Kuang, Augustin Luna
abstract: Background: For translational impact, accurate drug response prediction and biological plausibility of predictive features are needed. We present drGT, a heterogeneous graph deep learning model over drugs, genes, and cell lines that couples prediction with mechanism-oriented interpretability via attention coefficients (ACs). Results: We assess predictive generalization (random, unseen-drug, unseen-cell, and zero-shot splits) and biological plausibility (text-mined PubMed co-mentions and comparison to a structure-based DTI predictor) on GDSC, NCI60, and CTRP datasets. Across benchmarks, drGT delivers top regression performance while maintaining competitive classification accuracy for drug sensitivity. Under random 5-fold cross-validation, drGT attains an AUROC of up to 0.945 (3rd overall) and an R2 of up to 0.690, outperforming baselines on regression. In leave-one-out tests for unseen cell lines and drugs, drGT achieves AUROCs of 0.706 and 0.844, and R2 values of 0.692 and 0.022, the only model yielding positive R2 for unseen drugs. In zero-shot prediction, drGT achieves an AUROC of 0.786 and a regression R2 of 0.334, representing the highest scores among models. For interpretability, AC-derived drug-gene links recover known biology: among 976 drugs with known DTIs, 36.9% of predicted links match established DTIs, and 63.7% are supported by either PubMed abstracts or a structure-based predictive model. Enrichment analyses of AC-prioritized genes reveal drug-perturbed biological processes, providing pathway-level explanations. Conclusions: drGT advances predictive generalization and mechanism-centered interpretability, offering state-of-the-art regression accuracy and literature-supported hypotheses, leveraging graph learning from heterogeneous data for biological discovery. title: Hypothesis-Driven Analysis of Gut Microbiome in Subclinical ASCVD
authors: Shreya Chindepalli, Anita Shlesinger, Joshua Granek, Francois Haddad, Jessilyn Dunn
abstract: Host-microbe interactions contribute to pathways relevant to atherosclerosis pathogenesis, including lipid metabolism, bile acid metabolism, and vascular inflammation. Alterations in human gut microbial composition have been reported in atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease (ASCVD), though evidence in early, subclinical stages remains limited. Subclinical ASCVD is characterized by measurable plaque burden prior to onset of symptomatic cardiovascular disease. Studying this stage enables investigation of biological processes associated with disease development. This study examines associations between gut microbiome taxonomic composition and subclinical ASCVD. Stool metagenomic sequencing data from 485 samples across 136 participants (68 with subclinical ASCVD, defined as coronary artery calcium score > 100; 68 matched controls with no coronary artery calcium) was obtained from the Project Baseline Health Study. Participants were propensity-matched on age, sex, race, ethnicity, BMI, hypertension, ASCVD risk score, and type 2 diabetes status. Species-level taxonomic profiles were generated using MetaPhlAn v4. Based on published findings linking specific gut taxa to ASCVD, four genera were selected for prespecified hypothesis-testing: Collinsella, Roseburia, Eubacterium, and Streptococcus. Wilcoxon rank-sum tests with multiple testing correction identified higher relative abundance of genera Collinsella and Roseburia in the subclinical ASCVD group. Species-level tests identified three taxa, Eubacterium ventriosum, Eubacterium ramulus, and Streptococcus gordonii, as significantly associated with subclinical ASCVD status after multiple testing correction. These findings suggest that some microbial associations with ASCVD reported in the literature are also detectable in subclinical ASCVD. This work represents an initial hypothesis-testing analysis within an ongoing investigation of this longitudinal data from the Project Baseline Health Study cohort.

title: Using Large Language Models to Automate Cancer Gene Prioritization for 898 Cancer Subtypes from the OncoTree Ontology for Exploration in cBioPortal
authors: Suhasini Lulla, Ino de Bruijn, Karl Pichotta, Christopher Fong, Augustin Luna, Sharon Plon
abstract: Disease-specific gene sets are central to genomic data interpretation. However, curation at the cancer subtype resolution remains incomplete and difficult to scale. Therefore, we developed 'OncoTree2Genes-LLM' (https://github.com/SuhasiniLulla/OncoTree2Genes-LLM), a programmatic framework that leverages large language models (LLMs) to generate and evaluate gene-cancer subtype associations across the comprehensive OncoTree ontology of cancer subtypes. Using the December 2025 OncoTree release, we prompted an LLM to generate structured lists of genes classically implicated for each subtype. We then compared these lists with established pan-cancer lists. Associations absent in these lists were evaluated through automated PubMed queries. For each association, abstracts were retrieved and assessed using a second LLM acting as an independent evaluator ('LLM-as-a-judge', LLMaJ) to determine literature evidence support. Supported associations were retained. Human review of selected subtypes assessed concordance with LLMaJ. The pipeline generated gene sets for 896 of 898 cancer subtypes, yielding 11,129 associations (median 12 genes per subtype). Of these, 85.1% were supported by established lists or literature-based LLMaJ evaluation. Manual review demonstrated agreement between LLMaJ and human judgment (17 of 18 correct classifications). Subtype-specific gene sets showed concordance with curated resources for selected cancers where curations were available. Lists generated by OncoTree2Genes-LLM were integrated into a local deployment of cBioPortal for cohort filtering and visualization. This work demonstrates a scalable approach for structured knowledge extraction and evaluation in combination with pre-existing ontologies that enables continuous updating in pace with evolving literature. Applications include expert gene curation, focused research, and clinical workflows.

title: Role of Genomics and Proteomics in disease diagnosis
authors: Sara Munir, Muhammad Waqar Ali, Arfeen Siddique
abstract: Background:Genomics and proteomics are quickly transforming the practice of clinical medicine with regard to disease diagnosis through early, precise and personalized detection of complex disorders. In this study, we explore how whole-exome sequencing and mass spectrometry-based proteomic profiling can be combined to produce greater diagnostic utility in three key clinical areas: breast cancer, Alzheimer disease, and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Method: A group of 120 participants (patients and healthy controls) were enrolled to undergo comprehensive genomic and proteomic analysis. Important disease specific genetic mutations, e.g. BRCA1/2/HER2 in breast cancer, APOE 4 in Alzheimer disease, TCF7L2 in diabetes and their relationship with respective protein biomarkers, e.g. HER2 protein, tau, and amyloid-82, inflammatory cytokines were identified. Results: The diagnostic accuracy of statistical and machine learning models were high (up to 94.2%), and gene variants were strongly correlated with protein expression levels (r > 0.7). These results affirm that multi-omics in tandem increases the classification of disease and biomarker identification in a grand magnitude compared to traditional methods. Conclusions: The article underlines the potential of genomics and proteomics in enabling earlier accurate diagnosis and informing customized medicine, but also points to the issue of validation upon greater scale and the application of apparatus to clinical practice

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: From Single-Cell Decisions to Tissue-Scale Disease: A Multiscale Modeling Framework
authors: Shayn Peirce-Cottler
abstract: Many of the most prevalent and challenging human diseases—including cancer, cardiovascular disease, and fibrotic disease—emerge from dynamic, multiscale interactions among heterogeneous cell populations and their evolving microenvironments. Yet most therapeutic strategies and computational models focus on isolated molecular targets, limiting their ability to predict or influence emergent tissue-level behavior or patient-specific outcomes. Addressing this gap requires mechanistic models that explicitly link intracellular signaling, cell phenotypic decision-making, and tissue-scale remodeling across space and time. In this talk, I will present our laboratory’s work developing multiscale mechanistic computational models that integrate molecular, cellular, and tissue-level processes to study disease onset and progression. Our approach centers on agent-based modeling, enabling explicit 2 representation of individual cells, stochastic behaviors, and cell–cell interactions while capturing emergent, tissue-scale dynamics. These models are specified and parameterized using data-driven, machine learning approaches, allowing us to incorporate high-dimensional experimental data while preserving mechanistic interpretability. Importantly, our modeling efforts are tightly coupled to experiments in an iterative loop. We design experiments to probe single-cell behaviors and microenvironmental cues, use these data to refine model structure and parameters, and then generate testable predictions regarding tissue-scale adaptations. Using this framework, we have studied microvascular network and tissue remodeling in development, regeneration following injury, and fibrotic disease. Together, these studies demonstrate how multiscale mechanistic models can reveal causal links between cellular decision-making and tissue-level disease phenotypes, providing a predictive foundation for rational therapeutic design.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: VAPOR: A variational autoencoder with transport operators to disentangle latent dynamics in single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data
authors: Jie Sheng, Noah Cohen Kalafut, Daifeng Wang
abstract: Complex systems exhibit dynamics governed by the interplay of intrinsic, co-occurring processes. For instance, emerging single-cell and spatial transcriptomics data reveal that changes in cellular gene expression entangle simultaneous biological processes such as maturation, proliferation, and spatial organization. Current trajectory inference methods for dynamic analysis typically impose a global smoothness constraint, ordering cells into an aggregated, uni-scale progression that conflates distinct processes and thus overlook their specific dynamic patterns. To address this, we developed VAPOR, a generative framework to infer and disentangle latent dynamics for co-occurring biological processes from single-cell data. To reconstruct continuous transitions from static observations, we employ a Markov process that leverages graph transport on a local stochastic neighborhood graph to estimate feasible state transitions for each cell in the variational autoencoder latent space. Using such transitions, VAPOR models and infers latent dynamics as ordinary differential equations. More importantly, it decomposes the latent dynamics into a set of process-specific components parameterized by transport operators (TOs) and their corresponding weights. Each TO defines a process-specific dynamic component, and its weight for each cell quantifies the process's contribution to the cell's dynamics with associated dynamic genes. After simulation studies and benchmarking, we applied VAPOR to diverse real-world datasets, including cross-species brain development, multiplexed cancer drug responses, and spatial transcriptomics of the mouse hippocampus. VAPOR disentangled a variety of temporally and spatially co-occurring processes, such as neuronal differentiation, cell cycle, and extracellular signal-regulated kinase (ERK) suppression after drug treatment. Furthermore, VAPOR also identified corresponding dynamic genes for those processes, such as RBFOX3, showing an earlier progression in macaque than human neurogenesis.
keywords: disentangle latent dynamics; VAPOR; transport operators; variational autoencoder; spatial transcriptomics

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Mechanistic ODE Modeling of MAPK/ AKT Signaling Reveals Scheduling-Dependent Control of Persister Dynamics in BRAF-Mutant Melanoma
authors: Ethan Wang, Aayan Alwani
abstract: Melanoma relapse is frequently associated with drug-tolerant persister cells, rare tumor subpopulations that survive targeted therapy through adaptive signaling rather than stable genetic resistance. Because these cells remain dependent on MAPK and RTK/AKT signaling, combination strategies that disrupt both pathways may improve control of drug-tolerant populations. Here, we present a mechanistic ordinary differential equation (ODE)-based model to investigate treatment scheduling strategies combining a PROTAC degrader targeting mutant BRAF with an RTK inhibitor. The model integrates MAPK and AKT signaling dynamics, downstream transcriptional programs, and tumor population behavior, with drug action represented through two-compartment pharmacokinetics, bolus dosing, and Hill-type pharmacodynamics. Treatment performance was evaluated using a persister index (PI) together with a composite optimization score (COS) that balances persister burden and drug exposure. Screening across a large set of candidate regimens identified scheduling strategies that reduce simulated persister populations relative to baseline conditions. Regimens incorporating early PROTAC exposure followed by sustained RTK inhibition achieved the largest reductions in PI while maintaining lower modeled toxicity penalties. Additional analysis across simulated tumor phenotypes revealed variability in optimal schedules, reflecting differences in underlying signaling dynamics. Overall, this framework demonstrates that, within a mechanistic modeling context, treatment scheduling can substantially influence persister dynamics and comparative performance metrics. These results provide a basis for exploring combination treatment strategies and generating hypotheses for future experimental validation of scheduling-based approaches to targeting melanoma persister cells.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Computational pipeline elucidates how single-cell, lymphocyte motility behaviors drive B-T interactions that mediate the antibody response.
authors: Nikita Sivakumar, Chanhong Min, Kibaek Choe, Wendy Beguelin, Jude Phillip, Feilim Mac Gabhann
abstract: Lymphocytes rely on cell motility to navigate tissue environments and engage in cell-cell interactions that support the adaptive immune response. Within germinal centers, B-cells and T-cells rely on cell motility to encounter and engage in B-T interactions that enable antibody affinity maturation. Systematically quantifying how B-cell and T-cell motility influences B-T interactions within germinal centers can inform what cellular mechanisms support a healthy antibody response to infection or vaccination. Experimental methods, alone, cannot simultaneously image single-cell motility in vivo and all B-T interactions within high-density tissue environments, like the germinal center. To close this gap, we developed and validated PRISMM (Pipeline for Recapitulating Cell-Cell Interactions using Spatial Motility Modelling). PRISMM first applies unsupervised machine learning to learn single-cell, lymphocyte motility behaviors from intravital, time-lapse imaging data. PRISMM then applies agent-based simulations to infer how these motility behaviors drive B-T interactions. The application of our pipeline identified that germinal center T-cells tend to take on fast and exploratory movements, while B-cells tend to move more slowly. Our simulations show that these distinct motility behaviors allow B-cells to maximize unique interactions with T-cells within confined volumes. This result suggests that baseline lymphocyte motility behaviors optimize B-T interactions during a physiological antibody response. PRISMM leverages the single-cell nature of motility data to identify distinct, in vivo cell motility behaviors. Our pipeline can then predict how these single-cell motility behaviors drive emergent cell-cell interactions. Using PRISMM we can understand how cell motility influences cell-cell interactions in healthy and disease contexts.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Metabolic signatures of immune checkpoint inhibitor response in gynecologic cancers: Insights from flux balance analysis
authors: Gideon Idumah, Lin Li, Lamis Yehia, Haider Mahdi, Ying Ni
abstract: Modifiers of immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) responses in cancer patients are complex and remain poorly characterized, especially in gynecologic cancers. In this study, we explored fluxomic biomarkers that differentiate responders from non-responders to ICIs in a series of 49 patients with gynecologic cancers, including ovarian, cervical, and endometrial cancers. By applying metabolic enzyme expression as constraints, we utilized an objective-customizable flux balance analysis within a genome-scale metabolic model to predict the metabolic flux differences between responders versus non-responders of ICI treatment. We identified three reactions with consistent differential activity across all ten different optimization objectives: Succinate Dehydrogenase (SUCD1m) in the citric acid cycle, NADH: Guanosine-5-Phosphate Oxidoreductase (r0276) involved in purine catabolism, and Ornithine Transaminase Reversible, Mitochondrial (ORNTArm) in the urea cycle. Additionally, reactions within the folate cycle subsystem, particularly involving MTHFD2, demonstrated significance in distinguishing treatment responses, aligning with previous findings linking MTHFD2 to immune evasion and tumor progression. To further analyze the association between metabolic features and survival outcomes, we implemented machine learning models that integrate multi-omics data. Our model included clinical-pathologic, molecular-genomic features (gene expression, TGF-beta score, immune cell abundance from transcriptomic deconvolution), and significant reaction fluxes. Our findings suggest that SUCD1m, MTHFDm and ORNTArm are important metabolic biomarkers that could serve as predictive indicators for ICI response and, if validated in a larger cohort, may guide the development of targeted therapies to enhance treatment efficacy for gynecologic cancer patients. This study highlights the use of genome-scale metabolic modeling to identify clinically relevant biomarkers and improve therapeutic strategies.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: SPECIMEN powered by refineGEMs for streamlined automated high-quality genome-scale modeling
authors: Carolin Brune, Gwendolyn Olivia Döbel, Andreas Dräger
abstract: Background: Systems biology aims to provide a systematic, comprehensive understanding of living systems at all scales through context-specific computational models. Metabolism has been identified as a primary aspect for this endeavor because of its well-defined physico-chemical foundations and its involvement in all aspects of life. In many applications, genome-scale metabolic models (GEMs) have demonstrated their usefulness to predict various phenotypic features based on firm principles. Even though GEMs follow relatively simple mathematical structures, their reconstruction and curation are demanding and still involve many manual steps. Results: We introduce SPECIMEN, a collection of workflows designed for automated, standardized strain-specific metabolic modeling and GEM curation. SPECIMEN primarily utilizes the toolbox refineGEMs, which provides a database of defined growth media and a plethora of functions for reading, manipulating, and curating individual aspects of GEMs, including mass/charge curation and the assignment of SBO terms and EC numbers. RefineGEMs demonstrated its usefulness in reconstructing five C.-striatum models. SPECIMEN combines these functions to provide two principal reconstruction pipelines, both based on previously published methods: the High-Quality Template-Based (HQTB) and the CarveMe-ModelPolisher (CMPB) workflow. CMPB starts from a CarveMe-generated draft model, refines and extends it into a high-quality, strain-specific model, whereas HQTB employs a user-provided template model and genome as its basis for reconstructing a new model. Conclusion: The combination of both tools drastically reduces manual effort while semi-automatically producing directly usable, high-quality GEMs that comply with all current standard operating procedures and best-practice guidelines. Availability: Both Python-based open-source software solutions are freely available at github.com/draeger-lab/SPECIMEN and github.com/draeger-lab/refineGEMs.

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Temporal competence windows govern four discrete phases of neural progenitor fate commitment in a multi-layer ODE framework of CNS development
authors: Batuhan Safa Kar
abstract: BACKGROUND How positional signals are translated into discrete neuronal identities across developmental time remains incompletely understood. Transcription factor (TF) competence windows”periods during which progenitors respond to inductive signals”constrain fate decisions, but their system-level dynamics remain uncharacterized. METHODS We developed a six-layer ODE framework modeling CNS progenitor fate commitment along anterior-posterior and dorsal-ventral axes, integrating: (1) a bistable GSE/SVE switch via Lhx3-Phox2b mutual inhibition (Hill n=4), (2) rhombomer boundary sharpening via Hoxb1-Hoxb2 cross-repression (Hill n=6), (3) Notch-Delta lateral inhibition, (4) Eph-Ephrin contact barrier, (5) CN VII axon guidance, and (6) temporal TF competence gating across 18 transcription factors. Validity was assessed against 11 quantitative biological criteria, including SHH dose-response benchmarking against Dessaud et al. (2008). RESULTS Systematic variation of ODE integration time (t_norm=0.03-1.0) revealed four discrete commitment phases. Phase I (t<0.125): complete progenitor indeterminacy. Phase II (t=0.16-0.38): rapid commitment via sequential TF window opening”somatic motor neurons commit before branchiomotor neurons, recapitulating known in vivo temporal ordering. Phase III (t=0.38-0.875): full commitment, zero residual progenitor fraction. Phase IV (t=1.0): partial reversion caused by Chx10 window closure, isolating ARAS progenitors as a structurally irreducible population. GSE-axis parameters showed R²=0.995 concordance with Dessaud dose-response data (EC50 deviation: 2.6%). CONCLUSIONS Temporal TF competence gating ”not morphogen signal strength or bistable switch kinetics”is the dominant determinant of commitment timing. The four-phase structure and Hill coefficient independence of commitment rates are emergent properties unreachable by individual subsystem analysis

track: SysMod: Computational Modeling of Biological Systems
title: Decoding Anti-TNF Therapy Outcomes from Pre-Treatment Single-Cell Data via Network-Based Perturbation Modeling
authors: Mathilde Meyenberg, Matthew Leipner, Alan James Mueller-Breckenridge, Jörg Menche
abstract: Despite anti-TNF therapies being a cornerstone of IBD management, non-response rates remain as high as 40%. To address the lack of predictive baseline biomarkers, we developed a computational framework that leverages multi-layer network integration and in silico perturbation modeling to predict drug response from pre-treatment single-cell transcriptomics. Using longitudinal data from UC and CD patients treated with adalimumab, we construct cell-type-specific networks by mapping Wilcoxon-ranked genes to a protein-protein interaction (PPI) network. To ensure disease relevance, networks are filtered using LCC-based z-scores, retaining only those where IBD-associated modules show significant connectivity. These layers are integrated into multiplex networks, where cell-specific disease neighborhoods are defined via a multiplex random walk with restart (RWR). These network neighborhoods define subnetworks that reveal distinct differences in connectivity around IBD genes for CD and UC. To model perturbations, layer-specific subnetworks are merged into union graphs representing disease (inflamed cells) and reference states (non-inflamed cells) from pre-treatment data. We simulate therapy by deleting target nodes and edges, evaluating the impact via a graph hopper kernel. This kernel utilizes semantic gene embeddings and topological features to compare graph similarity. By deriving a normalized effect score from the resulting distance matrices, we successfully recover a differential signal of anti-TNF response from baseline data alone. By investigating the cell-specific connectivity around TNF on the multiplex networks, we gain biological insights into how pre-treatment cellular signaling influences clinical outcomes.

title: PIMENTO: a Physics and bIology-inforMed Neural network for dynamic inference of gene regulatory networks to model plant response to biotic stresses
authors: Xavier Amorós-Gabarrón, Alessandra Goncalves Ribeiro, Krishna Kumar, Pratila Debnath, Regis Duvigneau, Justyna J. Olas, Lorenzo Sala, Silvia Bottini
abstract: In a scenario of climate change, plants are exposed to an increasing variety of pathogens, accompanied by additional hostile conditions. Comprehensive understanding of plant immunity is essential to ensure food production and security. Gene regulatory networks (GRNs) provide a powerful representation of these intricate regulatory systems. However, most inference methods measure only static properties and face the trade-off between scalability and mechanistic interpretability. Here, we propose PIMENTO, a novel hybrid model based on physics-informed neural-networks to infer fully interpretable GRNs from time-series omics data. This approach exploits the ability of neural-networks to approximate high-dimensional systems in combination with explicit ODEs and prior biological knowledge. PIMENTO showed robustness on synthetic data compared to random predictors when inaccurate prior is provided, when trained on as few as 4 timepoints and noise. PIMENTO on 21 time-series (3-7 timepoints, 2-8 replicates) of tomato (Solanum lycopersicum) plants upon infection by diverse economically important pathogens, with prior network composed of 11822 genes, 277 transcription factors (TFs) and 66343 edges, yielded several TFs with pivotal role in plant defense. Among the top 10, Solyc12g009240-ERF16 and Solyc06g070900-TCP17 were functionally validated using the virus-induced gene-silencing system in tomato, demonstrating their key role in the response to Botrytis cinerea infection, as silencing of either TF resulted in increased susceptibility. Overall, PIMENTO showed good performances regarding scalability, interpretability, predictivity and suitability to model time-series with few timepoints, which will fulfil a gap in the literature. PIMENTO can be used beyond plants, since the model is agnostic of the biological system

title: Mechanistic Modeling of rTMS-Mediated Quiescent Cell Targeting in Glioblastoma
authors: Chitransh Dave, Vrutti Mehta, Kenza Benzeroual, Nicolas Gallo
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) remains highly resistant to therapy in part because hypoxia, impaired perfusion, and treatment-associated cell-state transitions create a microenvironment that favors quiescent, therapy-resistant tumor populations. These latent physiological states are not well captured by models that evaluate treatments in isolation, despite their major influence on therapeutic response. We developed a mechanistic ODE-based computational framework to test whether repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation (rTMS) can shift this balance by modulating intratumoral perfusion and oxygenation, thereby reducing quiescent-cell burden. The model couples proliferating, quiescent, and necrotic tumor compartments with hypoxia–perfusion dynamics and rTMS as an upstream physiological perturbation. In this framework, rTMS is not treated as a direct cytotoxic agent, but as a driver of downstream changes in perfusion, oxygenation, delivery, and cell-state transitions that alter treatment sensitivity. Simulations across a heterogeneous Monte Carlo virtual patient cohort, combined with scenario exploration and sensitivity analysis, reveal parameter regimes in which modest hemodynamic changes reshape tumor burden and alter combination response. Together, these results establish an in silico test platform for studying neuromodulation-enabled therapeutic synergy in GBM.

title: Leveraging LLMs for accurate and confidence calibrated cell type and state identification
authors: Parashar Dhapola
abstract: Accurate cell type and cell state annotation remains a bottleneck in single-cell transcriptomics. Reference-based methods depend on curated atlases that are incomplete for disease contexts, rare populations, and transitional states. LLM-based approaches offer contextual reasoning over gene expression, but prior implementations suffer from hallucination, selective evidence use, and poor reproducibility across runs. We present a deterministic AI workflow that constrains LLM reasoning within a programmatic scaffold to achieve reference-free annotation with calibrated confidence. The workflow operates on pseudo-bulk expression profiles and proceeds through three structured stages. First, candidate cell identities are generated from expression data and challenged through an adversarial elimination process. Surviving candidates enter pairwise tournaments where competing hypotheses are evaluated against the full expression profile, not a pre-selected marker set. Cell identity and functional state are resolved in separate stages to prevent conflation of lineage with activation or differentiation status. Each annotation is linked to the Cell Ontology and accompanied by a structured argument documenting supporting evidence, eliminated alternatives, and rejection reasoning. Confidence scores are calibrated against empirical accuracy: annotations assigned high confidence are demonstrably more accurate than those flagged for manual review, giving researchers a principled basis for allocating curation effort. We benchmarked the workflow across 977 clusters in 20 datasets spanning PBMC, bone marrow, tumour microenvironment, and cross-species samples. Compared to expert-curated labels, the workflow achieved accuracy improvements of 388% over GPTCellType, 268% over CellTypist, and 101% over SingleR. In production, the system has annotated over 50,000 clusters across 3,000+ datasets. We discuss architectural decisions that govern where LLMs add value and where programmatic control is essential, offering a practical framework for integrating language models into reproducible computational biology pipelines.

title: Decoding IBD Risk: A Transformer-Based approach to Predict Allelic Regulatory Impact of IBD associated Variants Across Multiple Cell Lines
authors: Sanjoy Dey, Vibha Anand, Pablo Meyer Rojas, Scott Espenschied, Thaddeus Stappenbeck, Jianying Hu
abstract: Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) is a complex immune-mediated disorder with strong genetic underpinnings, yet the functional consequences of disease-associated single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) on gene expression remain poorly characterized across relevant cell types. To address this, we leveraged BMFM-DNA, a pretrained transformer-based foundation model that integrates SNP tokens at the earliest stage of sequence encoding and was pretrained on the human reference genome. The model was fine-tuned on the TewheyMPRA dataset, which quantifies the in vivo regulatory impact of SNPs via lenti-MPRA technology across three functionally distinct cell lines — K562, HepG2, and SK-N-SH — enabling cell-type-resolved predictions of allelic regulatory activity. We curated 241 SNPs previously reported as statistically significant IBD risk variants and applied the fine-tuned model to predict allelic skewness, defined as the difference in MPRA-measured expression between reference and alternative alleles (logâ‚‚FC_ref âˆ’ logâ‚‚FC_alt), as a quantitative measure of variant-driven regulatory perturbation. Prioritizing SNPs by the magnitude and consistency of their allelic skew across three cell lines, we identified five SNPs exhibiting robust and concordant impacts on gene expression regardless of cell context. Two SNPs (rs4821544 and rs6426833) had skewness score >0.5 representingdownregulation of gene expression in all three cell lines whereas three SNPs (rs907611, rs4676408 and rs1569328) has skewness score<-0.5 representing genetic up-regulation. These high-impact variants mapped to genes involved in immune regulation, receptor tyrosine kinase signaling, and broader cell signaling pathways, suggesting that a small but functionally critical subset of IBD-associated variants may exert broad, cell-type-independent regulatory effects with direct relevance to disease pathogenesis.

title: Genome-wide detection of human 5′ UTR variants that impact protein translation
authors: Matthieu Chaldebas, Khoren Ponsin, Jonathan Bohlen, Clément Conil, Haralambos Mourelatos, Peter D. Stenson, David N. Cooper, Laurent Abel, Jean-Laurent Casanova, Aurélie Cobat, Peng Zhang
abstract: The 5′ untranslated region (5′ UTR) of messenger RNAs (mRNAs) plays a central role in regulating protein synthesis initiation, particularly through the Kozak sequence and upstream open reading frames (uORFs). Genetic variants within these regulatory elements could affect translation, altering gene expression and contributing to clinical phenotypes in humans. We developed a computational method called 5ULTRA (5′ Untranslated Region Annotation) for analysis of whole-exome sequencing and whole-genome sequencing data to detect, annotate, and prioritize 5′ UTR variants with potential translation impact. 5ULTRA identifies single-nucleotide variants, indels, and splicing variants that affect uORFs by creating or disrupting start/ stop codons and that alter Kozak sequence strength of either the uORFs or the main coding sequence. 5ULTRA incorporates recent uORF databases and provides comprehensive annotations. 5ULTRA implements a machine-learning score to prioritize candidate variants with predicted effects on translation and also provides specific mechanistic predictions. The score correlates strongly with experimentally measured protein-level effects of 5′ UTR variants. We applied 5ULTRA to multiple genetics datasets across diverse disease contexts, identifying candidate variants including potential cancer-driving somatic mutations predicted to decrease ABI1 level or increase NRAS abundance; common variants associated with traits such as multiple sclerosis, lung function, and cardiovascular function, by altering protein levels of TAGAP, VRTN, and SPAAR, respectively; and rare germline variants in our cohort, including a splicing variant of RPSA leading to 5′ UTR sequence alteration that causes congenital asplenia and a variant of TNF that could predispose to tuberculosis.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: eGoT: Enhanced Graph-of-Thoughts for Multi-Hop Knowledge Retrieval and Hypothesis Generation in Biomedicine
authors: Nihar Sanda, Benjamin Gyori, Vito Quaranta, Auroop Ganguly, Ayan Paul
abstract: Motivation: Research on biological mechanisms and disease processes is limited by fragmented findings across unstructured text in publications. Question answering and hypothesis generation that can reason across multiple sources can overcome this limitation. However, Large language models (LLMs) are prone to inaccuracies and lack clear provenance to primary evidence. Retrieval augmented generation approaches that have provenance to the original source of evidence address these shortcomings. However, the response richness is dependent on the retrieval process design. Current approaches often fail to produce responses requiring multi-hop reasoning across multiple domains. Results: To address this, we propose eGoT, which combines automated knowledge graph construction from biomedical literature with a novel graph-of-thoughts approach to query the knowledge base and construct comprehensive responses to natural language questions. Given a corpus of documents, eGoT first uses an LLM-based pipeline to identify and normalize entities and relationships and constructs graph and vector databases. Given an input question, eGoT performs multi-round LLM-based querying of the databases to construct a response. Benchmarking on datasets like MultiHopRAG, HotpotQA, and Ultradomain demonstrates eGoT's superiority over state-of-the-art retrieval methods, including HopRAG, SireRAG, HiRAG, and HippoRAG. We demonstrate eGoT on two biomedical use cases: (i) generate responses to domain expert-curated questions on small cell lung cancer using 1,046 PubMed Central publications, and (ii) demonstrate eGoT’s ability to find plausible connections between Lupus and climate factors (UV exposure) that affect disease trajectory. Availability and Implementation: https://github.com/NNeuralDynamics/eGOT-ISMB.git

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: DrugAgent: Explainable Multi-Agent Reasoning for Aggregating Heterogeneous Biomedical Evidence
authors: Yoshitaka Inoue, Tianci Song, Xinling Wang, Augustin Luna, Tianfan Fu
abstract: Large Language Model (LLM)-based systems can integrate heterogeneous biomedical evidence but often produce unfaithful reasoning due to hallucinations of source material, leading to unsupported mechanistic claims. We introduce a triangulation framework using multiple LLM-based agents for drug-target interaction (DTI) reasoning, enforcing agreement across three complementary sources: ML-based affinity prediction, multi-hop knowledge graph (KG) reasoning, and PubMed retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). A reasoning module aggregates these signals under an explicit cross-source consistency constraint, thereby restricting inference by preventing the composition of unsupported cross-source evidence. We evaluate DrugAgent on 900 kinase drug-target pairs using an LLM-as-a-judge protocol for biological plausibility by citing multiple evidence sources. Without this multi-source triangulation, two-source combinations (ML+KG, ML+RAG, KG+RAG) produce 15-20% unfaithful explanations due to unsupported evidence bridging and speculative reasoning. Enforcing agreement across all three sources reduces unfaithful outputs to ≤0.2%, reaching near-zero failure rates while maintaining competitive predictive performance. The framework shows high stability (98.3% label agreement) and strong semantic consistency (>0.7 cosine similarity). It also improves biological plausibility, producing more calibrated predictions citing various evidence sources. Evidence combination analysis shows that triangulation resolves conflicts and prevents dominance of noisy sources, while stabilizing prediction trajectories and preserving consensus signals. These failures arise from under-constrained reasoning, where evidence is combined without sufficient cross-validation. Cross-source agreement acts as a regularizer for scientific reasoning, preventing hallucinated mechanisms and constraining inference to evidence-grounded pathways. This highlights triangulation as a general design principle for reliable multi-source reasoning in biomedical AI and other knowledge-intensive domains.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: MedHopQA: Benchmarking Multi-Hop Reasoning in LLM-Based Biomedical Question Answering with a Disease-Centered Corpus
authors: Rezarta Islamaj, Robert Leaman, Zhiyong Lu
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have transformed biomedical information retrieval, yet existing evaluation benchmarks fail to keep pace with their capabilities. Widely used datasets such as MedQA, MedMCQA, and MMLU Medical suffer from multiple-choice format constraints, saturation at near-ceiling performance, training data contamination, and single-hop reasoning requirements that do not reflect the complexity of real biomedical questions. A benchmark capable of distinguishing genuine multi-step reasoning from pattern-matched retrieval is critically needed. To address this gap, we present MedHopQA, a disease-centered biomedical question answering corpus of 1,000 expert-curated, multi-hop question–answer pairs developed as a shared task at BioCreative IX. Each question requires synthesizing information across at least two distinct Wikipedia articles, with open-ended free-text answers rather than closed option sets. The dataset was constructed through a multi-stage human–AI pipeline combining seed curation, GPT-o1-based augmentation, blind triage, iterative verification, and an LLM-as-a-judge validation framework. Gold annotations were enriched with ontology-derived synonyms from MONDO, NCBI Gene, and NCBI Taxonomy to support robust lexical and concept-level evaluation. To prevent leakage, the 1,000 scored questions are embedded within a 10,000-question package on CodaBench, with answers withheld. Evaluation of four frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting revealed that multi-hop biomedical reasoning remains genuinely challenging. GPT-5.1 achieved the highest accuracy at 83.7%, followed by Gemini-2.5-Pro (80.0%), Claude Sonnet 4.5 (78.7%), and GPT-4o (66.8%), with 77 questions unanswered correctly by any model. MedHopQA provides the community with a contamination-resistant, reasoning-focused benchmark and a reusable dataset construction framework applicable across biomedical subdomains.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Outcome-aware feature generation from unstructured metadata using LLMs for cross-study transcriptomic analysis
authors: Christine Hou, Jihua Liu, Colin Dewey
abstract: Public data repositories such as the Sequence Read Archive (SRA) contain many RNA-sequencing studies, providing valuable resources for cross-study analyses. Successful data integration requires correction for biological and technical factors that are often described in unstructured, study-level text. We investigated whether large language models (LLMs) can extract concise, interpretable sets of binary features from unstructured metadata that capture the major sources of transcriptomic variance across studies. We formalize this task as constructing M binary features from study-level metadata that maximize the variance explained in a high-dimensional outcome. We distinguish between two classes of feature generation methods: those that define features from metadata alone (outcome-independent), and those that additionally take the outcome of interest as input (outcome-dependent). We implemented methods of both classes, including outcome-independent n-gram and LLM-based approaches and two outcome-dependent LLM methods that differ in how outcome information is incorporated. For each method, we used best subset selection to identify the most informative M features that it generated with respect to the outcome, for small values of M. To evaluate these approaches, we analyzed 74 healthy human blood RNA-seq studies from the SRA. For small subsets of features, the LLM-based methods outperformed the n-gram baseline with respect to both variance explained and interpretability. In addition, outcome-dependent methods outperformed outcome-independent approaches by generating more targeted features relevant to transcriptomic variance. Our results indicate that outcome-dependent LLM-based feature generation is a scalable strategy for uncovering informative features from unstructured metadata to support cross-study integration and large-scale transcriptomic analysis.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: KLaR: Fusing Knowledge Graphs and Language Models for Biomedical Target Discovery
authors: Yinghui Jiang, Zixian Li, Yanchao Xu, Haotong Sun, Bocheng Xu, Xiangrong Liu
abstract: Motivation: Biomedical knowledge relevant to disease mechanisms and therapeutic discovery is distributed across structured knowledge graphs (KGs) and unstructured text. Although pretrained language models provide strong semantic embeddings, adapting them to biomedical link prediction typically requires domain-specific fine-tuning and may weaken explicit structural constraints. An open challenge is to enhance link prediction with principled knowledge–language fusion while keeping language encoders lightweight and controllable. Results: We propose KLaR, a knowledge–language representation framework for biomedical KG link prediction. Given a query entity, KLaR encodes its local k-hop neighborhood with a relational GNN and constructs mechanism-consistent textual contexts by template-based textualization of random-walk paths within the same subgraph. These contexts are embedded using a frozen sentence-embedding model (without external retrieval or task-specific fine-tuning), and structural and textual views are aligned and fused via gated integration. To model heterogeneous biomedical interactions, KLaR employs a sparse mixture-of-experts decoder for triple scoring. On PharmKG, HetioNet, and DTINet, KLaR yields consistent gains over structure-only and KG–language hybrid baselines under standard filtered evaluation. We additionally report text-only LLM reference results under a candidate-restricted protocol due to the infeasibility of full-entity ranking for prompted generation. Case studies suggest that KLaR can recover biologically plausible disease–gene and drug–target associations missing from the original graphs, supporting hypothesis generation without domain-specific language model fine-tuning. Availability and implementation: Code and processed data are available at: https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ KLaR-F531. track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: FAIR-SMART: Enabling FAIR Access to Supplementary Materials for Biomedical Text and Data Mining
authors: Chih-Hsuan Wei, Robert Leaman, Zhizheng Wang, Po-Ting Lai, Don Comeau, Shubo Tian, Zhiyong Lu
abstract: Supplementary materials (SM) accompany a substantial proportion of biomedical articles and often contain detailed datasets, including gene expression matrices, variant lists, and pathway analysis results that are not fully represented in the main text. In PubMed Central (PMC), 27% of full-length articles include at least one SM file, increasing to approximately 40% in recent years. However, SM files are distributed across heterogeneous formats and are not systematically indexed by conventional search engines, limiting large-scale reuse. We present FAIR-SMART (FAIR access to Supplementary MAterials for Research Transparency), a system that aggregates SM files from the PMC Open Access subset, converts them into BioC-compliant XML and JSON, and provides a web API for programmatic access and semantic retrieval. As of December 20, 2024, 5,112,828 textual SM files were processed, with 99.46% successfully converted. Tabular content was categorized into 40 semantic clusters using MedCPT embeddings and K-means clustering. Articles can be retrieved based on contextual queries and specified SM data types (e.g., Gene/ Protein Expression Data). Across 14 representative SM categories, FAIR-SMART achieved higher top-10 precision than PubMed and PMC full-text search. In GSEA-related queries, 76% of the top 50 FAIR-SMART results contained gene sets, compared to 26% from PubMed. FAIR-SMART was further used to curate 102 differentially expressed gene sets from 31 disease-related articles for contextual Gene Set Analysis benchmarking. The system enables structured access to supplementary data and supports systematic dataset assembly for biomedical research. FAIR-SMART is freely available as an API for SM data retrieval: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/research/bionlp/RESTful/supplmat.cgi.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Temporally annotated textual time series from PubMed Open Access clinical case reports
authors: Sayantan Kumar, Shahriar Noroozizadeh, Jeremy C. Weiss
abstract: Clinical narratives encode temporal dynamics essential for modeling patient trajectories, yet large-scale temporally annotated resources are scarce. We introduce PMOA-TTS, a corpus of 124,699 single-patient PubMed Open Access case reports converted into structured textual timelines of (event, time) pairs using a scalable large-language-model pipeline (Llama 3.3 70B and DeepSeek-R1). The corpus comprises over 5.6 million timestamped events, alongside extracted demographics and diagnoses. Technical validation uses a clinician-curated gold set and three measures: semantic event matching, temporal concordance (c-index), and alignment error summarized with Area Under the Log-Time CDF (AULTC). We benchmark alternative prompting and model choices and provide documentation to support reproduction. PMOA–TTS enables research on timeline extraction, temporal reasoning, survival modeling and event forecasting from narrative text, and offers broad diagnostic and demographic coverage. Data and code are openly available in public repositories.
