track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: Transferring semantic knowledge from scientific literature to metadata for comprehensive annotation of hundreds of thousands of public human and mouse biomedical datasets
authors: Mansooreh Ahmadian, Parker Hicks, Souha Tifour, Keenan Manpearl, Arjun Krishnan
abstract: Vast amounts of genomic and biomedical data are publicly available in specialist and generalist repositories. However, their reuse remains limited because sample and study metadata is primarily unstructured natural language. This lack of standardized ontology-based annotation makes it difficult for researchers to efficiently identify datasets relevant to specific diseases, tissues, cell types, experimental conditions, biological processes, or phenotypes. We previously developed txt2onto, a machine-learning framework that tags free-text samples and study metadata with controlled-vocabulary terms, enabling ontology-aware search and retrieval. However, the accuracy of these classifiers depends heavily on the availability of high-quality labeled training data, data that must typically be curated manually, a process that is slow, inconsistent, and often infeasible for under-studied biological concepts. To address these limitations, we developed OntoTagger, a scalable annotation framework that uses distant supervision to automatically construct high-quality training data across diverse biomedical ontologies. For each ontology, including MONDO, HPO, CL, UBERON, GO-BP, DOID, XCO, EFO, MAXO, and Upheno we generate positive examples from ontology terms and their lexical variants and derive negative examples from PubMed text after removing any ontology mentions. Using these distant-supervised corpora, we fine-tune specialized BioBERT models for each ontology type to perform both entity recognition and ontology normalization. We then apply the resulting OntoTagger models to large collections of biomedical text and extract short snippets surrounding each predicted ontology mention. These snippets, rather than raw sample or study metadata, serve as the input features for training our downstream machine-learning classifiers. Preliminary analyses show that these literature-derived snippets contain terms strongly predictive of their corresponding ontology concepts, demonstrating that semantic knowledge from biomedical literature can be effectively transferred to metadata annotation tasks. By transforming the previously labor-intensive process of label generation into an automated pipeline, our approach enables accurate annotation even for poorly studied attributes and generalizes across species rather than being limited to human data. In general, this work greatly improves the ease with which publicly available biomedical datasets can be found and reused.

track: Text Mining: Text Mining for Healthcare and Biology
title: GenPTM: A Generalizable Framework for Protein Post-Translational Modification Information Extraction from the Scientific Literature
authors: Shovan Bhowmik, Chuming Chen, Karen Ross, Cathy Wu, K. Vijay-Shanker
abstract: Protein post-translational modification (PTM) plays a central role in protein functions, cellular activities and biological processes. Although several databases curate PTM information, most cover only a limited number of PTMs and are not regularly updated, while the scientific literature continues to accumulate vast amounts of PTM-related knowledge. These growing studies highlight the need for automated information extraction (IE) systems that can identify modified proteins and their amino acid sites directly from the literature. While numerous PTMs have been reported in scientific articles, most existing tools are designed only for specific PTMs, and developing separate systems for every PTM is not feasible. To address these challenges, we developed GenPTM, a generalized IE tool that identifies modified proteins and sites from PubMed abstracts using a unified text representation strategy. GenPTM replaces PTM-specific modification names and/or chemical group mentions with generic placeholders, allowing a transformer model to learn shared textual patterns, motivated by our hypothesis that modification events are described by these two common ways across different PTM types. A BiomedBERT-based classifier is fine-tuned to determine whether a candidate protein or site is truly modified, and a post-processing module assembles the final modified entities. Trained on four major PTM types (e.g., Ubiquitination, Phosphorylation) and evaluated on ten additional PTMs, including PTMs that are not frequently mentioned (e.g., Citrullination, AMPylation), GenPTM achieves F1-scores ranging from 91% to 95% for three different evaluation categories. These results demonstrate strong generalization capability and outperform existing PTM-specific tools, providing a scalable path toward PTM-agnostic IE.

title: Optimizing transformer-based language model performance for named entity recognition of cell phenotypes in literature.
authors: LaToya McDonald, Noam Rotenberg, Robert Leaman, Rezarta Islamaj, Zhiyong Lu, Richard Scheuermann
abstract: LaToya McDonald, Noam Rotenberg, Robert Leaman, Rezarta Islamaj, Zhiyong Lu, Richard H. Scheuermann Division of Intramural Research, National Library of Medicine, Bethesda, MD, USA Transformer based models, such as Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers (BERT) and its domain specific variants, have demonstrated strong performance in general biomedical named entity recognition (NER). However, their relative success depends on how effectively they are guided to learn task-related requirements in preparation for fine tuning. This limitation is particularly pronounced in complex tasks such as cell phenotype extraction, where phenotype-related terminology is highly variable across publications. In this study, we present a comparative analysis of different BERT models-BERT, BioBERT, SciBERT, and PubMedBERT-with a focus on their capacity to learn cell phenotype representations for NER from the CellLink Corpus which includes over 22,000 annotated mentions of human and mouse cell populations in the biomedical literature. For methodological consistency, all models were fine-tuned using identical grids of hyperparameters, training procedures, and evaluation protocols. Performance was assessed using token level and entity level precision, recall, and F1-sores. Findings indicate that domain specific pretraining plays a decisive role in model performance. Results demonstrated that the domain-adapted PubMedBERT model outperforms the general-purpose and other domain-specific BERT models. These findings highlight the significance of identifying the correct pretraining data and hyperparameter selection for optimization. These results underscore the importance of corpus alignment between pretraining and downstream tasks. This work provides a practical comparison of BERT-based architectures for cell phenotype extraction and emphasizes the necessity for domain-specific modeling choices in biomedical NLP applications.

title: AutoPCR: Automated Phenotype Concept Recognition by Prompting
authors: Yicheng Tao, Yuanhao Huang, Yiqun Wang, Xin Luo, Jie Liu
abstract: Motivation: Phenotype concept recognition (CR) is a fundamental task in biomedical text mining. However, existing methods either require ontology-specific training making them struggle to generalize across diverse text styles and evolving biomedical terminology, or depend on general-purpose large language models (LLMs) that lack necessary domain knowledge. Results: To address these limitations, we propose AutoPCR, a prompt-based phenotype CR method designed to automatically generalize to new ontologies and unseen data without ontology-specific training. To further boost performance, we also introduce an optional self-supervised training strategy. Experiments show that AutoPCR achieves the best average and most robust performance across datasets. Further ablation and transfer studies demonstrate its inductive capability and generalizability to new ontologies. title: How can AI agents help you advance biomedicine?
authors: Kuan-lin Huang
abstract: We used to build bioinformatics software and run it. AI agents change the job: they can write the tools, run the analysis, and even pose the right questions sometimes. The hard part is deciding how much to hand over. I'll organize this talk around that single axis: how much freedom the agent has, how much entropy is introduced into your workflow, and when AI agents can be useful for you. For deterministic workflows where the answer is fixed, less freedom required and the major job is algorithmic performance. With agentic coding, we are rebuilding several genomics tools in Rust: I will discuss how we build fastVEP, which labels a full human genome WGS in 71 seconds rather than 3 hours by the standard tool that was written mostly in Perl, with identical results, in a single small binary file that can be easily used by any coding agent or human teams. For many large-scale computational tasks, such as drug repurposing, many answers could be valid. I introduce the LinkD agent, which lets you choose what "best" means in combining binding, selectivity, cell effect, or real-world evidence, and re-ranks drug candidates across millions of options. Across 11.5 million patient records, it flagged common beta-blockers as protective against prostate cancer, which we confirmed from molecule to patient. For the highest amount of freedom, I will discuss AI co-scientists, fully/partly-automated agents that plan, gather data, write and run code, and report. An agent that can do science can also hallucinate. I provided an example that leads to the NIH replication prize, where our agent backed findings from solid papers at a 17 odds ratio compared to the retracted ones, for about $2 each target validation. How do you plan to use AI agents to advance biomedicine?

title: Large-scale clinical sequencing reveals the pan-cancer genetic and clinical landscape of telomere maintenance mechanisms
authors: Harshit Sahay, Bill Diplas, Oluchi Ezekwenna, Divya Koyyalagunta, Simran Chhabria, Madison Darmofal, Agnel Sfeir, Quaid Morris
abstract: Replicative immortality is a hallmark of cancer, requiring activation of telomere maintenance mechanisms (TMMs). While ~90% of tumors reactivate telomerase, 10–15% rely on alternative lengthening of telomeres (ALT), a recombination-driven mechanism with high prevalence in aggressive mesenchymal tumors. ALT can influence prognosis and drug response, and represents an attractive therapeutic target. While ALT is typically associated with ATRX/DAXX truncating mutations, many tumors show activation of ALT without these mutations. However, due to labor-intensive detection assays, studying ALT at scale has remained challenging. We reasoned that large-scale ALT-detection in clinically annotated pan-cancer cohorts could reveal novel genetic and clinical associations. To address this, we leveraged the MSK-IMPACT clinical cohort, comprising >100,000 tumors across 80+ cancer types profiled with an FDA-approved targeted sequencing panel. Using typically discarded off-target sequencing reads, we quantified telomere content and repeat composition. ALT-status was experimentally assessed in 700 tumors using the C-circle assay (CCA). We then trained an ALT-classifier using a Random Forest ensemble with stratified five-fold cross-validation, achieving robust performance (ROC-AUC=0.84;PR-AUC=0.76), which enabled predictions of ALT-activity for 78,704 IMPACT-profiled tumors. Predictions aligned with known ALT patterns, showing highest prevalence in sarcomas, gliomas, and neuroendocrine tumors. Prospective C-circle experiments validated predictions in atypical ALT cases and highlighted candidate novel genetic drivers. ALT status was associated with overall survival in a tumor-type-specific manner: ALT predicted better outcomes in glioma but worse outcomes in uterine sarcoma. Our cohort's scale further enabled survival analysis in tumor types with limited prior evidence, such as osteosarcomas and melanomas, and characterization of ALT-associated metastatic patterns. Overall, our framework provides the most comprehensive pan-cancer map of ALT prevalence to date, identifying novel genetic and clinical associations that can inform patient stratification and therapeutic decisions targeting TMMs.

title: Routine Clinical Time Series Predict Cancer Adverse Events
authors: Chenlian Fu, Ruian Shi, Michele Waters, Jie Yu, Andre Arfe, Nikolaus Schultz, Justin Jee, Quaid Morris
abstract: Predicting adverse events in cancer—treatment side effects and mortality—is critical for personalized oncology, enabling clinicians to prescribe personalized prophylaxis to prevent life-threatening complications. Lab and vital tests are central to diagnosing treatment complications, yet existing tools underuse their temporal aspects, underutilize advances in AI, and lack validation in cancer contexts. We present SPARC (Surveillance of Patient Adverse events using Routine Clinical data), a transformer-based foundation model pretrained on 78,991,523 measurements from 57,510 cancer patients at Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center using a novel Missingness and Time-aware Causal Language Model (MT-CLM) objective tailored to sparse, irregularly sampled outpatient oncology data, then fine-tuned to predict treatment side effects and mortality. Evaluated on seven clinically actionable tasks, SPARC consistently outperforms or matches a broad suite of tree-based and deep learning benchmarks on internal held-out data, prospective validation, and preliminary external cohorts. Pretrained embeddings cluster cancer subtypes by known physiological signatures without label supervision. SPARC-predicted neutropenia risk scores further stratify patients by observed neutropenia rates and identify those who derive significant benefit from G-CSF prophylaxis, demonstrating a concrete path toward clinical decision support in chemotherapy management. Together, these results establish SPARC as a generalizable model for AI-driven adverse event prediction in routine oncology care.

title: Validating PREDICT Breast v4.1.1 across racial groups and genomic risk strata in a Southern California cancer registry
authors: Devanshi Pratiher, Paul Pharoah, Pei-Chen Peng
abstract: PREDICT Breast is a widely used web-based tool estimating survival probability and adjuvant treatment benefit, endorsed by the American Joint Committee on Cancer and recommended by NICE, with over 400,000 global sessions annually. Its latest version, v4.1.1, has not been evaluated in a diverse single-institution registry, nor has the contribution of genomic risk scores (GRS) across ancestry groups been characterized. We applied PREDICT Breast v4.1.1 to 12,533 female patients from the Cedars-Sinai Cancer Registry (ER-positive: 10,786; ER-negative: 1,747). All-cause mortality was compared with observed mortality by age, race/ethnicity, tumor characteristics, and treatment. Discrimination was assessed using Harrell's C-statistic. An ancestry sensitivity analysis evaluated removing race as a model input. OncotypeDX genomic risk scores were extracted from free-text pathology notes using rule-based text parsing and integrated as GRS inputs. Overall calibration replicated the SEER validation (10-year |Δ|: 12.2% vs 10.6%). Non-Hispanic Black patients showed the largest gap (|Δ| = 25.7%; C = 0.694 [0.654, 0.733]). Removing ancestry worsened calibration for non-Hispanic Black (|Δ| widened from 7.5% to 11.6%) and Hispanic patients with negligible discrimination change (ΔC = âˆ’0.004), indicating ancestry encodes background mortality rather than tumor risk. GRS was extracted for 2,939 patients (35.7% of the ER+/ HER2âˆ’/N0 subgroup); adding GRS improved ER-positive discrimination (ΔC = +0.014) and halved the calibration gap for non-Hispanic White and Black patients. GRS coverage was lower in non-Hispanic Black patients (18.7% vs 26.1%). PREDICT Breast v4.1.1 generalizes well to a diverse Southern California registry. Racial disparities in calibration and genomic testing access warrant population-specific recalibration.

title: Surveying alternative splicing in non-small cell lung cancer identifies unique histological and population-specific differences
authors: Saman Zeeshan, Bhavik Dalal, Rony Arauz, Adriana Zingone, Curtis Harris, Hossein Khiabanian, Sharon Pine, Bríd Ryan
abstract: Background Lung cancer is the leading cause of cancer-related death in the United States, with non–small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) as the most common subtype. African American (AA) men have a higher incidence and poorer survival than European American (EA) men, partly due to healthcare disparities. Alternative splicing (AS), a key mechanism in cancer biology, remains understudied in NSCLC, particularly in minority populations. This study investigates genome-wide AS differences in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD) and lung squamous cell carcinoma (LUSC) across AA and EA groups. Method NSCLC patients were recruited through an approved case-control study with informed consent. Discovery and validation cohorts included paired tumor and adjacent non-tumor tissues from AA and EA patients. RNA sequencing was performed, and differential AS was analyzed using rMATS, with significance defined as >10% PSI difference and FDR <0.1. Events replicated across datasets were validated by qRT-PCR. Results Over 1,000 significant AS events distinguished tumors from normal tissue. About 40–50% were validated, with 60% shared between LUAD and LUSC. LUAD-specific events were enriched in protein kinase A and HIPPO pathways, while LUSC involved endocytosis pathways. Population-specific differences were observed, including ADAM15 (AA) and IL32 (EA) in LUAD, and DLG1 (AA) and CTNND1 (EA) in LUSC. Cancer drivers such as AFDN, FGFR2, and VEGFA showed altered splicing. Smoking and aspirin exposure were associated with hundreds of AS events. Conclusion Statement AS patterns differ by histology and population, contributing to tumor heterogeneity. Findings highlight gene–environment interactions and suggest AS as biomarkers and therapeutic targets, emphasizing the need for diverse population studies in precision oncology. This study was peer-reviewed and published in Nature Oncogene (PMID: 39789165; DOI: 10.1038/s41388-024-03267-y).

title: PORTALS: Integrating Plasma Proteomics and Clinical Features via Tabular Foundation Models for ALS Survival Prediction
authors: Yurui Chen, Marcel Weinreich, Andrew Strange, Peng Gao, Johnathan Cooper-Knock, Sai Zhang
abstract: Accurate survival prediction in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is essential for clinical management and trial stratification, yet current models rely on a limited set of clinical variables, rarely leverage molecular information, and still lack the accuracy needed for individualized prognosis. Plasma proteomics has demonstrated predictive value for ALS diagnosis and symptom-onset estimation, but its utility for survival modeling remains unexplored owing to the scarcity of cohorts with matched proteomic, longitudinal clinical, and mortality data. We present PORTALS (PrOteomics-enhanced suRvival prediction via Tabular foundation models for ALS), a machine learning framework that adapts TabPFN to right-censored survival prediction via horizon-specific binary classification with censoring-aware masks, coupled with multi-task learning to integrate proteomic and clinical features. In 5-fold cross-validation on the ALS cohort (AMBRoSIA, N=117), PORTALS achieved a C-index of 0.830, mean time-dependent AUC of 0.901, and median absolute error of 5.2 months among deaths within 3 years, reducing error by 21% over the best clinical+proteomic baseline and 31% over the best clinical-only model. Our framework offers a state-of-the-art clinical tool for ALS survival prediction and stratification.

title: Brain Ontology Expression (BRONTE) graph neural network model uncovers disease-linked spatial variation in gene regulation across the human brain
authors: Jianfeng Ke, Tingjian Ge, Rachel Melamed
abstract: Uncovering genes dysregulated in neuropsychiatric diseases promises to put forward therapeutic targets. By linking disease risk variants to tissue-specific gene regulation, the Genotype-Tissue Expression (GTEx) project has enabled discovery of disease genes and the brain tissues where these pathogenic effects occur. But, GTEx requires huge investment in obtaining human brain tissues, limiting the sample size and tissue diversity available. Crucially, this resource does not contain all key tissues where brain diseases are known to originate. Here, we propose a novel graph convolutional model that integrates the GTEx brain expression data with the Allen Brain Atlas, a resource spanning over 100 fine grained brain tissues that are annotated with an ontology of tissue organization. Our model, Brain Ontology Expression (BRONTE), allows completion of the GTEx data for 221 individuals to impute expanded expression in 103 uncollected detailed brain tissues. We show that expression data imputed by BRONTE recovers measured variation in expression across subjects, genes, and brain tissues. Most importantly, our method both recapitulates known relationships between genetic variations and gene expression, and simultaneously discovers both new genes impacted by genetic variants, and the tissues impacted. This allows us to put forward novel mechanisms of effect for genetic variation associated with 30 brain-related traits, supplying therapeutic targets in overlooked tissues of the brain.

title: Computational prediction of ARSA variant severity to support newborn screening: advances revealed in the CAGI 7 ARSA challenge
authors: Yu-Jen Lin, Michael Gelb, Steven Brenner
abstract: Metachromatic leukodystrophy (MLD), caused by deficiency of arylsulfatase A (ARSA), is a devastating neurodegenerative disease. Gene therapy can alter the disease course, but only if administered presymptomatically; treatment decisions rely in part on genetic variant interpretation, and only individuals with the most severe, early-onset form receive therapy. As genomic sequencing expands into newborn screening for MLD and other conditions, variant interpretation must go beyond pathogenic versus benign—computational methods are needed to address penetrance, expressivity, and severity. The CAGI 7 ARSA challenge, part of the Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation (CAGI), used blinded prediction and independent assessment to evaluate how well computational methods meet this need. A deep mutational scanning (DMS) stability assay quantified ARSA abundance for nearly all missense variants, providing truth data against which 86 submissions from 22 teams were evaluated, together with 23 state-of-the-art or baseline predictors. We used complementary metrics: overall agreement with experimental stability via Kendall rank correlation, and a clinically motivated severity threshold via high-specificity AUC. A novelty metric estimated each method’s contribution beyond existing predictors such as AlphaMissense. Several new methods outperformed state-of-the-art predictors. Variants that were experimentally stable yet consistently predicted as deleterious clustered near catalytic and metal-coordination regions, suggesting computational models capture loss-of-function mechanisms beyond stability alone. Although comprehensive experimental data now exist for ARSA, most disease genes lack such assays, making computational severity prediction essential. These findings demonstrate that variant interpretation methods are advancing toward the quantitative, severity-aware accuracy that newborn screening and early intervention will demand.

title: Discovering new molecular targets directly from electronic health records in neurology and oncology, using network models of drug off-target effects
authors: Jennifer Wilson
abstract: Using real world data including electronic health records (EHRs) is attractive for translational investigations, especially given the FDA's reduced requirements for animal data before clinical investigations. Many have used EHRs to discover drug repurposing opportunities, but few have used EHRs to derisk new molecular targets. Using an interpretable approach, we directly model drug unintended effects, uncovering nonintuitive commonalities for drugs with different therapeutic uses. We associated off-target effects with patient outcomes in multiple EHRs using standard target-comparator statistical approaches, including propensity score analysis to control for confounding, and inverse propensity score weighted Cox proportional hazards to study outcomes for patients on drug with similar off-target effects. We have applied the approach broadly: predicting rare drug-drug interactions (DDIs), recovering recently-approved drug targets in neurological conditions like myasthenia gravis (MG) (highlighting a recent publication), and anticipating combination partners in oncology (unpublished). Our platform had a high sensitivity (84%) for predicting DDIs in well-known databases and associated predictions with patient outcomes. We discovered off-target effects on complement proteins were associated with reduced overall survival in patients with MG (HR=1.098, 95% C.I. 1.018-1.183, p-value=0.0148). These results support the approval of complement inhibitors for these patients, which occurred 8 months after study end. Recently, we predicted sensitizing pathways to first-line oncology treatments, like enzalutamide in prostate cancer, and observed commonly used anti-hypertensives with off-target effects were modestly, but not statistically-significant associated with prolonged survival (HR=0.88, 95% C.I. 0.56-1.41). Overall, our approach suggests a new way for derisking and prioritizing disease-relevant pathways directly from patient data.

title: From Variants to Therapy: A Multi-Agent Framework for Traceable Genomic and Regulatory Reasoning in Precision Medicine
authors: Maaly Nassar
abstract: Whole-genome sequencing generates millions of variants per patient, yet most remain variants of unknown significance (VUS), limiting clinical utility. Interpreting these variants requires integrating fragmented evidence across genomic data, biomedical literature, and regulatory sources. We present a multi-agent framework that separates knowledge construction from reasoning to enable traceable precision medicine. Heterogeneous datasets, including genomic data (ClinVar, 1000 Genomes), biomedical literature (PubMed/PMC), and regulatory sources (FDA reviews, drug labels), are semantically annotated using ontology-driven methods and enriched with metadata and AI-based mutation normalization. Structured and unstructured data are integrated into a knowledge graph supporting GraphRAG with multi-hop reasoning across biological relationships. The framework employs specialised agents for literature reasoning (PubMedAgent), regulatory reasoning (RegAgent), and mutation-centric reasoning (MutAgent), coordinated through controlled tool-based orchestration with snippet-level evidence grounding. Using a temporally restricted (pre-2024) index, we evaluated the system on new FDA-approved indications (2025-2026), where the ground truth consisted of drugs later approved for those indications. The system achieved zero-shot temporal discovery performance of Hit@10 = 42.2%, Hit@20 = 46.9%, and Hit@50 = 54.7%, demonstrating its ability to recover future FDA-approved repurposed therapies from prior evidence. MutAgent achieved Hit@10 = 0.752 on ClinVar mutation-disease recovery. Regulatory reasoning achieved ~70% preference for RegAgent on 200 FDA clinical and pharmacology review pairs. In a clinical case study, the system identified a non-coding regulatory variant missed in routine analysis and linked it to therapeutic evidence. title: FIG: Fairness through Intersectional Grouping, A Post-Processing Framework for Domain-Specific Bias Mitigation
authors: Yongchao Huang, Beatriz Penalver Bernabe, Yang Dai
abstract: Machine learning models for healthcare and computational biology can achieve high average accuracy, yet their performance varies across groups, with the worst performance in groups with smaller sample sizes or lower-quality data. Post-processing methods are particularly attractive when retraining is infeasible due to data protection requirements (e.g., genomics or identifiable data) or proprietary software. Here, we introduce FIG, a model-agnostic post-processing framework that systematically identifies and mitigates bias arising from intersections of multiple attributes (e.g., age, sex, race). FIG operates through two stages. An outer loop selects combinations of the most biased features to define intersectional groups, and an inner loop learns group-specific probability adjustments. FIG tries to minimize a total loss function that combines prediction error (binary cross-entropy), fairness loss (false-positive and false-negative variational rates), and regularization to prevent extreme adjustments. We evaluated FIG on electronic medical records from 5,875 pregnant women who received obstetric care at a public hospital in the US to predict prenatal depression. Baseline elastic-net models exhibited substantial intersectional disparities. FIG identified unplanned pregnancies and maternal age as the most prominent drivers and reduced fairness loss by 62%, from 0.53 to 0.20, with minimal impact on AUC-ROC (63% to 60%). In summary, FIG is a robust, scalable, model-agnostic post-processing framework that operates on model outputs without retraining and can identify bias-driven variables without any prior knowledge of the system, which may also be biased. We expect FIG to advance equity in predictive modeling based on multi-omics data, enabling its translation into real-world applications.

title: Drug-wide association studies as a tool for drug discovery and methodological improvement
authors: Sonja Kleper, Panagiotis Nikolaos Lalagkas, Tingjian Ge, Rachel Melamed
abstract: Using real-world health records data can uncover the effects of drugs on disease incidence or outcome. This approach overcomes the limitations of randomized trials: they are slow and expensive, making them unsuitable for discovering unexpected drug effects. But a crucial challenge is that unlike clinical trials, which rigorously randomize treatment in order to isolate the effect of a drug, in real-world health records, treatment is not randomly prescribed, but is given based on patient health history. This means that results of observational studies suffer confounding bias. Standard practice emulates one precisely specified target trial at a time: proponents say that this meticulous approach is in theory less vulnerable to bias. But, here we aim to show that high-throughput emulation of many target trials in a drug-wide association study can also contribute to overcoming bias, while allowing discovery of unexpected drug effects. We showcase our recent drug combination-wide analysis of cancer, which both identified new drug relevance to cancer, and revealed remaining biases in the method. In order to identify computational models capable of overcoming these biases, we again turned to the drug-wide association study as a tool for benchmarking multiple such methods. Finally, we present a holistic temporal graph neural network model for confounding control incorporating knowledge graphs and language embeddings, and we compare the model to recent non-high throughput target trials in two case studies.

title: Integration of eye imaging with multi-omics data to explore targets for eye rejuvenation
authors: Roberto Bonelli, Victoria Jackson, Yue Wu, Nathan Kennedy, Martin Friedlander, Aaron Lee, Melanie Bahlo
abstract: Aging is a heterogeneous process, and different organs within an individual age differently. Using the UK Biobank, we perform the first study into the aging of 17 eye tissues and identify systemic factors associated with slower or faster aging. A machine learning algorithm was developed to measure spatial thickness over 32,768 pixels of seven cell-specific layers in retinal images. Thickness data were compressed via functional principal component analysis. Additional eye measurement data were extracted from the biobank, including imaging-derived vascular, optic disc, ocular pressure, visual acuity, refractivity, and corneal measurements. Each set of variables was used to train a support vector machine to predict the age of individuals. Each tissue aging rate was then estimated by subtracting the predicted tissue age from the chronological age of the individual. We correlated the age rate of the 17 eye tissues with genomics, blood metabolomics and proteomics, as well as disease diagnoses data, using weighted omics regression models. The dataset of 138,000 individuals showed that age gap correlations across tissues were stratified, demonstrating aging heterogeneity even within the eye. Although measured primarily in blood, multi-omics analyses revealed more than 5,000 significant associations between blood omics features and eye aging rate. Globally, we found that different aging rates are likely impacted by separate or partially overlapping biological mechanisms. The systemic factors prioritised in this work warrant further validation in in vivo and in vitro models, as they may offer easy-to-target pathways to improve eye health or actively reverse eye aging.

title: Integrative Single-Cell and Spatial Omics Reveal Temporal-Spatial Dynamics of Fibroblast Subtypes during AKI-to-CKD Transition
authors: Mengying Xia, Jia-Jun Liu, Qingqi Lin, Dong Zhou, Silvia Liu
abstract: Acute kidney injury (AKI) affects millions of patients worldwide and substantially increases the risk of progression to chronic kidney disease (CKD). Currently, most studies focus on tubular injury as primary damage, with immune cell infiltrations identified as key events. Recent findings highlight the important role of fibroblasts in AKI-to-CKD transition; however, their subtype diversity and dynamic state transitions remain incompletely resolved. Here, we developed a scalable cross-dataset integration and meta-analysis pipeline to resolve fibroblast heterogeneity across three major murine AKI models, including ischemia–reperfusion injury (IRI), unilateral ureteral obstruction (UUO), and cisplatin-induced AKI (CIA). We reconstructed spatiotemporal state transitions during injury and repair using SCTransform-based integration, single-cell and spatial omics analysis, fibroblast subtyping, cell-cell communication analysis, and trajectory inference. Our analysis identifies both conserved and injury-specific fibroblast subpopulations and reveals a shared progression continuum from quiescent to an overactivated state in response to acute injury, followed by a bifurcation into two trajectories: an adaptive branch associated with transitional reprogramming, and a maladaptive branch that promotes fibrotic progression. While this trajectory is broadly conserved, distinct injury models exhibit divergent temporal dynamics. Cross-cohort meta-analysis further uncovers conserved and context-specific gene signatures underlying fibroblast activation and fibrosis. Importantly, cross-species comparison demonstrates partial conservation of fibroblast programs between mouse models and human AKI, supporting the translational relevance of our findings. Together, this study provides a comprehensive framework for dissecting fibroblast heterogeneity and dynamics in the AKI-to-CKD transition and highlights potential targets for therapeutic interventions.

title: Tutorial VT1: Genomic LLMs in Practice: A Hands-On Introduction with Hugging Face pt1
abstract: Though originally developed for natural language processing, large language models (LLMs) are also well suited to modelling the language of life. DNA sequences can be treated as sentences over a four-letter alphabet, with overlapping k-mer segments acting as “words”, hence enabling natural-language approaches to extracting biological information. Transformer-based LLMs are especially well-suited to this task, using multi head attention to capture long-range interactions within genomic sequences, and avoiding the vanishing gradient problems common in recurrent networks. Contemporary genomic LLMs, such as DNABERT and its successors, leverage this Transformer architecture in conjunction with specialised tokenisation methods to represent DNA and, after fine-tuning, have proven effective on tasks such as enhancer classification and splice site annotation. Recent work extends these models to multimodal omics data, integrating genomic sequences with transcriptomics and spatial data to tackle a whole new range of tasks. Such models have made strides in areas such as variant effect prediction, with DeepMind’s AlphaMissense achieving an 89% accuracy in classifying missense variant effects by combining structural context with evolutionary conservation data. This full-day tutorial will provide attendees with a theoretical and practical foundation in LLMs for genomics research. Instructors will explain why Transformers are well-suited to modelling DNA, review tokenisation strategies (single-nucleotide, k-mer, and byte-pair encoding), and discuss how to deal with long-context genomic data. Participants will gain hands-on experience in loading genomic datasets, tokenising sequences, and using pre-trained models from Hugging Face for inference and fine-tuning on DNA variant effect prediction problems. A guided walkthrough of the Hugging Face Trainer API will cover setting training arguments, monitoring loss via early stopping, and saving fine-tuned models. The tutorial will conclude with a session where attendees will work through a mini-project applying these skills, with instructors on hand to answer questions and provide guidance. By the end of this tutorial, participants will understand the principles behind genomic LLMs and be able to implement state-of-the-art Transformer-based models for DNA variant effect prediction.

title: Tutorial VT3: Hello Nextflow: Getting started with workflows for bioinformatics
abstract: Nextflow is a powerful and flexible open-source workflow management system that simplifies the development, execution, and scalability of data-driven computational pipelines. It is widely used in bioinformatics and related scientific fields to automate complex analyses, making it easier to manage and reproduce large-scale data analysis workflows. Hello Nextflow is intended as a “getting started” course for students and early-career researchers who are completely new to Nextflow. The tutorial aims to equip participants with foundational knowledge and skills in three key areas: (1) understanding the logic of how data analysis workflows are constructed, (2) Nextflow language proficiency and (3) command-line interface (CLI) execution. Through guided, goal-oriented exercises, participants will learn to: Use core components of the Nextflow language to construct simple multi-step workflows effectively. Launch Nextflow workflows locally, navigate output directories to access results, interpret log outputs for insights into workflow execution, and troubleshoot basic issues that may arise during workflow execution. By the end of the tutorial, participants will be well-prepared for tackling the next steps in their journey to develop and apply reproducible workflows for their scientific computing needs. Additional study-at-home materials will be provided for them to continue learning and developing their skills further. The training materials are open-source and freely available on the Nextflow training portal at https://training.nextflow.io/latest/ hello_nextflow

title: Tutorial VT4: Multimodal Integration and Multimodal Causal Inference using R/ Bioconductor
abstract: Biological and biomedical studies increasingly generate multimodal datasets that combine multiple molecular layers, such as genomics, transcriptomics, epigenomics, microbiome profiles, metabolomics, imaging data, and clinical or environmental measurements. While the availability of such data creates new opportunities to study complex biological systems, it also raises fundamental analytical challenges. Researchers must decide how to represent heterogeneous data types, how to integrate signals across modalities, and how to move beyond association toward mechanistic understanding. Many existing multimodal analysis workflows focus primarily on predictive performance or exploratory associations, often treating integration as a purely technical exercise. However, in many biological and clinical applications, the central goal is not only prediction but also understanding how and why an exposure, perturbation, or intervention affects an outcome through multiple biological layers. Addressing such questions requires principled approaches to multimodal integration that are compatible with causal reasoning and uncertainty quantification. This tutorial aligns directly with the ISMB Tutorials program by providing hands-on, educational training in multimodal integration and multimodal causal inference using open-source tools in R and Bioconductor. The emphasis is on methodological foundations, reproducible workflows, and balanced comparison of widely used integration strategies rather than on presenter-specific software. By combining practical instruction on multimodal data representation with causal mediation concepts, the tutorial fills an important gap for ISMB participants seeking to translate integrated multi-omics analyses into biologically interpretable and mechanistically grounded insights.

title: Tutorial VT2: Building Interactive Visualizations of Single-Cell and Spatial Data in Python
abstract: As single-cell and spatial biology datasets grow larger and more complex, with more modalities and types of downstream analysis results, tasks such as visualization also become more difficult. Using interactive techniques can help to alleviate challenges, enabling users to navigate to regions of interest in large spatial datasets, select genes of interest among all of those profiled, and select particular cells or cell types for follow-up analyses. However, creating such interactive visualizations often requires using unfamiliar tools, and it can be challenging to switch between producing static and interactive outputs. Once created, sharing interactive visualizations with collaborators can be challenging, as the corresponding data and software (as opposed to plain image files) must be made accessible to the visualization recipients. The Vitessce visualization framework for single-cell and 2D/3D spatial biology data (https://vitessce.io/) provides building-blocks to compose scalable and interactive visualizations and share them on the web, with support for common data formats defined in the Scverse and Open Microscopy Environment (OME) ecosystems. Vitessce is deployed in numerous data portals to provide thousands of single-cell and spatial data visualizations, e.g., in the NIH HuBMAP Data Portal, in the NIH Cellular Senescence Data Portal, in the NIH Kidney Precision Medicine Project Atlas, and many other academic and commercial resources (see https:/ vitessce.io/docs/showcase/). In Vitessce, multiple interactive visualizations can be linked together to construct applications that display information from multiple data types and modalities. The EasyVitessce Python package is designed to enable computational biologists to quickly author Vitessce-based visualizations with their own data using familiar Scverse plotting syntax. In our tutorial, we introduce core concepts of single-cell and spatial biology data visualizations and illustrate how they can be applied through hands-on training with Vitessce and EasyVitessce in Jupyter Notebooks.

title: Tutorial VT6: Programming robust LLM Agents for assisting scientific tasks
abstract: Work in computational biology can often benefit from LLM assistance, especially tasks like programming, file management, search, retrieval, and summarizing scientific texts. When we augment LLMs with tools, they become LLM Agents, gaining the ability to perform tasks outside of simple text generation, and assist us more directly with a larger degree of autonomy. However, tools and the ability to autonomously operate come with issues like security and error propagation in multi-step tasks, that hinder the usefulness of such agents. To use agents in a reliable and secure way, we need to utilize secured isolated environments, enforce structured outputs, and use programmatic validation of intermediate steps. Combining these approaches, we can create reliable agents that produce outputs with the correct format and functionality, and avoid relying on time consuming manual verification. In this tutorial, you will use Python, PydanticAI, and Docker to learn the basics of using LLM Agents to programmatically automate simple tasks. From there, you will automate more complicated tasks that require multiple steps, and ensure the robustness of the results with custom agent validators. You will learn to automate tasks like machine learning experimentation, creating reusable scripts, and extracting structure from scientific literature. title: Tutorial VT8: Foundation model and graph learning for modeling, analyzing, and interpreting single-cell omics and histopathology data
abstract: Emerging single-cell and spatial omics technologies, together with next generation AI/ML-driven digital histopathology, present both unprecedented opportunities and challenges for integrating molecular biology and pathology. How to model vast sequencing and imaging data in diverse modalities, perform computational analyses, and reveal and interpret biological and pathological mechanisms by identifying biologically and pathologically meaningful cell types, niches, and key markers are central questions in this area. Computational methods and tools, particularly foundation models and graph learning approaches, offer a promising approach to addressing these challenges. Loki1 is a visual–omics foundation model OmiCLIP designed to bridge omics data and hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) images. Targeting single-cell multi-omics data, scPEFT2 introduces a flexible Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning framework to enhance the adaptation of single-cell large language models. TrimNN3 uses a graph learning approach to infer the conservative cellular community patterns in spatial omics. FUSION4 provides a one-stop web application platform for in-depth exploration of multi-omics data with brightfield histology. Our tutorial will cover key advancements in foundation models and graph learning developed on singlecell omics and histopathology research over the past few years, emphasizing new opportunities in bioinformatics enabled by these advancements. We will start with a technical talk about the machine learning algorithms covered in approaches, including Loki, scPEFT, TrimNN, and FUSION, and from model training to model interpretation (discovery on cell types, niches, and key markers). We will then demonstrate the impact of machine learning on uncovering the underlying mechanisms of complex diseases, such as cancer, Alzheimer’s disease, and kidney disease.

abstract: The nf-core project is a widely recognized community resource that provides a rich collection of modular, reusable workflows and developer tools, along with best practices for building high-quality bioinformatics pipelines. While these resources are highly valuable, the breadth and sophistication of nf-core can be daunting for newcomers, making it challenging to know where to start. title: Tutorial IP1: Agentic AI System for In Silico Team Science: From LLM Basics to Lab Assistant Agents
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used in biomedical research for code generation and decision support. However, going from chatbots to reliable lab assistant AI agents that can work closely with biomedical data and tools remains challenging. This tutorial aims to bridge the gap between concepts and production. This tutorial balances conceptual introductions to various topics in biomedical agentic AI with hands-on exercises. The first half of the tutorial focuses on the basics. We begin with a background introduction to the definition of agentic AI and the untapped opportunities in biomedical research. We then dive into common LLM techniques and building blocks of agentic AI systems, the combination of which shape agentic AI system performance and behaviors. The attendees will experiment with various LLM and agentic AI techniques through hands-on exercises. The second half of the tutorial guides the attendees to develop their own agentic AI systems. The attendees will have the opportunity to construct an agent that parses a natural-language task, selects the appropriate tools, runs the data analyses, and produces a useful report. Finally, we discuss advanced topics on multi-agent systems, human-in-the-loop workflow, lightweight logging, and cost tracking. Through guided exercises, participants will: Configure an agent for their preferred LLM provider. Register bioinformatics-relevant tools (e.g., local Python scripts for sequence analysis or variant annotation) and versatile biomedical MCP servers. Orchestrate single-agent, multi-agent, and human-in-the-loop agentic AI systems. Build a simple end-to-end “bioinformatics assistant” or “bioinformatics team” that can propose, explain, and automate a small computational biology workflow. All code (Python scripts, Jupyter notebooks, example tools) and slides will be shared via an open GitHub repository.

title: Tutorial IP3: From Trees to Networks
abstract: Phylogenetic trees are the standard representation of evolutionary relationships, yet many biological datasets contain conflicting signals that cannot be explained by a single tree. Processes such as incomplete lineage sorting, recombination, hybridization, and horizontal gene transfer require more general evolutionary models based on phylogenetic networks. In parallel, Bayesian phylogenetic inference has shifted the focus from single optimal trees to distributions of plausible trees, increasing the demand for methods that summarize and interpret complex tree sets. This half-day tutorial introduces participants to the complete workflow from sequence data to phylogenetic networks. The first half covers gene tree reconstruction using maximum-likelihood methods and Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. The second half focuses on the construction, visualization, and interpretation of phylogenetic networks. We will explore how to compute networks from distances, sequences and trees, using the latest SplitsTree release. Participants will learn how to use PhyloSketch to sketch, capture and layout trees and networks. We will look into the use of phylogeny GPTs to plan analyses. The tutorial combines conceptual foundations with practical application. By the end of the session, participants will be able to assess when network approaches are appropriate, compute networks from real data, and critically interpret network structures in a biological context. The tutorial is aimed at researchers with basic knowledge of phylogenetic analysis who wish to extend their analyses toward modern network-based evolutionary inference.

title: Tutorial IP5: Computational Network Analysis of Omics Data
abstract: Gene regulatory networks capture how transcription factors and other regulators control gene expression in cells. Biological pathways, such as signaling cascades or metabolic routes, describe coordinated molecular interactions that drive cellular responses to internal and external stimuli. Curated pathways and gene regulatory network models provide useful high-level views of molecular organization, but they are often incomplete and fail to capture the condition-specific interactions and regulatory processes that arise in response to particular stimuli or disease states. Both gene regulatory networks and pathways can be studied through network analysis, specifically through gene regulatory network inference methods and pathway reconstruction algorithms, which uses high-throughput omics data (such as genomic, proteomic, transcriptomic, or metabolomic) assays to construct and analyze condition-specific networks. Pathway reconstruction algorithms identify plausible condition specific pathways by combining omics datasets with prior knowledge of molecular interactions. For example, given a protein-protein interaction network and measurements of changes in protein phosphorylation or abundance in response to a treatment, these algorithms can infer a pathway that explains how the observed changes arise. Gene regulatory network inference methods identify condition-specific regulatory relationships from gene expression data. Given transcriptomic measurements, such as single-cell RNA sequencing data, these methods infer regulatory interactions between transcription factors and their target genes that explain observed expression patterns. Dozens of both pathway reconstruction and gene regulatory network inference approaches have been developed across the network biology community. Despite their potential and prevalence, pathway reconstruction algorithms and gene regulatory network inference methods can be difficult to use in practice. Fragmented software environments, inconsistent or unmaintained implementations, limited data standards, and complex parameter tuning all create barriers for new and experienced users alike. The current challenges make it difficult to select appropriate tools, manage inputs, compare outputs across methods, and interpret the resulting subnetworks. These barriers limit the broader adoption of pathway reconstruction approaches, even though the underlying methods are powerful and widely applicable. Recent efforts have begun to address these problems by developing software tools and frameworks that aim to make these types of network analysis more accessible and easier to use. SPRAS and BEELINE are software frameworks that tackle these issues for pathway reconstruction and gene regulatory networks, respectively. This tutorial will provide participants an introduction to pathway reconstruction and gene regulatory network inference, highlight two open source platforms (SPRAS and BEELINE) that simplify running and comparing different algorithms, and give examples of how predicted pathways and gene regulatory networks can be used to generate biological insights. It is designed for participants with entry-level computational skills, such as running command-line operations and editing YAML files, along with a basic understanding of omics data. No prior experience with pathway reconstruction algorithms or gene regulatory network inference methods are required. The tutorial will offer practical guidance for incorporating pathway reconstruction tools and gene regulatory network inference tools into real biological research. All tutorial material and the underlying software are available online with open source licenses.

title: Tutorial IP7: Quantum Computing for Multi-omics analyses
abstract: Single-cell and population-level multi-omics analyses are transforming our understanding of biological complexity by integrating genomics, proteomics, and transcriptomics to reveal the molecular underpinnings of disease. As these datasets grow in scale and dimensionality, emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and quantum computing (QC) are poised to overcome classical computational limits. Recent breakthroughs in QC have demonstrated remarkable potential for machine learning, optimization, and biomedical discovery, spanning applications from biomarker identification, clinical trials, to therapeutic design [1-5]. This tutorial introduces participants to the fundamentals of quantum computing and its practical application in multi-omics analysis. Through guided, hands-on exercises, participants will learn how to preprocess and encode biological data for quantum algorithms, explore quantum machine learning and tensor decomposition, and use data complexity measures to understand when quantum approaches can outperform classical ones. The session concludes with quantum–classical hybrid workflows applied to real-world multi-omics datasets, offering actionable insights into how QC can accelerate therapeutic discovery and precision medicine.

title: Tutorial IP8: Metagenomic sequence analysis using k-mer based methods
abstract: Modern metagenomics has greatly benefited from k-mer–based methods due to their scalability and accuracy on large and complex datasets. A variety of methods with somewhat different goals and philosophies fit under the broad banner of “k-mer–based”, and it has been difficult for users to keep this breadth in mind. This tutorial provides a comprehensive overview of k-mer–based approaches for analyzing metagenomic samples, focusing on both methodological foundations and practical applications. The tutorial brings together developers of widely used tools to present complementary perspectives on tasks such as taxonomic profiling and classification, phylogenetic placement, and virus identification, together with tips on downstream analysis and comparison of metagenomic samples. Fundamentally, these methods use k-mers to avoid alignment. However, they differ in the specific computational tasks and in approach. Participants will learn about core concepts underlying both short and long k-mer–based analysis, including sketching, minimizers, and distance estimation, and how choices affect accuracy, resolution, and computational efficiency. They will learn about methods that analyze each read, then summarize results, methods that jointly analyze all reads of a sample, and methods that bridge the two approaches. Hands-on exercises will allow participants to apply the tools they are interested in to example datasets. Emphasis will be placed on understanding the strengths, limitations, and appropriate applications of each approach. title: Tutorial IP1: Agentic AI System for In Silico Team Science: From LLM Basics to Lab Assistant Agents
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are now widely used in biomedical research for code generation and decision support. However, going from chatbots to reliable lab assistant AI agents that can work closely with biomedical data and tools remains challenging. This tutorial aims to bridge the gap between concepts and production. This tutorial balances conceptual introductions to various topics in biomedical agentic AI with hands-on exercises. The first half of the tutorial focuses on the basics. We begin with a background introduction to the definition of agentic AI and the untapped opportunities in biomedical research. We then dive into common LLM techniques and building blocks of agentic AI systems, the combination of which shape agentic AI system performance and behaviors. The attendees will experiment with various LLM and agentic AI techniques through hands-on exercises. The second half of the tutorial guides the attendees to develop their own agentic AI systems. The attendees will have the opportunity to construct an agent that parses a natural-language task, selects the appropriate tools, runs the data analyses, and produces a useful report. Finally, we discuss advanced topics on multi-agent systems, human-in-the-loop workflow, lightweight logging, and cost tracking. Through guided exercises, participants will: Configure an agent for their preferred LLM provider. Register bioinformatics-relevant tools (e.g., local Python scripts for sequence analysis or variant annotation) and versatile biomedical MCP servers. Orchestrate single-agent, multi-agent, and human-in-the-loop agentic AI systems. Build a simple end-to-end “bioinformatics assistant” or “bioinformatics team” that can propose, explain, and automate a small computational biology workflow. All code (Python scripts, Jupyter notebooks, example tools) and slides will be shared via an open GitHub repository.

title: Tutorial IP8: Metagenomic sequence analysis using k-mer based methods
abstract: Modern metagenomics has greatly benefited from k-mer–based methods due to their scalability and accuracy on large and complex datasets. A variety of methods with somewhat different goals and philosophies fit under the broad banner of “k-mer–based”, and it has been difficult for users to keep this breadth in mind. This tutorial provides a comprehensive overview of k-mer–based approaches for analyzing metagenomic samples, focusing on both methodological foundations and practical applications. The tutorial brings together developers of widely used tools to present complementary perspectives on tasks such as taxonomic profiling and classification, phylogenetic placement, and virus identification, together with tips on downstream analysis and comparison of metagenomic samples. Fundamentally, these methods use k-mers to avoid alignment. However, they differ in the specific computational tasks and in approach. Participants will learn about core concepts underlying both short and long k-mer–based analysis, including sketching, minimizers, and distance estimation, and how choices affect accuracy, resolution, and computational efficiency. They will learn about methods that analyze each read, then summarize results, methods that jointly analyze all reads of a sample, and methods that bridge the two approaches. Hands-on exercises will allow participants to apply the tools they are interested in to example datasets. Emphasis will be placed on understanding the strengths, limitations, and appropriate applications of each approach. By the end of the tutorial, participants will gain a sufficient understanding of the key differences between approaches and the trade-offs involved. They will learn how to evaluate which approaches are most suitable for specific metagenomic tasks, and gain insights for designing analyses for their own applications and datasets

title: Tutorial IP7: Quantum Computing for Multi-omics analyses
abstract: Single-cell and population-level multi-omics analyses are transforming our understanding of biological complexity by integrating genomics, proteomics, and transcriptomics to reveal the molecular underpinnings of disease. As these datasets grow in scale and dimensionality, emerging technologies like artificial intelligence and quantum computing (QC) are poised to overcome classical computational limits. Recent breakthroughs in QC have demonstrated remarkable potential for machine learning, optimization, and biomedical discovery, spanning applications from biomarker identification, clinical trials, to therapeutic design [1-5]. This tutorial introduces participants to the fundamentals of quantum computing and its practical application in multi-omics analysis. Through guided, hands-on exercises, participants will learn how to preprocess and encode biological data for quantum algorithms, explore quantum machine learning and tensor decomposition, and use data complexity measures to understand when quantum approaches can outperform classical ones. The session concludes with quantum–classical hybrid workflows applied to real-world multi-omics datasets, offering actionable insights into how QC can accelerate therapeutic discovery and precision medicine.

title: Tutorial IP5: Computational Network Analysis of Omics Data
abstract: Gene regulatory networks capture how transcription factors and other regulators control gene expression in cells. Biological pathways, such as signaling cascades or metabolic routes, describe coordinated molecular interactions that drive cellular responses to internal and external stimuli. Curated pathways and gene regulatory network models provide useful high-level views of molecular organization, but they are often incomplete and fail to capture the condition-specific interactions and regulatory processes that arise in response to particular stimuli or disease states. Both gene regulatory networks and pathways can be studied through network analysis, specifically through gene regulatory network inference methods and pathway reconstruction algorithms, which uses high-throughput omics data (such as genomic, proteomic, transcriptomic, or metabolomic) assays to construct and analyze condition-specific networks. Pathway reconstruction algorithms identify plausible condition specific pathways by combining omics datasets with prior knowledge of molecular interactions. For example, given a protein-protein interaction network and measurements of changes in protein phosphorylation or abundance in response to a treatment, these algorithms can infer a pathway that explains how the observed changes arise. Gene regulatory network inference methods identify condition-specific regulatory relationships from gene expression data. Given transcriptomic measurements, such as single-cell RNA sequencing data, these methods infer regulatory interactions between transcription factors and their target genes that explain observed expression patterns. Dozens of both pathway reconstruction and gene regulatory network inference approaches have been developed across the network biology community. Despite their potential and prevalence, pathway reconstruction algorithms and gene regulatory network inference methods can be difficult to use in practice. Fragmented software environments, inconsistent or unmaintained implementations, limited data standards, and complex parameter tuning all create barriers for new and experienced users alike. The current challenges make it difficult to select appropriate tools, manage inputs, compare outputs across methods, and interpret the resulting subnetworks. These barriers limit the broader adoption of pathway reconstruction approaches, even though the underlying methods are powerful and widely applicable. Recent efforts have begun to address these problems by developing software tools and frameworks that aim to make these types of network analysis more accessible and easier to use. SPRAS and BEELINE are software frameworks that tackle these issues for pathway reconstruction and gene regulatory networks, respectively. This tutorial will provide participants an introduction to pathway reconstruction and gene regulatory network inference, highlight two open source platforms (SPRAS and BEELINE) that simplify running and comparing different algorithms, and give examples of how predicted pathways and gene regulatory networks can be used to generate biological insights. It is designed for participants with entry-level computational skills, such as running command-line operations and editing YAML files, along with a basic understanding of omics data. No prior experience with pathway reconstruction algorithms or gene regulatory network inference methods are required. The tutorial will offer practical guidance for incorporating pathway reconstruction tools and gene regulatory network inference tools into real biological research. All tutorial material and the underlying software are available online with open source licenses.

title: Tutorial IP3: From Trees to Networks
abstract: Phylogenetic trees are the standard representation of evolutionary relationships, yet many biological datasets contain conflicting signals that cannot be explained by a single tree. Processes such as incomplete lineage sorting, recombination, hybridization, and horizontal gene transfer require more general evolutionary models based on phylogenetic networks. In parallel, Bayesian phylogenetic inference has shifted the focus from single optimal trees to distributions of plausible trees, increasing the demand for methods that summarize and interpret complex tree sets. This half-day tutorial introduces participants to the complete workflow from sequence data to phylogenetic networks. The first half covers gene tree reconstruction using maximum-likelihood methods and Bayesian phylogenetic analysis. The second half focuses on the construction, visualization, and interpretation of phylogenetic networks. We will explore how to compute networks from distances, sequences and trees, using the latest SplitsTree release. Participants will learn how to use PhyloSketch to sketch, capture and layout trees and networks. We will look into the use of phylogeny GPTs to plan analyses. The tutorial combines conceptual foundations with practical application. By the end of the session, participants will be able to assess when network approaches are appropriate, compute networks from real data, and critically interpret network structures in a biological context. The tutorial is aimed at researchers with basic knowledge of phylogenetic analysis who wish to extend their analyses toward modern network-based evolutionary inference.

title: Tutorial IP2: Large Language Models and Agentic AI for Biomedical Informatics
abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) such as ChatGPT have demonstrated strong capabilities in understanding, generating, and reasoning over natural language. In bioinformatics and biomedical informatics, these models are rapidly emerging as a new computational paradigm with the potential to transform literature mining, data integration, workflow automation, and biomedical reasoning. This tutorial provides a practical, introductory, and hands-on guide to understanding and applying LLMs and agentic AI systems in biomedical data science research. The tutorial begins with a concise introduction to LLMs and their evolution, followed by an overview of both commercial and open-source models commonly used in scientific applications. Participants will learn core techniques including prompt design, retrieval-augmented generation for biomedical literature and databases, text-to-SQL query generation, and bioinformatics code generation in Python. Building on these foundations, the tutorial introduces agentic AI systems that enable multi-step reasoning, tool use, and workflow orchestration for complex bioinformatics and biomedical informatics tasks. Through guided hands-on exercises and real-world case studies, participants will gain practical experience applying LLMs and agentic AI to realistic biomedical research scenarios. The tutorial also emphasizes responsible and rigorous use of these models, addressing limitations such as hallucination, bias, robustness, and reproducibility in scientific and clinical contexts. By the end of the tutorial, attendees will be equipped with foundational knowledge, practical skills, and best practices to responsibly integrate LLMs and agentic AI into biomedical research workflows.

title: Tutorial IP4: Generating realistic synthetic biological data using phylogenetics
abstract: Synthetic data are essential for developing bioinformatics tool and for constructing training datasets for artificial intelligence model development. More specifically, synthetic biological data with known true parameter values are crucial for evaluating the performance of the developed methods. However, selecting appropriate parameters for producing biologically realistic data requires substantial biological knowledge. In this tutorial, we provide foundational theoretical and biological background for generating synthetic biological data, including species trees, gene trees within those species trees, and sequence data derived from those gene trees, along with hands-on experience in computationally generating them. We discuss the Yule model and the birth-death model for species tree generation, the multispecies coalescent for gene tree generation, and models of sequence evolution ranging from the simplest Jukes-Cantor to more complex General Time Reversible models for DNA sequence generation. We utilize R package phytools for species tree generation, ms for gene tree generation, and seq-gen for DNA sequence generation. Finally, we examine critical assumptions underlying these simulations and how altering parameter settings such as speciation and extinction rates, population sizes and speciation times, and base frequencies and transition rates produces datasets that convey specific biological scenarios.

title: Tutorial IP6: Network Biology Workflows with Cytoscape and NDEx: Visualization, Analysis, Sharing, Automation, and Apps
abstract: Biological networks provide a powerful framework to organize and interpret high-throughput data, from protein interactions and pathway models to disease-associated networks and knowledge graphs. Cytoscape is a widely used open-source platform for interactive network visualization and analysis, supported by an ecosystem of interoperable tools and services, including NDEx (Network Data Exchange) for publishing and sharing networks, Cytoscape Web for browser-based visualization, and automation interfaces for integrating network analysis into reproducible pipelines. This half-day, in-person tutorial is structured as two consecutive blocks. Block 1 is geared toward participants who are new to Cytoscape and/or network biology. Through short concept overviews and guided exercises, attendees will import a simple edge list dataset, apply data-driven visual styles and layouts, retrieve a biologically relevant network from a public source (e.g., STRING or NDEx), run a basic analysis workflow, and publish results to NDEx (including exporting CX2 and Cytoscape session files) for sharing and reuse in desktop and web contexts. Block 2 is geared toward bioinformaticians and tool/workflow developers. Participants will learn practical integration patterns (e.g., launching Cytoscape from an external application), drive Cytoscape programmatically from Python using py4cytoscape and the Cytoscape Automation/REST interfaces, and extend Cytoscape via a hands-on Service App exercise using a provided template repository and an optional AI-assisted coding demonstration. We will also briefly situate Cytoscape and NDEx within the broader network-analysis landscape (e.g., igraph/networkx, Gephi) and discuss when interactive visual analytics versus scripted workflows are most appropriate

title: Advances in computational variant impact prediction: findings from the Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation, seventh edition (CAGI 7)
authors: Critical Assessment Of Genome Interpretation Consortium, Steven Brenner
abstract: CAGI, the Critical Assessment of Genome Interpretation, is the community experiment that establishes the state of the art in computational variant impact prediction and aims to drive the field toward the most important new goals. Participants make blinded predictions; independent assessors evaluate them against experimental or clinical truth data. Diagnostic sequencing has had a transformative impact, but cancer and newborn and prenatal screening will become yet larger applications of genomic sequencing. These demand assessment of penetrance, expressivity, and actionability, well beyond distinguishing pathogenic or benign. CAGI 7 conducted 14 blinded prediction challenges. Missense variant impact was assessed against deep mutational scans of ARSA, BARD1, TSC2, LPL, and ATP7B. Gain-of-function and regulatory variant challenges addressed FGFR kinase domain activating mutations and lentiMPRA enhancer variants, respectively. Splicing and polygenic risk score challenges were conducted. The Rare Genomes Project challenge called for identification of clinical diagnostic variants. Annotation Accumulation Accuracy Assessment (A4) challenges track predictor performance longitudinally across CAGI editions, continuing for missense and now expanded to nonsense, frameshift, and indel variants. Top missense predictions consistently outperformed widely used methods such as AlphaMissense and REVEL, with striking advances since CAGI 6. This held across different proteins, datasets, and assessors. Leading methods integrate evolutionary and protein language model information, with structural and biophysical features emerging as beneficial. Regulatory variant predictions clearly improved over prior benchmarks. The gain-of-function challenge revealed current methods are not yet adequate, an important frontier. CAGI 7 demonstrates substantial, reproducible progress while highlighting critical new directions for the field.

title: Mapping, manipulating, and modelling regulatory DNA to link disease variants to functions
authors: Jesse Engreitz, Maya Sheth, Andreas Gschwind, Michael Montgomery, Wei-Lin Qiu, Rosa Ma, Stephanie Conley, Gabriella Martyn, James Galante, Judhajeet Ray, Dulguun Amgalan, William Goodyer, Robin Andersson
abstract: To understand how genomic variation affects disease risk, we need a Gene Regulation Map to predict which DNA elements and variants regulate which genes in which of the 1000s of cell types and states in the human body. To build such a map, we implement a “Map-Perturb-Predict” strategy in which we combine single-cell mapping, CRISPR perturbations, and predictive modelling to interpret and rewrite noncoding DNA. First, we collect and integrate a dataset of >20,000 CRISPR perturbations to elements and noncoding variants from CRISPRi and prime editing screens. Second, we benchmark existing predictive models, including Enformer and AlphaGenome, revealing limitations in distal prediction and cross-cell-type transfer. Third, we construct new predictive models that improve the ability to link distal enhancers to target genes. Finally, we apply these models to single-cell atlases to build cell-state-resolved regulatory maps of complex tissues. The resulting Gene Regulation Maps can link noncoding variants to causal genes, cell types, and gene programs. In the human fetal heart, noncoding variants associated with quantitative valve traits link to congenital heart disease genes in valvular interstitial cells. In immune cells, predictive models enable rewriting regulatory DNA to modulate disease gene expression. Together, our approach enables systematic, cell-type-resolved enhancer-gene mapping, providing a foundation to link variants to disease mechanisms and develop genetic medicines targeting regulatory DNA.
