title: PPI-seq: A Massively Parallel System to Decode Genetic Variant Impacts on Protein Interactions
authors: Justin Delano, Patrick Cann, Nicolas Rey, Tian Yu, Luca Pinello, Richard Sherwood
abstract: Protein-protein interactions organize cellular function, yet quantitative measurement of how they change across partners, conditions, and coding variants remains scarce. No existing approach combines native mammalian cellular context, variant-level resolution, and multiplexed throughput-a gap that particularly limits variant interpretation. We developed PPI-seq, a pooled two-hybrid assay that couples protein-protein interaction to a sequence-readable signal inside mammalian cells. Each bait protein is fused to an adenine base editor, and each prey protein is fused to an RNA binding protein; interaction between the two proteins triggers editing of a barcoded RNA reporter, and sequencing quantifies such edits in parallel. Extracting reliable interaction scores from these count data requires accounting for library size, transfection efficiency, and sample-to-sample variation. We therefore developed PyroPPI, a Bayesian hierarchical model that isolates the interaction-specific signal from confounders and reports calibrated confidence intervals. We applied PPI-seq to the BCDX2 complex, a DNA repair complex whose pairwise contacts are well established from biochemical studies. PyroPPI recovered the known binding pairs that were obscured in the unprocessed data. We then performed deep mutational scanning of RAD51D and XRCC2, testing ~3200 variants. Stop-gain variants showed the greatest reduction in binding, synonymous variants remained near baseline, and missense variants exhibited graded intermediate effects, with positions in the conserved Walker A and B ATPase motifs among the most sensitive. PPI-seq and PyroPPI together provide a scalable platform for quantifying how coding variation reshapes protein interaction networks in their native setting.

title: High content phase separation profiling of genetic variants reveals principles of complex heredity in disease
authors: Sumanta Ghosh, Xingxin Pan, Daniel McGrail, Juan Fuxman Bass, Marc Vidal, Joshua Riback, S. Stephen Yi, Daniel Jarosz, Nidhi Sahni
abstract: Biomolecular condensates formed through phase separation orchestrate many aspects of biology. However, the extent to which phase separation impacts human disease remains largely enigmatic. Herein we performed a high-content imaging-based functional profiling of ~3,000 missense variants across a broad spectrum of Mendelian disorders. While common variants rarely affect condensates, more than 10% of disease-associated alleles alter phase separation, with a significant fraction showing gain-of-condensate phenotype. Different mutations in the same gene often exhibit distinct effects on condensate formation, resulting in pleiotropic outcomes. Dominant disease alleles in the TGIF1 homeobox domain drive aberrant condensation, and sequester wild-type TGIF1, providing a mechanism for the genetic dominance of such alleles. Furthermore, we developed a first-in-time variant-centric deep learning framework to accurately predict mutation-mediated gain or loss of condensates. Together, our large-scale study suggests phase separation as a potentially widespread mechanism underlying human disease, which could help explain many variants with unknown significance.

title: Deconvolving mutation effects on protein stability and function with disentangled protein language models
authors: Kerr Ding, Ziang Li, Tony Tu, Jiaqi Luo, Yunan Luo
abstract: Understanding how evolutionary constraints shape protein sequences is fundamental to deciphering the molecular mechanisms underlying protein stability and function, with broad implications for protein engineering and therapeutic development. Recent advances in protein language models (pLMs) have enabled accurate prediction of mutation effects, capturing the evolutionary pressure that governs protein sequence variation. A critical challenge, however, remains in disentangling the intertwined mutation effects on protein stability and function, as evolutionary signals conflate stability-driven and function-driven pressures, obscuring the mechanistic basis of mutation effects. In this work, we introduce DETANGO, a deep learning framework that explicitly deconvolves the mutation effects on protein functions by removing components attributable to stability perturbations from pLM-predicted mutation effects. DETANGO estimates a functional plausibility score for each single-point mutation that is the component of the mutation effect not accounted for by changes in stability. Single-point mutations with low functional plausibilities are predicted to be stable-but-inactive (SBI) variants, whose compromised activities are caused by direct perturbations on functional mechanisms rather than stability. Residues enriched for such variants are inferred to be functionally critical, as indicated by the strong pressures to maintain protein function. Through extensive benchmarking experiments, we show that DETANGO accurately identifies SBI variants and pinpoints functional sites across contexts, including ligand binding, catalysis, and allostery. Moreover, extending DETANGO from individual proteins to homologous protein families reveals shared and distinctive functional patterns across protein families. Collectively, these results establish DETANGO as a biologically grounded framework for disentangling evolutionary constraints and advancing mechanistic understanding of protein function.

title: Position-dependent variant effects reveal importance of context in genomic regulation
authors: Sambina Islam Aninta, Ryan Tewhey, Carl de Boer
abstract: Gene expression is governed by the DNA sequence, which is read out through complex interactions between transcription factors (TFs), co-activators, and chromatin. Massively Parallel Reporter Assays (MPRAs) provide a high-throughput framework for functionally characterizing how regulatory DNA sequences impact the expression of a model gene. MPRAs have also proven to be useful for measuring the effects of genetic variation, where each allele is typically tested in the center of ~200 bp of genomic context cloned into the MPRA; but the impact of variant position and local context remains largely unexplored. In this study, we systematically investigate how shifting the position of a variant within an MPRA probe influences its regulatory activity using models that predict expression in MPRAs from DNA sequence. We find that while the direction of variant effects is usually preserved across positions, the magnitude of expression changes can vary substantially depending on where the variant is placed within the construct. This positional bias appears to be largely explained by the strong position-dependent activity of TFs whose binding the variants perturb. In a subset of cases, disruption of TF-TF cooperative interactions also contributes to position-specific effects. In ~1% of cases, positional-dependence of variants resulted from the variants impacting RNA polymerase III (Pol III) promoters within Alu elements, where boxes A and B form a bipartite promoter and are both required for function and exclusion of either motif due to window shifts disrupted observed variant effect. However, we saw little evidence to support the hypothesis that the positional dependence of variant effects resulted from redundancy of motifs. Overall, our study demonstrates the complexity of cis-regulatory grammar and how it can confound the interpretation of regulatory variants.

title: Machine Learning Approaches for Predicting Functional Consequences of Human Genetic Variants
authors: Yuval Itan
abstract: Despite the rapid growth of patient genomic data worldwide, key limitations continue to impede effective computational variant assessment. We recently developed LoGoFunc, the first machine-learning method to accurately identify pathogenic gain-of-function (GoF) and loss-of-function (LoF) variants at genome-wide scale. We also introduce variant-to-phenotype (V2P), a framework to estimate specific disease phenotypes for human genetic variants, moving beyond current tools that primarily predict general pathogenicity. In addition, we present network-based heterogeneity clustering (NHC), an approach designed to enable case-control gene association analyses in very small disease cohorts. Finally, leveraging major multi-ancestry biobanks, we conducted extensive phenome-wide association studies (PheWAS) to estimate both population-specific and shared phenotypes associated with pathogenic human GoF and LoF variants. Together, these advances enable precise functional classification, phenotype prediction, and improved association power across the spectrum of human genetic variation and diseases.

title: Machine Learning-Based Deconstruction of Polygenic Risk Scores for Identification of Age-Dependent Genetic Effects
authors: Frederick Kamanu, Yi-Pin Lai, Kyungah Im, Sabina Murphy, Nicholas Marston, Andrea Bellavia
abstract: Background: Polygenic risk scores (PRS) quantify genetic predisposition to disease by aggregating genotype dosages weighted by effect sizes. Interactions between PRS and clinical factors have been identified, yet specific variants remain unclear, limiting risk stratification. This study introduces a machine-learning workflow aimed at PRS deconstruction to identify variants involved in age-related interactions with coronary artery disease (CAD) PRS. Methods: We developed a gradient-boosted survival analysis framework to predict incident CAD. Using the UK Biobank, we modeled a 238-variant CAD PRS based on risk-allele dosages and GWAS effect sizes, incorporating baseline age. Gradient Boosting Models (GBM) were trained via 5-fold cross-validation (300 rounds, learning rate 0.05, max depth 6). Interpretable techniques ranked variants and quantified age interactions using Friedman’s H-statistics, validated through Cox proportional hazards models adjusted for sex and genetic ancestry. Results: Among 472,392 participants (median age: 58; 55% female), 15,681 developed CAD over 12 years. The mean cross-validated C-index for the GBM was 0.68. Top-ranked interaction with age was identified for rs2891168 on CDKN2B-AS1. Stratifying by rs2891168 genotypes, individuals with AG/GG alleles showed a significant interaction between PRS and age (p < 0.0001), while AA genotypes did not (p = 0.104). Age-stratified analysis revealed rs12952244 on KAT2A for those under median age, and rs28451064 on NCRNA00310 for those above the median, highlighting substantial heterogeneity in genetic risk architecture across the lifespan. Conclusion: Variants within a CAD PRS exhibit heterogeneous, non-linear interactions with age. Machine learning-based interaction metrics and stratification provide a scalable framework for more precise age-specific risk prediction.

title: Genetic data-driven prioritization of druggable transcription factors in Alzheimer's Disease
authors: Alena Orlenko, Mythreye Venkatesan, Dennis Hazelett, Li Shen, Marylyn Ritchie, Zhiping Wang, Katie Cardone, Tayo Obafemi-Ajayi, Jason Moore
abstract: Identifying high-yield targets for drug repurposing in complex and heterogeneous diseases such as Alzheimer’s disease is challenging due to high dimensionality of genetic data and limited functional annotation of associated variants. This highlights the need for novel, biology-informed feature selection approaches to effectively guide drug target discovery. One strategy is to target transcription factors upstream of one or more known Alzheimer’s effector genes. We present a machine learning framework that integrates gene regulatory mechanisms, particularly transcription factor–gene interactions, to prioritize potential novel, druggable transcription factors that may have clinical relevance in Alzheimer’s disease. Given that interpretation at the single-nucleotide polymorphism level remains challenging, we constructed machine learning models using gene-level risk scores, which reflect aggregated influence of gene-affiliated variants. Building on prior work, we show that models based on gene level summary scores are at least as good or slightly better than computationally less efficient models based on all variants. The findings also demonstrate that feature sets based on known Alzheimer’s disease effector genes interacting with transcription factors yield higher performance compared to effector genes alone, affirming our hypothesis that upstream transcription factors contain untapped signal for Alzheimer’s detection. Some transcription factor-effector gene pairs display synergistic interactions based on permutation feature importance analysis and explicit tests of epistasis, suggesting that these interactions are not merely additive. Several of these gene sets also participate in key pathways governing neural development, maintenance, and protection, and disruption of which has been linked to neurological disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease. title: Biobank-scale whole-genome sequence variance component estimation in subquadratic time and space
authors: Seyed Alireza Rasoulzadeh Hosseini, Oona Shigeno Risse-Adams, Xinzhu Wei, Richard Border
abstract: Variance component estimation (VCE), including SNP heritability and partitioned heritability, is among the most computationally demanding classes of genomic analyses. Standard REML implementations require O(n^2) memory and O(n^3) compute to factorize the genetic relatedness matrix, rendering them infeasible beyond ~100,000 individuals. Iterative alternatives still scale as O(nm) per iteration, limiting feasibility at biobank scale. Consequently, partitioned heritability at biobank scale relies on summary-statistic methods such as S-LDSC, which cannot incorporate individual-level covariates or rare variants. Individual-level methods that can fit corrected models remain computationally infeasible at these sample sizes. We present a VCE framework built natively on genotype representation graphs (GRGs), directed acyclic graphs encoding shared genealogical structure. GRG traversals replace O(nm) genotype-matrix products with O(| V|+|E|) graph operations, an ~8,000-fold reduction for the UK Biobank WGS dataset. We implement randomized Haseman-Elston regression (RHEMC) on this platform. Unlike S-LDSC, RHEMC directly adjusts for individual-level covariates and incorporates rare variants, but its O(nm) cost has previously limited its use at scale. We introduce a fast block jackknife computing leave-one-block-out standard errors via score decomposition, requiring only traversals per probe regardless of block count. Benchmarked against GENIE, the reference RHEMC implementation, our approach achieves 8.2x speedup and 9.6x memory reduction on VCF-derived GRGs at n=50,000, with speedups reaching 79x on optimally compressed GRGs. Individual-level partitioned heritability at whole-genome sequence scale, previously limited to summary-statistic approximations, is now computationally feasible.

title: Resolving Variants of Uncertain Significance at Scale with Calibrated Computational and Experimental Evidence
authors: Predrag Radivojac
abstract: Resolving variants of uncertain significance (VUS) is a key challenge in genomic medicine, with about 90% of missense variants in ClinVar classified as VUS. This limits the clinical utility of genetic testing for patients with suspected Mendelian disease and is a hindrance to improving human health and well-being. Two major sources of evidence hold promise for resolving VUS at scale: (1) variant effect predictors, which generate computational scores for any variant, and (2) high-throughput experimental assays, which directly measure the impact of variants on gene function. Realizing the clinical potential of these evidence types requires systematic data generation, rigorous calibration (the mapping of scores and measurements to probabilities of pathogenicity), and data sharing. In this highlights presentation, we will focus on new calibration strategies for computational and experimental evidence, and demonstrate their combined power to dramatically reduce the burden of VUS. For computational evidence, current calibration practices aggregate pathogenic and benign control variants across genes to apply genome-wide thresholds that exhibit variability in predictor performance for specific genes. To address this, we developed a framework that performs gene-specific calibration when sufficient control variants are available. For genes with limited control variant data, we aggregate protein domains with similar prediction score distributions to enable robust domain-based calibration. Applying this framework across 2,769 genes, we show that gene-and domain-based calibration increase the proportion of variants with assigned evidence while improving evidence accuracy relative to genome-wide calibration. For experimental evidence, current guidelines for clinical variant classification rely on establishing gene-and assay-specific score thresholds that separate pathogenic from benign variants. This approach is inherently subjective, inconsistent across laboratories, and lacks the statistical rigor of formal calibration. To overcome these limitations, we introduce a semi-supervised framework to jointly model pathogenic, benign, synonymous, and population variants and produce variant-specific probabilities of pathogenicity. The approach was evaluated across 80 datasets from 39 genes and substantially outperformed existing standards. Towards the goal of reducing VUS, we generated experimental measurements for 62,215 variants across ten genes using multiplexed assays and curated another 193,139 existing variant effect measurements across 30 genes from the literature. Using the new calibration framework, we developed a scalable classification workflow relying solely on experimental and predictive evidence that enables reclassification of 75% of 16,115 VUS across these genes as pathogenic or benign, with error below 1%. The framework was also applied prospectively. Among more than 90,000 variants not yet observed in clinical databases, 62% carried sufficient evidence to be “preclassified" before ever appearing in a patient record. This approach establishes a blueprint for how coordinated data generation, calibration, and open dissemination through the IGVF Catalog and MaveMD, can transform genomic medicine by bringing actionable diagnoses to many patients.

title: Interpreting indel mutational signatures in 6,975 tumors based on more informative indel classification schemes
authors: Mo Liu, Mi Ni Huang, Xue Ming Wu, Qi Zheng, Runtian Yao, Ying Yang, Runxi Shen, Steven G. Rozen
abstract: Mutational signatures can be viewed as latent factors underlying observed mutational spectra that ideally correspond to specific mutagenic mechanisms. They are important for variant interpretation in cancers in several ways. First, they can show that tumors were exposed to exogenous carcinogenic mutagens or to endogenous mutagenic processes. Second, they can sometimes guide treatment. Third, they can estimate the rates of different types of mutations, and therefore help distinguish elevated mutation rates from selection. The mutational signatures of small insertions and deletions (“indels" ) have been under-studied, but Koh, Nanda, and colleagues recently published two new classifications that recognize 89 types and 476 types of indels. We show that both these classifications provide better discrimination than the older and more widely used classification into 83 types of indel. We analyzed somatic indels in 6,975 whole genomes from 32 cancer types to create comprehensive collections of indel signatures. We identified signatures in all three classification schemes (476, 89, and 83 types of indels) using two unrelated algorithms. We identified 44 89-type mutational signatures and, independently, their corresponding 476-type signatures. We found that the new classification schemes are in most cases superior, in that they detect differences between spectra and signatures that the 83-type classification does not. In one example we use the new system to accurately identify the mutational signature of deficient RNase H2B activity. We provide a website for exploring indel signatures and their relationships across the three classifications, as well as signatures’ relationships to genomic topography.

title: Allele-aware spatial RNA-seq simulator enables comprehensive benchmarking of copy number variation analysis across methods and spatial patterns
authors: Jiamu Qiao, Xianjie Huang, Rongting Huang, Yuanhua Huang
abstract: Copy number variations (CNVs) are prevalent somatic mutations driving the development and progression of various cancers. While single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) enables high-resolution CNV detection, its inherent technical sparsity poses significant challenges. Recent spatial transcriptomics (ST) technologies preserve the spatial context of RNA transcripts, offering critical insights into tumor clonal architecture. However, the lower sequencing coverage of ST further complicates CNV inference. Several computational tools have been developed for CNV detection from scRNA-seq and ST data, including XClone, InferCNV, CopyKAT, Numbat, and CalicoST. However, most tools, including XClone, InferCNV, CopyKAT, and Numbat, were designed primarily for single-cell data. Their efficacy on ST data remains largely unexplored. Furthermore, the performance of ST-specific tools like CalicoST across diverse clonal architectures remains untested. The limited availability of public ST datasets, compounded by high assay costs, restricts the comprehensive benchmarking of these tools. Moreover, most ST datasets lack reliable ground truth for both CNV profile and potential CNV clonality, thereby urgently demanding a powerful simulator. Although some simulation frameworks have been developed for scRNA-seq data to generate synthetic datasets, none of the few simulators are designed for the simulation of CNV counts or reads. To address this gap, we developed scCNVSim, an allele-specific spatial RNA-seq simulator. Seeded with real-world ST data, scCNVSim accurately simulates allele-specific events, generating phased reads via its read simulation module and count matrices via its count simulation module. The resulting simulated dataset exhibits high fidelity to real-world data across critical metrics, including read coverage and allele frequency. Utilizing scCNVSim, we generated diverse ST datasets encompassing a wide range of CNV events and clonal patterns to systematically benchmark existing algorithms. We evaluated tool performance across varying sequencing depths, cell counts, and tumor purities. Multiple CNV events were simulated, including copy loss and copy-neutral loss-of-heterozygosity (CNLOH) across different alleles, whole-genome duplication (WGD), and complex clonal structures. Tools incorporating allelic information (XClone, Numbat, and CalicoST) significantly outperformed others in detecting CNLOH and allele-specific copy loss. For subclonal structure inference, CalicoST demonstrated superior overall performance. Numbat excelled in tumor cell identification generally, though its accuracy degraded sharply at low tumor purities. Conversely, XClone, InferCNV, and CopyKAT exhibited greater robustness at extreme (very high or low) tumor purities. Additionally, evaluating CalicoST's spatial dependency revealed that its CNV inference accuracy inversely correlates with spatial complexity in general, such as irregular clone shapes, small inter-clonal spatial distance, and high infiltration rates. To further validate the benchmarking results, these tools were applied to real-world hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) and prostate cancer ST datasets. XClone and Numbat achieved the highest overall CNV calling accuracy, followed by CalicoST, CopyKAT, and InferCNV. Notably, CopyKAT outperformed others in subclonal structure detection in the HCC dataset. Furthermore, XClone facilitated the discovery of a novel tumor subclone characterized by unique copy losses on chromosomes 15 and 18, which we orthogonally validated using mitochondrial single-nucleotide variant (SNV) analysis. In summary, scCNVSim enables the simulation of highly customizable, complex CNV events and clonal structures, providing a robust framework for benchmarking CNV callers. Our comprehensive evaluation highlights that algorithm performance is highly context-dependent, emphasizing the need for scenario-specific tool selection. Generally, allele-aware methods demonstrate superior capability in resolving complex CNV events. Finally, integrating CNV inference with orthogonal molecular analyses, such as SNV profiling, is highly recommended to maximize biological insights from real-world spatial datasets.

title: PGViS: Personal Genome Variant interpretation Score for lung cancer genomes
authors: Pallavi Surana, Pratik Dutta, Paolo Boffetta, Ramana Davuluri
abstract: The inherited genetic risk of lung cancer is shaped not only by protein-coding mutations but also by functionally impactful non-coding germline variants that remain largely uncharacterized. Conventional polygenic risk scores and genome-wide association studies focus predominantly on coding regions and common variants, overlooking the regulatory landscape shaped by germline mutations in non-coding regions. Unlike coding variants, non-coding mutations do not produce altered proteins but instead dysregulate gene expression at multiple levels, making their interpretation inherently challenging. DNA foundation models like DNABERT, Nucleotide Transformer offer powerful approaches to decode non-coding variant effects in smaller cohorts without requiring large-scale GWAS, yet a robust patient-level framework for integrating these predictions with population-level mutation prevalence for cancer risk quantification remains lacking. We present PGViS (Personal Genome Variant interpretation Score), a statistical framework for quantifying individual non-coding germline regulatory risk in non-small cell lung cancer. Applied to whole-genome sequencing data from 1,102 patients across TCGA and CPTAC, PGViS integrates three complementary signals: functional variant impact scores from fine-tuned DNABERT models targeting gene regulatory elements; allele frequency shifts between disease; and a weighted allelic imbalance metric inspired by polygenic risk scores. These are aggregated into a single cohort-normalized, interpretable patient-level score. PGViS reveals distinct inherited regulatory variant burden profiles between adenocarcinoma and squamous cell carcinoma subtypes and enables risk stratification across independent cohorts. Validation on asymptomatic individuals demonstrates its utility for predicting cancer risk in general populations. Its modular design supports integration into clinical genomic workflows and adaptation across other cancer types.
